skill.hx.surg.history_scheme.title: Surgical case taking: history framework
skill.hx.surg.history_scheme.oneLine: Chief complaints in chronological sequence, history of present illness, and past surgical background
skill.hx.surg.history_scheme.why: A surgical diagnosis rests on the exact chronological sequence of symptoms. Hurrying through complaints or failing to establish the precise mode of onset leads to misinterpreting pathology, missing operative contraindications, and overlooking previous surgical interventions.

asks.text: Record patient demographics: name, age, gender, occupation, and residence.
Elicit chief complaints in chronological order with exact duration for each complaint.
Explore history of present illness: mode of onset, progress, site, character, aggravating and relieving factors, and associated systemic symptoms.
Enquire about past medical and surgical illness: previous operations, jaundice, tuberculosis, diabetes, hypertension, and bleeding tendencies.
Review personal habits: tobacco use (smoking, chewing bidi or gutkha), alcohol intake, diet, and bowel or urinary changes.
Document family history of hereditary disease, familial polyposis, breast or colorectal carcinoma, or bleeding disorders.

skill.hx.surg.history_scheme.practice: Take a complete surgical history from an elective surgical inpatient. Record each symptom with its exact date or duration of onset in chronological sequence. Present the case in under three minutes without reading notes.
pitfalls: Recording complaints in order of severity rather than chronological sequence.
Omitting previous surgical operations, scar revisions, or past anaesthetic complications.
Failing to ask about tobacco chewing and bidi smoking in patients with head, neck, or abdominal pathology.
Accepting vague durations such as some days instead of establishing the exact time course.

probes.q: Why must chief complaints in a surgical case be recorded in chronological order rather than order of severity?
probes.a: Chronological order reveals the natural progression and underlying pathology of the surgical disease, showing which symptom initiated the process and which were secondary complications.

probes.q: What specific aspects of past anaesthetic and surgical history must be explored prior to planning surgery?
probes.a: Enquire about previous operations, difficult airway or intubation, prolonged recovery, malignant hyperthermia, deep vein thrombosis, and adverse drug reactions.

probes.q: How does eliciting a patient's specific occupation alter surgical diagnosis and operative management?
probes.a: Occupation reveals occupational hazards, physical stress predisposing to hernia or varicose veins, chemical exposures, and dictates the choice and timing of incision, recovery duration, and rehabilitation needs.

rubric.text: Records chief complaints in strict chronological order with exact durations
Explores onset, progression, and relieving factors of the primary complaint
Enquires specifically about previous surgeries, anaesthesia, and comorbidities
Documents tobacco, alcohol, and drug history accurately

teach.heading: Chronological framework of surgical history
teach.body:
In surgical case taking, the chief complaints must always be recorded in the order of their appearance. The symptom that began first is listed first, accompanied by its exact duration. A common error is listing the most painful or dramatic symptom first.

Establishing exact dates or durations allows the clinician to reconstruct the natural history of the illness, differentiating acute surgical emergencies from progressive chronic disease processes.

teach.heading: Components of a comprehensive surgical history

rows: Differentiates acute emergency from chronic disease

teach.heading: Preoperative inquiry into personal habits
teach.body:
Personal history in the surgical clinic carries direct operative implications. Tobacco smoking impairs microvascular perfusion, increases wound breakdown, and heightens postoperative pulmonary atelectasis and pneumonia risks.

Alcohol intake increases the risk of acute withdrawal, liver impairment, and altered drug metabolism. Bidi and smokeless tobacco chewing predispose to oral premalignant lesions and aggressive squamous carcinomas across the upper aerodigestive tract.

skill.gen.surg.survey.title: General survey of the surgical patient
skill.gen.surg.survey.oneLine: Attitude, build, facies, systemic stigmata, and vital signs before examining the local lesion
skill.gen.surg.survey.why: Jumping directly to a surgical lump or wound without a general survey causes catastrophic misses: overlooking toxic facies in peritonitis, missing severe pallor before urgent intervention, or failing to recognise systemic dehydration and shock.

steps.text: Observe the patient from the bedside: attitude in bed, comfort level, posture, and facial expression.
Assess nutritional status, body habitus, height, weight, and general skeletal build.
Inspect the face for toxic or sunken facies (Hippocratic facies), periorbital oedema, or icteric sclerae.
Examine systematically for the six cardinal general signs: pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, generalized lymphadenopathy, and pedal oedema.
Check hydration: tongue moisture, skin turgor, sunken eyes, and capillary refill time.
Record baseline vital signs: pulse rate, rhythm, volume, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and axillary temperature.

skill.gen.surg.survey.normal: Alert, comfortable in bed without distress, well nourished, moist pink mucous membranes, no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy or oedema, and normal vital signs.
skill.gen.surg.survey.abnormal: Restless or motionless posture with knees drawn up, hollow sunken cheeks (Hippocratic facies), dry furrowed tongue, pallor, deep icterus, peripheral cyanosis, pedal pitting oedema, tachycardia, and hypotension.
skill.gen.surg.survey.significance: A patient lying completely motionless with knees drawn up indicates generalised peritonitis, where any movement causes agony. Sunken eyes, dry tongue, and toxic facies indicate severe dehydration or septicaemia demanding immediate resuscitation before any surgical procedure.
skill.gen.surg.survey.practice: Conduct a two-minute general survey on every patient before touching a localized surgical lesion. Verbally report attitude, facies, hydration, the six cardinal physical signs, and vital signs.
pitfalls: Focusing immediately on a surgical lump or ulcer without inspecting the general condition and facies.
Missing dehydration by failing to inspect the dorsal and ventral surfaces of the tongue.
Failing to note tachycardia and hypotension in an apparently calm patient with internal bleeding.
Neglecting to examine both ankles and the sacrum for dependent oedema.

probes.q: What is the classical Hippocratic facies and what does it signify in surgery?
probes.a: Sunken eyes, hollow cheeks, sharp nose, cold leaden skin, and relaxed lips, signifying advanced generalized peritonitis, profound dehydration, and impending collapse.

probes.q: Why does a patient with generalized peritonitis lie motionless with knees flexed, unlike a patient with renal colic?
probes.a: In peritonitis, any movement of the inflamed parietal peritoneum causes intense agony, whereas in colic, smooth muscle spasm causes restlessness without somatic peritoneal inflammation.

probes.q: How does identifying pedal oedema and jaundice alter perioperative surgical risk assessment?
probes.a: Pedal oedema suggests cardiac, renal, or hepatic failure, while jaundice points to hepatobiliary dysfunction or biliary obstruction, predisposing to coagulopathy, altered drug clearance, and hepatorenal syndrome.

rubric.text: Notes patient posture, comfort, and spontaneous movements in bed
Inspects facial expression, eye contours, and mucous membrane hydration
Systematically checks for pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, clubbing, and oedema
Verifies pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and temperature

teach.heading: General survey as a life-safety gate
teach.body:
The general survey is the first and most critical component of surgical physical examination. Before examining an ulcer, lump, or abdomen, the surgeon must evaluate whether the patient is stable, toxic, or in impending circulatory collapse.

Recognizing severe dehydration, pallor, or tachypnoea early directs urgent resuscitation, securing intravenous access and blood typing before proceeding with detailed elective examinations.

teach.heading: Key general signs in surgical assessment

rows: Sunken temples, dry tongue, pinched nose

teach.heading: Attitude and posture in bed
teach.body:
The patient's spontaneous posture yields diagnostic clues. In acute pancreatitis or severe peritonitis, patients often lie still with knees flexed to relax the abdominal musculature and minimize peritoneal friction.

In acute biliary or ureteric colic, patients are restless, constantly twisting or rolling in bed attempting to find relief. This stark behavioral difference reliably discriminates hollow viscus colic from true somatic peritonitis.

skill.hx.surg.pain.title: Surgical pain assessment: somatic, visceral, and referred patterns
skill.hx.surg.pain.oneLine: Onset, character, site, radiation, and discriminating colic from peritonitic pain
skill.hx.surg.pain.why: Pain is the commonest presenting surgical symptom. Failure to dissect its character confuses visceral colic with peritonitic irritation, obscures early hollow viscus perforation, and delays emergency laparotomy.

asks.text: Clarify the exact onset: sudden and instantaneous (perforation, rupture, torsion) versus gradual and insidious (inflammation, obstruction).
Locate the exact site of origin and whether the patient can point to it with one fingertip (somatic) or uses a flat hand (visceral).
Determine the character of the pain: burning, throbbing, dull ache, sharp stabbing, or periodic cramping colic.
Trace any radiation or referred path: back (pancreas, aortic aneurysm), shoulder tip (diaphragmatic irritation), or groin (ureteric colic).
Identify aggravating factors (movement, coughing, respiration, food) and relieving factors (vomiting, antacids, flexion of knees).
Distinguish subjective pain felt by the patient from tenderness elicited by the examiner.

skill.hx.surg.pain.practice: Interview a surgical patient presenting with acute or subacute pain. Map the symptom using the SOCRATES framework (Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Timing, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity). Distinguish visceral from parietal components.
pitfalls: Confusing pain (subjective sensation reported by the patient) with tenderness (objective sign elicited by the doctor).
Failing to recognize that sudden cessation of severe appendicular colic may indicate gangrenous perforation rather than recovery.
Ignoring shoulder tip pain in a patient with upper abdominal trauma or suspected ruptured ectopic gestation.
Neglecting to ask about radiation to the back in severe epigastric pain.

probes.q: What is the physiological difference between visceral pain and somatic parietal pain in the abdomen?
probes.a: Visceral pain is mediated by autonomic afferents, is dull, cramping, poorly localized, and referred to the midline, whereas somatic pain is mediated by cerebrospinal nerves, is sharp, severe, and precisely localized.

probes.q: Why does diaphragmatic peritoneal irritation produce pain referred to the tip of the shoulder?
probes.a: The central diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5), which shares spinal cord segments with the supraclavicular nerves supplying the skin over the acromion and shoulder tip.

probes.q: Describe the clinical pain characteristics of true colic and how it differs from peritonitic pain.
probes.a: True colic is caused by smooth muscle contraction against an obstruction, featuring regular crescendos of intense cramping pain with complete pain-free intervals and motor restlessness, unlike constant peritonitic pain aggravated by movement.

rubric.text: Differentiates instantaneous catastrophic onset from gradual progressive pain
Identifies character: burning, sharp, throbbing, or periodic spasmodic colic
Traces radiation to the back, shoulder, or groin systematically
Identifies aggravating factors (cough, movement) and relieving posture

teach.heading: Four anatomical categories of surgical pain
teach.body:
Surgical pain is categorized into four distinct anatomical types. Superficial somatic pain arises from skin and superficial tissue, is sharp, prickling, and precisely located with a finger.

Segmental pain follows a specific dermatome from sensory nerve root compression. Deep visceral pain arises from abdominal viscera, is dull, poorly localized, and referred to embryological midline zones. Psychogenic pain lacks organic anatomical boundaries.

teach.heading: Referred pain pathways in clinical surgery
teach.body:
Referred pain occurs when visceral afferents converge on the same dorsal horn spinal segments as somatic sensory nerves. The cerebral cortex perceives the sensation as originating from the somatic dermatome.

Classic surgical examples include biliary pain referred to the right infrascapular region (T7-T9), diaphragmatic irritation referred to the shoulder tip (C3-C5), and ureteric colic radiating to the groin and hemiscrotum (T11-L1).

skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.title: Eliciting tenderness, guarding, and rebound tenderness
skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.oneLine: Gentle progressive palpation, involuntary muscular rigidity, and the release sign of peritonitis
skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.why: Violent or sudden palpation frightens the patient and induces voluntary guarding, destroying the clinical examination. Eliciting rebound tenderness gently and distinguishing true involuntary rigidity from voluntary defence confirms parietal peritoneal inflammation.

steps.text: Position the patient flat on the back with one pillow under the head and knees slightly flexed to relax abdominal muscles.
Ask the patient to point with one finger to where the pain hurts most, and state that this area will be examined last.
Warm hands and begin palpating gently in the quadrant furthest away from the site of reported pain.
Palpate with the palmar surface of relaxed fingers, watching the patient's face continuously for wincing.
Assess for muscular guarding: distinguish voluntary guarding (relaxes on gentle expiration) from involuntary rigidity (constant, board-like).
Test for rebound tenderness (Blumberg sign): press gently and deeply into the affected area, hold for several seconds, then release the hand suddenly while watching the face.

skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.normal: Abdomen soft, non-tender, relaxed abdominal wall musculature moving freely with respiration, no guarding or rebound tenderness.
skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.abnormal: Localized tenderness on light touch, involuntary muscular rigidity (board-like hardness), and severe sharp pain accentuated immediately upon sudden release of palpating fingers (positive Blumberg sign).
skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.significance: True involuntary rigidity indicates acute peritonitis, where inflamed parietal peritoneum reflexly contracts overlying abdominal wall muscles. Rebound tenderness confirms parietal peritoneal inflammation, as sudden recoil of the abdominal wall shakes the inflamed serosa.
skill.exam.surg.tenderness_rebound.practice: Practice abdominal palpation starting at the non-tender quadrant. Rehearse slow deep depression followed by instantaneous withdrawal of the fingers while keeping eyes fixed on the subject's face.
pitfalls: Poking with stiff fingertips instead of palpating flat with the palmar pads of relaxed fingers.
Looking down at the abdomen instead of watching the patient's face for signs of discomfort.
Palpating the tenderest area first, which causes generalised muscle spasm and loss of patient trust.
Performing aggressive or repeated rebound tests when severe rigidity is already obvious.

probes.q: What is the difference between tenderness and pain?
probes.a: Pain is a subjective symptom felt and reported by the patient, whereas tenderness is an objective physical sign elicited by the clinician on palpation.

probes.q: How does the clinician distinguish voluntary muscular guarding from true involuntary rigidity?
probes.a: Voluntary guarding relaxes when the patient is distracted, breathes deeply with mouth open, or during expiration, whereas involuntary rigidity remains board-like and constant throughout the respiratory cycle.

probes.q: Explain the physical mechanism of the Blumberg rebound tenderness sign and when it should be avoided.
probes.a: Slow deep depression stretches the parietal peritoneum; sudden release allows it to snap back rapidly, provoking acute pain if inflamed. It should be avoided when obvious board-like rigidity already confirms peritonitis, as it inflicts unnecessary agony.

rubric.text: Positions patient supine with knees semi-flexed and arms by the side
Starts palpation in the quadrant furthest from the site of reported pain
Watches patient facial expression continuously during examination
Distinguishes voluntary muscular defence from involuntary rigidity
Elicits rebound tenderness gently without violent jerking

teach.heading: Principles of gentle abdominal palpation
teach.body:
Palpation must never begin at the site of suspected acute pathology. Beginning over an acutely inflamed appendix or gallbladder provokes severe pain, causing immediate voluntary guarding that obscures all subsequent findings.

Warming hands and beginning in the furthest quadrant establishes patient confidence, relaxes abdominal wall musculature, and allows subtle differences in tone and localized tenderness to be accurately mapped.

rows: Fear, cold hands, anxiety, anticipated pain
Reflex motor spasm from parietal peritonitis
Muscles relax transiently on deep expiration
Often non-surgical or early localized issue

teach.heading: Eliciting rebound tenderness safely
teach.body:
Rebound tenderness (Blumberg sign) is a specific sign of parietal peritoneal irritation. To elicit it, the examiner depresses the abdominal wall deeply and steadily over several seconds, allowing the underlying inflamed serosa to adapt to the pressure.

The hand is then withdrawn suddenly and cleanly. The sudden release of tension causes the abdominal wall and inflamed peritoneum to rebound, triggering a sharp lancinating wince. If generalized rigidity is already present, rebound testing is redundant and cruel.

skill.gen.surg.surgical_fever.title: Surgical fever: postoperative timeline and septic patterns
skill.gen.surg.surgical_fever.oneLine: Evaluating postoperative pyrexia across the five Ws and recognizing septic intermittent spikes
skill.gen.surg.surgical_fever.why: Fever after surgery is not an automatic call for antibiotics. Misunderstanding the postoperative timeline leads to missing atelectasis on day one, overlooking surgical site sepsis on day five, or failing to recognise life-threatening ascending cholangitis.

steps.text: Review the surgical temperature chart: verify timing, height of spikes, daily fluctuations, and baseline trends.
Categorize fever pattern: continuous (fluctuation under 1 degree), remittent (fluctuation over 2 degrees without normal baseline), or intermittent (spikes touching normal).
Enquire about associated chills and rigors, pointing to bacteraemia or suppurative collections.
Examine according to the postoperative timeline: chest examination for atelectasis or pneumonia (days 1 to 2).
Inspect intravenous cannula sites, urinary catheter, and urine appearance (days 3 to 5).
Inspect the surgical wound for erythema, induration, warmth, and purulent discharge (days 5 to 7), and check calves for deep vein thrombosis.

skill.gen.surg.surgical_fever.normal: Postoperative temperature within normal physiological range (36.5 to 37.2 degrees Celsius), or transient mild atelectatic rise under 38 degrees resolving within 48 hours.
skill.gen.surg.surgical_fever.abnormal: Sustained pyrexia above 38 degrees Celsius, swinging hectic fever with severe rigors, late secondary temperature spike after day five, or Charcot triad (fever with rigors, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain).
skill.gen.surg.surgical_fever.significance: A fever within 24 to 48 hours is usually pulmonary atelectasis, managed with chest physiotherapy rather than antibiotics. A new fever on day five to seven suggests surgical site infection or deep intra-abdominal collection. Charcot intermittent fever indicates acute ascending cholangitis.
skill.gen.surg.surgical_fever.practice: Review temperature charts of three surgical inpatients. Correlate the postoperative day with the physical examination of lungs, urinary tract, wound, and peripheral veins. Determine the probable source using the five Ws rule.
pitfalls: Prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics for day one postoperative atelectatic fever instead of initiating chest physiotherapy.
Failing to inspect the surgical wound beneath dressings in a patient with day six pyrexia.
Overlooking thrombophlebitis at peripheral intravenous cannula sites as a cause of unexplained pyrexia.
Missing pelvic or subdiaphragmatic collections because superficial wound inspection appears clean.

probes.q: What is the classical Five Ws mnemonic for postoperative fever and its timeline?
probes.a: Wind (atelectasis/pneumonia, days 1-2), Water (urinary tract infection, days 3-5), Wound (surgical site infection, days 5-7), Walking (deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism, days 7+), and Wonder drugs (drug-induced fever, any time).

probes.q: What is Charcot intermittent biliary fever and what does it indicate?
probes.a: A swinging intermittent fever with chills and rigors accompanied by right upper quadrant pain and jaundice, indicating acute cholangitis secondary to common bile duct obstruction.

probes.q: How does a hectic or swinging septic fever pattern arise in surgical patients?
probes.a: Hectic fever arises from intermittent showers of bacteria and endotoxins released from a walled-off pus collection (such as a subdiaphragmatic or pelvic abscess) into the systemic circulation, producing high evening spikes with severe morning sweats.

rubric.text: Analyzes the temperature chart for pattern, spike timing, and duration
Applies the postoperative timeline correctly to guide system examination
Inspects surgical incision, cannula sites, and calves thoroughly
Formulates non-antibiotic versus targeted antibiotic management plans

teach.heading: The postoperative pyrexia timeline
teach.body:
Postoperative fever follows a predictable temporal pattern that dictates the clinical search. Fever in the first 48 hours is overwhelmingly respiratory in origin, caused by hypoventilation, airway mucus plugging, and alveolar atelectasis.

From day three onwards, catheter-associated urinary infection emerges. Wound infections and deep intra-abdominal collections typically declare themselves between postoperative days five and eight, when wound erythema, oedema, and purulence develop.

teach.heading: Special surgical fever patterns
teach.body:
Intermittent fever featuring high spikes accompanied by shaking chills and rigors indicates bacteraemia or a concealed deep abscess (subphrenic, pelvic, or appendicular).

Charcot intermittent biliary fever is pathognomonic for ascending cholangitis, demanding urgent biliary decompression. A persistent continuous fever unresponsive to therapy must prompt examination of all intravenous access lines for cannula thrombophlebitis.

skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.title: Recognition of surgical shock and tissue hypoperfusion
skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.oneLine: Bedside identification of hypovolaemic, septic, cardiogenic, and neurogenic circulatory collapse
skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.why: Waiting for blood pressure to drop means waiting for decompensated shock. Early surgical shock manifests as tachycardia, tachypnoea, cool periphery, delayed capillary refill, and oliguria; missing these bedside signs leads to irreversible end-organ ischaemia.

steps.text: Assess neurological responsiveness: alertness, agitation, confusion, or lethargy indicating cerebral hypoperfusion.
Evaluate peripheral circulation: feel temperature of hands and feet, note skin pallor or mottling, and measure capillary refill time on the nail bed or sternum (normal under 2 seconds).
Examine peripheral and central pulses: note rate, volume (thready pulse), and rhythm.
Measure blood pressure and calculate pulse pressure: note narrow pulse pressure in early hypovolaemia.
Inspect jugular venous pressure: flat veins in hypovolaemia versus distended neck veins in cardiogenic or obstructive shock (tension pneumothorax, tamponade).
Monitor urinary output via catheter: oliguria under 0.5 mL per kg per hour confirms inadequate renal perfusion.

skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.normal: Warm dry periphery, pink nail beds with capillary refill under 2 seconds, full volume pulse of 60 to 90 beats per minute, normal blood pressure and pulse pressure, and urine output over 0.5 mL per kg per hour.
skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.abnormal: Cold, clammy, mottled extremities, prolonged capillary refill over 2 seconds, rapid thready pulse over 100 beats per minute, tachypnoea, systolic blood pressure under 90 mmHg with narrow pulse pressure, and acute oliguria.
skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.significance: Tissue hypoperfusion with anaerobic metabolism is the core physiological defect in shock. In hypovolaemic surgical shock, compensatory vasoconstriction preserves blood pressure initially; detecting tachycardia, cool peripheries, and oliguria allows lifesaving fluid and blood resuscitation before hypotensive arrest.
skill.gen.surg.surgical_shock.practice: Perform a bedside shock screen on an acutely ill patient. Check capillary refill time on the digit, feel limb temperature gradients, examine neck veins, and calculate pulse pressure.
pitfalls: Relying on normal systolic blood pressure to rule out shock; young patients maintain blood pressure until severe blood loss occurs.
Failing to expose the patient to search for concealed external or pelvic bleeding sources.
Overlooking warm, flushed extremities in early hyperdynamic septic shock.
Administering fluid boluses without checking neck veins and chest sounds for tension pneumothorax or tamponade.

probes.q: What is the earliest reliable bedside sign of hypovolaemic shock in a young surgical trauma patient?
probes.a: Persistent resting tachycardia and tachypnoea with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill, occurring well before systolic blood pressure falls.

probes.q: How does jugular venous pressure distinguish hypovolaemic shock from cardiogenic or obstructive surgical shock?
probes.a: In hypovolaemic shock, JVP is flat or unrecordable due to reduced venous return, whereas in cardiogenic shock, cardiac tamponade, or tension pneumothorax, JVP is markedly elevated.

probes.q: Explain why early septic shock may present with warm extremities, unlike hypovolaemic shock.
probes.a: Early septic shock features endotoxin-mediated peripheral vasodilation with high cardiac output (hyperdynamic or warm shock), causing bounding pulses and warm extremities, before capillary leakage and myocardial depression induce cold shock.

rubric.text: Assesses peripheral temperature, skin mottling, and capillary refill time
Measures heart rate, blood pressure, and calculates pulse pressure
Inspects jugular venous pressure to differentiate hypovolaemic from obstructive shock
Checks urine output threshold (0.5 mL/kg/h) as a marker of end-organ perfusion

teach.heading: Pathophysiology and early bedside markers of shock
teach.body:
Shock is defined as an acute failure of the circulatory system to maintain adequate tissue perfusion, leading to cellular hypoxia, anaerobic glycolysis, and lactic acidosis. Normal blood pressure does not rule out shock.

Compensatory baroreceptor activation releases catecholamines, causing tachycardia and selective cutaneous and splanchnic vasoconstriction. Cold clammy extremities and delayed capillary refill are early warnings before systolic pressure collapses.

rows: Low JVP, high pulse, low cardiac output
Early warm periphery, bounding pulse, low SVR
Elevated JVP, pulmonary crackles, low output

teach.heading: Physical differentiation of obstructive shock
teach.body:
In surgical trauma, obstructive shock must be recognized instantly. Tension pneumothorax presents with hypotension, severe respiratory distress, hyperresonant hemithorax, absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side.

Cardiac tamponade presents with Beck triad: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds. Both cause severe shock with distended neck veins, demanding immediate needle decompression rather than fluid infusion alone.

skill.exam.surg.crepitus.title: Surgical crepitus: surgical emphysema, bone, joint, and tendon varieties
skill.exam.surg.crepitus.oneLine: Differentiating gas in tissues, fractured bone fragments, degenerate cartilage, and tenosynovitis
skill.exam.surg.crepitus.why: Crepitus has four distinct physical forms with completely different diagnostic implications. Confusing subcutaneous gas of necrotising infection with joint crepitation delays life-saving debridement, while forcefully seeking bone crepitus inflicts severe pain and causes neurovascular injury.

steps.text: Identify the clinical context: soft tissue swelling, trauma, joint pain, or tenosynovitis.
For surgical emphysema (subcutaneous crepitus): place the palm flat over the swollen tissue and compress gently, feeling for a delicate bubbling, spongy crackling sensation beneath the skin.
Note the extent of subcutaneous crepitus: trace its boundaries across the neck, chest wall, or scrotum.

For tenosynovitis: place fingers lightly over the tendon sheath (e.g. wrist abductor pollicis longus) and ask the patient to actively flex and extend the digit, feeling for fine, silken, leathery friction.
For joint crepitus: place one palm over the joint (e.g. patellofemoral) and gently guide the joint through passive range of motion, noting coarse, grating, or fine rub.
For suspected bone fracture: recognize that bone crepitus (grating of fractured ends) must NEVER be deliberately elicited due to severe pain and risk of neurovascular damage.

skill.exam.surg.crepitus.normal: Smooth, silent, frictionless gliding of tendons and joints without crackling, bubbling, or grating on palpation or movement.
skill.exam.surg.crepitus.abnormal: Spongy, crackling bubbles under the skin (subcutaneous surgical emphysema or gas gangrene), fine leathery friction along tendon sheaths, coarse grating joint crepitation, or bone crepitus with fracture mobility.
skill.exam.surg.crepitus.significance: Subcutaneous emphysema following chest trauma indicates tracheobronchial rupture, pneumothorax, or oesophageal perforation. In an inflamed limb wound, subcutaneous gas indicates life-threatening clostridial myonecrosis or necrotising fasciitis requiring immediate radical operative debridement.
skill.exam.surg.crepitus.practice: Palpate a model of subcutaneous emphysema (such as bubble wrap beneath a thin cloth). Practice light palpation along tendon sheaths during active finger movement to recognize silken tenosynovial crepitus.
pitfalls: Deliberately rubbing suspected fracture bone fragments together to elicit bone crepitus, which causes severe pain and risks neurovascular transection.
Mistaking benign subcutaneous air from laparoscopy or chest drain insertion for acute spreading necrotising clostridial infection.
Failing to palpate the neck and supraclavicular fossae for surgical emphysema after blunt thoracic trauma.
Overlooking the fine silken crepitus of tenosynovitis by pressing too hard on the tendon.

probes.q: What physical sensation characterizes subcutaneous crepitus (surgical emphysema) on light touch?
probes.a: A spongy, crackling sensation similar to pressing on bubble wrap or dry snow underfoot, caused by microbubbles of gas shifting through subcutaneous connective tissue spaces.

probes.q: Why is bone crepitus strictly avoided as a diagnostic test during clinical fracture examination?
probes.a: Deliberately grating jagged fractured bone ends together inflicts excruciating pain, damages surrounding periosteum, muscles, and vessels, and risks converting a closed fracture into an open or neurovascular injury.

probes.q: How does subcutaneous crepitus from clostridial gas gangrene differ clinically from benign traumatic surgical emphysema?
probes.a: Gas gangrene presents with profound systemic toxicity, severe disproportionate wound pain, sweet foul discharge, skin bronzing, and rapid spreading necrosis, whereas traumatic emphysema is painless, clean, and without toxic shock.

rubric.text: Identifies the anatomical variety of crepitus: subcutaneous, tendon, joint, or bone
Uses gentle, flat compression to elicit subcutaneous bubbles without pain
Strictly avoids attempting deliberate bone crepitus in fracture assessment
Recognizes signs of gas-forming necrotising infection versus benign air

teach.heading: Four clinical varieties of surgical crepitus
teach.body:
Crepitus describes four completely different physical signs that share a sensory vibration. Subcutaneous crepitus (surgical emphysema) is a fine crackling caused by gas bubbles shifting through connective tissue planes.

Tendon crepitus is a fine, silken, leathery vibration felt when an inflamed tendon glides through its sheath. Joint crepitus is a coarse friction caused by worn articular cartilage. Bone crepitus is the harsh grating of fractured ends.

teach.heading: Emergency implications of subcutaneous gas
teach.body:
Subcutaneous gas carries urgent implications. In thoracic trauma or tracheostomy, air tracks along tissue planes into the neck and chest wall, usually benign once the underlying pneumothorax is drained.

In an acute wound or diabetic perineum (Fournier gangrene), subcutaneous crepitus accompanied by profound systemic toxicity, tachycardia, and dishwater fluid marks gas-forming necrotising infection requiring immediate radical surgical excision.

skill.hx.surg.lump.title: History of a lump or swelling
skill.hx.surg.lump.oneLine: Duration, mode of appearance, rate of growth, pain, and secondary changes
skill.hx.surg.lump.why: The temporal evolution of a lump establishes its pathological nature. A swelling present since birth indicates a congenital anomaly; rapid enlargement with pain suggests acute inflammation or high-grade malignancy; a painless lump enlarging slowly over years indicates a benign neoplasm.

asks.text: Determine the exact duration: when was the lump first noticed by the patient, and was it present since birth?
Enquire about the mode of onset: did it appear spontaneously, follow blunt trauma (haematoma), or emerge during sudden physical strain?
Trace the rate of growth: has it enlarged steadily, rapidly over weeks, remained stationary for years, or fluctuated in size?
Investigate pain: is it painless, accompanied by a dull ache, or characterized by throbbing pain and tenderness?
Ask if the swelling changes in size with coughing, straining, standing, or lying down (hernia, saphena varix, meningocele).
Enquire about secondary complications: overlying skin ulceration, purulent discharge, spontaneous bleeding, or systemic weight loss.

skill.hx.surg.lump.practice: Take a focused history from a patient presenting with a peripheral mass or neck swelling. Construct a timeline charting duration, initial size, growth velocity, and the presence or absence of pain.
pitfalls: Confusing the duration of patient awareness with the actual duration of the swelling.
Failing to ask whether the swelling disappears on lying down or increases during coughing.
Dismissing a history of blunt trauma that may merely have drawn the patient's attention to an existing tumour.
Overlooking weight loss, fever, or night sweats in a patient with an enlarging painless lump.

probes.q: What is the critical clinical difference between a lump present since birth and one that appeared recently in adult life?
probes.a: A lump present since birth indicates a congenital malformation or hamartoma (such as cystic hygroma or meningocele), whereas one appearing in adult life suggests acquired inflammatory, benign, or malignant neoplastic pathology.

probes.q: How does the rate of growth of a swelling help differentiate a benign neoplasm from a malignant tumour?
probes.a: Benign neoplasms typically enlarge slowly and smoothly over months to years without pain, whereas malignant tumours grow rapidly over weeks to months, often displaying invasive fixity and secondary necrosis.

probes.q: What causes a surgical lump to fluctuate in size over time?
probes.a: Fluctuations in size occur in reducible hernias, saphena varix, retention cysts that empty and refill, branchial cysts with intermittent secondary infection, or vascular malformations during postural shifts.

rubric.text: Distinguishes first awareness from congenital presence since birth
Characterizes the velocity and trajectory of swelling enlargement
Enquires about postural variation, straining, and reducibility
Documents associated pain, discharge, weight loss, and constitutional symptoms

teach.heading: Temporal progression of surgical lumps
teach.body:
The history of a swelling is dominated by time and rate of progression. A swelling present since birth represents a congenital lesion, such as a cystic hygroma, branchial fistula, or teratoma. Lumps appearing rapidly over days with throbbing pain indicate acute pyogenic abscesses.

A slow, imperceptible enlargement over several years is the hallmark of a benign tumour like a lipoma or fibroma. Rapid growth over weeks in an adult warns of malignant sarcoma or carcinoma.

teach.heading: Diagnostic clues in the history of a swelling
Associated secondary phenomena
teach.body:
A swelling cannot be assessed in isolation from secondary cutaneous and systemic changes. Ask specifically if the skin over the lump has become red, stretched, or shiny, indicating rapid distension or acute secondary infection.

Inquire about numbness, paresthesia, or motor weakness in the distal limb, which signals nerve compression. Constitutional weight loss and anorexia point toward advanced malignant neoplasia or disseminated tuberculosis.

skill.exam.surg.lump_inspect.title: Inspection of a lump or swelling
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspect.oneLine: Anatomical site, shape, dimensions, surface, margins, and overlying cutaneous signs
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspect.why: Touching a lump before systematic inspection misses critical surface clues: visible pulsation, cough impulse, punctum of an epidermoid cyst, erythema of cellulitis, peau d'orange, and movement with deglutition or respiration.

steps.text: Expose the anatomical region fully with good ambient lighting, comparing the affected area with the contralateral normal side.
Define the exact anatomical position and spatial relationship to underlying bones, muscles, and joint creases.
Record the size (estimating horizontal and vertical visible diameters in centimetres) and overall shape (spherical, ovoid, lobulated, or irregular).
Inspect the surface texture (smooth, lobulated, or nodular) and clarity of margins (well-defined or fading into adjacent tissue).
Examine the overlying skin for erythema, dilated tortuous veins, oedema (peau d'orange), surgical scars, pigmentation, or a central punctum.
Observe for dynamic signs: visible expansile pulsation, expansile cough impulse, movement on swallowing (thyroid), or movement on tongue protrusion (thyroglossal cyst).

skill.exam.surg.lump_inspect.normal: Bilateral symmetrical anatomical contours, smooth unbroken skin of uniform colour, absence of visible masses, engorged vessels, puncta, or abnormal pulsations.
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspect.abnormal: Visible localized elevation, asymmetrical contour, erythema, engorged subcutaneous veins, peau d'orange skin pitting, central black punctum, visible pulsation, or movement on swallowing or coughing.
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspect.significance: A central punctum confirms an epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst anchored to the epidermis. Movement on deglutition proves attachment to the pretracheal fascia or thyroid gland. Peau d'orange indicates subdermal lymphatic obstruction by invasive carcinoma.
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspect.practice: Inspect a clinical swelling from the front, profile, and tangentially under oblique lighting. Systematically dictate site, size, shape, surface, margins, skin changes, and dynamic movement before palpating.
pitfalls: Placing hands on the swelling immediately before completing a deliberate visual inspection.
Missing a subtle central punctum by failing to inspect the summit of the mass under bright light.
Failing to observe the neck during swallowing when inspecting a midline cervical mass.
Inspecting only in portrait view rather than viewing tangentially across the skin surface to judge elevation.

probes.q: What does the presence of a central punctum on a subcutaneous swelling indicate?
probes.a: A central punctum represents the plugged orifice of an obstructed sebaceous gland duct, confirming the diagnosis of an epidermoid or sebaceous cyst adherent to the skin.

probes.q: Why does a thyroid swelling move upward during deglutition?
probes.a: The thyroid gland is enclosed within the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia, which is firmly attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, lifting the gland during laryngeal elevation in swallowing.

probes.q: What pathological mechanism produces the peau d'orange appearance of the skin overlying a lump?
probes.a: Peau d'orange occurs when malignant tumor emboli block cutaneous subdermal lymphatics, producing localized cutaneous oedema where hair follicles remain tethered to deep tissue, creating a pitted orange-peel texture.

rubric.text: Exposes lesion completely and compares with the contralateral normal anatomy
Describes exact anatomical site, size in centimetres, shape, and surface contours
Inspects skin for erythema, dilated veins, scars, peau d'orange, and punctum
Tests for movement with deglutition, respiration, or coughing when relevant

teach.heading: The discipline of visual inspection before touching
teach.body:
In surgical examination, the eye must precede the hand. Rushing to touch a lump disturbs the skin, causes reactive muscular contraction, and risks missing subtle surface findings that only exist before palpation.

Oblique lighting across the surface highlights subtle lobulation, fine cutaneous puckering, and gentle rhythmic pulsations that are invisible under direct perpendicular light.

rows: Map to bony landmarks and triangles
Look for erythema, scars, veins, punctum
Ask to swallow, cough, or protrude tongue

teach.heading: Cutaneous clues overlying tumours
teach.body:
The skin overlying a lump provides direct evidence of its depth and biological behavior. Dilated tortuous subcutaneous veins indicate high vascularity or collateral flow around a deep venous obstruction.

Skin tethering and peau d'orange signify malignant lymphatic permeation. A visible scar directly over the mass may represent recurrence of a previously excised benign or malignant neoplasm.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

skill.exam.surg.lump_palpate.title: Palpation of a lump: temperature, tenderness, and consistency
skill.exam.surg.lump_palpate.oneLine: Local heat, tenderness, accurate dimensional measurement, surface texture, and hardness grading
skill.exam.surg.lump_palpate.why: Palpation establishes the physical architecture of a tumour. Grading consistency from soft and cystic through firm to stony hard directs the differential diagnosis between cysts, benign fibromas, chronic granulomas, and invasive carcinomas.

steps.text: Confirm the patient is relaxed and warm hands before touching.
Assess local temperature using the dorsal surface of the fingers, comparing the skin over the lump with adjacent and contralateral normal tissue.
Elicit tenderness by gently pressing the lump, continuously watching the patient's face for discomfort.
Measure exact dimensions in centimetres (length, breadth, and depth) using a calibrated tape or ruler rather than subjective fruit comparisons.
Palpate the surface: determine if it is smooth (simple cyst), lobulated (lipoma), nodular (fibroadenoma), or craggy irregular (carcinoma).
Palpate margins around the entire circumference: note if edges are clearly defined (benign) or diffuse and indistinct (infiltrative).
Assess consistency: classify as soft, cystic/fluctuant, tense, firm, hard, or stony hard.

skill.exam.surg.lump_palpate.normal: Uniform skin temperature, non-tender tissue, anatomical planes without palpable discrete masses, smoothly yielding subcutaneous fat, and absence of indurated margins.
skill.exam.surg.lump_palpate.abnormal: Palpable discrete mass with elevated local temperature, exquisite tenderness, lobulated or craggy surface, ill-defined infiltrative margins, and firm to stony-hard consistency.
skill.exam.surg.lump_palpate.significance: Elevated local temperature indicates acute inflammation or hypervascular sarcomatous tumour. A lobulated soft mass suggests a lipoma. A stony-hard, craggy mass with ill-defined margins strongly indicates malignant carcinoma with desmoplastic stroma.
skill.exam.surg.lump_palpate.practice: Palpate clinical lumps or teaching manikins of varying hardness. Practice grading consistency against standard anatomical benchmarks (soft as lip, firm as nose tip, hard as forehead). Measure exact axes in centimetres.
pitfalls: Describing lump dimensions using fruits (lemon-sized, pea-sized) instead of recording metric measurements.
Assessing local temperature with the palm or fingertips instead of the dorsal skin of the fingers.
Pressing aggressively on a tender inflammatory mass, causing guarding and severe distress.
Failing to trace the entire circumference of the margin to verify deep infiltration.

probes.q: Why is the dorsum of the hand preferred over the palm for evaluating local temperature?
probes.a: The skin on the dorsal surface of the fingers is significantly thinner, richer in temperature receptors, and less prone to moisture or sweat than the thick palmar skin.

probes.q: What physical consistency characterizes a scirrhous carcinoma, and what histopathological feature causes it?
probes.a: A scirrhous carcinoma feels stony hard and craggy, caused by intense reactive fibroblastic proliferation known as dense desmoplastic stroma around invading malignant cells.

probes.q: How does an examiner grade the spectrum of lump consistency using standard physical landmarks?
probes.a: Soft mimics relaxed lip or cheek; cystic feels like fluid tense balloon; firm feels like the cartilaginous tip of the nose; hard feels like the bony forehead or patella.

rubric.text: Tests local temperature using the dorsal surface of fingers against contralateral skin
Measures exact dimensional axes in centimetres using a measuring tape
Characterizes surface contours (smooth, lobulated, craggy) and edge definition
Grades consistency accurately from soft through cystic, firm, to stony hard

teach.heading: Temperature and tenderness assessment
teach.body:
Palpation begins with the assessment of local warmth and tenderness. Always use the dorsal aspect of the middle phalanges, comparing the skin overlying the swelling with the corresponding area on the opposite side of the body.

Increased local temperature indicates increased vascular perfusion, typical of acute bacterial abscesses, cellulitis, arteriovenous malformations, or rapidly vascularized malignant bone and soft tissue sarcomas.

teach.heading: Mapping boundaries and surfaces
teach.body:
Systematically trace the entire perimeter of the mass. A benign swelling usually has smooth, rounded, well-circumscribed edges that allow the examining fingers to define its exact boundaries.

Malignant or chronic inflammatory lesions invade surrounding tissue planes, producing ragged, indistinct margins that blend imperceptibly into adjacent muscles and fascial structures.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

skill.exam.surg.lump_mobility_plane.title: Determining the anatomical plane of a swelling
skill.exam.surg.lump_mobility_plane.oneLine: Mobility testing against skin, subcutaneous plane, deep fascia, muscle contraction, and bone
skill.exam.surg.lump_mobility_plane.why: Surgical resectability and tissue of origin depend entirely on the anatomical plane. Failing to test mobility with the underlying muscle contracted leads to mistaking an intramuscular sarcoma for a harmless subcutaneous lipoma.

steps.text: Test skin mobility: attempt to glide the skin over the lump, then attempt to pinch up the skin directly over the summit of the mass.
If skin cannot be pinched separately, the lump arises from the skin (sebaceous cyst) or has invaded it (malignancy); if skin pinches freely, the lump is subcutaneous or deeper.
Test mobility in the relaxed state: move the mass in two orthogonal directions (longitudinal and transverse) across the underlying anatomical structures.
Put the underlying muscle into active contraction against resistance (e.g. contracting biceps by flexing elbow against resistance, or pectoralis major by pressing hands on hips).
Re-test mobility while the muscle is contracted: if the lump becomes fixed and less mobile, it arises from or is attached to the muscle or deep fascia.

If the lump becomes more prominent and completely fixed on muscle contraction, it is superficial to or attached to deep fascia; if it becomes less prominent or disappears, it lies deep to the muscle (submuscular).
Test relation to underlying bone: verify whether the mass can be moved in any direction over bone, or is completely immobile and fixed to periosteum.

skill.exam.surg.lump_mobility_plane.normal: Subcutaneous tissues move freely over deep fascia and muscle; skin pinches up easily in all regions except palms and soles; underlying contracted muscles harden without fixed masses.
skill.exam.surg.lump_mobility_plane.abnormal: Skin tethered and unpinchable over mass; lump mobile in relaxed state but becoming immobile and prominent upon active muscle contraction; or mass rigidly fixed to underlying skeletal bone.
skill.exam.surg.lump_mobility_plane.significance: A subcutaneous lipoma remains mobile when underlying muscle contracts. A mass fixed only when muscle contracts originates from muscle or deep fascia (intramuscular sarcoma or fibromatosis). Fixation to bone indicates osteosarcoma, chondroma, or advanced bony invasion.
skill.exam.surg.lump_mobility_plane.practice: Demonstrate anatomical plane testing on an arm or thigh mass. Perform skin pinch test, test mobility in two directions with muscles relaxed, and repeat mobility testing while throwing biceps or quadriceps into active isometric contraction.
pitfalls: Testing lump mobility in only one direction instead of testing two perpendicular axes.
Failing to ask the patient to contract the underlying muscle against resistance during palpation.
Assuming a lump is subcutaneous because it moves freely when the underlying limb muscles are completely relaxed.
Mistaking a mobile deep fascial tumour for a superficial subcutaneous lipoma.

probes.q: What does an inability to pinch the skin over a subcutaneous swelling indicate?
probes.a: It indicates that the swelling either originates directly from the dermis or epidermis (such as a sebaceous cyst) or that a deeper tumour has infiltrated and tethered the overlying skin.

probes.q: How does contracting the underlying muscle differentiate an intramuscular lump from a submuscular lump?
probes.a: When the muscle contracts, an intramuscular lump becomes firm, fixed, and more prominent, whereas a submuscular lump becomes obscured, less prominent, and impalpable beneath the hardened muscle belly.

probes.q: Why does a swelling arising from a nerve or artery move sideways across the structure but not along its long axis?
probes.a: The tumour is anchored along the longitudinal axis by the continuous nerve sheath or arterial adventitia, restricting longitudinal displacement while allowing lateral mobility.

rubric.text: Performs skin pinch and skin sliding tests over the summit of the swelling
Tests mobility in two perpendicular axes while underlying muscles are relaxed
Applies resistance to throw the specific underlying muscle into contraction
Accurately deduces whether the plane is skin, subcutaneous, fascial, muscular, or bone

teach.heading: The anatomical hierarchy of planes
teach.body:
Every surgical swelling must be assigned to its precise anatomical depth: skin, subcutaneous tissue, deep fascia, muscle belly, submuscular space, or bone. Resectability, surgical margins, and biopsy approach depend on this localization.

The skin pinch test is the first filter. If the skin pinches freely, the mass is beneath the dermis. If the skin is tethered and moves with the mass, cutaneous origin or malignant infiltration is confirmed.

teach.heading: Technique for contracting underlying muscles
teach.body:
To test muscle involvement, the specific muscle beneath the lump must be actively contracted against resistance. For a chest wall mass, press hands against hips to contract pectoralis major.

For an anterior thigh mass, extend the knee against resistance to contract quadriceps femoris. If a mass is arising from muscle, its mobility decreases markedly across the direction of muscle fibres upon contraction.

skill.exam.surg.fluctuation.title: Testing for fluctuation in swellings
skill.exam.surg.fluctuation.oneLine: Two-finger displacement technique in perpendicular planes and Paget test for small lumps
skill.exam.surg.fluctuation.why: Fluctuation confirms fluid within a cavity. Performing the test in only one plane leads to false positives across muscle fibres, while using standard two-hand technique on lumps smaller than two centimetres merely displaces the mass without testing fluid displacement.

steps.text: Position the patient comfortably so that the swelling is well supported and muscles in the region are completely relaxed.
Place two fingers of one hand (the watching or receiving fingers) gently on one side of the swelling, maintaining light, stationary contact.
Place one finger of the opposite hand (the displacing or active finger) on the diametrically opposite aspect of the swelling.
Gently press the displacing finger toward the centre of the swelling to displace fluid within the cavity.
Feel for the hydraulic push: the watching fingers should feel passively lifted and separated by the displaced fluid.
Perform the test in two orthogonal planes: rotate hands 90 degrees and repeat the manoeuvre to ensure fluid displacement occurs equally in both planes.
For small swellings under 2 cm: perform Paget test by steadying the periphery with two fingers and pressing the centre with a third, noting if the centre is softer than the margin.

skill.exam.surg.fluctuation.normal: Solid soft tissue without hydraulic fluid transmission; displacing pressure is absorbed locally without expanding opposite watching fingers in multiple planes.
skill.exam.surg.fluctuation.abnormal: True fluctuation: displacement of the active finger produces an immediate, passive outward thrust on stationary watching fingers in two planes at right angles to each other.
skill.exam.surg.fluctuation.significance: True fluctuation proves the presence of fluid (pus, serum, blood, synovial fluid, or cyst contents) contained within an encapsulated cavity or tissue space. It is the cardinal physical sign distinguishing an abscess or cyst from a solid tumour.
skill.exam.surg.fluctuation.practice: Practice eliciting fluctuation on a fluid-filled balloon or latex glove filled with water. Rehearse the two-plane test and Paget test on small cystic models under 2 cm in diameter.
pitfalls: Testing in only one plane: soft fleshy muscles (such as quadriceps) yield false-positive fluctuation across fibres but not along fibres.
Pressing with both hands simultaneously instead of keeping watching fingers completely passive and stationary.
Attempting standard two-finger fluctuation on tiny swellings under 2 cm, which merely pushes the mass sideways.
Confusing pseudofluctuance of soft vascular lipomas or myxomas with true fluid fluctuation.

probes.q: Why must the fluctuation test always be performed in two planes at right angles to each other?
probes.a: Fleshy muscle tissue yields to pressure across its fibres giving a false sensation of fluctuation, but yields no transmission along the line of its fibres; true fluid transmits equally in all planes.

probes.q: What is the Paget test and when is it indicated?
probes.a: Paget test is used for small swellings under 2 cm where standard two-hand testing is impossible; two fingers fix the periphery while a third presses the centre, which feels softer and fluctuant compared to the edge.

probes.q: Which solid soft tissue tumours can produce pseudofluctuance mimicking fluid collections?
probes.a: Very soft lipomas, myxomas, soft fibromas, and vascular sarcomas can give a false impression of fluctuation due to their high water content and extreme cellular elasticity.

rubric.text: Keeps watching fingers passive and stationary while displacing finger presses
Tests fluctuation in two planes perpendicular to each other to exclude muscle artefact
Applies Paget test appropriately for lumps smaller than two centimetres
Distinguishes true fluid fluctuation from soft tissue pseudofluctuance

teach.heading: Hydraulic principles of the fluctuation test
teach.body:
Fluctuation is governed by Pascal principle: pressure exerted on a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions. One finger acts as the displacing piston while two stationary watching fingers receive the fluid wave.

The watching fingers must remain completely passive. If the examiner presses with both hands, the sense of fluid movement is destroyed by opposing muscular tension.

rows: Wide displacement across large fluid volume
Index and thumb receptive, opposite finger displaces
Fix periphery with two fingers, press softer centre

teach.heading: Avoiding the muscular false positive
teach.body:
The commonest bedside trap is testing over a relaxed muscle belly, such as the quadriceps, gastrocnemius, or deltoid. Striated muscle displaces readily when compressed transverse to its fibres, mimicking fluid.

Rotating the examining fingers by 90 degrees aligns the test along the longitudinal axis of the muscle fibres. Longitudinal compression encounters fibrous resistance and abolishes false fluctuation instantly.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.transillumination.title: Testing for transillumination in cystic swellings
skill.exam.surg.transillumination.oneLine: Dark-room torch technique with roll of paper to differentiate clear fluid from blood or solid tissue
skill.exam.surg.transillumination.why: Transillumination proves a swelling contains clear, serous, or lymphatic fluid. Failing to darken the room or directing the light directly onto the face of the mass produces false reflections that mislead the clinician.

steps.text: Perform the test in a completely darkened room, or shade the examination field with a dark sheet.
Roll a dark paper or cardboard tube (such as an X-ray film or stiff paper) to fit over one side of the swelling.
Place the viewing end of the paper cylinder against the examiner's eye and seat the opposite end firmly against the side of the swelling.
Place a bright, focused pencil torch firmly against the diametrically opposite aspect of the swelling.
Ensure that the entire mass intervenes directly between the torch and the viewing cylinder, avoiding superficial light scatter.
Look through the cylinder: observe whether the body of the swelling lights up with a brilliant reddish-yellow glow (translucent) or remains dark (opaque).

skill.exam.surg.transillumination.normal: Normal solid tissues and thick blood-filled structures do not transilluminate; light is absorbed and scattered within millimeters, yielding an opaque dark view.
skill.exam.surg.transillumination.abnormal: Brilliant red or golden translucency across the entire swelling, confirming the presence of clear serous fluid, lymph, or water.
skill.exam.surg.transillumination.significance: Transillumination confirms clear fluid content. A vaginal hydrocele, epididymal cyst, cystic hygroma, and ranula transilluminate brilliantly. Swellings containing blood (haematocele), thick pus, pultaceous sebaceous matter, or solid testicular neoplasms remain completely opaque.
skill.exam.surg.transillumination.practice: Perform the transillumination test in a dark room on a water-filled glove versus a milk-filled glove using a focused torch and paper roll. Rehearse eliminating ambient light leakage.
pitfalls: Attempting the test in a brightly lit outpatient clinic without a viewing tube or dark room.
Placing the torch directly on top of the swelling facing the examiner, producing glaring surface reflection.
Assuming all fluctuant cysts transilluminate; sebaceous cysts and cold abscesses contain thick matter that is completely opaque.
Failing to place the entire mass between the light source and the viewing tube.

probes.q: What physical property of the contents determines whether a fluctuant swelling will transilluminate?
probes.a: Transillumination requires clear, non-turbid, low-cellularity fluid such as serum, water, or lymph; fluid containing red cells, thick pus, cholesterol crystals, or sebaceous material absorbs light and remains opaque.

probes.q: Why is a hollow tube or rolled paper cylinder recommended when testing for transillumination in daytime?
probes.a: The cylinder cuts out peripheral ambient light glare and ensures that the examiner only observes light that has traversed the entire depth of the swelling, preventing false-positive reflections.

probes.q: Name three classic surgical swellings that characteristically transilluminate brilliantly.
probes.a: Primary vaginal hydrocele of the testis, cystic hygroma (lymphangioma) of the neck, and epididymal cyst (spermatocele).

rubric.text: Achieves adequate darkness using a dark room or viewing cylinder
Places light source and viewer on opposite sides of the swelling
Prevents ambient light leakage around the edges of the torch
Differentiates clear serous fluid from opaque blood, pus, or solid tissue

teach.heading: Optical physics of surgical transillumination
teach.body:
Transillumination (translucency) depends on the passage of photons through a fluid medium without significant scattering or absorption. Clear serous fluid, lymph, and normal saline allow photons to travel straight through.

Suspended particles such as erythrocytes in a haematocele, polymorphs in an abscess, or desquamated epithelial cells in a sebaceous cyst scatter and absorb light completely, rendering the swelling opaque.

teach.heading: The cardboard cylinder technique
teach.body:
In tropical and daytime clinics, a roll of dark X-ray film or black cardboard is essential. Press the cylinder firmly onto one side of the mass so that skin seals the rim against daylight.

The torch is placed on the diametrically opposite aspect. Looking down the dark cylinder reveals a fiery crimson illumination if translucent. This technique eliminates false positives from superficial cutaneous rim reflections.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.lump_pulsation.title: Differentiating expansile from transmitted pulsation in a lump
skill.exam.surg.lump_pulsation.oneLine: Two-finger separation test to distinguish true arterial aneurysms from overlying solid tumours
skill.exam.surg.lump_pulsation.why: Mistaking an aneurysm for an abscess or innocent lump and attempting aspiration or incision leads to catastrophic haemorrhage. The two-finger test confirms whether the fingers are pushed apart in all directions (expansile) or merely lifted upward together (transmitted).

steps.text: Inspect the swelling under tangential light for visible, rhythmic surface expansion synchronous with the cardiac cycle.
Place the tips of the index fingers of both hands on diametrically opposite borders of the swelling.
Keep the fingers stationary and relaxed, feeling for the direction of pulsatile displacement with each arterial beat.
Observe whether the two fingers are pushed apart laterally in all directions (expansile pulsation, characteristic of an aneurysm or vascular tumour).
Observe whether the fingers are merely lifted forward or upward in parallel without lateral separation (transmitted pulsation from an underlying normal artery).
Attempt to gently mobilize the swelling off the underlying vessel: a mass with transmitted pulsation can often be displaced away, abolishing the pulse.
Compress the proximal feeding artery if accessible: an aneurysm softens and ceases to pulsate, whereas a tumour overlying a vessel remains unchanged in consistency.

skill.exam.surg.lump_pulsation.normal: No visible or palpable pulsation over soft tissue masses; fingers placed on opposite margins remain stationary without lateral separation or elevation.
skill.exam.surg.lump_pulsation.abnormal: Expansile pulsation pushing fingers apart in all three dimensions with each heartbeat, or transmitted forward heave without lateral separation.
skill.exam.surg.lump_pulsation.significance: Expansile pulsation confirms an aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation, or highly vascular tumour (such as carotid body tumour or bone sarcoma). Transmitted pulsation indicates a non-vascular mass (lymph node, cyst, fibroma) lying directly over an artery.
skill.exam.surg.lump_pulsation.practice: Simulate expansile versus transmitted pulsation using an arterial pulse model. Practice resting two index fingertips on opposite margins to observe separation versus simple upward elevation.
pitfalls: Incision or needle aspiration of a pulsatile mass assumed to be an abscess, resulting in torrential hemorrhage.
Confusing strong transmitted heave from a thin patient's aorta for an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Using only one finger to palpate a pulsatile lump, which cannot assess lateral displacement.
Failing to check for a vascular thrill and systolic bruit over a pulsatile swelling.

probes.q: What is the physical hallmark of expansile pulsation during the two-finger test?
probes.a: The examining fingers placed on opposite borders are pushed apart laterally as well as lifted upward, demonstrating true multi-directional volume expansion of the mass with each cardiac systole.

probes.q: How does transmitted pulsation occur and how does gentle lateral displacement clarify the diagnosis?
probes.a: Transmitted pulsation occurs when a solid mass overlies an artery and is lifted passively upward; displacing the mass laterally off the arterial line abolishes the pulsation, proving it is transmitted.

probes.q: Which solid neoplasms may exhibit true expansile pulsation mimicking an aneurysm?
probes.a: Carotid body tumour (paraganglioma), telangiectatic osteosarcoma, vascular renal cell carcinoma metastases to bone, and thyroid vascular tumours.

rubric.text: Places index fingers on diametrically opposite margins of the mass
Distinguishes lateral finger separation from simple upward parallel heave
Tests proximal arterial compression to observe reduction in pulse or volume
Auscultates for systolic bruit or continuous machinery murmur

teach.heading: Biomechanics of expansile versus transmitted pulsation
teach.body:
Pulsation in a lump originates either from within its lumen or from an underlying artery. Expansile pulsation occurs when blood is driven into the swelling under cardiac pressure, expanding its volume in all directions.

Transmitted pulsation occurs when a solid mass rests on an artery. The pulse wave lifts the mass forward, but because no blood enters the mass, its internal volume does not increase.

rows: Pushed apart laterally in all axes
Cannot be moved away from artery
Can be pushed off the artery

teach.heading: Dangers of the pulsatile mass
teach.body:
A pulsatile swelling must be approached with extreme caution. Chronic aneurysms are often lined by laminated thrombus that feels firm, and inflammatory adventitial reaction can produce overlying erythema and tenderness.

Inexperienced clinicians frequently mistake such inflammatory aneurysms for subcutaneous abscesses. Incision and drainage yields catastrophic arterial haemorrhage that can be fatal without immediate proximal vascular control.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.compressibility_reducibi.title: Differentiating compressibility from reducibility in swellings
skill.exam.surg.compressibility_reducibi.oneLine: Testing volume reduction by fluid emptying versus anatomical reduction into a body cavity
skill.exam.surg.compressibility_reducibi.why: Compressibility and reducibility are frequently confused by students. A compressible vascular malformation collapses under direct pressure but refills immediately when pressure is released, whereas a reducible hernia disappears into an anatomical cavity and remains reduced until abdominal pressure rises.

steps.text: Inspect the baseline dimensions and vascular appearance of the swelling.
Apply firm, steady, continuous pressure over the mass with the flat of the fingers or palm.
Observe if the swelling shrinks or empties completely under manual compression.

To test compressibility: release the manual pressure abruptly while observing the swelling closely; note whether it refills rapidly and spontaneously without any patient effort (characteristic of cavernous haemangioma or lymphangioma).
To test reducibility: guide the contents through an anatomical defect or orifice into a body cavity (abdominal, thoracic, cranial, or spinal); note that the mass disappears entirely.
Keep the patient relaxed: note that the reduced mass remains inside the cavity, and reappears only when the patient coughs, strains, or stands up (characteristic of hernia or meningocele).

skill.exam.surg.compressibility_reducibi.normal: Normal solid tissues do not collapse under compression, and anatomical boundaries prevent displacement of tissues into closed body cavities.
skill.exam.surg.compressibility_reducibi.abnormal: Compressibility: swelling collapses on direct compression and refills spontaneously on release. Reducibility: swelling disappears through an orifice and remains reduced until coughing or standing.
skill.exam.surg.compressibility_reducibi.significance: Compressibility indicates a liquid-filled, multi-locular vascular or lymphatic space with communicating venous channels (cavernous haemangioma, venous malformation, cystic hygroma). Reducibility proves communication with a preformed anatomical body cavity (hernia, saphena varix, psoas abscess, meningocele).
skill.exam.surg.compressibility_reducibi.practice: Demonstrate the difference between a sponge model (compressibility, refilling instantly on release) and a balloon model pushed through a ring (reducibility, remaining inside until pressure pushes it out).
pitfalls: Using the terms compressible and reducible interchangeably in case presentations.
Failing to observe the behavior of the mass after releasing compressive pressure.
Forcing a tense, non-reducible groin swelling, causing bowel perforation or strangulation.
Overlooking rapid venous refilling in a subcutaneous vascular malformation.

probes.q: What is the defining clinical difference between a compressible swelling and a reducible swelling?
probes.a: A compressible swelling collapses under direct pressure and refills spontaneously as soon as pressure is released, whereas a reducible swelling empties into a body cavity and stays reduced until intra-cavity pressure forces it out.

probes.q: Why does a cavernous haemangioma refill immediately after manual compression is released?
probes.a: Direct pressure empties blood from the large cavernous vascular spaces into draining veins; when released, arterial and venous pressure instantly refills the vascular channels.

probes.q: Name two surgical swellings that are reducible and two that are compressible.
probes.a: Reducible: inguinal hernia, saphena varix, psoas abscess, or meningocele. Compressible: cavernous haemangioma, venous malformation, or cystic hygroma.

rubric.text: Applies firm, even compression to test volume reduction of the lump
Observes spontaneous refilling upon release to verify compressibility
Guides contents through an anatomical defect to confirm true reducibility
Checks whether a reduced swelling returns only on coughing or standing

teach.heading: The mechanical distinction between compression and reduction
teach.body:
Compressibility and reducibility represent two distinct anatomical mechanisms. A compressible mass contains fluid in communicating spaces that can be squeezed out into surrounding venules, capillaries, or lymphatic channels.

When pressure is removed, internal pressure drives fluid straight back, refilling the mass immediately. A reducible mass contains mobile viscera or fluid that pass bodily through a defect into an adjacent cavity.

teach.heading: Clinical examples at the bedside
teach.body:
Classic compressible lesions include cavernous haemangiomas, glomus tumours, and cystic hygromas. Squeezing them between two fingers blanches and flattens the tissue, which engorges with blood within seconds of release.

Classic reducible lesions include inguinal and femoral hernias, saphena varix, and cranial meningoceles. They disappear with a characteristic gurgle or slip, and remain absent until intra-abdominal or intra-cranial pressure rises.
