skill.exam.surg.cough_impulse.title: Testing for expansile cough impulse in swellings
skill.exam.surg.cough_impulse.oneLine: Inspection and palpation of expansile impulse at hernia orifices and body wall defects
skill.exam.surg.cough_impulse.why: An expansile impulse on coughing indicates a direct connection between the swelling and a high-pressure body cavity. Failing to verify true expansion rather than simple movement leads to misdiagnosing lymph nodes as hernias or overlooking saphena varix.

steps.text: Expose the swelling and related anatomical regions (groin, scrotum, chest wall, or cranial defect) with the patient standing if possible.
Instruct the patient to turn their head away from the examiner to prevent droplet transmission during coughing.
Inspect the swelling while asking the patient to cough firmly: observe whether the lump visibly bulges, expands, or emerges from an orifice.
Place the palmar surface of the fingers gently but firmly over the swelling and the suspected anatomical ring.
Ask the patient to give a series of short, sharp, resonant coughs while your fingers remain on the mass.
Palpate for true expansile impulse: feel whether the swelling expands outwards in all directions, driving the fingers apart, rather than merely being bumped forward.
In infants or uncooperative patients, observe crying or straining, which generates equivalent intra-cavity pressure.

skill.exam.surg.cough_impulse.normal: No visible or palpable expansion over hernial orifices or body wall margins when the patient coughs; tissue may be pushed forward by underlying muscle contraction but does not expand.
skill.exam.surg.cough_impulse.abnormal: Visible bulge and palpable expansile impulse on coughing, where the mass expands outward and impacts against the examining fingers.
skill.exam.surg.cough_impulse.significance: An expansile impulse on coughing confirms a direct communication between the swelling and a high-pressure cavity containing mobile viscera or fluid. It is the hallmark of reducible hernias (inguinal, femoral, umbilical), saphena varix, laryngocele, and meningocele.
skill.exam.surg.cough_impulse.practice: Palpate the superficial inguinal ring while asking a subject to turn their head and cough. Discriminate the true fluid expansile impulse of a hernia from the simple muscular twitch of the conjoined tendon.
pitfalls: Confusing a transmitted forward thrust from contracting abdominal muscles with a true expansile impulse.
Allowing the patient to cough directly toward the examiner's face.
Examining for cough impulse only while the patient is lying supine, which can mask subtle reducible hernias.
Assuming absence of cough impulse rules out a hernia; an incarcerated or strangulated hernia loses its cough impulse.

probes.q: What is the physical difference between an expansile cough impulse and a simple transmitted thrust?
probes.a: An expansile impulse features true outward expansion in all dimensions, pushing the examining fingers apart, whereas a transmitted thrust merely displaces the fingers forward without volume expansion.

probes.q: Why does a strangulated or incarcerated hernia lose its expansile cough impulse?
probes.a: The neck of the hernia is tightly constricted by the rigid hernial ring, blocking the transmission of intra-abdominal pressure waves and visceral movement into the hernial sac.

probes.q: What sign in the groin mimics an inguinal or femoral hernia by giving an expansile impulse on coughing?
probes.a: A saphena varix (dilatation of the terminal great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction), which produces a fluid thrill and expansile cough impulse in the groin.

rubric.text: Instructs patient to turn head away before coughing to prevent droplet spray
Inspects for visible bulge before placing hand over the orifice
Palpates with flat fingers to detect true expansile outward expansion
Examines in the erect position when supine examination is equivocal

teach.heading: Mechanism of the expansile cough impulse
teach.body:
Coughing causes sudden contraction of the diaphragm and anterolateral abdominal wall muscles against a closed glottis, driving intra-abdominal pressure above 100 mmHg. This pressure wave travels through any patent defect.

If an anatomical defect exists, abdominal contents (omentum, bowel, or fluid) are pushed into the preformed sac, producing a sudden, momentary expansion that can be seen and felt.

rows: Viscera pushed into sac by abdominal pressure
Venous pressure wave transmitted up saphenous vein
Increased intraglottic pressure during forced expiration
Cerebrospinal fluid wave forced through bone defect

teach.heading: The danger of the absent impulse
teach.body:
Students often assume that every hernia has an expansile cough impulse. An uncomplicated reducible hernia always demonstrates an impulse. However, when a hernia becomes irreducible, incarcerated, or strangulated, the impulse disappears.

The neck is tightly occluded by oedematous tissue and inflammatory exudate, cutting off pressure transmission. An absent cough impulse in a tender, tense groin mass is a surgical emergency, not a benign finding.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.slip_sign.title: Testing the slip sign for subcutaneous lipoma
skill.exam.surg.slip_sign.oneLine: Gentle marginal pressure causing a lobulated subcutaneous tumour to slip from under the finger
skill.exam.surg.slip_sign.why: The slip sign is the classical physical hallmark of a subcutaneous lipoma. Because a lipoma is soft and encapsulated, tangential pressure on its edge causes it to slide away into the lax subcutaneous fat, whereas a sebaceous cyst or fibroma yields or stays anchored.

steps.text: Position the patient so that the subcutaneous mass is well supported and the overlying skin is relaxed.
Locate the peripheral border of the swelling by gentle circumferential palpation.
Place the tip of the examining index finger directly upon the edge of the swelling.
Press down gently and steadily against the edge in a tangential direction toward the underlying deep fascia.
Observe and feel whether the encapsulated edge slips away from underneath the examining finger and slides into adjacent subcutaneous fat.
Compare with the edge of a cyst or fibroma: a cyst edge yields gently without sliding away, while a fibroma or cyst stays fixed in its subcutaneous bed.

skill.exam.surg.slip_sign.normal: Subcutaneous fat yields smoothly without discrete encapsulated margins slipping away beneath the examining fingertip.
skill.exam.surg.slip_sign.abnormal: Positive slip sign: the discrete margin of the swelling slips away readily from beneath the pressing finger, sliding sideways into the surrounding tissue.
skill.exam.surg.slip_sign.significance: A positive slip sign is pathognomonic for a benign encapsulated subcutaneous lipoma (the universal tumour). It confirms that the mass has a well-defined fibrous capsule, a lobulated architecture, and lies entirely within the mobile subcutaneous adipose plane.
skill.exam.surg.slip_sign.practice: Demonstrate the slip sign on a subcutaneous lipoma model (or a smooth, soft, encapsulated gel disc beneath a fabric layer). Practice sliding the finger over the edge to appreciate the sudden slip.
pitfalls: Pressing vertically into the centre of the lump instead of pressing tangentially on its peripheral margin.
Pressing too forcefully, which pins the mass against deep fascia and prevents it from sliding.
Mistaking the yield of a tense sebaceous cyst for the slip of a lipoma.
Failing to confirm lobulation and pseudo-fluctuance, which accompany a true lipoma.

probes.q: What physical phenomenon occurs during a positive slip sign?
probes.a: When the examining finger presses on the margin of the lump, the encapsulated edge slips out from under the finger and glides sideways into the loose subcutaneous adipose tissue.

probes.q: Why does a subcutaneous lipoma slip away, whereas an epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst does not?
probes.a: A lipoma is surrounded by loose subcutaneous connective tissue and a thin capsule, allowing lateral displacement, whereas a sebaceous cyst is tethered to the overlying epidermis via its punctum and yields without slipping.

probes.q: What combination of physical signs makes the diagnosis of a subcutaneous lipoma virtually certain?
probes.a: A subcutaneous mass with a positive slip sign, lobulated surface, soft doughy consistency, pseudofluctuance, and freely mobile overlying skin.

rubric.text: Identifies the exact peripheral margin of the lump before testing
Applies gentle tangential downward pressure on the edge of the swelling
Correctly appreciates the mass slipping away into adjacent subcutaneous tissue
Corroborates findings with surface lobulation and skin pinch testing

teach.heading: Anatomical basis of the slip sign
teach.body:
The subcutaneous lipoma is encapsulated by a delicate layer of compressed areolar tissue that separates it from surrounding adipose lobules. The mass floats within the lax subcutaneous fat plane.

When a finger presses directly onto its sloping edge, the rounded, slippery contour offers minimal friction. Instead of compressing, the mass glides rapidly away from the point of pressure, producing the classic slip sign.

teach.heading: Lipoma versus sebaceous cyst at the bedside
Palpatory characteristics of adipose tumours
teach.body:
In addition to the slip sign, a lipoma exhibits a soft, doughy consistency and pseudo-fluctuance. The liquid fat inside adipocytes gives an impression of fluid on palpation.

However, true fluctuation in two orthogonal planes is absent. Gently pushing the skin from the sides accentuates the characteristic surface lobulation, making individual fat clusters visible beneath the stretched dermis.

skill.exam.surg.lump_auscultation.title: Auscultation of a lump or swelling
skill.exam.surg.lump_auscultation.oneLine: Listening for systolic bruits, continuous machinery murmurs, venous hums, and peristaltic sounds
skill.exam.surg.lump_auscultation.why: Auscultation is often forgotten when examining swellings. Detecting a systolic bruit confirms a high-flow arteriovenous communication or aneurysm, while hearing peristaltic bowel sounds confirms that an abdominal or groin swelling contains bowel (enterocele).

steps.text: Warm the diaphragm and bell of the stethoscope before placing it on the patient's skin.
Place the diaphragm lightly over the summit and margins of the swelling without exerting heavy pressure that could compress underlying vessels.
Listen systematically for vascular bruits: identify systolic bruits (turbulent arterial flow in aneurysms or carotid body tumours).
Listen for continuous machinery murmurs with systolic accentuation (arteriovenous fistulae).
Listen for a soft continuous venous hum (large venous collaterals or Cruveilhier-Baumgarten syndrome over umbilical veins).
In groin or abdominal swellings, listen for gurgling, tinkling bowel peristaltic sounds confirming an enterocele.
Auscultate while gently compressing the proximal feeding artery: note whether the bruit diminishes or disappears completely.

skill.exam.surg.lump_auscultation.normal: Silent soft tissue masses without bruits, vascular murmurs, venous hums, or bowel sounds.
skill.exam.surg.lump_auscultation.abnormal: Harsh systolic bruit, continuous machinery murmur with systolic accentuation, soft venous hum, or active tinkling, gurgling bowel sounds.
skill.exam.surg.lump_auscultation.significance: A systolic bruit confirms turbulent arterial blood flow in an aneurysm, vascular neoplasm, or thyroid goitre. A continuous machinery murmur is diagnostic of an arteriovenous fistula. Bowel sounds within a groin swelling prove the presence of viable intestine inside a hernia sac.
skill.exam.surg.lump_auscultation.practice: Auscultate over a dialysis arteriovenous fistula to appreciate a continuous thrill and machinery murmur. Auscultate over an umbilical or inguinal hernia to detect intermittent bowel sounds.
pitfalls: Pressing too heavily with the stethoscope bell, which can artificially create a systolic bruit by compressing a normal underlying artery.
Omitting auscultation entirely during the routine examination of swellings and hernias.
Failing to auscultate the thyroid gland in a suspected toxic goitre (bruit indicates Graves disease).
Confusing ambient room noise or muscle tremor with a true vascular bruit.

probes.q: What does a systolic bruit heard over a swelling signify?
probes.a: It signifies turbulent blood flow through a narrowed, dilated, or tortuous arterial lumen, as seen in an arterial aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation, or hypervascular tumour.

probes.q: What auditory finding distinguishes an arteriovenous fistula from a simple arterial aneurysm?
probes.a: An arteriovenous fistula produces a continuous machinery murmur that persists throughout both systole and diastole with systolic accentuation, whereas an aneurysm produces only a systolic bruit.

probes.q: Why is auscultation valuable when examining an inguinoscrotal swelling?
probes.a: Hearing peristaltic gurgling bowel sounds over an inguinoscrotal swelling confirms that it contains intestine (enterocele) rather than omentum, hydrocele fluid, or a testicular mass.

rubric.text: Applies stethoscope diaphragm lightly to avoid compressing vessels
Correctly classifies sounds as systolic bruit, machinery murmur, or bowel sounds
Tests proximal arterial compression to observe changes in the bruit
Auscultates for peristalsis in abdominal and groin masses

teach.heading: Acoustic physics of vascular swellings
teach.body:
Auscultation of a mass detects sound waves produced by turbulent fluid flow. When blood accelerates through an irregular or dilated arterial segment, laminar flow is disrupted into turbulent vortices.

These vortices vibrate the vessel wall and surrounding soft tissues, producing a harsh, blowing systolic bruit. In an arteriovenous fistula, high pressure differential creates continuous turbulent flow through systole and diastole.

teach.heading: Technique for auscultating lumps
teach.body:
The examiner must place the stethoscope diaphragm with minimal pressure. Heavy pressure indents an underlying normal artery, creating artificial turbulence and a false systolic bruit.

In toxic goitre, auscultate specifically over the superior poles where the superior thyroid arteries enter. Always coordinate auscultation with simultaneous palpation of the contralateral carotid pulse to time murmurs to the cardiac cycle.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.title: Systematic examination of regional lymph nodes
skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.oneLine: Palpating drainage basins for enlargement, tenderness, consistency, matting, and fixity
skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.why: Every surgical swelling, ulcer, and infection drains into a specific lymph node basin. Omitting regional lymph node examination fails to stage malignant neoplasms, misses metastatic spread, and overlooks chronic infections like tuberculosis.

steps.text: Identify the primary lesion (swelling, ulcer, or inflammatory focus) and determine its exact anatomical lymphatic drainage basin.
Position the patient to relax the overlying muscles of the node basin (e.g. flex neck slightly for cervical nodes; support patient arm for axillary nodes).
Palpate with the palmar pads of relaxed fingers, rolling the soft tissues against underlying firm muscular or bony structures.
Examine systematically all anatomical stations in the basin (e.g. submental, submandibular, jugular chain, posterior triangle, supraclavicular in neck).
Document the number, exact anatomical group, and size (in centimetres) of palpable nodes.

Assess physical characteristics: tenderness (inflammatory), consistency (soft, firm, rubbery, stony hard), discrete versus matted (tuberculosis, lymphoma), and mobility or fixity to skin and deep fascia.

skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.normal: Lymph nodes not palpable, or small (under 1 cm), soft, discrete, non-tender, freely mobile, and non-matted.
skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.abnormal: Enlarged palpable lymph nodes: tender and soft (acute pyogenic infection), matted and firm with cold abscess or sinus (tuberculosis), firm and rubbery (lymphoma), or stony hard, discrete initially, later matted and fixed to deep structures (metastatic carcinoma).
skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.significance: Regional lymphadenopathy establishes whether a lump or ulcer is benign, tuberculous, or malignant. Stony-hard fixed nodes indicate regional metastatic cancer (e.g. Virchow node in gastrointestinal malignancy). Matted nodes with periadenitis indicate tuberculosis.
skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.practice: Perform a complete regional lymph node examination of the neck, axilla, or groin on a clinical subject. Methodically report anatomical station, size, consistency, tenderness, matting, and mobility.
pitfalls: Concluding the examination of an ulcer or lump without palpating its regional lymph node drainage basin.
Palpating axillary or cervical nodes with the patient's overlying muscles tensed and unrelaxed.
Assuming stony-hard lymph nodes are benign because they are completely painless.
Missing Troisiers sign (left supraclavicular Virchow node) in upper abdominal malignancy.

probes.q: What physical consistency of enlarged lymph nodes is characteristic of metastatic carcinoma?
probes.a: Stony hard consistency, initially discrete and painless, later becoming craggy, conglomerate, and fixed to adjacent deep tissues and overlying skin.

probes.q: What does matting of lymph nodes mean, and which surgical condition classically produces it?
probes.a: Matting means individual nodes are glued together into a conglomerate mass by periadenitis and capsular inflammation, classically seen in tuberculous lymphadenitis and advanced malignancy.

probes.q: What is Troisier sign, what is the involved node called, and what does it indicate?
probes.a: Troisier sign is the enlargement of a hard left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow node) nestled between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid, indicating metastatic spread from an abdominal or pelvic malignancy via the thoracic duct.

rubric.text: Correctly identifies the lymphatic drainage basin corresponding to the lesion
Positions the patient to ensure complete relaxation of overlying musculature
Palpates all anatomical groups within the drainage territory systematically
Assesses and documents size, tenderness, consistency, matting, and fixity

teach.heading: Anatomical imperative of lymphatic examination
teach.body:
In clinical surgery, an examination of any lump, ulcer, or inflammatory focus is incomplete until its regional lymph node basin has been examined. Tumour cells and pathogens travel via afferent lymphatics to regional filter stations.

Palpation must follow the known drainage pathways: head and oral lesions drain to cervical nodes, upper limb and breast lesions to axillary nodes, and lower limb, perineal, and lower abdominal lesions to inguinal nodes.

teach.heading: Physical characteristics of pathological lymph nodes

rows: Discrete initially, later fixed to deep plane

teach.heading: Technique for relaxing regional node basins
teach.body:
Lymph nodes lie deep to muscular and fascial layers. To palpate the anterior cervical chain, flex the patient neck slightly forward and toward the side being examined to relax the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

For the axilla, support the patient arm in your own to fully relax pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi, allowing fingers to sweep high into the apex of the axillary pyramid against the rib cage.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.surg.ulcer.title: History of an ulcer: onset, chronicity, and predisposing factors
skill.hx.surg.ulcer.oneLine: Mode of onset, duration, pain, discharge, systemic comorbidities, and previous wound therapies
skill.hx.surg.ulcer.why: An ulcer is a manifestation of an underlying pathology rather than a disease in isolation. Exploring diabetes, venous insufficiency, peripheral arterial disease, neuropathy, and previous scar trauma is essential to direct targeted management.

asks.text: Determine the mode of onset: did the ulcer follow mechanical trauma, a thermal burn, insect bite, or arise spontaneously from a pre-existing swelling, blister, or mole?
Record the exact duration: how long has the ulcer been open, and has it shown any periods of spontaneous healing or recurrence?
Assess pain: is the ulcer excruciatingly painful (ischaemic, aphthous), mildly uncomfortable (venous), or completely painless (neuropathic, trophic, syphilitic)?
Enquire about the character and quantity of discharge: serous, blood-stained, thick purulent, or foul-smelling.
Investigate predisposing systemic conditions: long-standing diabetes mellitus, varicose veins, deep vein thrombosis, smoking history, leprosy, tuberculosis, or syphilis.
Enquire whether the ulcer arose within the dense, unstable scar of a previous burn, radiotherapy, or chronic osteomyelitis sinus (Marjolin ulcer).

skill.hx.surg.ulcer.practice: Take a complete history from a patient with a chronic lower limb ulcer. Systematically trace the original precipitating event, duration, pain characteristics, and screen for vascular, neuropathic, and malignant risk factors.
pitfalls: Focusing only on local wound care without asking about underlying diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, or venous reflux.
Dismissing a painless ulcer on the sole of the foot as a minor callosity or blister without evaluating peripheral neuropathy.
Overlooking malignant transformation (Marjolin ulcer) when a chronic burn scar or venous ulcer rapidly expands or changes character.
Failing to ask about previous surgical debridements, skin grafts, or long-term topical applications.

probes.q: What does a completely painless, deep ulcer over a bony weight-bearing area of the foot suggest?
probes.a: A trophic or neuropathic ulcer (mal perforant) caused by loss of protective pain sensation, commonly due to diabetic sensory neuropathy, leprosy, or tabes dorsalis.

probes.q: What is a Marjolin ulcer and what classic history precedes its appearance?
probes.a: A squamous cell carcinoma arising within a long-standing, unstable, poorly vascularized scar, classically preceding by decades from a chronic burn scar, venous ulcer, or osteomyelitic sinus.

probes.q: How does the pain history differentiate a venous stasis ulcer from an arterial ischaemic ulcer?
probes.a: A venous ulcer produces a dull ache relieved by limb elevation and walking, whereas an arterial ulcer produces severe, sharp, unrelenting pain aggravated by elevation and relieved by hanging the leg dependent.

rubric.text: Identifies spontaneous appearance versus antecedent trauma, burn, or blister
Characterizes pain severity and relationship to limb elevation or dependency
Screens systematically for diabetes, vascular disease, and neuropathy
Enquires about long-standing scars to assess risk of malignant transformation

teach.heading: Etiological classification of surgical ulcers
teach.body:
An ulcer is defined as a discontinuity in the epithelial surface of the skin or mucous membrane. It results from cellular death following trauma, vascular insufficiency, metabolic failure, chronic infection, or malignant neoplasia.

Eliciting the exact initial event is vital. Traumatic ulcers in healthy tissue heal rapidly. When an ulcer persists beyond a few weeks, chronic underlying systemic pathology must be identified.

teach.heading: History clues in major lower limb ulcers

rows: Spontaneous or minor scratch over gaiter area
Dull ache, relieved by leg elevation
Trauma to toes, heels, or pressure points
Severe rest pain, relieved by hanging leg
Painless blister or foreign body in sole
Completely painless, loss of protective sense
Rapid change in long-standing burn scar

teach.heading: Discharge characteristics and chronicity
teach.body:
The nature of the discharge reveals the microbiological and pathological activity within the ulcer bed. A serous discharge indicates clean healing or venous weeping.

A thick, yellow, purulent exudate indicates pyogenic infection. Foul-smelling, greenish exudate indicates Pseudomonas colonisation, while dirty, blood-stained, serosanguinous discharge with necrotic debris suggests aggressive malignant breakdown.

skill.exam.surg.ulcer_inspect.title: Systematic inspection of an ulcer
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_inspect.oneLine: Site, size, shape, number, the five edge varieties, floor characteristics, and surrounding skin
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_inspect.why: The anatomical site and the morphology of the edge provide immediate diagnostic clues. Failing to recognize the raised everted edge of squamous carcinoma, the undermined edge of tuberculosis, or the punched-out edge of neuropathy leads to erroneous treatment.

steps.text: Expose the ulcer and the entire anatomical limb under excellent illumination, removing all dressings gently without damaging granulation tissue.
Note the exact anatomical site: gaiter area above medial malleolus (venous), pressure points of toes or heel (arterial/trophic), sun-exposed face (rodent ulcer), or burn scar (Marjolin).
Record size (measuring longest perpendicular diameters in centimetres) and overall shape (circular, oval, irregular, or geographic).
Count the number of ulcers: single (neoplastic, venous) versus multiple (tuberculous, syphilitic, vasculitic).

Inspect the edge and margin systematically: classify into sloping (healing), punched-out (trophic/syphilitic), undermined (tuberculous), rolled and beaded (basal cell carcinoma), or raised and everted (squamous cell carcinoma).
Inspect the floor of the ulcer: examine granulation tissue (healthy pink velvet versus pale, flabby, exuberant), slough, exposed tendon, or bare bone.
Examine the surrounding skin: look for stasis pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, eczema, erythema, loss of hair, trophic nail changes, or unstable scar tissue.

skill.exam.surg.ulcer_inspect.normal: Intact, healthy skin without ulceration, abnormal pigmentation, induration, slough, or denuded epithelium.
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_inspect.abnormal: Cutaneous defect with sloping edge and healthy red granulation tissue (healing); deep punched-out defect over pressure points (trophic); undermined bluish margin (tuberculosis); rolled beaded border (basal cell carcinoma); or raised everted cauliflower-like edge with necrotic floor (squamous cell carcinoma).
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_inspect.significance: A sloping edge with pink granulation tissue indicates active healing. An undermined edge with pale flabby granulations indicates tuberculous ulceration. A raised, everted edge is diagnostic of squamous cell carcinoma or Marjolin ulcer.
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_inspect.practice: Inspect an ulcer systematically using a clinical checklist: site, size, shape, number, edge, floor, discharge, and surrounding skin. Dictate findings cleanly in under sixty seconds.
pitfalls: Confusing the edge (the boundary between normal skin and the ulcer floor) with the margin (the perimeter line).
Overlooking exposed bone or tendon deep within the floor of a chronic ulcer.
Failing to inspect the surrounding skin for signs of chronic venous insufficiency (hemosiderin pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis).
Missing a rodent ulcer by confusing its rolled beaded edge with a benign chronic scab.

probes.q: What are the five classic morphological types of ulcer edges and their primary pathological associations?
probes.a: Sloping (healing ulcer), punched-out (trophic or gummatous ulcer), undermined (tuberculous ulcer), rolled and beaded (basal cell carcinoma), and raised and everted (squamous cell carcinoma).

probes.q: What visual features in the floor of an ulcer distinguish healthy healing granulation tissue from unhealthy infected granulation tissue?
probes.a: Healthy granulation tissue is bright pink or red, finely granular (velvety), moist, and does not bleed easily; unhealthy granulation tissue is pale, flabby, exuberant (proud flesh), covered with yellowish slough, and bleeds readily.

probes.q: Why does a tuberculous ulcer characteristically develop an undermined edge?
probes.a: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection spreads more rapidly in the loose, less vascular subcutaneous adipose tissue than in the tough overlying dermis, causing destruction of the subcutaneous plane so the epidermis overhangs the floor.

rubric.text: Records exact anatomical site, orientation, and metric dimensions in centimetres
Accurately classifies the edge into one of the five classic morphological varieties
Describes floor contents: granulation tissue quality, slough, and exposed structures
Inspects surrounding skin for pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, and trophic changes

teach.heading: The anatomical framework of ulcer inspection
teach.body:
Inspection of an ulcer requires a disciplined anatomical progression: site, size, shape, number, margin, edge, floor, and surrounding skin. The anatomical location alone strongly suggests the aetiology.

Venous ulcers occur characteristically in the gaiter area above the medial malleolus. Arterial ulcers appear on the tips of the toes or over the heel. Neuropathic ulcers occur beneath metatarsal heads or the calcaneal pressure pad.

teach.heading: The five classic ulcer edge configurations

rows: Gently sloping gradient with three colour zones
Perpendicular, vertical walls dropping like a punch
Edge curls over with pearly beaded nodules
Tissue heaps up, outgrows lumen, and rolls out

teach.heading: The floor versus the base of an ulcer
teach.body:
Students must never confuse the floor with the base of an ulcer. The floor is the visible surface of the ulcer bed seen on inspection, consisting of granulation tissue, slough, or necrotic debris.

The base is the deeper anatomical foundation upon which the ulcer rests, palpated between fingers to assess induration and deeper fixation to deep fascia, tendons, or periosteum.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.ulcer_palpate.title: Palpation of an ulcer: tenderness, induration, and base mobility
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_palpate.oneLine: Palpating the margin for malignant induration and testing base fixity to deep structures
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_palpate.why: Induration of the ulcer edge is the clinical hallmark of malignancy. Palpating the base determines depth of invasion and fixation to deep fascia, tendon, or bone, which dictates the surgical margin required for excision.

steps.text: Wear sterile gloves and ensure the patient is comfortable; explain what you are about to do.
Palpate the skin around the ulcer to test local temperature: compare warmth with adjacent and contralateral normal tissue.
Assess tenderness by gentle digital pressure on the edge and periwound skin, continuously watching the patient's face.
Palpate the edge: gently grasp the ulcer margin between index finger and thumb to assess for induration (hardness and thickening).
Confirm whether the edge feels soft (healing), firm (chronic inflammation), or stony hard with woody induration (malignancy).
Palpate the base: gently press the ulcer bed and attempt to mobilize it in two orthogonal planes over underlying deep fascia, tendons, and bone.
Check for friability and contact bleeding: note whether gentle touch produces brisk capillary bleeding (friable malignant tissue versus stable healing granulation).

skill.exam.surg.ulcer_palpate.normal: Periwound tissue supple, soft, and non-tender; absence of palpable induration; ulcer bed mobile over deeper planes without fixation or contact bleeding.
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_palpate.abnormal: Marked local heat and exquisite tenderness (acute infection); stony hard, unyielding induration of the edge (carcinoma); rigid fixation of the base to underlying periosteum or deep fascia; or exuberant friable tissue that bleeds briskly upon touch.
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_palpate.significance: Stony-hard induration of the edge is the clinical hallmark of malignant ulceration (epithelioma, Marjolin ulcer). Fixity of the base to underlying bone or tendon proves deep anatomical invasion, ruling out simple superficial wide local excision and demanding en bloc composite resection.
skill.exam.surg.ulcer_palpate.practice: Palpate simulated ulcer models with varying edge firmness. Practice grasping the margin between finger and thumb to test edge induration, and pinch the base to assess mobility over deep planes.
pitfalls: Failing to wear sterile gloves when touching open ulcer beds and exudate.
Pressing aggressively into an acutely inflamed, tender floor, causing agonizing pain and patient distrust.
Omitting the pinch test of the edge to assess induration, which is the primary bedside discriminator of cancer.
Neglecting to test mobility of the base over underlying muscle and bone.

probes.q: What does stony-hard induration of the edge and base of a chronic ulcer indicate?
probes.a: It indicates malignant infiltration, classically squamous cell carcinoma (epithelioma) or Marjolin ulcer, where invasive tumour cells and desmoplastic fibrosis produce rock-hard induration.

probes.q: How does the surgeon test whether an ulcer is fixed to the underlying deep bone or periosteum?
probes.a: By grasping the base and edges of the ulcer between fingers and attempting to move it in two perpendicular directions over the bone; complete immobility in both planes proves bony invasion.

probes.q: Why does a malignant ulcer bleed on gentle touch (contact bleeding)?
probes.a: Malignant neoplasms induce abnormal, chaotic, friable tumour neo-vasculature that lacks normal smooth muscle and basement membrane support, rupturing easily upon light tactile pressure.

rubric.text: Applies sterile gloves and explains the gentle examination to the patient
Grasps the ulcer margin between finger and thumb to assess induration
Tests mobility of the base over deep fascia, tendon, and underlying bone
Observes tissue friability and notes any contact bleeding

teach.heading: Technique for assessing ulcer induration
teach.body:
Induration is the cardinal sign sought during ulcer palpation. The examiner must gently take the margin of the ulcer between the index finger and thumb, lifting and pinching the tissue.

In a healing or benign chronic ulcer, the edge feels pliable, soft, or moderately firm. In an epithelioma, the edge feels like a piece of cartilage or hard stone embedded in the skin, extending into surrounding normal tissue.

rows: Fixed to deep fascia, tendon, or bone

teach.heading: Testing mobility and depth of invasion
teach.body:
After the edge is evaluated, the base must be palpated flat against underlying structures. Attempt to slide the ulcer bed transversely and longitudinally across underlying tendons and bones.

If the base moves freely, the disease is confined to the skin and subcutaneous plane. If it is completely anchored, malignant or osteomyelitic invasion of deep fascia, periosteum, or bone is confirmed, altering surgical resectability.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.annex.surg.ulcer_edges.title: Ulcer edges: morphological classification and pathological correlates
skill.annex.surg.ulcer_edges.oneLine: The five classic edge patterns: sloping, punched-out, undermined, rolled-beaded, and raised-everted
skill.annex.surg.ulcer_edges.why: Accurately naming the edge configuration distinguishes benign healing ulcers from granulomatous infections and malignant neoplasms. Misidentifying an everted or rolled edge as a chronic inflammatory wound delays biopsy and definitive oncological resection.
skill.annex.surg.ulcer_edges.practice: Rehearse sketching cross-sectional diagrams of the five classic ulcer edges from memory. Correlate each architectural shape with its underlying histopathological mechanism and clinical disease entity.
pitfalls: Confusing the terminology of an edge (the cross-sectional contour) with a margin (the boundary line on surface view).
Assuming that all deep ulcers with vertical walls are syphilitic; diabetic trophic ulcers are far more common today.
Failing to take an incisional punch biopsy from the active everted edge of a suspected malignant ulcer.
Misdiagnosing a basal cell carcinoma as a benign healing ulcer because of slow progression.

probes.q: What are the three distinct colour zones visible on the sloping edge of an active healing ulcer?
probes.a: An outer white zone of multiplying keratinized epithelium, a middle bluish-grey zone of thin transparent growing epithelial cells, and an inner red zone of vascular healthy granulation tissue.

probes.q: What histopathological process produces the raised and everted edge of a squamous cell carcinoma?
probes.a: Rapid, uncontrolled malignant epithelial cell proliferation outstrips the floor of the ulcer, heaping up cancerous tissue that rolls outward and overhangs normal surrounding skin.

probes.q: Why is an incisional biopsy taken from the edge rather than the center of an ulcer for histological diagnosis?
probes.a: The edge contains actively proliferating, viable diagnostic pathology at the junction with normal tissue, whereas the center often contains non-diagnostic necrotic debris, slough, and secondary bacterial colonisation.

rubric.text: Names and sketches all five classic edge configurations accurately
Correlates cross-sectional anatomy with specific underlying pathological processes
Explains why biopsies must include the active edge and viable junctional tissue

teach.heading: Architectural classification of ulcer edges
teach.body:
The edge of an ulcer is defined as the cross-sectional contour between the surrounding intact skin and the ulcer floor. Classical surgical pathology recognizes five distinct edge patterns, each reflecting a specific disease mechanism.

Recognizing these edge shapes allows the clinician to reach a provisional diagnosis on inspection alone, separating benign reparative processes from chronic granulomas and aggressive neoplasms.

rows: Gentle incline with white, blue, red zones
Inverted pearly roll with fine telangiectasia
Heaped up, rolled outward cauliflower mass

teach.heading: Clinical biopsy rules based on edge architecture
teach.body:
When an ulcer presents with a raised-everted or rolled edge, or when any chronic ulcer fails to heal after several weeks, biopsy is mandatory. Biopsy tissue must always be taken from the active edge of the lesion.

Sampling necrotic slough from the centre yields only non-viable debris. An adequate wedge or punch biopsy must include the advancing edge with a small margin of adjacent normal epidermis for precise histological orientation.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_ulcer.title: Wagner-Meggitt classification of diabetic foot lesions
skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_ulcer.oneLine: Six-grade clinical staging from intact high-risk skin to extensive gangrene of the entire foot
skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_ulcer.why: The Wagner classification provides a standardized surgical grading system that guides immediate management, from conservative offloading for grade 1 to emergency surgical debridement or major amputation for advanced gangrene.
skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_ulcer.practice: Grade three clinical scenarios of diabetic foot disease using the Wagner-Meggitt scale. Formulate the immediate surgical management strategy corresponding to each grade.
pitfalls: Underestimating a grade 3 ulcer by focusing on a small skin opening while missing extensive deep plantar abscess or osteomyelitis.
Treating dry localized toe gangrene (grade 4) with soaking or wet dressings, converting it into wet spreading gangrene.
Delaying radical surgical debridement in grade 3 or 4 infections with systemic toxicity.
Failing to probe for bare bone with a sterile metal probe in deep diabetic foot ulcers.

probes.q: What clinical feature marks the transition from Wagner grade 2 to Wagner grade 3 in diabetic foot disease?
probes.a: Wagner grade 2 is a deep ulcer penetrating to tendon or capsule without abscess, whereas Wagner grade 3 is complicated by deep abscess formation, osteomyelitis, or joint sepsis.

probes.q: What is the definition of Wagner grade 0 and what is the primary management focus?
probes.a: Grade 0 represents intact skin with high-risk pre-ulcerative foot deformity or calluses; the focus is preventive offloading, custom diabetic footwear, patient education, and tight glycaemic control.

probes.q: How do Wagner grade 4 and Wagner grade 5 differ in anatomical extent and surgical intervention?
probes.a: Grade 4 is localized gangrene confined to the forefoot or digits (amenable to minor toe or transmetatarsal amputation), whereas Grade 5 is extensive gangrene involving the entire foot, requiring major below-knee amputation.

rubric.text: Correctly defines all six grades (0 to 5) of the Wagner-Meggitt classification
Accurately differentiates superficial ulceration, deep tissue, and bone involvement
Distinguishes localized forefoot gangrene from extensive whole-foot gangrene

teach.heading: Principles of the Wagner-Meggitt staging system
teach.body:
The Wagner-Meggitt classification is the classical, universally utilized surgical grading system for diabetic foot lesions. It categorizes lesions into six grades based on depth of tissue penetration, presence of osteomyelitis, and extent of gangrene.

The system provides a clear roadmap for surgical triage, distinguishing superficial wounds treatable in outpatients from deep infections requiring emergency hospitalisation, surgical debridement, or definitive amputation.

rows: Intact skin, pre-ulcerative deformity, bony prominence
Superficial ulcer involving skin and subcutaneous fat
Deep ulcer penetrating to tendon, ligament, or joint
Deep ulcer complicated by abscess or osteomyelitis
Radical debridement, bone resection, IV therapy
Localized gangrene of digits or forefoot
Extensive gangrene involving the entire foot

teach.heading: Clinical interpretation of Wagner grades
teach.body:
In grade 3 lesions, the probe-to-bone test is critical. Palpating hard, rough, gritty bone with a sterile metal probe has a high positive predictive value for underlying osteomyelitis.

Grade 4 gangrene requires urgent vascular assessment. If vascular flow is adequate or reconstructable, localized digital amputation preserves a functional heel and midfoot. Grade 5 lesions with ascending sepsis demand urgent life-saving major amputation.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
