skill.hx.surg.sinus_fistula.title: History of a sinus or fistula
skill.hx.surg.sinus_fistula.oneLine: Congenital versus acquired origin, discharge nature, antecedent abscess, and previous surgery
skill.hx.surg.sinus_fistula.why: Differentiating a blind sinus from a communicating fistula requires identifying antecedent events: prior incision and drainage, persistent stitch discharge, passage of bowel contents, or recurrent painful perineal swellings.

asks.text: Determine congenital versus acquired origin: has the opening been present since birth (preauricular sinus, branchial fistula, patent vitello-intestinal duct) or did it develop later in life?
Enquire about antecedent events: did the opening follow a painful acute abscess that ruptured spontaneously or was surgically drained (perianal fistula, stitch abscess, osteomyelitis)?
Trace the exact duration and whether the discharge is continuous, intermittent, or ceases temporarily followed by painful recurrent swelling.
Analyze the nature of the discharge: clear serous, purulent, blood-stained, bone chips, hair, faeces, flatus, urine, bile, saliva, or milk.
Ask about previous surgical operations, implants, mesh, sutures, foreign body impaction, or abdominal trauma.
Enquire about underlying systemic diseases: chronic inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease), tuberculosis, actinomycosis, or pelvic radiotherapy.

skill.hx.surg.sinus_fistula.practice: Take a focused history from a patient with a discharging perianal or abdominal wall opening. Map out the original abscess, any previous operative interventions, and determine whether the discharge represents enteric or urinary leakage.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about the passage of flatus or faecal matter through an abdominal or perianal opening.
Overlooking previous surgical operations or mesh repair that point to a retained infected suture or foreign body sinus.
Assuming a sinus has healed when the external opening closes, missing recurrent abscess formation due to trapped deep infection.
Neglecting to enquire about symptoms of Crohn disease (chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, oral ulcers) in young patients with complex anal fistulae.

probes.q: What is the defining anatomical difference between a sinus and a fistula?
probes.a: A sinus is a blind-ending track leading from an epithelial surface down into deeper tissues, whereas a fistula is an abnormal communicating track connecting two epithelial-lined surfaces.

probes.q: What does a history of intermittent discharge followed by recurrent painful swelling over the site indicate?
probes.a: It indicates temporary occlusion of the external opening with retained discharge and recurrent abscess formation, followed by spontaneous burst or re-drainage when internal pressure rises.

probes.q: Which specific discharge contents point to chronic osteomyelitis, pilonidal disease, and actinomycosis respectively?
probes.a: Small gritty bone chips (sequestrum) indicate chronic osteomyelitis; tufts of hair indicate pilonidal sinus; sulphur granules in purulent discharge indicate actinomycosis.

rubric.text: Distinguishes congenital origin from post-abscess or postoperative onset
Identifies the specific material discharged (pus, bone chips, hair, faeces, urine)
Explores previous abscess drainage, surgical history, and retained implants
Screens for systemic inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, and radiotherapy

teach.heading: Anatomical definitions and historical inquiry
teach.body:
A sinus is a blind track lined by granulation tissue connecting an epithelial surface to a deep focus of tissue breakdown. A fistula is an abnormal communication between two epithelial surfaces (organ to skin or organ to organ).

History must establish the antecedent event. A chronic bone sinus almost always begins with acute osteomyelitis and high fever; an anal fistula is typically preceded by a painful ischiorectal or perianal abscess.

teach.heading: The cycle of temporary closure
teach.body:
Patients frequently report that the sinus heals completely for several weeks, only to become intensely painful, hot, and swollen again before suddenly discharging pus. This cyclical pattern is diagnostic.

Epithelialisation or scab formation at the orifice temporarily blocks outflow. Pus re-accumulates under tension until pressure ruptures the opening, relieving pain. True permanent healing never occurs until the deep source is excised.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_inspect.title: Inspection of a sinus or fistula opening
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_inspect.oneLine: Anatomical site, opening morphology, sprouting granulations, puckering, and surrounding excoriation
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_inspect.why: The appearance of the opening reveals the underlying etiology: sprouting exuberant granulation tissue points to a foreign body or sequestrum, a puckered opening indicates tuberculosis, and excoriated surrounding skin indicates active digestive enzyme leakage.

steps.text: Expose the area completely under bright direct illumination, cleaning away crusts gently with saline to inspect the actual orifice.
Note the exact anatomical site: preauricular, midline or lateral neck, midline natal cleft, perianal clock position, groin, or abdominal wall scar.
Count the number of external openings: single versus multiple (actinomycosis, hidradenitis suppurativa, complex fistula-in-ano).
Inspect the morphology of the orifice: flush with skin, depressed, puckered with bluish undermined skin, or raised on a button of granulation.
Look for sprouting exuberant granulation tissue (proud flesh) projecting from the mouth of the opening, indicating a deep foreign body or bone sequestrum.
Look for a raised, rolled, or everted margin around the opening, warning of malignant transformation in a chronic sinus.
Inspect the surrounding skin: look for excoriation and chemical digestion from proteolytic enzymes (enterocutaneous fistula), eczema, hyperpigmentation, or induration.

skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_inspect.normal: Intact, smooth skin without discharging orifices, abnormal pits, granulation buds, scarring, or chemical excoriation.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_inspect.abnormal: Cutaneous orifice discharging fluid; sprouting cauliflower-like granulation tissue protruding from the mouth; puckered bluish depressed opening; multiple cribriform openings; or severe raw cutaneous excoriation.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_inspect.significance: Sprouting granulation tissue at the mouth confirms a foreign body (retained suture, surgical mesh) or necrotic bone sequestrum in the depth. A puckered, scarred orifice indicates tuberculous sinus. Excoriated surrounding skin confirms leakage of proteolytic enzymes from small bowel.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_inspect.practice: Inspect simulated or clinical photographs of sinus orifices. Contrast the projecting red granulation button of a foreign body sinus with the puckered, depressed, bluish scar of a tuberculous sinus.
pitfalls: Failing to clean away dry discharge crusts, mistaking a plugged sinus opening for a simple skin papule.
Overlooking secondary pits or tiny hair-containing openings in the midline natal cleft in suspected pilonidal disease.
Dismissing sprouting granulation tissue as innocent proud flesh without searching for a deep foreign body or sequestrum.
Failing to protect the surrounding skin from digestive enzymatic excoriation in enterocutaneous fistulae.

probes.q: What does exuberant, sprouting granulation tissue projecting from the mouth of a chronic sinus indicate?
probes.a: It indicates a persistent deep mechanical irritant in the cavity, classically a necrotic bone sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis or a retained non-absorbable surgical foreign body (suture or mesh).

probes.q: What physical appearance of a sinus opening is classical for tuberculous lymphadenitis or bone disease?
probes.a: A depressed, puckered opening surrounded by thin, bluish, undermined skin with pale, watery granulation tissue, often leaving a scarred, stellate depression upon healing.

probes.q: Why does the skin surrounding an enterocutaneous fistula become raw and severely excoriated?
probes.a: Active proteolytic digestive enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin) and bile salts from small bowel effluent digest the stratum corneum and superficial dermis, producing painful chemical burns.

rubric.text: Cleans crusts gently to inspect the true anatomical orifice and margin
Accurately describes opening as flush, depressed, puckered, or sprouting
Recognizes protruding proud flesh as a marker of a deep foreign body or sequestrum
Evaluates surrounding skin for enzymatic excoriation, eczema, or induration

teach.heading: Visual morphology of the external opening
teach.body:
The mouth of a sinus or fistula provides immediate clues regarding the pathology at its base. When the orifice is flush with surrounding skin and epithelialised, the track is mature and unlikely to close spontaneously.

If the opening is surrounded by a raised, hyperplastic rim of pink tissue that bleeds easily, active granulation tissue is proliferating in response to persistent deep irritants like infected sutures or necrotic bone.

rows: Sunken, scarred, surrounded by bluish skin
Midline pits containing visible hair tufts

teach.heading: Enzymatic excoriation in enterocutaneous fistulae
teach.body:
The condition of the periorificial skin distinguishes high-output small bowel fistulae from low-output colonic fistulae. Duodenal and proximal jejunal effluent is rich in activated trypsin, lipase, and bile salts.

Within hours of contact, these enzymes strip the epidermal barrier, causing raw, bleeding, agonizingly painful excoriation that mimics a partial-thickness chemical burn, demanding barrier appliances and stoma paste.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_palpate.title: Palpation of a sinus or fistula track
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_palpate.oneLine: Eliciting tenderness, feeling cord-like induration, and expressing discharge along the track
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_palpate.why: Palpating along the suspected course of a sinus or fistula reveals the extent of chronic induration and determines whether compression expresses pus, serum, or alimentary content, confirming the axis of the track.

steps.text: Wear sterile gloves and ensure the patient is comfortably supported.
Palpate the skin around the opening to evaluate local warmth and localized tenderness.
Roll the tissues between the index finger and thumb (or compress flat against deep bone) along the suspected axis of the track.
Feel for a firm, fibrous, cord-like or pencil-like induration tracing from the skin opening toward deeper structures.
Apply gentle, progressive pressure along the indurated track moving toward the external orifice.
Observe the mouth of the sinus during compression: note the emergence and nature of expressed discharge (pus, droplets of serous fluid, or gas bubbles).
In perianal fistula cases, perform a digital rectal examination to palpate the internal opening and trace the indurated track through the anal sphincter.

skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_palpate.normal: Soft, pliable, non-tender subcutaneous tissues without palpable fibrous cords, deep induration, or discharge expressed on compression.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_palpate.abnormal: Palpable, firm, fibrous cord-like track beneath the skin leading to a deep focus; localized deep tenderness; and active expression of pus, blood, or gas bubbles from the opening upon pressure.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_palpate.significance: A palpable cord-like induration outlines the anatomical course and branching of the fistulous track. Expression of pus confirms active suppurative infection within a deep reservoir. Tracing the track into the anal canal establishes the relation to the sphincter complex.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_fistula_palpate.practice: Palpate a simulated fistula track (such as a firm silicone cord embedded within soft foam beneath a thin skin layer). Practice feeling the cord-like boundary and milking pressure toward the orifice.
pitfalls: Applying aggressive, painful pressure over an acutely tender inflammatory swelling.
Failing to observe the mouth of the sinus while expressing the track from behind.
Neglecting digital rectal examination in a patient presenting with an external perianal opening.
Mistaking a normal tendon or blood vessel for an indurated fibrous fistulous track.

probes.q: What physical sensation does a chronic fistulous track convey to the palpating fingers?
probes.a: A firm, thickened, fibrous, cord-like or pencil-like indurated band running subcutaneously from the external opening toward the deeper origin.

probes.q: Why is gentle expression of the track performed during palpation?
probes.a: Compressing the track toward the opening reveals hidden discharge, allows collection of fresh purulent fluid for microbiological culture, and confirms that the indurated cord communicates with the orifice.

probes.q: What specific palpatory findings are sought during digital rectal examination in a case of fistula-in-ano?
probes.a: An indurated pit or nodule marking the internal opening at the dentate line, a palpable cord traversing the anal wall, and assessment of anal sphincter tone.

rubric.text: Applies sterile gloves and positions patient comfortably for palpatory tracing
Rolls subcutaneous tissues to palpate the fibrous cord-like track
Applies gentle directional pressure toward the orifice to express discharge
Performs digital rectal examination for internal opening when perianal

teach.heading: Palpation of the chronic fibrous track
teach.body:
Long-standing infection and continuous drainage stimulate intense chronic fibroblastic proliferation around the granulation track. This reaction transforms the soft fistulous channel into a dense fibrous tube.

On light palpation, rolling the tissues between thumb and forefinger reveals this tube as a palpable, firm, cord-like structure. Palpation maps its orientation, depth, and anatomical direction.

rows: Identify the distal limit of the indurated cord
Determines depth and extent of track
Press smoothly with fingertip along the cord
Stroke gently toward the external opening
Expresses accumulated fluid from deep pocket
Watch the orifice as fluid emerges
Identifies purulence, gas, or bone fragments

teach.heading: Mapping perianal tracks into the sphincter
teach.body:
In fistula-in-ano, digital rectal examination is indispensable. With the index finger in the anal canal and thumb on the perianal skin, bidigital palpation pinches the tissues between the external opening and anal verge.

The examiner feels the cord-like track traversing the sphincter. At the dentate line, the internal opening is frequently palpated as a distinct indurated nodule or small pitted depression.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.sinus_probing.title: Surgical principles and technique of probing a sinus
skill.exam.surg.sinus_probing.oneLine: Aseptic gentle exploration using a blunt malleable probe and avoiding false passage creation
skill.exam.surg.sinus_probing.why: Blind, forceful probing in an uncooperative patient or acute infection causes intense pain, induces bacteremia, creates false tracks, and risks visceral perforation. Probing must be gentle, aseptic, and replaced by fistulography or MRI when deep.

steps.text: Verify indications and strict contraindications: never probe an acutely inflamed, tender, non-draining opening in an outpatient setting.
Cleanse the skin with antiseptic and maintain strict surgical asepsis.
Select an appropriate sterile, blunt-ended, malleable metal probe (silver or stainless steel).
Introduce the probe tip gently into the orifice holding it loosely like a pen, allowing it to find its own path along the track under gravity without applying force.
Determine the direction, depth, and termination of the track: note if it passes superficial, deep to fascia, or into a cavity.

Feel for the end of the track: note a soft springy stop (fibrous tissue), an open stop (deep cavity), or a hard, gritty, moveable object at the depth of the track indicating a loose sequestrum. Fixed, unyielding bare bone is involucrum, not a loose sequestrum, so never force the probe.
If resistance is encountered, cease advancing immediately to prevent perforating tissues or creating a false passage; transition to radiological contrast sinography or MRI.

skill.exam.surg.sinus_probing.normal: Smooth, gentle entry of the blunt probe without resistance, following a preformed track without pain, bleeding, or creation of false passages.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_probing.abnormal: Severe pain on gentle insertion (acute inflammation); probe entering a deep body cavity; or probe striking a rough, hard, gritty, mobile object (bone sequestrum in osteomyelitis).
skill.exam.surg.sinus_probing.significance: Probing confirms whether the track is superficial or traverses deep fascia, and demonstrates bare bone or sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis. When the track is tortuous or deep, contrast sinography or MRI fistulography replaces blind probing to prevent visceral injury.
skill.exam.surg.sinus_probing.practice: Practice inserting a blunt malleable probe into a transparent anatomical track model. Rehearse holding the probe lightly between thumb and two fingers, letting gravity guide the tip without pushing.
pitfalls: Using excessive force, driving the probe through the fibrous wall to create a painful, bleeding false passage.
Probing an acutely inflamed, infected sinus in the clinic without anaesthesia, precipitating severe pain and bacteremia.
Probing an abdominal wall sinus blindly, risking perforation of underlying adherent small intestine.
Using a sharp or rigid needle instead of a sterile, blunt-ended malleable probe.

probes.q: What tactile sensation does a probe convey when it strikes a sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis?
probes.a: A hard, rough, gritty sensation with a dull metallic click, confirming bare necrotic cortical bone separated from vascular living tissue.

probes.q: Why must blind probing be strictly avoided in an abdominal wall sinus?
probes.a: Underlying intestinal loops, colon, or bladder may be densely adherent to the peritoneum directly beneath the sinus; blind probing risks visceral perforation, peritonitis, or faecal fistula.

probes.q: What imaging investigations provide a safe, non-invasive alternative to clinical probing for complex sinuses and fistulae?
probes.a: Contrast sinography or fistulography under fluoroscopy, high-resolution ultrasound, and pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI fistulogram).

rubric.text: Selects a sterile, blunt-ended malleable probe and prepares the field aseptically
Guides the probe gently between fingers without pushing or forcing resistance
Accurately interprets tactile stop (soft, cavity, or gritty bone sequestrum)
Stops immediately upon resistance and recommends sinography or MRI when indicated

teach.heading: Surgical rules for probing tracks
teach.body:
Probing a sinus is an invasive diagnostic manoeuvre requiring strict aseptic precautions. The cardinal rule of probing is that force must never be applied. The probe must be held lightly like a pen between the fingertips.

Allow the probe to slide in gently, following the path of least resistance. Forcing the probe creates a false passage through granulation tissue into healthy muscle or viscera, causing haemorrhage and tracking infection.

teach.heading: Radiological replacement of blind probing
teach.body:
Modern surgical practice increasingly replaces metal probing with cross-sectional imaging and contrast studies. In complex perianal fistulae, pelvic MRI demonstrates the track, secondary branches, and internal opening with pinpoint accuracy.

For complex abdominal or extremity sinuses, injecting water-soluble iodinated contrast (sinography) under fluoroscopy outlines deep cavities, tortuous channels, and visceral communications safely without tissue trauma.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.annex.surg.sinus_persistence.title: Mechanisms of persistence in sinuses and fistulae
skill.annex.surg.sinus_persistence.oneLine: Pathological causes preventing spontaneous healing: foreign body, epithelialisation, and distal obstruction
skill.annex.surg.sinus_persistence.why: Sinuses and fistulae persist because specific pathological barriers prevent granulation tissue from obliterating the track. Systematic evaluation for necrotic sequestrum, epithelial lining, tuberculosis, or distal obstruction is mandatory before definitive surgical repair.
skill.annex.surg.sinus_persistence.practice: Review the classic surgical causes of persistent sinus and fistula. Apply the clinical framework to explain why an osteomyelitic sinus or enterocutaneous fistula fails to heal spontaneously.
pitfalls: Attempting simple superficial cauterisation or curettage of a sinus while leaving a deep necrotic sequestrum or mesh in place.
Overlooking distal bowel obstruction in an enterocutaneous fistula, where healing is impossible until the distal lumen is cleared.
Failing to biopsy the wall of a long-standing sinus that has undergone malignant degeneration into squamous carcinoma.
Assuming a tuberculous sinus will heal with surgical curettage alone without full systemic anti-tubercular chemotherapy.

probes.q: What are the common foreign bodies that cause a surgical sinus to persist indefinitely?
probes.a: Non-absorbable surgical sutures (silk, braided polyester), infected prosthetic mesh, retained gauze or swabs, bone sequestra in osteomyelitis, and foreign implants.

probes.q: Why does epithelialisation of a sinus or fistulous track prevent spontaneous obliteration?
probes.a: Granulation tissue can only adhere to and fuse with opposing raw mesenchymal tissue; once the track is lined by mature stratified or columnar epithelium, healing cannot occur until the lining is completely excised.

probes.q: What classic mnemonic or framework summarizes the systemic and local factors that prevent fistula healing?
probes.a: The classic surgical causes include Foreign body, Epithelialisation, Specific infection (TB/actinomycosis), Malignancy, Inadequate rest/drainage, Distal obstruction, and High-pressure output (the FRIENDS framework).

rubric.text: Lists the major pathophysiological causes of persistent sinus and fistula
Explains how necrotic tissue and non-absorbable foreign bodies perpetuate drainage
Recognizes that distal lumen obstruction maintains high-pressure fistulous flow

teach.heading: Biological barriers to sinus and fistula healing
teach.body:
Normal tissues possess an intrinsic drive to obliterate tracks through granulation tissue formation, collagen synthesis, and scar contraction. When a sinus or fistula persists beyond several weeks, a definitive pathological barrier exists.

Surgical intervention succeeds only when this underlying cause is identified and eradicated. Superficial cautery or dressing changes are futile as long as the primary inciting factor remains in the depth.

rows: Retained silk stitch, mesh, bone sequestrum
Bowel stricture distal to enterocutaneous fistula

teach.heading: Additional mechanical and biological factors
teach.body:
Lack of physical rest prevents wound edges from adhering. Persistent movement over a joint, or continuous contraction of the anal sphincter in fistula-in-ano, repeatedly tears delicate advancing granulation buds.

Dense surrounding fibrous tissue, as seen in chronic empyema thoracis, prevents the rigid cavity walls from collapsing together. Finally, high-pressure outflow of irritant digestive juices continually washes away healing fibrin seals.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.annex.surg.goodsall_rule.title: Goodsall rule for fistula-in-ano
skill.annex.surg.goodsall_rule.oneLine: Anterior straight versus posterior curved tracks in relation to the transverse anal line
skill.annex.surg.goodsall_rule.why: Goodsall rule predicts the course of the fistulous track from the position of the external perianal opening. Anticipating a curved posterior midline track or a straight radial anterior track guides surgical lay-open or seton placement and protects sphincter integrity.
skill.annex.surg.goodsall_rule.practice: Draw the anal verge with a transverse horizontal line passing through the center of the anus. Plot anterior and posterior external openings, and draw the expected tracks according to Goodsall rule, including the major exception.
pitfalls: Applying Goodsall rule to patients with Crohn disease, where tracks are notoriously atypical, multiple, and complex.
Overlooking the exception: an anterior opening situated more than 3.75 cm (1.5 inches) from the anal verge usually curves to the posterior midline.
Cutting directly toward the anus from an anterior opening without verifying whether the track is an exception.
Failing to perform digital rectal examination to verify the true location of the internal opening at the dentate line.

probes.q: State the classical Goodsall rule for anal fistulae with posterior external openings.
probes.a: If the external opening lies posterior to a transverse line bisecting the anus, the fistulous track usually curves around to enter the anal canal in the posterior midline at the 6 o'clock position.

probes.q: State the classical Goodsall rule for anal fistulae with anterior external openings.
probes.a: If the external opening lies anterior to the transverse anal line, the fistulous track usually runs directly in a straight radial direction into the anal canal at the corresponding clock position.

probes.q: What is the classic exception to Goodsall rule regarding anterior external openings?
probes.a: An anterior external opening situated more than 3.75 cm (1.5 inches) from the anal verge does not run radially straight; it curves backward to enter the anal canal in the posterior midline.

rubric.text: Identifies the transverse horizontal line through the anal canal as the reference axis
Describes curved course of posterior tracks entering the posterior midline
Describes straight radial course of anterior tracks entering directly
States the 3.75 cm distance exception for anterior openings accurately

teach.heading: Anatomical principles of Goodsall rule
teach.body:
Goodsall rule provides an empirical anatomical guide to the path of a fistula-in-ano. Imagine a transverse horizontal line bisecting the anal canal with the patient in the lithotomy position.

The location of the external skin opening relative to this transverse line predicts whether the fistulous track takes a direct radial course or curves backward into the posterior midline crypt at the 6 o'clock position.

teach.heading: Summary of Goodsall rule and its exception
Surgical relevance and precautions
teach.body:
Understanding Goodsall rule prevents false passage creation during operative probing. In a posterior opening, advancing a rigid straight probe directly into the anus tears the external sphincter.

The surgeon must use a flexible malleable probe curved to match the natural arc toward the posterior midline. In Crohn disease or recurrent complex fistulae, MRI fistulography is mandatory because atypical anatomy renders clinical rules unreliable.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.surg.pvd_claudication_restpain.title: Arterial claudication and rest pain
skill.hx.surg.pvd_claudication_restpain.oneLine: Quantify walking distance, identify the anatomical level of pain, and screen for critical rest pain
skill.hx.surg.pvd_claudication_restpain.why: Intermittent claudication indicates muscular ischemia on exercise, while rest pain signals critical limb-threatening ischemia where microvascular perfusion fails even basal metabolic needs. Confusing claudication with venous heaviness or spinal pseudoclaudication leads to delayed revascularization or inappropriate spinal surgery.

asks.text: What exact distance can you walk on level ground before the pain starts, and does it compel you to stop?
Where is the pain felt: foot arch, calf, thigh, or buttock, and does it disappear within minutes of standing still?
Do you have severe pain in the toes or foot at night that wakes you from sleep and improves when you hang the foot over the edge of the bed?
Have you noticed skin colour changes, coldness, tingling, numbness, or slow-healing sores on the toes?
What is your smoking history, including cigarettes or bidis per day and years of use, and do you have diabetes, hypertension, or heart disease?
In men with bilateral buttock claudication, do you experience difficulty achieving or maintaining an erection (Leriche syndrome)?

skill.hx.surg.pvd_claudication_restpain.practice: Rehearse taking a vascular history from a colleague, mapping the anatomical site of claudication to the occluded arterial segment and differentiating nocturnal ischemic rest pain from muscle cramps and spinal canal stenosis.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about rest pain and nocturnal leg dependency, which are cardinal markers of critical limb-threatening ischemia.
Confusing spinal pseudoclaudication (relieved by sitting or spine flexion) with true vascular claudication (relieved by standing still).
Not quantifying claudication distance against fixed objective landmarks such as city blocks, lamp posts, or metres.

rubric.text: Quantifies initial claudication distance and absolute walking tolerance
Localises pain to specific muscle compartments to predict the level of arterial stenosis
Screens specifically for nocturnal rest pain, burning character, and relief on dependency
Documents smoking burden (pack-years or bidis/day), diabetes, hypertension, and coronary disease

probes.q: What defines vascular intermittent claudication?
probes.a: Ischemic muscle pain brought on by a constant amount of exercise and rapidly relieved within minutes by standing still without sitting down.

probes.q: How does vascular claudication differ from neurogenic pseudoclaudication due to lumbar spinal stenosis?
probes.a: Vascular claudication occurs at a constant walking distance and is relieved by standing still, whereas neurogenic pseudoclaudication is variable, aggravated by walking downhill or standing erect, and relieved only by bending forward or sitting down.

probes.q: Why does ischemic rest pain worsen when the patient is lying flat in bed and improve when hanging the leg over the edge?
probes.a: Lying flat removes the hydrostatic pressure column of gravity, reducing capillary perfusion pressure across severe arterial stenosis below the critical closing threshold; dependency adds hydrostatic pressure and improves distal microvascular blood flow.

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of claudication and rest pain
teach.body: Intermittent claudication occurs when arterial blood flow is adequate at rest but cannot increase to meet the metabolic demands of contracting muscle. Accumulation of lactic acid and ischemic metabolites in muscle beds stimulates sensory nerve endings, producing an aching cramp that compels the patient to halt. Standing still allows blood flow to clear metabolites within two to five minutes.

teach.heading: Ischemic rest pain as the cry of dying nerves
teach.body: Rest pain indicates critical limb ischemia. Capillary perfusion pressure falls below thirty millimetres of mercury, depriving sensory nerve endings of oxygen even at basal metabolic rates. Pain is severe, burning, worse at night when cardiac output and limb elevation drop perfusion pressure, and compels patients to sleep in a chair with the limb dependent.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.pvd_inspection.title: Inspection of the ischemic limb
skill.exam.surg.pvd_inspection.oneLine: Inspect limb colour, trophic skin changes, guttered veins, and the characteristics of dry versus wet gangrene
skill.exam.surg.pvd_inspection.why: Visual inspection provides immediate clues to the chronicity and severity of arterial insufficiency. Missing shiny atrophic skin, hair loss, nail dystrophies, guttered dorsal veins, or an unheralded necrotic toe leads to underestimating limb threat until irreversible gangrene occurs.

steps.text: Position the patient supine in good natural light with both lower extremities fully exposed from groin to toes.
Compare the colour of both limbs side by side, observing for cadaveric pallor, mottled cyanosis, or dependent rubor.
Inspect skin texture, noting thinning, loss of subcutaneous tissue, dryness from sympathetic denervation, and loss of hair over the digits, dorsum of foot, and lower third of leg.
Examine the toenails for transverse ridges, thickening, brittleness, and fungal dystrophy (onychomycosis).
Inspect veins on the dorsum of the foot to observe whether they are flat and empty (guttered veins) when the limb is resting horizontally.
Inspect between all web spaces and beneath the heels for ischemic fissures, punched-out ulcers with pale dry bases, or blackened necrotic tissue.
Note the characteristics of any gangrene present: dry and mummified versus wet, swollen, foul-smelling, and spreading.

skill.exam.surg.pvd_inspection.normal: Healthy pink skin colour matching the contralateral limb, normal hair distribution, smooth pliable skin, flat but non-guttered dorsal veins, and intact nail plates.
skill.exam.surg.pvd_inspection.abnormal: Cadaveric pallor or dusky cyanosis, guttered dorsal veins, loss of hair, thin shiny parchment skin, brittle ridged nails, and black necrotic mummified or purulent digits.
skill.exam.surg.pvd_inspection.significance: Guttered dorsal veins and dependent rubor indicate severe microvascular collapse. Dry gangrene reflects pure chronic ischemia with tissue mummification, whereas wet gangrene indicates secondary bacterial infection with tissue liquefaction, demanding urgent surgical decompression.
skill.exam.surg.pvd_inspection.practice: Practise systematic inspection of the lower limbs on clinical rounds, documenting skin changes, hair distribution, dorsal vein filling, and web space integrity in patients with diabetes or suspected peripheral vascular disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking the purplish-red discoloration of dependent rubor for adequate warmth or good circulation.
Failing to separate the toes and inspect the interdigital web spaces and plantar pressure points for occult necrosis.
Overlooking guttered dorsal veins while the patient is supine, which is an unmistakable sign of severe arterial hypoperfusion.

rubric.text: Exposes both lower limbs completely from groin to toes in good illumination
Systematically compares colour, trophic changes, and hair distribution between both limbs
Inspects dorsal foot veins for guttering and collapse in the supine position
Inspects interdigital web spaces, pressure points, and nail beds for occult ulceration or necrosis

probes.q: What causes the dependent rubor observed in an ischemic foot?
probes.a: Paralysis of precapillary arterioles due to chronic severe hypoxia, causing maximal vasodilatation so that on dependency, unoxygenated blood pools in dilated cutaneous capillary beds.

probes.q: How do dry gangrene and wet gangrene differ clinically?
probes.a: Dry gangrene is dry, shrivelled, black, mummified, and sterile with a clear line of demarcation; wet gangrene is swollen, edematous, putrid, moist, rapidly spreading, and infected without a clear line of demarcation.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of guttered veins on the dorsum of the foot in a supine patient?
probes.a: It indicates that arterial inflow is so critically diminished that resting perfusion pressure cannot even keep the superficial venous capillaries filled, representing advanced critical limb ischemia.

teach.heading: Trophic signs of chronic tissue ischemia
teach.body: Severe chronic ischemia starves dermal and epidermal appendages of essential nutrients. This produces classical trophic changes: thinning of skin to a fragile parchment-like texture, loss of hair follicles over the dorsum of foot and lower tibia, brittle ridged nails, and wasting of subcutaneous fat pads, exposing underlying extensor tendons and bones.

rows: Pure arterial occlusion with tissue desiccation
Arterial or venous occlusion with bacterial superinfection
Sharp line of demarcation between living and dead tissue
Poorly defined margin with proximal erythema and cellulitis
Keep dry, protect from trauma, elective amputation
Emergency surgical debridement or amputation with IV antibiotics

teach.heading: Significance of guttered veins
teach.body: In a healthy person lying flat, superficial veins on the dorsum of the foot contain blood and appear rounded. In severe peripheral arterial disease, resting blood flow drops so low that blood drains completely, leaving dorsal veins collapsed into sunken linear grooves termed guttered veins. This is an ominous bedside sign of critical ischemia.

skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.title: Palpation of lower extremity arterial pulses
skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.oneLine: Systematically palpate and grade femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally
skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.why: Accurate palpation of all lower extremity arterial pulses maps the precise level of occlusive disease from the aorta to the foot. Mistaking the examiner's own digital pulse for the patient's, or misidentifying the dorsalis pedis artery, leads to erroneous diagnostic and revascularization plans.

steps.text: Position the patient supine, relaxed, and warm with clothing removed to expose the abdomen and both lower extremities.
Palpate the femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point (midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis), compressing the artery against the femoral head with two fingers.

Palpate the popliteal artery with the patient supine: flex the knee to forty to sixty degrees with the heel resting on the couch, place both thumbs in front of the patella, curl the fingers of both hands into the popliteal fossa, and press against the upper posterior surface of the tibia.
If the popliteal pulse is difficult to feel, turn the patient prone, flex the knee to ninety degrees to relax the popliteal fascia, and compress the neurovascular bundle in the midline of the fossa.
Palpate the posterior tibial pulse midway between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon, using the pulps of the index and middle fingers curving gently behind the medial malleolus.

Palpate the dorsalis pedis pulse on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon over the tarsal bones, having the patient actively extend the great toe to identify the tendon landmark.
If a pulse feels doubtful or absent, verify that you are not feeling your own pulse by simultaneously checking your own radial pulse or having a colleague cross-check.

skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.normal: Bilateral, strong, synchronous femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses with normal vessel wall compressibility.
skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.abnormal: Diminished or absent pulses below an arterial occlusion, expansile pulsatile swelling indicating an aneurysm, or palpable vessel wall calcification.
skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.significance: A palpable femoral pulse with absent distal pulses localises occlusion to the superficial femoral artery. An absent femoral pulse indicates aortoiliac disease. Absence of dorsalis pedis can occur as a normal anatomical variant in eight to ten percent of individuals, but absent posterior tibial pulse is almost always pathological.
skill.exam.surg.arterial_pulses_lower.practice: Practise palpating the popliteal pulse bimanually in supine and prone positions on multiple colleagues, and confirm the exact anatomical relationship of the dorsalis pedis to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.
pitfalls: Mistaking the examiner's own digital pulsation for a faint patient pulse; eliminate this by cross-checking your own radial pulse.
Searching for the dorsalis pedis artery too far distally beyond the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space.
Attempting to palpate the popliteal pulse with the knee in full extension, which stretches the deep fascia and prevents compression of the artery against the tibia.

rubric.text: Palpates femoral artery accurately at the mid-inguinal point against the femoral head
Palpates popliteal artery bimanually with knee relaxed in flexion
Palpates posterior tibial artery midway between medial malleolus and Achilles tendon
Identifies extensor hallucis longus tendon and palpates dorsalis pedis just lateral to it
Systematically compares pulse volume and symmetry between both limbs

probes.q: Where is the mid-inguinal point located for femoral artery palpation?
probes.a: Midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.

probes.q: Why is the dorsalis pedis pulse sometimes absent in a healthy person without arterial disease?
probes.a: The dorsalis pedis artery is congenitally absent or replaced by the perforating branch of the peroneal artery in about eight to ten percent of healthy individuals.

probes.q: What is the disappearing pulse sign and what does it indicate?
probes.a: A peripheral pulse that is palpable at rest but disappears immediately after the patient exercises to the point of claudication; it indicates hemodynamically significant proximal arterial stenosis unmasked by exercise-induced peripheral vasodilatation.

teach.heading: Surface anatomy and landmarks of the lower limb arteries
teach.body: The femoral artery emerges beneath the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis (not the midpoint of the inguinal ligament). The popliteal artery runs deep in the popliteal fossa between the condyles. The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus, and the dorsalis pedis lies lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

teach.heading: Stepwise technique for popliteal palpation
points: Flex the patient's knee to forty to sixty degrees with the foot resting flat on the examining couch.
Place both hands around the knee with thumbs resting on the patella and fingertips meeting in the midline of the popliteal fossa.
Press the pulps of the middle fingers firmly anteriorly against the posterior surface of the tibial condyles.
If negative, roll the patient into the prone position, flex the knee to ninety degrees to relax the deep fascia, and palpate the neurovascular bundle.

rows: Complete occlusion of the feeding arterial trunk
Significant proximal stenosis or collateral reconstitution
Unobstructed proximal and local arterial lumen
Arteriomegaly, aneurysm, or wide pulse pressure

skill.exam.surg.buerger_postural_test.title: Buerger's postural test and capillary refilling
skill.exam.surg.buerger_postural_test.oneLine: Elicit postural colour changes to determine Buerger's vascular angle and assess microvascular refilling times
skill.exam.surg.buerger_postural_test.why: Buerger's test is the definitive bedside provocative test for chronic lower limb ischemia. It quantifies the degree of arterial compromise through the vascular angle and verifies the functional microvascular capacity upon dependency. Omitting it misses subtle but critical ischemia in limbs with borderline resting pulses.

steps.text: Position the patient supine in broad daylight or good artificial illumination.
Elevate both lower limbs with knees straight to an angle of forty-five to ninety degrees for one to two minutes, supporting the heels.
If pallor does not develop immediately, have the patient actively dorsiflex and plantarflex the ankles repeatedly to the point of muscular fatigue.
Observe the soles of the feet: note the angle of elevation at which cadaveric pallor appears (Buerger's vascular angle) and whether dorsal veins become collapsed and guttered.
Lower the legs and ask the patient to sit up with both legs hanging down over the edge of the examining couch.
Record the capillary filling time: the time required for the blanched pale skin of the toes and foot to turn pink upon dependency.
Record the venous refilling time: the time taken for the empty dorsal foot veins to bulge and become prominent.
Observe for the subsequent appearance of a striking dark purplish-red discoloration (dependent rubor or sunset foot).

skill.exam.surg.buerger_postural_test.normal: Limbs remain pink even on elevation to ninety degrees; on dependency, pink skin colour returns within ten seconds and superficial veins refill within ten to fifteen seconds without dependent rubor.
skill.exam.surg.buerger_postural_test.abnormal: Cadaveric pallor appearing at an elevation angle under thirty degrees (vascular angle under thirty degrees indicates severe ischemia), capillary filling time prolonged beyond twenty to thirty seconds, and development of intense dependent cyanotic rubor.
skill.exam.surg.buerger_postural_test.significance: A vascular angle of less than twenty to thirty degrees indicates critical limb-threatening ischemia. Dependent rubor reflects blood pooling in dilated, paralyzed capillary beds. Delayed venous refilling beyond twenty seconds confirms severe reduction in arterial inflow.
skill.exam.surg.buerger_postural_test.practice: Practise performing Buerger's test on healthy volunteers and vascular patients, documenting the vascular angle and timing capillary and venous refilling times with a stopwatch.
pitfalls: Performing the test in poor lighting, which prevents accurate detection of early sole pallor.
Misinterpreting the intense redness of dependent rubor as healthy perfusion rather than capillary vasomotor paralysis.
Failing to exercise the ankles during elevation when resting pallor is equivocal.

rubric.text: Elevates legs with straight knees and supports limbs adequately
Determines Buerger's vascular angle of pallor accurately
Instructs patient to flex and extend ankles to unmask latent ischemia
Places patient in sitting position with legs dependent and times capillary and venous filling
Recognises and correctly interprets the development of dependent rubor

probes.q: What is Buerger's vascular angle of elevation?
probes.a: The angle between the elevated limb and the horizontal examining bed at which cadaveric pallor appears in the foot.

probes.q: What does a Buerger's angle of less than thirty degrees indicate?
probes.a: Severe arterial ischemia and critical limb threat.

probes.q: Why do superficial veins take longer to refill upon dependency in an ischemic limb?
probes.a: Venous refilling depends entirely on arterial inflow entering the microvasculature; when feeding arteries are occluded, blood trickles slowly through high-resistance collaterals, delaying venous filling.

teach.heading: Physiology of Buerger's postural test
teach.body: Gravity acts against arterial perfusion pressure. In a healthy limb, systolic pressure is sufficient to drive blood into dermal capillaries even against a ninety degree vertical column of hydrostatic pressure. In an ischemic limb with stenosed or occluded arteries, perfusion pressure cannot overcome gravity, causing blood to drain rapidly from capillaries and leaving the sole chalky pale.

teach.heading: Capillary and venous refilling sequence
teach.body: When an ischemic limb is lowered into dependency, oxygen-depleted blood slowly creeps into dilated capillaries. Normal pink colour returns within ten seconds, but in severe ischemia it requires twenty to thirty seconds. Veins that normally refill within ten to fifteen seconds take over thirty to forty-five seconds to rise above skin level, confirming severe reduction in inflow.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.upper_limb_vascular.title: Upper limb vascular and thoracic outlet examination
skill.exam.surg.upper_limb_vascular.oneLine: Assess upper limb pulses, confirm palmar arch patency with Allen's test, and elicit thoracic outlet compression signs
skill.exam.surg.upper_limb_vascular.why: Upper limb ischemia, though less common than lower limb disease, occurs in thoracic outlet syndrome, Raynaud's phenomenon, subclavian steal, and thromboangiitis obliterans. Palmar arch patency must also be proven before radial artery cannulation or harvesting to prevent iatrogenic digital gangrene.

steps.text: Palpate the subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial, and ulnar pulses sequentially and compare bilateral pulse volumes.
Perform Allen's test: instruct the patient to clench the fist tightly for thirty seconds while you compress both radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist with your thumbs.
Have the patient open the hand without hyperextending the fingers: observe the blanched, pale palm.
Release pressure from the ulnar artery while maintaining firm occlusion of the radial artery: observe whether pink colour flushes across the entire palm within five to seven seconds.
Repeat the procedure, releasing the radial artery while keeping the ulnar artery occluded, to verify radial arch patency.

Perform Adson's test: feel the radial pulse with the patient sitting upright, have the patient take a full deep inspiration, extend the neck, and turn the chin toward the affected side; observe for pulse obliteration or subclavian bruit.
Perform the costoclavicular manoeuvre: palpate the radial pulse while the patient braces the shoulders downwards and backwards into an exaggerated military posture.

Perform the elevated arm stress test: have the patient abduct both arms to ninety degrees with elbows flexed to ninety degrees and open and close the hands slowly for three minutes, noting early ischemic pain, paresthesias, or arm dropping.

skill.exam.surg.upper_limb_vascular.normal: Bilateral equal pulses throughout; Allen's test shows full palmar flush within five to seven seconds from both arteries; thoracic outlet tests do not produce ischemic arm pain or premature fatigue.
skill.exam.surg.upper_limb_vascular.abnormal: Asymmetrical or absent pulses, palmar pallor persisting beyond ten seconds during Allen's test (incomplete palmar arch), obliteration of radial pulse on Adson's test, and inability to maintain elevated arm exercise for three minutes.
skill.exam.surg.upper_limb_vascular.significance: A positive Allen's test (delayed ulnar refill) contraindicates radial artery cannulation or harvest. Adson's and costoclavicular signs suggest neurovascular compression at the thoracic outlet (cervical rib, scalenus anticus, or first rib compression).
skill.exam.surg.upper_limb_vascular.practice: Practise Allen's test on multiple colleagues, timing palmar reperfusion with a stopwatch, and practise palpating the radial pulse during Adson's and costoclavicular manoeuvres.
pitfalls: Hyperextending the fingers during Allen's test, which stretches palmar fascia and causes false-positive pallor.
Assuming pulse reduction on Adson's test alone is diagnostic without corresponding symptoms, as pulse dampening can occur in healthy people.
Cannulating a radial artery without performing or documenting a prior Allen's test.

rubric.text: Palpates radial, ulnar, brachial, and subclavian pulses bilaterally
Completely occludes both radial and ulnar arteries while fist is clenched
Releases ulnar artery and observes palmar reperfusion time
Performs Adson's manoeuvre with deep inspiration, neck extension, and head rotation
Executes elevated arm stress test to screen for thoracic outlet neurovascular fatigue

probes.q: What is the primary clinical indication for performing Allen's test before arterial puncture?
probes.a: To verify that the ulnar artery provides adequate collateral flow through the palmar arches to maintain hand viability if the radial artery becomes occluded.

probes.q: How is Adson's test performed for suspected cervical rib or scalenus anticus syndrome?
probes.a: The radial pulse is palpated while the patient takes a deep breath, extends the neck, and rotates the head toward the affected side; diminution or obliteration of the pulse suggests subclavian artery compression.

probes.q: Why is a pulse dampening on Adson's test alone not considered definitive proof of thoracic outlet syndrome?
probes.a: Diminution or obliteration of the radial pulse during Adson's manoeuvre occurs in up to ten to fifteen percent of normal healthy individuals without any anatomical abnormality.

teach.heading: Vascular anatomy of the palmar arches
teach.body: The hand receives dual arterial inflow from the radial and ulnar arteries, which anastomose through the deep and superficial palmar arches. In approximately eighty percent of individuals, the superficial arch formed predominantly by the ulnar artery is complete. In twenty percent, it is incomplete, meaning occlusion or cannulation of the radial artery can cause devastating ischemic necrosis of digits.

rows: Scalenus anticus spasm or cervical rib
Radial pulse attenuation with subclavian systolic bruit
Compression between clavicle and first rib
Pulse dampening in exaggerated military backward shoulder bracing
Loss of radial pulse when arm is passively hyperabducted beyond 90 degrees
Inability to open and close hands above shoulder for 3 minutes

teach.heading: Raynaud's phenomenon in the upper limb
teach.body: Raynaud's phenomenon represents paroxysmal digital vasospasm triggered by cold exposure or emotional stress. The classical triphasic attack consists of: local syncope (blanching and dead-white digits from digital artery spasm), local asphyxia (dusky cyanosis from sluggish capillary deoxygenation), and local recovery (reactive rubor and throbbing pain from reactive hyperemia).

skill.ix.surg.abpi.title: Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI)
skill.ix.surg.abpi.oneLine: Measure systolic pressures with Doppler and cuff to calculate and interpret the ankle-brachial ratio
skill.ix.surg.abpi.why: Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) is the primary non-invasive hemodynamic measurement for diagnosing and staging peripheral arterial disease. Applying compression bandages or undertaking ulcer debridement without knowing the ABPI risks causing acute arterial necrosis in an unsuspected ischemic limb.

steps.text: Position the patient supine and resting comfortably in a warm room for at least ten minutes before measurement.

Place an appropriately sized blood pressure cuff around the upper arm, locate the brachial pulse using a five to eight megahertz Doppler ultrasound probe angled at forty-five to sixty degrees against blood flow, and measure the brachial systolic pressure in both arms.
Use the higher of the two brachial systolic pressures as the systemic reference denominator.
Place the blood pressure cuff smoothly around the lower calf just above the malleoli.

Apply acoustic gel and identify the dorsalis pedis arterial Doppler signal; inflate the cuff twenty to thirty millimetres of mercury above pulse disappearance, deflate slowly at two millimetres per second, and record the pressure when the Doppler signal reappears.
Identify the posterior tibial arterial Doppler signal behind the medial malleolus and record its systolic opening pressure in the same manner.
Select the higher of the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressures as the numerator for that leg.
Calculate ABPI by dividing the higher ankle pressure of that limb by the higher of the two brachial systolic pressures.

skill.ix.surg.abpi.practice: Practise measuring Doppler pressures in both arms and both ankles on peers and clinical patients, mastering probe angling at forty-five to sixty degrees, gel application, and ratio calculation.
pitfalls: Using a regular stethoscope instead of a continuous-wave Doppler probe, which makes distal pulse detection in low-flow states impossible.
Using the lower brachial pressure as the denominator, which falsely inflates the calculated ABPI.
Misinterpreting an ABPI greater than 1.3 to 1.4 as normal circulation rather than recognizing medial arterial calcification (Monckeberg sclerosis).

rubric.text: Ensures patient rests supine for ten minutes prior to measurement
Measures systolic pressures in both arms with Doppler and selects the higher value
Measures both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial systolic pressures in the target ankle
Calculates ABPI correctly as higher ankle pressure divided by higher brachial pressure
Correctly categorises ABPI value into normal, mild, moderate, severe, or calcified vessels

probes.q: How is the ankle-brachial pressure index calculated?
probes.a: By dividing the highest systolic pressure measured at the ankle (dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial) by the highest brachial systolic pressure measured between the two arms.

probes.q: What does an ABPI of 0.35 in a diabetic patient with a foot ulcer indicate?
probes.a: Critical limb-threatening ischemia with severe arterial insufficiency, indicating that the ulcer will not heal without revascularization and that compression therapy is strictly contraindicated.

probes.q: A patient with long-standing diabetes has an ABPI of 1.45. How should this be interpreted?
probes.a: The vessels are artificially incompressible due to medial arterial calcification (Monckeberg arteriosclerosis); the reading is falsely elevated and does not exclude severe distal ischemia, requiring toe-brachial index or duplex scanning.

teach.heading: Principles of Doppler blood pressure measurement
teach.body: The ankle-brachial pressure index compares systolic blood pressure in the ankle with systemic pressure in the arm. In a healthy resting supine person, ankle systolic pressure is slightly higher than brachial pressure due to pulse wave reflection and arterial compliance, giving a normal ABPI of 1.00 to 1.29. Significant stenoses cause a systolic pressure drop downstream.

rows: Adequate flow, compression bandaging safe if indicated
Moderate to severe claudication, vascular referral indicated
Rest pain, ulceration, tissue loss; urgent revascularization needed
Medial sclerosis in diabetes or renal failure; measure toe pressures

teach.heading: Safety rules in compression therapy
teach.body: Before applying therapeutic compression bandages for venous leg ulcers or lymphedema, an ABPI must be measured. If the ABPI is below 0.80, standard high-compression bandaging (forty millimetres of mercury) is unsafe and can trigger acute arterial necrosis or gangrene. For ABPI values between 0.50 and 0.80, only modified reduced-compression bandaging can be considered under specialist vascular supervision.

skill.annex.surg.fontaine_rutherford.title: Fontaine and Rutherford staging of chronic limb ischemia
skill.annex.surg.fontaine_rutherford.oneLine: Clinical staging classifications correlating symptom severity with objective hemodynamic thresholds
skill.annex.surg.fontaine_rutherford.why: Fontaine and Rutherford staging systems provide standardized clinical classifications used globally to communicate disease severity, guide treatment decisions between supervised exercise and surgical bypass or angioplasty, and assess outcomes in peripheral vascular disease.

rows: Normal resting exam, ABPI 0.90 or reduced post-exercise
Moderate to severe claudication, walking distance < 200 m
Ischemic rest pain (nocturnal, relieved by dependency)
Ankle pressure < 50 mmHg, toe pressure < 30 mmHg, ABPI < 0.40
Tissue loss (ischemic ulceration or frank gangrene)
Ankle pressure < 50 mmHg, toe pressure < 30 mmHg, unhealing tissue defect

skill.annex.surg.fontaine_rutherford.practice: Classify five clinical vignettes of lower extremity vascular patients into their exact Fontaine stages and Rutherford categories, stating whether critical limb-threatening ischemia criteria are met.
pitfalls: Failing to separate Fontaine stage II into IIa (> 200 metres) and IIb (< 200 metres), which determines whether surgical intervention is indicated.
Misclassifying ischemic rest pain as claudication because the patient also complains of walking difficulty.
Omitting the distinction between minor tissue loss (Rutherford 5) and major gangrene extending above the transmetatarsal level (Rutherford 6).

rubric.text: Distinguishes asymptomatic, claudication, rest pain, and tissue loss stages
Applies 200-metre threshold to separate Fontaine stage IIa from IIb
Identifies Fontaine stages III and IV as critical limb-threatening ischemia

probes.q: What defines Fontaine Stage IIb peripheral arterial disease?
probes.a: Intermittent claudication occurring after walking less than two hundred metres on level ground.

probes.q: Which Fontaine stages constitute critical limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI)?
probes.a: Fontaine Stage III (ischemic rest pain) and Fontaine Stage IV (ischemic ulceration or gangrene).

probes.q: Why is the two hundred metre walking distance threshold clinically pivotal in Fontaine staging?
probes.a: Patients with claudication distance greater than two hundred metres (Stage IIa) generally maintain social independence and respond well to supervised exercise and cilostazol, whereas walking distance under two hundred metres (Stage IIb) significantly impairs daily living and frequently warrants revascularization.

teach.heading: Historical evolution of limb ischemia classifications
teach.body: Rene Fontaine introduced his four-stage clinical classification in the mid-twentieth century based on bedside symptoms. Robert Rutherford refined this in subsequent surgical consensus by adding objective physiological criteria (treadmill distances and Doppler pressures) and subdividing tissue loss into minor non-healing ulceration and major gangrene extending past the transmetatarsal level.

teach.heading: Defining critical limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI)
teach.body: Critical limb-threatening ischemia (Fontaine III or IV, Rutherford 4 to 6) is defined by chronic ischemic rest pain persisting for more than two weeks, or ischemic ulceration or gangrene, associated with an ankle systolic pressure under fifty millimetres of mercury or toe systolic pressure under thirty millimetres of mercury. Without urgent revascularization, major limb loss is imminent.

teach.heading: Clinical management stratified by stage
points: Fontaine Stage I: Lifestyle modification, statin therapy, antiplatelet agent, risk factor control.
Fontaine Stage IIa: Supervised exercise therapy, cilostazol, smoking cessation; surgery rarely required.
Fontaine Stage IIb: Supervised exercise trial; endovascular or surgical bypass if disabling and refractory.
Fontaine Stage III and IV: Urgent vascular surgical consult, diagnostic imaging, and urgent revascularization.

skill.hx.surg.varicose_veins.title: History of varicose veins and venous insufficiency
skill.hx.surg.varicose_veins.oneLine: Elicit heaviness, evening swelling, cramps, skin changes, bleeding risk, and deep vein thrombosis history
skill.hx.surg.varicose_veins.why: Varicose vein history distinguishes primary superficial venous incompetence from secondary hypertension caused by deep vein thrombosis or pelvic masses. Operating on secondary varicosities with deep venous obstruction destroys the essential collateral return and can cause limb-threatening venous gangrene.

asks.text: What symptoms trouble you most: aching heaviness, tiredness, throbbing, evening swelling, or cosmetic embarrassment?
Does the discomfort worsen after prolonged standing or at the end of the day, and does elevation of the leg or walking bring relief?
Have you experienced sudden severe pain or swelling in the whole leg in the past (deep vein thrombosis), particularly after surgery, trauma, childbirth, or prolonged travel?
Have you noticed skin darkening, hardening, itching, eczema, or an open sore around your ankle?
Have you ever had profuse bleeding from a burst vein, or episodes of painful, red, hard lumps along the veins (superficial thrombophlebitis)?
In women, ask about previous pregnancies, whether veins appeared or worsened during pregnancy, and use of oral contraceptive pills.

skill.hx.surg.varicose_veins.practice: Take a structured venous history from a partner, systematically distinguishing primary uncomplicated varices from chronic venous insufficiency with deep venous pathology.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about past deep vein thrombosis, which changes management from simple ablation to deep vein investigation.
Omitting questions about sudden profuse venous hemorrhage, which requires immediate patient education on leg elevation and direct pressure.
Attributing joint or radicular nerve pain to visible minor spider veins without verifying whether the pain improves with leg elevation.

rubric.text: Identifies cardinal symptoms: aching, heaviness, evening swelling, and nocturnal cramps
Confirms that pain worsens on dependent standing and improves on leg elevation
Specifically screens for past deep vein thrombosis, pelvic surgery, and contraceptive use
Asks about episodes of superficial thrombophlebitis, bleeding, skin changes, and ulceration

probes.q: Why does the aching pain of varicose veins worsen at the end of the day and improve on leg elevation?
probes.a: Prolonged standing increases hydrostatic venous hypertension in incompetent superficial veins, stretching vein walls and pooling blood; elevation uses gravity to drain blood and reduce venous pressure.

probes.q: Why is a past history of deep vein thrombosis crucial before planning varicose vein surgery?
probes.a: If deep veins remain chronically occluded or damaged, the dilated superficial veins act as the primary collateral drainage of the limb; stripping them can produce severe venous congestion and phlegmasia.

probes.q: What is the emergency first-aid management if a large thin-walled varicosity ruptures and bleeds profusely?
probes.a: Immediately lie the patient flat, elevate the bleeding leg well above the level of the heart, and apply firm direct pressure with a clean pad and bandage; a tourniquet should not be used.

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of ambulatory venous hypertension
teach.body: In a healthy person, muscular contractions of the calf pump blood upward through deep veins, while competent bicuspid valves prevent retrograde reflux, reducing venous pressure from ninety to twenty millimetres of mercury. In varicose veins, defective or destroyed valves allow blood to reflux back into superficial veins on standing, creating chronic ambulatory venous hypertension that transmits high pressure to dermal capillary beds.

rows: Idiopathic weakness of vein wall and valvular cusps
Post-thrombotic syndrome, pelvic tumour, AV fistula
Occluded, recanalised with destroyed valves, or compressed
Greatly relieved by elevation and elastic stockings
Often persists as bursting calf pain during walking
Safe for endovenous ablation or surgical stripping
Ablation contraindicated if deep veins are non-functional

teach.heading: Dermatological sequelae of chronic venous disease
teach.body: High capillary hydrostatic pressure forces red blood cells into dermal tissues, where extravasated erythrocytes lyse and release hemosiderin pigment, producing brown staining (gaiter zone stasis hyperpigmentation). Extravasated fibrinogen polymerises into pericapillary fibrin cuffs that impede oxygen diffusion. Chronic subcutaneous fat necrosis and fibrosis produce a rigid wooden cuff termed lipodermatosclerosis.

skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.title: Examination of varicose veins: inspection and palpation
skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.oneLine: Examine the standing patient for saphenous distributions, saphena varix, blow-outs, and trophic skin changes
skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.why: Examining varicose veins with the patient lying down is a classic clinical error because collapsed veins hide incompetence. Systematic standing inspection and palpation define whether the long saphenous, short saphenous, or perforator systems are diseased, detect saphena varix, and identify pre-ulcerative trophic skin changes.

steps.text: Have the patient stand upright on a raised examination step with both lower extremities fully exposed from groin to toes.
Inspect the course of the great (long) saphenous vein from the medial malleolus, up the medial calf and knee, to the saphenofemoral junction in the groin.
Inspect the patient from behind to trace the small (short) saphenous vein from behind the lateral malleolus up the midline of the calf into the popliteal fossa.
Inspect for localized saccular bulges (perforator blow-outs) along the medial calf, mid-thigh, and lower thigh.
Inspect the medial groin four centimetres below and lateral to the pubic tubercle for a visible bulge (saphena varix).
Palpate the saphenofemoral junction while the patient coughs, noting any palpable fluid thrill or expansive cough impulse (Morrissey cough test).
Palpate along the course of the varicose veins with light fingertip pressure to detect fascial defects (Fegan pits) where incompetent perforators penetrate the deep fascia.

Inspect and palpate the gaiter area of the lower leg for pitting edema, stasis eczema, brown hemosiderin pigmentation, atrophie blanche, lipodermatosclerosis (inverted champagne bottle appearance), and active or healed venous ulcers.

Perform the Schwartz tap test: place the fingers of one hand over the saphenous opening in the groin and tap a distended varicosity in the lower leg with the other hand to feel a transmitted fluid wave.

skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.normal: No visible or palpable venous dilatation in the standing position; no saphenofemoral cough impulse, no fascial perforator pits, and healthy gaiter skin without pigmentation or induration.
skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.abnormal: Tortuous dilated long or short saphenous trunks, expansile saphena varix at the saphenofemoral junction, palpable fascial defects over perforators, and gaiter lipodermatosclerosis with venous ulceration.
skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.significance: Saphena varix confirms severe saphenofemoral junction valve incompetence. Palpable fascial pits localise incompetent perforators that pump high deep venous pressure into superficial veins. Inverted champagne bottle induration reflects advanced chronic venous insufficiency.
skill.exam.surg.varicose_inspection_palp.practice: Practise examining the standing lower limbs in the surgical outpatient clinic, tracing great and small saphenous anatomy, detecting fascial pits using Fegan's method, and eliciting Morrissey's cough impulse on a saphena varix.
pitfalls: Examining the patient only while lying flat on the couch, which collapses superficial veins and masks significant disease.
Mistaking a saphena varix for a femoral hernia: both present at the groin, but saphena varix disappears on lying down and produces a venous thrill on coughing.
Failing to examine the back of the calf, thereby missing small saphenous vein incompetence entering the popliteal fossa.

rubric.text: Examines the patient in the erect standing position with limbs fully exposed
Traces both great saphenous and small saphenous systems systematically
Examines the saphenous opening for saphena varix and elicits cough impulse
Palpates along the vein course for fascial defects to localise incompetent perforators
Documents presence of lipodermatosclerosis, pigmentation, eczema, and ulceration

probes.q: Why must a patient stand during the examination of varicose veins?
probes.a: Gravity fills the incompetent superficial veins with blood, making tortuosity, valvular incompetence, blow-outs, and saphena varix visible and palpable.

probes.q: How do you distinguish a saphena varix from a femoral hernia?
probes.a: Both lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with a cough impulse, but a saphena varix has a fluid thrill on coughing, empties immediately when the patient lies flat, and transmits a percussion tap wave from the lower leg (Schwartz test).

probes.q: What causes the inverted champagne bottle appearance of the lower leg in severe chronic venous disease?
probes.a: Severe circumferential subcutaneous fibrosis and lipodermatosclerosis around the lower calf and gaiter area constrict the ankle, while the upper calf remains swollen with edema or normal muscle mass.

teach.heading: Anatomy of the superficial and perforating veins
teach.body: The great saphenous vein originates in front of the medial malleolus, ascends the anteromedial calf and thigh, and pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening to enter the common femoral vein four centimetres below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. The small saphenous vein runs behind the lateral malleolus up the midline of the calf to enter the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.

rows: Connects femoral vein to great saphenous trunk
Frequent source of thigh varicosity recurrence
Upper medial calf (below medial knee joint line)
Connects posterior tibial veins to great saphenous
Medial ankle (5, 10, and 15 cm above medial malleolus)
Directly implicated in medial gaiter venous ulcers

teach.heading: Differentiating saphena varix from groin swellings
teach.body: A saphena varix is a saccular dilatation of the upper great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening. It presents as a soft, bluish swelling in the groin. Unlike a femoral hernia or psoas abscess, it is compressible, disappears completely when the patient lies down, gives a fluid thrill on coughing, and demonstrates an impulse when the calf varicosity is tapped (Schwartz test).

skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.title: Trendelenburg and tourniquet tests for venous incompetence
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.oneLine: Perform Brodie-Trendelenburg and multiple tourniquet tests to localise saphenofemoral and perforator incompetence
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.why: The Brodie-Trendelenburg and multiple tourniquet tests are classic clinical manoeuvres that pinpoint the exact anatomical site of venous reflux. Confusing saphenofemoral reflux with perforator leak leads to incomplete surgery and early varicosity recurrence.

steps.text: Position the patient supine and elevate the limb to sixty degrees to empty all blood from the superficial varicosities (milking gently proximally if needed).

Locate the saphenofemoral junction (four centimetres below and lateral to the pubic tubercle) and occlude it firmly with your thumb, or place a soft rubber tourniquet around the upper thigh just below the junction.
While maintaining continuous pressure over the saphenofemoral junction, instruct the patient to stand up quickly.

Observe the superficial veins for thirty seconds while pressure is maintained: if the varicosities fill rapidly from below, incompetent perforating veins are present (Trendelenburg positive for perforators).

If the veins remain collapsed and empty while the saphenofemoral junction is compressed, release the thumb pressure: if blood surges down from above and rapidly distends the veins, saphenofemoral junction valve incompetence is confirmed (Trendelenburg test positive for saphenofemoral incompetence).
Perform the multiple tourniquet test: elevate the limb to empty veins, then apply three tourniquets simultaneously (upper thigh below saphenofemoral junction, above the knee, and below the knee).
Have the patient stand: observe which venous segment fills between the tourniquets, thereby localising the level of the incompetent perforator.

skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.normal: Superficial veins remain collapsed upon standing while the junction is occluded, and fill only very slowly from below (after thirty seconds) via normal capillary bed drainage upon release.
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.abnormal: Rapid retrograde filling from above within two seconds of releasing saphenofemoral compression, or rapid filling from below within thirty seconds while the saphenofemoral junction is still compressed.
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.significance: Retrograde surge from above on release indicates saphenofemoral junction valve incompetence requiring flush ligation at the femoral vein. Rapid filling while compressed proves incompetent perforators (Hunterian, Dodd, Boyd, or Cockett) that require separate subfascial ligation or ablation.
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_tourniquet.practice: Practise performing the Brodie-Trendelenburg test with both thumb occlusion and rubber tourniquets on surgical patients, mastering rapid standing transitions and accurate observation of venous filling dynamics.
pitfalls: Applying the upper thigh tourniquet too tightly, which compresses the deep femoral vein and prevents normal deep venous return.
Applying pressure too low on the thigh, leaving the saphenofemoral junction unoccluded.
Releasing the thumb before observing whether filling occurs from below while the junction is occluded.

rubric.text: Elevates limb adequately to completely empty superficial veins before occlusion
Accurately occludes saphenofemoral junction four centimetres below and lateral to pubic tubercle
Observes for rapid filling from below while occlusion is maintained
Releases occlusion and observes for retrograde reflux from above
Correctly classifies test as showing saphenofemoral, perforator, or dual incompetence

probes.q: What does it mean if superficial veins fill rapidly from below while the saphenofemoral junction remains compressed during Trendelenburg testing?
probes.a: It indicates incompetence of communicating perforator veins between the deep and superficial systems, allowing retrograde flow into the superficial veins.

probes.q: What does a rapid surge of blood filling the varicosity from above immediately after releasing saphenofemoral compression demonstrate?
probes.a: Incompetence of the saphenofemoral junction valve, allowing retrograde reflux down the great saphenous vein from the common femoral vein.

probes.q: How does the multiple tourniquet test isolate the level of an incompetent thigh perforator?
probes.a: By placing tourniquets at the upper thigh, above the knee, and below the knee; when the patient stands, the venous segment that distends between two tourniquets localises the incompetent perforator to that anatomical compartment.

teach.heading: Historical terminology of the Trendelenburg test
teach.body:
Friedrich Trendelenburg described this test in the late nineteenth century. Surgical nomenclature can be confusing: Trendelenburg positive historically meant rapid filling from above upon release (saphenofemoral incompetence).

Trendelenburg negative meant veins filled while the tourniquet was on (perforator incompetence). Modern practice avoids ambiguous labels and explicitly states whether saphenofemoral, perforator, or dual incompetence exists.

rows: Veins fill rapidly within 10 to 30 seconds
Rapid cascade of blood fills veins from above
Fills from below, then fills more from above

teach.heading: Role of colour duplex ultrasound
teach.body: While clinical tourniquet tests remain essential clinical examination skills in surgical vivas and bedside teaching, duplex ultrasound has become the gold standard diagnostic modality. Duplex scanning directly visualises valve closure, measures retrograde reflux duration (pathological if greater than 0.5 seconds in superficial veins or greater than 1.0 second in deep veins), and maps every perforator.
