skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.title: Perthes' test for deep venous patency
skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.oneLine: Perform Perthes' and modified walking tourniquet tests to verify deep venous patency before surgery
skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.why: Perthes' test verifies that deep veins are patent and capable of clearing venous blood under the action of the calf muscle pump. Operating on or sclerosing superficial varicose veins when deep veins are blocked causes severe acute venous congestion, burst calf pain, and venous gangrene.

steps.text: Have the patient stand until the varicose veins are fully engorged and distended.
Apply a rubber tourniquet around the upper or mid-thigh firmly enough to occlude the superficial veins (great saphenous trunk) without obstructing deep venous or arterial flow.
Instruct the patient to walk briskly around the room or stand on tiptoes thirty to forty times for five minutes with the tourniquet in place.
Observe the superficial varicose veins continuously during and immediately after exercise.
Note whether the varicose veins collapse and shrink, remain unchanged, or become tense, turgid, and more prominent.
Ask the patient specifically whether the walking caused relief of leg heaviness or produced intense, bursting, cramp-like pain in the calf.

In the classic bandage test (original Perthes' test), wrap the entire leg firmly with an elastic bandage from toes to upper calf and have the patient walk: note whether walking is well-tolerated or provokes agonizing calf pain.

skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.normal: Varicose veins collapse and empty during walking with the tourniquet on, and the patient experiences no calf discomfort, confirming patent deep veins and functional calf pump.
skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.abnormal: Varicose veins become more congested and prominent, and the patient develops severe bursting calf pain, indicating deep venous obstruction or post-thrombotic deep venous valve destruction.
skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.significance: Normal collapse of varicosities confirms that deep veins are patent and that superficial vein stripping or endovenous ablation can be performed safely. Distension of veins and bursting pain indicate deep venous obstruction, representing an absolute contraindication to superficial vein ablation.
skill.exam.surg.perthes_deep_vein_patenc.practice: Practise performing the modified Perthes' test on clinical patients, noting changes in varicosity caliber during active calf exercise and correlating with duplex ultrasound findings.
pitfalls: Applying the tourniquet too loosely so that superficial reflux continues, causing false interpretation of deep vein blockage.
Applying the tourniquet so tightly that deep venous and arterial inflow are compromised.
Stripping or ablating superficial varicose veins in a patient who failed Perthes' test without obtaining a deep vein duplex scan.

rubric.text: Ensures superficial veins are fully distended before applying tourniquet
Applies tourniquet with correct pressure to occlude superficial veins only
Instructs patient to walk briskly or perform repeated tiptoe contractions for five minutes
Observes whether varicose veins collapse or become more distended
Inquires specifically regarding development of bursting calf pain

probes.q: What is the primary clinical objective of Perthes' test?
probes.a: To determine whether the deep veins of the lower limb are patent and competent to carry venous return.

probes.q: How does the calf muscle pump empty superficial veins when deep veins are normal during Perthes' test?
probes.a: Contraction of calf muscles compresses deep veins, pumping blood towards the heart; during relaxation, blood is sucked from superficial veins into deep veins through competent perforating veins, emptying the varicosities.

probes.q: What does the development of severe bursting calf pain during Perthes' test indicate, and what is its surgical implication?
probes.a: It indicates deep venous thrombosis or chronic post-thrombotic deep venous obstruction; superficial vein ablation or stripping is strictly contraindicated because the varicosities represent essential collateral drainage.

teach.heading: Physiology of the calf muscle pump
teach.body: The calf muscle pump functions as the peripheral heart. Contraction of gastrocnemius and soleus generates pressures exceeding two hundred millimetres of mercury within the deep fascial compartment. This forcefully expels blood upward through the popliteal vein. During muscular relaxation, intramuscular deep veins reopen under low pressure, aspirating blood from superficial veins through one-way perforators.

teach.heading: Why superficial ablation can be disastrous in DVT
teach.body: When deep veins are blocked by organized thrombus or scarred by post-thrombotic syndrome, venous return from the foot and calf has only one available exit: dilated superficial saphenous channels. If an unwary surgeon strips or ablates these superficial varices, the limb loses its sole remaining venous outflow pathway, culminating in acute venous hypertension, massive swelling, and venous gangrene.

skill.annex.surg.ceap_classification.title: CEAP classification of chronic venous disorders
skill.annex.surg.ceap_classification.oneLine: Clinical staging classification for chronic venous disorders from telangiectasias to active venous ulceration
skill.annex.surg.ceap_classification.why: The CEAP classification (Clinical, Etiologic, Anatomic, Pathophysiologic) is the international standard for reporting chronic venous disease. It standardizes diagnosis, tracks disease progression from cosmetic spider veins (C1) to active ulceration (C6), and governs treatment selection in surgical practice.

rows: No visible or palpable signs of venous disease
Scarred skin over prior venous defect
Full-thickness skin defect in gaiter zone

skill.annex.surg.ceap_classification.practice: Classify clinical photographs and case histories of venous disease into their exact CEAP clinical stages (C0 to C6), identifying the threshold between uncomplicated varices and chronic venous insufficiency.
pitfalls: Failing to recognize that chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) strictly refers to CEAP classes C3 through C6, and not simple C2 varicose veins.
Confusing C4a (pigmentation, eczema) with C4b (lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche), which carries much higher ulceration risk.
Misclassifying a healed venous ulcer as C6 instead of C5.

rubric.text: Accurately categorises clinical presentations from C0 to C6
Defines the onset of chronic venous insufficiency at stage C3 (edema)
Correctly distinguishes healed ulcer (C5) from active ulcer (C6)

probes.q: What clinical findings characterize CEAP Class C4 venous disease?
probes.a: Skin changes secondary to chronic venous hypertension, subdivided into C4a (pigmentation or stasis eczema) and C4b (lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche).

probes.q: What is the difference between CEAP Class C5 and Class C6?
probes.a: Class C5 represents healed venous ulceration, whereas Class C6 represents an active, open venous ulceration.

probes.q: What do the E, A, and P components of the full CEAP classification represent?
probes.a: E represents Etiology (congenital, primary, or secondary), A represents Anatomy (superficial, perforator, or deep), and P represents Pathophysiology (reflux, obstruction, or both).

teach.heading: Structure and components of the CEAP classification
teach.body: Formulated by consensus panel by the American Venous Forum and updated in recent consensus guidelines, CEAP assesses four distinct domains: Clinical class (C0 to C6, with a for asymptomatic and s for symptomatic), Etiology (Ec congenital, Ep primary, Es secondary, En no venous cause), Anatomy (As superficial, Ap perforator, Ad deep), and Pathophysiology (Pr reflux, Po obstruction, Pr,o both).

teach.heading: Distinction between varicose veins and venous insufficiency
teach.body: Varicose veins (CEAP C2) are dilated, palpable subcutaneous veins three millimetres or larger in diameter. By international consensus, chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) is reserved for advanced disease: classes C3 (edema), C4 (pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis), C5 (healed ulcer), and C6 (active ulcer). Simple varices without edema do not constitute chronic venous insufficiency.

teach.heading: Atrophie blanche and ulcer risk
points: Atrophie blanche represents localized, circular, ivory-white avascular skin patches surrounded by dilated capillary loops.
It results from microvascular thrombosis and intense dermal ischemia in severe chronic venous hypertension.
The fibrotic tissue has fragile epithelial coverage that easily breaks down into agonizingly painful recurrent ulcers.
Presence of atrophie blanche categorises the patient as CEAP C4b and demands aggressive venous treatment.

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.surg.lymphedema_lymphadenopathy.title: History of lymphedema and lymphadenopathy
skill.hx.surg.lymphedema_lymphadenopathy.oneLine: Differentiate primary from secondary lymphedema, elicit filarial exposure and ADLA attacks, and screen for malignant lymphadenopathy
skill.hx.surg.lymphedema_lymphadenopathy.why: Lymphedema history separates primary aplasia or hypoplasia (congenital, praecox, tarda) from secondary causes (filariasis, post-mastectomy axillary clearance, pelvi-inguinal node dissection, radiotherapy, or malignant obstruction). Missing recurrent acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADLA) attacks leaves lymphatic damage unarrested, while overlooking B-symptoms misses occult lymphoma or metastatic carcinoma.

asks.text: When and where did the swelling begin: at birth, around puberty, or in adult life, and did it start in the foot and creep up the leg?
Have you lived in or visited areas endemic for lymphatic filariasis (e.g. coastal Odisha, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh), or walked barefoot?
Do you experience recurrent episodes of high fever with chills, rigors, headache, and intense redness, heat, and pain spreading up the limb (acute dermatolymphangioadenitis attacks)?
Have you undergone prior surgeries such as radical mastectomy, axillary or groin node dissection, or received regional radiotherapy?
If lymph nodes are enlarged, are they painful or painless, how fast have they grown, and have you noticed fevers (Pel-Ebstein fever), drenching night sweats, or significant weight loss?
Are there any compressive symptoms: shortness of breath, facial puffiness, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, or limb swelling?

skill.hx.surg.lymphedema_lymphadenopathy.practice: Rehearse taking a lymphatic history from a patient with lower extremity swelling, systematically distinguishing primary lymphedema (Milroy, Meige, tarda) from filarial elephantiasis and pelvic neoplastic obstruction.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about recurrent fever and chills (ADLA attacks), which accelerate lymphatic destruction in endemic filariasis.
Omitting a travel or residential history in filariasis-endemic regions of India.
Treating painless progressive unilateral lower limb lymphedema in an elderly patient as simple benign disease without searching for pelvic malignancy.

rubric.text: Establishes precise age of onset to categorize primary versus secondary lymphedema
Asks regarding endemic residence, barefoot walking, and microfilarial exposure
Screens for recurrent acute dermatolymphangioadenitis episodes (fever, chills, ascending erythema)
Screens for systemic B-symptoms: drenching night sweats, weight loss, and unexplained fever

probes.q: How is primary lymphedema classified based on the patient's age at presentation?
probes.a: Congenital lymphedema (Milroy disease, presenting at birth or before one year), lymphedema praecox (Meige disease, presenting at puberty up to thirty-five years), and lymphedema tarda (presenting after thirty-five years of age).

probes.q: What is an ADLA attack in lymphatic filariasis and why is it clinically important?
probes.a: Acute dermatolymphangioadenitis; an acute bacterial dermato-hypodermatitis presenting with high fever, chills, and painful retrograde lymphangitis, which triggers progressive irreversible lymphatic obliteration and fibrosis.

probes.q: Why should new-onset unilateral lower extremity lymphedema in a middle-aged or elderly patient prompt pelvic imaging?
probes.a: To exclude pelvic or retroperitoneal malignancy (such as cervical, uterine, ovarian, prostate, or rectal carcinoma, or lymphoma) compressing or infiltrating the iliac and para-aortic lymph nodes.

teach.heading: Classification of primary lymphedema
teach.body: Primary lymphedema stems from congenital lymphatic hypoplasia, aplasia, or valvular incompetence. It is classified by age of onset: congenital lymphedema (present at birth or within the first year, often familial as Milroy disease caused by VEGFR3 mutations), lymphedema praecox (the commonest form, emerging around menarche or young adulthood, often termed Meige disease), and lymphedema tarda (appearing after age thirty-five).

teach.heading: Secondary lymphedema and lymphatic filariasis
teach.body: Worldwide, the commonest cause of secondary lymphedema is lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. In India, hyperendemic pockets span Odisha, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and coastal belts. Adult worms lodge in pelvic and inguinal lymphatics, inciting sterile inflammation. Secondary bacterial entry through interdigital fissures triggers recurrent ADLA attacks that drive progressive elephantiasis.

teach.heading: Alarm symptoms in lymphadenopathy
points: Rapidly enlarging painless lymph nodes in an adult demand histological evaluation to rule out lymphoma or metastasis.
B-symptoms (unexplained fever > 38 C, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss > 10% over 6 months) suggest systemic lymphoma.
Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical high fever lasting several days alternating with afebrile periods) is classically associated with Hodgkin lymphoma.
Pruritus, alcohol-induced nodal pain, and chronic dry cough from mediastinal compression warrant immediate chest imaging.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.lymphedema_signs.title: Examination of lymphedema: physical signs and limb girth
skill.exam.surg.lymphedema_signs.oneLine: Elicit Stemmer's sign, inspect buffalo hump and square toes, evaluate brawny induration, and measure girth
skill.exam.surg.lymphedema_signs.why: Lymphedema is distinguished from venous and systemic edema by specific pathognomonic physical signs. Missing Kaposi-Stemmer sign or failing to standardize circumferential measurements leads to misdiagnosis, ineffective diuretic prescriptions, and inability to monitor decongestive therapy.

steps.text: Position the patient supine with both lower extremities fully exposed from groin to toes in good illumination.

Inspect the distribution of swelling: observe whether the dorsum of the foot has a hump-like cushion of edema (buffalo hump) and whether the toes have lost their tapered shape and appear blunt and boxy (square toes).
Inspect the skin for verrucous hyperkeratosis, mossy papillomatosis, lymph vesicles, lichenification, and interdigital fungal maceration (tinea pedis).
Perform Kaposi-Stemmer's sign: grasp and attempt to pinch or tent a fold of skin at the dorsal base of the second toe between your thumb and index finger.

Test for pitting edema by pressing your thumb firmly over the medial malleolus, anterior tibia, and dorsum of foot for thirty seconds: note whether a persistent pit remains or whether the tissue feels rubbery and non-pitting (brawny induration).

Measure limb circumferences with a non-stretch measuring tape at standardized anatomical levels: at the ankle (narrowest point above malleoli), ten centimetres and twenty centimetres below the tibial tuberosity, and ten centimetres and twenty centimetres above the superior pole of the patella.
Compare all circumference measurements symmetrically with the contralateral unaffected limb.

skill.exam.surg.lymphedema_signs.normal: Skin on the dorsal base of the second toe pinches and lifts easily into a thin fold (Stemmer sign negative); toes are tapered; no buffalo hump; tissues pit not at all or rapidly recover, and bilateral limb circumferences are equal.
skill.exam.surg.lymphedema_signs.abnormal: Inability to pinch or lift the skin fold at the base of the second toe (Stemmer sign positive); prominent buffalo hump on the dorsum of the foot; square boxy toes; deep non-pitting brawny induration; mossy verrucous papillomatosis; and limb circumference increased by more than two centimetres compared with the opposite side.
skill.exam.surg.lymphedema_signs.significance: A positive Kaposi-Stemmer sign is pathognomonic of lymphedema and reliably rules out uncomplicated venous or cardiac edema. Transition from pitting to non-pitting brawny induration marks the onset of irreversible subcutaneous fibrosis (ISL Stage 2 to 3).
skill.exam.surg.lymphedema_signs.practice: Practise eliciting Stemmer's sign on both normal individuals and patients with ankle swelling, and master standardized limb circumference measurements using fixed bony landmarks.
pitfalls: Diagnosing lymphedema as cardiac or renal edema and prescribing long-term diuretics, which dehydrates the patient without reducing fibrotic lymphedematous tissue.
Failing to examine the interdigital web spaces for tinea pedis, which acts as the major portal of entry for streptococcal ADLA attacks.
Measuring limb girth at arbitrary points without referencing fixed bony landmarks (tibial tuberosity or patella), making longitudinal comparison impossible.

rubric.text: Performs Kaposi-Stemmer sign at the base of the second toe accurately
Inspects for buffalo hump, square toes, and interdigital fungal infection
Applies sustained thirty-second thumb pressure to assess pitting versus brawny non-pitting induration
Measures limb circumferences using standardized distances from bony landmarks
Documents presence of hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, and lymphorrhea

probes.q: What is Kaposi-Stemmer's sign and how is it performed?
probes.a: An inability to pinch or lift a fold of skin at the dorsal base of the second toe due to subcutaneous fibrosis and lymphatic fluid accumulation; a positive sign is pathognomonic of lymphedema.

probes.q: Why do chronic lymphedematous limbs become non-pitting over time?
probes.a: Stagnant, protein-rich lymphatic fluid stimulates chronic inflammation, macrophage activation, fibroblast proliferation, and extensive collagen deposition in the subcutaneous fat, converting soft fluid into dense fibrotic tissue.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of interdigital tinea pedis in a patient with elephantiasis?
probes.a: Interdigital fungal fissures disrupt the epidermal barrier, serving as the primary entry portal for beta-hemolytic streptococci that precipitate recurrent acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADLA) attacks.

teach.heading: Pathognomonic foot signs in lymphedema
teach.body: Lymphedema characteristically starts distally on the foot. Fluid and fibro-adipose tissue accumulate on the dorsum of the foot, producing a rounded cushion termed buffalo hump, while deep transverse skin creases are accentuated. Toes swell into cylindrical, blunt structures termed square toes. In contrast, venous edema characteristically spares the toes and the anterior dorsum of the foot.

teach.heading: Differentiating lymphedema from chronic venous edema

rows: Involves dorsum of foot and toes (buffalo hump)
Spares dorsum of foot and toes; peri-malleolar
Positive (cannot pinch base of second toe)
Pitting early, brawny and non-pitting late

teach.heading: Standardized limb circumference measurement
teach.body: Limb volume changes must be documented objectively. Using a non-stretch tape, measure circumferences at fixed distances: the ankle (narrowest circumference proximal to malleoli), ten and twenty centimetres above the medial malleolus, and ten and twenty centimetres above the superior pole of the patella. A difference greater than two centimetres between matching points confirms clinically significant lymphedema.

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.lymph_node_groups.title: Systematic examination of peripheral lymph node groups
skill.exam.surg.lymph_node_groups.oneLine: Systematically palpate cervical, axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal nodal basins and evaluate size, consistency, and fixation
skill.exam.surg.lymph_node_groups.why: Systematic palpation of peripheral lymph nodes detects primary lymphomas, staging for malignant metastases, and chronic infections such as tuberculosis. Inadvertently skipping the supraclavicular basin (Virchow's node) or examining axillary nodes with a tense pectoralis muscle causes missed advanced malignancy.

steps.text: Position the patient comfortably sitting on a chair or the examination couch for cervical and axillary examination, and supine for inguinal examination.

Stand behind the sitting patient to examine the cervical chains: use the pulps of the fingers of both hands to palpate submental, submandibular, preauricular, postauricular, occipital, upper deep cervical (jugulodigastric), middle deep cervical, lower deep cervical, and posterior triangle groups.

Palpate the supraclavicular fossae systematically while the patient flexes the neck slightly forward: feel behind the clavicles, specifically checking the left supraclavicular fossa for an enlarged, hard node (Virchow's node / Troisier sign).
Examine the axillary lymph nodes from the front: support the patient's right forearm with your right arm to completely relax the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi muscles.

Use your left hand to palpate the five anatomical groups of the right axilla: anterior (pectoral) along the lateral border of pectoralis major, posterior (subscapular) along the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral along the upper humerus and axillary vein, central in the axillary fat pad against the chest wall, and apical at the apex of the axilla behind the pectoralis minor.
Switch arms to palpate the left axilla in the identical relaxed manner.
Palpate the epitrochlear lymph node in the groove three centimetres above and anterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus, supporting the patient's flexed elbow.

Have the patient lie supine to examine the inguinal lymph nodes: palpate the horizontal chain parallel to and just below the inguinal ligament, and the vertical chain along the upper terminal segment of the great saphenous vein.

For any enlarged node, record: exact anatomical site, size, number, discrete versus matted, consistency (soft, cystic, rubbery, stony hard), tenderness, mobility in both planes, and fixation to skin or deep structures.

skill.exam.surg.lymph_node_groups.normal: Small (under one centimetre), soft, non-tender, discrete, mobile, or impalpable lymph nodes in all anatomical basins; no supraclavicular fullness.
skill.exam.surg.lymph_node_groups.abnormal: Enlarged nodes (> 1 cm), matted clusters with cold abscess or discharging sinuses (tuberculosis), firm rubbery painless discrete nodes (Hodgkin lymphoma), stony hard fixed nodes (metastatic carcinoma), or soft tender erythematous nodes (acute lymphadenitis).
skill.exam.surg.lymph_node_groups.significance: A stony hard node fixed to deep structures is metastatic carcinoma until proven otherwise. Matted nodes with overlying violaceous skin or sinus indicate tuberculosis. Rubbery discrete nodes suggest lymphoma. Left supraclavicular node enlargement (Troisier sign) signals transcoelomic metastasis from gastric, pancreatic, or pelvic cancer.
skill.exam.surg.lymph_node_groups.practice: Practise examining the cervical and axillary nodes on colleagues, ensuring the arm is fully supported and relaxed during axillary examination and that Virchow's node is examined with relaxed clavicular heads.
pitfalls: Examining the axilla while the patient's arm is abducted or unsupported, causing muscular contraction that shields deep nodes from palpation.
Missing the left supraclavicular fossa (Virchow's node) in patients presenting with upper gastrointestinal symptoms or abdominal masses.
Forgetting to inspect and examine the primary drainage territory (skin, scalp, breast, perineum, or extremities) corresponding to an enlarged node.

rubric.text: Palpates all cervical lymph node levels systematically from behind the patient
Examines supraclavicular fossae specifically for Virchow's node with neck flexed
Supports the patient's arm to achieve complete pectoral relaxation during axillary palpation
Palpates all five axillary groups (anterior, posterior, lateral, central, apical)
Accurately characterizes size, consistency, matting, tenderness, and deep fixation

probes.q: Why must the patient's arm be supported and relaxed during axillary lymph node palpation?
probes.a: Contraction of the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi muscles tightens the axillary fascia, preventing the examiner's fingers from pressing against the chest wall and axillary apex.

probes.q: What is Troisier's sign and what is its anatomical route of spread?
probes.a: Enlargement of the left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow's node) due to metastatic spread from abdominal or pelvic malignancy (such as stomach cancer) via the thoracic duct into the left jugulo-subclavian venous confluence.

probes.q: How does the consistency of lymph nodes differ among acute lymphadenitis, tuberculous lymphadenitis, Hodgkin lymphoma, and metastatic carcinoma?
probes.a: Acute lymphadenitis is soft and tender; tuberculosis produces matted nodes with cold abscesses or sinuses; Hodgkin lymphoma produces firm, rubbery, discrete, painless nodes; and metastatic carcinoma produces stony hard, fixed nodes.

teach.heading: Levels and basins of the cervical lymph nodes
teach.body: Surgical oncology classifies cervical nodes into six levels: Level I (submental IA, submandibular IB), Level II (upper jugular, skull base to hyoid), Level III (middle jugular, hyoid to cricoid), Level IV (lower jugular, cricoid to clavicle), Level V (posterior triangle along spinal accessory nerve), and Level VI (anterior central compartment around thyroid and trachea). Supraclavicular nodes lie in the lower part of Level IV and V.

rows: Matted by periadenitis, cold abscess, sinus
Discrete, mobile, like tennis balls in a bag
Fixed to underlying muscles, vessels, or skin

teach.heading: Technique of axillary node examination
teach.body: Palpating the axilla requires methodical positioning. To examine the patient's right axilla, cup the patient's right wrist or elbow with your right hand, lifting the arm slightly away from the chest to relax the axillary folds. Slide the fingers of your left hand high into the apex behind the pectoralis major. Gently press toward the thoracic cage and slide downward, feeling the central, anterior, posterior, and lateral walls.

skill.annex.surg.isl_lymphedema_stages.title: International Society of Lymphology (ISL) staging of lymphedema
skill.annex.surg.isl_lymphedema_stages.oneLine: Consensus staging of peripheral lymphedema based on edema reversibility, tissue consistency, and skin changes
skill.annex.surg.isl_lymphedema_stages.why: The International Society of Lymphology (ISL) staging system provides the global clinical standard for staging lymphedema. It distinguishes early fluid-predominant reversible swelling from irreversible fibro-adipose elephantiasis, dictating whether conservative compression, complete decongestive therapy, or surgical debulking is indicated.

rows: Impaired lymphatic transport; asymptomatic, may feel heaviness
Swelling completely reverses on leg elevation
Pitting edema, accumulation of protein-rich fluid, no fibrosis
Elevation rarely reduces swelling without compression
Pitting becomes difficult; moderate subcutaneous tissue fibrosis
Non-pitting brawny induration; extensive fibro-adipose proliferation
Severe non-pitting induration, hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, acanthosis

skill.annex.surg.isl_lymphedema_stages.practice: Apply the ISL classification to five clinical vignettes of patients with secondary post-mastectomy or filarial lymphedema, identifying the stage where compression therapy transitions from reversible to maintenance.
pitfalls: Failing to recognize Stage 0 (latent phase) in post-axillary clearance or post-radiotherapy patients who complain of tightness before visible swelling develops.
Assuming that all lymphedema pits on pressure, missing the fact that Stage 2 late and Stage 3 are completely non-pitting due to fibrosis.
Promising a Stage 3 elephantiasis patient that elevation or simple compression wraps will restore normal limb contour without surgical excision.

rubric.text: Accurately categorises clinical cases into ISL Stages 0, 1, 2, and 3
Identifies reversibility on limb elevation as the hallmark separating Stage 1 from Stage 2
Recognises non-pitting fibrosis and trophic skin overgrowths as the defining criteria of Stage 3

probes.q: What defines ISL Stage 1 lymphedema?
probes.a: Early accumulation of protein-rich fluid that produces pitting edema and completely subsides upon limb elevation.

probes.q: How does ISL Stage 2 differ from Stage 1 lymphedema?
probes.a: In Stage 2, limb elevation alone rarely reduces the swelling because progressive subcutaneous tissue fibrosis and adipogenesis develop, making pitting increasingly difficult to elicit.

probes.q: What skin and soft tissue features characterize ISL Stage 3 lymphostatic elephantiasis?
probes.a: Severe non-pitting brawny edema accompanied by prominent trophic skin changes including hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, warty papillomatosis, fat deposits, and recurrent fungal or bacterial infections.

teach.heading: Pathophysiological basis of ISL staging
teach.body: Lymphatic staging reflects progressive structural remodelling. In Stage 0, transport capacity is impaired but matches normal lymph load. In Stage 1, microvascular filtration exceeds lymphatic drainage, accumulating interstitial fluid that pits easily. Over months and years, high protein concentrations recruit fibroblasts and adipocytes, converting reversible edema into irreversible fibrotic tissue (Stage 2 and 3).

teach.heading: Management strategies linked to ISL stages
points: Stage 0 (Latent): Patient education, limb protection, avoidance of venipuncture/blood pressure cuffs, early surveillance.
Stage 1 (Reversible): Complete decongestive therapy (CDT), multilayer bandaging, manual lymphatic drainage, and flat-knit compression garments.
Stage 2 (Established): Intensive phase CDT, compression garments, skin care; microsurgical lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) may be considered.
Stage 3 (Elephantiasis): Rigorous antimicrobial skin hygiene, long-term bandaging, and reductive excisional surgery (Charles procedure or debulking) for disabling deformity.

teach.heading: Monitoring lymphedema volume and severity
teach.body: In addition to clinical staging, severity within each stage is subclassified by volume difference compared to the healthy contralateral limb: mild (less than 20 percent increase in volume), moderate (20 to 40 percent volume increase), and severe (greater than 40 percent volume increase). Volume can be calculated from serial circumferential measurements using the frustum formula.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.surg.nerve_injury.title: History of peripheral nerve injury and entrapment
skill.hx.surg.nerve_injury.oneLine: Determine the trauma mechanism, classify sharp versus blunt injury, map neurological deficits, and screen for leprosy
skill.hx.surg.nerve_injury.why: A detailed history of peripheral nerve injury establishes whether the nerve was sharply transected (requiring primary exploration and repair) or suffered closed traction or compression (favouring conservative observation for axonotmesis). It identifies trophic vulnerability to painless burns and distinguishes traumatic transection from entrapment neuropathies or leprosy.

asks.text: What was the exact mechanism and timing of injury: a sharp laceration (broken glass, knife), a high-energy fracture, traction, a crush injury, or an intramuscular injection?
For sharp wounds, was the injury clean or contaminated, was there arterial bleeding or tendon division, and was the wound explored or sutured?
When did the weakness or numbness begin: immediately at the moment of trauma, or did it develop insidiously weeks or months later (tardy palsy or callus entrapment)?
Which specific movements or tasks are impossible: gripping objects, opening jars, buttoning shirts, picking up a key, or lifting the foot while walking?
What is the distribution of sensory loss: numbness, tingling, electric shocks, or hyperesthesia, and have you sustained painless burns, blisters, or ulcers?

In non-traumatic or insidious weakness, screen for systemic causes: diabetes mellitus, chronic alcohol misuse, occupational repetitive strain, exposure to heavy metals, and hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation (leprosy).

skill.hx.surg.nerve_injury.practice: Practise taking a peripheral nerve injury history, mapping the timeline of deficit onset to determine whether neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis, or delayed tardy palsy is present.
pitfalls: Failing to ask whether motor loss occurred immediately at the time of injury or developed during plaster immobilisation (iatrogenic compartment syndrome or cast compression).
Omitting questions about painless cigarette burns or hot-water scalds, which reflect loss of protective pain sensation.
Overlooking leprosy as an endemic cause of painless neuropathic deformities (claw hand, foot drop) in the Indian clinical setting.

rubric.text: Defines injury mechanism (sharp laceration, blunt crush, fracture, traction, or compression)
Establishes immediate versus delayed onset of motor and sensory deficits
Screens for loss of protective pain sensation, painless burns, and trophic ulcers
Screens for leprosy, diabetes mellitus, chronic alcohol use, and injection palsy

probes.q: Why is it vital to determine whether a nerve deficit followed a sharp laceration or a closed blunt fracture?
probes.a: Sharp lacerations usually cause neurotmesis with complete transection requiring early surgical exploration and repair, whereas closed blunt fractures usually cause neurapraxia or axonotmesis which often recover spontaneously.

probes.q: What is tardy ulnar nerve palsy and what is its typical antecedent history?
probes.a: Delayed ulnar neuropathy at the elbow appearing years after a malunited lateral humeral condyle fracture that caused cubitus valgus deformity, stretching the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.

probes.q: Why should an unexplained peripheral nerve lesion in the Indian setting prompt examination of the skin for hypopigmented patches?
probes.a: Leprosy (Hansen disease) caused by Mycobacterium leprae is a neurotropic infection that preferentially invades superficial peripheral nerves and dermal cutaneous nerves, presenting with hypopigmented anesthetic skin patches and nerve thickening.

teach.heading: Mechanism of injury and nerve continuity
teach.body: Nerve injuries divide fundamentally into open and closed insults. Open lacerations by glass, knives, or industrial machinery sever epineurium and axons (neurotmesis), creating a physical gap filled by scar tissue that halts regeneration without microsurgical suture. Closed injuries from bone displacement, tourniquets, or crush maintain endoneurial sheath alignment (axonotmesis), enabling spontaneous axon regrowth at one millimetre per day.

teach.heading: Trophic consequences of denervation
teach.body: Interruption of postganglionic sympathetic fibres running within peripheral nerves abolishes sudomotor, pilomotor, and vasomotor function. The skin becomes completely dry (anhidrosis), glossy, thin, and vulnerable to microtrauma. Loss of protective pain sensation leads to unperceived thermal burns from cooking utensils, cigarette burns, or painless pressure sores that destroy underlying joints.

rows: Knife wound, humerus fracture, shoulder dislocation

skill.exam.surg.radial_nerve.title: Examination of the radial nerve
skill.exam.surg.radial_nerve.oneLine: Demonstrate wrist drop, test brachioradialis and finger extension, and map first dorsal web space sensation
skill.exam.surg.radial_nerve.why: The radial nerve is the most frequently injured major nerve in fractures of the humerus shaft. Misinterpreting finger extension mediated by interossei and lumbricals as intact radial nerve function, or failing to test its autonomous sensory zone, leads to missed diagnoses of complete radial transection.

steps.text: Inspect the resting attitude of the affected upper limb: observe for characteristic wrist drop, finger drop at the metacarpophalangeal joints, and thumb drop.
Inspect the extensor compartment of the forearm for muscle wasting compared to the normal contralateral side.
Test triceps brachii (high lesion above spiral groove): have the patient abduct the shoulder to ninety degrees and extend the elbow against resistance.
Test brachioradialis: have the patient flex the elbow against resistance with the forearm in the mid-prone position (thumbs up); palpate and observe the taut muscle belly on the lateral forearm.
Test wrist extension: instruct the patient to extend the wrist against resistance with fingers flexed into a loose fist (to prevent trick extension by extensor tendons).

Test extensor digitorum communis: have the patient actively extend the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints against your resistance, noting that extension of proximal and distal interphalangeal joints is mediated by intact lumbricals and interossei.
Test extensor pollicis longus: instruct the patient to place the hand flat on the table, palm down, and extend the thumb backward off the tabletop against resistance (hitch-hiker thumb).

Test sensation in the autonomous sensory zone of the radial nerve: test light touch with cotton wool and pinprick over the dorsal aspect of the first web space (between first and second metacarpal bases).

skill.exam.surg.radial_nerve.normal: Strong wrist and finger extension at metacarpophalangeal joints, prominent contraction of brachioradialis in mid-prone flexion, and intact sensation over the dorsal first web space.
skill.exam.surg.radial_nerve.abnormal: Complete wrist drop, finger drop at metacarpophalangeal joints, inability to lift thumb off the tabletop, absent brachioradialis contraction, and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space.
skill.exam.surg.radial_nerve.significance: Intact triceps with wrist drop localises injury to the spiral groove (associated with midshaft humerus fracture). Spared brachioradialis and wrist extensors with isolated finger drop indicates a posterior interosseous nerve lesion. Preserved interphalangeal joint extension confirms intact ulnar and median nerve lumbrical-interosseous function.
skill.exam.surg.radial_nerve.practice: Practise examining the radial nerve on a colleague, verifying isolation of extensor digitorum at the metacarpophalangeal joints and mapping the exact boundary of the dorsal first web space autonomous zone.
pitfalls: Mistaking interphalangeal joint extension (performed by ulnar and median innervated lumbricals and interossei) for intact radial nerve function.
Testing wrist extension with fingers fully extended, allowing passive tenodesis recoil to simulate active extension.
Testing sensory function on the dorsal forearm or lateral hand rather than the solitary reliable autonomous zone on the dorsal first web space.

rubric.text: Inspects for classical wrist drop, finger drop, and thumb drop
Tests brachioradialis in mid-prone elbow flexion against resistance
Specifically isolates extensor digitorum at the metacarpophalangeal joints
Tests extensor pollicis longus by lifting thumb off tabletop against resistance
Tests cutaneous sensation accurately over the dorsal first web space

probes.q: Why can a patient with complete radial nerve transection and wrist drop still extend their interphalangeal joints?
probes.a: Extension of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints is performed by the lumbricals and interossei, which insert into the extensor expansion and are supplied by the median and ulnar nerves.

probes.q: Where is the solitary autonomous sensory zone for the radial nerve located?
probes.a: The dorsal aspect of the first web space between the bases of the first and second metacarpals on the back of the hand.

probes.q: How do you clinically differentiate a high radial nerve injury in the axilla from an injury in the spiral groove?
probes.a: In a high axillary lesion, the triceps brachii is paralyzed (loss of elbow extension and absent triceps reflex), whereas in a spiral groove lesion, branches to the triceps arise proximally and are spared, preserving elbow extension.

teach.heading: Topographical anatomy of radial nerve branching
teach.body: The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. In the axilla, it gives off branches to all three heads of the triceps and posterior cutaneous nerves. It winds around the posterior humerus in the spiral groove, where it is vulnerable to shaft fractures. At the lateral epicondyle, it supplies brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus before bifurcating into the posterior interosseous nerve and superficial radial nerve.

rows: Loss of elbow extension plus full wrist drop
Dorsal web space, posterior arm and forearm
Finger drop, intact wrist extension (radial deviation)
Sensory loss over dorsal first web space

teach.heading: Trick movements and pitfalls in testing
teach.body: Examiners frequently test students on trick movements in radial nerve palsy. A patient with complete wrist drop can produce apparent wrist extension by strongly flexing the fingers, utilizing passive recoil of extensor tendons (tenodesis). To eliminate trick movements, always test wrist extension with fingers relaxed or curled, and test finger extension specifically at the metacarpophalangeal joints.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.median_nerve.title: Examination of the median nerve
skill.exam.surg.median_nerve.oneLine: Demonstrate thenar wasting, test abductor pollicis brevis with the pen test, and test index pulp sensation
skill.exam.surg.median_nerve.why: The median nerve is the labourer's nerve and the eye of the hand. It controls precision opposition and sensation to the working digits (thumb, index, and middle). Missing abductor pollicis brevis weakness or failing to test the index fingertip autonomous zone leaves motor and sensory deficits unaddressed, risking permanent hand disability.

steps.text: Inspect the hand resting palm up: observe for thenar eminence wasting, flattening of the thenar contour (ape thumb / simian hand deformity), and pointing index (failure of index DIP flexion).
Inspect the palmar skin of the radial three and a half digits for trophic dryness, smoothing of dermal ridges, glossy skin, and unperceived burn scars.

Perform the pen test for abductor pollicis brevis: have the patient place the hand flat on a table with the palm facing up; hold a pen horizontally above the palm and instruct the patient to point the thumb straight up towards the ceiling to touch the pen against your downward resistance.

Test opponens pollicis: instruct the patient to touch the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, keeping the thumbnail in a plane parallel to the palm; attempt to pull the thumb away while palpating thenar contraction.
Test flexor pollicis longus (anterior interosseous / high median nerve): hold the proximal phalanx of the thumb steady and have the patient bend the distal interphalangeal joint against resistance.
Test flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger: hold the middle phalanx of the index finger extended and instruct the patient to flex the distal interphalangeal joint against resistance.

Perform Ochsner's clasp test: ask the patient to clasp both hands together interlocking the fingers tightly; observe whether the index finger of the affected hand remains extended and straight (pointing index).
Test sensation in the autonomous sensory zone of the median nerve: test light touch with cotton wool and two-point discrimination over the palmar pulp of the index fingertip.

skill.exam.surg.median_nerve.normal: Full rounded thenar eminence, powerful thumb abduction perpendicular to the palm in the pen test, forceful opposition, vigorous DIP flexion of thumb and index, and normal sensation on the index fingertip pulp.
skill.exam.surg.median_nerve.abnormal: Flattened thenar eminence, inability to abduct the thumb vertically off the palm in the pen test, inability to oppose thumb to little finger, pointing index on hand clasping, and complete sensory loss over the index fingertip pulp.
skill.exam.surg.median_nerve.significance: Failure of the pen test (abductor pollicis brevis weakness) is the most sensitive and specific clinical sign of median nerve lesion and carpal tunnel syndrome. Inability to flex the index DIP and thumb IP indicates a high median nerve lesion or anterior interosseous nerve injury. Sensory loss over the index pulp deprives the hand of stereognosis.
skill.exam.surg.median_nerve.practice: Practise the pen test for abductor pollicis brevis and Ochsner's clasping test on colleagues, ensuring the thumb moves strictly perpendicular to the palmar plane without adductor substitution.
pitfalls: Allowing the patient to substitute adductor pollicis (ulnar nerve) during opposition testing by sweeping the thumb across the palm without true vertical abduction.
Testing sensation on the thenar eminence rather than the index fingertip pulp; the thenar skin is supplied by the palmar cutaneous branch, which spares carpal tunnel compression.
Testing superficial flexors instead of deep flexors when evaluating high median nerve injury.

rubric.text: Inspects thenar eminence for wasting, ape thumb attitude, and trophic skin changes
Performs pen test for abductor pollicis brevis with thumb moving perpendicular to palm
Tests opponens pollicis maintaining thumbnail parallel to the palmar plane
Performs Ochsner clasping test to demonstrate pointing index finger
Tests light touch and two-point discrimination over the index fingertip pulp

probes.q: How is the pen test performed to test the abductor pollicis brevis muscle?
probes.a: The patient rests the hand flat on a table with the palm facing upward and abducts the thumb vertically towards the ceiling against resistance to touch a pen held above the palm.

probes.q: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence classically spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
probes.a: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the wrist and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, escaping compression within the carpal tunnel.

probes.q: What is Ochsner's clasp test and which muscle paralysis produces the pointing index?
probes.a: When the patient clasps hands with interlocking fingers, the index finger remains extended (pointing index) due to paralysis of the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus supplied by the median nerve.

teach.heading: Anatomy and clinical significance of the median nerve
teach.body: The median nerve is formed by medial and lateral cords of the brachial plexus. It runs down the arm with the brachial artery, enters the forearm between heads of pronator teres, and travels beneath flexor digitorum superficialis. At the wrist, it passes through the unyielding carpal tunnel with nine flexor tendons. Because it innervates thenar muscles and sensory pulps of the radial digits, it is the primary nerve of precision grip.

teach.heading: High versus low median nerve lesions

rows: Pronators, FCR, FDS, lateral FDP, FPL, thenar muscles
Pointing index (Ochsner test), ape thumb, weak wrist flexion
Palmar digits 1 to 3 and lateral half of ring finger
Abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, lumbricals 1 and 2
Ape thumb deformity, positive pen test, thenar wasting
Fingertip pulps of digits 1 to 3; thenar skin spared
FPL, lateral FDP, pronator quadratus (pure motor)
Inability to form OK sign (pulp-to-pulp pinch instead of tip-to-tip)

teach.heading: Testing abductor pollicis brevis without trick substitution
teach.body: The abductor pollicis brevis is innervated exclusively by the median nerve and is the premier diagnostic muscle. When testing it, ensure the hand lies flat on a firm surface with the palm upwards. The patient must lift the thumb straight up towards the ceiling, perpendicular to the palm. If the thumb moves sideways in the plane of the palm, the patient is using the ulnar-innervated adductor pollicis.

skill.exam.surg.ulnar_nerve.title: Examination of the ulnar nerve
skill.exam.surg.ulnar_nerve.oneLine: Demonstrate claw hand deformity, perform the card test and Froment's sign, and map little finger sensation
skill.exam.surg.ulnar_nerve.why: The ulnar nerve is the musician's nerve, innervating all intrinsic interossei and the adductor pollicis to provide fine digital dexterity. Failing to elicit the card test, misinterpreting Froment's sign, or misunderstanding the ulnar paradox leads to incorrect anatomical localisation and delayed decompression.

steps.text: Inspect the resting hand: observe for classical claw hand deformity (main en griffe) with hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, most marked in the ring and little fingers.
Inspect the dorsum and palm of the hand for hollowing and guttering between the metacarpals (wasting of dorsal interossei) and flattening of the hypothenar eminence.
Note the degree of clawing: recognize that clawing is more severe in low lesions at the wrist than in high lesions at the elbow (the ulnar paradox).

Perform the card test for palmar interossei: place a stiff card between two fully extended adjacent fingers (e.g. index and middle, or ring and little) and instruct the patient to grip it tightly; pull the card out and assess resistance.

Test dorsal interossei (abduction): have the patient place the hand flat on the table, palm down, and actively spread the fingers apart against your resistance, palpating the first dorsal interosseous muscle belly in the first web space.

Test adductor pollicis using Froment's sign (the book or paper test): instruct the patient to grasp a sheet of paper or thin book firmly between the pad of the extended thumb and the radial border of the index finger with both hands; pull the paper firmly.

Observe the thumb: in ulnar nerve paralysis, the patient cannot adduct the thumb and involuntarily flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb using flexor pollicis longus (median nerve) to maintain grip (positive Froment sign).

Perform Egawa's test: with the hand resting flat on a table palm down, instruct the patient to keep the middle finger straight and move it from side to side (abducting and adducting using dorsal interossei).
Test sensation in the autonomous sensory zone of the ulnar nerve: test light touch with cotton wool and two-point discrimination over the palmar and dorsal aspects of the little finger pulp.

skill.exam.surg.ulnar_nerve.normal: No claw deformity, full hypothenar contour, strong grip on the card between adjacent fingers, firm pinch grip with extended thumb in Froment's test, and intact sensation over the little finger pulp.
skill.exam.surg.ulnar_nerve.abnormal: Hyperextension of MCP and flexion of IP joints of ring and little fingers (claw hand), guttering between metacarpals, inability to hold a card between fingers, acute flexion of thumb IP joint on pulling paper (positive Froment sign), and sensory loss over the little finger.
skill.exam.surg.ulnar_nerve.significance: A positive card test proves palmar interosseous paralysis. Froment's sign confirms adductor pollicis paralysis. High ulnar lesions produce less clawing than low lesions because the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is paralyzed (ulnar paradox). Sensory loss over the hypothenar and little finger confirms ulnar distribution.
skill.exam.surg.ulnar_nerve.practice: Practise performing the card test, Froment's book test, and Egawa's test with a colleague, and rehearse explaining the anatomical mechanism of the ulnar paradox out loud.
pitfalls: Allowing the patient to flex the fingers during the card test, which substitutes long flexors for palmar interossei.
Missing Froment's sign by failing to observe the hyperflexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint during strong paper pull.
Expecting more severe clawing in a high elbow lesion than in a low wrist lesion, forgetting the ulnar paradox.

rubric.text: Inspects for claw hand attitude, interosseous guttering, and hypothenar wasting
Performs card test correctly with fingers fully extended to isolate palmar interossei
Tests first dorsal interosseous muscle abduction in the first web space
Elicits Froment's paper grip sign and identifies compensatory thumb IP flexion
Tests cutaneous sensation over the palmar and dorsal pulp of the little finger

probes.q: What is Froment's sign and which muscle weakness causes it?
probes.a: When a patient tries to grip a piece of paper between thumb and index finger, the thumb interphalangeal joint flexes compensatory using flexor pollicis longus (median nerve) because the adductor pollicis (ulnar nerve) is paralyzed.

probes.q: Explain the ulnar paradox in peripheral nerve lesions.
probes.a: A high ulnar nerve lesion at or above the elbow produces less clawing of the fingers than a low lesion at the wrist, because the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus is paralyzed, removing the deep flexor force that curls the interphalangeal joints.

probes.q: Why does claw hand deformity affect the ring and little fingers much more severely than the index and middle fingers in an isolated ulnar nerve injury?
probes.a: The third and fourth lumbricals (ring and little fingers) are innervated by the ulnar nerve and paralyzed, while the first and second lumbricals (index and middle fingers) are innervated by the intact median nerve and continue to extend their IP joints.

teach.heading: Pathomechanics of the claw hand deformity
teach.body: Lumbricals and interossei normally flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend both proximal and distal interphalangeal joints via the extensor expansion. In ulnar paralysis, loss of these intrinsic muscles allows the unopposed long extensor (extensor digitorum communis) to hyperextend the MCP joints, while unopposed long flexors pull the IP joints into acute flexion, producing the claw hand.

teach.heading: Clinical tests for intrinsic ulnar muscles

rows: Card pulled out easily without resistance
Weak abduction, visible guttering in web spaces
Key pinch grip with flat extended thumb
Thumb IP joint flexes acutely (FPL substitution)
Side to side middle finger movement
Inability to swing middle finger off table plane

teach.heading: The ulnar paradox explained
teach.body: The ulnar paradox describes a counterintuitive surgical rule: the higher the nerve lesion, the less severe the deformity. In low lesions at the wrist, intrinsic muscles are paralyzed but the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus remains active, pulling the denervated ring and little fingers into acute clawing. In high lesions at the elbow, FDP is also paralyzed, relaxing the interphalangeal joints and lessening the claw deformity.

skill.exam.surg.common_peroneal_nerve.title: Examination of the common peroneal nerve
skill.exam.surg.common_peroneal_nerve.oneLine: Demonstrate foot drop, test tibialis anterior and eversion, and map first dorsal web space sensation
skill.exam.surg.common_peroneal_nerve.why: The common peroneal (lateral popliteal) nerve is the most frequently injured nerve in the lower extremity due to its subcutaneous winding around the fibular neck. Missing early foot drop or confusing it with an L5 radiculopathy leads to delayed surgical decompression or irreversible equinovarus deformity.

steps.text: Observe the patient's gait: look for classical high-stepping (cock-walk / equine) gait where the patient lifts the knee excessively high to prevent the dropped, inverted toes from scraping along the ground.
Inspect the resting attitude of the foot: note the talipes equinovarus posture with the foot dropped into plantarflexion and inversion.
Inspect the anterolateral compartment of the lower leg for muscle wasting of tibialis anterior and the peroneal muscles.
Test tibialis anterior (deep peroneal nerve): have the patient actively dorsiflex the ankle against your resistance, observing and palpating the tendon as it crosses the anterior ankle.
Test extensor hallucis longus (deep peroneal nerve): instruct the patient to actively dorsiflex the great toe towards the ceiling against resistance.

Test peroneus longus and brevis (superficial peroneal nerve): have the patient actively evert the foot against resistance with the ankle in plantarflexion, palpating the peroneal tendons behind the lateral malleolus.
Test the autonomous sensory zone of the deep peroneal nerve: test light touch and pinprick over the dorsal first web space between the first and second toes on the foot.

Test the sensory distribution of the superficial peroneal nerve: test light touch over the lower anterolateral calf and the dorsum of the foot, noting preservation of the lateral border (sural nerve) and medial border (saphenous nerve).
Palpate the common peroneal nerve as it winds subcutaneous and superficial around the lateral aspect of the neck of the fibula for thickening, tenderness, or a positive Tinel sign.

skill.exam.surg.common_peroneal_nerve.normal: Normal heel-strike gait without foot drop; powerful ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension, and foot eversion; intact sensation over the dorsal first web space and foot dorsum; non-tender nerve at fibular neck.
skill.exam.surg.common_peroneal_nerve.abnormal: High-stepping gait, foot drop in equinovarus, complete inability to dorsiflex or evert the foot, wasting of anterolateral leg muscles, and sensory loss over the first dorsal web space and foot dorsum.
skill.exam.surg.common_peroneal_nerve.significance: Foot drop with loss of eversion confirms common peroneal nerve lesion. Preserved foot inversion (tibialis posterior, supplied by tibial nerve) distinguishes common peroneal palsy from an L5 root lesion (which paralyzes both dorsiflexion and inversion).
skill.exam.surg.common_peroneal_nerve.practice: Practise examining the common peroneal nerve on colleagues, contrasting deep peroneal (dorsiflexion) with superficial peroneal (eversion) motor testing and palpating the nerve trunk at the fibular neck.
pitfalls: Failing to test foot inversion (tibialis posterior), which is normal in common peroneal palsy but weak in an L5 radiculopathy.
Missing iatrogenic nerve compression caused by a tight plaster cast, splint, or incorrect leg positioning during lithotomy or prolonged lateral decubitus.
Testing sensory loss on the sole of the foot, which is supplied by the tibial nerve and unaffected in peroneal injury.

rubric.text: Observes gait for characteristic high-stepping compensatory foot drop
Tests ankle dorsiflexion against resistance to assess deep peroneal nerve
Tests foot eversion against resistance to assess superficial peroneal nerve
Palpates common peroneal nerve trunk at the neck of the fibula for tenderness
Maps sensory loss over the first dorsal web space and dorsum of the foot

probes.q: Why does a patient with common peroneal nerve injury walk with a high-stepping gait?
probes.a: Due to paralysis of the ankle and toe dorsiflexors (foot drop), the patient must excessively flex the hip and knee to lift the dangling foot clear of the ground and prevent tripping.

probes.q: Where is the autonomous sensory zone of the deep peroneal nerve on the foot?
probes.a: The dorsal first web space on the skin between the great toe and the second toe.

probes.q: How do you distinguish a common peroneal nerve lesion at the fibular neck from an L5 lumbar nerve root radiculopathy?
probes.a: Test foot inversion: in common peroneal nerve palsy, tibialis posterior is innervated by the tibial nerve and inversion is preserved; in an L5 radiculopathy, both dorsiflexion and foot inversion are paralyzed.

teach.heading: Vulnerable anatomy of the common peroneal nerve
teach.body: The common peroneal nerve diverges from the sciatic nerve in the upper popliteal fossa, passes along the medial border of biceps femoris, and winds around the lateral surface of the fibular neck directly beneath the skin and deep fascia. It then pierces peroneus longus, dividing into deep and superficial peroneal branches. Its superficial bony location makes it exceedingly vulnerable to direct blows, lacerations, and cast pressure.

rows: Tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL, peroneus tertius, EDB
Dorsal first web space between toes 1 and 2
Lower anterolateral leg and dorsum of foot
Both deep and superficial branches paralyzed
Complete foot drop in equinovarus deformity
Entire dorsum of foot and first web space

teach.heading: Differentiating peripheral palsy from radiculopathy
teach.body: Foot drop is a frequent clinical dilemma. An L5 radiculopathy paralyzes both ankle dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior) and foot inversion (tibialis posterior), and may impair hip abduction (gluteus medius). In contrast, a common peroneal nerve lesion paralyzes dorsiflexion and eversion while leaving foot inversion perfectly preserved, because tibialis posterior is innervated by the tibial nerve.

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.nerve_thickening_tinel.title: Palpation of thickened nerves and Tinel's sign
skill.exam.surg.nerve_thickening_tinel.oneLine: Palpate peripheral nerve trunks for leprous thickening and elicit Tinel's percussion sign for regenerating axons
skill.exam.surg.nerve_thickening_tinel.why: Palpation of peripheral nerve trunks identifies leprosy (the commonest non-traumatic cause of peripheral neuropathy in India) and localises nerve sheath tumours. Tinel's sign maps the advancing front of regenerating sensory axons, allowing the clinician to objectively track nerve recovery or diagnose entrapment without invasive studies.

steps.text: Position the patient comfortably with the neck, upper limbs, and lower limbs relaxed and adequately exposed.

Palpate the greater auricular nerve: turn the patient's head to the opposite side to make the sternocleidomastoid prominent; roll your fingers across the muscle where the nerve crosses obliquely towards the ear lobe.

Palpate the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus: flex the elbow slightly and roll the nerve gently against the retrocondylar groove, assessing thickness, consistency, nodularity, and tenderness compared to the contralateral side.
Palpate the superficial radial nerve: roll your fingers over the lateral border of the radius five to eight centimetres proximal to the radial styloid process.
Palpate the common peroneal nerve: roll the nerve against the bone just behind and below the head and neck of the fibula.
Palpate the posterior tibial nerve: feel behind and below the medial malleolus at the ankle.

Elicit Tinel's sign: identify the anatomical course of the injured or regenerating nerve; begin tapping lightly with the tip of your index finger or a reflex hammer far distally and advance systematically proximal toward the site of injury.
Ask the patient to report the precise instant a tingling, electric shock-like sensation (pins and needles) shoots into the cutaneous distribution of the nerve.
Mark the most distal point along the nerve course where tapping elicits paresthesia, and measure its distance from the repair site to document the rate of axonal regeneration over serial visits.

skill.exam.surg.nerve_thickening_tinel.normal: Nerves are smooth, non-tender, cord-like, uniform in caliber matching the opposite side, and free from nodularity; light percussion produces no radiating electric paresthesias (Tinel sign negative).
skill.exam.surg.nerve_thickening_tinel.abnormal: Enlarged, thickened, irregular, tender, or beaded nerve trunks (characteristic of leprosy); positive Tinel sign with tingling radiating into the sensory autonomous zone upon gentle percussion over the nerve trunk.
skill.exam.surg.nerve_thickening_tinel.significance: Thickened peripheral nerves in an Indian patient with hypopigmented anesthetic skin patches confirm leprosy. An advancing Tinel sign indicates regenerating sensory axons progressing down the distal nerve sheath (typically one millimetre per day). A stationary Tinel sign at a repair site indicates an obstruction or neuroma requiring surgical re-exploration.
skill.exam.surg.nerve_thickening_tinel.practice: Practise palpating the greater auricular, ulnar, and common peroneal nerves on colleagues, mastering light rolling palpation against bony surfaces without causing discomfort, and elicit Tinel's sign over the median nerve at the wrist.
pitfalls: Tapping too forcefully during Tinel testing, which mechanically stimulates normal axons and produces false-positive paresthesias.
Advancing from proximal to distal instead of distal to proximal during Tinel testing, which stimulates the proximal neuroma prematurely and prevents accurate localisation of the advancing axon front.
Overlooking greater auricular nerve enlargement in suspected leprosy because the neck was not examined.

rubric.text: Palpates greater auricular nerve crossing the sternocleidomastoid correctly
Palpates ulnar nerve in the retrocondylar groove assessing thickness and nodularity
Palpates common peroneal nerve against the fibular neck
Performs Tinel percussion systematically from distal to proximal
Identifies and measures the advancing front of regenerating axons

probes.q: What does Tinel's sign signify after peripheral nerve suture?
probes.a: It indicates the presence of growing, unmyelinated or thinly myelinated sensory axon sprouts that are sensitive to mechanical percussion as they regenerate down the distal nerve sheath.

probes.q: Why must Tinel's percussion be performed from distal to proximal along the nerve course?
probes.a: To locate the most advanced distal point reached by regenerating axons; tapping proximally first stimulates all downstream axons and prevents identifying the true regenerating front.

probes.q: Name four peripheral nerve trunks that should be routinely palpated for thickening in suspected leprosy in India.
probes.a: The ulnar nerve at the elbow, the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck, the greater auricular nerve on the sternocleidomastoid, and the superficial radial nerve at the wrist.

teach.heading: Mechanism and clinical utility of Tinel's sign
teach.body:
Described by Jules Tinel, this sign relies on the mechanical hypersensitivity of regenerating unmyelinated axon sprouts. Gentle percussion over these fine sprouts triggers action potentials that travel centrally, perceived by the patient as tingling in the cutaneous sensory distribution.

Tracking the distal movement of Tinel's sign at sequential clinical visits confirms axonal regeneration at approximately one millimetre per day.

rows: Roll gently over muscle belly with head turned
Pearly beaded enlargement in tuberculoid leprosy
Roll with elbow flexed; note nodularity and pain
Claw hand deformity, hypothenar sensory loss
Winding around lateral aspect of fibular neck
Compress against fibular neck below joint line
Foot drop, trophic ulceration on dorsum of foot
Over radius 5 cm proximal to radial styloid
Sensory patch over dorsal first web space

teach.heading: Stationary versus advancing Tinel sign
teach.body: The behavior of Tinel's sign over time carries immense prognostic value. If the tingling sign advances progressively down the limb, nerve regeneration is proceeding satisfactorily. If Tinel's sign remains arrested at the site of trauma or suture line after two to three months, the axon sprouts are blocked by dense intraneural fibrosis (amputation neuroma), indicating that re-exploration and grafting are required.

skill.annex.surg.seddon_sunderland.title: Seddon and Sunderland classifications of nerve injury
skill.annex.surg.seddon_sunderland.oneLine: Classifications correlating anatomical tissue disruption with electrophysiological recovery and surgical prognosis
skill.annex.surg.seddon_sunderland.why: Sir Herbert Seddon in clinical practice and Sir Sydney Sunderland in subsequent anatomical studies established the definitive histological and prognostic classifications of peripheral nerve trauma. These classifications dictate whether a nerve injury will recover spontaneously or requires urgent microsurgical exploration and nerve grafting.

rows: Focal demyelination; axon and connective tissue sheaths completely intact
Complete spontaneous recovery within days to weeks; surgery contraindicated
Axonal transection with Wallerian degeneration; endoneurial tubes intact
Complete recovery at 1 mm/day; excellent functional alignment without surgery
Axon and endoneurial sheath disrupted; perineurium and epineurium intact
Incomplete recovery due to intrafascicular fibrosis and axon misdirection
Complete fascicular disruption; epineurium intact; scarred neuromas-in-continuity
No spontaneous recovery; requires surgical excision of neuroma and nerve grafting
Complete anatomical transection of axon and all connective tissue sheaths
Zero recovery without surgery; requires immediate microsurgical direct suture or graft

skill.annex.surg.seddon_sunderland.practice: Map five clinical nerve injury scenarios into their exact Seddon and Sunderland grades, stating whether Wallerian degeneration occurs and predicting the necessity for surgical intervention.
pitfalls: Confusing second-degree axonotmesis (endoneurium intact, perfect recovery) with fourth-degree injury (scarred neuroma, requires resection and grafting).
Believing that Wallerian degeneration occurs in neurapraxia (it occurs only when the axon is physically disrupted in second degree and higher).
Operating prematurely on closed fracture-associated nerve injuries that represent second-degree axonotmesis capable of spontaneous regeneration.

rubric.text: Defines the three classic Seddon categories: neurapraxia, axonotmesis, and neurotmesis
Correlates Seddon types with the five anatomical Sunderland grades
Identifies which injury grades undergo distal Wallerian degeneration

probes.q: What defines neurapraxia in Seddon's classification?
probes.a: A temporary physiological conduction block due to focal myelin damage, with intact axons and connective tissue sheaths, resulting in rapid and complete spontaneous recovery without Wallerian degeneration.

probes.q: What is the key pathological difference between Sunderland second-degree and third-degree axonotmesis?
probes.a: In second-degree injury, the endoneurial tube remains intact, guiding regenerating axons perfectly to their original targets; in third-degree injury, the endoneurium is ruptured, causing intrafascicular scarring and axonal misdirection.

probes.q: Why does Sunderland fifth-degree neurotmesis have zero potential for spontaneous functional recovery?
probes.a: Because the nerve trunk and all supporting connective tissue sheaths are completely transected, leaving a physical gap that fills with fibrous scar tissue through which advancing axons cannot navigate without surgical repair.

teach.heading: Histological anatomy of peripheral nerve sheaths
teach.body: An individual nerve axon is surrounded by Schwann cells and wrapped in endoneurium. Multiple axons are bundled into fascicles bounded by the blood-nerve barrier of the perineurium. Multiple fascicles embedded in loose vascular connective tissue are enclosed by the tough outer epineurium. Sunderland grades describe damage penetrating progressively deeper through these connective tissue barriers.

teach.heading: Wallerian degeneration sequence
points: Within 24 to 48 hours of axonal transection, the axon skeleton and neurofilaments fragment distal to the injury.
The myelin sheath breaks down into fatty droplets, and Schwann cells proliferate into longitudinal columns (bands of Bungner).
Macrophages clear myelin debris over two to three weeks, leaving hollowed endoneurial tubes ready to receive new axonal sprouts.
Proximal axon sprouts advance at approximately 1 mm per day (about 1 inch per month) until end-organs are reinnervated.

teach.heading: Electrodiagnostic timing and reaction of degeneration
teach.body: Following axonal interruption, denervated muscle fibers become hypersensitive, exhibiting spontaneous fibrillations and positive sharp waves on electromyography (EMG). These electrical changes require ten to twenty-one days to develop. Performing EMG immediately after acute trauma is uninformative because Wallerian degeneration is incomplete; baseline electrodiagnostic testing should be scheduled three weeks post-injury.

skill.hx.surg.tendon_fascia_disorders.title: History of tendon, muscle, and fascial disorders
skill.hx.surg.tendon_fascia_disorders.oneLine: Elicit pain patterns, repetitive mechanical stress, clicking or locking, and functional finger contractures
skill.hx.surg.tendon_fascia_disorders.why: Tendon, muscle, and fascial disorders are primarily diagnosed through functional mechanical history. Correlating pain with specific resisted joint motions distinguishes enthesopathies (tennis elbow, golfer's elbow) from intra-articular arthritis, and distinguishes stenosing tenosynovitis from fixed joint contractures.

asks.text: What is the exact site of pain, and does it flare with specific repetitive manual actions (e.g. gripping, racquet sports, typing, or prolonged walking)?
In shoulder pain, does the pain catch during the middle phase of lifting your arm sideways, and does it wake you when lying on that side?
In elbow or wrist pain, does discomfort worsen when extending your wrist backwards (tennis elbow) or flexing it forwards against resistance (golfer's elbow)?
Does any digit catch, click, or lock in the palm when you bend your fingers, requiring you to pry it straight with your other hand (trigger finger)?
Have you noticed thick painless cords or puckering in your palm that gradually pull your ring or little finger down towards the palm (Dupuytren's contracture)?
Do you wake at night with burning pain, tingling, or numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers that improves when you shake your hand (carpal tunnel syndrome)?

skill.hx.surg.tendon_fascia_disorders.practice: Rehearse taking a musculoskeletal history from a partner presenting with hand or elbow pain, differentiating local tendonitis from nerve entrapment and inflammatory arthritis.
pitfalls: Mistaking the nocturnal dysesthesias of carpal tunnel syndrome for cervical radiculopathy without asking about the hand-shaking sign.
Failing to ask about sudden popping sensations in the calf or upper arm during strenuous exertion (Achilles or biceps tendon rupture).
Treating a trigger finger as arthritis without inquiring about mechanical locking or snapping on awakening.

rubric.text: Correlates pain with specific resisted joint movements and mechanical strain
Specifically screens for digital snapping, clicking, or locking (trigger digit)
Elicits onset, progression, and digit involvement in palmar fascial thickening
Inquires about nocturnal numbness and wrist splinting response in carpal tunnel syndrome

probes.q: What symptom in the morning is characteristic of a trigger finger?
probes.a: The affected finger is locked in flexion upon waking and snaps straight abruptly or must be straightened forcefully with the other hand.

probes.q: How does the pain of plantar fasciitis characteristically behave during the day?
probes.a: Pain is most excruciating upon taking the very first steps out of bed in the morning or after resting, gradually eases with walking, and worsens again after prolonged standing.

probes.q: What conditions are classically associated with Dupuytren's diathesis?
probes.a: Liver cirrhosis, chronic epilepsy treated with phenytoin, diabetes mellitus, heavy alcohol consumption, and fibromatoses such as Ledderhose disease and Peyronie disease.

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of overuse enthesopathies
teach.body: Enthesopathy represents inflammation and micro-tearing at the insertion of tendons or ligaments into bone. Repetitive eccentric loads exceed the tensile strength of the tendon origin, triggering avascular degeneration and fibroblastic repair rather than acute inflammatory infiltration. Understanding which muscle group originates from a bony epicondyle immediately explains why resisted wrist extension strains the lateral epicondyle.

teach.heading: Symptom profiles of common tendon and fascial conditions

rows: Inability to lift a kettle or turn a doorknob
Localized ache during pull or swing actions
Pain pinching objects or lifting an infant
Sharp stabbing heel pain taking first steps

teach.heading: Mechanical locking versus fixed contracture
teach.body: It is clinically vital to distinguish dynamic stenosing tenosynovitis from static fascial contracture. In trigger finger, the finger moves normally until a swollen nodule on the flexor tendon impacts against the tight A1 pulley, catching the finger in flexion. In Dupuytren's contracture, irreversible shortening of palmar fascial pretendinous cords mechanically tethers the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints.
