skill.exam.surg.tendinitis_enthesopathy.title: Examination of tendinitis and enthesopathies
skill.exam.surg.tendinitis_enthesopathy.oneLine: Demonstrate the painful arc of supraspinatus, Cozen's tennis elbow test, golfer's elbow, and plantar fascia tenderness
skill.exam.surg.tendinitis_enthesopathy.why: Enthesopathies and tendinopathies cause disabling pain that is easily misdiagnosed as joint arthritis or cervical radiculopathy. Systematic provocation tests (painful arc, Cozen test, medial epicondyle stress, and calcaneal palpation) isolate the precise tendon insertion and prevent unnecessary intra-articular interventions.

steps.text: For supraspinatus tendinitis, observe the patient actively abduct the arm from zero to one hundred and eighty degrees in the scapular plane: look for the classical painful arc between sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees, with no pain from zero to sixty degrees and easing of pain above one hundred and twenty degrees.

Palpate the insertion of the supraspinatus tendon: place your thumb just below the anterior edge of the acromion on the greater tuberosity with the patient's arm held in passive extension and internal rotation; elicit localized tenderness.
For lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), palpate the lateral epicondyle of the humerus and common extensor origin: identify maximal tenderness just anterior and distal to the epicondylar tip.

Perform Cozen's test for tennis elbow: stabilize the patient's elbow with your thumb over the lateral epicondyle, instruct the patient to make a fist, pronate the forearm, and radially deviate and extend the wrist against your firm downward resistance; observe for sudden sharp pain at the lateral epicondyle.
Perform Mills' test: passively pronate the forearm, flex the wrist fully, and extend the elbow; observe for exacerbation of lateral epicondylar pain.

For medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow), palpate the medial epicondyle for focal tenderness; instruct the patient to supinate the forearm and flex the wrist against resistance, observing for sharp medial epicondylar pain.

For plantar fasciitis, position the patient supine or prone, dorsiflex the toes with one hand to tighten the plantar aponeurosis (windlass mechanism), and palpate with your thumb firmly over the anteromedial aspect of the plantar calcaneal tuberosity to elicit focal tenderness.

For Achilles tendinitis, palpate the Achilles tendon two to six centimetres proximal to its calcaneal insertion between your thumb and index finger: elicit focal tenderness and palpable nodular thickening that moves with tendon excursion.

skill.exam.surg.tendinitis_enthesopathy.normal: Full, smooth, pain-free active shoulder abduction without a painful arc; no epicondylar tenderness during resisted wrist extension or flexion; non-tender plantar calcaneal insertion and Achilles tendon.
skill.exam.surg.tendinitis_enthesopathy.abnormal: Painful arc between sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees of shoulder abduction; severe localized pain at the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist extension (positive Cozen test); sharp medial epicondylar pain on resisted wrist flexion; point tenderness on the plantar calcaneal tuberosity; and tender nodular Achilles thickening.
skill.exam.surg.tendinitis_enthesopathy.significance: A painful arc indicates subacromial impingement and supraspinatus tendinopathy. Cozen's test confirms lateral epicondylitis (extensor carpi radialis brevis origin). Medial epicondyle pain confirms golfer's elbow (pronator teres / flexor carpi radialis origin). Plantar calcaneal tenderness confirms plantar fasciitis.
skill.exam.surg.tendinitis_enthesopathy.practice: Practise performing Cozen's and Mills' tests for tennis elbow, the painful arc test for supraspinatus tendinitis, and the windlass palpation test for plantar fasciitis on clinical colleagues.
pitfalls: Testing tennis elbow with the elbow flexed, which reduces tension on the extensor carpi radialis brevis and produces false-negative results.
Confusing supraspinatus tendon rupture (inability to initiate abduction, zero to thirty degrees) with tendinitis (painful arc between sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees).
Palpating the posterior calcaneum instead of the plantar anteromedial tubercle when examining for plantar fasciitis.

rubric.text: Evaluates active shoulder abduction, identifying pain between sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees
Performs Cozen's test with resisted wrist extension and pronated forearm
Tests medial epicondyle with resisted wrist flexion and forearm supination
Palpates anteromedial calcaneal tuberosity with dorsiflexed toes (windlass mechanism)
Palpates Achilles tendon two to six centimetres proximal to insertion for tender nodules

probes.q: What defines the painful arc syndrome in supraspinatus tendinitis?
probes.a: Shoulder abduction is painless from zero to sixty degrees, becomes painful between sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees as the degenerated tendon is compressed beneath the acromion, and eases above one hundred and twenty degrees.

probes.q: Which specific tendon origin is primarily involved in tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis)?
probes.a: The extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon at its attachment to the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.

probes.q: How does the windlass mechanism assist in clinical testing for plantar fasciitis?
probes.a: Passive dorsiflexion of the metatarsophalangeal joints winds the plantar fascia around the metatarsal heads, tightening the aponeurosis and reproducing pain at its calcaneal insertion.

teach.heading: Biomechanics of the subacromial painful arc
teach.body: The supraspinatus initiates the first fifteen to thirty degrees of shoulder abduction before the deltoid takes over. As the humerus elevates between sixty and one hundred and twenty degrees, the greater tuberosity rotates beneath the rigid coracoacromial arch. In supraspinatus tendinopathy, this narrows the subacromial space, pinching the swollen, degenerated tendon and overlying subacromial bursa and eliciting acute pain.

rows: Resisted active wrist extension and radial deviation
Sharp pain at lateral epicondyle (tennis elbow)
Passive extension of elbow with wrist flexed
Tension stretch reproduces lateral epicondyle pain
Resisted active wrist flexion and pronation
Sharp pain at medial epicondyle (golfer's elbow)
Resisted active extension of middle finger

teach.heading: Achilles tendinopathy and critical hypovascular zone
teach.body: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the human body, but possesses a relatively avascular watershed zone located two to six centimetres proximal to its calcaneal insertion. Repetitive microtrauma in runners or unaccustomed walking causes micro-tears and non-inflammatory mucoid degeneration (tendinosis) in this zone, presenting as a tender spindle-shaped swelling that moves with ankle excursion.

skill.exam.surg.dequervain_trigger_finge.title: Examination of stenosing tenovaginitis: De Quervain's and trigger finger
skill.exam.surg.dequervain_trigger_finge.oneLine: Perform Finkelstein's test for De Quervain's disease and demonstrate the A1 pulley nodule and snapping in trigger finger
skill.exam.surg.dequervain_trigger_finge.why: Stenosing tenovaginitis results from friction between tendons and thickened fibrous sheaths. Performing Finkelstein's test incorrectly causes false-positive results, while failing to palpate the flexor tendon nodule in trigger finger leads to confusing dynamic snapping with an irreducible joint dislocation.

steps.text: For suspected De Quervain's tenosynovitis, inspect the radial border of the wrist over the radial styloid process for visible swelling or fullness.
Palpate the first dorsal extensor compartment (containing abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis) directly over the radial styloid for localized tenderness and thickening.
Perform Finkelstein's test: instruct the patient to fold the thumb across the palm, curl the fingers firmly over the thumb to form a fist, and steady the forearm.
With the patient's fist closed over the tucked thumb, passively deviate the wrist sharply in an ulnar direction.
Observe the patient's response: sharp, excruciating pain localized precisely over the radial styloid confirms a positive Finkelstein test.

For trigger finger or trigger thumb, inspect the affected digit during active flexion and extension: observe whether the digit moves smoothly or hitches, catches, and snaps abruptly into extension like a trigger.
Palpate the palmar aspect of the hand directly over the metacarpophalangeal joint: feel for a firm, tender, rounded nodule on the flexor tendon sheath at the level of the A1 pulley.
Keep your palpating finger over the nodule while the patient actively flexes and extends the digit: feel the nodule snap underneath your finger as it forces its way through the constricted A1 pulley.
If the digit becomes locked in flexion, determine whether the patient can release it by powerful extensor effort or requires gentle passive extension with the other hand.

skill.exam.surg.dequervain_trigger_finge.normal: Painless ulnar deviation of the wrist with tucked thumb; smooth, silent digital flexion and extension without catching or palpable nodules over flexor sheaths.
skill.exam.surg.dequervain_trigger_finge.abnormal: Agonizing sharp pain over the radial styloid on passive ulnar wrist deviation with thumb tucked in fist (positive Finkelstein test); palpable tender nodule over the A1 pulley with audible and tactile clicking, popping, or locking in flexion.
skill.exam.surg.dequervain_trigger_finge.significance: A positive Finkelstein test confirms stenosing tenovaginitis of the first extensor compartment (De Quervain's disease). A palpable nodule with snapping confirms trigger finger (stenosing tenovaginitis of the flexor tendon sheath at the A1 pulley), indicating readiness for pulley release.
skill.exam.surg.dequervain_trigger_finge.practice: Practise performing Finkelstein's test correctly on colleagues and palpating the A1 pulley over the metacarpal head in surgical outpatients presenting with digital clicking.
pitfalls: Deviating the wrist without having the thumb tucked inside the closed fingers, which fails to stretch the first dorsal compartment tendons.
Confusing De Quervain's disease with osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint.
Forcing open a locked trigger digit violently, which risks acute tendon rupture or joint sprain.

rubric.text: Palpates first dorsal extensor compartment directly over the radial styloid process
Executes Finkelstein's test with thumb tucked into fist followed by passive ulnar deviation
Confirms that sharp pain localises strictly to the radial styloid process
Palpates palmar aspect of MCP joint over the A1 pulley for a tender nodule
Demonstrates mechanical hitching, popping, or locking during digital movement

probes.q: How is Finkelstein's test performed for De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
probes.a: The patient folds the thumb into the palm, closes the fingers tightly over it to make a fist, and the examiner passively deviates the wrist into ulnar deviation, producing sharp pain over the radial styloid.

probes.q: Which two tendons pass through the first extensor compartment of the wrist in De Quervain's disease?
probes.a: The abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) tendons.

probes.q: What is the anatomical mechanism of snapping in trigger finger?
probes.a: A focal reactive nodular thickening on the flexor tendon becomes caught proximal to the constricted, thickened A1 pulley; powerful flexors force the nodule through into the palm, but weaker extensors fail to pull it back, snapping abruptly or locking.

teach.heading: Pathoanatomy of the first dorsal extensor compartment
teach.body: The extensor retinaculum at the wrist binds extensor tendons into six distinct fibro-osseous compartments. The first compartment lies directly over the radial styloid process and transmits abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. Repetitive thumb abduction and wrist deviation cause friction, sheath thickening, and narrowing of the tunnel lumen, frequently with an internal fibrous septum that must be divided during surgical decompression.

teach.heading: Eichhoff versus Finkelstein test nuances
teach.body: In classic surgical literature, tucking the thumb into the fist followed by passive ulnar deviation is termed the Eichhoff manoeuvre, while Fritz de Quervain's original sign described active ulnar traction. In modern surgical examinations and textbooks, folding the thumb inside the fingers and passively deviating the wrist ulnarward is universally evaluated as Finkelstein's test. Pain must localize strictly over the radial styloid.

teach.heading: Anatomy of the flexor pulley system in trigger finger

rows: Primary site of thickening and stenosis
Never divided during trigger finger release
Impacts against proximal edge of A1 pulley
Congenital nodule in paediatric trigger thumb
Causes fixed flexion deformity of thumb IP joint

skill.exam.surg.dupuytren_contracture.title: Examination of Dupuytren's contracture
skill.exam.surg.dupuytren_contracture.oneLine: Inspect palmar nodules and cords, test skin tethering, and perform Hueston's table top test
skill.exam.surg.dupuytren_contracture.why: Dupuytren's contracture is a progressive fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar aponeurosis. Differentiating pretendinous cord contractures from flexor tendon adhesions or spastic contractures governs surgical timing, where Hueston's table top test indicates when fasciectomy or collagenase injection is mandatory.

steps.text: Position the patient seated with both hands resting palm up on the examining table under direct overhead lighting.
Inspect the palmar skin: look for firm nodules, longitudinal pretendinous cords, skin puckering, deep pits, and flexion deformities of the fingers.
Note which fingers are affected: observe that the ring finger is most commonly involved, followed in frequency by the little finger, middle finger, and thumb.
Palpate the palmar aponeurosis: feel the hard, non-tender nodules and follow the thick fibrous cords extending from the mid-palm into the proximal and middle phalanges of the affected digits.
Test skin tethering: observe that the palmar skin is firmly adherent and anchored to the underlying fibrotic cords, unlike tendon swellings where the skin moves freely.
Measure joint flexion contractures using a goniometer: record passive extension deficit at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints.
Perform Hueston's table top test: instruct the patient to place the hand flat on a firm, hard tabletop with the palm facing down, and attempt to flatten the palm completely against the table surface.
Observe whether the palm and all fingers lie perfectly flat, or whether the hand arches up off the tabletop (positive table top test).

Examine for ectopic fibromatosis elsewhere: inspect the plantar fascia of both feet (Ledderhose disease), the dorsum of the proximal interphalangeal joints for knuckle pads (Garrod pads), and palpate the penis for Peyronie's plaques.

skill.exam.surg.dupuytren_contracture.normal: Smooth, pliable, unpuckered palmar skin; no palpable nodules or fibrous cords; hand lies completely flat on the table with palm and all digits in full contact (Hueston's table top test negative).
skill.exam.surg.dupuytren_contracture.abnormal: Firm palmar nodules, thick pretendinous cords tethering skin, fixed flexion deformity of ring and little fingers, and inability to lay the palm flat on the tabletop (Hueston's table top test positive).
skill.exam.surg.dupuytren_contracture.significance: A positive Hueston table top test is the standard surgical indication for intervention (fasciectomy, fasciotomy, or collagenase). Fixed PIP contractures develop irreversible joint capsule shortening if operation is delayed.
skill.exam.surg.dupuytren_contracture.practice: Practise performing Hueston's table top test and measuring MCP and PIP joint contractures with a goniometer on clinical patients, documenting pretendinous cords and knuckle pads.
pitfalls: Confusing Dupuytren's cords with flexor tendons: flexor tendons lie deep beneath the palmar fascia and move during finger excursion, whereas Dupuytren cords are superficial and fixed to skin.
Waiting until PIP joint contracture exceeds forty-five degrees before referral, after which full joint extension is rarely restored even with radical surgery.
Failing to examine the feet (Ledderhose) and knuckles (Garrod pads) for systemic fibromatosis (Dupuytren diathesis).

rubric.text: Inspects palmar skin for nodules, pretendinous cords, and skin puckering
Palpates cords confirming adherence to skin and lack of movement during flexion
Measures extension deficits at MCP and PIP joints accurately
Performs Hueston's table top test to identify surgical threshold
Examines for associated knuckle pads (Garrod pads) and plantar nodules

probes.q: How is Hueston's table top test performed and what constitutes a positive result?
probes.a: The patient attempts to place the hand completely flat on a tabletop with the palm down; if the fingers or palm arch off the surface due to fixed flexion contracture, the test is positive.

probes.q: How do you distinguish a Dupuytren's cord from a thickened flexor tendon on physical examination?
probes.a: A Dupuytren cord lies in the palmar fascia superficial to the tendons, is firmly tethered to the overlying puckered skin, and does not move when the fingers are passively flexed and extended.

probes.q: What clinical features define Dupuytren's diathesis and what is its prognostic significance?
probes.a: Onset at an early age (under forty), bilateral hand involvement, family history, and ectopic fibromatoses (Garrod knuckle pads, Ledderhose plantar disease, Peyronie disease); it predicts aggressive progression and high surgical recurrence.

teach.heading: Pathology and myofibroblast proliferation
teach.body: First described by Baron Guillaume Dupuytren, this condition involves benign fibroblastic proliferation of the palmar and digital fascia. Normal type I collagen is replaced by type III collagen synthesized by contractile myofibroblasts. Progression proceeds through three histological stages: proliferative (nodule formation), involutional (longitudinal cord alignment), and residual (dense, acellular, contracted collagen scar).

rows: Urgent surgery before collateral ligament shortening
Z-plasty or local flap release required

teach.heading: Clinical significance of Hueston's table top test
teach.body: Hueston's table top test marks the dividing line between observation and surgical intervention. When a patient can no longer place the hand flat on the table, the MCP contracture typically exceeds thirty degrees or the PIP contracture is progressive. At this point, activities of daily living (washing face, shaking hands, putting on gloves) become impaired, and postponing surgery risks permanent articular contracture.

skill.exam.surg.ganglion_cyst.title: Examination of a ganglion cyst
skill.exam.surg.ganglion_cyst.oneLine: Demonstrate a tense cystic swelling, verify transillumination, and test mobility with tendon excursion
skill.exam.surg.ganglion_cyst.why: A ganglion is the commonest benign soft tissue swelling of the hand and wrist. Because the cyst is tensely distended with viscous mucinous fluid, it is frequently mistaken for a solid fibroma or bone tumour unless transillumination is performed and its mobility across versus along tendons is evaluated.

steps.text: Inspect the anatomical location of the swelling: observe whether it lies on the dorsum of the wrist (scapholunate joint), the volar radial wrist (between FCR and radial artery), the flexor tendon sheath of a digit, or the dorsum of the foot.
Inspect the contour, size, and overlying skin: note that the skin is healthy, normal in colour, and not tethered to the underlying lump.
Palpate the swelling for warmth and tenderness: ganglia are non-warm and typically non-tender unless acutely inflamed or compressing a nerve.
Palpate the consistency and borders: note the well-defined, smooth, globular or lobulated shape and distinctly tense, firm consistency that is softest at its centre.
Test for fluctuation: gently press one side of the swelling while feeling for a fluid impulse on the opposite side, noting that high internal fluid tension often makes fluctuation subtle.

Perform transillumination testing: dim the room lights, place a narrow-beam pen torch tightly against one side of the swelling, and observe whether light brilliantly illuminates the entire lump (transillumination positive).
Test mobility in relation to tendons: instruct the patient to keep the fingers relaxed while you move the lump transversely across the tendon and longitudinally along the tendon axis.
Have the patient actively flex and extend the fingers to make the extensor tendons taut: note whether the lump becomes less mobile or completely fixed when the tendon is contracted.
In volar wrist ganglia, carefully palpate the radial pulse adjacent to the cyst to document its anatomical relationship and avoid puncture injury.

skill.exam.surg.ganglion_cyst.normal: Smooth anatomical wrist contours without palpable cysts; no transilluminant subcutaneous lumps; full painless joint and tendon excursion.
skill.exam.surg.ganglion_cyst.abnormal: Smooth, tense, well-circumscribed, painless or mildly tender cystic swelling; brilliantly transilluminant with clear fluid; mobile perpendicular to tendon fibers when relaxed but fixed when tendon is made taut.
skill.exam.surg.ganglion_cyst.significance: Brilliant transillumination confirms a fluid-filled cystic lesion, reliably differentiating a ganglion from a solid giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath or a sarcoma. Reduced mobility upon tendon contraction localises origin to the tendon sheath or joint capsule.
skill.exam.surg.ganglion_cyst.practice: Practise transilluminating wrist swellings in a darkened room using a pencil torch and evaluating cyst mobility before and during active tendon contraction on clinical patients.
pitfalls: Failing to dim ambient lights during transillumination, missing brilliant fluid illumination in a small tense ganglion.
Misdiagnosing a tense ganglion as an osteoma or fibroma because high intracystic pressure masks classic fluctuation.
Attempting blind needle aspiration on a volar wrist ganglion without confirming the exact position of the radial artery.

rubric.text: Identifies precise joint or tendon sheath anatomical relations
Performs transillumination with a pencil torch in a darkened room
Demonstrates smooth margins, firm-cystic consistency, and central softness
Tests mobility transverse versus longitudinal with tendon relaxed and taut
Palpates radial artery in volar wrist swellings to ensure safe margin

probes.q: Why does a ganglion cyst often feel hard and solid rather than fluctuant?
probes.a: The cyst is filled with thick, highly viscous gelatinous fluid under intense hydrostatic pressure within a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, masking conventional fluctuation.

probes.q: What physical sign reliably differentiates a ganglion from a giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath?
probes.a: A ganglion brilliantly transilluminates light because it contains clear gelatinous fluid, whereas a giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath is solid and completely opaque.

probes.q: How does the mobility of a tendon-sheath ganglion change when the underlying muscle contracts?
probes.a: When the tendon is relaxed, the ganglion can be moved slightly from side to side across the tendon; when the tendon is made taut by active contraction, the ganglion becomes completely fixed.

teach.heading: Pathogenesis and structure of a ganglion
teach.body: A ganglion is a non-neoplastic mucinous cyst arising from mucoid degeneration of collagenous tissue in a joint capsule or tendon sheath. Repetitive microtrauma or capsular stretching produces micro-cysts that coalesce into a multilocular cavity lined by compressed fibrous pseudocapsule without an epithelial or synovial lining. A tortuous pedicle frequently connects the cyst base to the underlying joint, acting as a one-way valve.

rows: Lies between EDC and EPL tendons
Adjacent to radial artery and FCR
Small (2 to 5 mm), hard seed ganglion
Painful on gripping hard steering wheel

teach.heading: Diagnostic transillumination technique
teach.body: Transillumination requires a high-intensity pencil torch applied firmly against the margin of the swelling in a dark room. Normal surrounding skin may show faint red glow, but a ganglion exhibits brilliant crystal-clear illumination throughout its entire volume. Solid soft-tissue tumours such as giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath, neurofibroma, or sarcoma absorb light and remain totally opaque.

skill.exam.surg.tendon_rupture_tests.title: Clinical examination for tendon ruptures
skill.exam.surg.tendon_rupture_tests.oneLine: Demonstrate Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test for Achilles rupture and Popeye sign for biceps rupture
skill.exam.surg.tendon_rupture_tests.why: Major tendon ruptures are frequently missed on initial presentation because secondary muscle groups provide compensatory movement. Performing the Simmonds-Thompson test detects complete Achilles tendon rupture where missed diagnosis causes chronic gait disability, while recognizing the Popeye sign distinguishes long head biceps rupture from soft tissue tumours.

steps.text: For suspected Achilles tendon rupture, place the patient in the prone position with both feet hanging freely over the end of the examination couch.
Inspect the posterior calves and ankles: observe for loss of the normal resting ankle equinus tone (the injured foot hangs more vertically in dorsiflexion compared to the healthy foot).
Inspect for a visible dip or depression along the course of the Achilles tendon two to six centimetres above the calcaneal insertion.
Palpate gently along the tendon: feel for a distinct palpable gap or defect in the tendon fibers, frequently accompanied by localized tenderness and hematoma.
Perform Simmonds' / Thompson's calf squeeze test: with the patient prone and feet relaxed over the couch edge, firmly squeeze the middle third of the calf muscle belly with your hand.
Observe the foot: in a healthy limb, squeezing the gastrocnemius-soleus bulk mechanically produces passive plantarflexion of the foot.
In complete Achilles tendon rupture, squeezing the calf produces no plantarflexion of the foot whatsoever (positive Simmonds-Thompson test).

For suspected rupture of the long head of the biceps brachii, inspect the anterior arm: observe for an abnormal distal bunched-up muscular bulge in the lower arm (Popeye muscle sign) that becomes prominent and ball-like when the patient flexes the elbow against resistance.

skill.exam.surg.tendon_rupture_tests.normal: Symmetrical resting ankle equinus; squeezing the calf produces brisk passive plantarflexion of the foot (Simmonds-Thompson test negative); biceps muscle belly remains uniform during resisted elbow flexion.
skill.exam.surg.tendon_rupture_tests.abnormal: Loss of resting ankle equinus with foot hanging in passive dorsiflexion; absence of passive plantarflexion on squeezing the calf (positive Simmonds-Thompson test); palpable gap in Achilles tendon; and ball-like distal muscular bulge on elbow flexion (Popeye sign).
skill.exam.surg.tendon_rupture_tests.significance: A positive Simmonds-Thompson test proves complete Achilles tendon rupture requiring urgent cast immobilization in equinus or surgical repair. The Popeye sign confirms rupture of the long head of the biceps brachii, which is usually managed conservatively in elderly patients but may require tenodesis in active young workers.
skill.exam.surg.tendon_rupture_tests.practice: Practise performing the Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test on colleagues to observe the normal passive plantarflexion response, and rehearse explaining why active plantarflexion can persist via deep flexors.
pitfalls: Ruling out Achilles rupture because the patient can still weakly plantarflex the ankle while non-weight-bearing (mediated by intact deep flexors: tibialis posterior, FHL, and FDL).
Mistaking the bunched-up muscle belly of a ruptured biceps (Popeye sign) for a soft tissue sarcoma of the upper arm.
Squeezing the lower third of the calf or Achilles tendon directly instead of the upper muscular belly during the Thompson test.

rubric.text: Positions patient prone with feet hanging freely over the edge of the couch
Inspects resting ankle posture for loss of normal equinus tone
Palpates Achilles tendon two to six centimetres proximal to calcaneus for a defect
Executes Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test observing for passive plantarflexion
Demonstrates Popeye muscle sign during resisted elbow flexion and supination

probes.q: How is the Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test performed and what is a positive result?
probes.a: With the patient prone and feet hanging over the couch, the examiner squeezes the calf muscle belly; failure of the foot to passively plantarflex indicates complete Achilles tendon rupture.

probes.q: Why can a patient with a completely ruptured Achilles tendon still actively plantarflex the foot when seated on the couch?
probes.a: Deep flexor muscles of the calf (tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and peroneus longus) remain intact and can produce weak non-weight-bearing plantarflexion.

probes.q: What causes the Popeye muscle deformity in the upper arm?
probes.a: Rupture of the long head of the biceps brachii tendon, allowing the muscle belly to retract distally into the lower arm and form a prominent rounded bulge when the elbow is flexed.

teach.heading: Biomechanics of Achilles tendon rupture
teach.body: The Achilles tendon withstands immense tensile forces during sprinting and jumping. Rupture typically strikes middle-aged individuals participating in sudden unaccustomed sports. The patient experiences a sudden violent snap like being kicked in the back of the ankle. The injury occurs through the hypovascular watershed zone two to six centimetres above the calcaneal insertion.

teach.heading: Physical signs in acute Achilles tendon disruption

rows: Inspect feet hanging prone over couch edge
Foot hangs in 20 to 30 degrees of equinus
Foot hangs vertically in increased dorsiflexion
Squeeze mid-calf muscle bulk with hand
Slide finger along Achilles tendon course
Palpable gap with hematoma 2 to 6 cm from heel
Patient attempts to stand on toes of one foot
Inability to lift heel off ground

teach.heading: Rupture of the long head of biceps brachii
teach.body: The long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and passes through the bicipital groove. Chronic impingement beneath the acromion leads to degenerative fraying and eventual rupture during modest lifting. The detached tendon retracts distally, and when the patient flexes the elbow against resistance, the bunched muscle belly forms a conspicuous lump in the lower arm (Popeye sign). Forearm supination is weakened by approximately twenty percent.

skill.hx.surg.bone_pain_swelling.title: History of bone pain and swelling
skill.hx.surg.bone_pain_swelling.oneLine: Analyse patient age, anatomical bone zone, expansion rate, and nocturnal pain pattern
skill.hx.surg.bone_pain_swelling.why: Bony pathologies show strict predilections for specific age groups and anatomical zones (epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis). Eliciting whether swelling is solitary or multiple, rapidly enlarging or indolent, and whether pain is nocturnal or throbbing distinguishes infection from benign and malignant neoplasms prior to radiography.

asks.text: What is your exact age, and when did you first notice this bone swelling or deep ache?
Which bone is affected, and is the swelling located near a joint (metaphysis) or along the mid-shaft (diaphysis)?
Has the swelling grown rapidly over weeks (malignancy, infection) or remained unchanged for years (benign tumour)?
Is the pain worse at night, and does a simple dose of aspirin or paracetamol relieve it completely (suggesting osteoid osteoma)?
Have you had high fevers, chills, weight loss, or previous lung, breast, thyroid, kidney, or prostate cancer?
Did the swelling appear after a minor injury, or did the bone crack during normal activity (pathological fracture)?

skill.hx.surg.bone_pain_swelling.practice: Practise taking a structured bone tumour history, focusing on age brackets, skeletal site, rate of growth, and nocturnal pain.
pitfalls: Attributing a rapidly growing bone swelling entirely to a recent trivial bump or fall rather than considering it an inciting symptom of a tumour.
Failing to ask about night pain relieved by salicylates, which is the classic bedside signature of osteoid osteoma.
Omitting inquiry regarding previous carcinomas of the breast, thyroid, lung, kidney, or prostate that cause secondary bone metastases.

probes.q: Which anatomical zone of long bones is the commonest site for primary osteosarcoma and acute haematogenous osteomyelitis?
probes.a: The metaphysis is the commonest site for both conditions because of its rich vascular hairpin loops and rapid bone turnover.

probes.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with severe bone pain at night that is dramatically relieved by aspirin. What benign lesion should you suspect?
probes.a: Osteoid osteoma, characteristically driven by high prostaglandin production within the vascular radiolucent nidus.

probes.q: Why does a solitary bone swelling in a patient over 50 years of age warrant urgent search for a non-skeletal primary?
probes.a: Metastatic carcinoma and multiple myeloma are far commoner in this age group than primary bone sarcomas, with primary sites in breast, bronchus, prostate, kidney, and thyroid.

rubric.text: Establishes exact age, duration, and anatomical bone segment
Explores nocturnal pain pattern and response to salicylates or analgesics
Differentiates rapid aggressive enlargement from indolent stationary swelling
Screens for constitutional symptoms and primary visceral malignancies

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Age and anatomical zone determine the diagnosis
teach.body:
Primary bone lesions follow defined rules of skeletal maturity. Under 20 years, acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and simple cysts dominate.

Between 20 and 40 years, giant cell tumour (osteoclastoma) emerges after epiphyseal fusion. Over 40 years, secondary metastases and multiple myeloma account for the vast majority of bony lesions.

teach.heading: Pain character reflects underlying pathology
teach.body:
Constant, deep, boring pain that intensifies at night and awakens the patient suggests malignancy or subperiosteal tension from acute infection.

Sharp nocturnal pain relieved within 20 minutes by aspirin suggests osteoid osteoma. Pain starting only after weight-bearing suggests mechanical joint pathology or early stress fracture.

skill.exam.surg.bone_swelling.title: Examination of a bony swelling
skill.exam.surg.bone_swelling.oneLine: Confirm fixity to bone, define margins, test for local warmth, eggshell crackling, and bruit
skill.exam.surg.bone_swelling.why: Differentiating a true bone swelling from an overlying soft tissue mass requires demonstrating that the mass remains fixed to the skeleton in all planes regardless of muscle contraction. Identifying localized warmth, eggshell crackling, dilated veins, and vascular bruits separates aggressive sarcomas from quiescent benign lesions.

steps.text: Expose the entire limb and the contralateral symmetrical limb to compare contour, length, and joint alignment in daylight.
Inspect the swelling for location (epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis), shape, smooth or bosselated surface, skin stretched or shiny, and dilated collateral veins.
Palpate the local skin temperature using the dorsum of the fingers, comparing the swelling directly with the identical area on the opposite limb.
Palpate with overlying muscles completely relaxed to confirm fixity to the underlying cortex in both longitudinal and transverse axes.
Feel the margins to determine if the edge rises smoothly from normal bone (expanded cortex) or blends abruptly into surrounding soft tissues (cortical breach).
Test consistency across the mass: bony hard (osteochondroma), firm and resilient, or springy with eggshell crackling (giant cell tumour).
Auscultate with the stethoscope diaphragm directly over warm, vascular swellings to detect an arterial systolic bruit in vascular osteosarcomas.
Examine the joint immediately proximal and distal to the swelling, and palpate the regional lymph nodes.

skill.exam.surg.bone_swelling.normal: Smooth skeletal contours with no localized elevation, normal skin temperature, absence of venous prominence, and full painless active movement of neighbouring joints.
skill.exam.surg.bone_swelling.abnormal: Fixed bony mass arising from the cortex, localized heat, dilated superficial veins, eggshell crackling, systolic bruit, or restricted range of motion in adjacent joints.
skill.exam.surg.bone_swelling.significance: A warm, rapidly growing metaphyseal mass with dilated veins suggests osteosarcoma. A subarticular mass in a young adult with eggshell crackling indicates giant cell tumour. A pedunculated painless bony mass pointing away from the nearest joint indicates osteochondroma.
skill.exam.surg.bone_swelling.practice: Rehearse palpating bone landmarks and testing fixity across relaxed and contracted muscles, feeling for temperature differences and eggshell crackling.
pitfalls: Failing to relax the overlying muscles, leading to confusion between an intramuscular tumour and a true bony mass.
Omitting temperature assessment with the dorsum of the hand, missing the marked hyperaemia of osteosarcoma or Ewing sarcoma.
Forgetting to auscultate for a systolic bruit over a suspected malignant bone tumour.

probes.q: How do you distinguish a swelling arising from bone from one arising in overlying skeletal muscle?
probes.a: A bone swelling is completely immobile in both longitudinal and transverse planes, and contracting the overlying muscle does not alter its fixity.

probes.q: What pathological process produces eggshell crackling on gentle palpation of a bone swelling?
probes.a: Thinning and expansion of the overlying cortical bone into a delicate parchment-like shell that yields under finger pressure, classic for giant cell tumour.

probes.q: Why may a high-grade telangiectatic osteosarcoma be mistaken clinically for an aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation?
probes.a: It possesses extensive blood-filled vascular spaces that create marked local warmth, prominent dilated veins, arterial pulsation, and a systolic bruit.

rubric.text: Exposes bilaterally and inspects position, shape, skin, and collateral veins
Assesses local temperature and proves absolute bony fixity in two planes
Determines margin definition and feels for bony hardness or eggshell crackling
Auscultates for systolic bruit and checks adjacent joints and regional nodes

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Establishing bony origin
teach.body:
The essential test of a bone swelling is demonstrating that it cannot be moved independently of the skeleton in any direction.

Ask the patient to contract the overlying muscles against resistance. A soft-tissue intramuscular lesion hardens and becomes restricted, while a subcutaneous mass stays mobile. A bony mass remains unchanged and fixed to the skeletal frame.

teach.heading: Consistency provides histological guidance
teach.body:
The tactile feel of a bone lesion directly reflects its mineral content. Hardness like ivory is typical of an osteoma. Firm, resilient lobulation suggests chondroma or chondrosarcoma.

Eggshell crackling happens when an expansile lesion attenuates the cortex to paper thinness, classically in giant cell tumour and aneurysmal bone cyst.

teach.heading: Physical signs of vascularity
teach.body:
Rapidly growing bone sarcomas stimulate dramatic neo-angiogenesis. The examiner detects distinct skin hyperaemia, prominent blue collateral veins draining toward the torso, and an audible systolic bruit.

These vascular signs can be so intense that novice examiners sometimes mistake osteosarcoma for an acute bacterial infection or an arteriovenous fistula.

skill.exam.surg.chronic_osteomyelitis.title: Examination of chronic osteomyelitis and discharging sinuses
skill.exam.surg.chronic_osteomyelitis.oneLine: Inspect puckered scars, palpate irregular thickened bone, and identify sequestrum and cloacae
skill.exam.surg.chronic_osteomyelitis.why: Chronic osteomyelitis follows untreated acute infection or open skeletal trauma, producing persistent bone necrosis and discharging sinuses. Examining for thickened irregular involucrum, deep adherent puckered scars, discharged bone spicules (sequestra), and joint contractures directs surgical sequestrectomy and prevents Marjolin ulceration.

steps.text: Inspect the affected limb for cutaneous sinuses, puckered adherent scars, discoloration, and eczema from chronic purulent discharge.
Examine the active sinus opening: note surrounding pink granulation tissue, skin tethering, and character of the discharge (pus, blood, gritty bone sand).
Palpate the bone shaft along its entire length to appreciate thickened, irregular, widened cortical bone (involucrum formation).
Gently test for localized bone tenderness over the involucrum and around the sinus openings.
Test mobility of the skin and scar over the bone: observe deep puckering where the tract adheres directly to the periosteum.
Assess the active and passive range of motion of the joint immediately proximal and distal to detect stiffness or fixed contractures.
Measure limb length bilaterally to detect shortening from physeal damage or lengthening from chronic hyperaemia.
Inspect long-standing sinuses (>10 years) for everted, raised, indurated edges signaling malignant transformation (Marjolin ulcer).

skill.exam.surg.chronic_osteomyelitis.normal: Smooth, uniform bone contours without cortical thickening, supple freely mobile skin without sinuses or scarring, and equal limb lengths.
skill.exam.surg.chronic_osteomyelitis.abnormal: Widened irregular bone shaft (involucrum), puckered sinus discharging pus and gritty bone fragments, scarred tethered skin, joint stiffness, or limb length discrepancy.
skill.exam.surg.chronic_osteomyelitis.significance: A puckered sinus discharging gritty bone sand confirms a dead piece of bone (sequestrum) encased by new bone (involucrum) with draining holes (cloacae). A long-standing sinus developing raised everted margins indicates squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer).
skill.exam.surg.chronic_osteomyelitis.practice: Practise inspecting sinuses for puckering, palpating thickened irregular bone, and systematically measuring limb length.
pitfalls: Blindly probing a sinus tract with a metal probe at the bedside, which introduces new pathogens and causes severe pain without aiding diagnosis.
Overlooking chronic limb length discrepancy resulting from childhood metaphyseal growth plate involvement.
Failing to inspect the margins of a chronic decades-old discharging sinus for malignant transformation into a squamous cell carcinoma.

probes.q: What is the pathological definition of a sequestrum and an involucrum in chronic osteomyelitis?
probes.a: A sequestrum is a piece of dead necrotic bone separated from living bone; an involucrum is the sheath of new periosteal bone formed around it.

probes.q: Why does a sinus in chronic osteomyelitis typically present with deep skin puckering?
probes.a: The fibrous sinus tract extends directly from the underlying bone and periosteum, tethering and pulling the skin inward as it scars.

probes.q: What dangerous complication should you suspect if a 30-year-old osteomyelitic sinus develops foul-smelling, raised, everted, indurated edges?
probes.a: Marjolin ulcer, which is a squamous cell carcinoma developing in a site of chronic inflammation and scarring.

rubric.text: Inspects sinus for puckering, discharge character, and granulation tissue
Palpates thickened irregular bone shaft and checks skin tethering
Examines adjacent joint mobility and measures limb lengths bilaterally
Screens chronic sinus edges for induration and malignant changes

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Triad of sequestrum, involucrum, and cloaca
teach.body:
When purulent exudate strips the periosteum, cortical bone loses its blood supply and dies, forming a detached piece of dead bone known as a sequestrum.

The elevated periosteum lays down a dense subperiosteal casing of new bone called the involucrum. Defects in the involucrum through which pus and bone fragments escape are cloacae.

teach.heading: Clinical features of the discharging sinus
teach.body:
The osteomyelitic sinus is puckered and depressed because fibrous bands anchor the dermal margin down to the rigid bone cortex.

Discharge is seropurulent and intermittent. Spontaneous discharge of gritty white sand or bony spicules proves that sequestra are actively separating from the living skeletal bed.

teach.heading: Complications of long-standing infection
points: Pathological fracture through a weakened bone segment where involucrum is incomplete.
Amyloidosis (secondary AA type) presenting with proteinuria, hepatosplenomegaly, and renal failure after decades of suppuration.
Joint contractures and stiffness from fibrous ankylosis of neighbouring joints.
Marjolin ulcer: low-grade squamous cell carcinoma arising in the chronic sinus tract epithelium.

skill.annex.surg.bone_tumour_sites.title: Bone tumour localization by anatomical zone and age predilection
skill.annex.surg.bone_tumour_sites.oneLine: Cross-tabulate epiphyseal, metaphyseal, and diaphyseal predilections against age cohorts
skill.annex.surg.bone_tumour_sites.why: Primary bone neoplasms exhibit distinct anatomical predilections within long bones based on local cellular kinetics and blood supply. Correctly categorizing a lesion by its anatomical compartment (epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis) and patient age narrows the differential diagnosis to two or three possibilities before biopsy.

asks.text: What is the exact chronological age of the patient?
Is the lesion centered in the epiphysis, metaphysis, or diaphysis on imaging?
Are the physis plates open or fused?

skill.annex.surg.bone_tumour_sites.practice: Rehearse placing clinical case vignettes of bone tumours into the anatomical zone matrix by age cohort.
pitfalls: Placing giant cell tumour in a child before epiphyseal plate closure; GCT occurs almost exclusively after physeal fusion.
Confusing diaphyseal Ewing sarcoma with acute osteomyelitis because both cause fever, high white cell counts, and bone pain.
Forgetting that secondary metastatic carcinoma is the single commonest malignant bone tumour in adults over 45 years.

probes.q: Name the classic epiphyseal bone tumour occurring in skeletally mature young adults aged 20 to 40 years.
probes.a: Giant cell tumour of bone (osteoclastoma).

probes.q: Name three distinct pathological lesions characteristically found in the metaphysis of growing long bones.
probes.a: Osteosarcoma, acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, osteochondroma, and aneurysmal bone cyst.

probes.q: Which primary malignant bone tumours typically arise within the diaphysis of long bones?
probes.a: Ewing sarcoma, multiple myeloma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma of bone.

rubric.text: Correctly localizes lesion to epiphysis, metaphysis, or diaphysis
Correlates lesion type with patient age and physeal maturity
Derives the top two pathological diagnoses from the matrix

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Classification of bone tumours: site and age

teach.heading: Age cohort distribution of bone tumours
Clinical utility of the zone matrix
teach.body:
The metaphysis possesses high vascular flow and bone remodelling, rendering it prone to osteosarcoma and haematogenous infection.

The epiphysis receives an isolated epiphyseal circulation that supports chondroblastoma and giant cell tumours. The diaphysis houses marrow elements, explaining its predilection for small round blue cell Ewing sarcoma and multiple myeloma.

skill.hx.surg.fracture_injury.title: History of bone and joint trauma
skill.hx.surg.fracture_injury.oneLine: Establish kinetic energy, impact vector, snapping sensation, and pre-existing bone disease
skill.hx.surg.fracture_injury.why: The kinetic energy and vector of mechanical violence distinguish low-energy fragility fractures from high-energy comminuted injuries prone to soft tissue disruption and compartment syndrome. Inquiring about preceding bone ache or minimal trivial trauma identifies pathological fractures.

asks.text: What was the exact mechanism of injury: fall from height, motor vehicle collision, direct blow, or twisting force?
Did you hear or feel an audible snap or crack at the moment of impact?
Were you able to bear weight on the limb immediately after the accident?
Was the violence minor or trivial (such as turning in bed or coughing), suggesting a pathological fracture in weakened bone?
Did you feel numbness, tingling, or severe coldness in the fingers or toes following the injury?
Did the bone end poke through the skin at any stage, or was there an open wound with bleeding?

skill.hx.surg.fracture_injury.practice: Rehearse interrogating an acute trauma patient to extract the velocity, impact vector, snap sensation, and pre-injury status.
pitfalls: Failing to recognize trivial trauma as a hallmark of a pathological fracture through metastasis or osteoporosis.
Accepting 'I fell' without establishing whether the fall was caused by syncope, stroke, or mechanical tripping.
Overlooking distal neurovascular symptoms because the patient is distracted by intense fracture site pain.

probes.q: What fracture pattern is characteristically produced by a twisting or torsional indirect force on a long bone?
probes.a: A spiral fracture.

probes.q: What is the clinical definition of a pathological fracture?
probes.a: A fracture occurring in a bone that is pre-weakened by a local or systemic disease, produced by trivial violence that would not fracture normal bone.

probes.q: Why is an open fracture where a bone spike momentarily pierced the skin and receded still treated as an open contaminated injury?
probes.a: The retreating bone spike carries clothing, soil, and external surface bacteria directly into the deep marrow space and haematoma.

rubric.text: Establishes mechanical force, velocity, and impact vector
Inquires about immediate functional loss and weight-bearing ability
Screens for trivial trauma and pre-existing local bone ache
Inquires about skin puncture, external bleeding, and distal sensation

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
ATLS

teach.heading: Mechanisms of mechanical violence
teach.body:
Fractures result from direct, indirect, or muscular violence. Direct tapping violence causes transverse fractures with localized contusion.

Crushing violence creates comminution and severe soft tissue crushing. Indirect twisting forces cause spiral fractures, while bending forces generate transverse fractures with a triangular butterfly fragment.

teach.heading: Recognizing a pathological fracture
teach.body:
When a bone breaks under trivial stress, such as rolling over in bed or stepping off a low curb, underlying bone pathology must be presumed.

Ask about preceding dull bone aches, unexplained weight loss, or known malignancy. Common culprits include metastatic carcinoma, osteoporosis, Paget disease, and multiple myeloma.

teach.heading: Immediate bedside functional clues
points: An audible snap accompanied by immediate incapacitating pain strongly points to bone disruption.
Inability to bear weight immediately following ankle or leg trauma carries high sensitivity for fracture.
Distal paresthesia or coldness warns of acute vascular entrapment or nerve traction requiring urgent intervention.

skill.exam.surg.fracture_signs.title: Examination of cardinal physical signs of fracture
skill.exam.surg.fracture_signs.oneLine: Identify localized point tenderness, gross deformity, and unnatural mobility without seeking crepitus
skill.exam.surg.fracture_signs.why: Clinical examination confirms skeletal disruption while safeguarding the surrounding soft-tissue envelope. Eliciting unnatural mobility or deliberate bony crepitus causes excruciating pain, tears periosteal vessels, and converts closed fractures into open wounds. Careful inspection and gentle point tenderness palpation establish the diagnosis safely.

steps.text: Inspect the injured limb for visible deformity: angulation, rotation, and shortening compared to the uninjured side.
Inspect the overlying skin for swelling, bruising, ecchymosis, blebs, and open puncture wounds.
Gently palpate along the bone with a single fingertip to locate the exact site of maximum point bone tenderness.
Gently observe for unnatural mobility across a long bone shaft only during necessary splinting, never by deliberate bending.
Do not deliberately rub bone ends together to elicit bone crepitus; note it only if felt incidentally during gentle alignment.
Assess active loss of function: ask the patient to gently move distal joints without manipulating the fracture site.
Immediately evaluate distal peripheral pulses, capillary refill, and motor and sensory nerve function.
Apply a temporary rigid splint to immobilize the joint above and the joint below the fracture before sending for radiographs.

skill.exam.surg.fracture_signs.normal: Anatomical skeletal alignment, non-tender bone shaft on palpation, intact active joint motion, normal distal pulses and sensation.
skill.exam.surg.fracture_signs.abnormal: Visible limb deformity (angulation, rotation, shortening), localized point bone tenderness, unnatural mobility, incidental bone crepitus, loss of function.
skill.exam.surg.fracture_signs.significance: Localized point bone tenderness following trauma is the single most reliable clinical sign of an undisplaced fracture. Deliberately eliciting crepitus or testing unnatural mobility is contraindicated as it risks neurovascular injury and converts closed fractures to open ones.
skill.exam.surg.fracture_signs.practice: Rehearse systematic fracture inspection and gentle point tenderness palpation on clinical simulation models.
pitfalls: Deliberately moving bone ends to elicit crepitus, which tears adjacent nerves and vessels and causes immense pain.
Failing to remove splints or clothing to inspect the entire limb for occult open puncture wounds.
Splinting without immobilizing both the joint above and the joint below the fracture site.

probes.q: What is the single most reliable clinical sign of an undisplaced fracture on physical examination?
probes.a: Localized point bone tenderness directly over the fracture line.

probes.q: Why is testing for bone crepitus strongly condemned in modern trauma management?
probes.a: It causes severe pain, risks shredding adjacent nerves and vessels, and can convert a closed fracture into an open fracture.

probes.q: Which two joints must be immobilized by a splint when managing a fractured long bone shaft?
probes.a: The joint immediately above and the joint immediately below the fracture site.

rubric.text: Inspects for angulation, rotation, shortening, and open puncture wounds
Palpates gently to localize exact point bone tenderness
Avoids deliberate testing of unnatural mobility or bone crepitus
Checks distal neurovascular status and immobilizes joint above and below

sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: The examination of bone and joint injuries: fractures

teach.heading: Cardinal signs of fracture
teach.body:
The classical signs fall into visual and tactile clues. Visible signs include deformity (angulation, rotation, shortening), swelling, and ecchymosis.

Tactile signs include localized point tenderness, unnatural mobility, and bone crepitus. Loss of active movement reflects mechanical discontinuity and pain.

teach.heading: The danger of testing crepitus
teach.body:
Crepitus is the dry, grating sensation produced when fractured bone ends rub together. Historical texts emphasized it, but modern surgical practice forbids eliciting it deliberately.

Attempting to produce crepitus causes agonizing distress and can shred adjacent neurovascular bundles, converting a closed fracture into an open wound.

teach.heading: Rules of splinting
points: Check and document distal pulses and neurological function before placing any splint.
Immobilize the joint above and the joint below the fracture to abolish rotational and shearing forces.
Pad all bony prominences under the splint to prevent pressure necrosis and nerve compression.

skill.exam.surg.neurovascular_injury.title: Distal neurovascular examination and acute compartment syndrome check
skill.exam.surg.neurovascular_injury.oneLine: Document distal pulses, capillary refill, motor-sensory nerves, and pain on passive digital stretch
skill.exam.surg.neurovascular_injury.why: Fractures and dislocations frequently injure adjacent major vessels and nerves (e.g. supracondylar fracture injuring brachial artery; knee dislocation tearing popliteal artery). Missed acute compartment syndrome leads to irreversible muscle necrosis and claw contracture within six hours. Documenting neurovascular status before and after reduction is vital.

steps.text: Palpate distal peripheral pulses (radial and ulnar in upper limb; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial in lower limb) and compare amplitude bilaterally.
Assess capillary refill time in all digits by compressing the nail bed for five seconds and observing return of pink colour within two seconds.
Palpate the muscular compartments of the limb (e.g. deep and superficial flexor compartments of forearm, four leg compartments) for tense, woody fullness.
Perform passive stretch of the digits: gently extend the fingers or toes to stretch the compartment muscles; observe for agonizing deep pain.
Test cutaneous sensation in autonomous zones: radial nerve (dorsal first web space), median nerve (index fingertip), ulnar nerve (little fingertip).
Test cutaneous sensation in lower limb: peroneal nerve (dorsal first web space), tibial nerve (plantar aspect of heel).
Test motor function: radial nerve (wrist and thumb extension), median nerve (thumb abduction / OK sign), ulnar nerve (finger abduction).
Test motor function in lower limb: deep peroneal (ankle and great toe dorsiflexion), tibial (plantarflexion), superficial peroneal (eversion).

skill.exam.surg.neurovascular_injury.normal: Easily palpable distal pulses, brisk capillary refill (<2 seconds), soft compressible muscle compartments, painless passive digital stretch, intact sensation and motor power.
skill.exam.surg.neurovascular_injury.abnormal: Tense, woody, non-compressible compartment; agonizing pain on passive digital stretch; diminished or absent distal pulses; delayed capillary refill; progressive paresthesias or motor paralysis.
skill.exam.surg.neurovascular_injury.significance: Disproportionate pain and severe pain on passive stretch of compartment muscles are the earliest and most sensitive signs of acute compartment syndrome. Pulselessness and paralysis are late signs indicating irreversible myonecrosis. Immediate emergency fasciotomy is required.
skill.exam.surg.neurovascular_injury.practice: Rehearse testing autonomous nerve sensory zones, motor power, and performing gentle passive digital stretch on all four limbs.
pitfalls: Waiting for pulselessness before diagnosing compartment syndrome; capillary perfusion and distal pulses persist until late in the syndrome.
Failing to re-examine neurovascular status immediately following fracture reduction or cast application.
Attributing agonizing, escalating limb pain solely to 'normal fracture pain' and administering escalating opioids without releasing tight dressings.

probes.q: What is the earliest and most sensitive physical sign of acute compartment syndrome in an alert patient?
probes.a: Severe pain disproportionate to the injury, aggravated intensely by passive stretching of the muscles in that compartment.

probes.q: What is the autonomous sensory zone for testing the radial nerve and the median nerve in the hand?
probes.a: The dorsal first web space for the radial nerve, and the palmar aspect of the index fingertip for the median nerve.

probes.q: Why is the presence of a strong distal pulse misleading in early acute compartment syndrome?
probes.a: Intracompartmental tissue pressure needs only to exceed capillary and venular pressure (30 mmHg) to cause muscle ischaemia, which is far below systolic arterial blood pressure.

rubric.text: Palpates distal pulses and checks capillary refill time bilaterally
Palpates muscle compartments and performs passive digital stretch
Tests sensation in specific autonomous zones for all major peripheral nerves
Tests targeted motor function for individual peripheral nerves

teach.heading: The 5 Ps of acute ischaemia and compartment syndrome
teach.body:
The classic signs are Pain out of proportion, Paresthesia, Pallor, Paralysis, and Pulselessness.

Crucially, pain on passive muscle stretch and paresthesia appear first. Pulselessness, pallor, and paralysis are late, terminal manifestations indicating that irreversible muscle necrosis has already occurred.

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of compartment syndrome
teach.body:
Closed osteofascial compartments cannot expand. Bleeding or post-ischaemic edema raises intracompartmental pressure.

When tissue pressure exceeds microvascular capillary perfusion pressure (typically within 30 mmHg of diastolic pressure), tissue ischaemia ensues. Irreversible muscle infarction develops within 4 to 6 hours if fasciotomy is delayed.

teach.heading: High-risk injury patterns
points: Supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children: brachial artery and median nerve injury.
Knee dislocations: popliteal artery rupture and common peroneal nerve palsy.
Proximal tibial shaft fractures: acute anterior and deep posterior leg compartment syndrome.
Fractures treated with circumferential plaster casts: iatrogenic constriction.

skill.annex.surg.gustilo_salter_harris.title: Classification of open fractures and paediatric physeal injuries
skill.annex.surg.gustilo_salter_harris.oneLine: Apply the Gustilo-Anderson open fracture grading and Salter-Harris physeal fracture types
skill.annex.surg.gustilo_salter_harris.why: Gustilo-Anderson grading dictates the urgency of surgical debridement, antibiotic selection, and soft tissue coverage strategies. The Salter-Harris classification predicts the risk of premature physeal arrest and progressive angular growth deformities in paediatric skeletal trauma.

asks.text: What is the size of the skin wound, and was it caused by an inside-out spike or external crushing energy?
Is there extensive soft tissue stripping, periosteal exposure, or gross farmyard or sewage contamination?
Is there an associated major vascular injury requiring urgent arterial repair to save the limb?
In a child, does the fracture line cross the radiolucent cartilaginous physis, metaphysis, or articular epiphysis?

skill.annex.surg.gustilo_salter_harris.practice: Rehearse classifying complex clinical vignettes of open fractures into Gustilo grades and paediatric X-rays into Salter-Harris types.
pitfalls: Underestimating a small 1 cm puncture wound caused by high-energy crush or shotgun blast; high energy elevates it to Grade IIIA automatically.
Waiting for definitive X-rays before administering intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics in open fractures.
Confusing Salter-Harris Type II (metaphyseal corner fragment) with Type IV (which crosses both epiphysis and metaphysis).

probes.q: What defines a Gustilo-Anderson Grade IIIC open fracture regardless of wound size?
probes.a: An open fracture associated with a major arterial injury requiring surgical repair to preserve limb viability.

probes.q: What is the Thurston-Holland sign in paediatric fractures, and which Salter-Harris fracture type does it define?
probes.a: A triangular metaphyseal bone fragment remaining attached to the epiphyseal plate, defining a Salter-Harris Type II fracture.

probes.q: Why does a Salter-Harris Type V physeal injury carry a high risk of permanent limb shortening and angular deformity?
probes.a: It involves a severe crushing force across the germinal zone of the physis, causing premature growth arrest and bony bridge formation.

Identifies anatomical plane of fracture relative to the physis (Types I-V)

teach.heading: Clinical significance of the classification
teach.body:
Gustilo Grade IIIC denotes any open fracture with arterial disruption requiring repair. Farmyard contamination elevates any wound to Grade III regardless of skin size.

Salter-Harris Type V represents a direct crush injury to the physis without obvious initial displacement, often discovered only retrospectively when limb shortening or angular deformity appears months later.

skill.exam.surg.shoulder_dislocation.title: Examination of anterior shoulder dislocation
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_dislocation.oneLine: Elicit loss of deltoid roundness, prominent acromion, Hamilton ruler test, and axillary nerve test
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_dislocation.why: Anterior glenohumeral dislocation is the commonest major joint dislocation. Differentiating dislocation from a surgical neck fracture before attempting reduction is critical. Associated axillary nerve paralysis (sensory loss over the regimental badge area) must be documented prior to any reduction manoeuvre.

steps.text: Strip the patient to the waist and inspect from the front, lateral side, and behind with the patient standing or sitting upright.
Observe the characteristic attitude: the injured arm is held in slight abduction and external rotation, supported by the contralateral hand.
Inspect the shoulder contour: observe loss of normal deltoid roundness producing a flattened, squared-off shoulder with prominent acromion.
Palpate the subacromial space: feel that the normal glenoid fossa is empty beneath the sharp lateral border of the acromion.
Palpate the anterior infraclavicular region to identify the displaced humeral head resting in the subcoracoid or subglenoid position.
Perform Hamilton ruler test: place a straight ruler along the lateral aspect of the arm from the lateral epicondyle up toward the acromion.
Perform Callaway test: measure the circumference of both shoulders through the axilla over the acromion; observe increased girth on the affected side.
Perform Dugas test: ask the patient to place the hand of the injured arm on the opposite shoulder while bringing the elbow flat against the chest.
Test pinprick sensation over the lateral aspect of the upper arm (regimental badge area) to evaluate the axillary nerve.
Palpate the radial pulse to confirm that the axillary and brachial arterial pulses remain intact.

skill.exam.surg.shoulder_dislocation.normal: Smoothly rounded deltoid contour, humeral head palpable in glenoid beneath acromion, ruler cannot touch both acromion and epicondyle, intact sensation over lateral deltoid.
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_dislocation.abnormal: Flattened deltoid with squared-off shoulder, prominent acromion, empty glenoid fossa, humeral head felt anteriorly below coracoid, positive Hamilton ruler, positive Dugas test, sensory loss over regimental badge.
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_dislocation.significance: Anterior dislocation displaces the humeral head anteromedially. Hamilton ruler test and Dugas test confirm dislocation and distinguish it from fracture of the humeral neck (where the head stays in the glenoid). Axillary nerve palsy occurs in 10 to 15 percent of anterior dislocations.
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_dislocation.practice: Rehearse performing Hamilton ruler test, Callaway test, Dugas test, and mapping the regimental badge sensory area on a clinical model.
pitfalls: Attempting closed reduction without first checking and documenting axillary nerve sensation over the regimental badge area.
Confusing a dislocated shoulder with a fracture of the neck of the humerus, where the humeral head remains in the glenoid cavity.
Missing an associated posterior shoulder dislocation, where the arm is locked in internal rotation and the anterior shoulder is flattened.

probes.q: What is the normal anatomical structure responsible for the smooth roundness of the shoulder contour?
probes.a: The greater tuberosity of the humerus projecting laterally beneath the fleshy belly of the deltoid muscle.

probes.q: What is Hamilton ruler test, and what does a positive test indicate?
probes.a: A straight ruler placed on the lateral arm touches the acromion and lateral epicondyle simultaneously, confirming glenohumeral dislocation.

probes.q: Which peripheral nerve is most vulnerable in anterior shoulder dislocation, and how is its function tested at the bedside?
probes.a: The axillary nerve, tested by checking pinprick sensation over the regimental badge area on the lateral aspect of the deltoid.

rubric.text: Inspects flattening of deltoid, prominent acromion, and attitude of limb
Palpates empty glenoid beneath acromion and locates displaced humeral head
Executes Hamilton ruler test, Callaway test, and Dugas test accurately
Tests axillary nerve in regimental badge area and palpates radial pulse

teach.heading: Anatomical basis of the deformity
teach.body:
Normal shoulder roundness is created by the greater tuberosity projecting laterally beneath the deltoid muscle.

When the humeral head dislocates anteriorly into the subcoracoid space, the deltoid drops vertically downward from the acromion, transforming the rounded shoulder into a characteristic squared-off outline.

teach.heading: Classic physical diagnostic tests
teach.body:
Hamilton ruler test: normally, a straight line cannot connect the lateral epicondyle and the acromion because the greater tuberosity bulges between them. In dislocation, the ruler lies flat against both points.

Dugas test: the patient cannot touch the opposite shoulder with the elbow held against the chest wall.

teach.heading: Neurological and vascular hazards
points: The axillary nerve curves around the surgical neck of the humerus and is stretched over the dislocated head.
Loss of sensation over the lower half of the deltoid (regimental badge area) confirms neuropraxia.
Check the radial pulse: the axillary artery can be compressed or torn by the displaced head in elderly patients.

skill.exam.surg.elbow_three_point.title: Examination of the elbow three-point bony relationship in trauma
skill.exam.surg.elbow_three_point.oneLine: Palpate olecranon tip and epicondyles: equilateral triangle in flexion, straight line in extension
skill.exam.surg.elbow_three_point.why: In acute elbow trauma, distinguishing an extra-articular supracondylar fracture of the humerus from an intra-articular posterior dislocation of the elbow is the classic bedside surgical dilemma. The three-point relationship remains preserved in supracondylar fractures but is disrupted in dislocations. Brachial artery and median nerve integrity must be urgently established to prevent Volkmann contracture.

steps.text: Inspect the injured elbow compared with the sound side: note posterior prominence, forearm shortening, and swelling in the cubital fossa.
Flex both elbows to 90 degrees (if tolerated) and palpate the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and tip of the olecranon process.
Assess the geometric relationship in 90 degrees flexion: determine whether the three points form a symmetrical equilateral triangle.
Gently extend the elbow and verify whether the three bony points lie along a straight horizontal line.
In supracondylar fracture: note that the three bony points retain their normal relationship but are displaced posteriorly en bloc with bone crepitus above the joint.
In posterior dislocation: note that the olecranon is displaced backward and upward, completely disrupting the equilateral triangle.
Palpate the radial and brachial pulses, compare pulse volume, and evaluate capillary refill in all five fingernails.
Test the anterior interosseous nerve (branch of median nerve): ask patient to make an OK sign by flexing distal phalanges of thumb and index finger.
Test radial nerve (active extension of wrist and thumb) and ulnar nerve (abduction of fingers against resistance).
Gently stretch the fingers into extension: observe for deep, agonizing forearm pain indicating acute compartment ischaemia.

skill.exam.surg.elbow_three_point.normal: Equilateral triangle at 90 degrees flexion; straight horizontal line in extension; strong radial pulse; intact OK sign; painless passive finger extension.
skill.exam.surg.elbow_three_point.abnormal: Disrupted three-point relationship in posterior dislocation; preserved three-point relationship with posterior displacement of lower shaft in supracondylar fracture; absent radial pulse; loss of OK sign; severe pain on passive finger extension.
skill.exam.surg.elbow_three_point.significance: Intact three-point relationship confirms an extra-articular supracondylar fracture; disruption confirms an intra-articular elbow dislocation. Loss of radial pulse with passive stretch pain warns of acute brachial artery entrapment and impending Volkmann ischaemic contracture.
skill.exam.surg.elbow_three_point.practice: Palpate your own elbow epicondyles and olecranon in flexion and extension, then practise eliciting the OK sign and testing radial/ulnar function.
pitfalls: Assuming a palpable radial pulse excludes acute compartment syndrome or impending Volkmann ischaemia in a swollen elbow.
Failing to test the anterior interosseous nerve (OK sign), which is the commonest nerve injured in extension-type supracondylar fractures.
Forcefully flexing a severely swollen elbow with a supracondylar fracture, which can completely occlude the brachial artery.

probes.q: What geometrical shape is formed by the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and olecranon tip in a normal elbow at 90 degrees flexion?
probes.a: An equilateral triangle.

probes.q: How does the three-point bony relationship distinguish a supracondylar fracture of the humerus from a posterior dislocation of the elbow?
probes.a: The three-point relationship remains preserved in supracondylar fractures, whereas it is completely disrupted in posterior elbow dislocation.

probes.q: How do you test for an anterior interosseous nerve injury in a child with a displaced supracondylar fracture?
probes.a: Ask the child to make an OK sign by flexing the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger and the interphalangeal joint of the thumb.

rubric.text: Palpates medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and olecranon tip in flexion and extension
Correctly deduces preserved vs disrupted bony relationship
Assesses radial and brachial pulses and capillary refill in all digits
Tests anterior interosseous nerve (OK sign) and checks pain on passive finger stretch
