teach.heading: Anatomy of the three bony points
teach.body:
When the elbow is flexed to 90 degrees, the tips of the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and olecranon form an equilateral triangle.

When the joint is fully extended, the olecranon ascends to lie in the exact horizontal line connecting the two epicondyles. In children, massive swelling can obscure these points, requiring deliberate deep palpation.

teach.heading: The menace of Volkmann ischaemia
teach.body:
The sharp proximal fragment in extension-type supracondylar fractures points anteriorly, directly threatening the brachial artery and median nerve.

Kinking or spasm of the brachial artery causes deep flexor compartment ischaemia. The earliest warning sign is severe, agonizing pain when the examiner passively extends the patient's fingers.

skill.exam.surg.colles_wrist_injury.title: Examination of Colles fracture and wrist deformity
skill.exam.surg.colles_wrist_injury.oneLine: Evaluate dinner-fork deformity, dorsal tilt, and loss of radial styloid distal projection
skill.exam.surg.colles_wrist_injury.why: Colles fracture (distal radial metaphyseal fracture within 2.5 cm of articular surface with dorsal displacement and tilt) is the commonest fracture of the upper limb in adults over 50. Identifying the classic dinner-fork deformity and relative styloid positions prevents malunion, median nerve compression, and complex regional pain syndrome.

steps.text: Inspect the wrist from the lateral profile: observe the dorsal hump created by backward displacement of the distal fragment, producing the classic dinner-fork deformity.
Inspect from the dorsal view: observe radial deviation (shift) of the hand producing a bayonet-like appearance, with prominence of the distal ulnar styloid.
Inspect the palmar aspect: observe fullness at the anterior wrist crease created by the forward-projecting proximal radial shaft fragment.
Palpate the radial and ulnar styloid processes simultaneously with your index fingers to assess their relative levels.
Verify whether the radial styloid retains its normal 1 cm distal projection beyond the ulnar styloid, or has become level with or proximal to it.
Palpate gently over the distal radius metaphysis (approximately 2 to 2.5 cm proximal to joint line) to localize point bone tenderness.
Test cutaneous sensation over the palmar aspect of the index and middle fingertips to rule out acute median nerve compression.
Palpate the radial pulse and check capillary refill in all five digits.

skill.exam.surg.colles_wrist_injury.normal: Radial styloid projects approximately 1 cm (8 to 12 mm) distal to ulnar styloid; smooth dorsal wrist profile without step-off; intact median nerve sensation.
skill.exam.surg.colles_wrist_injury.abnormal: Dinner-fork deformity (dorsal displacement and dorsal tilt); radial shift of hand; radial styloid at same level as or proximal to ulnar styloid; numbness in median nerve distribution.
skill.exam.surg.colles_wrist_injury.significance: Loss or reversal of the normal 1 cm styloid height difference confirms radial shortening and impaction. Acute median nerve paresthesias warrant urgent closed reduction and release of any constricting dressings.
skill.exam.surg.colles_wrist_injury.practice: Practise simultaneously palpating the radial and ulnar styloid levels on both wrists and sketching the six displacements of a Colles fracture.
pitfalls: Failing to simultaneously palpate both styloids to detect subtle radial shortening in impacted fractures with minimal deformity.
Omitting median nerve sensory testing over the index fingertip before and after manipulation.
Confusing Colles fracture (dorsal displacement) with Smith fracture (volar displacement / garden spade deformity).

probes.q: What classic eponym describes the characteristic lateral profile deformity of a Colles fracture?
probes.a: Dinner-fork deformity.

probes.q: How does the relative level of the radial and ulnar styloid processes change in a displaced Colles fracture?
probes.a: The radial styloid, which normally lies 1 cm distal to the ulnar styloid, ascends to the same level or proximal to the ulnar styloid.

probes.q: Which peripheral nerve is most commonly compressed acutely in a displaced Colles fracture, and what symptom results?
probes.a: The median nerve, producing numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers.

rubric.text: Inspects lateral profile for dinner-fork deformity and dorsal view for radial shift
Simultaneously palpates radial and ulnar styloid processes to assess relative height
Tests sensation in the median nerve distribution over the index and middle fingertips
Checks radial pulse and digital capillary refill

teach.heading: The six classic displacements of Colles fracture
points: Dorsal displacement of the distal fragment.
Dorsal tilt (reversing normal 11-degree volar tilt to backward angulation).
Lateral (radial) displacement of the distal fragment.
Lateral (radial) tilt of the articular surface.
Supination of the distal fragment.
Impaction or proximal shift causing radial shortening.

teach.heading: Anatomical styloid relationship
teach.body:
In a normal wrist, the tip of the radial styloid process extends roughly 1 cm distal to the tip of the ulnar styloid.

When impaction occurs at the distal radial fracture site, the radial styloid is pulled proximally. In a displaced Colles fracture, both styloids lie at the same horizontal level, or the radial styloid is higher.

rows: Fall on back of flexed hand

skill.exam.surg.scaphoid_fracture.title: Examination for scaphoid fracture
skill.exam.surg.scaphoid_fracture.oneLine: Palpate the anatomical snuffbox, scaphoid tubercle, and test axial thumb compression
skill.exam.surg.scaphoid_fracture.why: Scaphoid fractures often follow a fall on an outstretched hand with minimal initial radiographic findings. Because the retrograde arterial blood supply enters from the distal pole, missed or un-immobilized waist fractures frequently result in proximal pole avascular necrosis, non-union, and secondary wrist osteoarthritis.

steps.text: Inspect the radial aspect of the wrist and hand for swelling, fullness, or loss of the normal depression in the anatomical snuffbox.
Identify the boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox: extensor pollicis longus tendon medially, and extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus tendons laterally.
Place the wrist in gentle ulnar deviation to expose the waist of the scaphoid.
Palpate with a single fingertip directly in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox; assess for sharp, localized bone tenderness.
Palpate the volar aspect of the wrist at the base of the thenar eminence to test for tenderness over the scaphoid tubercle.
Apply longitudinal axial compression along the first metacarpal shaft toward the scaphoid while stabilizing the wrist.
Test active and passive wrist dorsiflexion and radial deviation, noting terminal pain and restriction.
Check radial pulse and sensation over the dorsal first web space and thumb.

skill.exam.surg.scaphoid_fracture.normal: Well-defined hollow depression in the anatomical snuffbox; painless palpation of snuffbox floor and scaphoid tubercle; painless axial compression of thumb.
skill.exam.surg.scaphoid_fracture.abnormal: Fullness and obliteration of the snuffbox hollow; exquisite point tenderness in the snuffbox floor; tenderness over the volar scaphoid tubercle; sharp radial wrist pain on axial thumb compression.
skill.exam.surg.scaphoid_fracture.significance: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox combined with scaphoid tubercle tenderness and pain on axial thumb loading carries over 90 percent sensitivity for scaphoid fracture. Clinical fracture warrants cast immobilization even if initial radiographs appear normal.
skill.exam.surg.scaphoid_fracture.practice: Identify your own anatomical snuffbox tendons with active thumb extension and practise palpating the scaphoid waist and tubercle.
pitfalls: Dismissing a scaphoid fracture as a simple 'wrist sprain' based solely on normal initial plain radiographs.
Failing to palpate the scaphoid tubercle on the volar wrist, which distinguishes scaphoid pathology from radial styloid injury.
Omitting repeat imaging or MRI at 10 to 14 days when clinical signs are positive despite normal initial X-rays.

probes.q: What anatomical tendons form the medial and lateral boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox?
probes.a: Medial boundary is extensor pollicis longus; lateral boundary is formed by extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus.

probes.q: What vascular anatomical vulnerability makes fractures of the scaphoid waist prone to avascular necrosis of the proximal pole?
probes.a: The blood supply enters the scaphoid from the distal pole in a retrograde direction, so a waist fracture shears the blood supply to the proximal fragment.

probes.q: What is the mandatory clinical policy if a patient has clear anatomical snuffbox tenderness following trauma but initial X-rays are reported normal?
probes.a: Immobilize the wrist in a scaphoid plaster cast or splint and repeat radiographs or perform an MRI after 10 to 14 days.

rubric.text: Identifies tendon boundaries and palpates floor of anatomical snuffbox in ulnar deviation
Palpates volar scaphoid tubercle at the base of the thenar eminence
Tests longitudinal axial compression of the thumb metacarpal
Explains protocol for clinically suspected fracture with negative initial X-ray

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Triad of physical signs in scaphoid injury
points: Point tenderness directly in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox during ulnar deviation.
Tenderness on deep pressure over the scaphoid tubercle on the anterior wrist crease.
Sharp wrist pain elicited by compressing the thumb longitudinally along its axis into the carpus.

teach.heading: The retrograde blood supply problem
teach.body:
The scaphoid receives its major nutrient branches from the radial artery via dorsal and volar ridges near its distal waist.

Intraosseous branches travel retrogradely to supply the proximal pole. A fracture through the narrow waist deprives the proximal pole of arterial blood, leading to avascular necrosis and non-union in up to 30 percent of cases.

teach.heading: Management of occult fractures
teach.body:
In the first 48 hours, a fine crack fracture may not create enough bone resorption to be visible on standard plain radiographs.

A patient with positive clinical triad signs must be placed in a thumb spica cast. Repeat X-rays in 10 to 14 days will reveal the fracture line due to osteoclastic resorption, or an urgent MRI will show marrow edema.

skill.exam.surg.hip_injury_attitude.title: Examination of hip fracture: attitude, shortening, and rotational deformity
skill.exam.surg.hip_injury_attitude.oneLine: Distinguish intracapsular neck fracture from extracapsular trochanteric fracture by external rotation
skill.exam.surg.hip_injury_attitude.why: Proximal femoral fractures in elderly patients carry high mortality and morbidity. Examining the resting attitude of the lower limb differentiates intracapsular femoral neck fractures (moderate external rotation 45 degrees, high avascular necrosis risk) from extracapsular intertrochanteric fractures (complete external rotation 90 degrees with patella touching bed, massive occult bleeding).

steps.text: Inspect the patient supine: observe the resting attitude of both lower limbs, focusing on the patellae, feet, and malleoli.

Note the degree of external rotation: in intracapsular neck fracture, external rotation is moderate (approximately 45 degrees); in extracapsular trochanteric fracture, external rotation is complete (80 to 90 degrees, lateral border of foot rests flat on couch).
Compare the overall apparent length of the limbs: observe definite shortening on the injured side.
Inspect the groin and greater trochanteric area: look for fullness, swelling, or ecchymosis (prominent in extracapsular fractures, minimal in intracapsular).
Palpate the femoral pulse in the femoral triangle, noting full volume.
Palpate for tenderness over the anterior hip joint line (groin) and over the greater trochanter.
Ask the patient to perform an active straight leg raise (test of continuity): note complete inability to lift the heel off the bed.
Do not aggressively rotate the limb or deliberately seek bony crepitus, which causes excruciating pain and disrupts retinacular vessels.

skill.exam.surg.hip_injury_attitude.normal: Symmetrical lower limb alignment with feet pointing slightly outward (10 to 15 degrees); equal limb lengths; painless active straight leg raise; non-tender groin and trochanter.
skill.exam.surg.hip_injury_attitude.abnormal: External rotation and shortening of the injured lower limb; moderate external rotation (45 degrees) in intracapsular neck fracture; extreme external rotation (80 to 90 degrees) in trochanteric fracture; inability to lift heel off bed.
skill.exam.surg.hip_injury_attitude.significance: The degree of external rotation directly reflects the anatomy of the hip capsule. Complete external rotation occurs in extracapsular fractures because the distal fragment is free of capsular constraint. Intracapsular fractures carry high risk of avascular necrosis due to retinacular vessel shearing.
skill.exam.surg.hip_injury_attitude.practice: Observe clinical attitudes of hip injuries, practise estimating rotational angles, and rehearse testing active heel elevation.
pitfalls: Vigorously rotating the fractured leg internally and externally to elicit crepitus, which shreds remaining retinacular vessels.
Missing an impacted femoral neck fracture (Garden I) where the patient can still bear weight and has minimal rotational deformity.
Failing to recognize that complete external rotation flat against the bed indicates an extracapsular, not intracapsular, fracture.

probes.q: What is the typical attitude of the lower limb in a displaced fracture of the proximal femur?
probes.a: External rotation and shortening.

probes.q: Why is external rotation limited to approximately 45 degrees in an intracapsular femoral neck fracture, but reaches 90 degrees in an intertrochanteric fracture?
probes.a: In an intracapsular fracture, the intact joint capsule and iliofemoral ligament restrict rotation, whereas an extracapsular fracture is completely outside capsular restraint.

probes.q: What vascular complication threatens displaced intracapsular fractures of the femoral neck, and which artery is the primary source?
probes.a: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head, caused by disruption of retinacular vessels arising primarily from the medial circumflex femoral artery.

rubric.text: Inspects resting attitude and quantifies degree of external rotation (45 vs 90 degrees)
Evaluates limb shortening and ecchymosis over trochanteric region
Tests active straight leg raise and avoids aggressive rotational manipulation
Checks femoral and distal pulses and distal neurological sensation

teach.heading: Anatomical basis of limb attitude
teach.body:
When the proximal femur fractures, the iliopsoas, gluteus medius, and adductor muscles pull the shaft proximally, causing shortening.

The weight of the foot and the unopposed external rotators rotate the shaft externally. The joint capsule checks this rotation at roughly 45 degrees in intracapsular neck fractures.

teach.heading: Active straight leg raise as continuity test
teach.body:
Ask the supine patient to raise the heel off the bed. In a displaced femoral fracture, the patient cannot lift the leg at all.

In undisplaced or impacted Garden I fractures, the patient may still manage a weak straight leg raise. Never force hip flexion if fracture is suspected.

skill.exam.surg.knee_ligaments_drawer.title: Examination of knee cruciate ligaments: Lachman and drawer tests
skill.exam.surg.knee_ligaments_drawer.oneLine: Perform the Lachman test for ACL integrity and drawer tests for anteroposterior stability
skill.exam.surg.knee_ligaments_drawer.why: Cruciate ligament ruptures cause disabling knee instability, recurrent giving way, and accelerated post-traumatic osteoarthritis. The Lachman test is the most sensitive bedside test for acute anterior cruciate ligament rupture because it can be performed at 20 to 30 degrees of flexion before protective hamstring spasm locks the joint.

steps.text: Place the patient supine and completely relaxed on the examination couch.
Lachman test: flex the patient's knee to 20 to 30 degrees; stabilize the anterior distal femur with one hand and grasp the posterior proximal tibia with the other hand.
Apply a firm, brisk anterior translating force to the proximal tibia while maintaining femoral stability.
Assess the degree of anterior tibial translation and feel for the presence of a crisp, firm endpoint versus a mushy, absent endpoint.

Inspect for posterior sag sign (Godfrey test): flex both hips to 45 degrees and knees to 90 degrees with feet resting flat; look from the lateral profile for posterior sagging of the tibial tuberosity.
Anterior drawer test: flex knee to 90 degrees with hip at 45 degrees; sit gently on the forefoot to stabilize it; verify that the hamstring tendons are completely relaxed.
Grasp the proximal tibia with both hands, placing thumbs along the medial and lateral joint lines, and pull the tibia anteriorly.
Posterior drawer test: from the same 90-degree position, push the tibia firmly backward to evaluate posterior cruciate ligament integrity.

skill.exam.surg.knee_ligaments_drawer.normal: Firm, abrupt stop (endpoint) with minimal anterior translation (<3 to 5 mm); no posterior sag of tibial tuberosity; identical to uninjured knee.
skill.exam.surg.knee_ligaments_drawer.abnormal: Increased anterior tibial translation (>5 mm) with a soft, mushy endpoint on Lachman and anterior drawer tests; posterior displacement or posterior sag of tibial tuberosity.
skill.exam.surg.knee_ligaments_drawer.significance: A positive Lachman test confirms an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. Lachman test has over 90 percent sensitivity in acute injury, whereas anterior drawer test is often falsely negative due to haemarthrosis and hamstring spasm at 90 degrees. Posterior sag confirms a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) rupture.
skill.exam.surg.knee_ligaments_drawer.practice: Rehearse positioning the knee at 20 degrees, relaxing hamstrings, and applying brisk anterior tibial translation during the Lachman test.
pitfalls: Performing the anterior drawer test before checking for a posterior sag; pulling a posteriorly subluxated tibia back to neutral mimics a false-positive anterior drawer.
Attempting Lachman testing with tense, contracted hamstrings, which restrains anterior tibial translation.
Relying on the anterior drawer test at 90 degrees in an acute knee, where severe hemarthrosis blocks deep flexion.

probes.q: At what degree of knee flexion is the Lachman test performed?
probes.a: At 20 to 30 degrees of knee flexion.

probes.q: Why is the Lachman test significantly more sensitive than the anterior drawer test in an acutely injured knee?
probes.a: At 20 degrees of flexion, the posterior horn of the medial meniscus is not wedged and hamstring muscle spasm is minimal, allowing free translation.

probes.q: What happens if you perform an anterior drawer test without first checking for a posterior sag sign in a patient with a torn posterior cruciate ligament?
probes.a: The posteriorly displaced tibia is pulled forward to its normal anatomical position, creating a false-positive anterior drawer sign.

rubric.text: Executes Lachman test at 20 to 30 degrees flexion with firm femoral stabilization
Distinguishes a firm abrupt endpoint from a soft mushy endpoint
Checks for posterior sag sign (Godfrey test) before performing anterior drawer
Performs anterior and posterior drawer tests at 90 degrees with relaxed hamstrings

Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.heading: Biomechanics of the cruciate ligaments
teach.body:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) passes upward, backward, and laterally from the anterior tibial plateau to the lateral femoral condyle, resisting anterior tibial translation.

The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) passes upward, forward, and medially from the posterior tibia to the medial femoral condyle, resisting posterior tibial translation.

teach.heading: Superiority of the Lachman test
teach.body:
In acute ACL rupture, acute haemarthrosis makes 90-degree flexion painful and triggers intense hamstring spasm that restrains anterior movement.

At 20 to 30 degrees, the joint capsule has maximum compliance, the hamstrings are relaxed, and the primary restraint against anterior translation is solely the ACL.

teach.heading: The trap of the posterior cruciate sag
points: Always inspect the lateral knee profile at 90 degrees flexion before touching the leg.
If the PCL is torn, gravity pulls the tibial tuberosity backward, creating a visible concave step-off below the patella.
Pulling this sagging tibia forward produces an apparent drawer motion that inexperienced examiners mistake for an ACL tear.

skill.exam.surg.knee_meniscus_mcmurray.title: Examination for meniscal tear of the knee: McMurray test and joint line tenderness
skill.exam.surg.knee_meniscus_mcmurray.oneLine: Palpate the joint line for point tenderness and elicit the McMurray rotational click
skill.exam.surg.knee_meniscus_mcmurray.why: Meniscal tears cause mechanical locking, recurrent joint effusion, and articular cartilage degradation. Accurate clinical evaluation localizes tears to the medial or lateral meniscus, guiding arthroscopic partial meniscectomy or repair to preserve joint biomechanics and delay post-traumatic osteoarthritis.

steps.text: Inspect the supine knee for quadriceps wasting (particularly vastus medialis) and localized joint effusion in the suprapatellar pouch.
Flex the patient's knee to 90 degrees and identify the medial and lateral joint lines with the knee relaxed.
Palpate systematically along the entire anterior, middle, and posterior joint lines with the thumb and index finger, seeking localized point tenderness.
McMurray test for medial meniscus: fully flex the knee, externally rotate the foot and tibia to trap the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, and apply gentle valgus stress.
Slowly extend the knee while maintaining external rotation and valgus stress, feeling along the medial joint line with your thumb.
McMurray test for lateral meniscus: fully flex the knee, internally rotate the foot and tibia, apply varus stress, and slowly extend while palpating the lateral joint line.
Note any palpable or audible click, thud, or pain as the torn meniscal fragment is caught between the condyles.
Perform Apley grind test: place patient prone with knee at 90 degrees; apply downward axial compression on the heel while rotating the tibia internally and externally.

skill.exam.surg.knee_meniscus_mcmurray.normal: Non-tender medial and lateral joint lines; smooth, silent knee extension without clicks, clunks, or pain during McMurray rotational testing; painless Apley grind test.
skill.exam.surg.knee_meniscus_mcmurray.abnormal: Localized point tenderness along the joint line; audible or palpable click accompanied by pain during rotational extension (positive McMurray test); sharp pain on axial grinding in prone position.
skill.exam.surg.knee_meniscus_mcmurray.significance: A positive McMurray test indicates a displaced meniscal tear (bucket-handle, flap, or complex cleavage tear) impinging between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau. Medial meniscal tears are three times commoner than lateral tears due to firm attachment to the medial collateral ligament.
skill.exam.surg.knee_meniscus_mcmurray.practice: Practise palpating the tibiofemoral joint lines in flexion and performing coordinated external rotation with extension during McMurray testing.
pitfalls: Performing the McMurray test too rapidly or violently, which causes diffuse pain and muscle guarding.
Mistaking patellofemoral crepitus or a snapping tendon for a true intra-articular meniscal click.
Overlooking isolated joint line tenderness, which is often more sensitive than the McMurray test in chronic tears.

probes.q: Which meniscal injury is three times more common: medial or lateral meniscus, and why?
probes.a: Medial meniscus tear, because the medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep medial collateral ligament and joint capsule, making it less mobile.

probes.q: What exact rotational position of the tibia stresses the medial meniscus during the McMurray test?
probes.a: External rotation of the foot and tibia while applying valgus stress during slow extension from full flexion.

probes.q: How does true mechanical locking of the knee differ from pseudo-locking caused by pain or hamstring spasm?
probes.a: In true locking, a mechanical block (displaced bucket-handle tear) abruptly stops full extension while flexion remains free; in pseudo-locking, all movements are restricted by pain.

rubric.text: Palpates medial and lateral joint lines systematically at 90 degrees flexion
Performs medial McMurray with external rotation, valgus stress, and slow extension
Performs lateral McMurray with internal rotation, varus stress, and extension
Executes Apley compression grind test in the prone position

teach.heading: Meniscal anatomy and mechanics
teach.body:
The fibrocartilaginous menisci deepen the shallow tibial plateaus, absorb axial shock, and distribute synovial lubrication across the joint.

The peripheral third has an active vascular supply (red-red zone) amenable to surgical repair. The inner two-thirds are avascular (white-white zone) and do not heal spontaneously, requiring partial meniscectomy.

teach.heading: Mechanism of McMurray test
teach.body:
Full flexion forces the posterior horns of the menisci backward into the joint space. External rotation of the tibia engages the posterior horn of the medial meniscus against the medial femoral condyle.

As the knee extends under valgus pressure, any torn or displaced flap is squeezed against the condyle, eliciting a distinct palpable pop or click.

skill.exam.surg.achilles_rupture.title: Examination of Achilles tendon rupture: Simmonds-Thompson test
skill.exam.surg.achilles_rupture.oneLine: Palpate the tendon gap and squeeze the calf to assess passive plantarflexion
skill.exam.surg.achilles_rupture.why: Complete rupture of the Achilles tendon (tendo calcaneus) is misdiagnosed as an ankle sprain in up to 25 percent of patients because weak active plantarflexion persists using accessory toe flexors and tibialis posterior. The Simmonds-Thompson test provides pathognomonic physical confirmation, guiding functional bracing or surgical repair.

steps.text: Place the patient prone on the couch with both feet hanging freely over the end, or ask them to kneel on a chair.
Inspect both Achilles tendons from behind: observe loss of normal tendon outline, localized swelling, and ecchymosis.
Observe the resting angle of the feet: note that the ruptured foot hangs in neutral or slight dorsiflexion (loss of normal slight equinus position).
Palpate along the entire course of the tendon from the gastrocnemius junction to the calcaneal tuberosity.
Identify a distinct palpable gap or depression across the tendon fibres (classically located 2 to 6 cm proximal to calcaneal insertion in the watershed zone).
Perform Simmonds-Thompson test: firmly squeeze the fleshy calf muscle bellies with your hand; observe for involuntary passive plantarflexion of the foot.
Compare immediately with the contralateral normal calf: note crisp plantarflexion on the healthy side versus complete absence on the ruptured side.
Ask the standing patient to attempt a single-leg heel raise on the injured limb: observe total inability to lift the heel off the floor.

skill.exam.surg.achilles_rupture.normal: Symmetrical tendon contours, slight resting plantarflexion of both feet, brisk passive plantarflexion on calf squeeze (negative Simmonds-Thompson), able to perform single-leg heel raise.
skill.exam.surg.achilles_rupture.abnormal: Palpable gap or defect in the tendon, foot hangs at 90 degrees or dorsiflexed, complete absence of plantarflexion on calf squeeze (positive Simmonds-Thompson test), inability to perform single-leg heel raise.
skill.exam.surg.achilles_rupture.significance: Absence of passive plantarflexion on calf squeeze confirms complete rupture of the Achilles tendon. Weak active plantarflexion in a non-weight-bearing position does NOT rule out rupture because long toe flexors and tibialis posterior remain intact.
skill.exam.surg.achilles_rupture.practice: Rehearse positioning the patient prone with feet hanging freely, palpating the tendon gap, and performing the calf squeeze test.
pitfalls: Ruling out rupture because the patient can feebly plantarflex their foot while lying down, which is accomplished by tibialis posterior and toe flexors.
Misdiagnosing the injury as a simple ankle sprain and applying an elastic bandage without formal immobilization.
Missing the injury in elderly patients with fluoroquinolone or corticosteroid exposure presenting with painless sudden weakness.

probes.q: How is the Simmonds-Thompson test performed, and what constitutes a positive result?
probes.a: The calf bellies are squeezed firmly while the patient is prone; absence of involuntary plantarflexion of the foot indicates a positive test.

probes.q: Why can a patient with complete Achilles tendon rupture still weakly plantarflex their ankle when lying on an examination couch?
probes.a: Intact secondary plantarflexor muscles (tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus, and peroneus longus) can move the unweighted foot.

probes.q: Why does the Achilles tendon typically rupture 2 to 6 cm proximal to its insertion on the calcaneus?
probes.a: This region represents an anatomical watershed hypovascular zone with poor arterial perfusion, rendering it vulnerable to microtrauma and rupture.

rubric.text: Positions patient prone with feet hanging free and inspects resting ankle angle
Palpates the palpable defect 2 to 6 cm proximal to calcaneus
Executes Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test and evaluates passive plantarflexion
Tests active single-leg heel raise to verify loss of weight-bearing propulsion

teach.heading: Anatomical vulnerability of the Achilles tendon
teach.body:
The tendo calcaneus is formed by the conjoined tendons of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, inserting onto the middle posterior calcaneus.

A watershed area of relative hypovascularity exists between 2 and 6 cm proximal to its insertion. Repeated micro-tearing in this zone precedes catastrophic rupture during push-off activities.

teach.heading: The classic patient presentation
teach.body:
Patients are typically middle-aged recreational athletes who describe an explosive sensation of being kicked or struck by a racket in the back of the ankle.

They turn around expecting to see an assailant, only to find no one there. Immediate pain is followed by inability to push off during normal gait.

teach.heading: Diagnostic triad of Achilles rupture
points: A visible and palpable gap in the tendon substance 2 to 6 cm proximal to the heel.
Loss of the normal resting equinus posture (the injured foot lies perpendicular or dorsiflexed).
A positive Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test with complete absence of passive plantarflexion.

skill.hx.surg.joint_pathology.title: History taking in diseases of joints
skill.hx.surg.joint_pathology.oneLine: Analyse onset tempo, joint pattern, morning stiffness, locking, and systemic associations
skill.hx.surg.joint_pathology.why: The history classifies joint disease into acute inflammatory/infective (septic arthritis), chronic inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), chronic granulomatous (tuberculous arthritis), or degenerative (osteoarthritis). Identifying diurnal stiffness patterns, mechanical locking, giving way, and night cries establishes the surgical pathology before imaging.

asks.text: How many joints are affected: a single joint (monoarthritis), a few joints (oligoarthritis), or multiple joints (polyarthritis)?
Did the joint swelling and pain explode over hours (septic, gout) or emerge insidiously over months (tuberculosis, osteoarthritis)?
Is the joint stiff when you wake up in the morning, and does it take more than 30 to 60 minutes of movement to loosen (inflammatory)?
Does the joint truly catch or lock, so you cannot straighten it until it clicks free (loose body, meniscal tear)?
Does the joint give way unexpectedly beneath you while walking (cruciate ligament tear, patellar subluxation)?
Do you awaken from deep sleep by sudden sharp pain when your muscles relax (nocturnal cries in tuberculous arthritis)?
Have you had high fevers, urethral discharge, red eyes, psoriasis, chronic cough, or family history of joint diseases?

skill.hx.surg.joint_pathology.practice: Practise taking a detailed arthritis history, categorizing symptoms into inflammatory versus mechanical patterns.
pitfalls: Confusing morning stiffness of short duration (<15 minutes in osteoarthritis) with prolonged inflammatory stiffness (>60 minutes in rheumatoid arthritis).
Accepting 'locking' without asking whether the joint physically jams at a specific angle (true locking) or is merely painful to move (pseudo-locking).
Failing to ask about nocturnal cries in children, which is a classic historical signature of tuberculous arthritis of the hip.

probes.q: How does the duration of morning joint stiffness distinguish inflammatory arthritis from degenerative osteoarthritis?
probes.a: Inflammatory arthritis causes prolonged morning stiffness lasting over 30 to 60 minutes that improves with activity, whereas osteoarthritis causes brief stiffness lasting under 15 to 30 minutes that worsens with activity.

probes.q: What pathological mechanism causes nocturnal cries in a child with early tuberculous arthritis of the hip?
probes.a: During the day, voluntary muscle spasm holds the joint immobile; when the child falls into deep sleep, the muscles relax and the raw articular surfaces rub together, triggering severe pain that wakes the child crying.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a patient describing true mechanical locking of the knee?
probes.a: It indicates a mechanical intra-articular obstruction, classically a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear or a loose body, that mechanically prevents full extension.

rubric.text: Determines mono-, oligo-, or polyarticular distribution and onset tempo
Distinguishes prolonged inflammatory morning stiffness from degenerative wear
Differentiates true locking from pseudo-locking and identifies giving way
Screens for nocturnal cries, constitutional features, and extra-articular signs

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Inflammatory versus degenerative patterns
teach.body:
Inflammatory joint diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis) cause pain that is worse at rest and improves with activity.

Morning stiffness is profound and prolonged, exceeding 60 minutes. Degenerative disease (osteoarthritis) causes pain that worsens with weight-bearing and is relieved by rest, with brief morning gelling under 15 minutes.

teach.heading: Mechanical symptoms: locking versus giving way
teach.body:
True locking means the joint suddenly becomes jammed in flexion and cannot achieve full extension. It indicates an intra-articular loose body or bucket-handle meniscal tear.

Pseudo-locking is restricted motion due to severe pain and muscle spasm without an actual mechanical block. Giving way indicates ligamentous instability or quadriceps inhibition.

skill.exam.surg.joint_examination_scheme.title: Systematic physical examination scheme for a pathological joint
skill.exam.surg.joint_examination_scheme.oneLine: Execute Look, Feel, Move, and Measure comparing always with the contralateral joint
skill.exam.surg.joint_examination_scheme.why: Joint diseases produce characteristic physical sequences of capsular distension, synovial hypertrophy, cartilage destruction, and fixed deformity. Following the rigorous Look, Feel, Move, Measure sequence prevents missing subtle joint line tenderness, minor contractures, and occult neurovascular complications.

steps.text: Expose both limbs completely and inspect in a good, uniform light comparing the affected joint with the healthy counterpart.
Look: observe the resting attitude, skin changes (scars, sinuses, erythema), localized or diffuse swelling, and surrounding muscle wasting.
Feel: test local skin temperature using the dorsum of the fingers, comparing with the contralateral joint and adjacent shaft.
Feel: palpate the joint lines and bony prominences systematically to map out localized point tenderness.
Feel: assess for synovial thickening (soft, boggy, doughy fullness) and test for intra-articular effusion.
Move: test active range of motion first, noting degrees of excursion and terminal pain or restriction.
Move: test gentle passive range of motion, placing a palm over the joint to detect fine soft synovial crepitus or coarse bony crepitus.
Measure: measure fixed deformities with a goniometer and measure limb length and muscle girth bilaterally.

skill.exam.surg.joint_examination_scheme.normal: Symmetrical joint contours without swelling or wasting, normal temperature, non-tender joint lines, absence of effusion or synovial thickening, smooth painless full active and passive range of motion.
skill.exam.surg.joint_examination_scheme.abnormal: Localized warmth, boggy synovial thickening, joint effusion, joint line tenderness, fine or coarse grating crepitus, restricted range of motion, fixed flexion or angular deformity, muscle wasting.
skill.exam.surg.joint_examination_scheme.significance: Fine soft crepitus with doughy thickening indicates chronic synovitis (rheumatoid or tuberculous arthritis). Coarse grating crepitus with irregular hard osteophytes indicates advanced osteoarthritis. Total restriction of all movements in all planes with agonizing spasm indicates acute septic arthritis.
skill.exam.surg.joint_examination_scheme.practice: Rehearse the complete Look, Feel, Move, Measure sequence on a knee, hip, or shoulder joint, comparing bilaterally.
pitfalls: Examining only the symptomatic joint without exposing and comparing with the contralateral normal joint.
Testing passive movements before observing active movement, causing patient guarding and distress.
Confusing coarse bone-on-bone crepitus of cartilage loss with fine silky crepitus of synovial hypertrophy.

probes.q: What are the four classical sequential steps in the clinical examination of any joint?
probes.a: Look (inspection), Feel (palpation), Move (range of motion), and Measure.

probes.q: How does the tactile quality of crepitus differ between chronic synovial hypertrophy and severe end-stage osteoarthritis?
probes.a: Chronic synovitis produces fine, silky, or soft crepitus, whereas end-stage osteoarthritis produces coarse, loud, grating bone-on-bone crepitus.

probes.q: What physical finding immediately distinguishes acute intra-articular arthritis from periarticular bursitis or tendinitis?
probes.a: In acute intra-articular arthritis, every single active and passive movement in all planes is restricted by pain and spasm, whereas in bursitis or tendinitis, restriction affects only specific movements that stress the inflamed tendon.

rubric.text: Exposes bilaterally and inspects resting attitude, swelling, and muscle wasting
Palpates local temperature, joint lines, and assesses for doughy synovial thickening
Assesses active followed by passive movements and palpates for crepitus
Measures fixed deformities, muscle girth, and limb length bilaterally

teach.heading: The Look, Feel, Move, Measure hierarchy
teach.body:
Systematic examination prevents premature focus on the main complaint. Look establishes the joint's resting attitude, presence of effusion, and periarticular muscle wasting.

Feel localizes heat, joint line tenderness, and doughy synovial proliferation. Move defines the functional arc and distinguishes extra-articular from intra-articular restriction.

teach.heading: Tactile types of crepitus
teach.body:
Placing a warm palm over the moving joint reveals internal articular friction. Fine soft crepitus feels like rubbing silk fibres together, typical of rheumatoid or tuberculous synovitis.

Coarse grating crepitus produces a harsh crunching sensation when eburnated subchondral bone rubs against exposed bone in severe osteoarthritis.

skill.exam.surg.joint_effusion.title: Clinical examination for joint effusion: patellar tap, bulge test, and cross-fluctuation
skill.exam.surg.joint_effusion.oneLine: Select the bulge test for minimal fluid, patellar tap for moderate effusion, and cross-fluctuation for tense distension
skill.exam.surg.joint_effusion.why: Differentiating true intra-articular fluid from periarticular bursitis (e.g. prepatellar bursitis / housemaid's knee) or soft tissue edema dictates whether diagnostic joint aspiration is indicated. Selecting the correct clinical test based on effusion volume prevents missed septic or tuberculous synovitis.

steps.text: Position the patient supine with quadriceps muscles fully relaxed and both knees in full extension.
Inspect the parapatellar hollows on both sides of the patella: note fullness or obliteration of the normal medial and lateral gutters.
Bulge / Stroke test (for minimal fluid, 5 to 15 mL): stroke the medial side of the joint proximally two or three times to empty fluid into the suprapatellar pouch.
Immediately stroke the lateral aspect of the knee downward; observe the medial gutter for a visible fluid bulge or wave reforming.
Patellar tap test (for moderate effusion, 20 to 50 mL): empty the suprapatellar pouch by sliding the palm of one hand downward from 10 cm above the patella, pressing firmly against the femur.
With the tips of two fingers of the other hand, push the patella sharply backward against the femoral condyles; feel for the patella tapping on bone and floating back up.
Cross-fluctuation test (for massive or tense effusion, >50 mL): place two fingers over the suprapatellar pouch and two fingers across the inferior parapatellar gutters.
Compress the suprapatellar pouch with one hand; feel the fluid wave transmitted directly to the inferior receiving fingers in two perpendicular planes.

skill.exam.surg.joint_effusion.normal: Sharp concave depressions visible medially and laterally around patella; negative bulge test; patella rests directly against femoral condyles without floating; no cross-fluctuation.
skill.exam.surg.joint_effusion.abnormal: Obliteration of parapatellar hollows; positive fluid wave on bulge test (small effusion); floating patella that taps against femur and rebounds (moderate effusion); transmitted impulse on cross-fluctuation (large effusion).
skill.exam.surg.joint_effusion.significance: Confirms true intra-articular effusion rather than prepatellar bursitis (where fluid sits anterior to the patella and the tap is negative). Acute effusion developing within two hours of trauma indicates haemarthrosis (cruciate ligament tear or osteochondral fracture).
skill.exam.surg.joint_effusion.practice: Practise the bulge test and patellar tap test on clinical simulation knee models, feeling for the crisp bone tap and rebound.
pitfalls: Attempting the patellar tap with contracted quadriceps, which pulls the patella tightly into the trochlear groove and prevents floating.
Misdiagnosing prepatellar bursitis as a knee joint effusion; in bursitis, the fluid is superficial to the patella and the joint gutters are empty.
Relying on the patellar tap to exclude small effusions; a tap requires at least 20 to 30 mL of fluid, whereas the bulge test detects 5 mL.

probes.q: Which clinical test is most sensitive for detecting a minimal knee joint effusion of 5 to 15 mL?
probes.a: The bulge test (fluid displacement or stroke test).

probes.q: How does the patellar tap test distinguish an intra-articular effusion from prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee)?
probes.a: In an intra-articular effusion, fluid lifts the patella off the femur so it taps on compression; in prepatellar bursitis, fluid is superficial to the patella and no tap occurs.

probes.q: What does rapid development of a tense knee effusion within two hours of a sports injury indicate?
probes.a: Acute haemarthrosis, most commonly resulting from an anterior cruciate ligament tear, peripheral meniscal tear, or osteochondral fracture.

rubric.text: Inspects parapatellar hollows with quadriceps completely relaxed in extension
Executes bulge stroke test for minor fluid displacement
Empties suprapatellar pouch and elicits patellar tap and rebound
Tests two-handed cross-fluctuation in two planes for large effusions

teach.heading: Technique of the patellar tap
teach.body:
The suprapatellar pouch extends up to 5 cm proximal to the patella deep to the quadriceps tendon.

Sliding the non-dominant hand downward forces pooled synovial fluid under the patella, floating it off the femoral condyles. Pushing the patella down produces a distinct metallic-like tap against bone.

teach.heading: Differential diagnosis of knee swelling
points: Prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee): swelling covers anterior patella, patellar tap negative.
Infrapatellar bursitis (clergyman's knee): swelling over patellar tendon and tibial tuberosity.
True effusion: fluid occupies the suprapatellar pouch and parapatellar gutters deep to the capsule.

skill.annex.surg.joint_ankylosis.title: Ankylosis: classification, differentiation of bony versus fibrous forms, and optimum positions
skill.annex.surg.joint_ankylosis.oneLine: Compare clinical mobility, pain, and radiologic features of true bony versus fibrous joint fusion
skill.annex.surg.joint_ankylosis.why: Ankylosis (complete or partial loss of joint motion) may be fibrous (intra-articular or extra-articular) or bony. Distinguishing true bony ankylosis from fibrous ankylosis determines whether non-operative mobilization, arthroplasty, or corrective osteotomy is indicated.

asks.text: Is there any detectable movement in the joint, even a springy jog of movement on forced examination?
Does attempting to force movement in the joint cause sharp pain (fibrous) or is it completely painless (bony)?
Was the preceding cause pyogenic infection (predisposing to bony ankylosis) or tuberculosis (predisposing to fibrous)?

skill.annex.surg.joint_ankylosis.practice: Rehearse testing for a jog of movement and memorizing the functional positions of election for joint arthrodesis.
pitfalls: Assuming absolute bony ankylosis without attempting gentle forced movement; even a 2-degree springy jog confirms fibrous fusion.
Attempting closed manipulation under anaesthesia on a fibrously ankylosed tuberculous joint, which reactivates dormant bacilli.
Arthrodesing a joint in full extension when a few degrees of flexion are necessary for functional sitting or walking.

probes.q: What is the key clinical difference in pain between bony and fibrous ankylosis when the examiner attempts to move the joint?
probes.a: Bony ankylosis is completely painless on attempted movement, whereas fibrous ankylosis is typically painful when forced.

probes.q: Why does pyogenic septic arthritis typically lead to bony ankylosis, whereas tuberculous arthritis results in fibrous ankylosis?
probes.a: Pyogenic organisms produce proteolytic enzymes that rapidly destroy articular cartilage, allowing bare bone ends to unite; tubercle bacilli lack proteolytic enzymes, leaving necrotic cartilage that forms fibrous adhesions.

probes.q: What is the optimum functional position of election for surgical arthrodesis of the adult knee joint?
probes.a: 5 to 10 degrees of flexion with neutral rotation and normal physiological valgus.

rubric.text: Differentiates bony from fibrous ankylosis by testing for a springy jog of movement and pain
Correlates aetiology (pyogenic vs tuberculous) with type of joint union
Names the functional position of election for arthrodesis of major joints

teach.heading: Comparison of bony versus fibrous ankylosis
Functional positions of election for arthrodesis
Pathological basis of healing
teach.body:
Staphylococcus aureus synthesizes aggressive proteolytic elastases that liquefy articular hyaline cartilage completely within days.

Denuded subchondral bone vascularizes, bridging the joint with true osteoid trabeculae. In tuberculosis, cartilage is slowly undermined by pannus without proteolysis, creating fibrous bridges.

skill.exam.surg.shoulder_impingement_cuf.title: Examination of rotator cuff pathology: impingement tests and cuff tears
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_impingement_cuf.oneLine: Elicit Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy, painful arc, drop arm sign, and external rotation lag
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_impingement_cuf.why: Rotator cuff tendinopathy and subacromial impingement are the commonest sources of non-traumatic shoulder disability. Clinically isolating the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis separates reversible subacromial bursitis from full-thickness tears requiring surgical repair.

steps.text: Inspect the shoulder girdle from front and behind: observe supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossa hollowing (muscle atrophy).
Painful arc test: ask patient to actively abduct the arm from 0 to 180 degrees in the scapular plane; observe for pain between 60 and 120 degrees that clears above 120 degrees.
Neer impingement sign: stabilize the scapula with one hand to prevent rotation; with the other hand, passively forward-flex the pronated arm fully overhead.
Hawkins-Kennedy test: forward-flex shoulder to 90 degrees and elbow to 90 degrees; forcefully internally rotate the humerus to jam the greater tuberosity against the coracoacromial ligament.
Jobe supraspinatus test (empty can test): abduct arms to 90 degrees with 30 degrees forward flexion in scapular plane and full internal rotation (thumbs pointing down); resist downward pressure.
Drop arm test: passively abduct the arm to 90 degrees and ask patient to lower it smoothly and slowly to the side; observe for sudden uncontrolled drop.

External rotation lag sign (infraspinatus / teres minor): with elbow flexed to 90 degrees, passively rotate arm externally to maximum; ask patient to hold it; observe for internal rotation spring-back.
Gerber lift-off test (subscapularis): place dorsum of patient's hand against lumbar spine; ask patient to push hand backward away from back against resistance.

skill.exam.surg.shoulder_impingement_cuf.normal: Smooth painless active abduction from 0 to 180 degrees; negative Neer and Hawkins tests; strong resistance on empty can test; smooth controlled descent of arm; no lag signs.
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_impingement_cuf.abnormal: Sharp pain between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction (painful arc); pain on maximal forward flexion (positive Neer); pain on internal rotation at 90 degrees (positive Hawkins); sudden arm drop (positive drop arm sign); unable to maintain external rotation (lag sign).
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_impingement_cuf.significance: Painful arc (60-120 degrees) and positive Neer/Hawkins signs confirm subacromial impingement. Drop arm test confirms full-thickness supraspinatus tear. External rotation lag sign confirms infraspinatus tear. Inability to lift hand off back confirms subscapularis tear.
skill.exam.surg.shoulder_impingement_cuf.practice: Rehearse performing the painful arc, Neer test, Hawkins-Kennedy manoeuvre, and empty can test with a partner.
pitfalls: Failing to stabilize the scapula during the Neer test, allowing compensatory scapulothoracic movement to mask impingement.
Performing the empty can test with thumb pointing up instead of down, which tests the biceps and anterior deltoid rather than supraspinatus.
Confusing subacromial impingement with adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder); frozen shoulder restricts passive external rotation, while impingement preserves passive motion.

probes.q: Between what degrees of active abduction does the classical painful arc of subacromial impingement occur?
probes.a: Between 60 and 120 degrees of active abduction.

probes.q: What anatomical structures impinge against each other during the Hawkins-Kennedy test?
probes.a: The greater tuberosity of the humerus and the supraspinatus tendon impinge against the coracoacromial ligament and acromion.

probes.q: What does a positive drop arm test indicate when the patient attempts to lower the arm from 90 degrees abduction?
probes.a: A full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon, preventing eccentric muscular control of descent.

rubric.text: Elicits painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of active abduction
Performs Neer sign with scapular stabilization and Hawkins-Kennedy internal rotation
Executes empty can test and drop arm sign to detect full-thickness tears
Evaluates external rotation lag sign and Gerber lift-off test

teach.heading: Pathomechanics of subacromial impingement
teach.body:
The coracoacromial arch consists of the anterior acromion, coracoid process, and coracoacromial ligament.

During arm elevation, the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa glide beneath this rigid arch. Swelling from overuse or osteophytes narrows the 1 cm space, compressing the tendon.

teach.heading: The painful arc mechanism
teach.body:
From 0 to 60 degrees of abduction, the supraspinatus tendon has not yet reached the coracoacromial arch, so movement is painless.

Between 60 and 120 degrees, the greater tuberosity squeezes under the arch, producing sharp pain. Above 120 degrees, the tuberosity passes beyond the arch, and pain clears.

rows: Empty can test, Drop arm sign

skill.exam.surg.epicondylitis_elbow.title: Examination of lateral and medial epicondylitis of the elbow
skill.exam.surg.epicondylitis_elbow.oneLine: Perform Cozen test for tennis elbow and resisted wrist flexion for golfer's elbow
skill.exam.surg.epicondylitis_elbow.why: Overuse tendinopathies of the common extensor origin (lateral epicondylitis / tennis elbow) and common flexor origin (medial epicondylitis / golfer's elbow) cause disabling occupational and sports disability. Localizing the exact site of micro-tearing and tendon degeneration separates epicondylitis from radial tunnel syndrome or cervical radiculopathy.

steps.text: Inspect the elbow contours: note that cutaneous redness and diffuse swelling are usually absent in uncomplicated epicondylitis.
Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow): flex the elbow to 90 degrees with the forearm pronated; palpate the anterior facet of the lateral epicondyle directly.
Identify the precise point of maximal tenderness directly over the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) origin.
Cozen test: ask the patient to make a fist, pronate the forearm, and radially deviate and extend the wrist actively against firm manual resistance while your thumb presses the lateral epicondyle.
Mill test: passively pronate the forearm, fully flex the wrist, and extend the elbow completely; note sharp pain over the lateral epicondyle.
Maudsley test: test resisted active extension of the middle finger; note localized pain over the lateral epicondyle due to isolated stress on ECRB.
Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow): palpate the medial epicondyle and test resisted active wrist flexion and pronation.
Palpate the radial tunnel (4 cm distal to lateral epicondyle over radial neck) to exclude posterior interosseous nerve entrapment.

skill.exam.surg.epicondylitis_elbow.normal: Non-tender epicondyles; painless resisted wrist extension, wrist flexion, and finger extension; full painless elbow range of motion.
skill.exam.surg.epicondylitis_elbow.abnormal: Exquisite localized point tenderness directly over the anterior facet of the lateral epicondyle; sharp pain reproduced by Cozen test, Mill test, or Maudsley test; medial epicondylar tenderness on resisted wrist flexion (golfer's elbow).
skill.exam.surg.epicondylitis_elbow.significance: A positive Cozen and Mill test confirms lateral epicondylitis (angiofibroblastic tendinosis of ECRB origin). Tenderness located 4 cm distal to the epicondyle over the supinator edge indicates radial tunnel syndrome rather than tennis elbow.
skill.exam.surg.epicondylitis_elbow.practice: Practise identifying the anterior facet of the lateral epicondyle and executing Cozen, Mill, and Maudsley tests with a partner.
pitfalls: Palpating too posteriorly or distally, mistaking the radiohumeral joint line or radial head for the extensor origin.
Missing radial tunnel syndrome, where maximal tenderness lies 4 cm distal to the epicondyle over the mobile muscle belly.
Failing to examine the cervical spine (C6-C7 radiculopathy) in patients presenting with refractory lateral elbow pain.

probes.q: Which specific muscle tendon origin is primarily involved in lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)?
probes.a: Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB).

probes.q: How is Cozen test performed, and what constitutes a positive result?
probes.a: The patient actively extends and radially deviates the wrist against resistance with elbow flexed; sharp pain localized to the lateral epicondyle is positive.

probes.q: How does radial tunnel syndrome clinically mimic tennis elbow, and how do you differentiate them on physical examination?
probes.a: Both cause lateral elbow pain, but in tennis elbow tenderness is directly on the lateral epicondyle, whereas in radial tunnel syndrome tenderness is 4 cm distal over the radial neck and supinator muscle.

rubric.text: Palpates anterior facet of lateral epicondyle to localize point tenderness
Executes Cozen test with resisted wrist extension and radial deviation
Performs Mill passive stretch test and Maudsley middle finger test
Palpates 4 cm distal to exclude radial tunnel nerve compression

teach.heading: Pathology of epicondylitis
teach.body:
Despite the '-itis' suffix, chronic epicondylitis is not an acute inflammatory disease but an angiofibroblastic tendinosis.

Repetitive microtrauma causes microscopic tearing, vascular hyperplasia, and disorganized collagen repair at the extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon origin on the lateral epicondyle.

teach.heading: The three provocative tests for tennis elbow
points: Cozen test: resisted active wrist extension with forearm pronated.
Mill test: passive wrist flexion with the elbow fully extended.
Maudsley test: resisted active extension of the middle finger, which specifically tensions ECRB.

skill.exam.surg.carpal_tunnel.title: Examination for carpal tunnel syndrome: Phalen, Tinel, and thenar wasting
skill.exam.surg.carpal_tunnel.oneLine: Elicit Phalen test, Durkan carpal compression, Tinel sign, and abductor pollicis brevis weakness
skill.exam.surg.carpal_tunnel.why: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest peripheral nerve entrapment neuropathy. Unrecognized chronic compression of the median nerve in the fibro-osseous canal leads to permanent sensory axon loss, irreversible thenar motor wasting, and loss of fine thumb opposition. Identifying provocative signs and thenar sparing directs prompt decompression.

steps.text: Inspect both hands: compare the thenar eminences to detect flattening, hollowing, or guttering (thenar muscle wasting).
Test cutaneous sensation using light touch and pinprick over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger.
Crucially test sensation over the thenar eminence: note normal sensation here because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the transverse carpal ligament.
Phalen test: ask the patient to hold both wrists in complete, unforced 90-degree flexion with dorsal surfaces touching for 60 seconds.
Note whether tingling, numbness, or burning paresthesias develop in the median nerve distribution during the 60 seconds.
Durkan carpal compression test: place both thumbs directly over the proximal edge of the transverse carpal ligament and apply steady pressure for 30 seconds.
Tinel sign: lightly tap with the tip of your index finger over the median nerve at the anterior wrist crease; ask if electric tingling shoots into the digits.

Motor testing: test abductor pollicis brevis by asking the patient to place the hand palm up and point the thumb vertically toward the ceiling against downward resistance, while palpating the thenar muscle belly.

skill.exam.surg.carpal_tunnel.normal: Full rounded thenar eminence; normal sensation across all digits and palm; negative Phalen test and Durkan test after 60 seconds; negative Tinel sign; strong thumb abduction against resistance.
skill.exam.surg.carpal_tunnel.abnormal: Paresthesias in radial 3.5 digits during Phalen test within 30 to 60 seconds; positive Durkan compression; radiating electric tingling on tapping (positive Tinel); thenar muscle wasting; weakness of abductor pollicis brevis with normal thenar eminence sensation.
skill.exam.surg.carpal_tunnel.significance: Sparing of thenar eminence sensation confirms entrapment within the carpal tunnel, as the palmar cutaneous branch branches proximal to the flexor retinaculum. Thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction indicate advanced motor axon loss warranting urgent open or endoscopic surgical decompression.
skill.exam.surg.carpal_tunnel.practice: Rehearse performing Phalen and Durkan tests, eliciting Tinel sign at the wrist crease, and testing abductor pollicis brevis power.
pitfalls: Failing to test sensation over the thenar eminence; loss of sensation over the thenar eminence indicates proximal median nerve or C6-C7 root pathology.
Testing thumb adduction instead of abduction; thumb adduction is performed by the ulnar-innervated adductor pollicis.
Ending the Phalen test after only 10 seconds; the test must be maintained for a full 60 seconds unless symptoms appear sooner.

probes.q: Which digits experience numbness and tingling in classic carpal tunnel syndrome?
probes.a: The thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the radial half of the ring finger.

probes.q: Why is sensation over the fleshy thenar eminence preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome despite profound numbness in the fingertips?
probes.a: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises 3 to 5 cm proximal to the wrist and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, bypassing the carpal tunnel.

probes.q: Which specific thenar muscle is tested clinically to evaluate median motor nerve loss in carpal tunnel syndrome, and how is it tested?
probes.a: Abductor pollicis brevis, tested by asking the patient to abduct the thumb vertically at 90 degrees to the palm against resistance.

rubric.text: Inspects thenar eminence for wasting and maps sensory loss in radial 3.5 digits
Demonstrates sparing of palmar cutaneous sensation over thenar eminence
Executes Phalen test for 60 seconds and Durkan carpal compression test
Tests abductor pollicis brevis power with thumb pointing vertically

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Anatomy of the carpal tunnel
teach.body:
The carpal tunnel is bounded deeply by the carpal bones (scaphoid, trapezium, hamate, triquetrum) and roofed by the thick transverse carpal ligament.

Ten structures pass through: the median nerve, four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus, and the tendon of flexor pollicis longus.

teach.heading: Provocative bedside diagnostic tests
points: Phalen test: wrist hyperflexion increases intracarpal pressure from 30 to over 100 mmHg, reproducing paresthesias within 60 seconds.
Durkan compression test: direct thumb pressure over the carpal tunnel has the highest sensitivity (over 85 percent) for reproducing symptoms.
Tinel sign: percussion over the compressed segment elicits tingling in regenerating or irritable nerve fibres.

teach.heading: The palmar cutaneous branch sign
teach.body:
The palmar cutaneous branch arises 5 cm proximal to the flexor retinaculum and travels superficially into the skin of the thenar eminence.

Because it does not enter the carpal tunnel, sensation over the thenar eminence remains completely normal. Sensation loss over the thenar eminence points instead to a C6 radiculopathy or pronator teres syndrome.

skill.exam.surg.de_quervain.title: Examination for de Quervain tenosynovitis: Finkelstein test
skill.exam.surg.de_quervain.oneLine: Palpate the first extensor compartment and elicit the Finkelstein stretch test
skill.exam.surg.de_quervain.why: Stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal extensor compartment (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis) causes disabling radial styloid pain in young mothers and manual workers. A positive Finkelstein test confirms tendon entrapment beneath the thickened extensor retinaculum, directing corticosteroid injection or surgical release.

steps.text: Inspect the radial aspect of the wrist: observe localized thickening, swelling, or fullness directly over the radial styloid process.
Palpate the radial styloid process and identify the first extensor tendon compartment passing across it.
Identify the two tendons of the first compartment: abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB).
Palpate directly along the tendon sheath for localized point tenderness and firm, tender fibrous thickening.
Finkelstein test: ask the patient to tuck the thumb into the palm and fold the other four fingers tightly over it into a fist.
Stabilize the patient's forearm with one hand and gently, firmly deviate the wrist toward the ulnar side.
Observe for an immediate, sharp, agonizing pain localized precisely over the first extensor compartment at the radial styloid.
Perform the thumb carpometacarpal grind test (axial compression and rotation of first metacarpal) to exclude base-of-thumb osteoarthritis.

skill.exam.surg.de_quervain.normal: Smooth non-tender radial styloid and first extensor compartment; painless passive ulnar deviation with thumb flexed in fist; negative CMC grind test.
skill.exam.surg.de_quervain.abnormal: Visible fullness or nodularity over radial styloid; exquisite localized tenderness over APL and EPB sheaths; severe lancinating pain on passive ulnar deviation with thumb enclosed (positive Finkelstein test).
skill.exam.surg.de_quervain.significance: A positive Finkelstein test confirms stenosing tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment. A negative thumb CMC grind test differentiates de Quervain disease from carpometacarpal osteoarthritis (rhizarthrosis).
skill.exam.surg.de_quervain.practice: Rehearse positioning the thumb inside the fingers and performing passive ulnar deviation (Finkelstein test) on clinical simulation models.
pitfalls: Performing the Finkelstein test violently, which causes extreme distress in a patient with severe tenosynovitis.
Confusing de Quervain tenosynovitis with first carpometacarpal osteoarthritis, where pain is reproduced by axial grinding of the thumb.
Overlooking an anatomical variation such as multiple slips of APL or a separate sub-compartment for EPB that causes treatment failure.

probes.q: Which two tendons pass through the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist?
probes.a: Abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB).

probes.q: How is the Finkelstein test performed, and what constitutes a positive result?
probes.a: The patient encloses the thumb inside a clenched fist, and the examiner passively ulnar-deviates the wrist; sharp localized pain over the radial styloid is positive.

probes.q: What bedside test distinguishes de Quervain tenosynovitis from osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint?
probes.a: The CMC grind test (axial compression and circumduction of the thumb metacarpal), which is positive in CMC arthritis but negative in de Quervain tenosynovitis.

rubric.text: Palpates radial styloid and localizes point tenderness over APL and EPB tendons
Executes Finkelstein test with thumb inside fist and passive ulnar deviation
Performs CMC grind test to rule out first carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis
Differentiates first compartment tenderness from anatomical snuffbox tenderness

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Anatomy of the first dorsal compartment
teach.body:
The first extensor compartment is a fibro-osseous tunnel over the lateral radial styloid containing the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

Repetitive thumb abduction and wrist deviation creates friction against the osteofascial roof, leading to synovial thickening and stenosis.

teach.heading: The Finkelstein test mechanism
teach.body:
Flexing the thumb across the palm pulls both APL and EPB tendons distally through their narrow tunnel.

Passive ulnar deviation of the wrist stretches the taut tendons firmly over the inflamed radial styloid ridge, producing an excruciating, reproducible lancinating pain.

teach.heading: Differential diagnosis of radial wrist pain

skill.exam.surg.thomas_hip_flexion.title: Thomas test for fixed flexion deformity of the hip
skill.exam.surg.thomas_hip_flexion.oneLine: Obliterate compensatory lumbar lordosis by flexing the sound hip to reveal true hip deformity
skill.exam.surg.thomas_hip_flexion.why: A patient with a fixed flexion deformity of the hip conceals the deformity when lying supine by exaggerating their lumbar lordosis, allowing the leg to lie flat on the couch. Thomas test eliminates spinal compensation, uncovering the true degree of fixed hip flexion in tuberculous arthritis, osteoarthritis, and Perthes disease.

steps.text: Place the patient supine on a firm, flat examination couch with legs extended.
Slide your flat hand under the patient's lumbar spine to evaluate baseline lumbar lordosis; note that the affected thigh appears to lie flat on the couch.
Fully flex the unaffected (sound) hip and knee onto the patient's abdomen until the thigh meets the chest.
Verify with your hand under the spine that the lumbar lordosis is completely flattened against the table (pelvis in neutral tilt).
Observe the affected lower limb: if the hip has no fixed flexion deformity, the thigh remains flat on the couch.
If a fixed flexion deformity is present, observe the affected thigh rise involuntarily off the couch as lordosis is flattened.
Measure the angle between the raised thigh and the examination table with a goniometer; this represents the true fixed flexion deformity angle.
Note that pressing the raised thigh down onto the couch causes the lumbar spine to arch upward off the table again.

skill.exam.surg.thomas_hip_flexion.normal: The affected thigh remains completely flat on the couch when the sound hip is fully flexed and lumbar lordosis is obliterated; no fixed flexion deformity (0 degrees).
skill.exam.surg.thomas_hip_flexion.abnormal: The affected thigh rises off the couch as lumbar lordosis is flattened; the angle between the thigh and the table measures the true fixed flexion deformity (e.g. 20 to 40 degrees).
skill.exam.surg.thomas_hip_flexion.significance: Unmasks concealed fixed flexion deformity of the hip. In tuberculous arthritis, Thomas test is positive early in the second and third stages. A positive test can also be caused by psoas spasm (psoas abscess, retrocaecal appendicitis) or advanced osteoarthritis.
skill.exam.surg.thomas_hip_flexion.practice: Rehearse sliding your hand beneath the lumbar spine, flexing the contralateral hip to flatten lordosis, and measuring the thigh angle.
pitfalls: Incompletely flexing the sound hip, leaving residual lumbar lordosis that masks part of the fixed flexion deformity.
Failing to place a hand under the lumbar spine to verify that the lordosis has been completely flattened against the couch.
Attempting Thomas test on a soft, yielding mattress where the pelvis sinks and distorts angular measurements.

probes.q: What compensatory mechanism does a patient use to hide a fixed flexion deformity of the hip when lying supine?
probes.a: Exaggeration of lumbar lordosis (anterior pelvic tilt).

probes.q: Why must the examiner place a hand under the patient's lumbar spine during Thomas test?
probes.a: To confirm that the compensatory lumbar lordosis is completely obliterated as the sound hip is flexed onto the abdomen.

probes.q: Name two non-articular conditions that can produce a positive Thomas test mimicking hip joint disease.
probes.a: Psoas abscess and iliopsoas muscle spasm from retrocaecal appendicitis or perinephric abscess.

rubric.text: Places flat hand under lumbar spine to assess compensatory lordosis
Fully flexes sound hip until lumbar lordosis is completely flattened
Measures angle of affected thigh rising off couch with goniometer
Tests passive hip extension and demonstrates lordosis returning on thigh depression

teach.heading: Biomechanics of pelvic compensation
teach.body:
The hip joint and lumbar spine function as a kinematic chain. When a hip develops a fixed flexion contracture, the patient cannot stand erect without compensation.

By tilting the pelvis forward and hyperextending the lumbar spine (hyperlordosis), the patient brings the flexed thigh into vertical alignment with the trunk.

teach.heading: Execution of Thomas test
teach.body:
When the patient lies on the couch, the flexed leg appears to lie flat because the lumbar spine arches off the table.

Flexing the normal hip rotates the pelvis backward and flattens the lumbar curve against the couch. Once the spine is flat, the true fixed flexion angle is unmasked as the affected thigh rises.

skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_hip.title: Trendelenburg test and the hip abductor mechanism
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_hip.oneLine: Assess pelvic tilt when standing on one leg: normal pelvis rises, deficient abductor mechanism dips
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_hip.why: Single-leg stance requires an intact hip abductor mechanism (gluteus medius and minimus, superior gluteal nerve, intact femoral neck lever arm, and stable femoral head fulcrum in the acetabulum). Trendelenburg test identifies abductor insufficiency in developmental dysplasia of the hip, ununited femoral neck fracture, coxa vara, and neurological paralysis.

steps.text: Stand behind the standing patient with the patient stripped from waist down to expose the buttocks, iliac crests, and thighs.
Inspect the symmetry of the gluteal folds and dimples of Venus (posterior superior iliac spines) at rest with both feet on the floor.
Ask the patient to lift one foot off the floor and stand solely on the other leg (the test stance leg) with the knee slightly flexed, without leaning.
Observe the non-weight-bearing (unsupported) hemipelvis and gluteal fold for 30 seconds.
Normal response: the unsupported hemipelvis rises above the horizontal, held up by the abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) of the stance leg.
Abnormal (positive) response: the unsupported hemipelvis dips or drops below the horizontal, indicating failure of the abductor mechanism of the stance hip.
Observe the patient's torso: note if the patient shifts their trunk laterally over the stance hip to balance their centre of gravity (Trendelenburg lurch).
Repeat the test with the patient standing on the opposite leg to compare bilaterally.

skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_hip.normal: Pelvis on the unsupported side rises above the horizontal when standing on one leg; torso remains erect without lateral lurching.
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_hip.abnormal: Pelvis on the unsupported side dips below the horizontal (positive Trendelenburg sign); lateral trunk shift toward the stance side (Trendelenburg lurch).
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_hip.significance: A positive test indicates failure of one of the four components of the hip abductor mechanism: 1. Paralysed muscle (poliomyelitis, superior gluteal nerve palsy); 2. Ineffective muscle (myopathy); 3. Defective lever arm (coxa vara, ununited femoral neck fracture); 4. Unstable fulcrum (developmental dysplasia/dislocation of hip, head destruction in septic arthritis).
skill.exam.surg.trendelenburg_hip.practice: Stand behind a partner and observe pelvic tilt on single-leg stance, then simulate a positive sign by relaxing stance abductors.
pitfalls: Permitting the patient to support their weight with hands against a wall, which stabilizes the pelvis and produces a false-negative result.
Missing the lurching torso shift (compensated Trendelenburg sign) where the patient leans over the stance hip to prevent pelvic drop.
Testing in an uncooperative or severely pained patient who cannot balance on one foot for at least 15 to 30 seconds.

probes.q: What happens to the unsupported pelvis during single-leg stance in a normal, healthy individual?
probes.a: The pelvis on the unsupported side rises slightly above the horizontal.

probes.q: What are the primary muscles and nerve supplying the abductor mechanism of the weight-bearing hip?
probes.a: Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles, innervated by the superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1).

probes.q: Name the four pathological categories that cause a positive Trendelenburg test.
probes.a: Paralysis of abductors (nerve injury), myopathic weakness, defective lever arm (coxa vara or non-union femoral neck), and unstable fulcrum (developmental dislocation of hip).

rubric.text: Stands behind patient and inspects resting gluteal folds and iliac crests
Instructs patient to stand on single leg without supporting hands on furniture
Observes whether unsupported pelvis rises (normal) or dips (positive sign)
Identifies compensatory lateral trunk shift (Trendelenburg lurch)
