teach.heading: The abductor lever mechanism
teach.body:
When standing on one leg, gravity pulls the unsupported pelvis downward. To keep the pelvis level, the gluteus medius and minimus on the stance side contract vigorously.

They act across the femoral neck lever arm, using the spherical femoral head seated in the acetabulum as a stable fulcrum.

teach.heading: Four anatomical requirements for a negative test
points: Intact muscle power in gluteus medius and minimus.
Intact nerve supply via the superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1).
Rigid, unshortened lever arm (normal femoral neck-shaft angle of 125 degrees and intact greater trochanter).
Stable articular fulcrum (femoral head securely located within the acetabular socket).

teach.heading: Trendelenburg gait versus lurch
teach.body:
When a patient with bilateral abductor insufficiency walks, the pelvis dips alternately from side to side, creating a waddling gait typical of bilateral DDH.

In unilateral disease, the patient leans their entire trunk over the weight-bearing side at each step (Trendelenburg lurch) to shift their center of gravity over the deficient fulcrum.

skill.exam.surg.limb_length_measurement.title: Limb length measurement: true versus apparent length and Bryant triangle
skill.exam.surg.limb_length_measurement.oneLine: Square the pelvis, measure true length from ASIS, and assess supratrochanteric shortening
skill.exam.surg.limb_length_measurement.why: Lower limb length discrepancy leads to pelvic obliquity, compensatory lumbar scoliosis, and abnormal gait. Differentiating true skeletal shortening (from bone defect or joint destruction) from apparent shortening (from pelvic tilt caused by fixed adduction contracture) determines whether skeletal lengthening, contralateral shortening, or soft-tissue contracture release is required.

steps.text: Place the patient supine on a firm, flat couch with legs extended.
Square the pelvis: ensure that a line connecting both anterior superior iliac spines (ASIS) is exactly perpendicular to the long axis of the trunk.
Place both lower limbs in identical attitudes of abduction, adduction, and rotation relative to the pelvis before measuring.

True length measurement: measure with a non-elastic tape from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the tip of the medial malleolus on each side, keeping the tape on the medial side of the patella.
Apparent length measurement: measure from a fixed midline point (xiphisternum or umbilicus) to the tip of the medial malleolus with limbs placed parallel.
Segmental bone measurements: measure femoral length (ASIS to lateral joint line) and tibial length (medial joint line to medial malleolus) bilaterally.

Bryant triangle: with patient supine, drop a vertical line down from the ASIS to the table; draw a horizontal line from the tip of the greater trochanter to meet the vertical line; measure the horizontal base of the triangle and compare with the healthy side.

Nelaton line: draw a line from the ASIS to the ischial tuberosity; verify whether the tip of the greater trochanter lies on or below this line (normal) or rides above it (supratrochanteric shortening).

skill.exam.surg.limb_length_measurement.normal: Equal true and apparent limb lengths bilaterally (difference <1 cm); symmetrical Bryant triangle bases; tip of greater trochanter touches or lies below Nelaton line.
skill.exam.surg.limb_length_measurement.abnormal: True shortening (ASIS-to-malleolus discrepancy); apparent shortening with normal true length (fixed adduction deformity with pelvic tilt); shortened base of Bryant triangle or trochanter riding above Nelaton line confirming supratrochanteric shortening.
skill.exam.surg.limb_length_measurement.significance: True shortening reflects anatomical bone loss or joint destruction (fracture, growth plate arrest, destroyed femoral head). Apparent shortening without true shortening indicates a fixed adduction contracture tilting the pelvis. A shortened Bryant triangle localizes shortening above the greater trochanter.
skill.exam.surg.limb_length_measurement.practice: Practise squaring the pelvis, measuring true and apparent lengths with a tape measure, and drawing Bryant triangle on a clinical model.
pitfalls: Measuring true limb length without squaring the pelvis first, producing erroneous measurements due to pelvic tilt.
Measuring the two limbs in different positions of abduction or adduction, which artificially alters tape distances.
Failing to perform segmental measurements to determine whether shortening is in the femur, tibia, or supra-trochanteric hip zone.

probes.q: Between which two anatomical bony landmarks is true lower limb length measured?
probes.a: From the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the tip of the medial malleolus.

probes.q: What clinical condition produces apparent shortening of a lower limb while the true limb length remains completely normal?
probes.a: A fixed adduction deformity of the hip, which forces the pelvis to tilt upward on the affected side when the limbs are brought parallel.

probes.q: How does Bryant triangle localize limb shortening to the supratrochanteric region of the hip?
probes.a: The horizontal base of the triangle (distance between greater trochanter and the vertical line dropped from ASIS) is shortened compared to the sound side.

rubric.text: Squares pelvis so line connecting ASIS is perpendicular to trunk axis
Measures true length from ASIS to medial malleolus with limbs in identical attitudes
Measures apparent length from xiphisternum or umbilicus with limbs parallel
Constructs Bryant triangle or Nelaton line to assess supratrochanteric shortening

teach.heading: True versus apparent shortening
teach.body:
True shortening is actual anatomical loss of skeletal length in the femur or tibia, measured between ASIS and medial malleolus.

Apparent shortening is an illusion created by pelvic obliquity. When a hip has a fixed adduction deformity, the patient must hike that side of the pelvis up to bring the legs parallel for walking, making the leg appear shorter.

teach.heading: Squaring the pelvis
teach.body:
Accurate measurement is impossible without squaring the pelvis. Palpate both anterior superior iliac spines and ensure the inter-ASIS line forms a 90-degree angle with the trunk.

Both limbs must be positioned at the identical angle of abduction or adduction. If one hip has a fixed 20-degree adduction deformity, abduct the sound hip by 20 degrees before measuring.

rows: Vertical from ASIS, horizontal from trochanter
Base shortened in neck fracture or coxa vara
Line from ASIS to ischial tuberosity
Trochanter rides above line in dislocation
Passes below umbilicus in hip displacement

skill.exam.surg.knee_osteoarthritis.title: Examination of knee osteoarthritis and angular deformities
skill.exam.surg.knee_osteoarthritis.oneLine: Identify varus malalignment, joint line osteophytes, patellofemoral crepitus, and Baker cyst
skill.exam.surg.knee_osteoarthritis.why: Osteoarthritis of the knee is the commonest degenerative joint disorder seen in surgical clinics. Comprehensive assessment of compartment involvement (medial tibiofemoral, lateral tibiofemoral, patellofemoral), varus or valgus deformity, fixed contractures, and secondary popliteal cysts determines conservative care versus high tibial osteotomy or unicompartmental / total knee arthroplasty.

steps.text: Inspect the standing patient from front, side, and behind: assess coronal alignment for genu varum (bow-leg deformity) or genu valgum (knock-knee).
Observe the patient walking: look for an antalgic limp and a dynamic lateral or varus thrust during the stance phase.
Inspect the supine knee: note quadriceps wasting (particularly vastus medialis), loss of parapatellar hollows, and popliteal fossa fullness.
Palpate the medial and lateral joint lines: identify localized tenderness and hard, irregular marginal bony ridges (osteophytes).
Test the patellofemoral joint: press the patella against the femoral trochlea and glide it side to side (patellar grind test); note coarse retropatellar crepitus and pain.
Palpate tibiofemoral crepitus: place your palm over the anterior knee while actively or passively flexing and extending through the full arc.
Evaluate fixed flexion deformity: gently push the posterior knee flat against the couch; measure any residual extension lag with a goniometer.
Palpate the popliteal fossa for a Baker cyst (popliteal cyst): note that the swelling tenses on knee extension and softens or disappears on 45-degree flexion (Foucher sign).

skill.exam.surg.knee_osteoarthritis.normal: Normal anatomical valgus (femoro-tibial angle 5 to 7 degrees); non-tender joint lines without osteophytes; smooth silent joint excursion without crepitus; full extension (0 degrees) and flexion (135 degrees); empty popliteal fossa.
skill.exam.surg.knee_osteoarthritis.abnormal: Genu varum (bow-leg) deformity; palpable irregular bony osteophytes along joint margin; coarse, grating crepitus during flexion-extension; retropatellar crepitus; fixed flexion deformity (>5 to 10 degrees); fluctuant popliteal mass with positive Foucher sign.
skill.exam.surg.knee_osteoarthritis.significance: Medial compartment osteoarthritis produces progressive varus deformity because weight-bearing forces concentrate medially during bipedal gait. Coarse bone-on-bone crepitus indicates full-thickness articular cartilage loss down to eburnated bone. A Baker cyst represents chronic synovial effusion herniating into the semimembranosus bursa.
skill.exam.surg.knee_osteoarthritis.practice: Practise identifying genu varum alignment on standing, palpating marginal osteophytes, and eliciting patellofemoral and tibiofemoral crepitus.
pitfalls: Examining coronal alignment only with the patient supine; varus and valgus malalignment must be evaluated in full standing weight-bearing.
Mistaking a pulsating popliteal artery aneurysm for a benign Baker cyst; always palpate for pulsation and auscultate for a bruit.
Overlooking an early fixed flexion contracture by not pressing the knee flat against the couch.

probes.q: Which tibiofemoral compartment is most commonly affected in primary knee osteoarthritis, and what angular deformity results?
probes.a: The medial tibiofemoral compartment, leading to a progressive genu varum (bow-leg) deformity.

probes.q: What physical sign characterizes a Baker cyst (popliteal cyst) on knee flexion and extension (Foucher sign)?
probes.a: The cyst becomes tense, firm, and prominent during full knee extension, and softens or disappears during 45 degrees of flexion.

probes.q: How does the patellar grind test evaluate patellofemoral osteoarthritis on physical examination?
probes.a: The patella is compressed posteriorly into the femoral trochlear groove and moved mediolaterally, eliciting coarse retropatellar crepitus and sharp pain.

rubric.text: Inspects standing coronal alignment for genu varum and observes gait for varus thrust
Palpates joint lines for localized tenderness and irregular bony osteophytes
Tests patellar grind and palpates for coarse tibiofemoral crepitus during motion
Measures fixed flexion deformity and palpates popliteal fossa for Baker cyst

teach.heading: Compartmental biomechanics of the knee
teach.body:
The knee consists of three functional compartments: medial tibiofemoral, lateral tibiofemoral, and patellofemoral.

During normal single-leg stance, the ground reaction force vector passes medial to the knee centre, directing 60 to 70 percent of body weight onto the medial compartment. This explains why medial wear and varus deformity are far commoner than lateral disease.

teach.heading: Physical triad of advanced osteoarthritis
points: Coarse grating crepitus: palpable crunching as denuded eburnated subchondral bone surfaces slide against each other.
Marginal osteophytes: prominent, irregular bony ledges felt along the joint margins, particularly the medial tibial plateau.
Fixed flexion deformity: inability to achieve full terminal extension (0 degrees) due to posterior capsular contracture and anterior osteophytes.

teach.heading: Anatomy and signs of a Baker cyst
teach.body:
A Baker cyst (popliteal synovial cyst) is a distension of the bursa between the medial head of gastrocnemius and the semimembranosus tendon.

It communicates with the knee joint via a one-way slit valve. In full knee extension, the muscles compress the cyst, making it tense and prominent (Foucher sign); flexing to 45 degrees relaxes tension.

skill.hx.surg.head_injury.title: History in head injury
skill.hx.surg.head_injury.oneLine: Mechanism, loss of consciousness, lucid interval, and post-traumatic amnesia
skill.hx.surg.head_injury.why: Establishes trauma kinematics, identifies patients requiring emergency neuroimaging or operative evacuation, and separates primary concussive injury from an expanding intracranial haematoma.

asks.text: What was the exact mechanism of injury: road traffic accident, fall from a height, or direct assault with a blunt or sharp weapon?
Was the patient conscious immediately following the impact, or was there immediate loss of consciousness?
If consciousness returned, was there a subsequent deterioration into drowsiness or coma (a lucid interval)?
How long was the period of retrograde amnesia (events before the trauma) and post-traumatic amnesia (until continuous memory returned)?
Has there been recurrent or projectile vomiting, severe worsening headache, or post-traumatic seizures?
Has there been watery fluid discharge or fresh bleeding from the nose (rhinorrhoea) or ears (otorrhoea)?
Was alcohol or any sedative ingested before the trauma, and is the patient taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications?

skill.hx.surg.head_injury.practice: Take a head injury history from a relative or bystander, specifically reconstructing the time course from impact to hospital arrival and documenting whether a lucid interval occurred.
pitfalls: Attributing altered sensorium solely to alcohol or substance intoxication without excluding an acute intracranial haematoma.
Failing to ask about a lucid interval, which can lead to delayed detection of an acute extradural haematoma.
Neglecting to record the exact duration of post-traumatic amnesia, which is the most reliable clinical indicator of injury severity.

probes.q: What is meant by a lucid interval in head trauma, and which intracranial lesion classically demonstrates it?
probes.a: A temporary period of normal consciousness between the initial traumatic loss of consciousness and subsequent coma, classically seen in acute extradural haematoma.

probes.q: How does the duration of post-traumatic amnesia correlate with the severity of traumatic brain injury?
probes.a: Post-traumatic amnesia lasting under one hour indicates mild injury, 1 to 24 hours moderate injury, and greater than 24 hours severe brain injury.

probes.q: Why is it essential to elicit an accurate medication history including anticoagulants in an elderly patient with minor head trauma?
probes.a: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs substantially elevate the risk of chronic and acute subdural haematomas even after trivial trauma.

rubric.text: Inquires about the exact mechanism of injury, velocity, and impact point
Clarifies instantaneous consciousness and screens specifically for a lucid interval
Quantifies retrograde and post-traumatic amnesia duration
Screens for vomiting, seizures, and cranial orifice fluid leaks

teach.heading: Mechanisms and forces in traumatic brain injury
teach.body:
Head injury results from direct impact, acceleration-deceleration forces, or penetrating trauma. High-speed vehicular collisions generate rotational forces that tear bridging veins or produce diffuse axonal shear injury.

Direct low-velocity blows more commonly produce local vault fractures and focal extradural or cortical contusions.

teach.heading: The diagnostic significance of the lucid interval
teach.body:
The classic lucid interval occurs when initial concussive stunning clears, followed hours later by progressive intracranial hypertension as an arterial bleed expands.

Although classically associated with middle meningeal artery laceration in extradural haematoma, it can also occur in acute subdural haematoma or developing cerebral oedema.

teach.heading: Amnesia as an objective index of concussion severity
teach.body:
Retrograde amnesia covers the period immediately before the impact, whereas post-traumatic amnesia extends from the injury until the return of continuous memory.

Post-traumatic amnesia correlates directly with the extent of diffuse axonal damage and serves as an objective clinical criterion to classify mild, moderate, and severe head trauma.

skill.exam.surg.gcs_pupils.title: Glasgow Coma Scale and pupillary examination
skill.exam.surg.gcs_pupils.oneLine: Objective level of consciousness and pupillary asymmetry in head trauma
skill.exam.surg.gcs_pupils.why: Tracks conscious level continuously to detect secondary deterioration, while pupillary asymmetry identifies uncal herniation demanding immediate surgical decompression.

steps.text: Assess Eye Opening (E): observe for spontaneous eye opening (4); if absent, call the patient by name (3); if absent, apply central pressure to the supraorbital ridge or trapezius (2); score 1 if no eye opening occurs.

Assess Best Verbal Response (V): ask the patient their name, location, and the current month. Score 5 for oriented, 4 for confused conversation, 3 for inappropriate words, 2 for incomprehensible sounds, and 1 for no vocal response.
Assess Best Motor Response (M): ask the patient to perform a two-step command such as squeezing and releasing fingers (6). If unresponsive, apply painful central stimulus to the trapezius muscle.

Classify the motor response to pain: hand moves above the clavicle to localise the stimulus (5); limb withdraws rapidly with normal flexion (4); slow decorticate posturing with adduction and internal rotation (3); decerebrate extension (2); or flaccid paralysis (1).
Inspect the pupils in ambient light for baseline diameter, roundness, and bilateral equality using a millimetre pupil gauge.
Test direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes in each eye using a bright pen torch, noting the briskness of constriction and any asymmetry.
Record the findings in split notation (for example E2 V2 M4, Total 8) alongside pupillary diameter and reactivity to establish a baseline for serial comparison.

skill.exam.surg.gcs_pupils.normal: GCS score 15 (E4 V5 M6), pupils equal, round, and briskly reactive to light (3 to 4 mm), with symmetric limb motor responses.
skill.exam.surg.gcs_pupils.abnormal: GCS score less than 15, unilateral dilated and unreactive pupil, sluggish light reflex, bilateral pinpoint pupils, decorticate flexion, or decerebrate extensor posturing.
skill.exam.surg.gcs_pupils.significance: A fall in GCS of 2 or more points or development of a unilaterally dilated pupil indicates expanding intracranial haematoma and impending transtentorial herniation, requiring immediate CT scanning and mannitol or burr-hole craniotomy.
skill.exam.surg.gcs_pupils.practice: Perform serial GCS scoring and pupillary evaluations on a simulated trauma scenario, recording the score in split E, V, and M notation.
pitfalls: Applying peripheral nailbed pressure instead of central trapezius or supraorbital pressure to distinguish purposeful localisation from withdrawal flexion.
Recording only the total numerical score (e.g., GCS 9) rather than the individual E, V, and M components, obscuring subtle motor deterioration.
Attributing an unreactive dilated pupil to direct ocular trauma before excluding ipsilateral third nerve compression from uncal herniation.
Failing to note physical barriers to evaluation such as endotracheal intubation (record as V1T) or severe bilateral periorbital swelling (record as E1C).

probes.q: What GCS score threshold universally defines severe head injury requiring definitive airway protection?
probes.a: A GCS score of 8 or less indicates severe head injury and warrants endotracheal intubation.

probes.q: What anatomical mechanism causes an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil during intracranial herniation?
probes.a: Medial displacement of the uncus of the temporal lobe compresses the oculomotor nerve against the tentorial edge, paralysing its parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibres.

probes.q: How does decorticate motor posturing differ pathophysiologically and clinically from decerebrate posturing?
probes.a: Decorticate posturing (flexion) reflects damage to the cerebral hemispheres or internal capsule with intact brainstem, whereas decerebrate posturing (extension) indicates more caudal midbrain or upper pontine dysfunction and carries a worse prognosis.

rubric.text: Applies appropriate central painful stimulus (trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure)
Accurately discriminates between localising, withdrawal, abnormal flexion, and extension
Assesses pupil size, symmetry, and both direct and consensual light reflexes
Records GCS in split component format (E, V, M) with appropriate modifiers

teach.heading: The three components of the Glasgow Coma Scale
teach.body:
The Glasgow Coma Scale provides a reproducible measure of consciousness by assessing eye opening (scored 1 to 4), best verbal response (scored 1 to 5), and best motor response (scored 1 to 6).

The motor score is the most prognostic component. Testing must always utilise central stimuli to assess purposeful localisation accurately.

teach.heading: Pupillary signs and transtentorial uncal herniation
teach.body:
The pupillomotor parasympathetic fibres travel on the superomedial periphery of the oculomotor nerve. Expanding supratentorial mass lesions force the uncus of the temporal lobe downward through the tentorial notch.

This compresses the third nerve, producing early ipsilateral pupillary sluggishness followed by dilatation and loss of the light reflex.

teach.heading: Serial evaluation and detection of the expanding haematoma
teach.body:
A single GCS reading provides a snapshot, but serial trend recordings detect deterioration before brainstem failure occurs.

A progressive drop of 2 points in GCS, worsening motor asymmetry, or newly sluggish pupillary reflexes signals decompensation, demanding immediate repeat scanning and surgical consultation.

skill.exam.surg.skull_base_fracture.title: Clinical signs of skull base fracture
skill.exam.surg.skull_base_fracture.oneLine: Periorbital ecchymosis, Battle sign, CSF leaks, and cranial nerve palsies
skill.exam.surg.skull_base_fracture.why: Identifies dural lacerations communicating the subarachnoid space with the exterior, warning of high meningitis risk and contraindicating blind nasogastric tube insertion.

steps.text: Inspect both orbits in good lighting for bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes or panda eyes), verifying that ecchymosis is strictly confined within the orbital margins.
Retract the eyelids gently and examine the bulbar conjunctiva with a torch, verifying that subconjunctival haemorrhage extends posteriorly without a visible posterior limit.
Inspect the skin overlying both mastoid processes behind the pinnae for postauricular ecchymosis (Battle sign).
Perform an otoscopic examination of both external auditory canals, checking for bloody discharge, clear watery fluid (CSF otorrhoea), or bluish bulging of the tympanic membrane (haemotympanum).
Examine both anterior nares using a nasal speculum and penlight, inspecting for clear, watery fluid drainage (CSF rhinorrhoea).

Perform the target or halo sign test if blood-tinged nasal or aural discharge is present, placing a drop onto clean filter paper or gauze to observe separation of a clear outer CSF ring from a central blood spot.
Test the function of cranial nerves I (olfaction if conscious), VII (facial symmetry and motor power), and VIII (gross hearing acuity and whisper test).

skill.exam.surg.skull_base_fracture.normal: No periorbital or mastoid ecchymosis, clear external auditory canals with pearly grey tympanic membranes, no nasal discharge, intact cranial nerve function.
skill.exam.surg.skull_base_fracture.abnormal: Bilateral raccoon eyes confined to orbital rims, subconjunctival ecchymosis lacking a posterior boundary, Battle sign over the mastoid, haemotympanum, CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea, facial nerve palsy.
skill.exam.surg.skull_base_fracture.significance: Confirms an anterior fossa fracture (raccoon eyes, subconjunctival bleed without posterior margin, CSF rhinorrhoea, anosmia) or middle fossa / petrous temporal fracture (Battle sign, haemotympanum, CSF otorrhoea, CN VII/VIII palsy), contraindicating nasogastric tube passage.
skill.exam.surg.skull_base_fracture.practice: Demonstrate inspection for Battle sign, the distinction between local black eye and raccoon eyes, and the filter-paper halo test on a clinical manikin.
pitfalls: Passing a nasogastric tube blindly in a patient with midface or anterior skull base trauma, risking intracranial insertion through the cribriform plate.
Packing the nose or external auditory meatus tightly when CSF leakage is present, which converts an open fistula into ascending intracranial infection.
Confusing direct facial contusion (black eye extending beyond orbital rims with a visible posterior conjunctival limit) with an anterior skull base fracture.
Failing to re-examine the postauricular area after 12 to 24 hours, as Battle sign is delayed in onset.

probes.q: What is the clinical hallmark of subconjunctival haemorrhage originating from an anterior skull base fracture?
probes.a: The haemorrhage has no visible posterior limit; its posterior boundary cannot be visualised even when the patient looks inward.

probes.q: What is Battle sign, and over what anatomical bony landmark does it appear?
probes.a: Ecchymosis over the mastoid process behind the ear, caused by blood extravasating along the posterior auricular artery from a petrous temporal bone fracture.

probes.q: How does the filter-paper halo or target test detect cerebrospinal fluid in blood-stained nasal discharge?
probes.a: Cerebrospinal fluid diffuses faster than whole blood through filter paper, producing a clear or pale outer ring around a denser central red blood spot.

rubric.text: Inspects orbits for raccoon eyes and confirms absence of a posterior conjunctival margin
Inspects postauricular mastoid area bilaterally for Battle sign
Examines ear and nose for CSF rhinorrhoea, otorrhoea, and haemotympanum
Explicitly avoids blind nasogastric tube insertion or nasal packing

teach.heading: Anterior cranial fossa fractures and orbital signs
teach.body:
Fractures of the orbital roof or cribriform plate allow blood and CSF to escape into the subconjunctival and periorbital spaces.

Tarsal plates strictly limit blood within the orbital margins, creating classic raccoon eyes, while subconjunctival blood tracks forward from the apex without a visible posterior limit.

teach.heading: Middle fossa fractures and petrous temporal bone injury
teach.body:
Fractures traversing the petrous temporal bone rupture the tympanic membrane or middle ear structures, producing haemotympanum, CSF otorrhoea, or bleeding from the meatus.

Blood tracking along the mastoid emissary vein creates postauricular ecchymosis (Battle sign), which characteristically takes 12 to 24 hours to become manifest.

teach.heading: Complications and contraindications in skull base injury
teach.body:
Dural tears breach the sterile intracranial compartment, introducing risk of pneumocephalus and bacterial meningitis.

Blind nasogastric tube passage is absolutely contraindicated because the tube can penetrate the fractured cribriform plate directly into the frontal lobe; an orogastric tube must be placed under direct vision.

skill.annex.surg.gcs.title: Glasgow Coma Scale Reference Table
skill.annex.surg.gcs.oneLine: Standard scoring criteria for Eye, Verbal, and Motor responses in acute trauma
skill.annex.surg.gcs.why: Standardised scoring prevents ambiguity between emergency, surgical, and intensive care teams, providing an objective threshold for intubation and urgent neurosurgical decompression.

rows: Opens eyes without requiring any stimulus
Opens eyes to spoken command or shouted name
Opens eyes to fingertip or central pressure
No eye opening to any stimulus
Accurately states name, current location, and month
Speaks in conversational phrases but is disoriented
Speaks isolated intelligible words; no conversation
Moans or groans; no recognisable words produced
No vocalisation produced to painful stimulus
Follows a two-step instruction such as releasing grip
Hand moves above clavicle toward central painful stimulus
Limb withdraws rapidly from pain without abnormal posturing
Slow decorticate posture with adducted arm and flexed wrist
Decerebrate posture with arm extension, adduction, pronation
No motor movement in response to painful stimulus

skill.annex.surg.gcs.practice: Calculate total GCS scores and write split notation for five emergency patient presentations, including cases with endotracheal intubation.
pitfalls: Conflating normal withdrawal flexion (M4) with abnormal decorticate flexion (M3), which underestimates midbrain compromise.
Recording total score alone without component breakdown, obscuring early motor asymmetry.
Failing to append standard clinical qualifiers like V1T for intubated patients or E1C for periorbital oedema.

probes.q: What is the minimum possible score on the Glasgow Coma Scale?
probes.a: The minimum score is 3, corresponding to E1 V1 M1.

probes.q: A trauma patient opens eyes to speech, speaks confused sentences, and localises pain. What is the GCS?
probes.a: GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5).

probes.q: How is the verbal component documented if a patient is intubated and mechanically ventilated?
probes.a: Documented as V1T, indicating that verbal response cannot be tested due to the endotracheal tube.

rubric.text: Accurately calculates total score from eye, verbal, and motor components
Correctly distinguishes localising from flexion withdrawal and decorticate posture
Correctly applies standard modifiers such as V1T and E1C

teach.heading: Stratification of traumatic brain injury severity
teach.body:
Traumatic brain injury severity is clinically stratified by post-resuscitation GCS score: mild injury corresponds to GCS 13 to 15, moderate injury to GCS 9 to 12, and severe injury to GCS 3 to 8.

Patients with GCS 8 or lower lose airway reflexes and require emergency endotracheal intubation.

teach.heading: Standardised testing stimuli and clinical modifiers
teach.body:
Reliable testing requires standardized central stimuli such as trapezius squeeze or supraorbital pressure, avoiding peripheral pinching.

When anatomical barriers prevent evaluation, standard modifiers must be appended: T for an artificial airway and C for closed eyes.

skill.hx.surg.icsol.title: History in intracranial space-occupying lesions
skill.hx.surg.icsol.oneLine: Triad of raised intracranial pressure, false localising symptoms, and focal deficits
skill.hx.surg.icsol.why: Identifies expanding intracranial mass lesions (neoplasms, abscesses, chronic subdural haematomas) before life-threatening brain herniation and irreversible neurological devastation occurs.

asks.text: What is the exact timing and character of the headache: is it throbbing or bursting, worse on waking in the morning, and aggravated by coughing, bending, or straining at stool?
Has there been vomiting, and is it projectile in nature without preceding nausea, occurring particularly at the peak of morning headache?
Have there been visual disturbances, such as transient obscurations of vision when bending, progressive blurring, or horizontal double vision (diplopia)?
Have close relatives noticed progressive changes in personality, memory loss, emotional apathy, or decline in intellectual and social functions?
Have there been seizures: focal twitching of a hand or face (Jacksonian march), sensory auras, olfactory hallucinations, or generalized convulsions?
Has there been progressive motor weakness, clumsiness of a limb, difficulty speaking or understanding language, or unsteadiness of gait?
Is there a past history of minor head trauma weeks earlier (chronic subdural haematoma), chronic ear discharge (otogenic brain abscess), or treated systemic malignancy (cerebral metastasis)?

skill.hx.surg.icsol.practice: Take a focused history from a patient presenting with progressive morning headache, distinguishing features of intracranial hypertension from migraine and tension headache.
pitfalls: Dismissing morning headache with vomiting as a gastrointestinal ailment or migraine, delaying neuroimaging.
Failing to ask family members about subtle progressive changes in personality and cognition.
Overlooking a history of chronic suppurative otitis media in a patient presenting with raised intracranial pressure, missing an otogenic temporal or cerebellar abscess.

probes.q: What three symptoms classically constitute the clinical triad of raised intracranial pressure?
probes.a: Headache (especially in the morning), projectile vomiting without nausea, and papilloedema (or visual blurring).

probes.q: Why is headache from raised intracranial pressure characteristically most intense in the early morning?
probes.a: Hypoventilation during recumbent sleep causes arterial carbon dioxide retention, leading to cerebral vasodilation and peak intracranial blood volume upon waking.

probes.q: Why is an isolated sixth cranial nerve palsy considered a false localising sign in patients with raised intracranial pressure?
probes.a: The abducens nerve has a long, tortuous intracranial course over the petrous temporal bone and is vulnerable to mechanical traction from generalised downward brain shift regardless of tumour location.

rubric.text: Inquires specifically about morning headache, projectile vomiting, and visual blurring
Details focal onset of seizures, motor march, and sensory or olfactory auras
Screens for chronic ear discharge, previous head trauma, and primary systemic malignancies
Asks family about personality shifts, apathy, and intellectual decline

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: The Monro-Kellie doctrine and raised intracranial pressure
teach.body:
The rigid cranium contains brain parenchyma, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid. Under the Monro-Kellie doctrine, an expanding space-occupying lesion is initially compensated for by displacement of venous blood and CSF into the spinal canal.

Once compensatory buffering is exhausted, small volume increases produce steep rises in intracranial pressure, presenting with morning headache and projectile vomiting.

teach.heading: Chronology and tempo of intracranial lesions
teach.body:
The clinical progression points to lesion pathology: acute onset over days suggests brain abscess or intra-tumoral haemorrhage; subacute evolution over weeks indicates glioblastoma multiforme or metastatic deposit.

An insidious progression spanning months or years characterises low-grade astrocytoma, meningioma, or acoustic schwannoma.

teach.heading: False localising signs and intracranial herniation vectors
teach.body:
Rising intracranial pressure causes mechanical brain displacement that creates signs unrelated to direct lesion location.

Traction on the sixth cranial nerve causes unilateral or bilateral lateral rectus palsy, while downward shift of the posterior cerebral arteries causes occipital infarction with hemianopia.

skill.exam.surg.icsol_focal.title: Neurological examination for focal intracranial lesions
skill.exam.surg.icsol_focal.oneLine: Lobar deficits, cranial nerve palsies, papilloedema, and cerebellar signs
skill.exam.surg.icsol_focal.why: Localises mass lesions to specific cerebral lobes, the cerebellopontine angle, or posterior fossa, directing targeted neuroimaging and urgent neurosurgical intervention.

steps.text: Examine higher mental functions and speech: test fluency of expressive speech (Broca area), comprehension of commands (Wernicke area), naming, and repetition.
Test visual pathways: perform confrontation visual field testing in all four quadrants to detect homonymous hemianopia or upper quadrantanopia.
Perform fundoscopy in a darkened room, inspecting optic disc margins for blurring, hyperemia, loss of spontaneous venous pulsations, elevation, and retinal flame haemorrhages (papilloedema).

Examine cranial nerves III, IV, and VI (extraocular movements and nystagmus); test cranial nerve V (corneal reflex and facial sensation); test cranial nerve VII (facial symmetry and motor power); and test cranial nerve VIII (whisper test and Rinne/Weber tuning fork examination).
Examine motor function in limbs: test muscle bulk, tone, power in major muscle groups, pronator drift, deep tendon reflexes, and extensor plantar (Babinski) response.
Examine parietal cortical sensory modalities: test stereognosis (identifying a coin or key by touch), graphaesthesia, and two-point discrimination.
Test cerebellar coordination: evaluate finger-nose pointing (dysmetria and intention tremor), rapid alternating hand movements (dysdiadochokinesia), heel-shin sliding, and tandem gait.

skill.exam.surg.icsol_focal.normal: Intact fluent speech and comprehension, sharp optic disc margins with spontaneous venous pulsations, full visual fields, symmetric cranial nerves, normal power and tone, brisk symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, intact cerebellar coordination.
skill.exam.surg.icsol_focal.abnormal: Papilloedema, homonymous hemianopia, expressive or receptive aphasia, absent corneal reflex, unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with facial palsy (CPA syndrome), contralateral hemiparesis, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar response, limb dysmetria, intention tremor, ataxic gait.
skill.exam.surg.icsol_focal.significance: Localises intracranial pathology: frontal lobe (contralateral hemiparesis, motor aphasia, grasp reflex); parietal lobe (astereognosis, sensory inattention, Gerstmann syndrome); temporal lobe (Wernicke aphasia, superior quadrantanopia); cerebellopontine angle (CN V, VII, VIII deficits); cerebellar hemisphere (ipsilateral limb ataxia).
skill.exam.surg.icsol_focal.practice: Perform a complete confrontation visual field assessment, corneal reflex test, and fundoscopic examination on a colleague.
pitfalls: Skipping fundoscopy in a patient with progressive headache, missing early papilloedema before optic atrophy supervenes.
Omitting the corneal reflex, which is the earliest and most sensitive sign of fifth nerve compression in acoustic schwannoma.
Confusing ipsilateral cerebellar limb incoordination with contralateral pyramidal corticospinal weakness.
Failing to test upper visual quadrants during confrontation testing, missing a temporal lobe lesion superior quadrantanopia.

probes.q: What ophthalmoscopic findings on fundoscopy indicate established papilloedema?
probes.a: Blurring of optic disc margins, hyperaemia of the disc, elevation of the optic cup, loss of physiological venous pulsation, and flame-shaped peripapillary haemorrhages.

probes.q: A patient presents with unilateral sensorineural deafness, absent corneal reflex, and peripheral facial weakness. What anatomical space is involved?
probes.a: The cerebellopontine angle, classically caused by a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) compressing cranial nerves VIII, V, and VII.

probes.q: What constellation of clinical deficits constitutes Gerstmann syndrome, and which cortical lobe does it localise to?
probes.a: Acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation, localising to the angular gyrus of the dominant parietal lobe.

rubric.text: Executes confrontation visual fields and fundoscopic examination for papilloedema
Tests corneal reflex (CN V), facial motor symmetry (CN VII), and acoustic nerve (CN VIII)
Evaluates pronator drift, limb power, tendon reflexes, and extensor plantar response
Performs finger-nose test, rapid alternating movements, and tandem gait

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Lobar syndromes of the cerebral hemispheres
teach.body:
Frontal lesions cause contralateral hemiparesis, motor aphasia in the dominant hemisphere, and disinhibition or urinary incontinence.

Parietal lesions impair cortical sensory processing (astereognosis and sensory inattention), while temporal lesions produce receptive aphasia, uncinate seizures, and homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

teach.heading: Cerebellopontine angle syndrome progression
teach.body:
Acoustic schwannomas arise from the vestibular nerve within the internal auditory meatus. Early symptoms are unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus.

Medial extension compresses the trigeminal nerve (manifesting earliest as loss of the corneal reflex), followed by the facial nerve, cerebellar hemisphere, and eventually the brainstem.

teach.heading: Posterior fossa lesions and hydrocephalus
teach.body:
Tumours of the cerebellum or fourth ventricle produce ipsilateral limb dysmetria, intention tremor, and nystagmus with hemispheric lesions, or truncal ataxia with vermian lesions.

Obstruction of CSF flow through the aqueduct of Sylvius or fourth ventricle generates acute obstructive hydrocephalus with rapid deterioration.

skill.ix.surg.neuroimaging_icsol.title: Neuroimaging in intracranial space-occupying lesions
skill.ix.surg.neuroimaging_icsol.oneLine: CT and contrast MRI evaluation of mass effect, midline shift, and ring lesions
skill.ix.surg.neuroimaging_icsol.why: Differentiates neoplastic, infective, and vascular intracranial mass lesions, assesses herniation risk, and provides stereotactic anatomical coordinates for biopsy or resection.
skill.ix.surg.neuroimaging_icsol.practice: Review axial CT and contrast-enhanced MRI brain scans, measuring midline shift of the septum pellucidum and identifying mass effect on the ventricles.
pitfalls: Performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with suspected ICSOL before imaging confirms absence of mass effect, triggering fatal tentorial or tonsillar herniation.
Relying solely on non-contrast CT when evaluating suspected cerebral abscess, metastates, or acoustic neuroma, which require gadolinium contrast.
Missing subtle midline shift by failing to measure deviation of the septum pellucidum and third ventricle from the anatomical midline.

probes.q: Why is lumbar puncture strictly contraindicated in a patient with suspected intracranial mass lesion and papilloedema?
probes.a: Sudden reduction of spinal subarachnoid pressure creates a pressure gradient that precipitates fatal transtentorial or cerebellar tonsillar herniation (coning).

probes.q: What are the commonest causes of ring-enhancing intracranial lesions seen on contrast-enhanced neuroimaging in Indian surgical practice?
probes.a: High-grade glioma (glioblastoma), cerebral metastasis, brain abscess, tuberculoma, and neurocysticercosis.

probes.q: What neuroimaging signs on axial brain CT indicate impending subfalcine or uncal brain herniation?
probes.a: Midline shift of the septum pellucidum exceeding 5 mm, effacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, obliteration of the basal cisterns, and compression of the midbrain.

rubric.text: Selects appropriate urgent non-contrast CT followed by contrast-enhanced MRI
Measures midline shift and evaluates ventricular effacement and basal cistern patency
Explicitly identifies lumbar puncture as contraindicated when mass effect is present
Lists differential diagnosis for ring-enhancing lesions in Indian clinical context

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Role of non-contrast CT as the initial emergency scan
teach.body:
Non-contrast computed tomography is the initial investigation of choice in acute presentations to exclude acute intracranial haemorrhage, major mass effect, and acute hydrocephalus.

It rapidly reveals hyperdense acute haematomas, areas of hypodense vasogenic oedema, bony erosion, and calcification within meningiomas or oligodendrogliomas.

teach.heading: Contrast-enhanced MRI in surgical planning
teach.body:
Magnetic resonance imaging with intravenous gadolinium provides superior soft tissue resolution, multiplanar imaging, and delineation of posterior fossa, brainstem, and sellar pathology.

T1-weighted post-contrast scans demarcate tumour margins and vascularity, while T2/FLAIR sequences demonstrate surrounding infiltrative oedema.

teach.heading: Differential diagnosis of ring-enhancing lesions
teach.body:
Intense peripheral ring enhancement on contrast scans results from breakdown of the blood-brain barrier.

In Indian surgical practice, tuberculomas (thick nodular ring with central caseation) and neurocysticercosis (small cystic lesion with eccentric scolex) must be differentiated from pyogenic abscess and glioblastoma multiforme.

skill.hx.surg.spine_trauma.title: History in acute spinal trauma
skill.hx.surg.spine_trauma.oneLine: Kinematics, mechanism of injury, tempo of neurological deficit, and girdle pain
skill.hx.surg.spine_trauma.why: Determines fracture vulnerability zones, identifies spinal cord compromise, and differentiates instantaneous transection from progressive compressive haematoma requiring emergent surgical decompression.

asks.text: What was the exact mechanism of spinal injury: fall from a height landing on feet or head, diving headfirst into shallow water, or vehicular collision with lap seat-belt restraint?
Was there immediate complete loss of movement or sensation in the limbs at the moment of impact, or did weakness develop hours later?
If paralysis developed, has it been static, improving, or ascending progressively up the trunk and limbs?
Is there a sensation of band-like tightness, burning, or constriction encircling the trunk (girdle pain) marking the level of nerve root irritation?
Is there acute retention of urine, loss of bladder fullness sensation, or involuntary fecal incontinence?
Where is the focal back or neck pain located, and does any attempt at movement exacerbate severe spasms?
Were there concurrent trauma impacts: head strike with loss of consciousness, blunt chest trauma, or pelvic crush injury?

skill.hx.surg.spine_trauma.practice: Take a focused spinal trauma history from an emergency attendant or conscious patient, determining trauma kinematics, neurological tempo, and presence of girdle sensation.
pitfalls: Overlooking shallow-water diving as a classic mechanism causing cervical fracture-dislocation and quadriplegia.
Failing to recognize that ascending paralysis hours after injury signals an expanding extradural haematoma or ascending cord oedema.
Neglecting to inquire about lap-type seat-belt restraint in vehicular trauma, missing flexion-distraction Chance fractures of the lumbar spine.

probes.q: What mechanism of spinal injury is characteristically produced by diving headfirst into shallow water?
probes.a: Cervical spine hyperflexion and axial loading, typically causing cervical fracture-dislocation at C5-C6 with cord compression.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of paraplegia that appears hours after trauma and gradually ascends upwards?
probes.a: It indicates progressive spinal cord compression from an expanding intraspinal haematoma (haematomyelia or extradural haemorrhage) or ascending oedema, requiring urgent decompression.

probes.q: What is girdle pain in spinal trauma, and what does its presence indicate?
probes.a: A band-like constricting pain radiating circumferentially around the trunk corresponding to the dermatomal distribution of the spinal root compressed at the level of vertebral injury.

rubric.text: Inquires into specific injury kinematics (axial load, diving, lap-belt deceleration)
Clarifies whether paralysis was instantaneous at impact or delayed and ascending
Screens for band-like girdle pain marking the level of root irritation
Inquires specifically regarding urinary retention and perineal sensation

teach.heading: Kinematics and transition zones in spinal trauma
teach.body:
Spinal injury severity correlates with applied kinetic forces: hyperflexion, hyperextension, axial loading, or rotation.

The junctional regions where a mobile segment meets a rigid segment (C5 to C7 in the cervical spine and T11 to L2 at the thoracolumbar junction) absorb the greatest mechanical stress and represent the commonest sites of fracture-dislocation.

teach.heading: Diagnostic value of the tempo of paralysis
teach.body:
Instantaneous flaccid paralysis developing at the split second of impact indicates mechanical contusion, crushing, or complete transection of neural pathways by displaced bone fragments.

In contrast, delayed or ascending paralysis developing over hours reflects progressive spinal epidural haematoma (haematorrhachis), central cord bleeding (haematomyelia), or expanding cord oedema.

teach.heading: Girdle sensation as an anatomical level marker
teach.body:
Compression or distortion of nerve roots exiting through damaged intervertebral foramina produces intense radicular irritation.

This is perceived as a constricting, band-like girdle sensation encircling the chest or abdomen, precisely matching the spinal segment of skeletal disruption.

skill.exam.surg.spine_logroll.title: Log-roll examination and spinal column palpation
skill.exam.surg.spine_logroll.oneLine: Coordinated multi-person log-roll with spinal immobilisation and column palpation
skill.exam.surg.spine_logroll.why: Prevents catastrophic secondary spinal cord injury during examination of the posterior column while identifying unstable fractures, hematomas, and rectal tone status.

steps.text: Assign roles to a four-person examination team: Leader maintains manual in-line cervical stabilisation at the head; two assistants manage the torso, pelvis, and lower limbs; fourth examiner performs inspection, palpation, and digital rectal examination.
The Leader controls all movement, giving the command to roll only when all team members are positioned with crossed hands securing the patient's shoulders, pelvis, knees, and ankles.
Roll the patient smoothly as a unified, rigid anatomical cylinder toward the assistants, maintaining neutral spinal alignment without torsional twist.
Inspect the entire posterior scalp, cervical spine, thoracic and lumbar spine, buttocks, and perineum for abrasions, contusions, penetrating wounds, and step deformities.
Systematically palpate the midline spinous processes from C2 down to the sacrum, feeling for focal point tenderness, abnormal gap between spinous processes, or a palpable step-off.
Perform a digital rectal examination while the patient is on their side, assessing resting anal sphincter tone and voluntary sphincter contraction if conscious.
On the Leader's command, roll the patient smoothly back into the supine position onto a firm surface, reapplying semi-rigid cervical collar, lateral head blocks, and straps.

skill.exam.surg.spine_logroll.normal: Continuous midline alignment of spinous processes without palpable steps, normal interspinous spacing, no focal tenderness, intact resting anal sphincter tone.
skill.exam.surg.spine_logroll.abnormal: Palpable gap between adjacent spinous processes, step-off deformity of the vertebral column, localized haematoma over the spine, severe focal spinous tenderness, flaccid anal sphincter with absent tone.
skill.exam.surg.spine_logroll.significance: A widened interspinous space or step-off confirms disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex and an unstable vertebral fracture-dislocation; flaccid anal tone indicates spinal cord disruption or spinal shock.
skill.exam.surg.spine_logroll.practice: Lead a four-person team in executing a log-roll on a trauma manikin, performing midline spinous palpation and simulated digital rectal examination.
pitfalls: Attempting to log-roll a trauma patient with fewer than four trained personnel, causing dangerous rotational twisting of an unstable fracture.
Palpating the lateral paraspinal musculature rather than systematically pressing firmly on each individual midline spinous process.
Omitting the digital rectal examination during the log-roll, missing critical assessment of anal sphincter tone and sacral sparing.
Releasing manual in-line head stabilisation before the cervical collar and lateral immobilisation blocks are securely refitted.

probes.q: Who directs and commands all patient movement during a trauma log-roll examination?
probes.a: The team leader stationed at the head of the bed maintaining manual in-line cervical immobilisation.

probes.q: What anatomical disruption is indicated by a palpable gap or widening between adjacent spinous processes on the back?
probes.a: Disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex (supraspinous and interspinous ligaments), indicating an unstable spinal fracture or dislocation.

probes.q: Why must a digital rectal examination be performed during the initial log-roll of a patient with suspected spinal cord trauma?
probes.a: To assess resting anal sphincter tone and perianal sensation, which determines whether spinal cord injury is complete or incomplete (sacral sparing).

rubric.text: Maintains continuous manual in-line cervical stabilisation throughout movement
Coordinates team roll as a single rigid anatomical axis on verbal command
Systematically palpates midline spinous processes from C2 to sacrum for steps and gaps
Performs digital rectal examination to evaluate anal sphincter tone and sacral sparing

teach.heading: Principles of spinal immobilisation and the log-roll
teach.body:
Unstable spinal column fractures are vulnerable to mechanical displacement during patient handling, which can convert an incomplete spinal injury into irreversible complete cord transection.

The log-roll maintains strict cervical and thoracolumbar alignment in a single anatomical axis under the explicit command of the leader at the head.

teach.heading: Palpating the posterior ligamentous complex
teach.body:
The supraspinous and interspinous ligaments form the primary tension band resisting hyperflexion. Rupture of these ligaments produces a palpable widening of the interspinous gap or a step-off deformity.

Palpation must travel midline from the suboccipital prominence to the sacrum, identifying focal tenderness or haematoma.

teach.heading: Assessment of sacral root function via rectal examination
teach.body:
Digital rectal examination assesses the lowest functional cord segments (S2 to S5).

Evaluation of resting tone reflects parasympathetic integrity; voluntary contraction demonstrates preserved corticospinal motor outflow (sacral sparing), establishing the injury as incomplete with far better functional prognosis.

skill.exam.surg.spinal_cord_level.title: Neurological level assessment in spinal cord injury
skill.exam.surg.spinal_cord_level.oneLine: Key sensory dermatomes, motor myotomes, sacral sparing, and bulbocavernosus reflex
skill.exam.surg.spinal_cord_level.why: Determines the exact neurological level of cord injury, differentiates complete from incomplete spinal cord syndromes, and identifies the resolution of spinal shock.

steps.text: Examine the 10 paired key motor myotomes systematically (scored 0 to 5): C5 (elbow flexors), C6 (wrist extensors), C7 (elbow extensors), C8 (finger flexors of distal phalanx), T1 (finger abductors), L2 (hip flexors), L3 (knee extensors), L4 (ankle dorsiflexors), L5 (long toe extensors), and S1 (ankle plantarflexors).
Examine sensory dermatomes bilaterally to light touch and pinprick, testing critical landmarks: C4 (clavicle), T4 (nipple line), T10 (umbilicus), L1 (groin crease), and S4-S5 (perianal skin).
Examine deep tendon reflexes: biceps (C5/C6), triceps (C7), patellar (L3/L4), and Achilles tendon (S1), noting hyporeflexia or hyperreflexia and clonus.

Test the bulbocavernosus reflex: with a gloved finger in the anal canal, gently squeeze the glans penis or clitoris, or apply gentle traction to an indwelling urinary catheter, feeling for reflex contraction of the anal sphincter.

Assess for sacral sparing: test sharp pinprick sensation at the mucocutaneous junction of S4-S5, evaluate deep anal pressure, and ask the patient to voluntarily contract the anal sphincter around the examining finger.
Classify the neurological level of injury as the lowest spinal cord segment possessing intact sensory function (score 2) and motor power grade 3 or greater, provided all proximal segments are normal.
Classify injury completeness: complete injury (absence of all sensory and motor function in lowest sacral segments S4-S5) versus incomplete injury (preservation of sacral sparing).

skill.exam.surg.spinal_cord_level.normal: Full motor power (grade 5/5) across all key myotomes, normal sensation across dermatomes C2 to S5, symmetrical deep tendon reflexes, intact bulbocavernosus reflex and voluntary anal contraction.
skill.exam.surg.spinal_cord_level.abnormal: Motor weakness or flaccid paralysis below a defined segment, distinct sensory level to pinprick, absent deep tendon reflexes (spinal shock), absent or recovered bulbocavernosus reflex, complete loss of perianal sensation and voluntary sphincter tone.
skill.exam.surg.spinal_cord_level.significance: Defines the exact anatomical level and severity of spinal cord injury. Sacral sparing confirms an incomplete cord lesion with substantial recovery potential; absence of bulbocavernosus reflex indicates spinal shock, during which injury completeness cannot be definitively diagnosed.
skill.exam.surg.spinal_cord_level.practice: Map the 10 key motor myotomes and 5 landmark dermatomes on a partner, stating the cord level and testing sequence.
pitfalls: Declaring a spinal cord injury permanently complete while the patient remains in spinal shock (bulbocavernosus reflex absent).
Failing to examine perianal pinprick sensation (S4-S5) and voluntary anal contraction, incorrectly categorising an incomplete injury as complete.
Attempting to test thoracic motor levels with limb movements (thoracic cord levels are determined purely by sensory dermatomal boundaries).
Overlooking acute priapism in a male trauma patient, which indicates immediate complete autonomic disruption from high spinal cord injury.

probes.q: What anatomical surface landmarks correspond to dermatomal sensory levels T4 and T10?
probes.a: T4 corresponds to the horizontal nipple line, and T10 corresponds to the level of the umbilicus.

probes.q: What clinical findings define sacral sparing, and what is its prognostic significance in acute spinal cord trauma?
probes.a: Preservation of sensory perception at the anal mucocutaneous junction (S4-S5), deep anal pressure, or voluntary anal sphincter contraction; it confirms an incomplete lesion with high potential for neurological recovery.

probes.q: What is the bulbocavernosus reflex and what does its return signify in a paraplegic trauma patient?
probes.a: Reflex anal sphincter contraction on squeezing the glans or tugging a catheter (S2-S4); its return marks the end of spinal shock, allowing permanent completeness of the cord lesion to be declared.

rubric.text: Tests key motor myotomes bilaterally and grades power from 0 to 5
Maps sensory level accurately using landmark dermatomes (C4, T4, T10, L1, S4-S5)
Explicitly assesses perianal sensation and voluntary anal contraction for sacral sparing
Checks bulbocavernosus reflex to evaluate for the presence or resolution of spinal shock

sources.locator: spinal_cord_injury_rehab: neurological level and ASIA classification

sources.source: ATLS - Advanced Trauma Life Support
sources.locator: Spine and spinal cord trauma: assessment

teach.heading: Defining the neurological level of spinal cord injury
teach.body:
The neurological level of injury is defined as the most caudal segment of the spinal cord that exhibits both normal sensory function and at least antigravity motor power (grade 3/5).

Because thoracic nerve roots do not supply distinct limb muscles, the thoracic cord level is defined strictly by the sensory dermatome level.

teach.heading: Spinal shock versus neurogenic shock
teach.body:
Spinal shock is the temporary complete cessation of all reflex, motor, and autonomic function below a transected or contused cord segment, characterized by flaccidity and an absent bulbocavernosus reflex.

Neurogenic shock is hemodynamic instability (hypotension with paradoxical bradycardia) caused by interruption of sympathetic descending outflow.

teach.heading: The imperative of sacral sparing in incomplete cord syndromes
teach.body:
Fibers serving the lowest sacral segments (S4 to S5) lie in the most peripheral, superficial portion of the spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts.

Preservation of perianal sensation or voluntary external anal sphincter contraction proves these peripheral tracts are intact, indicating an incomplete cord lesion with superior functional prognosis.

skill.hx.surg.back_pain.title: History in chronic back pain and spinal disorders
skill.hx.surg.back_pain.oneLine: Red flags, mechanical versus inflammatory back pain, and radicular sciatica
skill.hx.surg.back_pain.why: Distinguishes benign mechanical strain from spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease), disc herniation with cauda equina compression, and metastatic disease, preventing catastrophic neurological deterioration.

asks.text: What is the site, onset, and duration of the back pain: was it a sudden bursting pain while lifting a heavy weight, or an insidious dull ache?
Does the pain radiate down the buttock and leg along a specific dermatome below the knee (sciatica), accompanied by numbness or pins and needles?
What aggravates and relieves the pain: is it worsened by forward bending, sitting, coughing, or sneezing (disc prolapse) and relieved by lying flat?
Is the pain worse in the second half of the night, associated with morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes that eases with physical activity (inflammatory spondyloarthritis)?
Are there symptoms of neurogenic claudication: aching pain or heaviness in calves brought on by walking and relieved by sitting or bending forward (shopping cart sign)?
Are there red flag symptoms: unremitting night pain waking the patient, progressive unexplained weight loss, evening rise of temperature and night sweats (Pott's spine), or known primary cancer?
Are there sphincter disturbances: difficulty passing urine, urinary retention with overflow incontinence, loss of bowel control, or numbness around the anus and perineum (saddle anaesthesia)?

skill.hx.surg.back_pain.practice: Take a structured history from a patient presenting with severe sciatica, systematically screening for all five red flag features of cauda equina syndrome.
pitfalls: Failing to ask explicitly about urinary retention, altered stream, and perianal numbness in every patient with acute severe sciatica.
Attributing back pain in a young adult in an endemic area to simple mechanical muscle strain without screening for Pott's spine.
Overlooking inflammatory back pain characteristics such as prolonged morning stiffness (>30 minutes) that improves with exercise but worsens with rest.

probes.q: What clinical features constitute cauda equina syndrome, and why is it considered an emergency?
probes.a: Bilateral sciatica, lower limb motor weakness, saddle anaesthesia, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence; it requires emergency surgical decompression to prevent permanent sphincter paralysis.

probes.q: How does the pain of a prolapsed lumbar intervertebral disc differ from lumbar spinal canal stenosis regarding aggravating factors?
probes.a: Disc prolapse pain is aggravated by spinal flexion, sitting, and coughing; spinal canal stenosis pain is provoked by standing and walking (extension) and relieved by lumbar flexion (bending forward).

probes.q: What constitutional and nocturnal symptoms should prompt immediate suspicion of Pott's spine (spinal tuberculosis) in an Indian clinical context?
probes.a: Low-grade evening pyrexia, night sweats, anorexia, progressive weight loss, and severe nocturnal back pain with localized spinal rigidity.

rubric.text: Details pain onset, dermatomal radiation, and mechanical aggravating factors
Screens specifically for urinary retention, bowel incontinence, and saddle numbness
Inquires about evening fever, night sweats, weight loss, and previous tuberculosis exposure
Differentiates mechanical back pain from inflammatory morning stiffness

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: The spine: clinical presentation of spinal disorders

teach.heading: Mechanical versus inflammatory spinal pain profiles
teach.body:
Mechanical back pain from disc herniation or facet arthropathy worsens with prolonged standing, sitting, or forward bending, and is typically relieved by lying recumbent.

Inflammatory back pain from ankylosing spondylitis awakens the patient in the second half of the night, is accompanied by morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, and improves with movement.

teach.heading: Sciatica and radicular symptoms
teach.body:
Herniation of the nucleus pulposus impinges on an exiting or traversing nerve root.

Compression of L5 produces pain radiating along the lateral thigh and calf to the dorsum of the foot and great toe; compression of S1 produces pain down the posterior thigh and calf to the lateral foot and sole.

teach.heading: Cauda equina syndrome as a neurosurgical emergency
teach.body:
Massive central disc extrusion compresses the lumbosacral nerve roots of the cauda equina.

This generates bilateral radicular pain, motor weakness in feet, loss of perianal and saddle sensation, and painless urinary retention with overflow; emergency MRI and surgical decompression within 24 to 48 hours is mandatory.

skill.exam.surg.spine_inspection_mobilit.title: Examination of spinal curvature, posture, and mobility
skill.exam.surg.spine_inspection_mobilit.oneLine: Spinal alignment, angular gibbus in Pott's, Adams forward bend test, and lumbar mobility
skill.exam.surg.spine_inspection_mobilit.why: Differentiates structural from postural deformities, detects early tuberculous vertebral destruction (gibbus), and quantifies progressive lumbar spinal rigidity in spondylitis.

steps.text: Expose the patient from occiput to gluteal folds, observing posture from the posterior, lateral, and anterior aspects with feet together and knees straight.
Inspect the physiological spinal curves in the sagittal plane: cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, and lumbar lordosis. Note loss of lumbar lordosis (paraspinal spasm) or exaggerated lordosis.
Inspect specifically for an angular kyphosis: look for a sharp, localized posterior prominence (gibbus or knuckle) indicating structural collapse of anterior vertebral bodies as seen in Pott's spine.
Inspect the coronal plane for lateral curvature (scoliosis), checking for shoulder asymmetry, elevated scapula, waist asymmetry, and pelvic obliquity.

Perform the Adams forward bend test: instruct the patient to bend forward with knees straight and palms pressed together; view from behind at eye level to detect any persistent rotational thoracic rib hump or lumbar prominence.
Palpate each spinous process firmly for focal tenderness; run two fingers along the line of spinous processes to detect a step-off deformity (spondylolisthesis).

Perform the modified Schober test: mark the lumbosacral junction (level of dimples of Venus) and a point 10 cm above in upright posture; ask the patient to bend fully forward with knees straight and remeasure the distance (normal increase is at least 5 cm).
Palpate the lumbar triangle, iliac fossae, and groins for cold abscesses (psoas abscess tracking along the psoas sheath in spinal tuberculosis).

skill.exam.surg.spine_inspection_mobilit.normal: Smooth physiological curves, plumb line from occiput falls in natal cleft, symmetric shoulder levels, no rib hump on forward bending, Schober test increases by at least 5 cm, non-tender spine without palpable steps or cold abscesses.
skill.exam.surg.spine_inspection_mobilit.abnormal: Sharp localized angular kyphosis (gibbus), rotational rib hump on Adams test (structural scoliosis), flattened lumbar lordosis with intense paraspinal spasm, Schober test increase less than 5 cm, palpable fullness in iliac fossa or groin (psoas abscess).
skill.exam.surg.spine_inspection_mobilit.significance: An angular gibbus confirms anterior vertebral collapse typical of tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease); a persistent rib hump on forward bending defines structural scoliosis; restricted Schober test indicates ankylosing spondylitis or severe disc pathology.
skill.exam.surg.spine_inspection_mobilit.practice: Perform the Adams forward bend test and calculate a modified Schober test on a colleague, recording the exact expansion in centimetres.
pitfalls: Missing structural scoliosis by failing to observe the patient from eye level behind during the forward bend test.
Confusing the smooth round kyphosis of senile osteoporosis or Scheuermann disease with the sharp localized angular gibbus of Pott's spine.
Omitting palpation of the iliac fossae and femoral triangles for cold abscesses in patients presenting with spinal rigidity and suspected tuberculosis.
Allowing the patient to flex the knees during the Schober test, falsely inflating measured lumbar flexion.

probes.q: What is an angular gibbus and what infection classically causes it in the thoracic spine?
probes.a: A sharp, localized posterior bony prominence caused by the collapse of two or more adjacent tuberculous anterior vertebral bodies in Pott's spine.

probes.q: How does the Adams forward bend test differentiate structural scoliosis from postural or compensatory scoliosis?
probes.a: In structural scoliosis, fixed vertebral rotation produces an asymmetric rib hump or lumbar prominence that persists on forward bending, whereas postural curves disappear.

probes.q: How is the modified Schober test performed and what measurement indicates restricted lumbar spinal flexion?
probes.a: Mark lumbosacral junction and 10 cm above; upon full forward flexion, an increase in distance of less than 5 cm indicates pathological lumbar restriction.

rubric.text: Inspects physiological spinal curves and looks specifically for an angular gibbus
Executes Adams forward bend test to inspect for rotational rib hump
Measures lumbar spinal flexion excursion using the modified Schober test
Palpates the iliac fossae and groins for cold abscesses in suspected tuberculosis

teach.heading: Pathology of the angular gibbus in Pott's spine
teach.body:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis reaches the paradiscal anterior vertebral margins via haematogenous seeding through the Batson venous plexus.

Caseation destroys the anterior body while sparing the posterior neural arch; axial weight-bearing produces anterior wedging and structural collapse, resulting in a sharp, prominent angular deformity known as a gibbus or knuckle.

teach.heading: Structural scoliosis and the Adams forward bend test
teach.body:
Structural scoliosis incorporates lateral curvature coupled with obligate vertebral body axial rotation.

On forward bending (the Adams test), the rotated vertebral bodies thrust the attached posterior ribs upward on the convexity, creating an unmistakable posterior rib hump that confirms intrinsic structural deformity.

teach.heading: Anatomical tracking of tuberculous cold abscesses
teach.body:
Tuberculous pus breaks through the anterior periosteum and tracks along anatomical fascial planes under gravity.

From the lumbar spine, pus tracks down the sheath of the psoas major muscle, presenting as a non-tender, non-erythematous fluctuant cold abscess in the iliac fossa or beneath the inguinal ligament in the femoral triangle.

skill.exam.surg.nerve_root_tension.title: Nerve root tension tests: straight leg raise and femoral stretch
skill.exam.surg.nerve_root_tension.oneLine: Straight Leg Raise, Bragard, Bowstring, and Femoral Stretch tests for radiculopathy
skill.exam.surg.nerve_root_tension.why: Accurately differentiates true mechanical nerve root impingement from benign hamstring tightness, localising the level of disc herniation and guiding surgical discectomy decisions.

steps.text: Place the patient supine, relaxed, with the head flat without a pillow and both lower extremities fully extended.
Grasp the patient's heel with one hand while holding the knee fully extended with your other hand resting gently above the patella.
Elevate the lower limb slowly and smoothly, observing the patient's face for discomfort and asking the patient to report the moment pain begins.
Record the angle of elevation at which typical lancinating pain shoots below the knee down the leg (a positive SLRT occurs between 30 and 70 degrees).

Perform the Bragard test: lower the leg slightly until the radicular pain just subsides, then passively dorsiflex the foot at the ankle. Reproduction of sharp radicular pain confirms true nerve root tension.

Perform the Bowstring test: flex the knee slightly to 20 degrees, resting it on your shoulder, and press firmly with your thumbs into the popliteal fossa over the tibial nerve; recurrence of radicular pain confirms sciatic root irritation.
Perform the Crossed (Well-Leg) Straight Leg Raise test: elevate the asymptomatic contralateral limb; reproduction of radiating sciatic pain in the affected leg is highly specific for disc prolapse.

Perform the Femoral Stretch test: turn the patient prone, flex the knee to 90 degrees, and gently extend the hip at the couch; reproduction of anterior thigh pain indicates upper lumbar (L2, L3, L4) nerve root irritation.

skill.exam.surg.nerve_root_tension.normal: Lower limb can be raised to 80 to 90 degrees with only mild posterior thigh muscle stretch; negative Bragard, Bowstring, Crossed SLRT, and Femoral Stretch tests.
skill.exam.surg.nerve_root_tension.abnormal: Reproduction of sharp radicular pain radiating below the knee between 30 and 70 degrees of elevation (positive SLRT); aggravation by ankle dorsiflexion (positive Bragard); pain provoked by popliteal nerve pressure (positive Bowstring); positive crossed SLRT; anterior thigh pain on prone hip extension.
skill.exam.surg.nerve_root_tension.significance: A positive SLRT with Bragard sign indicates lower lumbar nerve root compression (L5 or S1, typical of L4-L5 or L5-S1 disc prolapse); positive Crossed SLRT strongly indicates a large paracentral or axillary disc extrusion; positive femoral stretch indicates L2, L3, or L4 root irritation.
skill.exam.surg.nerve_root_tension.practice: Perform SLRT, Bragard test, and bowstring manoeuvre on a partner, noting the angle of onset and distinguishing posterior hamstring tightness from simulated radicular pain.
pitfalls: Mistaking tightness in the posterior thigh (hamstring stretching, usually at >70 degrees) for true radicular pain (which must shoot below the knee).
Omitting the Bragard test (ankle dorsiflexion), which is critical to differentiate sciatic root tension from simple muscular resistance.
Failing to perform the crossed straight leg raise test on the unaffected leg, which has over 90% specificity for disc herniation.
Neglecting the femoral nerve stretch test in patients presenting with anterior thigh pain or quadriceps weakness.

probes.q: Between what angles of hip elevation is the Straight Leg Raise Test considered positive for nerve root tension?
probes.a: Between 30 and 70 degrees of elevation; below 30 degrees roots are slack, and beyond 70 degrees hamstrings tighten without further nerve excursion.

probes.q: How does the Bragard test confirm true sciatic nerve root irritation over hamstring tightness?
probes.a: By lowering the leg below the pain threshold and dorsiflexing the ankle, the tibial nerve is tractioned without altering hamstring length, reproducing true neural pain.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a positive Crossed (Well-Leg) Straight Leg Raise test?
probes.a: It is highly specific (over 90%) for a lumbar disc herniation, particularly a large central or axillary disc prolapse.

rubric.text: Raises extended lower limb smoothly with knee straight and records angle of pain onset
Lowers leg slightly and dorsiflexes ankle (Bragard test) to confirm nerve root tension
Performs crossed straight leg raise test on the contralateral asymptomatic limb
Executes femoral nerve stretch test in prone position to assess L2-L4 roots
