teach.heading: Biomechanics of the Straight Leg Raise Test
teach.body:
Lifting the extended leg draws the sciatic nerve and its contributory roots (L4, L5, S1) caudally through the intervertebral foramina.

Between 30 and 70 degrees, the nerve roots undergo maximum excursion (up to 6 mm) across the floor of the canal; an impinging herniated disc stretches the inflamed nerve root, reproducing lancinating radicular pain down the limb.

teach.heading: Bragard and Bowstring confirmatory signs
teach.body:
Because hamstrings attach to the ischial tuberosity and tibia, passive leg elevation stretches both muscle and nerve.

Dorsiflexion of the ankle (Bragard test) or direct popliteal compression of the tibial nerve (Bowstring test) pulls exclusively on neural tissue without altering hamstring tension, confirming true radicular irritation.

teach.heading: Crossed SLRT and the femoral stretch test
teach.body:
Elevating the healthy contralateral limb pulls the thecal sac caudally and swings the affected nerve root medially against an axillary disc fragment, producing positive crossed SLRT with exceptional specificity.

The femoral stretch test (prone hip extension) stretches the femoral nerve and upper lumbar roots (L2 to L4).

skill.exam.surg.sacroiliac_joint.title: Examination of the sacroiliac joint
skill.exam.surg.sacroiliac_joint.oneLine: FABER (Patrick) test, pelvic distraction, compression, and Gaenslen test
skill.exam.surg.sacroiliac_joint.why: Differentiates sacroiliitis (ankylosing spondylitis, enteropathic or pyogenic arthritis) from lumbar disc herniation and hip joint pathology, guiding targeted rheumatological and surgical care.

steps.text: Place the patient supine and relaxed on an examination couch.
Perform the FABER (Patrick) test: flex the hip and knee, abduct the thigh, and externally rotate the hip so the lateral malleolus rests on the opposite knee (figure-4 position).
Stabilise the contralateral anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) firmly with one hand while applying gentle downward pressure on the medial aspect of the flexed knee with your other hand.

Differentiate the pain location during FABER: ask whether pain is felt anteriorly in the groin (hip joint disease) or posteriorly in the buttock over the sacroiliac joint (sacroiliac joint pathology).

Perform the Pelvic Distraction (gapping) test: cross your arms and place palms firmly against both anterior superior iliac spines, applying a slow, firm posterolateral pressure to distract the anterior sacroiliac ligaments.

Perform the Pelvic Compression test: place the patient in the lateral recumbent position and apply downward vertical pressure over the upper iliac crest toward the couch, compressing the sacroiliac joints.

Perform the Gaenslen test: with the patient supine at the edge of the couch, have them flex one hip and knee maximally to the chest while the examined leg is allowed to hyperextend off the couch edge.
Palpate the sacroiliac joint sulcus directly: locate the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) and press firmly just medial to it along the joint line for localized point tenderness.

skill.exam.surg.sacroiliac_joint.normal: Full painless hip external rotation during FABER test with knee approaching the couch; no pain on pelvic distraction, compression, or Gaenslen test; non-tender sacroiliac sulci.
skill.exam.surg.sacroiliac_joint.abnormal: Posterior buttock pain elicited on stressing the flexed knee during FABER test; pain reproduced by pelvic distraction or compression; positive Gaenslen test; acute focal point tenderness over the sacroiliac joint line.
skill.exam.surg.sacroiliac_joint.significance: A cluster of positive provocative sacroiliac stress tests confirms sacroiliitis (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, or tuberculous/pyogenic sacroiliitis) rather than lumbar radiculopathy or hip osteoarthritis.
skill.exam.surg.sacroiliac_joint.practice: Demonstrate the figure-4 FABER test and pelvic distraction test on a peer, verifying firm stabilisation of the contralateral ASIS.
pitfalls: Failing to stabilise the opposite ASIS during the FABER test, allowing pelvic tilt that generates false-negative readings.
Confusing anterior groin pain during FABER (which indicates hip labral or articular pathology) with posterior buttock pain (which indicates sacroiliitis).
Relying on a single test rather than a provocative test cluster (distraction, compression, FABER, Gaenslen), which is required for diagnostic validity.
Overlooking acute unilateral sacroiliac tenderness with high fever in children or young adults, which signals pyogenic or tuberculous sacroiliitis.

probes.q: What does the clinical acronym FABER stand for in examination of the hip and sacroiliac joint?
probes.a: Flexion, Abduction, and External Rotation of the hip joint.

probes.q: How do you distinguish hip joint pathology from sacroiliac joint pathology during the FABER (Patrick) test?
probes.a: Anterior pain felt in the groin signifies hip joint pathology, whereas posterior pain felt in the buttock over the sacroiliac sulcus signifies sacroiliac joint pathology.

probes.q: In a young male presenting with chronic buttock pain and morning stiffness, what does bilateral pain on pelvic distraction signify?
probes.a: Bilateral active sacroiliitis, strongly suggesting an axial spondyloarthritis such as ankylosing spondylitis.

rubric.text: Positions leg in figure-4 and stabilizes contralateral ASIS while applying downward pressure
Explicitly differentiates anterior groin pain (hip) from posterior buttock pain (SI joint)
Executes pelvic distraction, compression, or Gaenslen tests to stress SI ligaments
Palpates the sacroiliac joint line medial to the PSIS for point tenderness

teach.heading: Functional anatomy of the sacroiliac joint
teach.body:
The sacroiliac joint is an L-shaped joint with an anterior synovial articular component and a massive posterior syndesmosis bound by the interosseous sacroiliac ligaments.

It transmits the entire upper body weight from the sacrum to the iliac bones with minimal rotatory motion but rich sensory innervation from S1 to S3 dorsal rami.

teach.heading: The FABER test and pain localization
teach.body:
Placing the hip in flexion, abduction, and external rotation tensions the anterior hip capsule and stresses the ipsilateral anterior sacroiliac joint.

Pain localized to the anterior groin indicates acetabular labral tear or osteoarthritis, whereas deep posterior pain over the PSIS reflects sacroiliitis.

teach.heading: Provocative test clusters in sacroiliitis
teach.body:
Because isolated physical signs have variable sensitivity, evidence-based assessment relies on a cluster of provocative stress tests: distraction, compression, FABER, and Gaenslen.

Reproduction of familiar posterior pain in at least three of these tests achieves over 85% sensitivity and specificity for sacroiliac pathology.

skill.hx.surg.hand.title: History in surgical disorders and infections of the hand
skill.hx.surg.hand.oneLine: Hand dominance, occupation, mechanism of trauma, bite wounds, and diabetes
skill.hx.surg.hand.why: The hand is an irreplaceable functional and tactile organ; subtle puncture wounds lead to limb-threatening space infections, and hand dominance governs reconstructive priorities.

asks.text: Which is your dominant hand (right or left), and what are the specific manual demands of your occupation, trade, or hobbies?
What was the exact mechanism of injury: sharp laceration (glass, blade), crush injury, high-pressure injection (grease gun, paint), or animal or human bite?
Was there a minor penetrating puncture wound (sewing needle, thorn, fish bone, splinter) that initially seemed trivial?
How many hours or days have elapsed since the injury or first symptom, and has there been intense, throbbing nocturnal pain keeping you awake (pulp space infection)?
Has there been rapid proximal progression of redness, swelling, or red streaks extending up the wrist and forearm (lymphangitis)?
Have you received any home treatment, poultices, or surgical incisions by unqualified practitioners prior to presenting?
Do you have diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression, and what is your tetanus immunisation status?

skill.hx.surg.hand.practice: Take a hand injury history from a manual labourer who sustained a puncture wound, documenting dominance, exact time elapsed, and screening for high-pressure injection or human bite risks.
pitfalls: Failing to record hand dominance, which is fundamental to surgical planning, disability assessment, and rehabilitation priorities.
Dismissing a small dorsal puncture wound over the metacarpophalangeal joint without inquiring about a clenched-fist human bite injury (fight bite).
Underestimating high-pressure paint or grease gun injection injuries, which cause extensive subterranean tissue necrosis despite an innocuous pinhole entry wound.

probes.q: Why is establishing hand dominance mandatory in every surgical consultation involving the hand?
probes.a: Because functional impairment of the dominant hand results in disproportionate occupational and personal disability, guiding surgical decisions, aggressive rehabilitation, and legal assessment.

probes.q: What dangerous complication and organism are associated with a puncture wound over the dorsal MCP joint sustained during a punch?
probes.a: A human bite injury (fight bite) inoculating oral flora including Eikenella corrodens and anaerobes directly into the extensor tendon and joint space, causing rapid septic arthritis.

probes.q: Why are high-pressure paint or grease gun injuries of the hand surgical emergencies despite minimal skin disruption?
probes.a: The high pressure injects toxic solvent deep along fascial planes and tendon sheaths, causing progressive compartment syndrome, widespread chemical necrosis, and high amputation risk.

rubric.text: Explicitly records hand dominance and occupational manual requirements
Inquires into precise trauma mechanism (puncture, crush, human/animal bite, grease gun)
Evaluates presence of throbbing nocturnal pain and speed of proximal swelling
Screens for diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, and tetanus prophylaxis status

teach.heading: The functional imperative of hand dominance
teach.body:
The human hand accounts for an immense proportion of cerebral motor cortex representation.

Injuries to the dominant hand threaten economic livelihood and daily activities of living; every documentation, triage decision, and surgical repair must be framed around hand dominance and occupational needs.

teach.heading: Closed space inoculation mechanisms
teach.body:
Because palmar skin is tough and keratinised, tiny punctures by contaminated foreign bodies (fish spines, wire, thorns) inoculate bacteria into unyielding compartments.

Microbial multiplication leads to rapidly escalating pressures within closed spaces, causing local vascular thrombosis and ischaemic tissue sloughing.

teach.heading: High-risk trauma mechanisms
teach.body:
Clenched-fist injuries (teeth striking the dorsal MCP joint) inoculate aggressive polymicrobial oral flora into the joint capsule, presenting initially as minor cuts but developing septic arthritis within 48 hours.

High-pressure fluid injection causes immediate subsurface dispersal of toxic chemicals demanding urgent decompression.

skill.exam.surg.hand_infections.title: Examination of localized and deep fascial space infections of the hand
skill.exam.surg.hand_infections.oneLine: Paronychia, felon, web space (collar-stud), thenar, and midpalmar space infections
skill.exam.surg.hand_infections.why: Unchecked fascial space infections produce digital necrosis, osteomyelitis of phalanges, and spread to the forearm, causing permanent functional hand crippling.

steps.text: Examine both hands side-by-side in good lighting, comparing skin color, resting posture, and contours of the fingers, thenar, and hypothenar eminences.
Inspect the nail folds of all digits for localized erythema, swelling, and purulent collections along the lateral nail fold or eponychium (paronychia).
Inspect the terminal pulp space of the fingers: look for tense swelling, induration, and pallor over the volar pad (felon / terminal pulp space infection).
Palpate the terminal pulp gently to assess tension and point tenderness, avoiding forceful pressure; check for fluctuance or ischaemic necrosis of the overlying skin.
Inspect the web spaces between digits: look for separation of adjacent fingers (V-sign) with fullness in the web and marked dorsal swelling (collar-stud / web-space abscess).
Inspect the palm: look for obliteration of the normal palmar concavity or a dome-shaped bulge in the center of the palm (midpalmar space infection).
Inspect the first web space: look for ballooning of the thenar web space with the thumb held in an abducted and forward posture (thenar space infection).
Inspect the dorsum of the hand and forearm for red streaks of lymphangitis; palpate the epitrochlear lymph nodes (above medial epicondyle) and axillary lymph nodes for tender enlargement.

skill.exam.surg.hand_infections.normal: Normal palmar concavity preserved, soft supple finger pulps, non-tender nail folds, fingers resting in natural gentle flexion cascade, thumb adducts easily, no dorsal oedema or lymphadenopathy.
skill.exam.surg.hand_infections.abnormal: Erythema and pus around the nail fold (paronychia); tense, throbbing induration of finger pulp (felon); separated adjacent fingers with dorsal and palmar web collection (collar-stud); dome-like bulging of midpalm; ballooned first web space; red lymphatic streaks up the forearm.
skill.exam.surg.hand_infections.significance: A felon demands urgent drainage to prevent digital artery occlusion and distal phalanx osteomyelitis; web space collar-stud abscess has dorsal and palmar pockets requiring dual clearance; midpalmar and thenar infections require urgent surgical drainage in theatre.
skill.exam.surg.hand_infections.practice: Identify the surface boundaries of the thenar space, midpalmar space, and the path of the digital arteries in a hand model or peer.
pitfalls: Incising the dorsal swelling of the hand in a midpalmar or thenar space infection, as dorsal swelling represents loose reactive lymphatic oedema rather than the primary pus collection.
Waiting for fluctuance in a felon before surgical drainage; tense induration with throbbing pain is the surgical indication, and waiting results in distal phalanx osteomyelitis.
Draining only the visible dorsal portion of a web-space collar-stud abscess, leaving the deeper palmar collection undrained.
Failing to examine the supratrochlear and axillary lymph nodes in every acute hand infection.

probes.q: Why does a felon (terminal pulp space infection) cause necrosis of the distal phalanx if not drained promptly?
probes.a: Vertical fibrous septa compartmentalise the pulp; rapidly rising tension compresses the digital vessels, leading to ischaemic necrosis and osteomyelitis of the distal two-thirds of the phalanx.

probes.q: Why is pronounced swelling seen on the dorsum of the hand in palmar fascial space infections, and why must it not be incised?
probes.a: Lymphatics from the palm drain dorsally where skin and subcutaneous tissue are loose; dorsal swelling is reactive inflammatory oedema, not the primary collection of pus.

probes.q: What is a collar-stud (collar-button) abscess of the hand and what anatomical structure creates its hourglass shape?
probes.a: A web-space abscess with two collections (palmar and dorsal) connected by a narrow tract traversing the deep transverse metacarpal ligament or palmar fascia.

rubric.text: Inspects nail folds, finger pulps, web spaces, and palmar concavity bilaterally
Assesses tension and induration in the terminal pulp space without awaiting fluctuance
Identifies dorsal hand swelling as reactive lymphatic oedema rather than primary pus
Examines forearm for lymphangitis and palpates epitrochlear and axillary lymph nodes

teach.heading: Anatomy and compartment mechanics of the finger pulp
teach.body:
The terminal pulp of the finger is divided into dozens of closed compartments by tough vertical fibrous septa running from the deep dermis to the periosteum of the distal phalanx.

Infection elevates closed compartment pressure, occluding digital branches supplying the diaphysis and causing avascular necrosis of the distal two-thirds of the phalanx while sparing the base (supplied by proximal digital branches).

teach.heading: Fascial spaces of the palm and web spaces
teach.body:
The deep palm is divided by a midline fibrous septum attached to the third metacarpal into the thenar space (radially) and the midpalmar space (ulnarly).

Midpalmar infections obliterate normal palmar concavity, producing a prominent central dome, while thenar infections distend the first web space, forcing the thumb into abduction.

teach.heading: The trap of dorsal oedema and collar-stud abscesses
teach.body:
The thick, unyielding palmar aponeurosis prevents palmar skin distension; lymphatic drainage flows directly toward the loose dorsal subcutaneous network.

Consequently, palmar infections produce massive dorsal swelling that tempts an unwary examiner to incise the wrong surface; web-space abscesses form hourglass collections across the deep transverse ligament.

skill.exam.surg.flexor_tenosynovitis.title: Examination for acute suppurative flexor tenosynovitis (Kanavel signs)
skill.exam.surg.flexor_tenosynovitis.oneLine: Kanavel four cardinal signs of purulent flexor tendon sheath infection
skill.exam.surg.flexor_tenosynovitis.why: Suppurative flexor tenosynovitis is a closed compartment infection; rising intrasheath pressure causes tendon ischemia, necrosis, and irreversible crippling within 24 to 48 hours.

steps.text: Inspect the resting posture of both hands side by side: observe whether the affected digit is held in uniform, slight flexion compared to adjacent digits (Kanavel Sign 1).
Inspect the contour of the affected digit: look for uniform, symmetrical sausage-like swelling along the entire length of the finger from base to tip (Kanavel Sign 2).

Palpate with a blunt probe or fingertip along the anatomical course of the flexor tendon sheath from the distal phalanx across the palm to the distal palmar crease, eliciting exquisite point tenderness along the entire sheath (Kanavel Sign 3).

Perform passive extension testing: grasp the tip of the affected digit gently and passively extend the distal interphalangeal joint, observing the patient's reaction for severe pain along the flexor sheath (Kanavel Sign 4: the most sensitive and earliest sign).
Compare passive extension pain in the affected digit with adjacent digits to confirm isolated sheath involvement.

In infections of the thumb or little finger, palpate both the thenar and hypothenar eminences and the distal forearm (space of Parona) to detect proximal spread into the radial and ulnar bursae (Horseshoe abscess).

skill.exam.surg.flexor_tenosynovitis.normal: Digits rest in normal progressive cascade of flexion, slender digits with normal skin creases, non-tender tendon sheaths, painless full passive extension.
skill.exam.surg.flexor_tenosynovitis.abnormal: The four Kanavel signs: (1) digit held in slight flexion at rest, (2) uniform symmetrical sausage swelling of the entire finger, (3) exquisite tenderness along the entire course of the flexor sheath, (4) severe pain elicited on passive extension of the digit (earliest sign).
skill.exam.surg.flexor_tenosynovitis.significance: Confirms acute suppurative flexor tenosynovitis requiring immediate admission, intravenous antibiotics, and urgent surgical sheath irrigation or drainage to prevent tendon sloughing and permanent contracture.
skill.exam.surg.flexor_tenosynovitis.practice: Demonstrate the elicitation of the four Kanavel signs on a partner, specifically performing the gentle passive extension test.
pitfalls: Forcefully hyperextending the finger during examination, which causes agonizing pain and risks rupturing an ischaemic tendon.
Confusing superficial cellulitis with suppurative tenosynovitis; cellulitis has erythema but lacks uniform sheath tenderness and pain on passive extension.
Missing a horseshoe abscess by failing to examine the little finger and hypothenar space when the thumb is infected (and vice versa).
Delaying surgical decompression while waiting for cutaneous redness, which is minimal on the palmar surface due to thick cornified skin.

probes.q: What four cardinal physical signs constitute Kanavel four signs of acute flexor tenosynovitis?
probes.a: Flexed posture at rest, uniform symmetrical sausage swelling of the entire digit, tenderness along the entire anatomical flexor sheath, and severe pain on passive extension of the digit.

probes.q: Which of Kanavel four signs is the earliest and most sensitive clinical indicator of flexor sheath infection?
probes.a: Severe pain elicited on gentle passive extension of the digit.

probes.q: What anatomical communication allows an infection of the thumb flexor sheath to spread to the little finger, creating a horseshoe abscess?
probes.a: The flexor pollicis longus sheath (radial bursa) and the little finger flexor sheath (ulnar bursa) communicate proximally in the space of Parona in the distal forearm.

rubric.text: Identifies flexed resting posture and uniform sausage digit contour
Systematically palpates along the entire length of the flexor tendon sheath
Gently performs passive extension test to elicit characteristic pain (earliest sign)
Checks radial and ulnar bursae in thumb and little finger infections for horseshoe spread

teach.heading: Surgical anatomy of the digital flexor synovial sheaths
teach.body:
The flexor sheaths of the index, middle, and ring fingers terminate proximally at the level of the metacarpal heads (the A1 pulley).

In contrast, the sheath of the thumb (radial bursa) and the sheath of the little finger (ulnar bursa) extend proximally through the carpal tunnel into the distal forearm (the space of Parona).

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of the Kanavel cardinal signs
teach.body:
Purulent exudate rapidly fills the unyielding closed synovial sheath, creating high internal pressures.

The digit assumes a flexed posture to maximize internal synovial volume and minimize pain; passive extension tensions the tendon against the inflamed sheath, producing excruciating pain.

teach.heading: The Horseshoe abscess and Parona space infection
teach.body:
In approximately 50 to 80% of individuals, the radial and ulnar bursae communicate in the deep fascial space of Parona (deep to the flexor digitorum profundus in the lower forearm).

Infection entering the thumb or little finger can cross through this communication to involve the opposite border of the hand, forming a classic horseshoe abscess.

skill.exam.surg.hand_tendons.title: Examination of flexor and extensor tendons of the hand
skill.exam.surg.hand_tendons.oneLine: Individual testing of FDS, FDP, extensor digitorum, mallet finger, and Boutonniere
skill.exam.surg.hand_tendons.why: Identifies divided or ruptured tendons in closed injuries and open lacerations; compensation by adjacent tendons frequently masks partial or complete tendon transection.

steps.text: Test the Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP): immobilise the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint in full extension; instruct the patient to actively flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Active DIP flexion confirms intact FDP.

Test the Flexor Digitorum Superficialis (FDS): hold all adjacent non-examined fingers in complete passive extension against a flat surface (inactivating the shared FDP muscle belly); ask the patient to actively flex the PIP joint of the free examined digit. Active PIP flexion confirms intact FDS.
Test the Flexor Pollicis Longus (FPL): stabilise the proximal phalanx of the thumb with your fingers and instruct the patient to actively flex the interphalangeal (IP) joint.
Test Extensor Digitorum Communis: ask the patient to actively extend the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints against resistance with the wrist in neutral position.
Inspect the distal digits for Mallet finger: observe for loss of active DIP extension with the distal phalanx held in a flexed attitude following traumatic impact to the tip of an extended finger.
Examine for Boutonniere deformity: look for flexion of the PIP joint accompanied by hyperextension of the DIP joint resulting from rupture of the central slip of the extensor expansion.

Perform the Elson test for central slip extensor rupture: flex the PIP joint 90 degrees over the edge of a table and ask the patient to extend the PIP joint against resistance. Weak PIP extension accompanied by a rigid, hyperextended DIP joint confirms central slip disruption.

skill.exam.surg.hand_tendons.normal: Active flexion at the DIP joint with PIP stabilised (intact FDP); active PIP flexion while adjacent fingers are restrained in extension (intact FDS); full active extension at MCP, PIP, and DIP joints without deformity.
skill.exam.surg.hand_tendons.abnormal: Inability to flex DIP joint actively (FDP division); inability to flex PIP joint with adjacent fingers restrained (FDS division); flexed DIP joint unable to extend actively (mallet finger); PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension (Boutonniere deformity); PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion (Swan-neck).
skill.exam.surg.hand_tendons.significance: Isolates and identifies individual tendon divisions and closed ruptures, defining the tendon zone (e.g., Zone 2 'No Man's Land') and dictating primary surgical repair versus specialised splinting.
skill.exam.surg.hand_tendons.practice: Perform isolated FDS and FDP examination on all four fingers of a colleague, ensuring proper restraint of adjacent digits.
pitfalls: Allowing adjacent fingers to curl during FDS testing, which recruits the FDP muscle and gives a false-positive impression of an intact FDS.
Assuming flexor tendons are intact simply because the patient can make a fist, failing to isolate individual FDS and FDP tendons.
Failing to recognize central slip extensor rupture early because intact lateral bands temporarily maintain weak PIP extension before sliding volarward.
Neglecting to test the flexor pollicis longus individually in lacerations over the thenar eminence or wrist.

probes.q: How is the Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) tendon clinically isolated and tested in an individual finger?
probes.a: By holding the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint in full extension and asking the patient to actively flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint.

probes.q: How do you isolate the Flexor Digitorum Superficialis (FDS) of a finger from the action of the FDP?
probes.a: By holding all other fingers in full passive extension (inactivating the shared FDP muscle belly) and asking the patient to flex the PIP joint of the free finger.

probes.q: What tendon disruption produces a Boutonniere deformity, and what is the characteristic posture of the PIP and DIP joints?
probes.a: Rupture of the central slip of the extensor tendon over the PIP joint, allowing the lateral bands to sublux volarward, producing PIP flexion and secondary DIP hyperextension.

rubric.text: Stabilises PIP joint in extension and tests isolated active DIP flexion for FDP
Restrains adjacent fingers in extension to inactivate FDP and tests PIP flexion for FDS
Stabilises thumb proximal phalanx and tests active IP flexion for FPL
Evaluates for mallet finger and central slip disruption using the Elson test

teach.heading: Anatomical relationship of the flexor digitorum tendons
teach.body:
The FDS tendon divides at the proximal phalanx into two slips (camper chiasm) that embrace the deeper FDP tendon before reuniting to insert into the middle phalanx.

The FDP tendon passes through the bifurcation to insert into the base of the distal phalanx; because FDP shares a common muscle belly for digits 3 to 5, restraining adjacent fingers neutralizes its action.

teach.heading: The extensor expansion and central slip mechanics
teach.body:
Over the proximal phalanx, the extensor tendon trifurcates into a central slip inserting onto the base of the middle phalanx and two lateral bands that fuse to insert into the distal phalanx.

Avulsion of the terminal tendon produces mallet finger, whereas rupture of the central slip allows lateral bands to slip volar to the PIP axis, generating the progressive Boutonniere deformity.

teach.heading: Flexor tendon zones and surgical prognosis
teach.body:
Flexor tendon injuries are categorized into five zones.

Zone 2 ('No Man's Land') extends from the A1 pulley at the distal palmar crease to the FDS insertion, where both tendons travel in a tight, unyielding fibro-osseous tunnel; repair in Zone 2 is notoriously complicated by postoperative adhesions.

skill.exam.surg.hand_nerves.title: Examination of peripheral nerves in the hand: radial, median, and ulnar
skill.exam.surg.hand_nerves.oneLine: Autonomous sensory zones and motor tests: APB pen test, Froment sign, and card test
skill.exam.surg.hand_nerves.why: Nerve lacerations and compression neuropathies cause devastating functional hand impairment; testing autonomous zones and isolated motor units accurately identifies nerve injury level.

steps.text: Test Radial Nerve Motor function: ask the patient to actively extend the wrist and fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints against resistance (check for wrist drop and finger drop).
Test Radial Nerve Sensory function: evaluate light touch and pinprick over its strictly autonomous sensory zone: the dorsum of the first web space (anatomical snuffbox area).

Test Median Nerve Motor function using the Abductor Pollicis Brevis (APB) / Pen Touch Test: place the hand flat on a table with the palm facing upward; instruct the patient to point the thumb straight up toward the ceiling (perpendicular to the palm) and touch an examiner's pen held above, resisting downward pressure.

Test Median Nerve Motor function with Ochsner clasp test: ask the patient to clasp both hands together; if the median nerve is divided at or above the elbow, the index and middle fingers fail to flex, creating the pointing index sign.
Test Median Nerve Sensory function: evaluate light touch and pinprick over its autonomous sensory zone: the palmar aspect of the tip of the index finger.

Test Ulnar Nerve Motor function using the Palmar Interossei Card Test: place a stiff card between two fully extended adjacent fingers and ask the patient to grip it tightly while you try to withdraw it.

Test Ulnar Nerve Motor function using Froment paper test for Adductor Pollicis: ask the patient to grip a sheet of paper tightly between the thumb pulp and radial aspect of the index finger; pull the paper away and observe whether the patient acutely flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb (positive Froment sign due to trick substitution by FPL).
Test Ulnar Nerve Sensory function: evaluate light touch and pinprick over its autonomous sensory zone: the palmar aspect of the tip of the little finger.

Inspect the resting posture of the hand for nerve injury attitudes: ape thumb deformity (median nerve), wrist drop (radial nerve), and ulnar claw hand (hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints of ring and little fingers; note the Ulnar Paradox where clawing is more severe in low ulnar lesions than high lesions).

skill.exam.surg.hand_nerves.normal: Full active wrist and finger extension, strong thumb abduction perpendicular to the palm (intact APB), firm card grip between fingers, flat thumb posture during paper pull (negative Froment), intact sensation at the three autonomous zones (index tip, little finger tip, first dorsal web).
skill.exam.surg.hand_nerves.abnormal: Wrist drop (radial); ape thumb with thenar wasting and weak APB (median); pointing index sign on clasping; ulnar clawing of digits 4 and 5; acute thumb IP flexion during paper pull (positive Froment sign); sensory loss in autonomous zones.
skill.exam.surg.hand_nerves.significance: Localises peripheral nerve injuries of the upper extremity, distinguishes high from low lesions, and separates true compressive neuropathy from acute traumatic laceration.
skill.exam.surg.hand_nerves.practice: Demonstrate the APB pen touch test, Froment paper test, and interossei card test on a partner, stating the autonomous sensory zones.
pitfalls: Testing thumb abduction in the plane of the palm (performed by abductor pollicis longus, innervated by the radial nerve) rather than perpendicular to the palm (abductor pollicis brevis, median nerve).
Missing Froment sign by looking at the paper rather than watching the distal interphalangeal joint of the thumb as the paper is pulled.
Testing sensation in overlapping territories instead of the three strictly autonomous zones (index tip for median, little finger tip for ulnar, first dorsal web space for radial).

Forgetting the Ulnar Paradox: a lesion at the wrist produces more pronounced claw deformity than a lesion at the elbow because the FDP to the ring and little fingers remains functioning in low lesions.

probes.q: What are the three autonomous sensory test zones for the radial, median, and ulnar nerves in the hand?
probes.a: Dorsum of the first web space for the radial nerve, palmar aspect of the tip of the index finger for the median nerve, and palmar aspect of the tip of the little finger for the ulnar nerve.

probes.q: How is the Abductor Pollicis Brevis (APB) tested to verify low median nerve motor function without trick movements?
probes.a: With the hand supinated flat on a table, the patient abducts the thumb vertically upward perpendicular to the plane of the palm against resistance (pen touch test).

probes.q: What is Froment sign, what paralysed muscle does it detect, and how does the patient compensate?
probes.a: Paralysis of the ulnar-innervated adductor pollicis; when gripping paper against resistance, the patient compensates using the median-innervated flexor pollicis longus, hyperflexing the thumb IP joint.

rubric.text: Tests sensation specifically at index tip (median), little finger tip (ulnar), and dorsal web (radial)
Executes pen touch test with thumb abducted perpendicular to the plane of the palm
Performs Froment paper grip test and observes for acute thumb IP joint hyperflexion
Tests palmar interossei adduction using the stiff paper or card test

teach.heading: Autonomous sensory territories of the hand
teach.body:
Because cutaneous sensory fields overlap extensively between the median, ulnar, and superficial radial nerves, sensation in the palm or middle fingers may remain preserved even after nerve division.

Reliable assessment demands testing the three strictly autonomous zones: the dorsal first web space (radial), the tip of the index finger (median), and the tip of the little finger (ulnar).

teach.heading: The plane of abduction and the APB test
teach.body:
Thumb abduction in the plane of the palm is performed by the abductor pollicis longus (posterior interosseous branch of the radial nerve).

True palmar abduction (moving the thumb vertically out of the plane of the palm toward the ceiling) is executed exclusively by the abductor pollicis brevis, serving as the benchmark motor test for low median nerve integrity.

teach.heading: Froment sign and the Ulnar Paradox
teach.body:
When adductor pollicis is paralysed in ulnar nerve injury, the patient grips paper by powerfully contracting flexor pollicis longus (median nerve), sharply flexing the thumb IP joint (Froment sign).

In the Ulnar Paradox, high ulnar lesions at the elbow paralyse FDP to digits 4 and 5, resulting in less severe clawing than low lesions at the wrist where intact FDP flexes the IP joints unrestrained.

skill.hx.surg.foot.title: History in surgical disorders and pain syndromes of the foot
skill.hx.surg.foot.oneLine: Pain localization, mechanical stress, marching fracture, plantar fasciitis, and footwear
skill.hx.surg.foot.why: The anatomical site and temporal pattern of foot pain accurately discriminates stress fractures, avascular necrosis, nerve entrapments, and biomechanical collapse prior to radiographic investigation.

asks.text: Where is the exact site of foot pain: heel, second metatarsal shaft, second metatarsal head, intermetatarsal web space, or the first metatarsophalangeal joint?
What is the timing of the pain: is there severe heel pain during the first few steps out of bed in the morning that eases after walking (plantar fasciitis)?
Did the pain start suddenly during or after unaccustomed prolonged walking or military marching (march fracture of second metatarsal)?
Is the pain a sharp, burning, or electric sensation in the forefoot radiating to the toes, accompanied by numbness or the feeling of walking on a pebble (Morton metatarsalgia)?
Was any deformity present since birth (congenital talipes equinovarus) or did it develop in adolescence or adulthood (hallux valgus, flatfoot)?
What type of footwear is worn routinely: tight military boots, high heels, narrow pointed shoes, or flat non-supportive sandals?
Is there a history of diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease, inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid or ankylosing spondylitis), or gout?

skill.hx.surg.foot.practice: Take a foot pain history from a simulated patient, identifying whether features correspond to plantar fasciitis, march fracture, or Morton metatarsalgia.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about the characteristic 'first-step morning pain' that differentiates plantar fasciitis from calcaneal stress fracture.
Dismissing insidious forefoot pain in an adolescent girl as growing pains without considering Freiberg disease (avascular necrosis of the second metatarsal head).
Attributing burning interdigital forefoot pain to generalized arthritis without screening for Morton interdigital neuroma.

probes.q: What is the classic clinical pattern of pain in plantar fasciitis regarding morning rising?
probes.a: Severe sharp pain under the heel during the first few steps out of bed in the morning, which gradually eases after walking as the plantar fascia stretches.

probes.q: What is a march fracture, which bone does it most frequently involve, and what history precipitates it?
probes.a: A stress fracture most commonly involving the neck or shaft of the second metatarsal, precipitated by prolonged unaccustomed walking or marching in recruits.

probes.q: What is Morton metatarsalgia, and what sensory symptom does the patient describe in the toes?
probes.a: Perineural fibrosis and entrapment of the third common plantar digital nerve between the third and fourth metatarsal heads, causing burning pain and numbness radiating into the adjacent third and fourth toes.

rubric.text: Pinpoints the exact anatomical location of foot pain (heel, metatarsal, interdigital)
Identifies morning first-step pain or exertion-related mechanical stress patterns
Distinguishes congenital deformities from progressive adult-acquired deformities
Inquires about footwear, military marching, diabetes, and inflammatory arthritis

teach.heading: Heel pain and the plantar fascia mechanism
teach.body:
The plantar aponeurosis originates from the medial tubercle of the calcaneus and fans out to the proximal phalanges, maintaining the longitudinal arch via the windlass mechanism.

Repetitive microtrauma causes insertional fasciosis; contraction of the aponeurosis during overnight recumbency produces intense pain on the first morning steps until fibers stretch.

teach.heading: Forefoot stress injuries and march fractures
teach.body:
The second metatarsal is the longest and most securely fixed metatarsal at the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) junction, absorbing the greatest mechanical load during the push-off phase of gait.

Unaccustomed walking or marching subjects the slender shaft to cyclical stress, resulting in microfractures (march fracture) that present with focal dorsal swelling and tenderness.

teach.heading: Morton interdigital neuroma pathophysiology
teach.body:
The third common plantar digital nerve receives communicating branches from both the medial and lateral plantar nerves, making it unusually thick and vulnerable.

Compression against the deep transverse metatarsal ligament during push-off causes repetitive perineural ischaemia and benign fibrous proliferation (neuroma), provoked by tight, pointed footwear.

skill.exam.surg.foot_deformities.title: Examination of foot deformities and structural alignment
skill.exam.surg.foot_deformities.oneLine: Pes planus, pes cavus, hallux valgus, toe deformities, and Achilles tendon integrity
skill.exam.surg.foot_deformities.why: Structural malalignment alters weight-bearing load distribution, causing chronic metatarsalgia, disabling arthritis, cutaneous ulceration, and gait dysfunction.

steps.text: Inspect both feet while the patient stands barefoot evenly on a flat surface, viewing from the front, lateral side, and posterior aspect.

Inspect the medial longitudinal arch: look for flattening with bulging of the navicular region against the floor (pes planus / flatfoot) versus an exaggerated high arch with clawing of toes (pes cavus).

Inspect from behind for hindfoot valgus or varus alignment and check for the 'too many toes' sign: viewing more than the fifth toe laterally while standing behind indicates forefoot abduction and hindfoot valgus.

Perform the Jack test (great toe extension test): with the patient standing, passively dorsiflex the great toe at the first MTP joint; reconstitution of the medial longitudinal arch indicates flexible flatfoot, whereas persistent flat arch indicates rigid flatfoot (e.g. tarsal coalition).

Inspect the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint for Hallux Valgus: assess lateral deviation of the great toe (>15 degrees), medial prominence of the first metatarsal head, and presence of an inflamed adventitious bursa (bunion).
Inspect the lesser toes for deformities: hammer toe (MTP extension, PIP flexion, DIP extension), claw toe (MTP hyperextension, PIP flexion, DIP flexion), and mallet toe (isolated DIP flexion).

Perform the Mulder test for Morton neuroma: compress the metatarsal heads transversely together with one hand while pressing the third interdigital space with your thumb; a palpable click accompanied by radiating pain is positive.

Perform the Simmonds-Thompson test for Achilles tendon rupture: place the patient prone with feet hanging freely over the end of the examination couch; squeeze the calf muscle firmly. Absence of passive ankle plantarflexion confirms complete rupture of the Achilles tendon.

skill.exam.surg.foot_deformities.normal: Medial longitudinal arch preserved on weight-bearing; neutral hindfoot; great toe aligned straight (<15 degrees valgus); painless metatarsal compression without click; calf squeeze produces brisk passive ankle plantarflexion.
skill.exam.surg.foot_deformities.abnormal: Flatfoot with collapsed medial arch (pes planus); high rigid arch with claw toes (pes cavus); hallux valgus with prominent inflamed bunion; hammer or claw toes with dorsal calluses; positive Mulder click; absent plantarflexion on calf squeeze (Achilles rupture).
skill.exam.surg.foot_deformities.significance: Distinguishes flexible flatfoot from rigid tarsal coalition; identifies hallux valgus and transfer metatarsalgia; confirms complete Achilles tendon rupture requiring surgical repair or rigid functional immobilisation.
skill.exam.surg.foot_deformities.practice: Perform the Jack test, Mulder compression test, and Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test on a colleague, recording findings.
pitfalls: Examining flatfoot only while non-weight-bearing on the couch, missing arch collapse that occurs strictly under gravitational loading.
Misdiagnosing an Achilles tendon tear because the patient can weakly plantarflex using long toe flexors when non-weight-bearing (the calf squeeze test is mandatory).
Confusing an adventitious bunion over the first metatarsal head with acute gouty arthritis without examining joint effusion and temperature.
Failing to look from behind for the 'too many toes' sign to recognize acquired flatfoot from tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction.

probes.q: How does the Jack test (passive great toe dorsiflexion) distinguish flexible from rigid flatfoot?
probes.a: Passive dorsiflexion of the great toe tightens the plantar fascia via the windlass mechanism; in flexible flatfoot the arch reconstitutes, whereas in rigid flatfoot the arch remains flat.

probes.q: How is the Simmonds-Thompson test performed to diagnose acute rupture of the Achilles tendon?
probes.a: With the patient prone and feet hanging over the bed, the examiner squeezes the calf muscle; failure of the foot to passively plantarflex confirms complete Achilles tendon rupture.

probes.q: What triad of structural deformities constitutes hallux valgus?
probes.a: Lateral deviation of the great toe at the first MTP joint, medial deviation of the first metatarsal (metatarsus primus varus), and formation of an adventitious bursa (bunion) over the medial metatarsal head.

rubric.text: Inspects medial longitudinal arch and hindfoot alignment while the patient is standing
Executes the Jack test (great toe dorsiflexion) to differentiate flexible from rigid flatfoot
Assesses 1st MTP valgus deviation, medial prominence, and bunion inflammation
Performs Simmonds-Thompson calf squeeze test to evaluate Achilles tendon integrity

teach.heading: The windlass mechanism and flatfoot biomechanics
teach.body:
The medial longitudinal arch is supported dynamically by the tibialis posterior tendon and statically by the spring ligament and plantar fascia.

Passive great toe extension tensions the plantar aponeurosis around the metatarsal head, pulling the calcaneus forward and elevating the medial arch (the windlass mechanism); failure to reconstitute indicates rigid tarsal coalition.

teach.heading: Structural pathology of Hallux Valgus
teach.body:
Hallux valgus involves lateral deviation of the proximal phalanx exceeding 15 degrees, medial deviation of the first metatarsal (metatarsus primus varus), and lateral subluxation of the extensor hallucis longus tendon and sesamoids.

Frictional shear against footwear induces an adventitious bursa over the prominent medial metatarsal head, termed a bunion.

teach.heading: Achilles tendon rupture and the Simmonds-Thompson sign
teach.body:
Complete rupture occurs characteristically 2 to 6 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion in an area of relative avascularity during sudden push-off.

Because intact deep toe flexors (FHL, FDL, tibialis posterior) can weakly plantarflex an unloaded foot, diagnosis relies on squeezing the gastrocnemius-soleus bulk, which fails to transmit passive plantarflexion when the tendon is severed.

skill.exam.surg.diabetic_foot.title: Surgical examination of the diabetic foot
skill.exam.surg.diabetic_foot.oneLine: Neuropathy screening, vascular perfusion, pressure points, and ulcer evaluation
skill.exam.surg.diabetic_foot.why: Diabetic foot complications account for the majority of non-traumatic lower extremity amputations; systematic detection of sensory loss, ischaemia, and deep space sepsis saves limbs.

steps.text: Inspect both feet completely barefoot: look for dry cracked skin, anhidrosis, loss of hair on dorsum and toes, thick dystrophic nails, clawed toes, and prominent metatarsal heads (motor and autonomic neuropathy).
Inspect all high-pressure plantar areas, heel, and web spaces between every toe for calluses, fissures, blisters, erythema, and ulcers.

Palpate skin temperature from the toes up to the knee, comparing both sides; palpate the dorsalis pedis artery (between 1st and 2nd metatarsal bases) and posterior tibial artery (behind medial malleolus) bilaterally.

Test protective sensation using the 10g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament: apply the filament perpendicular to the skin until it buckles for 1 to 2 seconds across standard plantar sites (plantar hallucal pulp, 3rd and 5th toes, 1st, 3rd, and 5th metatarsal heads, midfoot, and heel).
Test vibration perception using a 128 Hz tuning fork over the bony prominence of the interphalangeal joint of the great toe, noting premature loss of vibration sense.

Perform the probe-to-bone test on any open ulcer: using a sterile, blunt-ended metal probe, gently explore the ulcer base; feeling hard, gritty, unyielding bone directly confirms underlying osteomyelitis.
Grade any identified ulcer according to the Wagner classification (Grades 0 to 5) and palpate for deep plantar space fluctuance, subcutaneous crepitus (gas gangrene), and foul odour.

skill.exam.surg.diabetic_foot.normal: Warm skin, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, intact protective sensation to 10g monofilament at all testing sites, intact vibration perception, intact skin without calluses or ulceration.
skill.exam.surg.diabetic_foot.abnormal: Cold or abnormally warm pulseless foot, loss of 10g monofilament sensation, absent vibration sense, calluses over metatarsal heads, dry cracked skin, ulceration, positive probe-to-bone test, deep crepitus or purulent discharge.
skill.exam.surg.diabetic_foot.significance: Identifies the high-risk diabetic foot (sensory neuropathy combined with peripheral arterial disease); a positive probe-to-bone test has over 85% positive predictive value for osteomyelitis; guides urgent surgical debridement, revascularisation, and offloading.
skill.exam.surg.diabetic_foot.practice: Perform a 10-point 10g monofilament examination on a peer, applying sufficient force to bend the nylon filament into a C-shape.
pitfalls: Failing to remove shoes and socks and inspect between every toe and under the heel in every diabetic patient.
Omitting the probe-to-bone test in an open chronic diabetic ulcer, missing underlying cortical osteomyelitis.
Assuming a warm foot excludes severe vascular disease (neuropathic arteriovenous shunting or active infection often produces a warm, hyperaemic but ischaemic foot).
Neglecting to palpate both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses in every examination.

probes.q: How is the 10g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament applied to test protective sensation in the diabetic foot?
probes.a: Applied perpendicular to the skin surface until the monofilament buckles into a C-shape for 1 to 2 seconds, asking the patient to respond when touch is felt.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a positive 'probe-to-bone' test in a chronic diabetic foot ulcer?
probes.a: Gently probing with a sterile metal instrument feels hard, gritty bone; it carries a positive predictive value greater than 85% for underlying osteomyelitis.

probes.q: What triad of neuropathies contributes to the pathogenesis of the diabetic neuropathic ulcer?
probes.a: Sensory neuropathy (loss of protective pain sensation), motor neuropathy (lumbrical atrophy causing claw toes and high focal plantar pressures), and autonomic neuropathy (anhidrosis causing dry cracked skin).

rubric.text: Inspects skin, interdigital spaces between all toes, and plantar pressure points
Palpates dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally
Applies 10g monofilament until it buckles at standard plantar sites
Executes probe-to-bone test with a blunt metal probe on open ulcers

teach.heading: The diabetic foot triad: neuropathy, deformity, and ischaemia
teach.body:
Sensory neuropathy strips the patient of protective pain reflexes, allowing repetitive mechanical microtrauma to go unnoticed.

Motor neuropathy paralyse intrinsic lumbrical and interosseous muscles, creating claw toes that concentrate excessive shear stress under the metatarsal heads, while autonomic neuropathy impairs sweating, producing cracked skin susceptible to infection.

teach.heading: Technique of 10g monofilament sensory testing
teach.body:
The 10g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament delivers precisely 10 grams of linear force when pressed against the skin until it buckles.

Inability to perceive this tactile stimulus at two or more sites signifies loss of protective sensation, identifying a high-risk foot that warrants intensive prophylactic orthotics and offloading.

teach.heading: The probe-to-bone test and deep fascial sepsis
teach.body:
Palpating hard, rough cortical bone with a blunt sterile metal probe through an open ulcer bed confirms osteomyelitis without waiting for delayed radiographic changes.

Infection tracks along deep plantar fascial compartments (medial, lateral, and central), requiring urgent incision and drainage to avert major amputation.

skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_foot.title: Wagner Classification of Diabetic Foot Lesions
skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_foot.oneLine: Grading system for diabetic foot ulcers from pre-ulcerative risk to extensive gangrene
skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_foot.why: Standardised staging system stratifying ulcer depth, infection, and tissue necrosis to guide surgical decision-making from conservative offloading to urgent amputation.

rows: Intact skin with bony deformity, thick calluses, or healed prior ulcer
Pressure offloading, custom therapeutic footwear, callus debridement
Full-thickness skin ulcer not extending into tendon, capsule, or bone
Sharp debridement, moist wound dressings, non-weight-bearing offloading
Deep ulcer penetrating to tendon, joint capsule, or bone without abscess
Surgical debridement, culture-directed antibiotics, total contact cast
Deep ulcer complicated by deep abscess, osteomyelitis, or septic arthritis
Urgent surgical drainage, bone resection (partial ray), IV antibiotics
Localized gangrene involving digits or forefoot with necrosis
Urgent admission, vascular revascularisation, minor amputation (toe/ray)
Extensive gangrene involving the major portion of the foot
Emergency resuscitation, sepsis control, major amputation (below/above knee)

skill.annex.surg.wagner_diabetic_foot.practice: Review clinical photographs of diabetic foot ulcers and assign the correct Wagner grade, stating the management priority for each grade.
pitfalls: Assigning an ulcer with underlying bone contact to Grade 2 instead of Grade 3 (bone involvement qualifies as Grade 3).
Managing Grade 4 forefoot gangrene conservatively with local dressings alone without urgent vascular evaluation and surgical intervention.
Neglecting Grade 0 pre-ulcerative high-risk feet, which require custom footwear modifications to prevent initial ulcer formation.

probes.q: What differentiates a Wagner Grade 2 ulcer from a Wagner Grade 3 diabetic foot lesion?
probes.a: Wagner Grade 2 penetrates deep to tendon or bone without infection, whereas Grade 3 is complicated by deep abscess, osteomyelitis, or joint sepsis.

probes.q: What is the primary surgical management principle for a patient presenting with Wagner Grade 4 diabetic foot?
probes.a: Urgent hospitalisation, vascular assessment for revascularisation, and minor amputation (e.g., ray amputation or transmetatarsal amputation).

probes.q: What characterizes a Wagner Grade 0 diabetic foot, and why is its clinical identification vital?
probes.a: Intact skin with severe high-risk features such as deformities, calluses, or prior ulcers; identifying Grade 0 allows prophylactic offloading before ulceration occurs.

rubric.text: Accurately assigns Wagner grade based on tissue depth and infection
Correctly categorises bone involvement or deep abscess as Grade 3
Differentiates localised forefoot gangrene (Grade 4) from extensive gangrene (Grade 5)

teach.heading: Principles and architecture of the Wagner staging system
teach.body:
The Wagner system classifies diabetic foot pathology based on ulcer depth (Grades 0 to 2), presence of deep infection (Grade 3), and extent of ischaemic tissue necrosis (Grades 4 and 5).

This simple anatomical hierarchy directly informs whether treatment is conservative, reconstructive, or ablative.

teach.heading: Surgical escalation from Grade 1 to Grade 5
teach.body:
Grades 1 and 2 ulcers are managed with sharp debridement, offloading, and moist dressings.

Grade 3 demands surgical drainage and excision of infected bone (partial ray resection); Grade 4 requires urgent revascularisation and minor amputation; Grade 5 mandates major transtibial or transfemoral amputation to prevent fatal septic shock.

skill.exam.surg.scalp_swelling.title: Scalp Swelling Examination
skill.exam.surg.scalp_swelling.oneLine: Palpating anatomical plane, bone indentation, and cough impulse to separate benign cysts from cranial defects
skill.exam.surg.scalp_swelling.why: A scalp swelling may arise from the skin, subcutaneous fibrofatty tissue, galea aponeurotica, subaponeurotic space, pericranium, or underlying skull bone. Failing to establish the anatomical plane, test for underlying bone indentation, and check for a cough impulse risks mistaking an encephalocele, dermoid cyst with intracranial extension, or cirsoid aneurysm for a simple sebaceous cyst.

steps.text: Inspect the swelling under good illumination: record exact anatomical site, size, contour, skin colour, presence of a central punctum, local alopecia, and visible pulsations.

Palpate with warm hands: determine temperature, tenderness, and surface smoothness; gently pinch the overlying skin to see if it is tethered to the lump (sebaceous cyst) or moves freely over it (lipoma, dermoid cyst, bone tumour).
Test mobility over the skull: grasp the swelling and attempt to glide it in two perpendicular planes over the underlying cranial vault to determine whether it is mobile or fixed to bone.
Palpate the bony margin around the base: feel for a circular bone defect with a smooth raised saucer-like edge characteristic of an external angular or sequestration dermoid cyst.
Assess consistency and fluid signs: test for fluctuation across two axes, transillumination using a pen torch with a dark card cone, and expansile impulse on coughing or crying.
Auscultate with the bell of the stethoscope over the swelling: listen for a systolic vascular bruit if pulsations, thrill, or a compressible network of tortuous vessels is present (cirsoid aneurysm).

skill.exam.surg.scalp_swelling.normal: Scalp is uniform in thickness, smoothly contoured, non-tender, freely mobile over the cranium, without focal lumps, bone defects, pulsatile thrill, or audible bruits.
skill.exam.surg.scalp_swelling.abnormal: Spherical cyst fixed to overlying skin with a central punctum (sebaceous cyst / epidermoid cyst); tense cystic lump at suture line or outer canthus fixed to bone with a palpable saucer-like defect (dermoid cyst); soft, lobulated, slipping mass in subcutaneous plane (lipoma); pulsatile swelling of tortuous vessels with a systolic thrill and bruit (cirsoid aneurysm); stony hard non-tender mass arising from outer table (osteoma); soft reducible midline mass with expansile cough impulse (meningocele).
skill.exam.surg.scalp_swelling.significance: Distinguishes superficial cysts suitable for local excision from cranial vault osteomas, vascular malformations with intracranial communications, and congenital meningoceles where blind incision is catastrophic.
skill.exam.surg.scalp_swelling.practice: Rehearse examining a scalp lump by methodically testing three planes: pinch the skin over the lump, move the lump over the bone, and feel the bone contour around its circumference.
pitfalls: Attempting to excise a midline or outer canthus scalp lump without testing for a bone indentation defect and cough impulse, risking entry into an intracranial meningocele.
Confusing an ulcerated, infected, fungating sebaceous cyst with squamous cell carcinoma (Cock peculiar tumour).
Failing to auscultate a pulsating scalp mass for a systolic bruit, which identifies a cirsoid aneurysm and requires angiography rather than simple incision.

probes.q: What physical finding on the overlying skin distinguishes a sebaceous cyst from a lipoma of the scalp?
probes.a: A central punctum and adherence of the overlying skin to the dome of the cyst.

probes.q: What bone finding is characteristic when palpating the base of a congenital dermoid cyst on the skull?
probes.a: A saucer-shaped bone depression with a raised peripheral rim due to pressure erosion during skull growth.

probes.q: A pulsatile soft swelling on the temple feels like a bag of squirming earthworms. What is the diagnosis, and what must be excluded before surgery?
probes.a: Cirsoid aneurysm (arteriovenous malformation). Intracranial extension through skull erosion or perforation must be excluded by imaging before excision.

rubric.text: Tests whether overlying skin can be pinched free from the swelling
Palpates the bone margin around the circumference of the swelling
Checks for pulsation, thrill, and auscultates for a bruit in vascular lesions
Tests for an expansile impulse on coughing or crying in midline cranial masses

teach.heading: Anatomical planes of the scalp and their surgical lesions
teach.body:
The scalp comprises five distinct layers: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (galea), Loose areolar tissue, and Pericranium. Sebaceous cysts arise from the skin and move with it. Lipomas usually arise in the dense subcutaneous layer. Subaponeurotic collections spread widely beneath the galea down to the zygoma and orbital margins.

Cephalhaematoma is subpericranial, limited by suture lines because the pericranium is bound into skull sutures.

teach.heading: Diagnostic differences among common scalp swellings
Cock peculiar tumour and malignant mimickers
teach.body:
When a neglected sebaceous cyst of the scalp suppurates and ulcerates, exuberant granulation tissue grows out through the ruptured wall. This creates a fleshy, vascular, fungating granulomatous mass known historically as Cock peculiar tumour.

Although it alarmingly mimics a fungating squamous cell carcinoma, the edges are rounded rather than everted, and regional cervical lymphadenopathy is absent unless secondary sepsis supervenes.

skill.exam.surg.facial_ulcer.title: Facial Ulcer Examination
skill.exam.surg.facial_ulcer.oneLine: Evaluating anatomical zone, margin, base induration, and facial nerve invasion to distinguish rodent ulcer from squamous cancer
skill.exam.surg.facial_ulcer.why: Ulcers on the face commonly represent cutaneous malignancies driven by cumulative ultraviolet solar radiation. Basal cell carcinoma (rodent ulcer) is locally invasive with a rolled, beaded edge and rarely metastasises, whereas squamous cell carcinoma produces an indurated everted edge with early regional lymph node metastasis. Mistaking one for the other leads to inadequate margins or unnecessary radical nodal dissections.

steps.text: Inspect the ulcer location relative to the facial embryological lines: note whether it lies above or below the line joining the angle of the mouth to the tragus of the ear.
Examine the margins and edge: inspect for a raised, pearly, rolled, beaded margin with telangiectatic vessels (basal cell carcinoma) versus a raised, ragged, everted margin (squamous cell carcinoma).
Inspect the floor and base: note whether the floor contains a dark crust covering shallow raw tissue or irregular necrotic slough with bloody discharge.
Put on clean gloves and palpate the edge and base: assess for true cartilaginous or stony induration, extending beyond the visible margin of the ulcer.
Test fixation to deep structures: gently test mobility of the ulcer over the underlying malar bone, nasal cartilage, mandible, or facial musculature.
Examine regional lymph node basins: systematically palpate the preauricular, parotid, submental, and submandibular lymph node groups.

skill.exam.surg.facial_ulcer.normal: Facial skin is smooth, intact, uniform in pigmentation, without ulcers, hyperkeratotic plaques, induration, or regional lymphadenopathy.
skill.exam.surg.facial_ulcer.abnormal: Ulcer with raised rolled pearly beaded edges, central scabbing, and absence of regional lymphadenopathy (basal cell carcinoma); ulcer with raised everted irregular edges, indurated base, and hard enlarged regional lymph nodes (squamous cell carcinoma); painless indurated nodule with clean shallow base (primary syphilitic chancre); chronic reddish-brown ulcer with soft gelatinous apple-jelly nodules on glass slide pressure (lupus vulgaris).
skill.exam.surg.facial_ulcer.significance: A rolled beaded edge above the mouth-tragus line indicates a basal cell carcinoma, which destroys tissue locally but does not metastasise via lymphatics, whereas an everted edge requires wide resection and lymph node evaluation.
skill.exam.surg.facial_ulcer.practice: Practise inspecting ulcer margins with magnification and palpating base induration between gloved index finger and thumb to detect deep tissue tethering.
pitfalls: Removing a facial ulcer crust forcibly without gloved protection, precipitating brisk bleeding from friable tumour vessels.
Assuming an ulcer near the medial canthus is benign because of its slow growth, missing deep orbital bone erosion.
Failing to examine the parotid and submandibular lymph nodes in any suspicious facial ulcer.

probes.q: What describes the characteristic edge of a rodent ulcer (basal cell carcinoma)?
probes.a: A raised, rolled, beaded, pearly edge with fine telangiectatic vessels.

probes.q: What anatomical line historically separates the typical predilection zone of rodent ulcer from squamous cell carcinoma on the face?
probes.a: The line joining the angle of the mouth to the tragus of the ear.

probes.q: Why does a neglected basal cell carcinoma at the medial canthus carry a grave surgical prognosis despite being histologically non-metastasising?
probes.a: It invades directly into the orbit, ethmoid sinus, and cribriform plate along embryonic fusion planes, threatening blindness and intracranial entry.

rubric.text: Correctly describes the ulcer edge as rolled/beaded versus everted
Palpates the base and edge with gloved hands to grade induration
Tests mobility of the ulcer over the underlying facial bones
Palpates the preauricular, parotid, and submandibular lymph node stations

teach.heading: Rodent ulcer versus squamous cell carcinoma of the face
Pathological behaviour of the rodent ulcer
teach.body:
Basal cell carcinoma originates from the basal layer of the epidermis or hair follicle outer root sheath. It grows slowly over years, ulcerating in the centre while advancing at the beaded periphery. It does not metastasise through lymphatics.

However, its name rodent ulcer reflects its gnawing destruction of muscle, cartilage, and bone if left untreated, particularly around the eye, nose, and ear.

teach.heading: The danger zone and embryonic fusion planes
teach.body:
Lesions situated along embryonic fusion lines, such as the nasolabial fold, medial canthus, and retroauricular sulcus, behave with heightened local aggressiveness.

In these clefts, tumour cells can track deeply into periosteum and perichondrium with silent microscopic spread far beyond the visible margins, requiring Mohs micrographic surgery or wide margins.

skill.exam.surg.maxilla.title: Maxilla and Upper Jaw Examination
skill.exam.surg.maxilla.oneLine: Systematic assessment of the five maxillary surfaces to detect silent antral tumours and facial fractures
skill.exam.surg.maxilla.why: The maxilla encloses the pyramidal maxillary antrum and presents five distinct anatomical surfaces: anterolateral, superior (orbital floor), inferior (palatal), medial (nasal), and posterior (infratemporal). Neoplasms of the maxillary sinus (squamous cell carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, ameloblastoma) grow silently until they erode through one of these bony boundaries. Failing to examine all five surfaces delays the diagnosis until advanced skull base invasion has occurred.

steps.text: Inspect facial symmetry and anterolateral surface: look for fullness of the cheek, obliteration of the nasolabial sulcus, evert the upper lip, and palpate the canine fossa and gingivolabial gutter for bony expansion or tenderness.

Examine the superior (orbital floor) surface: inspect each profile for proptosis or dystopia; palpate the inferior orbital margin for step deformity or loss of sharpness; test extraocular movements for upward diplopia; test sensation of the cheek and upper lip supplied by the infraorbital nerve.

Examine the inferior (palatine) surface: ask patient to open the mouth; inspect the hard palate for unilateral fullness, ulceration, or expansion; inspect the upper dentition for unprovoked loosening of premolar and molar teeth.

Examine the medial (nasal) surface: test nasal patency by occluding each nostril in turn while the patient exhales; perform anterior rhinoscopy to inspect the lateral nasal wall for medial bulging, polypoid tissue, or blood-stained purulent discharge; check for epiphora from nasolacrimal duct obstruction.

Palpate the posterior (infratemporal) extension: palpate high in the buccal sulcus behind the zygomaticomaxillary buttress; measure inter-incisal mouth opening to detect trismus from pterygoid muscle invasion.
Palpate the regional cervical lymph nodes: examine the submandibular and upper deep cervical lymph nodes for firm or hard metastatic enlargement.

skill.exam.surg.maxilla.normal: Symmetrical facial contour, sharp and continuous inferior orbital margins, normal eyeball position, intact sensation in the infraorbital nerve distribution, symmetrical hard palate, stable upper dentition, and clear bilateral nasal airways.
skill.exam.surg.maxilla.abnormal: Cheek swelling with loss of nasolabial fold (anterolateral wall erosion); upward displacement of eyeball with proptosis, diplopia, and infraorbital anaesthesia (superior wall erosion); unilateral bulging of the hard palate with loose molar teeth (inferior wall erosion); unilateral nasal blockage, epistaxis, and epiphora (medial wall erosion); trismus with infratemporal fullness (posterior wall invasion); hard fixed submandibular lymphadenopathy.
skill.exam.surg.maxilla.significance: Directional expansion of the maxillary walls maps the anatomical spread of maxillary sinus carcinoma (Ohngren line of malignancy), distinguishing resectable infrastructure lesions from aggressive suprastructure tumours.
skill.exam.surg.maxilla.practice: Rehearse inspecting and palpating each of the five maxillary walls in sequence: facial contour, orbital rim with sensation, hard palate with teeth, nasal patency, and pterygoid/infratemporal fossa with mouth opening.
pitfalls: Extracting a loose upper molar tooth without examining the hard palate and antrum, which can create an oroantral fistula into a fungating maxillary carcinoma.
Attributing unilateral epistaxis and epiphora in an older adult to chronic rhinitis without inspecting the lateral nasal wall and orbital floor.
Failing to test cutaneous sensation over the cheek and upper lip, missing early infraorbital nerve entrapment by an orbital floor tumour.

probes.q: What cranial nerve sensory branch is commonly compromised when a maxillary antral tumour invades the orbital floor?
probes.a: The infraorbital nerve (branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, CN V2).

probes.q: What physical signs indicate that a maxillary tumour has breached its medial wall into the nasal cavity?
probes.a: Unilateral nasal obstruction, blood-stained nasal discharge (epistaxis), and epiphora due to nasolacrimal duct blockage.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of trismus in a patient presenting with an upper jaw swelling?
probes.a: It indicates posterior extension of the tumour into the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae with direct infiltration of the pterygoid muscles.

rubric.text: Examines all five surfaces of the maxilla (facial, orbital, palatal, nasal, posterior)
Tests sensory integrity in the infraorbital nerve distribution
Inspects the hard palate and checks for loose molar and premolar teeth
Tests nasal patency and checks for blood-stained discharge or epiphora

teach.heading: The five surfaces of the maxilla and their clinical signs
Ohngren classification of maxillary sinus carcinoma
teach.body:
Ohngren line is an imaginary plane extending from the medial canthus of the eye to the angle of the mandible. It divides the maxillary antrum into an anteroinferior infrastructure and a posterosuperior suprastructure.

Infrastructure tumours present with cheek or palatal swellings and carry a relatively favourable prognosis. Suprastructure tumours erode into the orbit, ethmoids, and pterygopalatine fossa, carrying a high rate of recurrence and poor survival.

teach.heading: Differentiating antral empyema from neoplasia
teach.body:
Acute empyema of the maxillary antrum causes marked tenderness over the cheek and unilateral foul purulent nasal discharge, but without bony expansion or facial deformity.

When bony expansion, egg-shell crackling, loose teeth, or cranial nerve deficit supervenes, the diagnosis is an expanding lesion: dentigerous cyst, ameloblastoma, or antral carcinoma.

skill.exam.surg.mandible.title: Mandible and Lower Jaw Examination
skill.exam.surg.mandible.oneLine: Bimanual palpation of internal and external cortices, dental alignment, and signs of fracture and odontogenic cysts
skill.exam.surg.mandible.why: The mandible is a subcutaneous horseshoe bone whose mucoperiosteum is tightly adherent to the alveolus, making virtually all fractures compound into the oral cavity. Odontogenic cysts, ameloblastomas, and fibro-osseous lesions cause insidious expansion of the outer and inner cortical plates. Bimanual palpation (one finger in the mouth and fingers outside) is mandatory to assess cortical destruction, egg-shell crackling, and dental alignment.

steps.text: Inspect facial contour from front, sides, and above: assess lower jaw symmetry, chin alignment, swelling over the body, angle, or ramus, and skin bruising or sinuses.
Inspect the oral cavity: assess dental occlusion, alignment of the dental arch, gaps between teeth, sublingual haematoma in the mouth floor, and blood-stained saliva.

Palpate the external lower border: trace the continuous bony rim from the symphysis menti along the body, angle, and posterior ramus to the condyle on each side, noting localized tenderness or step deformities.

Perform bimanual palpation: insert a gloved index finger into the buccal and lingual sulci while placing fingers of the opposite hand externally beneath the lower border, palpating the inner and outer cortical plates simultaneously.
Test for cortical thinning and egg-shell crackling: apply gentle pressure with the thumb over the most prominent part of any bony swelling to elicit yielding of paper-thin bone.
Palpate the mental nerve sensation and cervical lymph nodes: test touch and pinprick over the chin and lower lip; examine submental and submandibular lymph nodes.

skill.exam.surg.mandible.normal: Mandible is symmetrical, continuous, and non-tender from condyle to symphysis; dental occlusion is anatomical without gaps; no step deformity, egg-shell crackling, sublingual haematoma, or mental nerve hypoaesthesia.
skill.exam.surg.mandible.abnormal: Step deformity along lower border or alveolar ridge with malocclusion, sublingual ecchymosis, and mobile bone fragments (mandibular fracture); slow-growing expansile bone swelling with egg-shell crackling and honeycomb radiolucency (ameloblastoma / adamantinoma); smooth swelling associated with a missing permanent tooth (dentigerous cyst); tender fluctuant alveolar swelling with carious tooth (alveolar abscess); mental nerve anaesthesia (Vincent sign in mandibular osteomyelitis or malignancy).
skill.exam.surg.mandible.significance: Detects compound mandibular fractures requiring immediate stabilization and distinguishes benign dental cysts from locally invasive ameloblastoma, which demands segmental resection.
skill.exam.surg.mandible.practice: Practise bimanual palpation of the mandible on a peer, palpating the lingual plate internally while supporting the inferior border externally to trace the entire body and angle.
pitfalls: Failing to look for a sublingual haematoma Coleman sign in a suspected mandibular trauma, which confirms a compound fracture through the lingual cortex.
Pressing vigorously on an expansile jaw swelling with egg-shell crackling, causing painful cortical fracture.
Missing a bilateral fracture (parasymphyseal plus contralateral condyle) by stopping after finding the first fracture site.

probes.q: Why are fractures of the body of the mandible almost always compound?
probes.a: Because the gingival mucoperiosteum is tightly adherent to the underlying alveolar bone and tears when the bone fragments displace.

probes.q: What physical sensation on palpation indicates that an ameloblastoma or dentigerous cyst has thinned the outer mandibular cortex to parchment thickness?
probes.a: Egg-shell crackling (parchment-like yielding of thinned subperiosteal bone under finger pressure).

probes.q: What clinical sign in the mouth floor strongly indicates an unsuspected fracture of the mandibular body following blunt facial trauma?
probes.a: A sublingual haematoma (Coleman sign) caused by rupture of the lingual mucoperiosteum.

rubric.text: Performs gloved bimanual palpation of both the inner and outer mandibular surfaces
Inspects dental occlusion and traces the continuous inferior border for step deformity
Palpates expansile swellings gently for egg-shell crackling
Tests mental nerve sensation over the chin and lower lip

teach.heading: Odontogenic swellings and cysts of the mandible
Fracture patterns of the mandible
teach.body:
The mandible behaves like an arch: direct force frequently causes fractures at two sites, one at the point of impact and another contralaterally where indirect tensile strain peaks.

The canine region is inherently vulnerable because the deep socket of the canine tooth reduces bone mass. When examining trauma, finding a fracture in the mental area demands careful palpation of the contralateral condyle and vice versa.

teach.heading: Epulis: swellings upon the gum
teach.body:
An epulis is any discrete swelling arising from the gingiva or underlying alveolar periosteum.

Fibrous epulis is a benign, firm, slow-growing pedunculated mass from the periodontal membrane. Giant cell epulis (myelomatous epulis) is soft, purple-red, bleeds readily, and occurs in young adults. Carcinomatous epulis represents squamous cell carcinoma ulcerating and eroding bone.
