skill.exam.surg.tmj_trismus.title: Temporomandibular Joint and Trismus Examination
skill.exam.surg.tmj_trismus.oneLine: Measuring inter-incisal distance, palpating condylar translation, and separating true ankylosis from muscular trismus
skill.exam.surg.tmj_trismus.why: Restricted mouth opening impairs nutrition, speech, dental hygiene, and emergency airway access. The clinician must differentiate true joint pathology (articular disc displacement, osteoarthritis, fibrous or bony ankylosis) from extra-articular reflex muscular spasm (trismus) caused by impacted third molar pericoronitis, periapical abscess, quinsy, parotitis, oral submucous fibrosis, or systemic tetanus (risus sardonicus).

steps.text: Measure maximum inter-incisal mouth opening using a millimeter ruler or fingers breadth test: record the distance between the cutting edges of upper and lower central incisors (normal 35-50 mm, or at least three fingers breadths).

Palpate the condyles externally: place index finger pulps over the temporomandibular joints immediately anterior to the tragus on both sides while the patient opens and closes the mouth; note tenderness, swelling, and symmetry of condylar movement.

Palpate condylar translation via the external auditory canal: place the pulps of both little fingers into the external auditory meati facing forwards; feel the condyles glide forwards during opening and return backwards during closure.

Auscultate the joint during movement: place the bell of the stethoscope over the condyle; listen for a sharp click (internal derangement / displaced articular disc) or dry grating crepitus (osteoarthritis).
Observe mandibular excursion path: watch the chin during opening; note whether the jaw deviates to one side (deviates towards the affected side in unilateral disc displacement or ankylosis).

Examine for extra-articular causes of trismus: inspect for an impacted third molar with pericoronal inflammation, dental abscess, peritonsillar swelling (quinsy), blanching and fibrous bands in the cheek (oral submucous fibrosis), or generalized tetanic rigidity.

skill.exam.surg.tmj_trismus.normal: Inter-incisal opening 35-50 mm (at least 3 fingers breadths); smooth, symmetrical condylar translation palpable in preauricular region and external meatus without click, crepitus, pain, or lateral deviation.
skill.exam.surg.tmj_trismus.abnormal: Severe limitation of opening < 20 mm; audible or palpable clicking during jaw opening that disappears after clicking into place (anterior disc displacement with reduction); coarse dry crepitus with preauricular tenderness (temporomandibular osteoarthritis); complete immobility of the joint with jaw fixed (true bony or fibrous ankylosis); painful acute spasm with normal condylar anatomy (trismus due to pericoronitis or peritonsillar infection); tonic facial spasm with risus sardonicus (tetanus).
skill.exam.surg.tmj_trismus.significance: Separates true intra-articular pathology requiring joint arthroplasty or splints from extra-articular dental/pharyngeal sepsis or systemic tetanus requiring specific medical management.
skill.exam.surg.tmj_trismus.practice: Practise measuring inter-incisal opening with three vertical fingers on peers, and palpate the forward condylar translation using little finger pulps in the external auditory canals.
pitfalls: Attempting forceful mechanical jaw opening with a wedge in an acutely trismic patient, which can cause severe pain, muscle tearing, or trigger generalized tetanic convulsions.
Attributing chronic painless limitation of mouth opening in an Indian tobacco/supari chewer to TMJ disease rather than oral submucous fibrosis.
Missing unilateral condylar dislocation where the jaw is fixed open and deviated towards the opposite side.

probes.q: What is the normal inter-incisal distance during maximum mouth opening in a healthy adult?
probes.a: Between 35 and 50 millimetres, or the width of three fingers breadths placed vertically.

probes.q: How does the clinician verify symmetrical forward movement of the mandibular condyles during jaw opening?
probes.a: By placing the pulps of the little fingers into the external auditory canals facing forwards and feeling the condylar heads translate.

probes.q: In a unilateral dislocation of the temporomandibular joint, to which side does the chin deviate, and what is palpable behind the condyle?
probes.a: The chin deviates towards the opposite (unaffected) side, and an empty hollow is palpable immediately behind the dislocated condyle.

rubric.text: Measures the maximal inter-incisal distance accurately in millimetres or finger breadths
Performs condylar palpation via the external auditory canals during opening and closing
Auscultates the joint for clicking or crepitus
Inspects for oral sepsis, erupting third molars, and fibrous bands

teach.heading: True ankylosis versus false ankylosis and trismus
Internal derangement and clicking jaw
teach.body:
The temporomandibular joint contains a fibrocartilaginous biconcave meniscus attached to the lateral pterygoid muscle. Internal derangement typically involves anterior displacement of this articular disc.

On opening the mouth, the condyle rides over the posterior ridge of the displaced disc with a sharp, audible click (reduction). On full closure, the disc slips anteriorly again with a reciprocal click.

teach.heading: Risus sardonicus in tetanus
teach.body:
Tetanus produces sustained hypertonia of the facial and masticatory muscles due to tetanospasmin blocking inhibitory neurotransmitters.

Trismus (lockjaw) is typically the earliest symptom, accompanied by sustained retraction of the angles of the mouth and elevation of the eyebrows, producing the sardonic smile of risus sardonicus.

skill.hx.surg.oral_malignancy.title: Oral Cavity Malignancy History
skill.hx.surg.oral_malignancy.oneLine: Eliciting tobacco, supari, and gutka exposure, painless non-healing ulcer, referred otalgia, and salivation
skill.hx.surg.oral_malignancy.why: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity is an epidemic malignancy in India and South Asia, heavily driven by smokeless tobacco, betel quid (pan), areca nut (supari), gutka, and khaini. Patients present late because early cancerous ulcers and erythroplakia are painless. Identifying risk exposure, temporal progression, referred otalgia, speech changes, and excessive salivation establishes early suspicion before irresectable mandibular invasion occurs.

asks.text: When did you first notice the sore, ulcer, or lump in your mouth, and how has it changed over weeks and months?
Do you chew betel quid (pan), supari (areca nut), gutka, pan masala, or khaini, and do you keep the quid tucked in your cheek pouch during the day or overnight? For how many years?
Do you smoke bidis, cigarettes, cigars, or hookahs, or consume spirits? Calculate bidi or cigarette pack-years.
Was the ulcer painless when it first appeared, and has it become painful recently? A painless chronic ulcer in an older adult is highly suspicious of malignancy.
Do you experience pain shooting or radiating to your ear on the same side (referred otalgia via the lingual and auriculotemporal or glossopharyngeal nerves)?
Have you noticed excessive salivation, difficulty in speaking, painful swallowing, or difficulty sticking your tongue out?
Have you noticed any lump beneath your jaw or in your neck?

skill.hx.surg.oral_malignancy.practice: Rehearse taking a structured oral cavity risk history from a peer, specifically probing for smokeless tobacco types (gutka, khaini, pan with lime) and duration in years.
pitfalls: Accepting 'I do not smoke' without specifically asking about smokeless tobacco, betel quid, supari, and khaini, which are the primary drivers in South Asia.
Reassuring a patient because an oral ulcer is painless; painlessness is characteristic of early malignancy, whereas pain develops only in advanced infiltration or secondary sepsis.
Ignoring earache in a heavy tobacco user whose otoscopy is normal, missing referred pain from an occult carcinoma of the tongue base or tonsillar pillar.

probes.q: Why is early squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue or cheek frequently overlooked by patients?
probes.a: Because in its early stages the ulcer or nodule is entirely painless and causes no functional impairment.

probes.q: Explain the neural pathway causing referred ear pain (referred otalgia) in carcinoma of the oral tongue.
probes.a: Sensory irritation of the lingual nerve (branch of CN V3) is referred to the auriculotemporal nerve (also CN V3) supplying the pinna and external auditory meatus.

probes.q: Why does an elderly patient with carcinoma of the tongue frequently present holding a handkerchief to the mouth?
probes.a: Due to profuse salivation from taste and sensory nerve irritation, compounded by ankyloglossia and dysphagia preventing normal swallowing of saliva.

rubric.text: Quantifies smokeless tobacco, supari, gutka, and bidi/cigarette exposure
Inquires whether the initial lesion was painless or painful
Specifically asks about pain referred to the ipsilateral ear
Asks about speech changes, salivation, tongue mobility, and neck lumps

teach.heading: The epidemiology of oral cancer in the Indian subcontinent
teach.body:
Oral cancer ranks among the top three malignancies in India. The dominant aetiology is the habitual placement of betel quid with slaked lime, tobacco, and areca nut in the gingivobuccal sulcus (the Indian gutter).

Areca nut contains arecoline, which stimulates fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition, while tobacco-specific nitrosamines cause cellular dysplasia, driving progression from submucous fibrosis and leukoplakia to squamous carcinoma.

teach.heading: Clinical presentations of carcinoma of the tongue

rows: Slow infiltration, less early nodal spread
Diffuse woody induration of entire body

teach.heading: Referred otalgia: the anatomy of diagnostic error
teach.body:
Ear pain with a normal eardrum is known as referred otalgia. The tongue and oral floor are supplied by the lingual nerve (CN V3), while the posterior third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

Both nerves share central sensory pathways with nerves supplying the ear: the auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3) and Jacobson nerve (CN IX). An earache in an adult tobacco user demands thorough oral and hypopharyngeal examination.

skill.exam.surg.tongue_ulcer.title: Tongue Ulcer Examination
skill.exam.surg.tongue_ulcer.oneLine: Inspect at rest and palpate with relaxed tongue to detect true malignant induration
skill.exam.surg.tongue_ulcer.why: Carcinoma of the tongue most often arises on the lateral margin of the anterior two-thirds. The cardinal physical sign of malignancy is induration of the ulcer base and margins. If the examiner palpates while the tongue is protruded, the contracted lingual musculature creates false induration, leading to serious diagnostic error. Palpation must be performed bidigitally with the tongue completely relaxed within the mouth.

steps.text: Inspect the mouth and tongue in good light: note the ulcer site (lateral border, tip, dorsum, ventral surface), size, shape, and margins (everted and raised vs clean-cut vs punched out).
Inspect the floor and base: note whether the floor contains grey necrotic slough, red granulation tissue, or a clean surface; observe for contact bleeding.
Inspect the opposing dentition: check whether a jagged, sharp, carious tooth or fractured denture clasp impinges directly against the ulcer (traumatic dental ulcer).

Prepare for palpation: explain the manoeuvre, put on clean gloves, and instruct the patient to relax the tongue completely on the floor of the mouth; DO NOT permit the patient to keep the tongue protruded.

Perform bidigital palpation of the ulcer: grasp the lateral margin with gloved index finger on the ulcer and thumb on the ventral tongue or cheek; assess true cartilaginous or stony induration extending beyond the visible ulcer border.
Palpate bilateral cervical lymph node basins: examine submental, submandibular, jugulodigastric, and jugulo-omohyoid groups, remembering that lymphatic vessels decussate across the midline.

skill.exam.surg.tongue_ulcer.normal: Tongue surface is pink and papillated; margins are smooth and soft; no ulcers, fissures, induration, contact bleeding, or palpable cervical lymph nodes.
skill.exam.surg.tongue_ulcer.abnormal: Ulcer on lateral margin with raised everted edges, necrotic slough on floor, marked stony induration of base, and bleeding on touch (squamous cell carcinoma); painful shallow ulcer with soft base opposite a sharp tooth (dental ulcer); small painful yellow-based ulcer with red hyperaemic halo (aphthous ulcer); painless punched-out midline dorsum ulcer with wash-leather slough (syphilitic gumma); extremely painful shallow multiple ulcers with undermined edges in pulmonary tuberculosis (tuberculous ulcer).
skill.exam.surg.tongue_ulcer.significance: Stony hard induration at the base and everted edges are pathognomonic of squamous cell carcinoma, requiring incisional wedge biopsy. A dental ulcer resolves within 10-14 days of smoothing the offending tooth.
skill.exam.surg.tongue_ulcer.practice: Practise palpating the lateral border of the tongue on a model: first with tongue protruded (observing false firmness) and then with tongue relaxed within the oral cavity (verifying true muscular suppleness).
pitfalls: Palpating an ulcer while the tongue is protruded, mistaking active contraction of the genioglossus and superior longitudinal muscles for malignant induration.
Diagnosing a traumatic dental ulcer and continuing to observe it beyond two weeks when it fails to heal after extraction or filing of the offending tooth.
Palpating only the ipsilateral neck nodes, forgetting that lingual lymphatics decussate and readily metastasise to contralateral jugulodigastric nodes.

probes.q: Why must the tongue be resting inside the mouth rather than protruded when testing an ulcer for induration?
probes.a: Because contracted lingual muscles during protrusion feel firm and give a false impression of induration.

probes.q: What physical features distinguish a traumatic dental ulcer from a carcinomatous ulcer of the tongue?
probes.a: A dental ulcer has soft unindurated edges, is located opposite a sharp tooth, and heals promptly after dental treatment, whereas a cancer has everted indurated edges and bleeds easily.

probes.q: Why is examination of both sides of the neck mandatory even when a tongue carcinoma is strictly unilateral?
probes.a: Because lymphatic vessels from the tongue decussate across the midline, allowing unilateral tumours to produce bilateral or contralateral nodal metastases.

rubric.text: Ensures the tongue is relaxed inside the mouth before palpating the ulcer
Performs gloved bidigital palpation of the ulcer base and edges to assess induration
Inspects the adjacent teeth for jagged edges or ill-fitting dentures
Palpates cervical lymph nodes bilaterally across all jugular stations

teach.heading: Diagnostic differences among common tongue ulcers
The anatomical decussation of lingual lymphatics
teach.body:
The lymphatic drainage of the tongue follows a strict anatomical pattern. The tip drains to submental nodes and jugulo-omohyoid nodes. The lateral margins drain to submandibular and upper deep cervical nodes.

Crucially, lymphatic vessels from the dorsum and central musculature freely cross the median fibrous septum. As a result, midline and marginal tumours frequently metastasise to contralateral cervical nodes.

teach.heading: The danger of delayed biopsy in non-healing oral ulcers
teach.body:
Any solitary ulcer of the oral mucosa or tongue that persists for more than two weeks without clear evidence of healing requires incisional biopsy.

Extracting an offending sharp tooth is appropriate initial management for suspected trauma, but if the ulcer does not visibly heal within 10 to 14 days, malignancy must be assumed until histological proof is obtained.

skill.exam.surg.tongue_mobility.title: Tongue Mobility and Hypoglossal Nerve Examination
skill.exam.surg.tongue_mobility.oneLine: Protrusion excursion, lateral deviation, frenulum assessment, and floor-of-mouth tethering
skill.exam.surg.tongue_mobility.why: Testing tongue mobility assesses the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and extrinsic lingual muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus). In oral malignancy, inability to protrude the tongue or deviation towards the lesion indicates deep invasion of the genioglossus or floor of the mouth (ankyloglossia), upstaging the tumour to T3/T4 and altering the surgical approach. In children, a tight lingual frenulum restricts speech and dentition.

steps.text: Inspect the tongue at rest on the floor of the mouth: observe symmetry, muscle bulk, lateral furrowing, and visible fasciculations or hemiatrophy.
Instruct the patient to protrude the tongue straight out: observe the extent of excursion beyond the lower incisors and lower lip vermilion.
Assess midline deviation on protrusion: note whether the tongue tip stays in the midline or deviates towards one side (deviates towards the side of hypoglossal paralysis or tumour infiltration).
Test rapid lateral movements: ask the patient to move the tongue tip briskly from one corner of the mouth to the other, and to lick the upper and lower lips.

Inspect the ventral surface and lingual frenulum: ask patient to touch the roof of the mouth with the tongue tip; inspect for a tight, thick, short frenulum with anterior notched tethering (tongue-tie).
Gloved palpation of the tongue root and floor of the mouth: palpate the base of the tongue bidigitally to assess woody muscular fixation to the hyoid bone or mandible.

skill.exam.surg.tongue_mobility.normal: Tongue protrudes straight in the midline well past the lower lip; rapid, symmetrical lateral excursions; full elevation of the tip to the incisive papilla; supple lingual musculature without fasciculations, atrophy, or tethering.
skill.exam.surg.tongue_mobility.abnormal: Tip deviates to the affected side on protrusion (lower motor neuron hypoglossal palsy or unilateral genioglossus tumour infiltration); inability to protrude tongue past lower teeth with heart-shaped apical notch (ankyloglossia / tongue-tie); total immobility with tongue fixed to mouth floor and mandible ('frozen tongue' in advanced carcinoma); unilateral muscle wasting with fibrillary tremors (hypoglossal nerve injury).
skill.exam.surg.tongue_mobility.significance: Deviation towards a lesion indicates either destructive hypoglossal nerve involvement or direct extrinsic muscle infiltration. In oral cancer, deep muscle fixation signals advanced disease requiring composite mandibulolingual resection.
skill.exam.surg.tongue_mobility.practice: Rehearse testing tongue protrusion, lateral wagging, and lingual frenulum inspection on a peer, noting normal excursion 2 to 3 cm beyond the lower lip.
pitfalls: Failing to look at the tongue at rest on the mouth floor, missing fasciculations that disappear once active protrusion begins.
Confusing deviation caused by unilateral facial palsy (mouth asymmetry) with true hypoglossal tongue deviation; align the tongue against the central incisors, not the lips.
Assuming an inability to protrude the tongue in an elderly patient is congenital tongue-tie rather than advanced malignant infiltration of the floor of the mouth.

probes.q: When a patient with a unilateral hypoglossal nerve injury protrudes the tongue, to which side does the tip deviate?
probes.a: Towards the paralyzed (affected) side, pushed across by the unopposed contralateral genioglossus muscle.

probes.q: What congenital anomaly causes impaired speech and inability to protrude the tongue past the incisors in a child?
probes.a: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) caused by an abnormally short, thick lingual frenulum.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a 'frozen tongue' (inability to protrude or move the tongue) in an adult with an oral ulcer?
probes.a: It indicates extensive infiltration of the extrinsic tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus) and floor of the mouth, denoting advanced (T4) carcinoma.

rubric.text: Inspects the tongue at rest on the mouth floor for atrophy and fasciculations
Evaluates protrusion distance and checks for lateral deviation against incisors
Inspects the ventral surface and lingual frenulum with the tip elevated
Palpates the base and floor of the mouth to rule out muscular tumour tethering

teach.heading: The action of the genioglossus and mechanism of deviation
teach.body:
The genioglossus is the safety muscle of the tongue, arising from the superior mental spine of the mandible and fanning out into the lingual body. Its contraction pulls the tongue root forwards, protruding the tip out of the mouth.

When one hypoglossal nerve or one genioglossus is paralyzed or destroyed by tumour, the healthy contralateral muscle protrudes unopposed, pivoting the tip towards the weak side.

teach.heading: Malignant ankyloglossia as a surgical staging marker
teach.body:
In oral oncology, restriction of tongue mobility is a grave physical finding. While early superficial mucosal carcinomas remain mobile, invasion into the intrinsic and extrinsic musculature limits protrusion.

Fixation to the floor of the mouth or mandible upstages the cancer to T4 disease, mandating en bloc resection (commando operation) rather than partial glossectomy.

skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.title: Buccal Mucosa and Premalignant Lesions Examination
skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.oneLine: Retraction, bidigital palpation, Stensen orifice inspection, leukoplakia, and submucous fibrosis bands
skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.why: Carcinoma of the buccal mucosa accounts for the majority of oral cancers in India due to habitual betel quid and gutka placement in the gingivobuccal sulcus. Premalignant conditions like leukoplakia, erythroplakia, and oral submucous fibrosis (OSF) precede invasive carcinoma. A thorough examination requires full-thickness bidigital palpation of the cheek and measurement of mouth opening to detect early fibrosis and malignant infiltration.

steps.text: Retract the cheek with a wooden spatula or cheek retractor in good daylight or torchlight; inspect the entire buccal mucosa from the labial commissure to the anterior faucial pillar and retromolar trigone.
Inspect the gingivobuccal gutters: systematically look into the upper and lower sulci where tobacco quids are held, checking for erosion, white patches, or warty exophytic lesions.
Locate and inspect the parotid (Stensen's) duct orifice: identify the mucosal papilla opposite the crown of the upper second molar; inspect for erythema, stones, or ulceration.

Evaluate mucosal colour and texture: inspect for chronic blanched, pale, marble-like mucosa with loss of elasticity (oral submucous fibrosis), thick white non-scrapable plaques (leukoplakia), or fiery red velvety areas (erythroplakia).

Perform bidigital palpation: wearing clean gloves, place the index finger inside the cheek and the thumb or opposing fingers on the external skin; palpate the full thickness of the cheek muscle and skin for induration, lumps, or fibrous bands.

Palpate vertical fibrous bands in oral submucous fibrosis: sweep the intraoral finger along the pterygomandibular raphe and anterior cheek; note tough, blanching fibrous bands and quantify inter-incisal distance.

skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.normal: Buccal mucosa is pink, moist, smooth, supple, and elastic; Stensen's papilla is clean without erythema; no white patches, red velvety plaques, palpable fibrous bands, or cheek induration.
skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.abnormal: Firm, blanched, leathery mucosa with tough vertical fibrous bands and progressive trismus (oral submucous fibrosis); adherent, raised, cracked white plaque that cannot be scraped off (leukoplakia); fiery red velvety plaque with distinct margins (erythroplakia); indurated ulcer with everted margins in the lower gingivobuccal gutter (buccal carcinoma); soft, painless, bluish translucent fluctuant cyst on inner lip (mucous retention cyst).
skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.significance: Identifies high-risk premalignant lesions (erythroplakia carries up to 90% dysplasia/malignancy rate; oral submucous fibrosis carries a 7-8% malignant transformation rate) and detects early invasive carcinoma of the cheek.
skill.exam.surg.buccal_mucosa.practice: Practise retracting both cheeks with wooden spatulas, inspecting Stensen's papilla opposite the upper second molar, and performing full-thickness bidigital palpation on a peer.
pitfalls: Attempting to scrape off an oral white lesion with a spatula, mistaking candidiasis (which rubs off, leaving a raw bleeding base) for leukoplakia (which does not scrape off).
Inspecting only the central cheek, missing early ulcerative carcinomas hiding deep in the lower gingivobuccal sulcus or retromolar trigone.
Failing to palpate the cheek bidigitally, missing early submucosal induration when the surface epithelium appears minimally altered.

probes.q: What physical characteristic distinguishes oral leukoplakia from oral pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush)?
probes.a: Leukoplakia cannot be scraped off with a wooden spatula or gauze, whereas candidal pseudomembranes rub off easily leaving an erythematous base.

probes.q: What are the hallmark examination findings of oral submucous fibrosis (OSF) in the buccal mucosa?
probes.a: Blanching of the mucosa with a marble-like appearance, palpable tough vertical fibrous bands, and progressive reduction in mouth opening (trismus).

probes.q: Between oral leukoplakia and erythroplakia, which lesion carries a significantly higher risk of severe epithelial dysplasia or invasive carcinoma on biopsy?
probes.a: Erythroplakia, with histological dysplasia or invasive carcinoma present in up to 85 to 90 percent of cases.

rubric.text: Retracts cheeks fully to inspect the gingivobuccal sulci and retromolar trigone
Identifies the Stensen duct orifice opposite the crown of the upper second molar
Performs gloved bidigital palpation assessing full cheek thickness
Palpates for vertical fibrous bands and records maximum inter-incisal opening

teach.heading: Clinical spectrum of oral premalignant lesions

rows: White plaque, cannot be scraped off

teach.heading: Oral submucous fibrosis: pathogenesis and staging
teach.body:
Oral submucous fibrosis is a chronic progressive fibrosing disease of the oral cavity and oropharynx, triggered primarily by chewing areca nut (supari, gutka).

Flavonoids and copper in areca nut stimulate collagen synthesis while inhibiting collagenase. The mucosa loses its vascularity and turns leathery white, with dense fibrous bands in the cheeks, soft palate, and uvula, severely restricting mouth opening.

teach.heading: The Five 'S' risk factors of oral leukoplakia
teach.body:
Historically and clinically, five chronic irritants predispose to leukoplakia and carcinoma of the cheek: Smoking (bidis and cigarettes), Smokeless tobacco (gutka and khaini), Spirits (concentrated alcohol), Spices (pungent dietary chillies), and Sepsis (dental caries and sharp teeth).

Eliminating these irritants is the essential first step before considering biopsy or surgical excision.

skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.title: Floor of Mouth Examination
skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.oneLine: Bimanual palpation of the sublingual space, Wharton ducts, ranula, and signs of Ludwig angina
skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.why: The floor of the mouth is a critical anatomical crossroad bounded by the mandible, tongue root, and mylohyoid diaphragm. Lesions here (ranula, plunging ranula, sublingual dermoid, carcinoma, and calculus in Wharton's duct) can extend into the neck or elevate the tongue. In acute cellulitis (Ludwig's angina), bilateral sublingual and submandibular suppuration rapidly pushes the tongue against the palate, threatening immediate asphyxiation.

steps.text: Ask patient to open the mouth wide and elevate the tongue tip to touch the roof of the palate: thoroughly inspect the sublingual space in good light.
Inspect the sublingual caruncles and Wharton's duct orifices on either side of the lingual frenulum: observe for erythema, swelling, or an impacted yellow calculus.

Inspect for cystic swellings in the sublingual fold: note colour and position: a unilateral bluish translucent cyst pushing the tongue upwards is a ranula; a midline yellowish-white opaque doughy cyst is a sublingual dermoid.

Perform bimanual palpation: insert a gloved index finger into the mouth floor lateral to the tongue and place fingers of the opposite hand beneath the jaw in the submandibular/submental region; palpate between the two hands.

Test for cross-fluctuation in plunging ranula: press firmly on the sublingual intraoral component while palpating the cervical submandibular mass with the external hand; feel fluid transmit directly between mouth and neck.

Examine for Ludwig's angina in acute infections: inspect for marked elevation of the tongue, inability to swallow saliva, stridor, and palpate for tense, tender, brawny, woody induration of the submental and submandibular triangles.

skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.normal: Floor of the mouth is soft, symmetrical, and non-tender; sublingual folds are flat and pink; Wharton's duct orifices are patent without erythema or discharge; no palpable sublingual cysts, salivary stones, or cervical masses.
skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.abnormal: Unilateral bluish translucent fluctuant cyst in the sublingual space beneath Wharton's duct (ranula); cross-fluctuant cystic mass between sublingual space and submandibular neck triangle (plunging ranula); midline doughy non-translucent cystic mass above or below mylohyoid (sublingual dermoid); hard indurated ulcer tethered to lingual aspect of mandible (carcinoma of floor of mouth); board-like, woody, non-fluctuant swelling of bilateral submandibular and sublingual spaces elevating the tongue with impending airway occlusion (Ludwig's angina).
skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.significance: Differentiates superficial retention cysts from plunging ranulas and sublingual dermoids, and identifies Ludwig's angina as an acute surgical airway emergency requiring urgent tracheostomy and decompression.
skill.exam.surg.floor_of_mouth.practice: Practise inspecting Wharton's duct papillae with tongue elevated and performing bimanual palpation of the sublingual space between an intraoral index finger and external submandibular fingers.
pitfalls: Mistaking a plunging ranula for a branchial cyst or cold abscess, because the cervical component in the submandibular triangle is far more obvious than the intraoral component.
Waiting for fluctuation before diagnosing Ludwig's angina; the dense deep cervical fascia produces woody board-like induration without early fluctuant pus.
Aspirating a sublingual dermoid or ranula in the clinic, introducing secondary infection into the sublingual space.

probes.q: What is the characteristic clinical appearance of a simple ranula in the floor of the mouth?
probes.a: A unilateral, bluish, translucent, thin-walled cystic swelling resembling a frog's belly, situated lateral to the lingual frenulum.

probes.q: How does the clinician confirm that a neck swelling in the submandibular triangle is a plunging ranula?
probes.a: By demonstrating bimanual cross-fluctuation between the intraoral sublingual swelling and the cervical submandibular mass.

probes.q: What is the primary cause of death in untreated Ludwig's angina, and what physical sign indicates impending disaster?
probes.a: Asphyxiation from acute airway obstruction; indicated by elevation and backward displacement of the tongue against the palate, with stridor and inability to swallow secretions.

rubric.text: Inspects the floor of the mouth with the tongue tip actively elevated against the palate
Examines Wharton's duct orifices and sublingual folds bilaterally
Performs bimanual palpation between an intraoral finger and an external submental/submandibular hand
Evaluates for tongue displacement and woody induration of Ludwig's angina

teach.heading: Cystic swellings of the floor of the mouth

rows: Floor of mouth and submandibular neck

teach.heading: The anatomy of plunging ranula
teach.body:
A ranula is a mucus extravasation pseudocyst arising from the sublingual salivary gland following ductal rupture. When the cyst enlarges, it can herniate through a natural defect or perforation in the mylohyoid muscle.

Once through the mylohyoid, it expands freely into the loose fascial space of the submandibular triangle, presenting as a soft cervical mass with an intraoral tail.

teach.heading: Ludwig's angina: the surgical anatomy of rapid suffocation
teach.body:
Ludwig's angina is a rapidly spreading, bilateral cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental fascial spaces, typically originating from an infected lower second or third molar.

The unyielding deep cervical fascia holds inflammatory exudate under intense pressure, pushing the floor of the mouth and tongue upwards and backwards against the posterior pharyngeal wall, producing lethal asphyxia.

skill.hx.surg.salivary_swelling.title: Salivary Gland Swelling History
skill.hx.surg.salivary_swelling.oneLine: Differentiating mealtime salivary colic, slow-growing pleomorphic adenoma, and rapid malignant growth
skill.hx.surg.salivary_swelling.why: Salivary gland disorders have distinctive clinical tempos. Swelling and acute pain triggered specifically by the sight, smell, or ingestion of food indicate mechanical duct obstruction (sialolithiasis). A painless, slow-growing lump present for years is the hallmark of a pleomorphic adenoma. Sudden acceleration of growth, onset of continuous pain, skin ulceration, or facial muscle weakness in a longstanding lump signals malignant transformation (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma).

asks.text: When was the lump first noticed, where exactly did it start, and how has its size changed over months or years?
Does the swelling suddenly enlarge, become tense, and ache during meals, particularly when eating tart or spicy foods (mealtime syndrome)?
Has a longstanding, slow-growing lump recently started enlarging rapidly or become continuously painful?
What type of pain do you feel: throbbing (acute parotid abscess), colicky with food (calculus), or a constant deep boring ache (malignancy)?
Have you noticed any weakness or drooping of your face, difficulty closing your eye, or food accumulating in your cheek (facial nerve involvement)?
Have you experienced dry eyes, dry mouth, or joint stiffness and pains (Sjogren's syndrome)?
Have you had a previous parotid or neck operation, or noticed watery saliva discharging through the skin during meals (salivary fistula)?

skill.hx.surg.salivary_swelling.practice: Practise taking a salivary history from a peer, specifically contrasting the mealtime colicky pattern of ductal obstruction with the insidious, painless growth of a benign mixed parotid tumour.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about facial weakness in a parotid lump, missing a subtle marginal mandibular or zygomatic branch palsy that establishes malignancy.
Confusing the acute bilateral painful swelling of viral mumps with unilateral suppurative parotitis or ductal calculus.
Reassuring a patient with a parotid lump that has been present for twenty years without asking whether it has accelerated in growth or become painful in recent weeks.

probes.q: What pathognomonic symptom pattern points to a stone obstructing the submandibular or parotid duct?
probes.a: A rapid, tense, painful enlargement of the salivary gland occurring during meals (mealtime syndrome / salivary colic).

probes.q: What clinical triad in a longstanding painless parotid lump warns of malignant transformation into carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma?
probes.a: Sudden rapid acceleration of growth, onset of persistent pain, and development of facial nerve weakness or palsy.

probes.q: A patient experiences localized sweating and flushing over the cheek and preauricular skin during meals following parotid surgery. What is this condition, and what is the underlying mechanism?
probes.a: Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating), caused by misdirected regeneration of parasympathetic secretomotor fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve into sympathetic receptors supplying cutaneous sweat glands.

rubric.text: Specifically asks about swelling and pain related to meals
Evaluates duration and checks for recent acceleration of growth or pain
Screens for facial asymmetry, eye closure weakness, and mouth drooping
Asks about dry eyes, dry mouth, and joint symptoms of Sjogren's syndrome

teach.heading: The 80-80-80 rule of salivary neoplasms
teach.body:
Salivary gland tumours follow a well-known clinical distribution. Approximately 80 percent of all salivary neoplasms occur in the parotid gland. Of these parotid tumours, roughly 80 percent are benign.

Of the benign parotid tumours, about 80 percent are pleomorphic adenomas. In contrast, in the submandibular gland, nearly 50 percent of tumours are malignant, and in minor salivary glands, over 70 percent are malignant.

rows: Lifts ear lobule, CN VII intact

teach.heading: Capsular pseudopods and the danger of enucleation
teach.body:
A pleomorphic adenoma possesses a false capsule formed by compressed salivary tissue. Small microscopic tumour projections (pseudopods) regularly penetrate through deficiencies in this capsule.

Simple enucleation leaves these pseudopods behind, resulting in multifocal recurrence rates of 20 to 45 percent. The standard operation is therefore superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation.

skill.exam.surg.parotid_palpation.title: Parotid Gland Palpation
skill.exam.surg.parotid_palpation.oneLine: Assessing anatomical sulcus obliteration, mobility over contracted masseter, and bimanual deep lobe examination
skill.exam.surg.parotid_palpation.why: The parotid gland occupies the retromandibular fossa, extending anteriorly over the masseter and deeply through the stylomandibular tunnel into the parapharyngeal space. True parotid swellings elevate the ear lobule and obliterate the retromandibular hollow. Testing lump mobility while the patient clenches their teeth demonstrates whether the mass is confined to the superficial lobe or infiltrates the masseter muscle. Bimanual palpation against the tonsillar fossa is mandatory to detect deep lobe tumours.

steps.text: Inspect the parotid region from front and profile: observe whether the ear lobule is elevated and whether the natural depression between the posterior mandibular ramus and mastoid process is obliterated.
Inspect the skin over the gland: look for brawny oedema, redness, sinus openings, surgical scars, or skin tethering and ulceration.

Palpate the anatomical boundaries: outline the superior border along the zygomatic arch, posterior border along the mastoid process and anterior SCM, and anterior border extending across the masseter.

Assess consistency and surface: note whether the lump is smooth, bosselated, or nodular, and whether it exhibits variable consistency (firm and soft areas typical of pleomorphic adenoma) or stony hardness (carcinoma).

Perform the masseter contraction test: test mobility of the lump horizontally and vertically with the masseter relaxed; then instruct the patient to clench their teeth firmly to contract the masseter; re-test mobility over the taut muscle.

Perform bimanual palpation for the deep lobe: insert a gloved index finger into the mouth, placing the pulp against the lateral pharyngeal wall behind the third molar and tonsillar fossa, while pressing the external fingers inward behind the mandibular ramus.

skill.exam.surg.parotid_palpation.normal: Normal parotid gland is impalpable; the retromandibular hollow beneath the ear lobule is soft and clear; no intraoral bulging or displacement of the tonsil; masseter is soft at rest and firms on biting without palpable masses.
skill.exam.surg.parotid_palpation.abnormal: Firm, lobulated, painless mass lifting the ear lobule, mobile over the contracted masseter (superficial pleomorphic adenoma); soft cystic fluctuant lump overlying the angle of the jaw in an older man (Warthin's tumour); stony hard fixed mass tethered to skin and masseter with facial nerve palsy (parotid carcinoma); medial displacement of tonsil and soft palate with a full retromandibular sulcus (deep lobe parotid tumour); brawny pitting oedema with severe tenderness and heat (acute suppurative parotitis / parotid abscess).
skill.exam.surg.parotid_palpation.significance: A lump that remains mobile over the contracted masseter arises within or superficial to the parotid fascia and does not invade deep muscle. Bimanual palpation detects dumbbell parapharyngeal deep lobe tumours before they obstruct the airway.
skill.exam.surg.parotid_palpation.practice: Practise identifying the retromandibular sulcus and performing the masseter clenching test on a peer, verifying that the normal sulcus becomes taut when teeth are clenched.
pitfalls: Mistaking an enlarged upper deep cervical or preauricular lymph node for a parotid tumour; a lymph node does not elevate the ear lobule or obliterate the retromandibular sulcus.
Waiting for fluctuation before draining a suspected parotid abscess; the dense unyielding parotid fascia prevents early fluctuation, leading to extensive tissue necrosis.
Failing to examine inside the pharynx and perform bimanual palpation, missing a deep lobe 'dumbbell' tumour presenting only as a medial bulge of the tonsil.

probes.q: What physical landmark on inspection distinguishes an intrinsic parotid swelling from an enlarged cervical lymph node?
probes.a: A parotid swelling lifts the lobule of the ear and obliterates the retromandibular sulcus between the jaw angle and mastoid process.

probes.q: How does the clinician determine whether a parotid tumour is confined to the parotid gland or has infiltrated the masseter muscle?
probes.a: By testing the mobility of the lump while the patient clenches their teeth; a benign tumour remains mobile over the contracted masseter, whereas an infiltrating cancer becomes fixed.

probes.q: Why is fluctuation a dangerously late clinical sign in acute suppurative parotitis or parotid abscess?
probes.a: Because the gland is encased within the tough, unyielding deep parotid fascia, which holds inflammatory exudate under high tension without allowing superficial fluctuation.

rubric.text: Inspects for elevation of the ear lobule and obliteration of the retromandibular sulcus
Tests tumour mobility over the masseter muscle while the patient clenches their teeth
Performs bimanual palpation of the deep lobe against the tonsillar fossa
Assesses consistency across different portions of the swelling

teach.heading: The surgical anatomy of the parotid bed
teach.body:
The parotid bed is bounded anteriorly by the posterior border of the ramus of the mandible and masseter, posteriorly by the mastoid process and sternocleidomastoid, and superiorly by the external auditory meatus.

The gland is wrapped by the dense parotid fascia, derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. This unyielding envelope causes intense throbbing pain when the gland is acutely inflamed or distended by pus.

teach.heading: Superficial versus deep lobe and the stylomandibular tunnel

rows: Lump below and in front of ear
Both external mass and tonsillar bulge

teach.heading: Variable consistency in pleomorphic adenoma
teach.body:
Pleomorphic adenoma is termed 'mixed' because epithelial and myoepithelial cells are embedded in a diverse stroma of mucoid, myxoid, and chondroid matrix.

On clinical palpation, this produces the diagnostic sign of variable consistency: areas of soft, elastic, and firm cartilage-like tissue within the same lobulated mass, with intact overlying skin and facial nerve function.

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.stensen_duct.title: Stensen's Duct Examination
skill.exam.surg.stensen_duct.oneLine: Locating the orifice opposite the upper second molar, milking the duct, and bidigital palpation
skill.exam.surg.stensen_duct.why: Stensen's duct arises from the anterior border of the parotid gland, runs horizontally across the masseter, turns medially to pierce the buccinator, and opens into the oral cavity opposite the upper second molar. Inspecting the papilla and milking the duct from behind forwards demonstrates whether saliva is clear, absent (ductal calculus), frank pus (suppurative parotitis), or blood-stained (ductal carcinoma), confirming the diagnosis without invasive imaging.

steps.text: Position the patient in good light; use a wooden spatula or cheek retractor to gently retract the cheek mucosa away from the upper dental arcade.
Locate Stensen's duct orifice: identify the small mucosal papilla situated on the buccal mucosa directly opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth.
Inspect the papilla: note whether it is pale pink and flat, or inflamed, swollen, red, pouting, or occluded by an impacted yellow calculus.
Dry the orifice: gently blot the papilla dry with a clean cotton swab or gauze so that fresh emerging secretion can be observed clearly.

Perform expression milking: place fingers of one hand externally over the posterior parotid gland; compress gently and stroke forwards along the anatomical line of the duct across the masseter towards the cheek.
Inspect the extruded secretion: observe whether the duct yields a prompt bead of clear watery saliva, thick turbid saliva, droplets of frank yellow pus, or blood.

Perform bidigital palpation of the terminal duct: insert a gloved index finger inside the cheek and place the thumb outside on the cheek; roll the duct tissue between finger and thumb to detect an impacted calculus.

skill.exam.surg.stensen_duct.normal: Stensen's duct papilla is small, flat, pale pink, and non-tender; gentle parotid milking yields a prompt bead of clear, watery, non-viscid saliva; no palpable stones or induration along the duct.
skill.exam.surg.stensen_duct.abnormal: Red, swollen, pouting papilla exuding droplets of thick creamy pus upon milking (acute suppurative parotitis); blood-tinged saliva extruded from orifice (malignant ductal or glandular neoplasm); no saliva emerging despite parotid pressure with tender swollen duct (calculus obstruction or ductal stricture); firm, tender, mobile calculus palpable bidigitally in the cheek.
skill.exam.surg.stensen_duct.significance: Demonstrating pus confirms acute bacterial infection and provides an immediate specimen for Gram stain and culture. Frank blood mandates urgent core or excision biopsy for ductal malignancy.
skill.exam.surg.stensen_duct.practice: Practise identifying the papilla opposite the upper second molar on peers, drying the orifice, and observing normal salivation upon gentle external cheek pressure.
pitfalls: Looking for Stensen's duct on the floor of the mouth, confusing it with Wharton's duct of the submandibular gland.
Compressing an acutely inflamed, tender parotid gland forcefully, causing excruciating pain without drying the papilla first to observe the discharge.
Failing to bidigitally palpate the anterior mobile portion of the duct where a radiolucent stone or mucus plug may be lodged.

probes.q: Where does the parotid duct (Stensen's duct) open inside the oral cavity?
probes.a: On the buccal mucosa of the cheek opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth.

probes.q: What physical finding at Stensen's duct orifice confirms the diagnosis of acute suppurative parotitis?
probes.a: Expression of droplets of frank yellow pus or purulent saliva from the red, inflamed duct papilla upon gentle milking of the gland.

probes.q: Why are calculi significantly less common in Stensen's duct (parotid) compared to Wharton's duct (submandibular)?
probes.a: Parotid saliva is predominantly serous, watery, and flows horizontally, whereas submandibular saliva is viscid, mucinous, rich in calcium and phosphate, and flows uphill against gravity.

rubric.text: Accurately locates Stensen's duct orifice opposite the crown of the upper second molar
Dries the papilla before expression to accurately observe the emerging fluid
Performs gentle forward milking compression from the gland along the duct
Performs bidigital palpation of the terminal duct between index finger and thumb

teach.heading: Anatomical course of Stensen's duct
teach.body:
Stensen's duct is approximately 5 cm long. It emerges from the anterior border of the parotid gland, runs horizontally forwards across the middle third of the masseter muscle, one fingerbreadth below the zygomatic arch.

At the anterior border of the masseter, it turns sharply medially at right angles, pierces the buccal fat pad and buccinator muscle, and runs submucosally before opening opposite the upper second molar.

teach.heading: Suppurative parotitis in dehydrated surgical patients
teach.body:
Acute suppurative parotitis classically arises in debilitated, post-operative, or elderly patients who are dehydrated, kept nil-by-mouth, and maintain poor oral hygiene.

Diminished salivary flow permits retrograde ascent of oral commensals, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus, up Stensen's duct into the parotid parenchyma, leading to rapid suppuration under tension.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.facial_nerve.title: Facial Nerve Examination in Parotid Disease
skill.exam.surg.facial_nerve.oneLine: Motor testing of all five terminal branches to differentiate benign parotid tumours from malignancy
skill.exam.surg.facial_nerve.why: The facial nerve (CN VII) enters the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland and divides at the pes anserinus into temporofacial and cervicofacial divisions, giving rise to five terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. A fundamental surgical rule states that benign tumours (pleomorphic adenoma, Warthin's tumour) never cause facial paralysis regardless of size. The presence of facial nerve paresis or palsy in a parotid swelling is conclusive clinical proof of malignancy.

steps.text: Inspect facial symmetry at rest: look for loss of forehead furrows, widening of the palpebral fissure, flattening of the nasolabial fold, or drooping of the oral commissure on the side of the parotid mass.
Test the temporal branch (frontalis): instruct the patient to look up at the ceiling or wrinkle their forehead without moving their head; observe for symmetrical horizontal forehead furrows.

Test the zygomatic branch (orbicularis oculi): ask the patient to close their eyes tightly ('screw eyes shut'); attempt to gently pry the upper eyelids open with your thumbs, testing muscular resistance and observing for Bell's phenomenon.

Test the buccal branch (buccinator and zygomaticus major): ask the patient to puff out their cheeks with lips sealed; press gently on both cheeks to test for air leak; then ask them to show their teeth or smile broadly.

Test the marginal mandibular branch (depressor anguli oris and orbicularis oris): instruct the patient to whistle, purse their lips, or show their lower teeth; observe for asymmetrical depression of the lower lip.
Test the cervical branch (platysma): ask the patient to grimace forcefully or pull down the corners of their mouth; observe for visible contraction of the platysma muscle bands over the clavicles.

skill.exam.surg.facial_nerve.normal: Facial features symmetrical at rest; symmetrical, deep forehead wrinkling; forceful eye closure preventing lid elevation; cheeks puffed without air leak; symmetrical smile; symmetrical lower lip depression; active platysma contraction.
skill.exam.surg.facial_nerve.abnormal: Unilateral lag or inability to close the eye with scleral show (lagophthalmos / Bell's phenomenon); unilateral flattening of forehead furrows; drooping of the angle of the mouth with food pocketing in the cheek; air leaking from lips on cheek puffing; asymmetrical smile with mouth drawn to the healthy side; branch-specific paresis (e.g. isolated marginal mandibular droop in malignant parotid infiltration).
skill.exam.surg.facial_nerve.significance: Facial nerve weakness in a parotid lump confirms malignancy (adenoid cystic carcinoma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, or carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) or necrotising parotitis, mandating radical oncological resection rather than simple superficial parotidectomy.
skill.exam.surg.facial_nerve.practice: Rehearse testing all five terminal branches of the facial nerve systematically in cranial-to-caudal sequence on a peer: forehead wrinkle, tight eye closure, puffed cheeks, whistling smile, and platysma grimace.
pitfalls: Assuming that a massive, longstanding parotid lump with intact facial nerve function must be malignant; size does not determine malignancy, but facial nerve palsy does.
Testing only a smile and missing isolated marginal mandibular weakness, which presents as inability to evert the lower lip while the nasolabial fold remains intact.
Attributing facial droop in a patient with a parotid lump to idiopathic Bell's palsy, missing an infiltrating deep lobe parotid carcinoma.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy in a patient presenting with a firm parotid mass?
probes.a: It indicates malignant infiltration of the facial nerve, confirming parotid gland carcinoma.

probes.q: Can a very large benign pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland cause facial nerve paralysis?
probes.a: No; benign tumours displace and stretch the facial nerve branches over their capsule, but do not infiltrate or paralyze them.

probes.q: Which salivary malignancy is particularly notorious for microscopic perineural invasion and tracking along the branches of the facial nerve?
probes.a: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (cylindroma).

rubric.text: Inspects facial symmetry at rest for nasolabial flattening or eye fissure widening
Tests temporal (forehead wrinkle) and zygomatic (tight eye closure) branches
Tests buccal (cheek puff/smile) and marginal mandibular (whistle/lower teeth) branches
Identifies which specific branches are paretic or spared

teach.heading: The terminal branches of the facial nerve and their muscle targets

rows: Air leak, mouth drawn to normal side
Asymmetry of lower lip on depression

teach.heading: Surgical plane of the facial nerve: the pes anserinus
teach.body:
The facial nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen, passes lateral to the styloid process, and pierces the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland.

Within the gland, it branches like a goose foot (pes anserinus) into an upper temporofacial and lower cervicofacial division. This branching plane divides the parotid gland surgically into superficial and deep lobes.

teach.heading: Perineural tracking in adenoid cystic carcinoma
teach.body:
Adenoid cystic carcinoma exhibits an indolent clinical course but displays aggressive perineural invasion. Tumour cells track along nerve sheaths microscopically for centimetres beyond visible margins.

Patients may present with localized facial pain, dysaesthesia, or subtle muscle twitching months before frank motor paralysis becomes evident.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
