skill.exam.surg.submandibular_bimanual.title: Submandibular Gland Bimanual Palpation
skill.exam.surg.submandibular_bimanual.oneLine: Differentiating submandibular salivary gland from submandibular lymph nodes across the mylohyoid
skill.exam.surg.submandibular_bimanual.why: The submandibular triangle contains both the submandibular salivary gland and submandibular lymph nodes. Because the deep lobe of the salivary gland hooks around the posterior free margin of the mylohyoid muscle into the floor of the mouth, while lymph nodes lie entirely superficial (submylohyoid), bimanual palpation is the definitive bedside test to differentiate gland enlargement from lymphadenopathy. Missing this distinction leads to incorrect staging of oral cancers or misdiagnosis of sialolithiasis.

steps.text: Position the seated patient with head tilted slightly forwards and towards the side being examined to relax the platysma, deep cervical fascia, and strap muscles.
Inspect the submandibular triangle for visible swelling, redness, sinus formation, or scars; inspect the floor of the mouth for sublingual swelling or Wharton's duct redness.
Put on clean gloves; explain the procedure to the patient and instruct them to breathe quietly through the nose with the mouth slightly open.
Insert the gloved index finger into the floor of the mouth, medial to the mandible and lateral to the tongue, pressing as far back as the anterior pillar of the fauces.
Place the fingers of the opposite hand externally in the submandibular triangle beneath the lower border of the mandible, pushing the tissues upwards and medially.

Palpate the tissue trapped between the internal and external fingers: determine whether the mass is caught directly between the fingers (salivary gland) or slips away externally beneath the mylohyoid (lymph nodes).
Palpate the length of Wharton's duct: sweep the intraoral finger from posterior to anterior along the sublingual fold towards the caruncle to feel for an impacted stone.

skill.exam.surg.submandibular_bimanual.normal: Submandibular salivary gland is soft and barely perceptible on bimanual palpation; Wharton's duct is supple and non-tender; no palpable salivary calculi or enlarged lymph nodes.
skill.exam.surg.submandibular_bimanual.abnormal: Firm, smooth, lobulated mass distinctly palpable directly between internal and external fingers on both sides of the mylohyoid (enlarged submandibular salivary gland); discrete, firm, nodular lumps felt externally that cannot be engaged by the intraoral finger (submandibular lymph nodes); stony hard tenderness along the duct with arrested salivary flow (sialolithiasis of Wharton's duct); hard, fixed, infiltrating mass with lingual nerve anaesthesia (adenoid cystic or mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the submandibular gland).
skill.exam.surg.submandibular_bimanual.significance: A mass palpable directly between the intraoral and extraoral fingers is the submandibular salivary gland; a mass felt only from the outside is lymphadenopathy. Palpation along the duct identifies radio-opaque or radiolucent calculi.
skill.exam.surg.submandibular_bimanual.practice: Practise bimanual palpation on a peer, identifying the posterior free border of the mylohyoid muscle and feeling the supple submandibular gland between intraoral and external fingers.
pitfalls: Attempting bimanual palpation with the patient's neck extended, which tightens the cervical fascia and prevents the external fingers from invaginating the submandibular space.
Placing the intraoral finger medial to the tongue, gagging the patient instead of palpating the lateral sublingual sulcus.
Assuming multiple discrete submandibular lumps represent salivary gland pathology; multiple lumps are virtually always lymph nodes.

probes.q: Why is the submandibular salivary gland palpable bimanually between an intraoral and an extraoral finger, while submandibular lymph nodes are not?
probes.a: Because the deep lobe of the submandibular gland lies above the mylohyoid muscle in the mouth floor, whereas lymph nodes lie entirely below (superficial to) the mylohyoid.

probes.q: How does the clinician distinguish a single enlarged submandibular salivary gland from matted submandibular tuberculous lymph nodes on palpation?
probes.a: The salivary gland forms a single uniform lobulated mass felt bimanually, whereas lymph nodes present as multiple discrete or matted nodular swellings felt only from the exterior.

probes.q: If a stone is impacted at the ampulla of Wharton's duct, what clinical test using lemon juice demonstrates obstruction of that gland?
probes.a: Place dry swabs over both Wharton duct orifices, give lemon juice on the tongue; the normal side shows profuse saliva soaking the swab, while the obstructed side remains dry.

rubric.text: Positions the patient with neck slightly flexed to relax cervical fascia
Places one gloved finger in the lateral floor of mouth and opposite hand under mandible
Differentiates salivary gland from lymph nodes based on relation to the mylohyoid
Palpates the entire course of Wharton's duct from posterior to anterior

teach.heading: The anatomical relation of the submandibular gland to the mylohyoid
teach.body:
The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular diaphragm of the mouth floor. The submandibular gland is wrapped around the posterior free border of the mylohyoid in a C-shape.

Its large superficial lobe lies below the mylohyoid in the neck, while its small deep lobe extends above the mylohyoid into the sublingual space, accompanying Wharton's duct. This allows the gland to be grasped between internal and external fingers.

teach.heading: Submandibular gland versus submandibular lymph nodes

rows: Primary oral mucosal ulcer or tooth decay

teach.heading: Course of Wharton's duct and surgical precautions
teach.body:
Wharton's duct is about 5 cm long. It runs forwards from the deep lobe along the floor of the mouth, crossed twice by the lingual nerve (which spirals from lateral to inferior to medial).

It opens on the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum. When removing an impacted calculus near the caruncle, the duct is incised longitudinally; stone retrieval must avoid tearing the adjacent lingual nerve.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.surg.neck_swelling.title: Neck Swelling History
skill.hx.surg.neck_swelling.oneLine: Patient age, onset tempo, pain, compressive signs, constitutional symptoms, and primary search
skill.hx.surg.neck_swelling.why: A neck lump is a common presentation across surgical practice. The patient's age and temporal progression stratify the differential: congenital lesions appear in neonates and young adults (sternomastoid tumour, cystic hygroma, branchial cyst, thyroglossal cyst); acute painful swellings are infective (lymphadenitis, abscess); slowly progressive painless lumps represent tuberculosis or lymphoma; and any solitary hard neck mass in an adult over 40 must be considered metastatic carcinoma until proven otherwise.

asks.text: When did you first notice the swelling in your neck, and where was its exact original location?
Has the swelling grown slowly over months or years, or has it enlarged rapidly within days or weeks?
Is the swelling painful or tender? Acute inflammatory lymphadenitis is intensely painful, whereas tuberculous and malignant nodes are typically painless.
Does the swelling increase in size or ache specifically during meals (salivary calculus)?
Does the swelling move when you swallow water or when you stick your tongue out?
Have you noticed hoarseness of voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve), breathing difficulty or stridor (tracheal compression), or trouble swallowing food (oesophageal compression)?
Have you had evening fevers, drenching night sweats, or unintentional weight loss (tuberculosis, lymphoma)?
Have you noticed any non-healing sore, ulcer, bleeding, or lump in your mouth, throat, scalp, or skin, and do you consume tobacco, supari, or spirits?

skill.hx.surg.neck_swelling.practice: Practise taking a neck lump history from a peer, specifically probing for the rule of 80: congenital in youth, inflammatory in adults, and neoplastic in elderly patients.
pitfalls: Treating a persistent enlarged cervical lymph node in an adult with repeated courses of antibiotics without performing a complete upper aerodigestive examination to search for a primary malignancy.
Attributing an asymptomatic neck mass in an older patient to tuberculosis simply because it has been present for two months, delaying the diagnosis of occult carcinoma.
Failing to ask about voice change or stridor, missing critical aerodigestive compression from an invasive neck mass.

probes.q: What is the single commonest cause of an isolated swelling in the neck across all age groups?
probes.a: Enlarged cervical lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy).

probes.q: How does the duration and pain of a neck swelling distinguish acute cervical lymphadenitis from metastatic lymph node carcinoma?
probes.a: Acute lymphadenitis is of short duration (days) and is exquisitely painful and tender, whereas metastatic nodal carcinoma is painless and grows steadily over weeks to months.

probes.q: Why must every adult presenting with an unexplained firm cervical lymph node undergo panendoscopy (nasopharyngoscopy, laryngoscopy, and bronchoscopy)?
probes.a: To locate a hidden primary mucosal squamous cell carcinoma in the pyriform fossa, base of tongue, tonsil, or nasopharynx draining to that node.

rubric.text: Stratifies the history based on patient age and tempo of lump enlargement
Differentiates acute inflammatory tenderness from painless neoplastic growth
Screens for hoarseness, stridor, and dysphagia
Inquires about oral sores, scalp lesions, tobacco exposure, and B-symptoms

teach.heading: The surgical rule of 80s for non-thyroid neck lumps
teach.body:
In non-thyroid neck swellings in adults, a classic clinical rule of thumb applies: 80 percent of non-thyroid neck masses are neoplastic. Of these neoplastic masses, 80 percent are malignant.

Of these malignant neck masses, 80 percent represent metastatic carcinoma (predominantly squamous cell carcinoma) from a primary tumour in the head and neck. In contrast, in children, 90 percent of neck masses are inflammatory or congenital.

teach.heading: Age distribution of common neck swellings
Compressive red flag symptoms in neck masses
teach.body:
Because the neck encloses the cervical trachea, oesophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerves, and carotid sheath, expansion of a neck mass can cause vital functional impairment.

Hoarseness points to recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy; inspiratory stridor indicates critical tracheal compression; dysphagia indicates oesophageal indentation; and Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) indicates sympathetic trunk involvement.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: The neck: history and differential diagnosis

skill.exam.surg.neck_palpation.title: Neck Swelling Palpation
skill.exam.surg.neck_palpation.oneLine: Posterior approach with passive flexion, triangle mapping, and relation to contracted sternocleidomastoid
skill.exam.surg.neck_palpation.why: Palpating the neck from behind with the patient's neck passively flexed relaxes the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscles and investing cervical fascia. Establishing whether a swelling lies anterior, posterior, superficial, or deep to the SCM narrows the differential to a single anatomical compartment. Lumps deep to the SCM become less prominent and restricted on muscle contraction; superficial lumps remain mobile.

steps.text: Stand behind the seated patient; passively flex the patient's neck slightly by placing one hand on the occiput to relax the cervical fascia and muscles.
Passively tilt the patient's head slightly towards the side of the swelling to achieve maximum ipsilateral muscle relaxation.
Palpate the swelling systematically with warmed fingers: determine anatomical triangle (submental, submandibular, carotid, muscular, or posterior), size, shape, surface, margins, and consistency.

Test mobility in horizontal and vertical axes: determine whether the mass moves freely, moves in one direction only (carotid body tumour moves across but not along carotid axis), or is fixed to deep structures.

Test relationship to the sternocleidomastoid muscle: place your hand on the patient's chin opposite the lesion and ask them to turn the head against resistance (contracting ipsilateral SCM); palpate whether the lump is masked and restricted (deep to SCM) or prominent and mobile (superficial to SCM).

Differentiate pulsatility: place index and middle fingers across the mass; determine whether the fingers are pushed apart in all directions (expansile pulsation of an aneurysm) or merely lifted synchronously upwards (transmitted pulsation from an underlying carotid artery).

skill.exam.surg.neck_palpation.normal: Neck is symmetrical; anatomical triangles are soft and supple without palpable lumps; SCM and trapezius muscles are smooth and non-tender; carotid pulses are normally palpable without thrill or transmitted mass.
skill.exam.surg.neck_palpation.abnormal: Mass partly covered by anterior border of upper third of SCM that becomes masked during muscle contraction (branchial cyst, jugulodigastric node); mass in lower posterior triangle (cystic hygroma, supraclavicular node); firm pulsatile swelling at carotid bifurcation mobile laterally but fixed vertically (carotid body tumour); matted firm nodes deep to SCM with cold abscess (tuberculous lymphadenitis); stony hard mass fixed to SCM and carotid sheath (metastatic carcinoma).
skill.exam.surg.neck_palpation.significance: Localisation within anatomical triangles and depth relative to SCM distinguishes congenital cysts from nodal metastases and vascular neoplasms, preventing hazardous blind biopsies of carotid body tumours or aneurysms.
skill.exam.surg.neck_palpation.practice: Practise passive neck flexion from behind on a peer, identifying the anterior and posterior triangles and feeling how SCM contraction masks structures in the carotid triangle.
pitfalls: Attempting to palpate the neck with the patient's head extended, which stretches the strap muscles and SCM like tight steel cables, completely obscuring deep cervical lumps.
Mistaking the prominent greater cornu of the hyoid bone in a thin elderly patient for a hard metastatic lymph node; the hyoid cornu moves up with swallowing and is bilateral.
Failing to differentiate expansile from transmitted pulsation, mistaking a lymph node overlying the carotid bifurcation for a carotid aneurysm.

probes.q: Why is the neck best palpated with the examiner standing behind the patient and the neck slightly flexed?
probes.a: Because standing behind permits symmetrical access to all triangles, and slight passive flexion relaxes the sternocleidomastoid muscles and cervical fascia.

probes.q: How does the clinician determine whether a neck mass lies superficial or deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
probes.a: By testing lump prominence and mobility while the patient contracts the SCM against resistance; deep swellings become less prominent and restricted, whereas superficial swellings become more prominent.

probes.q: How does the clinician differentiate between expansile pulsation and transmitted pulsation in a pulsatile neck swelling?
probes.a: In expansile pulsation (aneurysm), two fingers placed on opposite sides are pushed apart in all directions; in transmitted pulsation (tumour over carotid), the fingers are merely lifted upwards.

rubric.text: Stands behind the patient with the neck passively flexed and tilted towards the lesion
Accurately maps the swelling to a specific anatomical neck triangle
Tests the relation of the mass to SCM during active muscle contraction
Differentiates expansile from transmitted pulsation using two fingers

teach.heading: Anatomical triangles of the neck and their key swellings
Fontaine sign in carotid body tumours
teach.body:
A carotid body tumour (chemodectoma / paraganglioma) arises at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery within the carotid sheath.

Because the tumour is firmly anchored to the carotid bifurcation, it can be moved freely from side to side across the neck, but CANNOT be moved vertically up and down along the vessel line. This pathognomonic finding is known as Fontaine sign.

teach.heading: Hyoid cornu: the commonest pseudo-tumour of the neck
teach.body:
In slender, elderly individuals, the greater cornu of the hyoid bone frequently presents as a hard, well-defined, tender lump high in the carotid triangle, readily mistaken for a hard metastatic node.

Palpating both sides simultaneously confirms symmetry; asking the patient to swallow demonstrates that the bony tip rises synchronously with the larynx.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.title: Deglutition and Tongue Protrusion Tests
skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.oneLine: Assessing deglutition excursion and tongue protrusion elevation to separate thyroglossal cysts from thyroid lesions
skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.why: Neck swellings connected to the larynx or trachea rise on deglutition because they are enclosed within or attached to the pretracheal fascia. A thyroglossal cyst develops along the embryonic thyroglossal tract between the foramen caecum and the thyroid isthmus, intimately related to the hyoid bone. Consequently, a thyroglossal cyst rises on swallowing AND rises upon active tongue protrusion (due to genioglossus traction on the hyoid and tract), distinguishing it definitively from thyroid and lymph node masses.

steps.text: Position the patient seated upright under tangential lighting; expose the neck fully from chin to suprasternal notch.
Inspect the midline of the neck: identify the hyoid bone, thyroid cartilage notch, and cricoid cartilage; note any cystic mass in the subhyoid, suprahyoid, or thyroid cartilage zone.

Perform the deglutition test: give the patient a sip of water; instruct them to hold the water in the mouth and swallow on command while you closely observe the mass; note whether the swelling rises and falls smoothly with the larynx.
Stabilize the mass: gently fix the lower border of the swelling between the index finger and thumb of one hand.

Perform the tongue protrusion test: ask the patient to open the mouth and stick the tongue straight out as far as possible without moving the head; observe whether the lump is pulled upwards and forwards beneath your fingers.
Observe tongue retraction: instruct the patient to pull the tongue back into the mouth; note whether the mass descends to its original resting position.

Inspect for a thyroglossal fistula: look for an indrawn transverse skin dimple or discharging opening near the midline below the hyoid, overlaid by a crescentic skin fold; repeat tongue protrusion to observe skin retraction.

skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.normal: Midline neck is smooth and supple; thyroid gland moves up smoothly with deglutition by 1.5 to 2.5 cm; no movement of midline tissues during tongue protrusion; no fistula opening or tethered skin fold.
skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.abnormal: Midline subhyoid cystic mass that moves up on deglutition AND rises distinctly with tongue protrusion (pathognomonic of thyroglossal cyst); midline swelling that moves up on deglutition but shows NO movement on tongue protrusion (thyroid isthmus lump, pyramidal lobe goitre, subhyoid bursa, prelaryngeal Delphian lymph node); lack of deglutition movement in a suspected thyroid mass (locally invasive anaplastic carcinoma or Riedel's thyroiditis); indrawn fistula opening that pulls upwards when tongue is protruded (thyroglossal fistula).
skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.significance: Upward movement on tongue protrusion proves anatomical continuity with the foramen caecum via the hyoid bone, confirming a thyroglossal cyst and mandating Sistrunk operation (en bloc excision of cyst, tract, and central hyoid body) to prevent recurrence.
skill.exam.surg.neck_deglutition_tongue.practice: Practise stabilizing a midline lump with thumb and index finger while the subject swallows and protrudes the tongue, feeling the distinct upward tug on tongue protrusion in a thyroglossal cyst.
pitfalls: Failing to ask the patient to protrude the tongue, mistaking a thyroglossal cyst for an ectopic thyroid nodule or Delphian lymph node.
Excising a midline subhyoid mass without pre-operative imaging (ultrasound / scan), accidentally removing the patient's only functioning thyroid tissue (lingual or ectopic thyroid).
Performing simple enucleation of a thyroglossal cyst without resecting the central body of the hyoid bone (Sistrunk procedure), resulting in a recurrence rate exceeding 50 percent.

probes.q: Why does a thyroid swelling move upwards during deglutition?
probes.a: Because the thyroid gland is enclosed within the pretracheal fascia, which is firmly attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages of the larynx.

probes.q: What physical examination finding definitively differentiates a thyroglossal cyst from an adenoma of the thyroid isthmus?
probes.a: A thyroglossal cyst moves upwards upon active protrusion of the tongue, whereas a thyroid isthmus adenoma does not.

probes.q: Explain the anatomical mechanism by which protruding the tongue pulls a thyroglossal cyst upwards.
probes.a: The thyroglossal tract passes from the foramen caecum of the tongue through or behind the hyoid bone to the cyst; active protrusion contracts the genioglossus, pulling the hyoid and tract upwards.

rubric.text: Administers a sip of water and observes swelling movement during swallowing
Stabilizes the mass gently with fingers to perceive traction
Tests for upward movement of the swelling during active tongue protrusion
Inspects for an indrawn fistula opening and crescentic skin fold

teach.heading: Swellings that move on deglutition
teach.body:
Any anatomical structure enclosed within or attached to the pretracheal fascia moves with the larynx on deglutition.

These include the thyroid gland (lobes, isthmus, and pyramidal lobe), thyroglossal cysts, subhyoid bursitis, laryngoceles, and prelaryngeal (Delphian) or pretracheal lymph nodes when adherent to the airway. Fixation by anaplastic cancer eliminates this movement.

teach.heading: Sistrunk operation: why the hyoid must be resected
teach.body:
In 1920, Walter Sistrunk demonstrated that the embryonic thyroglossal duct does not merely abut the hyoid bone; it passes through or intimately behind the central body of the hyoid, surrounded by microscopic ductal branches.

Simple cyst excision carries a recurrence rate over 50 percent, whereas core resection of the cyst, the central 1 to 2 cm of the hyoid body, and a tissue cone up to the foramen caecum reduces recurrence to under 4 percent.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: The neck: thyroglossal cyst and fistula

skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.title: Cervical Lymph Node Examination
skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.oneLine: Systematic palpation of levels I to VI, Virchow's node, and mapping primary drainage territories
skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.why: Cervical lymphadenopathy is the commonest surgical neck condition in India. Tuberculous adenitis dominates benign presentations, while metastatic squamous cell carcinoma dominates malignant presentations. Cervical nodes are classified into levels I through VI. A meticulous systematic examination maps the involved station to its specific primary mucosal drainage territory (oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, thyroid, or gastrointestinal tract), preventing missed occult primary malignancies.

steps.text: Stand behind the seated patient with their neck passively flexed and tilted towards the side being examined to relax the cervical fascia.
Palpate Level I: examine Level IA (submental) beneath the chin between anterior digastric bellies; examine Level IB (submandibular) in the submandibular triangle.

Palpate Levels II, III, and IV (internal jugular chain): gently hook fingers under the anterior border of the SCM; palpate Level II (upper jugular, skull base to hyoid), Level III (mid jugular, hyoid to cricoid), and Level IV (lower jugular, cricoid to clavicle).
Palpate Level V (posterior triangle): trace along the posterior border of SCM, anterior border of trapezius, and supraclavicular fossa (Level VA superior to cricoid arch, Level VB inferior).
Palpate Level VI (central anterior compartment): palpate prelaryngeal (Delphian), pretracheal, and paratracheal nodes between the hyoid and suprasternal notch.

Palpate the left supraclavicular fossa (Virchow's node / Troisier's sign): palpate deeply behind the clavicular head of the left SCM for hard, non-tender nodes indicating transdiaphragmatic abdominal metastasis.
Correlate with drainage territories: for any enlarged node, perform a directed inspection of the drained mucosa (oral cavity, tongue, tonsils, nasopharynx, larynx, scalp, or abdomen).

skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.normal: Cervical lymph nodes are not palpable, or palpable only as tiny (< 1 cm), soft, discrete, non-tender, mobile oval nodules in submandibular or upper jugular stations without matting, induration, or sinus formation.
skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.abnormal: Matted, rubbery nodes that soften into fluctuant cold abscesses with puckered discharging sinuses (tuberculous lymphadenitis); discrete, non-tender, rubbery, mobile nodes involving multiple cervical stations and axillae (lymphoma); stony hard, fixed, non-tender node tethered to carotid sheath or deep muscles (metastatic squamous cell carcinoma); hard, irregular left supraclavicular node (Troisier's sign of gastric, pancreatic, or testicular malignancy).
skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.significance: Nodal level directs the search for the occult primary: Level I drains lip and anterior mouth; Level II drains tonsil and tongue base; Level III/IV drains larynx and hypopharynx; Level VI drains thyroid; Virchow's node drains infradiaphragmatic viscera via the thoracic duct.
skill.exam.surg.cervical_nodes.practice: Rehearse palpating all six cervical lymph node levels in numerical sequence on a peer, rolling fingertips across each anatomical triangle from submental to supraclavicular.
pitfalls: Excising an enlarged cervical node in an adult for biopsy without first performing an endoscopic search for a primary mucosal cancer, breaching oncological planes and worsening prognosis.
Palpating only the superficial anterior neck and missing deep Level IV and Level V nodes tucked behind the clavicle and trapezius.
Dismissing a stony hard left supraclavicular node as local musculoskeletal tension, missing metastatic abdominal adenocarcinoma (Troisier's sign).

probes.q: What is Troisier's sign, and what anatomical structure explains its left-sided predominance?
probes.a: Enlargement of the left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow's node) due to metastatic abdominal cancer, transmitted via the thoracic duct which enters the left internal jugular-subclavian venous junction.

probes.q: What pathological stages characterise the progression of tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis to a 'collar-stud' abscess?
probes.a: Solid lymphadenitis progresses to periadenitis with matting, central caseation (cold abscess deep to deep fascia), perforation of deep fascia into superficial subcutaneous tissue (collar-stud), and skin ulceration with sinus.

probes.q: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with an isolated stony hard Level II (jugulodigastric) neck node. What primary mucosal sites must be systematically inspected?
probes.a: The ipsilateral tonsil, base of the tongue, soft palate, pyriform fossa, and nasopharynx.

rubric.text: Palpates all six cervical levels in systematic numerical anatomical order
Carefully palpates the posterior triangle and left supraclavicular fossa
Documents node size, consistency (rubbery vs stony hard), matting, and fixity
Identifies the primary mucosal drainage territory corresponding to the involved level

teach.heading: The Memorial Sloan Kettering cervical lymph node levels
Stages of tuberculous lymphadenopathy
teach.body:
Tuberculous lymphadenitis in South Asia proceeds through five well-defined pathological stages: (1) Stage of lymphadenitis: firm, discrete, mobile nodes; (2) Stage of periadenitis: nodes adhere to one another forming matted conglomerate masses.

(3) Stage of cold abscess: caseous liquefaction deep to the investing cervical fascia; (4) Stage of collar-stud abscess: necrosis through the deep fascia into subcutaneous fat; (5) Tuberculous sinus: bursting through skin with undermined blue edges.

teach.heading: Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) before open biopsy
teach.body:
In modern surgical practice, FNAC is the primary investigation of choice for any cervical lymphadenopathy.

Open incisional or excisional biopsy of a metastatic squamous cell node without prior imaging disrupts the fascial barrier, leads to tumour spillage, seeds the surgical neck scar, and significantly compromises subsequent neck dissection survival.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.lateral_neck_mass.title: Lateral Neck Mass Examination
skill.exam.surg.lateral_neck_mass.oneLine: Assessing transillumination, compressibility, and Fontaine's sign to distinguish branchial cyst, cystic hygroma, and carotid body tumour
skill.exam.surg.lateral_neck_mass.why: Lateral neck swellings include benign developmental cysts and vascular neoplasms requiring diametrically different surgical strategies. A branchial cyst presents as an ovoid fluctuant lump along the upper third anterior border of the SCM; a cystic hygroma is a multilocular lymphatic malformation in the posterior triangle; and a carotid body tumour arises at the common carotid bifurcation. Accurate clinical elicitation of transillumination, compressibility, and Fontaine's sign prevents catastrophic biopsy-induced haemorrhage.

steps.text: Inspect the lateral neck: observe the anatomical triangle (carotid triangle vs posterior triangle), contour, lobulation, skin colour, and visible pulsations.
Palpate the swelling to assess relation to the SCM: determine whether the mass lies under the upper anterior border of the SCM (branchial cyst) or fills the lower posterior triangle (cystic hygroma).
Test for fluctuation: place two fingers on opposite poles of the mass and press with a third finger; confirm true fluid presence in all axes.

Perform the transillumination test in a darkened room: press a focused bright pen torch against one side of the lump while viewing the opposite side through a rolled dark cardboard cylinder; note whether light shines through with a brilliant glow (cystic hygroma) or is blocked (branchial cyst containing opaque cellular fluid).

Test for compressibility: apply firm, steady pressure with the flat of the fingers over the mass; observe whether the swelling collapses completely under pressure and refills slowly when released (cystic hygroma or cavernous haemangioma).

Elicit Fontaine's sign for carotid bifurcation masses: grasp the lump between thumb and index finger; test mobility horizontally across the neck (mobile) and vertically along the line of the carotid vessels (fixed to bifurcation).
Auscultate for a vascular bruit: place the bell of the stethoscope over the mass; listen for a continuous or systolic murmur (carotid body tumour or carotid aneurysm).

skill.exam.surg.lateral_neck_mass.normal: Lateral neck triangles are symmetrical, smooth, and non-tender; no cystic or pulsatile masses; negative transillumination; clear carotid pulsations without thrill or bruit.
skill.exam.surg.lateral_neck_mass.abnormal: Smooth, painless, ovoid, fluctuant, non-translucent mass along the upper anterior border of SCM (branchial cyst); soft, lobulated, brilliantly transilluminant, highly compressible mass in the lower posterior triangle of an infant (cystic hygroma); firm pulsatile mass at the carotid bifurcation that moves laterally but not vertically, with an audible systolic bruit (carotid body tumour); expansile pulsatile mass with thrill along the carotid line (carotid artery aneurysm).
skill.exam.surg.lateral_neck_mass.significance: Brilliant transillumination and compressibility identify cystic hygroma. Fontaine's sign and systolic bruit identify a carotid body tumour, where incisional biopsy is absolutely contraindicated due to uncontrollable life-threatening bleeding.
skill.exam.surg.lateral_neck_mass.practice: Practise the transillumination test in a darkened room using a pen torch and dark cardboard tube on cystic versus solid models, and rehearse Fontaine's horizontal-versus-vertical mobility test.
pitfalls: Attempting needle aspiration or incisional biopsy of a carotid body tumour in the clinic, mistaking it for a lymph node, causing massive arterial haemorrhage.
Failing to darken the room completely when performing transillumination on a cystic hygroma, resulting in a false-negative result.
Mistaking an inflamed branchial cyst for an acute tuberculous cold abscess, leading to inappropriate incision and a persistent branchial fistula.

probes.q: What physical sign is classically positive in a cystic hygroma of the posterior triangle of the neck?
probes.a: Brilliant transillumination (translucency) and marked compressibility.

probes.q: What microscopic finding in the needle aspirate confirms the diagnosis of a branchial cyst?
probes.a: Abundant cholesterol crystals appearing as rectangular notched plates under light microscopy.

probes.q: Explain Fontaine's sign in the examination of a carotid body tumour.
probes.a: The tumour is mobile in the horizontal (transverse) plane but fixed in the vertical (longitudinal) plane because it is anchored to the carotid bifurcation.

rubric.text: Accurately maps the lump relative to the anterior and posterior borders of SCM
Performs transillumination test in a darkened room with a shaded tube
Tests for compressibility and refilling upon release of pressure
Tests horizontal versus vertical mobility (Fontaine's sign) and auscultates for bruit

teach.heading: Diagnostic differences among common lateral neck masses
Embryology of the branchial apparatus and cyst contents
teach.body:
A branchial cyst arises from the persistence of the cervical sinus of His, formed when the second branchial arch grows downwards over the third and fourth arches.

It is lined by squamous or columnar epithelium and filled with thick, opalescent fluid containing desquamated epithelial cells and characteristic notched cholesterol crystals, which gleam under the microscope.

teach.heading: Carotid body tumour: Shamblin classification and surgical risk
teach.body:
Carotid body paragangliomas arise from neural crest chemoreceptor cells at the carotid adventitia. The Shamblin classification grades them based on vessel encasement: Group I (minimally attached), Group II (partially surrounding), and Group III (completely encasing carotid vessels).

Because of intense vascularity, pre-operative angiography and embolisation are standard; biopsy is strictly forbidden.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.surg.thyroid.title: Thyroid Swelling and Functional History
skill.hx.surg.thyroid.oneLine: Evaluating goitre duration, growth tempo, aerodigestive compression, thyrotoxicosis, and goitre belt origin
skill.hx.surg.thyroid.why: Thyroid disorders present across three axes: anatomical enlargement (goitre), functional endocrine derangement (thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism), and invasive neoplasia. A structured surgical history must distinguish slow benign growth from sudden painful expansion (intra-nodular haemorrhage) or rapid invasive growth (anaplastic carcinoma), screen for compression of the trachea, oesophagus, and recurrent laryngeal nerve, and separate primary from secondary thyrotoxicosis.

asks.text: When did you first notice the swelling in your neck, and has it grown slowly over years or enlarged rapidly in recent weeks?
Did the lump suddenly enlarge accompanied by acute pain (haemorrhage into a thyroid nodule or subacute thyroiditis)?
Do you have difficulty breathing, choking when lying flat, or a whistling noise when breathing (stridor from tracheal compression)?
Have you noticed any change in your voice, roughness, or persistent hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion)?
Do you have difficulty swallowing solid food (dysphagia from retrotracheal oesophageal compression)?
Do you feel excessively hot when others are comfortable, sweat profusely, or prefer cold weather (heat intolerance)?
Have you lost weight despite an increased appetite, or do your hands shake when holding a cup (fine tremor)?
Do you have palpitations or feel your heart beating fast or irregularly (atrial fibrillation in toxic goitre)?
Where were you born and brought up, and do members of your family have neck swellings (endemic goitre belt, familial dyshormonogenesis)?

skill.hx.surg.thyroid.practice: Practise taking a thyroid history from a peer, specifically contrasting the nervous and ocular picture of primary thyrotoxicosis with the cardiovascular picture of secondary toxic goitre.
pitfalls: Dismissing recent rapid growth and hoarseness in a longstanding goitre as simple aging, missing anaplastic transformation or invasive follicular carcinoma.
Attributing atrial fibrillation and heart failure in an elderly patient to hypertensive heart disease without screening for an autonomous multinodular toxic goitre.
Failing to ask about residence in an endemic goitre belt (Himalayan or sub-Himalayan regions) or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.

probes.q: What event classically causes a painless longstanding thyroid nodule to enlarge suddenly and become acutely painful overnight?
probes.a: Spontaneous haemorrhage into an adenomatous or colloid cyst nodule.

probes.q: How do the clinical presentations of primary thyrotoxicosis (Graves' disease) and secondary thyrotoxicosis (toxic multinodular goitre) differ in organ system emphasis?
probes.a: Primary thyrotoxicosis mainly affects the nervous and ocular systems (anxiety, fine tremor, exophthalmos), whereas secondary thyrotoxicosis mainly affects the cardiovascular system (atrial fibrillation, arrhythmias, cardiac failure).

probes.q: Why does a patient with an enlarging goitre develop stridor and dyspnoea specifically when flexing the neck forwards or lying flat?
probes.a: Flexion forces the goitre downwards into the narrow thoracic inlet, exacerbating tracheal compression, and gravity allows retrosternal tissue to collapse against the trachea.

rubric.text: Determines duration, growth rate, and checks for acute painful enlargement
Screens systematically for dyspnoea/stridor, dysphagia, and hoarseness of voice
Evaluates symptoms of hyperthyroidism versus hypothyroidism
Inquires about endemic goitre belt origin and dietary goitrogens

rows: Eye signs usually absent (lid retraction only)

teach.heading: The three compressive symptoms in thyroid disease
teach.body:
Because the thyroid lobes hug the anterolateral aspect of the upper trachea and oesophagus, massive or invasive goitres produce mechanical symptoms.

Tracheal compression produces dyspnoea and stridor, worsening with neck flexion; oesophageal compression causes dysphagia, usually for solids; and recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion causes hoarseness, which is a strong pointer towards thyroid carcinoma.

teach.heading: Endemic goitre belts in India
teach.body:
Endemic goitre arises in regions where soil and water are leached of iodine by glaciation or intense monsoon flooding.

In India, the classical goitre belt extends along the entire Himalayan and sub-Himalayan ranges from Jammu and Kashmir through Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, the Terai, and North-East states, with additional pockets in the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.title: Thyroid Gland Inspection
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.oneLine: Posture, deglutition movement, Pizzillo's manoeuvre, lower border visibility, and dilated veins
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.why: A normal thyroid gland is neither visible nor palpable. Inspection establishes whether an anterior neck swelling moves with deglutition, confirming thyroid or thyroglossal origin. In obese or short-necked patients, goitres are easily missed; Pizzillo's manoeuvre projects the thyroid gland forward. Determining whether the lower border rises above the suprasternal notch during swallowing is the first clinical clue to retrosternal extension.

steps.text: Position the patient seated comfortably upright with the neck in neutral position or slightly extended, with the neck and upper chest fully exposed to the nipples in good tangential light.

Inspect the lower anterior neck between the thyroid cartilage and suprasternal notch: observe the symmetry, contours of both lateral lobes and the isthmus, and note whether the enlargement is diffuse or nodular.

Perform the deglutition test on inspection: give the patient a glass of water, ask them to take a sip, hold it in the mouth, and swallow on your instruction; watch the swelling ascend and descend smoothly with the larynx.

Observe the lower border of the swelling during swallowing: note whether the inferior margin rises completely above the suprasternal notch, or remains submerged beneath the manubrium (suggesting retrosternal goitre).

Perform Pizzillo's manoeuvre in short-necked, obese, or deeply muscled patients: instruct the patient to clasp both hands behind the occiput and push the head backwards against their hands; observe the thyroid projected forwards as strap muscles tighten.

Inspect the skin and venous network: check for dilated, engorged subcutaneous collateral veins over the upper chest (thoracic inlet obstruction), previous surgical collar scars, redness, or skin puckering.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.normal: Lower anterior neck is symmetrical; thyroid gland is invisible at rest and does not produce a visible bulge on swallowing; no dilated chest veins, scars, or Pizzillo prominence.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.abnormal: Symmetrical butterfly-shaped swelling rising on swallowing (diffuse hyperplastic or colloid goitre); discrete asymmetrical nodule moving with deglutition (solitary thyroid nodule); bosselated multinodular mass rising on deglutition (multinodular goitre); lower border that cannot be seen on swallowing because it extends beneath the sternum (retrosternal goitre); fixed mass that fails to rise on swallowing (locally invasive anaplastic carcinoma or Riedel's thyroiditis); engorged anterior chest collateral veins.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.significance: Upward movement on deglutition confirms attachment to the pretracheal fascia and larynx. Inability to visualize the lower border during swallowing indicates retrosternal prolongation requiring CT imaging.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_inspection.practice: Practise inspecting the thyroid in tangential light while administering sips of water, and rehearse Pizzillo's manoeuvre on a peer with a muscular neck to observe thyroid prominence.
pitfalls: Asking the patient to swallow without water; repetitive dry swallowing produces fatigue, inadequate laryngeal excursion, and uncoordinated muscle twitches.
Hyperextending the patient's neck excessively during inspection, which stretches the platysma and sternocleidomastoid muscles and flattens a soft goitre.
Overlooking small collar scars from remote childhood neck surgery or previous thyroid lobectomy in the lower neck skin crease.

probes.q: Why does a thyroid swelling move upwards when the patient swallows?
probes.a: Because the thyroid gland is enveloped by the pretracheal fascia, which anchors it firmly to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages of the larynx.

probes.q: What is Pizzillo's manoeuvre, and when is it particularly useful in clinical practice?
probes.a: The patient clasps both hands behind the head and pushes the head backwards against resistance; it projects a small or deeply situated goitre forwards in short-necked or obese individuals.

probes.q: What physical finding on inspection during swallowing strongly suggests a retrosternal goitre?
probes.a: The lower border of the swelling cannot be seen rising above the suprasternal notch during deglutition.

rubric.text: Exposes the neck fully to the nipples under tangential lighting with neck neutral
Observes movement of the lump during swallowing with a sip of water
Inspects whether the lower margin rises above the suprasternal notch
Demonstrates or describes Pizzillo's manoeuvre for short or muscular necks

teach.heading: The anatomical basis of deglutition movement
teach.body:
The thyroid gland is invested by the visceral layer of pretracheal fascia, which splits to enclose both lobes and the isthmus. Posterosuperiorly, this fascia thickens into the lateral suspensory ligament of Berry, attached to the cricoid cartilage and upper tracheal rings.

During swallowing, the suprahyoid muscles and stylopharyngeus elevate the larynx; because of Berry's ligament, the thyroid gland must ascend synchronously.

teach.heading: Diagnostic inspection features of common thyroid swellings

rows: Moves on swallow AND tongue protrusion

teach.heading: Pizzillo's manoeuvre: the biomechanics
teach.body:
In individuals with short, thick necks or bulky sternocleidomastoid muscles, a thyroid goitre can lie buried in the root of the neck.

When the patient clasps hands over the occiput and pushes back, isometric contraction of the neck extensors hyperextends the cervical spine while tensing the infrahyoid strap muscles. This compresses the visceral compartment and thrusts the thyroid gland forward.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.title: Thyroid Gland Palpation
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.oneLine: Posterior palpation, getting below the gland, Lahey's method, Kocher's test, and Berry's sign
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.why: Palpating the thyroid from behind with the neck slightly flexed relaxes the sternocleidomastoid muscles and investing cervical fascia. Determining whether the examiner's fingers can 'get below' the lower pole during swallowing excludes retrosternal extension. Palpating consistency, tracheal alignment, Kocher's test for stridor, and Berry's sign (carotid pulse encasement) establishes malignancy, airway danger, and surgical resectability.

steps.text: Stand behind the seated patient; passively flex the patient's neck slightly by placing both thumbs against the occiput and posterior neck, relaxing the sternocleidomastoid and strap muscles.

Place the index, middle, and ring fingers of both hands over the lateral lobes and isthmus in the lower anterior neck; palpate the gland systematically for size, contour, surface (smooth vs bosselated), and consistency (soft, firm, hard, or variable).

Perform the 'getting below the swelling' test: place finger pulps immediately above the suprasternal notch at the lower border of the thyroid; ask the patient to swallow a sip of water; feel whether the lower border slips completely above your fingertips.

Perform Lahey's method for each lateral lobe: stand in front or behind the patient; use the left hand to push the thyroid gland across to the patient's right side, making the right lobe prominent; palpate the right lobe thoroughly with the right fingers, then reverse hands.
Assess tracheal alignment: palpate the suprasternal trachea gently with the index finger to confirm whether the trachea is strictly midline or displaced to one side by an asymmetrical goitre.
Perform Kocher's test: apply gentle lateral compression with your fingers across both lateral lobes; observe whether inspiratory stridor is provoked, indicating a narrowed 'scabbard' trachea.

Test Berry's sign for carotid sheath encasement: palpate deeply along the posterior border of each thyroid lobe against the cervical spine; verify whether normal common carotid artery pulsations are felt (intact in benign goitre; obliterated/encased in thyroid carcinoma).

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.normal: Thyroid lobes are impalpable or barely perceptible as smooth, soft, non-tender tissue moving freely on swallowing; fingers easily get below the lower poles; trachea is central; Kocher's test is negative; carotid pulsations are easily felt behind both lobes.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.abnormal: Bosselated multinodular gland of variable consistency (multinodular goitre); stony hard, fixed mass infiltrating strap muscles (thyroid carcinoma or Riedel's thyroiditis); fingers cannot get below the lower border on deglutition (retrosternal goitre); marked tracheal deviation; positive Kocher's test with stridor on gentle lateral compression; positive Berry's sign (absent carotid pulse due to malignant encasement).
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.significance: Berry's sign distinguishes thyroid malignancy from benign goitre (benign goitres push the carotid artery posteriorly without obliterating its pulse). Positive Kocher's test warns of tracheomalacia or critical 'scabbard' tracheal compression.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_palpation.practice: Rehearse posterior thyroid palpation on a peer, verifying neck flexion, performing Lahey's lateral push to feel each lobe, and palpating the carotid pulse behind the thyroid lobe.
pitfalls: Attempting to palpate the thyroid with the patient's neck extended, which tightens the sternocleidomastoids and prevents fingertips from feeling the lobes.
Compressing the trachea forcefully during Kocher's test in a patient with severe airway narrowing, precipitating acute respiratory distress.
Mistaking the prominent greater cornu of the hyoid bone or an aberrant cervical lymph node for a solitary thyroid nodule.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance if the examiner's fingers cannot 'get below' the lower border of a thyroid swelling when the patient swallows?
probes.a: It indicates retrosternal (substernal or intrathoracic) extension of the goitre into the superior mediastinum.

probes.q: How does Lahey's manoeuvre facilitate detailed palpation of a thyroid nodule?
probes.a: By pushing the thyroid gland towards one side with one hand, the contralateral lobe is projected laterally away from the trachea, making it prominent for palpation with the other hand.

probes.q: Explain Berry's sign in the examination of a thyroid swelling and its diagnostic significance.
probes.a: The common carotid pulse is obliterated because a malignant thyroid tumour encases the carotid sheath; a benign goitre displaces the sheath posteriorly so the pulse remains palpable.

rubric.text: Stands behind the patient with the neck slightly flexed to relax strap muscles
Tests whether fingers can get below the lower thyroid poles during swallowing
Performs Lahey's lateral displacement method to examine each lobe individually
Tests Kocher's tracheal compression test and checks carotid pulses (Berry's sign)

teach.heading: Standard palpation methods: Crile versus Lahey

rows: Both hands over lobes, neck flexed
Best for overall symmetry and size
Push trachea to side, palpate opposite
Thumb on thyroid lobe during swallow
Sensitive for small nodules in isthmus

teach.heading: Kocher's test and the 'scabbard' trachea
teach.body:
Longstanding bilateral multinodular goitres can compress the cartilaginous tracheal rings from both sides, narrowing the lumen into a vertical slit known radiologically as a 'scabbard trachea'.

Kocher's test involves gently compressing both lateral lobes together. If this produces inspiratory stridor or respiratory distress, the trachea is critically narrowed, warning of possible tracheomalacia after thyroidectomy.

teach.heading: Berry's sign: malignant encasement versus benign displacement
teach.body:
The common carotid artery lies directly posterolateral to the thyroid lobes within the carotid sheath. A benign goitre expands smoothly and pushes the carotid sheath posteriorly and laterally, so the carotid pulse is readily felt at the posterior border of the mass.

An invasive thyroid carcinoma (papillary, follicular, or anaplastic) infiltrates and encases the carotid sheath, dampening or completely abolishing the palpable carotid pulse (positive Berry's sign).

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.title: Retrosternal Goitre Clinical Assessment
skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.oneLine: Pemberton's sign, manubrial percussion dullness, dilated collateral veins, and thoracic inlet compression
skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.why: Between 5% and 15% of thyroid goitres extend into the superior mediastinum beneath the sternum and clavicles. Because the thoracic inlet is a rigid ring of bone (manubrium, first ribs, and T1 vertebra), an expanding substernal goitre compresses the low-pressure internal jugular and brachiocephalic veins, trachea, and oesophagus. Eliciting Pemberton's sign (facial plethora, cyanosis, and venous distension upon elevating both arms) confirms thoracic inlet venous occlusion.

steps.text: Inspect the anterior chest wall, infraclavicular fossae, and root of the neck: look for dilated, engorged, tortuous subcutaneous collateral veins.

Palpate the lower border of the cervical thyroid: attempt to palpate the inferior margin during swallowing; record whether fingers can get below the swelling or whether it continues downwards behind the manubrium.
Perform Pemberton's sign: instruct the patient to raise both arms straight up above the head until they touch the sides of the ears.
Maintain the arm elevation for up to 60 seconds: observe the patient's face, neck veins, and breathing closely throughout the test.
Record the vascular and respiratory response: note whether progressive facial congestion, plethora, cyanosis, bulging of external jugular veins, and inspiratory stridor or distress develop.

Perform sternal percussion: percuss with a pleximeter finger directly over the manubrium sterni from the suprasternal notch downwards to the sternal angle of Louis; note whether the normal resonant bone note is replaced by dullness.

skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.normal: Fingers easily get below the lower thyroid poles on swallowing; no dilated anterior chest veins; manubrium sterni is resonant on percussion; Pemberton's test produces no facial flushing, cyanosis, venous engorgement, or dyspnoea after 60 seconds.
skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.abnormal: Lower border of thyroid cannot be reached on swallowing; manubrial percussion note is flat and dull; Pemberton's sign is positive, with progressive facial plethora, cyanosis, distension of external jugular veins, and inspiratory stridor developing within 60 seconds of arm elevation.
skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.significance: A positive Pemberton's sign confirms acute superior vena cava / thoracic inlet venous obstruction caused by a substernal goitre being pulled into the narrow inlet like a wedge, dictating urgent cross-sectional imaging (contrast CT of the neck and chest) and surgical decompression.
skill.exam.surg.retrosternal_goitre.practice: Practise performing Pemberton's test on peers, timing the arm elevation for 60 seconds and observing normal venous drainage, and percussing the manubrium sterni to master its normal resonance.
pitfalls: Terminating Pemberton's test after only 10 seconds; venous engorgement and plethora often require 30 to 60 seconds of sustained arm elevation to become clinically apparent.
Continuing Pemberton's test when the patient develops marked stridor or syncope; immediately lower the arms if severe respiratory distress or dizziness supervenes.
Assuming an elderly patient with dyspnoea when lying on one side has congestive heart failure without examining for a retrosternal goitre compressed by the trachea.

probes.q: How is Pemberton's sign performed at the bedside in a patient suspected of having a retrosternal goitre?
probes.a: The patient raises both arms vertically until they touch the sides of the head and ears, maintaining this position for up to 60 seconds.

probes.q: What physical changes indicate a positive Pemberton's sign?
probes.a: Facial plethora (flushing), cyanosis, distension of neck and forehead veins, and the development of inspiratory stridor or respiratory distress.

probes.q: Explain the anatomical mechanism that produces facial congestion during Pemberton's test.
probes.a: Arm elevation lifts the clavicles and forces the thyroid mass downwards into the rigid bony thoracic inlet like a wedge, compressing the internal jugular and brachiocephalic veins.

rubric.text: Inspects the upper anterior chest wall for dilated collateral venous channels
Correctly instructs patient to raise arms to touch ears and holds position for up to 60 seconds
Observes face for plethora, cyanosis, and external jugular venous distension
Percusses over the manubrium sterni to detect retrosternal dullness

rows: Mobile mass moving between neck and chest

teach.heading: The cork-in-the-bottle mechanism of Pemberton's sign
teach.body:
In 1946, Hugh Pemberton described the sign that bears his name. The thoracic inlet is bounded by the manubrium anteriorly, first ribs laterally, and T1 vertebra posteriorly.

When both arms are elevated, the clavicles move upwards and the inlet narrows, while traction on the cervical fascia forces the thyroid mass downwards like a cork into a bottle neck, abruptly obstructing venous return.

teach.heading: Tracheal deviation and 'scabbard' trachea
teach.body:
Retrosternal goitres frequently compress and deviate the trachea into a C-shaped curve or compress it bilaterally into an anteroposterior slot (scabbard trachea).

Patients report postural dyspnoea that worsens when turning the head or lying on one side. Plain chest radiograph reveals superior mediastinal widening and tracheal displacement, but contrast CT is the definitive investigation.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.title: Thyroid Auscultation and Bruit
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.oneLine: Superior pole auscultation to detect Graves' hyperaemia and separating thyroid bruit from carotid murmur and venous hum
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.why: In Graves' disease (primary toxic diffuse goitre), thyroid vascularity increases by up to ten-fold due to intense neo-angiogenesis. Auscultating a continuous vascular bruit with systolic accentuation over the superior thyroid poles confirms thyrotoxic hyperaemia. The clinician must reliably distinguish a true thyroid bruit from a transmitted carotid artery stenosis murmur, an aortic valve murmur, and a benign cervical venous hum, because a thyroid bruit warns of severe intraoperative haemorrhage.

steps.text: Warm the bell of the stethoscope with your palm; explain the examination to the seated patient.
Place the stethoscope bell lightly over the superior pole of each thyroid lobe anterolaterally, just beneath the thyroid cartilage lamina.
Instruct the patient to hold their breath in expiration for a few seconds to eliminate respiratory tracheal breath sounds.
Listen for a low-pitched, continuous vascular murmur with systolic accentuation: note whether it is accompanied by a fine palpable vascular thrill ('cat's purr') under your fingertips.

Differentiate from a carotid arterial bruit: move the stethoscope bell laterally over the carotid triangle and carotid bifurcation; a carotid bruit is loudest at the angle of the jaw and radiates along the vessel, whereas a thyroid bruit is loudest over the thyroid gland itself.

Differentiate from an aortic stenosis murmur: auscultate the aortic area (second right intercostal space) and carotid arteries; an aortic murmur radiates from the precordium into both carotids, whereas a thyroid bruit is confined to the neck.

Differentiate from a cervical venous hum: apply gentle finger pressure over the internal jugular vein immediately lateral to the thyroid lobe; a venous hum is abolished by light venous compression, whereas an arterial thyroid bruit persists unchanged.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.normal: No audible murmurs, bruits, hums, or palpable vascular thrills over the thyroid lobes or carotid sheath during breath-holding.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.abnormal: Continuous or systolic vascular bruit with systolic accentuation heard over the superior thyroid poles, often accompanied by a fine palpable thrill (Graves' disease); harsh systolic murmur radiating from the base of the neck to the jaw angle (carotid artery stenosis); continuous roaring hum abolished by gentle internal jugular compression (cervical venous hum).
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.significance: A true thyroid bruit confirms Graves' disease with extreme glandular vascularity. It indicates that preoperative preparation with Lugol's iodine or potassium iodide is necessary to reduce glandular blood flow before thyroidectomy.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_bruit.practice: Practise auscultating the superior thyroid pole with the stethoscope bell while the subject holds their breath in expiration, and test internal jugular compression to differentiate venous hums.
pitfalls: Pressing the stethoscope diaphragm too firmly over the neck, creating an artificial compression bruit over a normal carotid artery.
Failing to ask the patient to hold their breath, mistaking harsh bronchial tracheal breath sounds for a vascular murmur.
Mistaking an aortic valve stenosis ejection systolic murmur radiating into the neck for a thyroid bruit; always auscultate the precordium.

probes.q: What pathological condition of the thyroid is classically associated with an audible vascular bruit over the gland?
probes.a: Graves' disease (primary toxic diffuse goitre) due to marked glandular hypervascularity.

probes.q: At which anatomical site on the thyroid gland is a thyroid bruit most readily detected with the stethoscope?
probes.a: Over the superior poles of the lateral lobes, where the superior thyroid arteries enter the gland.

probes.q: How can the examiner definitively differentiate a true thyroid bruit from a cervical venous hum at the bedside?
probes.a: By applying gentle finger pressure over the internal jugular vein above the clavicle; a venous hum is completely obliterated, whereas a thyroid bruit persists.

rubric.text: Uses the bell of the stethoscope placed lightly over the superior thyroid poles
Instructs the patient to hold their breath during auscultation to eliminate breath sounds
Palpates for a corresponding vascular systolic thrill over the superior pole
Distinguishes the thyroid bruit from a transmitted carotid murmur and venous hum

teach.heading: Haemodynamics of the thyroid bruit in Graves' disease
teach.body:
Under intense stimulation by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), the follicular cells proliferate and secretomotor demands escalate. Total thyroid blood flow rises from a normal 5 mL/min/g to over 50 mL/min/g.

The superior and inferior thyroid arteries dilate markedly, and large arteriovenous shunts develop within the parenchyma, generating turbulent blood flow that produces a palpable thrill and an audible bruit.

teach.heading: Preoperative preparation with Lugol's iodine
teach.body:
Operating on a thyroid with an active thrill and bruit carries severe risk of catastrophic intraoperative bleeding from friable capsular vessels.

Administering Lugol's solution (5% iodine and 10% potassium iodide) for 10 to 14 days before surgery invokes the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, sharply reducing glandular vascularity, firming the gland, and abolishing the bruit.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.title: Thyrotoxic Eye Signs Examination
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.oneLine: Systematic elicitation of Dalrymple, Von Graefe, Stellwag, Moebius, and Joffroy signs
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.why: Ocular manifestations in thyrotoxicosis are divided into two distinct pathophysiological groups: sympathetic overactivity of the superior palpebral muscle of Muller (causing lid retraction and lid lag in any thyrotoxicosis) and autoimmune infiltrative Graves' orbitopathy (glycosaminoglycan deposition, retro-orbital fat expansion, extraocular muscle fibrosis, proptosis, and optic neuropathy). Accurately testing and differentiating these signs grades orbitopathy severity and prevents corneal ulceration and vision loss.

steps.text: Inspect the eyes from the front at eye level: observe for Dalrymple's sign (retraction of the upper eyelid with a rim of white sclera visible between the superior limbus and the upper lid margin in neutral gaze).
Observe blinking frequency and facial expression: note Stellwag's sign (infrequent, incomplete blinking with a wide, staring, apprehensive facial look).

Inspect from behind and above using Naffziger's method: stand behind the seated patient, tilt their head slightly backwards, and look down over the forehead along the superciliary ridges to detect true forward proptosis (exophthalmos) of the eyeballs.

Test for Von Graefe's sign (lid lag): hold your index finger 40 cm in front of the patient's eyes; instruct them to follow your finger downwards smoothly without moving the head; observe whether the upper lid lags behind the descending globe, exposing white sclera above the iris.

Test for Moebius' sign (convergence failure): hold your finger 30 cm in front of the patient's eyes in the midline and move it smoothly towards the bridge of the nose; observe whether both eyes converge symmetrically, or whether one or both eyes fail to maintain convergence within 10 cm.

Test for Joffroy's sign: ask the patient to look upwards towards the ceiling while keeping the head tilted slightly downwards; observe whether normal horizontal wrinkles on the forehead are absent despite upward gaze.

Inspect the conjunctiva and test extraocular movements: check for chemosis (oedema of conjunctiva causing crinkled jelly-like fold), corneal injection or ulceration, and test upward and outward gaze for ophthalmoplegia.

skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.normal: Upper eyelid covers the upper 1 to 2 mm of the cornea; no sclera visible above the limbus; normal blinking rate (15 to 20 per minute); upper lid descends smoothly and synchronously with the eyeball on downward gaze; eyes converge to within 8 to 10 cm of the nose; symmetrical forehead wrinkling on looking up; no proptosis or chemosis.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.abnormal: Sclera visible above superior limbus at rest (Dalrymple's sign); upper lid lags behind eyeball on down-gaze (Von Graefe's sign); staring look with infrequent blinking (Stellwag's sign); failure of ocular convergence within 10 cm of nose (Moebius' sign); lack of forehead wrinkling on looking up (Joffroy's sign); true forward proptosis > 20 mm; conjunctival chemosis with crinkling and corneal injection; limitation of elevation and abduction (ophthalmoplegia).
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.significance: Lid retraction and lid lag are non-infiltrative signs caused by sympathetic stimulation, occurring in any toxic state; true exophthalmos, chemosis, and ophthalmoplegia are infiltrative autoimmune markers exclusive to Graves' disease and can progress independently of thyroid hormone levels.
skill.exam.surg.thyroid_eye_signs.practice: Practise eliciting Von Graefe's sign smoothly by moving a finger downwards at moderate speed, and rehearse Naffziger's view from behind over the forehead on peers.
pitfalls: Moving the target finger down too rapidly during Von Graefe's test; rapid movement causes saccadic tracking and false lid lag in normal individuals.
Equating simple upper lid retraction with true exophthalmos; lid retraction is sympathetic overactivity, whereas exophthalmos is true anatomical forward displacement of the globe.
Missing malignant progressive exophthalmos with chemosis, which can lead to rapid exposure keratitis, corneal perforation, and blindness.

probes.q: What is Von Graefe's sign, and how is it elicited at the bedside?
probes.a: Lid lag: the upper eyelid lags behind the eyeball as the patient follows an examiner's finger moving slowly downwards, exposing white sclera above the iris.

probes.q: Differentiate Dalrymple's sign from Stellwag's sign in thyrotoxicosis.
probes.a: Dalrymple's sign is upper eyelid retraction with visible sclera above the superior limbus; Stellwag's sign is infrequent, incomplete blinking with a staring look.

probes.q: Why does infiltrative Graves' orbitopathy (exophthalmos and ophthalmoplegia) occur in Graves' disease but not in toxic multinodular goitre?
probes.a: Because Graves' orbitopathy is an autoimmune disorder driven by antibodies against TSH receptors on retro-orbital fibroblasts and adipocytes, which are absent in autonomous toxic multinodular goitre.

rubric.text: Inspects for upper lid retraction (Dalrymple) and infrequent blinking (Stellwag)
Performs smooth downward finger tracking to elicit Von Graefe's lid lag
Views the globes from above and behind (Naffziger's method) for true proptosis
Tests convergence (Moebius' sign) and forehead wrinkling (Joffroy's sign)

teach.heading: Summary of classical thyrotoxic eye signs

rows: Upper lid retraction, sclera seen above limbus
Sympathetic spasm of Muller's superior palpebral muscle
Upper lid lags behind globe on looking down
Spasm and fibrosis of levator palpebrae superioris
Infrequent, incomplete blinking with staring gaze
Inability to maintain convergence within 10 cm
Weakness / fibrosis of medial rectus muscles
Absence of forehead wrinkles on upward gaze

teach.heading: Non-infiltrative versus infiltrative ophthalmopathy
teach.body:
Non-infiltrative signs (Dalrymple, Von Graefe, Stellwag) are produced purely by excessive sympathetic stimulation of smooth muscle fibres in the eyelids. They improve promptly once euthyroid status or beta-blockade is established.

In contrast, infiltrative ophthalmopathy involves autoimmune infiltration by lymphocytes, mucopolysaccharide deposition, and retro-orbital oedema, leading to true exophthalmos and extraocular muscle tethering.

teach.heading: Malignant (progressive) exophthalmos and chemosis
teach.body:
When retro-orbital pressure rises excessively, venous and lymphatic drainage of the conjunctiva becomes obstructed, producing chemosis: the conjunctiva becomes boggy, crinkled, and protrudes between the lids.

The eyelids fail to close over the cornea (lagophthalmos), leading to exposure keratitis, corneal ulceration, and panophthalmitis, requiring emergency systemic steroids, orbital decompression, or tarsorrhaphy.

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.title: Thyrotoxic Systemic Status Examination
skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.oneLine: Assessing sleeping pulse rate, fine peripheral tremor, hot moist palms, hyperreflexia, and pretibial myxoedema
skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.why: Evaluating a thyroid patient requires a comprehensive general physical assessment. The severity of systemic thyrotoxicosis dictates medical treatment and surgical readiness. Subjecting an uncontrolled thyrotoxic patient to thyroidectomy carries an intolerable risk of intraoperative thyroid storm (malignant hyperpyrexia, cardiovascular collapse, and 20% mortality). The sleeping pulse rate is the most reliable clinical barometer of metabolic hyperfunction.

steps.text: Observe general appearance and demeanor: note psychomotor agitation, restlessness, fidgeting, thin emaciated habitus, and wearing light clothing on a cool day.

Palpate the radial pulse for a full 60 seconds: record rate, volume (high-volume bounding pulse), and rhythm; identify irregularity indicating atrial fibrillation; check the hospital temperature-pulse chart for the resting sleeping pulse rate.
Examine the hands and palms: hold the patient's hands immediately after checking the pulse; assess for hot, flushed, moist skin (warm vasodilation and diaphoresis) and palmar erythema.

Test for fine tremor of the hands: ask the patient to extend both arms horizontally forwards with fingers widely abducted; place a sheet of paper over the dorsum of the fingers to amplify and demonstrate the fine rapid tremor.
Test for fine tremor of the tongue: ask the patient to protrude the tongue straight out and maintain it for 30 seconds; observe for fine fibrillary muscle twitching.

Examine deep tendon reflexes: test the biceps and patellar reflexes; observe for brisk hyperreflexia with a characteristically rapid relaxation phase (pseudomyotonia is the opposite in hypothyroidism).

Inspect the lower limbs: examine the anterior shins for pretibial myxoedema (bilateral raised, brawny, non-pitting, violaceous plaques with prominent hair follicles resembling orange peel) and check fingers for thyroid acropachy (clubbing).

skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.normal: Resting pulse 60 to 80 beats per minute, regular; palms are cool and dry; no postural tremor of extended fingers or tongue; normal deep tendon reflexes; smooth, normal pretibial skin without plaques.
skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.abnormal: Tachycardia > 100 beats per minute at rest or irregularly irregular pulse of atrial fibrillation; sleeping pulse rate elevated > 90 bpm; hot, dripping wet palms; fine, rapid tremor shaking paper placed on extended fingers; fibrillary lingual tremors; brisk hyperreflexia with rapid relaxation; violaceous, brawny, non-pitting peau d'orange plaques over the shins (pretibial myxoedema).
skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.significance: Confirms systemic hyperthyroidism. A patient is considered prepared and safe for elective thyroidectomy only when euthyroid clinically (sleeping pulse rate below 80 beats per minute, weight stabilized, tremor eliminated) and biochemically.
skill.gen.surg.thyrotoxic_status.practice: Practise demonstrating the fine tremor of outstretched fingers using a lightweight sheet of paper, and rehearse palpating palmar temperature immediately following pulse examination.
pitfalls: Relying solely on daytime clinic pulse rates, which are elevated by anxiety; the sleeping pulse rate recorded during undisturbed sleep is the true metabolic index.
Operating on a thyrotoxic patient whose pulse rate is over 90 beats per minute, triggering fatal thyroid crisis during or after surgery.
Mistaking pretibial myxoedema for ordinary pitting dependent cardiac oedema; pretibial myxoedema is non-pitting, violaceous, and localized to the shins.

probes.q: How does the sleeping pulse rate grade the clinical severity of thyrotoxicosis?
probes.a: Mild thyrotoxicosis has a sleeping pulse rate under 90 beats/min; moderate is between 90 and 110 beats/min; and severe thyrotoxicosis is above 110 beats/min.

probes.q: What simple bedside manoeuvre makes a fine thyrotoxic hand tremor clearly visible to the examiner?
probes.a: Placing a plain sheet of paper over the dorsum of the patient's outstretched, widely spread fingers to amplify the rapid vibration.

probes.q: What cutaneous lesion on the lower limbs is specifically associated with Graves' disease, and what is its consistency?
probes.a: Pretibial myxoedema; it presents as brawny, non-pitting, violaceous or pinkish-brown plaques with prominent hair follicles (peau d'orange) over the anterior tibia.

rubric.text: Assesses radial pulse rate for 60 seconds and verifies resting/sleeping pulse rate
Checks palmar skin temperature and moisture immediately after pulse palpation
Tests for fine postural tremor of the fingers using a sheet of paper
Inspects and palpates the pretibial skin for non-pitting myxoedematous plaques

teach.heading: Grading thyrotoxicosis by sleeping pulse rate
Pathophysiology of pretibial myxoedema
teach.body:
Despite its confusing name, pretibial myxoedema occurs in hyperthyroid Graves' disease, not in ordinary hypothyroidism. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate TSH receptors on pretibial dermal fibroblasts.

These fibroblasts synthesize excessive hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulphate, binding water to produce dense, brawny, non-pitting mucinous infiltration with hyperkeratosis over the lower shins.

teach.heading: Thyroid storm (crisis): prevention at the bedside
teach.body:
Thyroid crisis is an acute life-threatening hypermetabolic surge caused by excessive release of T3 and T4, triggered by surgical trauma, infection, or abrupt withdrawal of antithyroid therapy.

It manifests with hyperpyrexia (over 40 deg C), extreme tachycardia, delirium, vomiting, and cardiovascular collapse. Meticulous preoperative preparation to achieve a euthyroid pulse prevents this catastrophe.

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
