skill.exam.surg.tetany_postop.title: Postoperative Hypocalcaemic Tetany Assessment
skill.exam.surg.tetany_postop.oneLine: Eliciting Chvostek-Weiss facial percussion and Trousseau's cuff ischaemia signs for latent tetany
skill.exam.surg.tetany_postop.why: Inadvertent devascularisation or excision of the parathyroid glands during total or subtotal thyroidectomy causes acute postoperative hypocalcaemia, typically declaring itself within 24 to 72 hours of surgery. Clinical tetany begins with subtle perioral numbness and tingling before escalating to excruciating carpopedal spasms and fatal laryngospasm. Bedside elicitation of Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign identifies latent hypocalcaemia before neuromuscular crises occur.

steps.text: Question the postoperative thyroid patient specifically about early sensory symptoms: ask about perioral tingling ('pins and needles' around lips and nose), numbness in fingertips, anxiety, and muscle cramps in calves or hands.
Elicit the Chvostek-Weiss sign: position the patient with facial muscles relaxed; identify the trunk of the facial nerve approximately 2 cm anterior to the tragus and just below the zygomatic arch.
Tap the facial nerve trunk sharply: use your index fingertip or a light percussion hammer to tap over the nerve trunk; observe for an immediate, brisk ipsilateral muscular twitch.
Grade the Chvostek response: Grade 1 (twitch of the angle of the mouth only); Grade 2 (twitch of mouth angle and ala of nose); Grade 3 (twitch of mouth, nose, and orbicularis oculi with eye blink).
Elicit Trousseau's sign: wrap a standard sphygmomanometer cuff around the patient's upper arm.
Inflate the cuff above systolic pressure: pump the cuff to 20 mm Hg above the patient's systolic blood pressure (at least 200 mm Hg) to produce complete arterial forearm ischaemia.

Maintain cuff occlusion for 3 full minutes: observe the hand and fingers closely for involuntary carpopedal spasm ('main d'accoucheur' / obstetrician's hand: flexion of wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints, extension of interphalangeal joints, and strong adduction of thumb into the palm).
Release cuff immediately when spasm occurs: verify relief of painful contraction and immediately order stat serum ionized and total calcium levels.

skill.exam.surg.tetany_postop.normal: No perioral or digital tingling; tapping anterior to tragus produces no facial twitch (negative Chvostek); 3 minutes of forearm cuff ischaemia produces no carpopedal spasm, pain, or paraesthesia (negative Trousseau).
skill.exam.surg.tetany_postop.abnormal: Brisk ipsilateral facial muscular twitch on tapping over the facial nerve trunk (positive Chvostek-Weiss sign); involuntary painful carpopedal spasm with thumb adducted, MCP joints flexed, and IP joints extended developing within 3 minutes of cuff occlusion (positive Trousseau's sign); overt tetany with generalized cramps, stridor from laryngospasm, or cardiac arrhythmias.
skill.exam.surg.tetany_postop.significance: Trousseau's sign is highly sensitive (94%) and specific for latent hypocalcaemia (Chvostek's sign is positive in 10-25% of healthy individuals). Recognition mandates immediate slow intravenous administration of 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate to prevent fatal laryngospasm.
skill.exam.surg.tetany_postop.practice: Practise measuring cuff inflation to 20 mm Hg above systolic pressure and monitoring the hand for 3 minutes, and rehearse tapping 2 cm anterior to the tragus to identify the facial nerve trunk.
pitfalls: Deflating the blood pressure cuff after only one minute during Trousseau's test; latent tetanic spasm often requires 2 to 3 minutes of ischaemia to manifest.
Waiting for overt carpopedal spasm or laryngospasm before testing serum calcium in a post-thyroidectomy patient reporting tingling around the mouth.
Pushing intravenous calcium gluconate rapidly through an IV line, risking acute bradycardia, heart block, and cardiac arrest.

probes.q: What classic hand posture constitutes carpopedal spasm (the obstetrician's hand) in hypocalcaemic tetany?
probes.a: Flexion of the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints, extension of the interphalangeal joints, and strong adduction of the thumb into the palm.

probes.q: Between Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign, which is more reliable and specific for latent hypocalcaemia, and why?
probes.a: Trousseau's sign is more reliable and specific (94% sensitivity), because Chvostek's sign is falsely positive in 10 to 25 percent of normal healthy individuals.

probes.q: What is the emergency pharmacological treatment for acute post-thyroidectomy tetany presenting with carpopedal spasm or stridor?
probes.a: Intravenous infusion of 10 millilitres of 10 percent calcium gluconate given slowly over 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring.

rubric.text: Specifically asks the post-thyroidectomy patient about perioral and finger tingling
Taps the facial nerve trunk 2 cm anterior to the tragus to elicit Chvostek's sign
Inflates cuff 20 mm Hg above systolic pressure and observes hand for up to 3 minutes
Accurately identifies the components of carpopedal spasm (MCP flexion, IP extension, thumb adduction)

teach.heading: Eponymous bedside signs of latent tetany

rows: Tap facial nerve trunk 2 cm anterior to tragus
Inflate cuff > systolic BP for 3 minutes

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of hypocalcaemic neuromuscular excitability
teach.body:
Extracellular ionized calcium stabilizes neuronal cell membranes by modulating voltage-gated sodium channels. In hypocalcaemia, the threshold potential shifts closer to the resting potential.

Sodium channels open with minimal depolarization, precipitating spontaneous and repetitive nerve action potentials that trigger muscular fasciculations, painful spasms, and tetany.

teach.heading: Anatomical risk in thyroidectomy and parathyroid preservation
teach.body:
The four parathyroid glands lie on the posterior capsule of the thyroid lobes, supplied mainly by delicate end-arterial branches of the inferior thyroid arteries.

During thyroid lobectomy, capsular dissection with meticulous ligation of tertiary thyroid vessels on the thyroid capsule preserves parathyroid perfusion. If a gland is inadvertently devascularised, it should be minced and autotransplanted into the sternocleidomastoid.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.annex.surg.who_goitre_grading.title: WHO Goitre Classification and Clinical Grading
skill.annex.surg.who_goitre_grading.oneLine: Bedside and epidemiological staging of thyroid enlargement into Grade 0, Grade 1, and Grade 2
skill.annex.surg.who_goitre_grading.why: Standardised grading of thyroid enlargement is essential for consistent clinical communication, tracking goitre evolution under thyroxine suppression, and epidemiological surveillance of iodine deficiency disorders (IDD). The simplified WHO/UNICEF/ICCIDD classification categorises goitre into objective grades based on palpability, visibility with neck extended, and visibility at normal head position.

rows: No goitre; each lateral lobe is smaller than subject thumb terminal phalanx
Each lobe larger than thumb phalanx; moves on swallowing; includes 1A and 1B
Visible with neck in normal position
Goitre clearly visible when looking straight ahead with neck in neutral posture

teach.heading: Historical Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) sub-classification

points.d: Goitre detectable only on palpation, with lateral lobes each larger than the terminal phalanx of the subject's thumb, but not visible even when the neck is fully extended.
Goitre that is palpable and also easily visible when the patient's neck is moderately or fully extended backwards (Pizzillo posture), but not visible in neutral position.
Goitre easily visible with the head and neck in normal anatomical posture at close distance.
Giant or monstrous goitre easily recognized from a distance of several metres, frequently with compressive aerodigestive distortion.

teach.heading: Epidemiological thresholds and endemic goitre definition
teach.body:
According to the World Health Organization, a geographic region is classified as an endemic goitre area when the Total Goitre Rate (TGR) exceeds 5 percent among school-age children between 6 and 12 years of age.

A TGR of 5.0 to 19.9% represents mild iodine deficiency; 20.0 to 29.9% represents moderate deficiency; and 30% or more indicates severe endemic deficiency requiring mandatory universal salt iodisation.

pitfalls: Using the examiner's thumb instead of the patient's own thumb terminal phalanx as the size comparator when evaluating thyroid lobe enlargement in children.
Classifying a goitre as Grade 2 when it is visible only when the patient tilts the head back; visibility in Grade 2 requires neutral, straight-ahead head posture.
Confusing an isolated solitary thyroid nodule with diffuse endemic goitre when calculating community goitre prevalence rates.

probes.q: According to the simplified WHO goitre classification, what anatomical comparator defines a palpable Grade 1 goitre?
probes.a: Each lateral thyroid lobe is larger than the terminal phalanx of the examined subject's own thumb.

probes.q: What physical feature distinguishes a Grade 1 goitre from a Grade 2 goitre under the simplified WHO criteria?
probes.a: A Grade 1 goitre is visible only when the neck is extended, whereas a Grade 2 goitre is clearly visible with the neck in the normal (neutral) position.

probes.q: What epidemiological threshold of Total Goitre Rate (TGR) in school-age children defines an endemic goitre region according to the WHO?
probes.a: A Total Goitre Rate exceeding 5 percent among children aged 6 to 12 years.

rubric.text: Compares thyroid lobe size against the terminal phalanx of the patient's thumb
Evaluates visibility with the patient's head and neck in the neutral straight-ahead position
Accurately assigns WHO Grade 0, Grade 1, or Grade 2 based on palpability and visibility

skill.hx.surg.chest_trauma.title: Chest trauma history
skill.hx.surg.chest_trauma.oneLine: Mechanism of thoracic impact, respiratory distress, and markers of tracheobronchial or visceral injury
skill.hx.surg.chest_trauma.why: Blunt and penetrating chest injuries can rapidly produce fatal hypoxia and hypovolaemia. Eliciting the precise mechanism, velocity, impact point, and symptoms such as haemoptysis guides immediate triage and alerts the surgical team to occult life-threatening injuries.

asks.text: What was the exact mechanism of injury: road traffic crash, fall from height, direct blow, crush injury, or stab wound?
If a vehicle crash, were you the driver or passenger, was a seatbelt worn, did the steering wheel hit your chest, and did the airbag deploy?
Did you experience immediate severe shortness of breath or a feeling of suffocation right after the impact?
Have you coughed up any blood or pink frothy sputum since the injury, which signals pulmonary contusion or tracheobronchial laceration?
Where is the pain located, does it worsen sharply on deep inspiration or coughing, and does it radiate to the shoulder or back?
Did you lose consciousness, and do you have pain in your abdomen, pelvis, neck, or extremities?

skill.hx.surg.chest_trauma.practice: Practise taking a rapid, structured history from an acute trauma patient within two minutes, focusing on velocity, steering wheel impact, seatbelt use, and haemoptysis.
pitfalls: Focusing exclusively on chest wall abrasions while missing the high-velocity deceleration mechanism that causes aortic tear.
Failing to inquire specifically about haemoptysis, which is the primary bedside clinical clue for pulmonary laceration or contusion.
Overlooking associated abdominal or pelvic injuries in crush trauma because chest wall pain dominates the clinical picture.

probes.q: What does coughing up frank blood following blunt chest trauma signify?
probes.a: It indicates pulmonary contusion, parenchymal laceration, or tracheobronchial airway injury.

probes.q: Why is impact against a steering wheel in a motor vehicle collision a critical historical detail?
probes.a: It produces rapid deceleration with direct sternal impact, predisposing to myocardial contusion, flail sternum, tracheobronchial rupture, and traumatic aortic transection.

probes.q: How does crushing trauma produce traumatic asphyxia, and what clinical clues must you seek in the history and appearance?
probes.a: Severe compression of the thoracic cage forces blood retrogradely into the avalvular veins of the head and neck, producing violent venous hypertension that causes extensive petechiae and subconjunctival haemorrhages.

rubric.text: Identifies precise mechanism and impact energy (speed, steering wheel impact, seatbelt)
Asks directly about haemoptysis and sputum character
Characterises pain aggravating factors (pleuritic, positional) and respiratory difficulty
Screens for polytrauma (head, abdominal, spinal, and extremity injuries)

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
ATLS
sources.locator: Thoracic trauma: initial assessment and primary survey

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Mechanism dictates the injury pattern
teach.body:
Thoracic injuries fall into blunt deceleration, crush, and penetrating violence. High-speed road collisions and falls over three metres cause rapid deceleration that places immense traction on the aortic isthmus, while steering wheel impacts fracture the sternum and contuse the myocardium.

Crush injuries between heavy vehicles or collapsed structures compress the chest wall, creating multiple segmental rib fractures and alveolar disruption.

teach.heading: Cardinial symptoms requiring immediate action
points: Immediate severe dyspnoea points to tension pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, or large flail chest.
Haemoptysis indicates alveolar haemorrhage from lung contusion or mucosal tear from tracheobronchial disruption.
Sudden hoarseness or surgical emphysema following blunt neck or chest impact warns of laryngeal or tracheal transection.
Severe interscapular or back pain following rapid deceleration raises high suspicion of acute traumatic aortic injury.

teach.heading: Traumatic asphyxia mechanism
teach.body:
Sudden massive compressive forces on the thorax against a closed glottis abruptly raise superior vena caval pressure. Because head and neck veins lack valves, this hydraulic wave engorges capillaries.

This produces a dramatic violaceous facial discoloration, extensive bilateral subconjunctival ecchymosis, and cutaneous petechiae across the face and upper neck that spare the lower torso.

skill.exam.surg.chest_trauma_survey.title: Chest trauma physical examination
skill.exam.surg.chest_trauma_survey.oneLine: Inspection for paradoxical movement, palpation for rib fractures and surgical emphysema, and thoracic compression testing
skill.exam.surg.chest_trauma_survey.why: Thoracic trauma produces acute mechanical instability and parenchymal injury that must be identified within seconds of patient arrival. Missing flail chest segments, undisplaced rib fractures, or spreading surgical emphysema leads to acute ventilatory failure, tension pneumothorax, and fatal hypoxia.

steps.text: Expose the chest completely from neck to waist with the patient supine, ensuring warm environment and cervical spine protection.
Inspect the chest wall surface for bruises, tyre tread marks, seatbelt signs, penetrating entry or exit wounds, and symmetry of chest contour.

Observe the respiratory pattern for tachypnoea, shallow excursions, intercostal indrawing, and paradoxical respiration where a chest wall segment moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration.
Palpate each rib systematically along its entire length from the sternum anteriorly to the angle posteriorly, feeling for point tenderness, bony steps, and crepitus.

Perform the thoracic compression test when rib fractures are suspected but not pinpointed: place one hand over the sternum and the other over the thoracic spine, applying gentle anteroposterior compression; pain elicited at a lateral rib site confirms a fracture.
Palpate the subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall, neck, face, and axillae for surgical emphysema, feeling the characteristic crackling bubble-wrap sensation.
Percuss both hemithoraces systematically from apex to base, comparing resonance, hyper-resonance, and dullness.
Auscultate breath sounds in all lung zones, noting diminished sounds, absent air entry, or added crackles of pulmonary contusion.

skill.exam.surg.chest_trauma_survey.normal: Symmetrical chest wall excursions without paradoxical indrawing, absence of bruising or penetrating wounds, non-tender rib cage on direct palpation and compression, no subcutaneous crepitus, resonant percussion notes bilaterally, and vesicular breath sounds throughout both lung fields.
skill.exam.surg.chest_trauma_survey.abnormal: Paradoxical chest wall movement with an unstable flail segment, localized bony crepitus and sharp rib tenderness, pain on anteroposterior thoracic compression, crackling subcutaneous emphysema extending across the chest wall and neck, unilateral percussion hyper-resonance or stony dullness, and absent or muffled breath sounds.
skill.exam.surg.chest_trauma_survey.significance: Paradoxical movement denotes a flail chest with underlying pulmonary contusion. Subcutaneous emphysema proves air leakage from a ruptured bronchus, lung laceration, or oesophagus. Sharp lateral rib pain on sternal compression localises an undisplaced rib fracture away from the examiner hands.
skill.exam.surg.chest_trauma_survey.practice: Perform the anteroposterior thoracic compression manoeuvre on a training mannequin, and practise palpating bubble-wrap beneath a sheet to replicate the sensation of subcutaneous emphysema.
pitfalls: Applying forceful thoracic compression in severe crushing injury, which can displace rib fragments into the underlying lung parenchyma or intercostal vessels.
Missing a flail chest segment early after trauma because powerful chest wall muscle splinting temporarily masks paradoxical movement.
Dismissing localized surgical emphysema without checking for an occult pneumothorax or major tracheobronchial tear.

probes.q: How do you perform the compression test for an occult rib fracture?
probes.a: Place one hand on the sternum and the other on the thoracic spine, then compress the thorax anteroposteriorly; pain felt at a lateral rib site away from the hands confirms a fracture.

probes.q: What anatomical definition constitutes a flail chest, and what is its physiological hallmark?
probes.a: Fracture of three or more contiguous ribs in two or more places (or ribs with sternum), creating an unstable segment that moves paradoxically inward during inspiration and outward during expiration.

probes.q: Why is the underlying pulmonary contusion more clinically significant than the paradoxical chest wall movement itself in flail chest?
probes.a: The severe contusion causes alveolar flooding, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, microvascular thrombosis, and loss of pulmonary compliance, which drive profound hypoxaemia requiring ventilatory support.

rubric.text: Fully exposes the chest and inspects for paradoxical respiration and skin marks
Palpates ribs individually and applies gentle anteroposterior compression correctly
Checks for subcutaneous surgical emphysema over chest, neck, and axilla
Percusses and auscultates both hemithoraces to assess symmetry of air entry

teach.heading: Detecting flail chest and paradoxical motion
teach.body:
Flail chest occurs when at least three consecutive ribs are broken in two places, detaching an unstable segment. During inspiration, falling intrapleural pressure sucks the flail segment inward while the normal chest expands.

During expiration, increasing intrathoracic pressure pushes the flail segment outward. This paradoxical motion impairs tidal volume and increases the work of breathing.

teach.heading: Subcutaneous surgical emphysema
teach.body:
Air escaping from a ruptured lung, bronchus, or open chest wound tracks along fascial planes into subcutaneous tissues. Palpation reveals a distinct crackling or bubble-wrap sensation.

While surgical emphysema itself is rarely dangerous, it is an unmistakable sign of underlying intrathoracic air leak and can swell the neck, face, scrotum, and eyelids closed.

teach.heading: Rib fracture compression test
points: Direct palpation over an undisplaced hairline rib fracture may cause only vague tenderness.
The clinician places the palm over the sternum and the other hand over the thoracic spine at the same level.
Gentle anteroposterior compression springs the thoracic cage outward at the mid-axillary line.
Sharp localized pain at the fracture site away from the examining hands confirms a broken rib.

skill.exam.surg.tension_pneumothorax.title: Tension and open pneumothorax evaluation
skill.exam.surg.tension_pneumothorax.oneLine: Rapid clinical differentiation of one-way valve pleural tension from sucking chest wounds and urgent needle thoracocentesis
skill.exam.surg.tension_pneumothorax.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis that must never await chest radiography. One-way valve air trapping progressively shifts the mediastinum, kinks the vena cava, abolishes venous return, and triggers rapid cardiac arrest unless immediately decompressed.

steps.text: Identify immediate signs of physiological distress: marked agitation, air hunger, cyanosis, diaphoresis, tachypnoea, and profound hypotension with tachycardia.
Inspect the neck for distended jugular veins caused by obstructed vena caval return, noting that hypovolaemia may attenuate vein distension.
Inspect the chest wall for unilateral hyperexpansion with absent respiratory excursions, and check for an open sucking chest wound where air hisses through the defect.
Palpate the trachea in the suprasternal notch, confirming deviation of the trachea away from the affected hemithorax.
Palpate the cardiac apex beat, identifying displacement away from the affected side.
Percuss the affected hemithorax, confirming widespread tympanitic hyper-resonance.
Auscultate the chest, confirming complete absence or severe reduction of breath sounds over the affected hemithorax.
For an open pneumothorax, immediately apply a sterile three-sided occlusive dressing to create a flutter-valve that allows air to escape during expiration but blocks ingress on inspiration.
For tension pneumothorax, initiate emergency needle decompression without waiting for radiological imaging.

skill.exam.surg.tension_pneumothorax.normal: Centred trachea in the suprasternal notch, apex beat in the normal anatomical fifth left intercostal space mid-clavicular line, flat jugular veins when upright, symmetrical percussion resonance, and equal bilateral vesicular breath sounds.
skill.exam.surg.tension_pneumothorax.abnormal: Trachea and apex beat pushed contralateral to the lesion, distended neck veins, unilateral hyper-expanded immobile hemithorax, hyper-resonant percussion note, total absence of breath sounds, severe hypotension, and cyanosis.
skill.exam.surg.tension_pneumothorax.significance: The constellation of unilateral hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation to the opposite side, and shock establishes tension pneumothorax. A sucking chest wound with hissing air movement causes mediastinal flutter and acute ventilatory collapse.
skill.exam.surg.tension_pneumothorax.practice: Practise tracheal palpation in the suprasternal notch with three fingers, and rehearse placing a three-sided flutter valve dressing over a simulated penetrating thoracic wound.
pitfalls: Sending a patient with clinical features of tension pneumothorax to the radiology suite for a chest radiograph, which can prove fatal in transit.
Failing to recognize that profound hypovolaemic shock can collapse neck veins, masking jugular venous distension in tension pneumothorax.
Taping all four edges of a dressing over an open chest wound without an intercostal tube, converting an open pneumothorax into a fatal tension pneumothorax.

probes.q: Why must tension pneumothorax never be diagnosed on a chest radiograph in the emergency bay?
probes.a: It is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate needle decompression; delaying treatment to obtain an X-ray can cause cardiovascular collapse and death.

probes.q: How does a sucking chest wound cause mediastinal flutter?
probes.a: On inspiration, air rushes through the defect pushing the mediastinum to the healthy side; on expiration, air leaves the wound and mediastinum shifts back, impairing venous return and oxygenation.

probes.q: Where is the recommended anatomical landmark for needle decompression of tension pneumothorax in modern trauma guidelines?
probes.a: The second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, or alternatively the fourth or fifth intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line on the affected side.

rubric.text: Recognises tension pneumothorax clinically without ordering an X-ray
Assesses tracheal deviation away from the lesion and checks neck vein distension
Demonstrates percussion hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on affected side
Applies three-sided flutter valve dressing for open sucking chest wound

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of the tension valve
teach.body:
A flap tear in the lung parenchyma or chest wall behaves as a one-way ball valve. Air enters the pleural space during inspiration but cannot exit during expiration.

Intrapleural pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure, causing total collapse of the ipsilateral lung, contralateral mediastinal displacement, and acute angulation of the superior and inferior venae cavae.

teach.heading: Comparison of tension and open pneumothorax

rows: In and out with loud sucking sound

teach.heading: Why three-sided dressings protect open wounds
teach.body:
If a chest wall defect exceeds two-thirds the tracheal diameter, air preferentially enters the chest wall defect during inspiration rather than the trachea.

Taping a sterile square dressing on three sides creates an impromptu flutter valve: air vents through the open bottom edge on expiration, but the dressing sucks flat on inspiration to prevent air ingress.

skill.exam.surg.haemothorax_tamponade.title: Massive haemothorax and cardiac tamponade signs
skill.exam.surg.haemothorax_tamponade.oneLine: Bedside physical distinction between massive pleural haemorrhage and pericardial tamponade using percussion and Beck triad
skill.exam.surg.haemothorax_tamponade.why: Massive haemothorax and cardiac tamponade are rapid killers in chest trauma that share profound hypotension and shock. Distinguishing them at the bedside is critical because massive haemothorax requires chest tube drainage and volume resuscitation, whereas tamponade requires subxiphoid decompression and pericardiocentesis.

steps.text: Assess systemic hemodynamics: evaluate skin pallor, cold clammy extremities, pulse volume, and record blood pressure.
Inspect the neck veins: observe whether the internal jugular veins are collapsed (massive blood loss) or distended (pericardial tamponade, tension pneumothorax).
Observe the chest wall contour and breathing movements, noting whether one side is flat and immobile or shows penetrating precordial wounds.
Palpate the trachea in the suprasternal notch, checking for deviation away from the side of a massive haemothorax.
Percuss both hemithoraces from apex to base: identify stony dullness over the lower and mid-zones on the affected side in haemothorax; note normal bilateral resonance in pure tamponade.
Auscultate the lung fields: confirm absent or severely muffled breath sounds on the affected side in haemothorax; note clear bilateral breath sounds in pure tamponade.
Auscultate heart sounds at the apex and left lower sternal border, listening specifically for distant, muffled heart sounds characteristic of pericardial fluid.
Examine for pulsus paradoxus: inflate the sphygmomanometer cuff and note an inspiratory systolic pressure drop greater than 10 mmHg.
Examine the epigastrium and chest for Beck triad: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds.

skill.exam.surg.haemothorax_tamponade.normal: Normotensive patient with warm extremities, flat neck veins when recumbent at 45 degrees, midline trachea, resonant percussion notes throughout both lungs, crisp dual heart sounds (S1 and S2), and no pulsus paradoxus.
skill.exam.surg.haemothorax_tamponade.abnormal: Profound hypotension with tachycardia; in haemothorax: flat neck veins, stony dull percussion note, and absent breath sounds on the affected side; in cardiac tamponade: distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, resonant lungs bilaterally, and marked pulsus paradoxus.
skill.exam.surg.haemothorax_tamponade.significance: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds and flat neck veins confirms massive haemothorax. Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) with clear lungs confirms cardiac tamponade and mandates immediate pericardial decompression.
skill.exam.surg.haemothorax_tamponade.practice: Auscultate heart sounds through a folded towel to experience the muffled sound of pericardial effusion, and practise measuring pulsus paradoxus using a manual sphygmomanometer.
pitfalls: Confusing cardiac tamponade with tension pneumothorax because both produce distended neck veins and shock; percussion resonance and breath sounds readily differentiate them.
Failing to recognize that neck veins will remain flat in cardiac tamponade if the patient has concurrent massive hypovolaemia.
Inserting an intercostal drain on the wrong side when breath sounds are falsely perceived due to transmitted sound from the contralateral lung.

probes.q: What three classical physical signs constitute Beck triad in acute cardiac tamponade?
probes.a: Hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure (distended neck veins), and muffled or distant heart sounds.

probes.q: How do percussion note and breath sounds distinguish massive haemothorax from cardiac tamponade at the bedside?
probes.a: Massive haemothorax produces stony dullness and absent breath sounds on the affected side, whereas pure cardiac tamponade has bilateral resonant percussion notes and clear breath sounds.

probes.q: What volume of acute pericardial blood collection is sufficient to cause fatal cardiac tamponade, and why?
probes.a: As little as 100 to 200 ml of blood acutely, because the fibrous parietal pericardium is non-distensible and rapidly compresses the thin-walled right atrium and right ventricle.

rubric.text: Evaluates vital signs, peripheral perfusion, and blood pressure
Inspects jugular venous distension to distinguish tamponade from hypovolaemia
Percusses for stony dullness and auscultates for absent breath sounds (haemothorax)
Auscultates for muffled heart sounds and checks for Beck triad (tamponade)

teach.heading: Bedside differentiation: haemothorax vs tamponade vs tension pneumothorax
Definition of massive haemothorax
teach.body:
Massive haemothorax is defined by the rapid accumulation of more than 1500 ml of blood (or one-third of the patient blood volume) in the pleural cavity.

It is caused by disruption of systemic vessels such as the internal mammary or intercostal arteries, or major hilar vessel laceration. It requires immediate large-bore tube thoracostomy and emergency thoracotomy if initial drainage exceeds 1500 ml.

teach.heading: Pulsus paradoxus mechanism
teach.body:
Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggeration of the normal physiological decline in systolic blood pressure during inspiration. An inspiratory drop greater than 10 mmHg is pathological.

In cardiac tamponade, the rigid pericardium restricts total ventricular volume. On inspiration, increased venous return fills the right ventricle, which bulges the interventricular septum leftward, drastically reducing left ventricular filling.

skill.hx.surg.chest_disease.title: Surgical chest disease history
skill.hx.surg.chest_disease.oneLine: Surgical history of chest pain, chronic cough with copious foul sputum, haemoptysis, and postoperative pulmonary collapse
skill.hx.surg.chest_disease.why: Thoracic surgical conditions such as lung abscess, bronchiectasis, empyema, and bronchogenic carcinoma present with distinctive symptom complexes. Eliciting precise sputum characteristics, pain radiation, and postoperative timing allows the clinician to distinguish parenchymal suppuration from mechanical collapse or malignant invasion.

asks.text: When did the chest complaints start, and was the onset sudden (pulmonary embolism, spontaneous pneumothorax) or gradual after pneumonia or tooth extraction?

Where is the chest pain located, is it sharp and catching on inspiration (pleurisy, empyema), throbbing (lung abscess), or a constant deep ache with shoulder and arm radiation (Pancoast apical tumour)?
Do you bring up sputum, how much in a 24-hour period (teaspoon, eggcup, or half cup), what is its colour, and does it have a putrid or foul odour?
Does coughing up large volumes of sputum depend on your body position, such as turning onto one side or bending forwards in the morning?
Have you ever coughed up blood (haemoptysis), was it blood-streaked phlegm or frank clots, and has an established smoker cough changed in character recently?
If you underwent a recent surgical operation, on which postoperative day did fever, tachypnoea, or sudden chest pain develop?

skill.hx.surg.chest_disease.practice: Practise taking a surgical chest history from a simulated patient presenting with copious foul sputum, quantifying daily volume with household containers and eliciting postural drainage positions.
pitfalls: Dismissing a change in the character of a chronic smoker cough as simple bronchitis without investigating for bronchial carcinoma.
Failing to ask about the smell of sputum, which is the pathognomonic clue separating foul anaerobic lung abscess from sweet-smelling bronchiectasis.
Overlooking the timing of postoperative fever and dyspnoea: atelectasis peaks at 24 to 48 hours, whereas pulmonary embolism typically strikes at 7 to 10 days.

probes.q: What does copious, foul-smelling, purulent sputum typically indicate in a patient with remittent fever?
probes.a: Putrid lung abscess caused by anaerobic pulmonary suppuration, frequently secondary to aspiration.

probes.q: How does the timing of postoperative respiratory deterioration distinguish atelectasis from pulmonary embolism?
probes.a: Pulmonary atelectasis typically develops on the first or second postoperative day with bronchial plugging, whereas pulmonary embolism usually occurs around the 7th to 10th postoperative day.

probes.q: What clinical syndrome is produced by an apical lung carcinoma invading the superior thoracic aperture?
probes.a: Pancoast syndrome (superior pulmonary sulcus tumour), causing severe shoulder and ulnar-distribution arm pain, Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), and wasting of hand intrinsic muscles.

rubric.text: Distinguishes pleuritic, throbbing, and constant aching chest pain
Quantifies sputum volume and specifically inquires about foul putrid odour
Asks about postural drainage triggers and screens for haemoptysis
Determines postoperative day of onset for acute respiratory symptoms

teach.heading: Surgical implications of chest pain character
teach.body:
Pleural pain is sharp, knife-like, and aggravated by inspiration and coughing. It occurs in acute pleurisy, early empyema, and pulmonary infarction. Throbbing pain suggests acute suppuration such as a tension lung abscess before rupture.

Constant, dull, boring chest pain in an older smoker indicates direct chest wall invasion by bronchogenic carcinoma, conveying an advanced prognostic stage.

teach.heading: Sputum characteristics in surgical suppurative disease
points: Bronchiectasis produces copious mucopurulent sputum that separates on standing into three layers: frothy mucus on top, turbid serous fluid in the middle, and dense pus debris at the bottom.
Lung abscess produces copious putrid, foul-tasting, and foul-smelling sputum caused by anaerobic organisms (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus) following aspiration.
Positional expectoration occurs when gravity allows a cavity or dilated bronchus to drain into the main bronchial tree upon turning in bed.
Haemoptysis ranges from streaking in bronchitis to massive volumes in cavitary tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, and cavitating lung cancer.

rows: Tachypnoea, low-grade fever, reduced basal air entry

skill.exam.surg.chest_wall_swelling.title: Chest wall swelling and deformity examination
skill.exam.surg.chest_wall_swelling.oneLine: Inspection of thoracic deformities and testing chest wall masses for cough impulse, compressibility, and rib fixity
skill.exam.surg.chest_wall_swelling.why: Chest wall swellings range from benign lipomas and chondromas to tuberculous cold abscesses and empyema necessitatis communicating directly with the pleural cavity. Missing a cough impulse or compressibility can cause catastrophic aspiration or open pneumothorax if incised in clinic.

steps.text: Position the patient seated stripped to the waist in good lighting, viewing the chest from the front, profile, and back.
Inspect thoracic contour for congenital or acquired deformities: pectus excavatum (funnel chest), pectus carinatum (pigeon chest), and thoracic kyphoscoliosis.
Identify any chest wall swelling, recording anatomical location, relation to ribs and intercostal spaces, overlying skin changes, and visible sinus openings.
Observe the swelling while asking the patient to turn their head and cough, checking for an expansile cough impulse.
Palpate the swelling for local temperature, tenderness, margin clarity, and consistency (soft, cystic, firm, or stony hard bony mass).
Test for fluctuation across two perpendicular planes to confirm fluid content in cystic swellings.

Perform the compressibility test: compress the swelling firmly with the fingers; if it partially disappears into the thorax and slowly refills, note whether refilling accelerates when the patient coughs.

Test for fixity to the rib: attempt to move the swelling along the long axis of the rib and across it; inability to move across the rib confirms origin from or attachment to the rib periosteum or cartilage.
Transilluminate the swelling in a darkened room to differentiate fluid-filled cysts from solid mesenchymal tumours.

skill.exam.surg.chest_wall_swelling.normal: Symmetrical chest wall contour without sternal depression or protrusion, absence of localized masses, no expansile impulse on coughing, ribs and intercostal spaces smoothly palpable without tenderness or gaps.
skill.exam.surg.chest_wall_swelling.abnormal: Pectus excavatum with deep sternal depression; pectus carinatum with prominent forward sternal projection; cystic, fluctuant swelling on the chest wall demonstrating an expansile cough impulse, compressibility into the pleural cavity (empyema necessitatis), or attachment to a rib (tuberculous cold abscess, chondroma).
skill.exam.surg.chest_wall_swelling.significance: An expansile cough impulse and compressibility confirm an empyema necessitatis or thoracic hernia communicating with the pleural space. A cold, non-tender, fluctuant swelling fixed to a costal cartilage represents a tuberculous collar-stud abscess arising from internal mammary lymph nodes or costal chondritis.
skill.exam.surg.chest_wall_swelling.practice: Practise distinguishing compressibility from reducibility on clinical models, and rehearse testing the mobility of a simulated mass along versus across the line of a rib.
pitfalls: Incision of an empyema necessitatis or tuberculous cold abscess mistaking it for a simple subcutaneous abscess, producing a chronic discharging thoracic fistula.
Failing to test for an expansile cough impulse in every cystic chest wall mass before attempting needle aspiration.
Missing the deep component of a collar-stud tuberculous abscess that passes through an intercostal space into the mediastinum.

probes.q: What does an expansile cough impulse in a cystic chest wall swelling prove?
probes.a: It proves that the swelling communicates directly with the pleural cavity or respiratory tract, such as empyema necessitatis or a lung hernia.

probes.q: How does an empyema necessitatis differ clinically from a tuberculous cold abscess of the chest wall?
probes.a: Empyema necessitatis is compressible, has an expansile cough impulse, and communicates with pleural pus, whereas a cold abscess is fluctuant and fixed to a rib or cartilage without an expansile cough impulse.

probes.q: What anatomical arrangement creates the collar-stud abscess of the chest wall in tuberculosis?
probes.a: Tuberculous lymphadenitis of the internal mammary chain or rib osteochondritis perforates the intercostal membrane, forming a superficial subcutaneous abscess connected by a narrow track to a deeper intrathoracic reservoir.

Elicits expansile cough impulse on coughing
Performs compressibility test and assesses refill dynamics
Tests mobility along and across the axis of the underlying rib

teach.heading: Compressibility versus reducibility
teach.body:
A compressible swelling disappears under gentle finger pressure because its fluid or vascular contents are squeezed into an internal chamber or venous lake.

Unlike a reducible hernia where contents slip into the abdomen through a defect with a sudden click, a compressible swelling empties gradually and spontaneously refills once the pressure is released.

teach.heading: Common cystic swellings of the chest wall

rows: Internal mammary node or rib TB

teach.heading: Why chest wall cold abscesses must never be incised
teach.body:
Incising a tuberculous cold abscess in the outpatients clinic introduces secondary pyogenic infection into a slow-healing cavity.

This creates a non-healing tuberculous sinus that discharges persistently. Proper management requires diagnostic needle aspiration through healthy non-dependent skin under systemic anti-tubercular coverage.

skill.exam.surg.empyema_thoracis.title: Thoracic empyema and lung suppuration signs
skill.exam.surg.empyema_thoracis.oneLine: Systematic examination for intercostal fullness, crowding of ribs, stony dullness, and signs of chronic pleural sepsis
skill.exam.surg.empyema_thoracis.why: Thoracic empyema is the accumulation of pus within the pleural space. Untreated acute empyema progresses into a chronic trapped lung encased in a thick fibrous peel, causing severe restrictive thoracic deformity, scoliosis, and bronchopleural fistula that requires complex surgical decortication.

steps.text: Inspect the patient general state: assess toxic appearance, swinging septic pyrexia, finger clubbing, and wasting.
Position the patient upright, stripped to the waist, and inspect the thorax from front, side, and back.

Observe the chest wall on the affected side: in acute empyema, look for restricted movement and bulging or fullness of intercostal spaces; in chronic empyema, look for hemithoracic contraction, flattening, crowding of ribs, and compensatory scoliosis.
Inspect the chest wall skin for localized erythema, oedema, spontaneous discharging sinuses, or previous thoracotomy scars.
Palpate the trachea in the suprasternal notch: note deviation to the opposite side in large acute collections, or deviation towards the affected side in chronic fibrotic fibrothorax.
Palpate the hemithoraces for intercostal tenderness and assess symmetrical chest expansion with hands placed firmly on the lower ribs.
Percuss the chest systematically from apex to base: map out the upper boundary of dullness (Ellis S-shaped curve), confirming stony dullness over the fluid collection.
Auscultate breath sounds: listen for absent or severely diminished vesicular breath sounds over the effusion, and tubular bronchial breathing just above the fluid level caused by compressed lung.
Auscultate for vocal resonance and aegophony: listen for the nasal bleating high-pitched quality (E-to-A transition) at the upper fluid margin.

skill.exam.surg.empyema_thoracis.normal: Symmetrical chest excursions without intercostal flattening or bulging, central trachea, resonant percussion notes throughout both lung fields, normal vesicular breath sounds without bronchial breathing, and normal vocal resonance.
skill.exam.surg.empyema_thoracis.abnormal: Swinging septic fever, prominent finger clubbing; ipsilateral chest wall fullness with intercostal tenderness in acute empyema; hemithoracic flattening with rib crowding in chronic empyema; stony dull percussion note with Ellis S-shaped upper line; absent breath sounds over the fluid with aegophony and bronchial breathing at the upper border.
skill.exam.surg.empyema_thoracis.significance: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds and high swinging fever in a patient following pneumonia confirms an empyema until proven otherwise. Hemithoracic contraction with tracheal pull towards the lesion proves chronic organized empyema with lung entrapment.
skill.exam.surg.empyema_thoracis.practice: Practise identifying the Ellis S-shaped curve by percussing a fluid container, and practise auscultating the E-to-A transition (aegophony) in patients with pleural effusions.
pitfalls: Assuming that absent breath sounds over stony dullness is simple pneumonia, delaying diagnostic pleural thoracocentesis for days while pus thickens.
Failing to notice rib crowding and scoliosis that signal transition from acute exsudative empyema into chronic organizing fibrothorax.
Missing a small discharging intercostal sinus hidden in the axillary fold or submammary crease.

probes.q: What does a stony dull percussion note over the lower hemithorax with absent breath sounds signify in a febrile patient?
probes.a: Pleural effusion or thoracic empyema (pus in the pleural cavity).

probes.q: What are the three progressive pathological stages of thoracic empyema described in surgery?
probes.a: Stage 1: exudative (thin fluid with mobile lung); Stage 2: fibrinopurulent (turbid pus, fibrin webs, and loculations); Stage 3: organizing / chronic (dense fibrous peel and trapped lung).

probes.q: Why does the trachea deviate towards the affected side in chronic empyema, but away from it in large acute empyema?
probes.a: In acute empyema, positive fluid pressure pushes the mediastinum to the opposite side; in chronic empyema, dense fibrous peel contraction and cicatricial atelectasis pull the mediastinum towards the affected hemithorax.

Distinguishes intercostal bulging (acute) from rib crowding and contraction (chronic)
Demonstrates tracheal position and confirms stony dullness
Identifies absent breath sounds with upper-margin aegophony and bronchial breathing

teach.heading: Pathological stages of pleural empyema
teach.body:
Stage 1 (exudative phase) involves sterile thin pleural fluid responding promptly to antibiotics and simple drainage. Stage 2 (fibrinopurulent phase) features heavy fibrin deposition, bacterial invasion, and loculations that impair tube drainage.

Stage 3 (organizing phase) develops after several weeks, forming a thick inelastic collagenous peel that traps the lung and pulls the chest wall inward, requiring surgical decortication.

teach.heading: Physical differences: acute versus chronic empyema
Ellis S-shaped curve of fluid dullness
teach.body:
When fluid accumulates freely in the pleural space, the upper border of dullness forms a line starting low near the spine, rising to its highest point in the mid-axillary line, and descending towards the sternum.

This S-shaped boundary occurs because negative intrapleural suction and lung capillary attraction are greatest in the lateral costophrenic recesses where lung recoil is maximal.

skill.ix.surg.thoracocentesis_icd.title: Pleural aspiration and chest tube thoracostomy
skill.ix.surg.thoracocentesis_icd.oneLine: Diagnostic thoracocentesis, safe triangle landmarks, and intercostal tube underwater seal management
skill.ix.surg.thoracocentesis_icd.why: Pleural fluid cannot be definitively classified as transudate, parapneumonic effusion, empyema, or haemothorax by examination alone. Diagnostic thoracocentesis provides essential biochemistry and microbiology, while correctly placed tube thoracostomy achieves lung re-expansion and evacuates pleural sepsis.
skill.ix.surg.thoracocentesis_icd.practice: Practise landmarking the safe triangle of chest drain insertion on a colleague, and assemble an underwater seal drainage bottle confirming the underwater tube depth of two centimetres.
pitfalls: Inserting an intercostal drain below the fifth intercostal space, risking direct puncture of the elevated diaphragm, spleen, or liver.
Advancing the needle or trocar below the rib instead of riding over the superior rib border, lacerating the intercostal neurovascular bundle.
Clamping an intercostal chest tube while air is actively bubbling, which rapidly converts a simple air leak into a fatal tension pneumothorax.

probes.q: What anatomical boundaries define the safe triangle for intercostal chest tube insertion?
probes.a: The anterior border of the latissimus dorsi, the lateral border of the pectoralis major, the horizontal line of the fifth intercostal space (nipple level in males), and the apex below the axilla.

probes.q: Why must an intercostal drain or aspiration needle always be inserted directly over the upper border of the rib?
probes.a: To avoid the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve, which run in the subcostal groove along the inferior border of the rib above.

probes.q: What biochemical findings on diagnostic pleural aspiration establish an empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring tube drainage?
probes.a: Frank pus, positive Gram stain or culture, pleural fluid pH below 7.20, low glucose (under 40 mg/dl), and markedly elevated LDH (over 1000 IU/L).

Specifies needle or trochar passage over the superior border of the rib

teach.heading: The safe triangle of thoracostomy
teach.body:
The British Thoracic Society safe triangle minimises danger to internal organs and major muscles. It is bounded anteriorly by the lateral edge of pectoralis major and posteriorly by the anterior edge of latissimus dorsi.

The base is formed by the fifth intercostal space (horizontal line across the nipple in men), and the apex sits in the base of the axilla. This region avoids the long thoracic nerve, internal mammary vessels, and subdiaphragmatic viscera.

rows: Turbid, cloudy, or frank thick pus

teach.heading: Principles of the underwater seal drain
teach.body:
The drainage tube from the chest is submerged two centimetres below sterile water in a drainage bottle placed below the patient bed.

During expiration and coughing, rising pleural pressure pushes air and fluid out through the water. During inspiration, negative intrapleural pressure pulls water up the tube, but the column height prevents air from re-entering the pleural cavity.

skill.hx.surg.breast.title: Breast disease surgical history
skill.hx.surg.breast.oneLine: Surgical history of breast lump, cyclical mastalgia, nipple discharge, and lifetime hormonal and familial risk factors
skill.hx.surg.breast.why: Presenting breast symptoms (lump, pain, nipple changes) overlap between physiological aberrations, benign lesions, and invasive carcinoma. A meticulous chronological history stratifies malignant risk, clarifies hormonal cyclicality, and identifies familial cancer syndromes requiring genetic evaluation.

asks.text: When was the lump first noticed, was it discovered accidentally during bathing or on self-examination, and has it grown rapidly or stayed unchanged?
Is there breast pain, and if so, is it bilateral, dull, and cyclical (worsening just before menstruation), or sharp, localized, and continuous?

Have you noticed any discharge from either nipple: is it spontaneous, does it come from a single duct or multiple ducts, and what colour is it (blood-stained, clear serous, yellow, or greenish-brown)?
Has either nipple recently become inverted, pulled to one side, or developed an itchy red rash that does not heal with creams?
What was your age at menarche, what is your obstetrical history (number of children, age at first full-term delivery), and did you breastfeed?
Has any first-degree relative (mother, sister, daughter) or maternal aunt been diagnosed with breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancer, particularly before age 50?

skill.hx.surg.breast.practice: Practise taking a complete breast history from a simulated patient within five minutes, establishing lump chronology, menstrual relationship, nipple discharge characteristics, and three-generation pedigree.
pitfalls: Assuming that because a breast lump is completely painless, it cannot be serious; classic early breast carcinoma is painless.
Failing to ask about the spontaneous nature and ductal origin (single versus multiple pores) of nipple discharge.
Omitting the family history of ovarian cancer, which is linked to the same BRCA mutations as hereditary breast cancer.

probes.q: What is the most common presenting symptom of early breast carcinoma in surgical outpatients?
probes.a: A painless, solitary, hard breast lump, often discovered accidentally during bathing or dressing.

probes.q: How does cyclical mastalgia differ from non-cyclical breast pain in clinical history?
probes.a: Cyclical mastalgia is diffuse, bilateral, and heaviness-like, peaking in the premenstrual week and easing with menses; non-cyclical pain is well-localized, constant, and unrelated to the menstrual cycle.

probes.q: Which characteristics of nipple discharge carry the highest suspicion for malignancy?
probes.a: Spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct discharge that is blood-stained (sanguinous) or clear serous, particularly in a woman over 50 years of age.

rubric.text: Elicits lump duration, mode of discovery, and rate of growth
Distinguishes cyclical mastalgia from non-cyclical or inflammatory pain
Asks about discharge character (spontaneous, single duct, bloody) and nipple inversion
Details reproductive history (parity, lactation) and family history of breast/ovarian cancer

teach.heading: Chronology and discovery of the breast lump
teach.body:
Fibroadenoma typically presents in women aged 15 to 30 as a firm, highly mobile lump growing very slowly. Fibrocystic changes fluctuate across cycles with premenstrual tenderness.

Carcinoma typically occurs over age 40 (though seen earlier in India), with an average interval of six weeks between accidental discovery and surgical attendance. Atrophic scirrhous carcinoma may exist for years without rapid enlargement.

teach.heading: Classification and significance of nipple discharge
Reproductive and genetic risk profile
teach.body:
Increased lifetime exposure to uninterrupted oestrogen cycles elevates breast cancer risk. Key historical factors include early menarche (before age 12), late menopause (after age 55), nulliparity, and first full-term pregnancy after age 30.

Conversely, multiple completed pregnancies and prolonged breastfeeding confer protective effects against hormone-receptor positive breast cancer.

skill.exam.surg.breast_inspection.title: Inspection of the breasts
skill.exam.surg.breast_inspection.oneLine: Systematic visual inspection in three postures: contour, symmetry, skin dimpling, peau d'orange, and nipple retraction
skill.exam.surg.breast_inspection.why: Inspection reveals skin tethering, contour flattening, and subtle nipple deviation that disappear once the patient lies flat or the breast is palpated. Dynamic manoeuvres that contract the pectoralis major unmask early malignant infiltration of Cooper suspensory ligaments.

steps.text: Ensure a private examination room with a female chaperone present; seat the patient comfortably, stripped to the waist, with arms resting relaxed by her sides in symmetrical lighting.
Inspect both breasts together: compare size, shape, symmetry, contour, and relative height of the breasts on the chest wall.
Inspect the skin over both breasts systematically: look for localized flattening, dimpling, erythema, prominent engorged subcutaneous veins, ulceration, or fungation.
Look specifically for peau d'orange: cutaneous lymphatic oedema where hair follicles appear pitted like an orange peel, denoting dermal lymphatic permeation.
Examine the nipple-areola complexes: compare the level of both nipples, noting elevation, deviation away from the midline, or asymmetrical enlargement.
Inspect the nipples for retraction or inversion, noting whether the inversion is slit-like (duct ectasia) or circumferential (underlying carcinoma), and whether it can be pulled out.
Inspect the areola and nipple surface for eczema, cracking, erosion, or superficial ulceration (distinguishing benign eczema from Paget disease of the nipple).
Ask the patient to raise both arms straight above her head: observe whether a hidden lump or tethering becomes visible, or if one nipple fails to elevate symmetrically.
Ask the patient to place both hands firmly on her hips and press inwards to contract the pectoralis major muscles: watch for skin puckering or accentuation of dimpling.
Ask the patient with large or pendulous breasts to lean forwards from the hips: observe whether both breasts swing freely away from the chest wall or if one remains fixed.

skill.exam.surg.breast_inspection.normal: Symmetrical breasts of equal or slightly differing volume, smooth convex contours without flattening or puckering, normal skin colour and vascular pattern without peau d'orange, everted nipples situated at identical horizontal levels pointing slightly downwards and outwards, and free breast excursion during postural manoeuvres.
skill.exam.surg.breast_inspection.abnormal: Asymmetrical breast enlargement or shrinkage; localized flattening or skin puckering; prominent engorged collateral veins; coarse pitted peau d'orange; recent nipple retraction, elevation, or axis deviation towards a quadrant; chronic unilateral nipple excoriation or ulceration (Paget disease); tethering accentuated on raising arms or pressing hips.
skill.exam.surg.breast_inspection.significance: Skin dimpling is caused by shortening of Cooper suspensory ligaments by malignant fibrosis. Peau d'orange indicates dermal lymphatic blockage by tumour emboli. Nipple elevation and deviation towards a tumour quadrant prove ductal contraction by underlying carcinoma. Paget disease represents intraepidermal spread of ductal adenocarcinoma.
skill.exam.surg.breast_inspection.practice: Perform the three visual inspection postures (arms at sides, arms elevated above head, hands pressed on hips) in front of a mirror or clinical model, reciting all visible signs systematically.
pitfalls: Beginning palpation immediately without performing dynamic inspection manoeuvres (raising arms, pressing hips), which unmask subtle ligamentous tethering.
Treating persistent unilateral nipple areolar eczema with topical steroid creams without suspecting and biopsying for Paget disease of the nipple.
Mistaking long-standing bilateral congenital inverted nipples for acute malignant nipple retraction.

probes.q: What pathological mechanism produces peau d'orange in locally advanced breast carcinoma?
probes.a: Malignant tumour emboli block the subdermal lymphatics, producing localized cutaneous oedema that accentuates the tethered hair follicles, resembling orange skin.

probes.q: Why does contracting the pectoralis major (by pressing hands on hips) accentuate skin dimpling over a breast tumour?
probes.a: Tension on the pectoral fascia pulls on the malignant fibrous tissue and shortens the attached Cooper ligaments, drawing the overlying skin inward as a visible dimple.

probes.q: How do you differentiate Paget disease of the nipple from benign bilateral areolar eczema?
probes.a: Paget disease is unilateral, starts on the nipple tip before spreading to the areola, destroys the nipple architecture, and does not respond to topical steroids; eczema is bilateral, starts on the areola sparing the nipple, is intensely pruritic, and heals with steroids.

rubric.text: Seats patient properly with chaperone, adequate exposure, and symmetrical lighting
Inspects for contour flattening, skin dimpling, peau d'orange, and nipple levels
Demonstrates arms raised, hands on hips pressed inward, and leaning forward
Examines nipple-areola complex for Paget disease versus eczema, cracks, and discharge

teach.heading: Cooper suspensory ligaments and skin tethering
teach.body:
Cooper ligaments run from the deep pectoral fascia through the breast parenchyma to insert into the deep dermis. When an invasive carcinoma infiltrates and incites desmoplastic fibrosis, these fibrous bands contract.

This shortens the distance between fascia and dermis, creating a characteristic skin pit or dimple that becomes strikingly visible when the breast is moved or the pectoralis muscle contracts.

teach.heading: Distinguishing Paget disease from eczema of the nipple

rows: Starts on the nipple, spreads to areola
Starts on areola, often spares nipple

teach.heading: Types and significance of nipple retraction
teach.body:
Congenital nipple inversion is bilateral, lifelong, and can be pulled out by gentle finger traction. In contrast, acquired malignant retraction is unilateral, recent, and fixed.

Duct ectasia produces a transverse slit-like slit retraction caused by periductal fibrosis, whereas underlying carcinoma pulls the nipple circumferentially inward and deviates it towards the tumour quadrant.

skill.exam.surg.breast_lump_palpation.title: Palpation of a breast lump
skill.exam.surg.breast_lump_palpation.oneLine: Technique with the flat of the fingers against the rib cage: quadrant mapping, consistency, margins, and fluctuation
skill.exam.surg.breast_lump_palpation.why: Pinching the breast tissue between thumb and forefinger creates a false impression of a lump in normal glandular lobules. Palpating with the palmar aspect of the fingers compresses breast tissue against the flat thoracic cage, allowing true pathology to be isolated and precisely characterised.

steps.text: Position the patient comfortably supine with the head resting on a low pillow; for lateral quadrant lumps, place a small pillow beneath the ipsilateral shoulder to spread breast tissue evenly over the chest wall.
Warm your hands before touching the patient, and ask whether any part of either breast is tender; examine the normal, non-tender breast first as a baseline.
Use the flat, palmar surfaces of the middle three fingers (not the fingertips or pinched fingers), keeping the hand relaxed and parallel to the chest wall.
Palpate systematically in a clockwise or lawn-mower pattern across all four anatomical quadrants (upper outer, upper inner, lower inner, lower outer) and the central retroareolar region.
Remember to palpate the axillary tail of Spence, which extends through the deep fascia into the anterior axillary fold.
When a lump is identified, compress it gently against the underlying chest wall to confirm it is a genuine mass (palpable between the flat hand and ribs) rather than normal physiological nodularity.
Record the lump exact anatomical quadrant and distance from the areolar margin using the clock-face notation (for example, 2 o'clock position, 3 cm from the nipple).

Assess the physical characteristics of the lump: size in centimetres (two dimensions), shape (spherical, discoid, irregular), surface (smooth, bosselated, rough), and margin (well-defined, lobulated, ill-defined and infiltrating).
Assess consistency: soft (lipoma), cystic (galactocoele, cyst), rubbery-firm (fibroadenoma), or stony hard (carcinoma).
Test for fluctuation in two planes if the lump feels cystic, and perform gentle transillumination in a dark room if fluid is suspected.

skill.exam.surg.breast_lump_palpation.normal: Soft, supple, diffusely lobular glandular breast tissue that compresses smoothly against the chest wall without focal masses, dominant lumps, distinct margins, or localized tenderness.
skill.exam.surg.breast_lump_palpation.abnormal: Palpable solitary or dominant mass; fibroadenoma: well-circumscribed, firm, smooth, highly mobile (breast mouse); breast cyst: round, tense-elastic or fluctuant, smooth; carcinoma: solitary, irregular, ill-defined margins, hard or stony consistency, merging imperceptibly into surrounding parenchyma.
skill.exam.surg.breast_lump_palpation.significance: A firm, well-circumscribed, highly mobile mass in a young woman is a fibroadenoma. A solitary, hard mass with ill-defined borders in a woman over 40 years is strongly suggestive of invasive breast carcinoma until proven otherwise by histological assessment.
skill.exam.surg.breast_lump_palpation.practice: Practise the flat-of-the-hand palpation technique on clinical breast phantoms, ensuring no pinching occurs, and document lump locations accurately using clock-face notation and centimetre distances.
pitfalls: Pinching the breast tissue between fingers, which gathers normal glandular lobules and creates a pseudo-lump in healthy breasts.
Failing to examine the axillary tail of Spence, where occult carcinomas can hide in the anterior axillary wall.
Examining the painful or affected breast first, causing guarding and losing the opportunity to establish the patient normal baseline texture.

probes.q: Why must the clinician use the flat of the fingers rather than pinching the breast tissue during palpation?
probes.a: Pinching picks up normal glandular lobules and gives a false sensation of a mass; the flat of the fingers compresses breast tissue against the rib cage to detect genuine pathology.

probes.q: Why is a fibroadenoma traditionally referred to as a breast mouse?
probes.a: Because it is completely unattached to surrounding breast parenchyma, slipping freely and easily beneath the examining fingers within its false capsule.

probes.q: What physical characteristics reliably distinguish a simple breast cyst from a scirrhous carcinoma on palpation?
probes.a: A cyst is well-circumscribed, smooth, tense-elastic or fluctuant, and mobile; a scirrhous carcinoma is hard or stony, irregular, poorly defined, and fixed to surrounding breast parenchyma.

rubric.text: Positions patient supine with shoulder supported to flatten breast tissue
Palpates with flat of three fingers without pinching normal glandular tissue
Covers all four quadrants, retroareolar area, and axillary tail of Spence
Documents location by clock face, size in centimetres, consistency, and margins

teach.heading: Pinching versus compression against ribs
teach.body:
The golden rule of breast palpation is never to pinch breast tissue between the thumb and index finger. Normal glandular tissue consists of lobules separated by fat and fibrous septa, which feel firm and discrete when grasped.

By laying the palmar pads of fingers flat and pressing gently against the underlying rib cage, normal lobules yield while genuine neoplastic or cystic masses stand out as discrete focal resistance.

teach.heading: Quadrant distribution and the axillary tail
teach.body:
Approximately 50 percent of all breast carcinomas develop in the upper outer quadrant, which contains the largest bulk of mammary parenchyma. The axillary tail of Spence pierces the deep fascia through the foramen of Langer.

Palpation must always track into the axillary fold. Carcinomas in the tail of Spence can be misdiagnosed as axillary lymphadenopathy or hidradenitis suppurativa.

teach.heading: Palpation profiles: fibroadenoma vs cyst vs carcinoma

rows: Fixed to tissue, skin, or muscle

skill.exam.surg.breast_mobility_fixity.title: Breast lump mobility and fixity testing
skill.exam.surg.breast_mobility_fixity.oneLine: Testing fixity to skin, breast parenchyma, pectoralis major, and serratus anterior on the chest wall
skill.exam.surg.breast_mobility_fixity.why: Determining the anatomical plane of fixity is the core clinical manoeuvre that separates localized breast disease from locally advanced T4 carcinoma. Fixity to pectoralis major or chest wall structures alters TNM staging, dictates neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and decides surgical resectability.

steps.text: Test fixity to the skin: gently pinch the skin overlying the lump between your thumb and index finger; if the skin cannot be pinched up independently, it is tethered or fixed to the mass.
Elicit skin dimpling: gently displace the lump away from the overlying skin in two opposite directions; observe whether the skin puckers or forms a shallow dimple over the tumour.

Test mobility within the breast tissue: hold the breast tissue firmly with one hand while attempting to move the lump with the other hand; a benign fibroadenoma moves freely, whereas a carcinoma moves only with the surrounding parenchyma.

Test fixity to the pectoralis major muscle: with the patient seated or supine, test lump mobility in two perpendicular directions (parallel and perpendicular to the muscle fibres) while the muscle is relaxed.
Contract the pectoralis major: instruct the patient to place both hands firmly on her hips and press inwards strongly against her pelvic bones.

Re-test lump mobility while the muscle is contracted: if the lump moves freely when relaxed but becomes fixed or restricted in mobility along the axis of muscle fibres when contracted, it is infiltrated into pectoralis major.
Test fixity to the chest wall and serratus anterior: with the patient seated, ask her to push her outstretched hands firmly against a wall or the examiner hand.

Palpate the lump during this pushing manoeuvre: if the lump is completely immobile in both directions even before and during pushing, it is fixed to the intercostal muscles, ribs, or serratus anterior (chest wall fixity).

skill.exam.surg.breast_mobility_fixity.normal: The lump moves freely in all directions when relaxed and contracted, overlying skin can be freely pinched off the lump without dimpling, and mobility is unaffected by pectoral or serratus contraction.
skill.exam.surg.breast_mobility_fixity.abnormal: Overlying skin cannot be pinched up (skin infiltration); visible skin dimple on moving the lump; lump mobility restricted across muscle fibres when hands press on hips (pectoralis major fixity); lump completely fixed to the bony thorax in both directions regardless of muscle action (chest wall fixity).
skill.exam.surg.breast_mobility_fixity.significance: Fixity to skin or Cooper ligaments represents local invasion. Fixity to pectoralis major indicates deep invasion of the retromammary space. True chest wall fixity (ribs, intercostal muscles, serratus anterior) classifies the tumour as clinical T4a, precluding immediate upfront mastectomy without downstaging.
skill.exam.surg.breast_mobility_fixity.practice: Perform the hands-on-hips and push-against-wall manoeuvres on a colleague, observing the contraction and hardening of pectoralis major and serratus anterior.
pitfalls: Confusing fixity to pectoralis major with true fixity to the chest wall; pectoralis involvement is T1 to T3 based on size, whereas rib/intercostal muscle fixity is T4a.
Testing pectoral fixity while the muscle is only partially contracted, leading to underestimation of deep infiltration.
Aggressively pinching a tense inflammatory tumour, causing intense pain and potential microvascular rupture.

probes.q: How do you contract the pectoralis major muscle to test for deep tumour fixity?
probes.a: Ask the patient to place both hands on her hips and press firmly inward against her pelvic bones.

probes.q: What does restriction of lump mobility during pectoralis contraction indicate compared to mobility when relaxed?
probes.a: It indicates that the tumour has infiltrated into the pectoralis major muscle or its covering deep pectoral fascia.

probes.q: Why is fixity to the pectoralis major muscle NOT classified as T4 in TNM staging, whereas fixity to ribs or intercostal muscles is T4a?
probes.a: The pectoralis major is an extrinsic muscle that can be safely excised en bloc with the breast, whereas chest wall structures (ribs, intercostals, serratus) represent deep thoracic wall invasion requiring major resection.

Assesses whether lump moves within breast tissue or moves with the breast
Tests mobility relaxed versus contracted during hands-on-hips manoeuvre
Distinguishes pectoral muscle fixity from true thoracic chest wall fixity

teach.heading: Stepwise testing of mobility planes
teach.body:
Mobility testing follows four anatomical planes from superficial to deep: the overlying skin, the glandular parenchyma, the pectoralis major muscle, and the skeletal chest wall.

Identifying which plane is tethered is essential for operative planning, determining whether breast-conserving surgery, mastectomy with pectoral fascial stripping, or full-thickness chest wall resection is required.

teach.heading: Pectoralis major fixity test manoeuvre
points: Grasp the lump between fingers while the patient arms rest at her sides, and assess mobility parallel and perpendicular to the direction of pectoral fibres.
Instruct the patient to press her hands firmly onto her hips, which strongly contracts both pectoralis major muscles.
Re-test lump mobility: if the lump becomes fixed or moves only with the muscle belly, it has invaded the pectoral fascia or muscle.
If the lump moves freely even during contraction, the retromammary space is clear of tumour infiltration.

teach.heading: Pectoral fixity versus true chest wall fixity

rows: T1, T2, or T3 (based on lump diameter)

skill.exam.surg.nipple_discharge.title: Examination of nipple discharge
skill.exam.surg.nipple_discharge.oneLine: Radial trigger-zone quadrant palpation, duct orifice identification, and colour characterisation of nipple discharge
skill.exam.surg.nipple_discharge.why: Pathological nipple discharge can arise from a benign intraductal papilloma, mammary duct ectasia, or an invasive ductal carcinoma. Systematic radial compression identifies the culprit duct and isolates the trigger quadrant, allowing targeted microdochectomy rather than blind major duct excision.

steps.text: Inspect the nipple and areola under bright illumination with a magnifying loupe if available, looking for crusted discharge, retraction, or visible dilated duct mouths.
Clean the nipple gently with an alcohol swab or saline-soaked gauze to clear dried secretions from the lactiferous duct orifices.
Begin systematic radial palpation: place the index finger at the outer periphery of the breast at the 12 o'clock position and press firmly while stripping inward towards the areola.
Repeat this radial compression manoeuvre systematically at every clock position (1, 2, 3 o'clock, continuing through all four quadrants) towards the nipple.
Watch the nipple face carefully during compression of each sector: identify the specific trigger zone where pressure reliably reproduces the discharge.
Inspect the nipple summit to determine whether fluid emerges from a single duct orifice or multiple duct openings across the lactiferous ampullae.

Examine the physical character of the discharge: collect a droplet on a white gauze swab to distinguish pure blood (sanguinous), serosanguinous, clear serous, greenish-brown, yellow pus, or milky secretions.
Perform chemical occult blood testing on the discharge using a bedside haemoccult strip if the fluid is dark or brown, confirming the presence of haemoglobin.
Prepare a direct smear on a glass slide for exfoliative cytology if indicated, fixing immediately in 95 percent ethanol.

skill.exam.surg.nipple_discharge.normal: No spontaneous discharge on gentle radial pressure; lactiferous duct orifices on the nipple summit are clean without crusts, blood, or inflammatory exudate.
skill.exam.surg.nipple_discharge.abnormal: Spontaneous or easily elicited discharge from a single duct orifice; blood-stained (bright red or dark brown) fluid; serous yellow fluid; thick greenish, toothpaste-like discharge from multiple ducts (duct ectasia); purulent discharge with periareolar tenderness (subareolar abscess); milky discharge from multiple ducts bilaterally (galactorrhoea).
skill.exam.surg.nipple_discharge.significance: Single-duct blood-stained or serosanguinous discharge in a patient over 40 years is strongly suspicious for intraductal papilloma or intraductal carcinoma, requiring microdochectomy. Multiduct greenish discharge with nipple slit-inversion denotes mammary duct ectasia.
skill.exam.surg.nipple_discharge.practice: Practise radial clock-face compression on a simulated model, identifying a localized trigger zone and transferring discharge onto white gauze to assess true colour against a bright background.
pitfalls: Squeezing the nipple summit directly between fingers, which empties all ampullae at once and obliterates the ability to locate the single offending duct.
Calling greenish-brown discharge bloody without testing on white gauze or a haemoccult strip; duct ectasia discharge often looks dark but contains no blood.
Reassuring a patient with single-duct serous discharge as benign without cytology or imaging, as ductal carcinoma in situ can present with non-bloody serous fluid.

probes.q: Why must the clinician compress each quadrant radially toward the areola instead of squeezing the nipple directly?
probes.a: To identify the specific trigger zone and culprit lactiferous duct; squeezing the nipple expresses fluid from multiple ducts simultaneously and conceals the anatomical origin.

probes.q: What is the most common pathological cause of spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct bloody nipple discharge in a 35-year-old woman?
probes.a: Benign intraductal papilloma (solitary duct papilloma within a major lactiferous duct).

probes.q: What clinical and surgical procedure is indicated for solitary single-duct blood-stained discharge when imaging is normal?
probes.a: Microdochectomy (selective excision of the single discharging lactiferous duct and its lobular segment using a fine lacrimal probe).

Performs radial quadrant compression systematically to identify trigger zone
Determines single-duct versus multi-duct origin on the nipple face
Expresses fluid onto white gauze to document colour and checks for blood

teach.heading: The radial trigger zone technique
teach.body:
Each lactiferous duct drains a discrete anatomical sector of the breast. Squeezing the nipple indiscriminately expresses fluid from several ducts at once, masking the pathology.

By pressing the finger at the periphery and stroking toward the areola clock hour by clock hour, the clinician discovers the precise wedge that provokes discharge, pinpointing the diseased duct.

teach.heading: Discharge colour on white gauze
teach.body:
Visualizing discharge against the patient skin can mislead the clinician; dark green or black fluid from duct ectasia looks bloody against pigmented skin.

Touching a sterile white gauze swab to the droplet resolves ambiguity: altered green-brown lipid pigment shows green edges on gauze, whereas genuine blood creates a red ring that haemoccult confirms.
