skill.exam.surg.axillary_nodes.title: Axillary and supraclavicular lymph node examination
skill.exam.surg.axillary_nodes.oneLine: Relaxation of the pectoral girdle, systematic palpation of the five axillary node groups, and supraclavicular assessment
skill.exam.surg.axillary_nodes.why: Axillary lymph node status is the single most powerful prognostic indicator in invasive breast carcinoma. Tense pectoral muscles obscure deep axillary nodes completely. Supporting the patient arm relaxes the fascia, allowing all five anatomical groups to be systematically palpated.

steps.text: Position the patient seated facing you; to examine the right axilla, support the patient right forearm with your right forearm, completely relaxing her shoulder girdle and pectoral muscles.
Use your left hand to palpate the right axilla (and vice versa: support the left arm with your left hand, palpating the left axilla with your right hand).

Palpate the anterior (pectoral) group: grasp the anterior axillary fold between your fingers inside the axilla and your thumb on the pectoralis major outside, palpating along the lower border of the muscle.
Palpate the posterior (subscapular) group: grasp the posterior axillary fold between your fingers and thumb, palpating along the anterior border of the latissimus dorsi and subscapularis.
Palpate the lateral (brachial) group: palpate against the upper medial aspect of the humerus along the axillary vein while moving the patient arm slightly through abduction.
Palpate the central group: press the pads of your extended fingers flat against the thoracic wall in the middle of the axilla (against the ribs and serratus anterior).
Palpate the apical (infraclavicular) group: push your fingers high into the apex of the axilla behind the pectoralis minor muscle towards the clavicle, asking the patient to shrug slightly.
Examine the supraclavicular fossa: stand behind the patient, have her tilt her head slightly forward, and palpate deeply behind the clavicle for enlarged supraclavicular lymph nodes.
Characterise any enlarged nodes: number, size in centimetres, consistency (soft, firm, rubbery, stony hard), tenderness, discrete nature versus matted clusters, and fixity to deep structures.

skill.exam.surg.axillary_nodes.normal: Axillary and supraclavicular fossae are soft, non-tender, and clear; no palpable lymph nodes in any of the five axillary groups or supraclavicular basins.
skill.exam.surg.axillary_nodes.abnormal: Palpable lymph nodes; metastatic carcinoma: stony hard, non-tender, discrete initially, becoming matted and fixed to chest wall or axillary vein in advanced disease; reactive/infective: tender, soft or elastic, mobile, discrete.
skill.exam.surg.axillary_nodes.significance: Palpable, firm or hard axillary nodes in breast cancer indicate lymphatic metastasis (clinical N1 or N2). Matted nodes fixed to underlying chest wall denote N2a disease. Metastatic supraclavicular lymph node involvement classifies the patient as clinical N3c (Stage IIIC locally advanced breast cancer).
skill.exam.surg.axillary_nodes.practice: Practise arm-support positioning with a colleague, palpating all five axillary boundaries (pectoral, subscapular, brachial, central, apical) and the supraclavicular fossa from behind.
pitfalls: Failing to support the patient arm, so the patient voluntarily holds her arm abducted, tensing the pectoralis major and making axillary palpation impossible.
Examining the right axilla with the right hand, which prevents proper cupping against the thoracic wall.
Forgetting to palpate the supraclavicular fossa, missing N3c metastatic disease that fundamentally changes surgical staging and treatment strategy.

probes.q: How must the examiner hold the patient arm to examine the right axilla properly?
probes.a: The examiner supports the patient right forearm with the examiner right forearm, leaving the left hand free to palpate the axilla while pectoral muscles are fully relaxed.

probes.q: What are the five anatomical groups of lymph nodes in the axilla?
probes.a: Anterior (pectoral), posterior (subscapular), lateral (brachial), central, and apical (infraclavicular).

probes.q: What surgical and clinical implication does the presence of an ipsilateral supraclavicular lymph node metastasis have in breast cancer?
probes.a: It denotes clinical N3c disease (Stage IIIC locally advanced breast cancer), indicating systemic lymphatic spread that precludes upfront curative surgery and mandates neoadjuvant systemic therapy.

Systematically palpates pectoral, subscapular, brachial, central, and apical groups
Stands behind patient and palpates supraclavicular fossae bilaterally
Characterises lymph node size, consistency (hard), mobility, and matting

teach.heading: Why arm support is mechanically essential
teach.body:
The axilla is a pyramidal space enclosed by thick muscular walls: pectoralis major anteriorly and latissimus dorsi with subscapularis posteriorly. If the patient holds her own arm up, these muscles contract vigorously.

Tensing the pectoral fascia creates an impenetrable rigid roof. Resting the patient forearm on the examiner arm removes all muscular tone, allowing the fingers to glide effortlessly into the apex.

teach.heading: Berg anatomical levels for axillary dissection
teach.body:
Surgeons divide axillary nodes into three levels based on their relationship to the pectoralis minor muscle: Level I lies lateral and inferior to pectoralis minor; Level II lies directly behind pectoralis minor; Level III lies medial and superior to pectoralis minor up to the apex.

Standard axillary lymph node dissection for invasive breast cancer clears Levels I and II, preserving Level III unless gross disease is present.

skill.ix.surg.triple_assessment.title: Triple assessment of breast lesions
skill.ix.surg.triple_assessment.oneLine: Multimodal diagnostic protocol: clinical examination, radiological imaging (mammography vs ultrasound), and tissue pathology
skill.ix.surg.triple_assessment.why: No single diagnostic modality has sufficient sensitivity and specificity to rule out breast malignancy alone. The triple assessment protocol achieves a diagnostic accuracy exceeding 99 percent when all three components concord, preventing missed cancers and unnecessary surgical excisions.
skill.ix.surg.triple_assessment.practice: Review a series of triple assessment vignettes, assigning numeric scores from 1 to 5 for clinical, radiological, and pathological findings, and applying the concordance rule.
pitfalls: Ordering mammography as the initial imaging modality in a 24-year-old woman; dense glandular tissue renders mammography uninterpretable, so ultrasound is mandatory.
Performing simple fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) instead of core needle biopsy when receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) is required before treatment.
Discharging a patient with a clinically suspicious stony hard lump because cytology or mammography was reported as benign (the rule of concordance requires excision).

probes.q: What are the three mandatory components of the triple assessment of breast disease?
probes.a: 1. Clinical examination; 2. Radiological imaging (mammography and/or ultrasound); 3. Pathological tissue assessment (core needle biopsy or FNAC).

probes.q: Why is breast ultrasound preferred over mammography in women under 35 years of age?
probes.a: Younger women have dense, radio-opaque glandular breast tissue that obscures microcalcifications and masses on mammography; ultrasound clearly differentiates solid from cystic lesions in dense breasts.

probes.q: What is the rule of concordance in triple assessment, and what action is required if one modality is suspicious while two are benign?
probes.a: All three modalities must agree (concord) to confirm a benign diagnosis; if any single component is suspicious or malignant (discordant), a definitive tissue biopsy or surgical excision is mandatory.

rubric.text: Names all three components of triple assessment (clinical, imaging, pathology)
Selects ultrasound under age 35/40 and mammography over age 40 correctly
Recommends core needle biopsy over FNAC for receptor status and invasive architecture
Explains concordance rule and mandates histological excision for discordant results

teach.heading: Components and scoring of triple assessment
teach.body:
Every patient attending a modern breast clinic undergoes three independent evaluations: clinical examination (E1 to E5), imaging by ultrasound or mammography (R1 to R5 / BI-RADS), and pathology by core biopsy or cytology (B1 to B5 / C1 to C5).

A score of 1 represents normal tissue, 2 represents benign, 3 is equivocal, 4 is suspicious, and 5 is definitively malignant.

rows: Dense glandular tissue is radio-opaque on X-ray; ultrasound separates cysts from solid lumps
Transition zone; ultrasound for focal lump, mammography for microcalcifications
Fatty breast replacement gives high mammographic contrast for microcalcifications

teach.heading: Core needle biopsy versus fine needle aspiration (FNAC)
teach.body:
While FNAC provides rapid cytological confirmation, it cannot distinguish ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) from invasive carcinoma because basement membrane architecture is lost.

Core needle biopsy provides histological tissue cores, reliably diagnosing invasion and allowing immunohistochemistry for oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2/neu status.

skill.annex.surg.tnm_breast.title: TNM staging and classification of breast carcinoma
skill.annex.surg.tnm_breast.oneLine: Clinical and pathological AJCC / UICC TNM criteria for tumour size, nodal spread, and anatomical stage grouping
skill.annex.surg.tnm_breast.why: Accurate TNM staging standardises breast cancer communication, determines eligibility for breast conservation versus modified radical mastectomy, dictates neoadjuvant systemic therapy, and establishes long-term survival prognosis.
skill.annex.surg.tnm_breast.practice: Practise staging five patient clinical vignettes using the T, N, M criteria and assigning the final AJCC anatomical stage group from Stage I to Stage IV.
pitfalls: Classifying pectoralis major muscle involvement as T4; only skin ulceration, skin nodules, peau d'orange, and chest wall fixity (ribs, intercostals) constitute T4.
Confusing clinical staging (cTNM, based on physical examination and imaging) with pathological staging (pTNM, based on histological resection).
Overlooking supraclavicular lymph node metastases, which are classified as N3c (Stage IIIC) rather than distant metastatic M1 disease.

probes.q: What tumour diameter cut-offs define T1, T2, and T3 in breast cancer TNM staging?
probes.a: T1 is 2.0 cm or less; T2 is greater than 2.0 cm up to 5.0 cm; T3 is greater than 5.0 cm.

probes.q: What clinical criteria define category T4 in breast carcinoma staging?
probes.a: T4 tumour of any size with direct extension to: T4a (chest wall: ribs, intercostals, serratus); T4b (skin ulceration, ipsilateral satellite nodules, or peau d'orange); T4c (both 4a and 4b); T4d (inflammatory carcinoma).

probes.q: How are ipsilateral internal mammary and supraclavicular lymph node metastases classified in N staging?
probes.a: Internal mammary nodes with axillary nodes are N3b; supraclavicular lymph nodes are N3c; either classifies the disease as Stage IIIC locally advanced breast cancer.

Distinguishes T4a (chest wall), T4b (skin/peau d'orange), and T4d (inflammatory)
Categorises N1 (mobile), N2 (fixed/matted), and N3 (supraclavicular/infraclavicular)
Assigns clinical Stage I, II, III, and IV based on TNM combinations

teach.heading: Regional lymph nodes (N) and stage grouping
teach.body:
N1 represents mobile ipsilateral level I/II axillary nodes. N2 represents matted or fixed axillary nodes (N2a) or clinically apparent internal mammary nodes without axillary disease (N2b).

N3 includes infraclavicular nodes (N3a), internal mammary with axillary nodes (N3b), or supraclavicular nodes (N3c). Stage I is T1N0M0; Stage II is early operable disease; Stage III is locally advanced; Stage IV is distant metastatic disease.

skill.hx.surg.dysphagia.title: Surgical history of dysphagia
skill.hx.surg.dysphagia.oneLine: Solids versus liquids differentiation, anatomical site of arrest, progression tempo, and red flag alarm symptoms
skill.hx.surg.dysphagia.why: Dysphagia represents mechanical obstruction or neuromuscular dysmotility until proven otherwise. A structured history distinguishes benign motility disorders from rapidly fatal oesophageal malignancy, localises the anatomical level of obstruction, and detects complications like aspiration pneumonia.

asks.text: Did the swallowing difficulty begin suddenly (foreign body impaction, acute esophagitis) or gradually over several months (carcinoma, achalasia, benign stricture)?

Do you have difficulty swallowing solids, liquids, or both: did it start with solids and progress to liquids (mechanical obstruction), or was it equal for solids and liquids from the onset (motility disorder)?
Where does the food feel like it sticks: in the throat/neck (oropharyngeal/cervical) or retrosternally behind the chest and epigastrium (mid or distal oesophagus)?
Do you experience regurgitation of undigested, foul-smelling food, particularly when lying flat at night, or sour acid reflux after meals?
Is swallowing painful (odynophagia), and do you have a sensation of retrosternal burning or chest tightness radiating to the back?
Have you noticed hoarseness of voice, persistent coughing or choking fits while eating (aspiration or tracheo-oesophageal fistula), and how much weight have you lost?

skill.hx.surg.dysphagia.practice: Take a focused five-minute dysphagia history from a simulated elderly patient, distinguishing progressive solid-to-liquid dysphagia from episodic motility spasm and screening for red flags.
pitfalls: Accepting a patient localization of obstruction at the suprasternal notch as proof of a cervical lesion; distal oesophageal lesions frequently refer sensation upwards to the neck.
Assuming that dysphagia for liquids before solids rules out mechanical cancer; patients occasionally drink liquids rapidly, triggering bolus impact against a tight malignant stricture.
Attributing dysphagia in an elderly smoker to benign acid reflux without arranging urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.

probes.q: How does the progression of dysphagia distinguish mechanical obstruction from a motility disorder?
probes.a: Mechanical obstruction begins with solids and progressively worsens to involve liquids; motility disorders cause dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the onset, often with episodic fluctuation.

probes.q: Why can a patient with a carcinoma of the lower third of the oesophagus complain of food sticking in the neck?
probes.a: Somatic sensory innervation of the lower oesophagus can refer obstruction sensations retrogradely to the suprasternal notch or throat; distal lesions can refer upwards, but cervical lesions never refer downwards.

probes.q: What does regurgitation of completely undigested, non-acidic, foul-smelling food eaten hours earlier suggest clinically?
probes.a: Oesophageal retention proximal to an obstruction, characteristic of achalasia cardia with mega-oesophagus or a Zenker pharyngeal pouch.

Inquires about the perceived anatomical level of swallowing arrest
Characterises regurgitation (acidic vs non-acidic) and separates dysphagia from odynophagia
Screens for alarm symptoms: marked weight loss, hoarseness, and choking on swallowing

teach.heading: Referred sensation and the level of arrest
teach.body:
While patients reliably point to where food seems to halt, the surgical aphorism holds true: distal lesions can refer sensation upwards, but proximal lesions never refer downwards.

A patient pointing to the lower sternum almost always has pathology at or below that level (gastro-oesophageal junction), whereas a patient pointing to the suprasternal notch may have a high pharyngeal lesion, a cervical stricture, or a carcinoma at the lower end of the oesophagus.

teach.heading: Red flag alarm symptoms in dysphagia
points: Rapid weight loss and profound anorexia point toward invasive oesophageal adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma.
Hoarseness of voice indicates recurrent laryngeal nerve infiltration, usually by mid-thoracic oesophageal tumour or mediastinal nodes.
Choking, coughing, and recurrent aspiration pneumonia on swallowing suggest tracheo-oesophageal fistula or neuromuscular pharyngeal paralysis.
History of accidental or intentional caustic acid/alkali ingestion indicates severe corrosive cicatricial stricture.

skill.exam.surg.dysphagia.title: Physical examination in dysphagia
skill.exam.surg.dysphagia.oneLine: Nutritional state, oral cavity survey, neck examination for Troisier sign and pharyngeal pouch, and abdominal palpation
skill.exam.surg.dysphagia.why: Physical signs in dysphagia identify metastatic dissemination, severe systemic malnutrition, and specific cervical pathologies like Zenker diverticulum or Paterson-Kelly syndrome. Detecting Virchow lymphadenopathy or hepatic metastases transforms clinical management from curative resection to palliative stenting.

steps.text: Assess general nutritional and systemic status: note temporal wasting, sunken eyes, skin turgor (dehydration), and loose clothes indicating cachexia.
Examine the hands, eyes, and mouth for stigmata of chronic iron deficiency anaemia (Paterson-Kelly / Plummer-Vinson syndrome): pallor, koilonychia (spoon nails), angular stomatitis, and cheilosis.

Examine the oral cavity and oropharynx with a pen torch and tongue depressor: inspect for tonsillar enlargement, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), palatal paralysis (say 'aah'), and smooth atrophic glossitis.

Inspect the neck for visible masses: look for thyroid enlargement, retrosternal goitre fullness, or a compressible pouch swelling in the lower posterior triangle (pharyngeal pouch / Zenker diverticulum).

Palpate the neck systematically: assess the thyroid gland, and check for Boyce sign by compressing a suspected left lower neck pouch; listen for gurgling and note regurgitation of stale food or gas into the mouth.

Test for Moure sign (laryngeal crepitus): grasp the thyroid cartilage between your thumb and forefinger and rock it gently from side to side against the cervical spine; normal laryngeal crepitus is lost when a post-cricoid or hypopharyngeal tumour infiltrates the retrovisceral space.

Palpate the left supraclavicular fossa with the patient neck slightly flexed: feel specifically for an enlarged, hard, non-tender Virchow lymph node (Troisier sign), indicating transcoelomic or thoracic duct metastasis.

Palpate the abdomen: check for an epigastric mass (carcinoma of the stomach or lower oesophagus), palpable nodular hepatomegaly (hepatic metastases), and test for shifting dullness (malignant ascites).

skill.exam.surg.dysphagia.normal: Well-nourished patient with normal skin turgor, pink conjunctivae, healthy tongue and nails, normal palatal elevation, absence of neck masses, presence of crisp laryngeal crepitus on rocking thyroid cartilage, clear supraclavicular fossae without lymphadenopathy, and soft non-tender abdomen without organomegaly.
skill.exam.surg.dysphagia.abnormal: Profound cachexia, dehydration, marked conjunctival pallor with koilonychia and atrophic glossitis; left posterior neck swelling that gurgles on compression (Boyce sign); absence of laryngeal crepitus (negative Moure sign); hard, non-tender left supraclavicular node (Troisier sign); hard, irregular epigastric mass, nodular hepatomegaly, or ascites.
skill.exam.surg.dysphagia.significance: Troisier sign confirms metastatic carcinoma (Stage IV). A negative Moure sign indicates invasive post-cricoid or cervical oesophageal carcinoma obliterating the prevertebral plane. Boyce sign establishes Zenker pharyngeal pouch. Koilonychia and glossitis indicate Paterson-Kelly syndrome with high risk of post-cricoid malignancy.
skill.exam.surg.dysphagia.practice: Practise eliciting normal laryngeal crepitus (Moure sign) on yourself or a colleague by gently rocking the thyroid cartilage across the cervical vertebrae, feeling and hearing the crisp click.
pitfalls: Missing a small, discrete Virchow node by palpating the left supraclavicular fossa with the patient neck extended; the neck must be slightly flexed to relax the sternocleidomastoid.
Dismissing mild conjunctival pallor and brittle nails in a middle-aged woman with upper dysphagia, missing Paterson-Kelly syndrome which is premalignant.
Omiting abdominal palpation in dysphagia; metastatic hepatomegaly or an epigastric tumour completely changes the operative plan.

probes.q: What is Troisier sign, and what does its presence indicate in a patient with progressive dysphagia?
probes.a: An enlarged, hard, non-tender left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow node); it indicates metastatic spread from gastric or lower oesophageal carcinoma via the thoracic duct.

probes.q: What is Moure sign (laryngeal crepitus), and why is it absent in post-cricoid carcinoma?
probes.a: Normal laryngeal crepitus is a friction sensation felt when the larynx is rocked against the cervical spine; it is lost when a post-cricoid tumour infiltrates between the cricoid cartilage and prevertebral fascia.

probes.q: What triad of features defines Paterson-Kelly (Plummer-Vinson) syndrome, and why is it surgically significant?
probes.a: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia, glossitis/koilonychia, and upper oesophageal web causing dysphagia; it is a recognised precancerous condition predisposing to post-cricoid squamous cell carcinoma.

Examines oral cavity, tonsils, and tests palatal movement
Palpates neck for Boyce sign and tests laryngeal crepitus (Moure sign)
Palpates left supraclavicular fossa for Troisier sign and checks liver/epigastrium

teach.heading: Moure sign: the laryngeal crepitus test
teach.body:
In a healthy individual, grasping the thyroid lamina and moving the larynx gently from side to side across the anterior surface of the cervical vertebral bodies produces a distinct, audible, and palpable grating or clicking sensation.

When a neoplasm arises in the post-cricoid region or hypopharynx, the tumour mass intervenes between the cricoid and the spine, cushioning the movement and abolishing this normal friction (negative Moure sign).

rows: Palpate left supraclavicular fossa behind clavicle
Compress swelling in left lower neck
Gurgling sound as pouch empties into pharynx (Zenker)
Rock thyroid cartilage sideways against vertebrae
Loss of crepitus indicates post-cricoid malignant infiltration
Raise both arms above head for one minute
Facial congestion indicates retrosternal goitre compression

teach.heading: Paterson-Kelly (Plummer-Vinson) syndrome
teach.body:
This syndrome occurs almost exclusively in middle-aged and elderly women with severe, long-standing iron deficiency anaemia. Patients exhibit spoon nails (koilonychia), atrophic glossitis, angular stomatitis, and splenomegaly.

A thin mucosal fold or web develops at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction, producing painless upper dysphagia. It is an aggressive precancerous lesion requiring endoscopic surveillance for post-cricoid carcinoma.

skill.ix.surg.dysphagia_workup.title: Investigation of dysphagia: endoscopy, barium swallow, and manometry
skill.ix.surg.dysphagia_workup.oneLine: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy, fluoroscopic barium contrast patterns, and high-resolution manometry
skill.ix.surg.dysphagia_workup.why: Dysphagia cannot be managed safely without direct visualization, tissue histopathology, and functional motility evaluation. Selecting the appropriate sequence of diagnostic modalities prevents instrumental perforation of a pharyngeal pouch and identifies early treatable mucosal neoplasia.
skill.ix.surg.dysphagia_workup.practice: Review a series of five classic barium swallow radiographs and match each image to its hallmark pattern: bird-beak, apple-core, smooth tapering, corkscrew, or Zenker pouch.
pitfalls: Blindly inserting a flexible endoscope without inspecting the pharynx first, risking catastrophic perforation into a Zenker pharyngeal pouch.
Taking superficial punch biopsies of a suspected achalasia cardia without sampling deeply, missing a submucosal infiltrating pseudoachalasia carcinoma.
Ordering high-resolution manometry before performing endoscopy; mechanical cancer must always be excluded before diagnosing primary motility spasm.

probes.q: What is the mandatory first-line investigation for any patient over 50 years presenting with progressive dysphagia?
probes.a: Upper gastrointestinal flexible endoscopy (oesophagogastroduodenoscopy / OGD) with direct visualization and biopsy of any mucosal abnormality.

probes.q: What classic radiological appearance is seen on barium swallow in: 1. Achalasia cardia; 2. Oesophageal carcinoma?
probes.a: 1. Achalasia shows a dilated, aperistaltic oesophagus with smooth, symmetrical, conical tapering at the lower end (bird-beak or rat-tail sign); 2. Carcinoma shows an irregular, shouldered, eccentric filling defect with mucosal destruction (apple-core sign).

probes.q: What manometric diagnostic criteria define achalasia cardia on high-resolution oesophageal manometry?
probes.a: Incomplete or absent relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (elevated integrated relaxation pressure / IRP) combined with 100 percent aperistalsis in the oesophageal tubular body.

Recognises bird-beak (achalasia), apple-core (carcinoma), and corkscrew (spasm) barium signs
Warns of perforation risk in Zenker diverticulum during blind endoscopic intubation
Explains role of high-resolution manometry (aperistalsis + non-relaxing LES) in motility workup

teach.heading: The diagnostic triad in dysphagia
teach.body:
The modern workup of dysphagia combines three complementary pillars: flexible endoscopy for direct luminal inspection and tissue biopsy; fluoroscopic barium swallow for dynamic bolus transit and anatomy; and high-resolution manometry for intraluminal pressure profiles.

Endoscopy is mandatory to exclude mucosal cancer, while barium swallow identifies extrinsic compression, tortuosity, and diverticula.

rows: Bird-beak or rat-tail smooth conical tapering
Hypertonic, non-relaxing lower sphincter with dilated mega-oesophagus
Irregular filling defect with shelf-like shouldering
Infiltrating malignant ulcer destroying mucosa and narrowing lumen
Circumferential fibrous cicatrix from chronic acid reflux

teach.heading: Endoscopic safety in Zenker pharyngeal pouch
teach.body:
Zenker diverticulum arises through Killian dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles. The pouch extends directly inferiorly in line with the pharyngeal lumen, while the true oesophageal entrance is displaced anteriorly.

Blind introduction of an endoscope or nasogastric tube enters the thin-walled pouch and perforates the retropharyngeal space, causing mediastinitis. Fluoroscopic barium swallow must always precede instrumentation if a pouch is suspected.

skill.annex.surg.dysphagia_score.title: Dysphagia grading scores and surgical aetiological classification
skill.annex.surg.dysphagia_score.oneLine: Atkinson / Mellow-Pinkas functional dysphagia grading scale and anatomical classification (intraluminal, intramural, extramural)
skill.annex.surg.dysphagia_score.why: Objective numerical grading of dysphagia standardises clinical communication, tracks disease deterioration, measures response to endoscopic dilation, stenting, or myotomy, and provides an objective benchmark for surgical oncology outcomes.
skill.annex.surg.dysphagia_score.practice: Practise assigning Atkinson dysphagia grades (0 to 4) to three patient scenarios and categorising ten causes of dysphagia into intraluminal, intramural, and extramural groups.
pitfalls: Documenting dysphagia as mild, moderate, or severe without anchoring to a validated functional score based on food consistency.
Failing to recognise that a score change from Grade 2 (semi-solids only) to Grade 4 (complete aphagia) within weeks indicates acute malignant luminal occlusion.
Forgetting extramural causes such as aortic aneurysm or retrosternal goitre, which present with dysphagia despite normal mucosal endoscopy.

probes.q: What dietary functional milestones define Grades 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 on the Atkinson dysphagia scale?
probes.a: Grade 0: Able to eat normal diet; Grade 1: Able to swallow some solids; Grade 2: Able to swallow semi-solids only; Grade 3: Able to swallow liquids only; Grade 4: Unable to swallow liquids / complete dysphagia (aphagia for saliva).

probes.q: How are causes of oesophageal dysphagia classified anatomically into three surgical groups?
probes.a: 1. Intraluminal (within the lumen, such as foreign bodies); 2. Intramural (in the oesophageal wall, such as carcinoma, stricture, webs, achalasia); 3. Extramural (extrinsic compression, such as retrosternal goitre, mediastinal nodes, aortic aneurysm, dysphagia lusoria).

probes.q: What vascular anomaly causes dysphagia lusoria, and which anatomical surgical group does it belong to?
probes.a: An aberrant right subclavian artery arising from the descending aorta and crossing behind the oesophagus; it is an extramural (extrinsic compression) cause of dysphagia.

rubric.text: Details Atkinson grades 0 to 4 based on food consistency milestones (normal, solid, semi-solid, liquid, aphagia)
Categorises surgical aetiology into intraluminal, intramural, and extramural
Names key extramural causes: retrosternal goitre, aortic aneurysm, and dysphagia lusoria
Explains how the score monitors post-stenting or post-dilatation recovery

teach.heading: The Atkinson / Mellow-Pinkas dysphagia grading scale

rows: Able to swallow some solid food; chews carefully
Able to swallow semi-solid or soft pureed food only
Able to swallow liquids only; solids completely blocked
Unable to swallow liquids; saliva drools or is spat out

teach.heading: Surgical anatomical classification of dysphagia causes

rows: Impacted foreign body (meat bolus, denture, coin), large polyp
Squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, peptic stricture, achalasia, spasm, web
Retrosternal goitre, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, aortic aneurysm, aberrant subclavian

teach.heading: Clinical utility of functional grading
teach.body:
Subjective terms such as severe or mild dysphagia fail to capture therapeutic response or disease progression. Applying the Atkinson scale provides an immediate numerical benchmark.

For example, successful palliative self-expanding metal stent (SEMS) deployment in inoperable oesophageal carcinoma is documented objectively by an improvement from Grade 3 (liquids only) to Grade 1 (soft solid diet).

skill.hx.surg.abdominal_trauma.title: History in abdominal trauma
skill.hx.surg.abdominal_trauma.oneLine: Mechanism, deceleration impact, weapon details, and urinary red flags
skill.hx.surg.abdominal_trauma.why: Closed injuries often mask catastrophic internal haemorrhage or visceral disruption behind minimal external signs. Uncovering the exact force, velocity, seat-belt deceleration, and time elapsed directs immediate resuscitation before circulatory collapse occurs.

asks.text: How did the injury happen: direct blunt impact, crush, blast wave, or high-speed vehicular collision?
Were you wearing a seat-belt, and did your body decelerate abruptly against the strap or steering assembly?
If wounded by a weapon, what was its length and trajectory, and was it a low-velocity blade or high-velocity firearm bullet?
Exactly how much time has passed between the trauma incident and arrival at the emergency department?
Have you vomited since the injury, and did the vomitus contain fresh red blood or coffee-ground material?
Have you passed urine since the trauma, did it contain blood, or do you feel an intense urge to void without being able to pass urine?

skill.hx.surg.abdominal_trauma.practice: Rehearse taking a rapid trauma history within two minutes, systematically identifying deceleration markers, seat-belt sign, and urinary warning signs.
pitfalls: Dismissing severe intra-abdominal injury because external abdominal wall bruising is absent or minor.
Failing to ask about micturition and haematuria, missing extraperitoneal or intraperitoneal bladder ruptures.
Overlooking deceleration forces from two-point lap seat-belts that cause mesenteric avulsion or small bowel transection.
Assuming early normal vital signs exclude major solid organ injury in young patients who compensate effectively.

probes.q: A trauma patient has an intense urge to void but passes only drops of blood at the meatus. What injury is suspected?
probes.a: Rupture of the membranous urethra or extraperitoneal rupture of the urinary bladder associated with pelvic fracture.

probes.q: Why do lap seat-belts cause mesenteric tears and hollow viscus injury during sudden deceleration?
probes.a: The anterior abdominal wall decelerates abruptly while mobile intra-abdominal viscera continue forward momentum, shearing the gut from its mesentery at points of anatomical fixation.

probes.q: How does the time interval since injury influence your interpretation of vital signs in blunt abdominal trauma?
probes.a: Young patients compensate for blood loss with tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, maintaining normal blood pressure until twenty to thirty percent of blood volume is lost; prolonged delay risks sudden unheralded decompensation.

rubric.text: Enquires about exact mechanism of trauma and impact vectors
Screens for haematuria, retention, and blood at the meatus
Records exact time elapsed from injury to clinical assessment
Identifies deceleration harness and steering wheel impact
Checks for haematemesis and contents of post-trauma vomitus

teach.heading: Mechanism determines the spectrum of visceral injury
teach.body:
Closed blunt trauma generates crushing waves and compression against the vertebral column, splitting solid organs like the spleen and liver. Rapid deceleration causes acute traction at fixed attachments, tearing the mesentery or renal pedicle.

Penetrating trauma severity depends on blade path and missile velocity. High-velocity projectiles transfer kinetic energy radially, creating temporary cavitation and devitalising tissue well beyond the apparent track.

teach.heading: Deceleration forces and seat-belt trauma
teach.body:
Seat-belt restraints reduce fatal ejection but generate distinctive injury patterns during abrupt deceleration. When the torso decelerates, inertia propels mobile bowel loops forward against fixed peritoneal reflections.

This produces mesenteric avulsion, devascularisation, or blow-out perforation of the small bowel, particularly near the duodenojejunal flexure and ileocaecal junction. Look specifically for the cutaneous seat-belt sign across the lower abdomen.

teach.heading: Urinary clues in pelvic and lower urinary tract disruption

rows: Urge but only meatal blood drops
Sheared membranous urethra in pelvic fracture
Bladder dome tear into peritoneal cavity
Anterior bladder wall laceration below reflection

skill.exam.surg.abdominal_trauma.title: Physical examination in abdominal trauma
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_trauma.oneLine: Inspection for seatbelt marks, gentle palpation, pelvic stability, and serial evaluation
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_trauma.why: Blunt and penetrating trauma can cause life-threatening internal haemorrhage or peritoneal contamination with deceptive early presentations. Rigorous physical examination detects evolving peritonitis, prevents dangerous urethral catheterisation, and establishes the need for immediate surgical exploration.

steps.text: Expose the entire torso and inspect the abdominal wall for abrasions, contusions, tyre marks, puncture sites, seat-belt bruising, and respiratory movements.
Assess general disposition, distinguishing the restless agitation of hypovolaemia and internal haemorrhage from the motionless stillness of peritonitis.
Palpate gently with warm hands, starting in the quadrant furthest from suspected pain, feeling for localized tenderness, muscular guarding, and board-like rigidity.
Test pelvic ring stability once by applying gentle manual compression across both anterior superior iliac spines and anteroposterior pressure on the pubic symphysis.
Inspect the perineum, scrotum, and external urethral meatus for blood drops or haematoma before considering urinary catheterisation.
Perform a digital rectal examination to assess sphincter tone, prostate position, pelvic bone fragments, and rectal mucosal integrity or intraluminal blood.
Establish a baseline abdominal girth measurement at the level of the umbilicus and schedule serial physical reassessments every thirty to sixty minutes.

skill.exam.surg.abdominal_trauma.normal: Symmetrical abdominal wall excursions with respiration, no visible contusions, soft non-tender abdomen without guarding or rigidity, normal bowel sounds, stable pelvic ring, and clear urethral meatus.
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_trauma.abnormal: Cutaneous ecchymosis, seat-belt contusion, absent respiratory movement, localized or generalized involuntary muscular rigidity, pelvic ring instability, blood at the urethral meatus, or a high-riding prostate.
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_trauma.significance: Involuntary rigidity indicates peritonitis from hollow viscus rupture or haemoperitoneum, pelvic instability signals massive retroperitoneal bleeding, and meatal blood warns against blind urethral catheterisation.
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_trauma.practice: Perform a complete trauma secondary survey of the abdomen on a simulated patient, demonstrating gentle palpation technique, single-attempt pelvic testing, and perineal inspection.
pitfalls: Repeatedly springing or rocking an unstable pelvis, which disrupts clotted retroperitoneal haematomas and accelerates exsanguination.
Inserting a Foley catheter when blood is present at the urethral meatus, transforming a partial urethral tear into a complete disruption.
Relying on a single physical examination in blunt trauma rather than instituting documented serial abdominal re-examinations.
Palpating vigorously over painful regions first, provoking intense voluntary guarding that obscures peritoneal signs.

probes.q: What must you check before inserting a urethral catheter in a male patient with abdominal and pelvic trauma?
probes.a: Inspect the external urethral meatus for blood, check the perineum for bruising, and perform a rectal examination to confirm normal prostate position.

probes.q: Why is pelvic compression testing performed only once during the physical examination?
probes.a: Repeated manipulation of an unstable pelvic fracture dislodges fragile haemostatic clots in the retroperitoneal venous plexus, provoking catastrophic haemorrhage.

probes.q: How do you distinguish voluntary muscular guarding from involuntary muscular rigidity at the bedside?
probes.a: Voluntary guarding relaxes during expiration and when the patient flexes their knees and breathes quietly; involuntary rigidity persists as an unyielding muscular spasm throughout the entire respiratory cycle.

rubric.text: Inspects entire abdominal wall and flanks for contusions and seat-belt mark
Palpates gently starting away from pain to detect involuntary rigidity
Assesses pelvic stability gently and performs test only once
Inspects external urethral meatus before any catheterisation attempt
Institutes scheduled serial physical reassessments and girth monitoring

teach.heading: Inspection and the geography of abdominal contusions
teach.body:
Physical signs in abdominal trauma are dynamic and evolve over hours. External bruises frequently reveal the direction and magnitude of blunt force. The classic seat-belt sign across the lower abdomen correlates strongly with small bowel and mesenteric tears.

Flank ecchymosis or periumbilical bruising often reflects retroperitoneal extravasation of blood, though these cutaneous manifestations may take hours or days to appear fully.

teach.heading: Guarding versus rigidity and peritoneal irritation
teach.body:
Distinguishing voluntary resistance from involuntary muscular rigidity is the cardinal clinical skill. Have the patient bend the knees and breathe slowly through an open mouth. Keep hands warm and palpate flat with the pulps of the fingers.

If the abdominal musculature remains board-like and unyielding during both inspiration and expiration, chemical or bacterial peritonitis is established, mandating urgent surgical exploration.

teach.heading: Pelvic fracture and urethral protection
teach.body:
Pelvic fractures frequently lacerate the presacral and paravesical venous plexuses, accumulating up to two to three litres of blood in the retroperitoneum with little external swelling.

Compress the pelvis gently once; if instability is elicited, halt further manipulation immediately and apply a pelvic binder. Never pass a catheter blindly if meatal blood or scrotal haematoma is identified, as retrograde urethrography is mandatory first.

skill.exam.surg.splenic_injury_signs.title: Clinical examination for splenic trauma
skill.exam.surg.splenic_injury_signs.oneLine: Kehr sign, Ballance sign, and detecting the delayed rupture of Baudet
skill.exam.surg.splenic_injury_signs.why: The spleen is the most frequently injured visceral organ in blunt abdominal trauma. Missing early signs of splenic tear or overlooking a subcapsular haematoma risks sudden catastrophic intraperitoneal exsanguination after a deceptive symptom-free interval.

steps.text: Inspect the left lower ribcage for abrasions, bruising, or paradoxical movement, noting any fracture of the left ninth to eleventh ribs.
Palpate the left hypochondrium gently, noting localized tenderness, muscular guarding, and restriction of diaphragm excursion.
Elicit Kehr sign by applying firm pressure over the left hypochondrium or placing the patient in a slight head-down position, enquiring if pain radiates to the left shoulder tip.
Percuss both flanks systematically, assessing for Ballance sign: fixed dullness in the left flank due to coagulated blood and shifting dullness in the right flank due to fluid blood.
Auscultate the left upper quadrant and abdomen for bowel sounds, noting silent paralytic ileus secondary to peritoneal irritation by blood.
Document baseline haemodynamic status and monitor closely for delayed rupture, warning the patient about the latent period of Baudet.

skill.exam.surg.splenic_injury_signs.normal: Normal respiratory excursion of the left costal margin, no local tenderness or guarding in the left hypochondrium, normal splenic dullness without flank dullness, and negative Kehr and Ballance signs.
skill.exam.surg.splenic_injury_signs.abnormal: Tenderness over fractured left lower ribs, localized guarding in left upper quadrant, left shoulder tip pain on left upper quadrant compression (Kehr sign), and fixed left flank dullness with right shifting dullness (Ballance sign).
skill.exam.surg.splenic_injury_signs.significance: Fractured lower left ribs and left hypochondrial tenderness strongly suggest splenic parenchymal laceration, Kehr sign indicates diaphragmatic irritation by subphrenic blood, and Ballance sign confirms extensive haemoperitoneum.
skill.exam.surg.splenic_injury_signs.practice: Demonstrate the elicitation of Kehr sign and explain the neuroanatomical pathway connecting diaphragmatic sensory fibres to the shoulder tip during surgical bed-side rounds.
pitfalls: Attributing left shoulder pain to a shoulder sprain or contusion following road traffic trauma, missing referred pain from splenic rupture.
Discharging a patient with lower left rib fractures and normal early vitals without observing or imaging for delayed splenic rupture.
Vigorously palpating the left upper quadrant in suspected subcapsular splenic haematoma, which can rupture the fragile capsule.
Assuming absence of shifting dullness rules out splenic laceration, as over one litre of free blood is typically needed for clear clinical shifting dullness.

probes.q: What is Kehr sign and what does it indicate in abdominal trauma?
probes.a: Referred pain to the left shoulder tip provoked by irritation of the inferior surface of the left hemidiaphragm by blood from a ruptured spleen.

probes.q: Explain the neurological basis of Kehr sign.
probes.a: Sensory innervation of the central diaphragmatic peritoneum travels via the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5), which shares spinal segments with the supraclavicular nerves supplying cutaneous sensation to the shoulder tip.

probes.q: What is the latent period of Baudet in splenic trauma and why is it dangerous?
probes.a: A deceptive symptom-free interval lasting days or weeks after initial trauma, during which an expanding subcapsular haematoma remains intact before bursting through the splenic capsule into the peritoneal cavity with sudden fatal shock.

rubric.text: Inspects and palpatesthe left lower ribs (ninth to eleventh) for fractures
Elicits and correctly interprets Kehr sign for diaphragmatic irritation
Demonstrates percussion for fixed left flank and shifting right flank dullness
Recognises the latent period of Baudet and counsel on delayed rupture risk

teach.heading: Anatomical vulnerability of the spleen to trauma
teach.body:
The spleen lies nestled in the left hypochondrium directly beneath the ninth, tenth, and eleventh ribs. It possesses a delicate capsule and extensive vascularity, receiving nearly ten percent of the cardiac output.

Fractures of the adjacent left lower ribs can drive bony fragments into the splenic pulp, or crushing blunt forces can compress the spleen against the vertebral bodies, causing catastrophic laceration.

teach.heading: Eponymous clinical signs: Kehr and Ballance
teach.body:
Kehr sign is elicited when blood accumulating beneath the left diaphragm irritates sensory branches of the phrenic nerve, causing referred pain to the top of the left shoulder via shared dermatomes C3 and C4.

Ballance sign describes fixed dullness to percussion in the left flank due to clotted blood surrounding the lacerated spleen, while dullness in the right flank remains fluid and shifts with change of patient position.

teach.heading: The latent period of Baudet and delayed rupture
teach.body:
In roughly fifteen percent of splenic injuries, bleeding initially remains contained beneath the intact splenic capsule, forming an expanding subcapsular haematoma, or is temporarily tamponaded by the greater omentum.

The patient experiences a symptom-free interval lasting from several days up to two weeks. Minor exertion or coughing may subsequently rupture the capsule, precipitating immediate peritoneal flooding and profound circulatory collapse.

skill.ix.surg.fast_dpl_trauma.title: Bedside investigation in abdominal trauma: FAST and DPL
skill.ix.surg.fast_dpl_trauma.oneLine: Four acoustic windows of FAST and the objective laboratory criteria of DPL
skill.ix.surg.fast_dpl_trauma.why: Haemodynamically unstable trauma patients cannot safely leave the resuscitation bay for CT imaging. FAST provides rapid, non-invasive confirmation of haemoperitoneum at the bedside, while diagnostic peritoneal lavage delivers definitive numerical criteria when ultrasound is inconclusive.
skill.ix.surg.fast_dpl_trauma.practice: Perform a simulated FAST examination on a phantom or ultrasound model, identifying all four acoustic windows within ninety seconds.
pitfalls: Delaying emergency laparotomy in an unstable patient with a positive FAST scan to obtain an abdominal CT scan.
Interpreting a negative FAST scan as complete exclusion of bowel perforation or retroperitoneal haemorrhage.
Attempting closed needle peritoneal lavage in a patient with previous abdominal midline scars without adopting an open cut-down technique.
Performing diagnostic peritoneal lavage before pelvic X-ray in pelvic trauma, where an anterior puncture can cause prevesical bleeding.

probes.q: Name the four anatomical acoustic windows evaluated during a standard FAST examination.
probes.a: Pericardial window (subxiphoid), right upper quadrant (hepatorenal pouch of Morison), left upper quadrant (splenorenal recess), and suprapubic (pelvic/rectovesical or rectouterine pouch).

probes.q: Which anatomical pouch is the most sensitive dependent site for detecting free peritoneal fluid on FAST in the supine patient?
probes.a: The hepatorenal recess (pouch of Morison) in the right upper quadrant.

probes.q: What laboratory criteria on aspirated lavage fluid define a positive Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage in blunt trauma?
probes.a: Aspiration of ten millilitres of frank gross blood, red blood cell count exceeding one hundred thousand per microlitre, white blood cell count exceeding five hundred per microlitre, or presence of bile, enteric contents, or food particles.

rubric.text: Identifies all four acoustic windows of FAST systematically
Recognises the hepatorenal pouch of Morison as the primary dependent fluid pocket
Recites the objective quantitative criteria for a positive DPL tap
Acknowledges FAST limitations in retroperitoneal and hollow viscus injuries

teach.heading: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
teach.body:
FAST is an essential point-of-care ultrasound protocol designed to detect free intraperitoneal and pericardial fluid in under two minutes during trauma resuscitation.

Four standard windows are visualised: subxiphoid to inspect the pericardium; right upper quadrant to examine Morisons pouch; left upper quadrant to evaluate the splenorenal recess; and suprapubic to scan the pelvis behind the bladder.

teach.heading: The hepatorenal pouch of Morison
teach.body:
In a supine patient, the hepatorenal space is the most dependent portion of the upper abdominal peritoneal cavity. Intraperitoneal fluid accumulates here before tracking down the right paracolic gutter into the pelvis.

As little as one hundred to two hundred millilitres of free blood can be identified as an anechoic black strip separating the bright echogenic reflections of the liver capsule and renal parenchyma.

rows: Peritoneal inflammation or hollow viscus injury

skill.hx.surg.acute_abdomen.title: History taking in the acute abdomen
skill.hx.surg.acute_abdomen.oneLine: Pain tempo, visceral vs somatic shift, vomiting sequence, and exacerbating factors
skill.hx.surg.acute_abdomen.why: The clinical history distinguishes surgical emergencies requiring laparotomy from non-surgical mimics before imaging is obtained. Establishing whether pain preceded vomiting, tracking somatic localisation, and mapping the onset curve identifies perforation, obstruction, colic, or mesenteric ischemia.

asks.text: When exactly did the pain start, and did it awaken you from sleep or start abruptly in seconds?
Did the pain start suddenly at its maximum intensity like an explosion, or did it build up gradually over several hours?
Where was the pain felt when it first began, and has it shifted or radiated to any other area?
What is the character of the pain: is it a twisting cramp that comes in waves with pain-free intervals, a burning sensation, or a continuous severe ache?
Did the pain come first or did the vomiting come first, and what does the vomitus look like?
Does coughing, walking, deep breathing, or bumping over a road pothole worsen your pain?

skill.hx.surg.acute_abdomen.practice: Take an acute abdomen history from a simulated patient in under five minutes, systematically establishing onset curve, radiation, and the pain-vomiting relationship.
pitfalls: Assuming vomiting that started before abdominal pain is a surgical emergency, when it typically signifies gastroenteritis.
Failing to ask about shifting pain, missing the classic visceral-to-somatic migration of acute appendicitis.
Treating colicky pain with opioids before establishing whether strangulated bowel or peritonitis is developing.
Overlooking atypical presentations of acute abdomen in the elderly, diabetics, or pregnant women.

probes.q: In acute abdominal pain, why is the sequence of pain and vomiting of critical surgical significance?
probes.a: In surgical conditions such as acute appendicitis, pain almost always precedes vomiting; in medical conditions like gastroenteritis or food poisoning, vomiting typically precedes or coincides with the onset of pain.

probes.q: Explain the embryological and neuroanatomical basis of shifting pain in acute appendicitis.
probes.a: Initial appendiceal distension stimulates visceral unmyelinated C-fibres of the midgut, producing vague periumbilical pain; once inflammation irritates the adjacent parietal peritoneum, somatic A-delta fibres produce sharp, well-localized pain in the right iliac fossa.

probes.q: How does true intestinal colic differ clinically from the constant severe pain of acute mesenteric ischemia?
probes.a: True intestinal colic features rhythmic spasms of griping pain separated by pain-free intervals; acute mesenteric ischemia produces severe unremitting pain that is strikingly disproportionate to the minimal abdominal tenderness found on physical examination.

rubric.text: Characterises exact speed of onset and temporal progression of pain
Determines whether abdominal pain preceded vomiting
Tracks any anatomical shift or radiation of the pain
Screens for aggravation by coughing, walking, or vehicle jolting

teach.heading: Onset curves and the tempo of surgical emergencies
teach.body:
The rapidity with which acute abdominal pain reaches peak intensity points directly to the underlying pathology. Sudden catastrophic pain reaching maximum severity in seconds indicates hollow viscus perforation, vascular catastrophe, or rupture of a vascular aneurysm.

Rapidly escalating pain over hours suggests acute pancreatitis, biliary colic, or intestinal strangulation. Insidious pain progressing over twenty-four hours indicates transmural inflammation such as acute appendicitis or diverticulitis.

teach.heading: Visceral versus somatic peritoneal pain
teach.body:
Visceral pain arises from distension or spasm of a hollow muscular organ and travels via bilateral sympathetic visceral afferents. It is dull, poorly localized, and referred to embryological midline zones: foregut to epigastrium, midgut to periumbilical region, and hindgut to hypogastrium.

Somatic parietal pain arises when exudate irritates the sensitive parietal peritoneum. It travels via somatic spinal nerves, becoming sharp, constant, and exquisitely localized directly over the inflamed organ.

rows: Visceral distension followed by parietal peritonitis
Hypoxic tissue damage with minimal early peritonitis

skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.title: Clinical examination for peritonitis
skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.oneLine: Involuntary muscular rigidity, percussion tenderness, rebound sign, and bowel sounds
skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.why: Peritonitis is an acute surgical emergency where chemical or bacterial contamination triggers reflex protective spasm of the abdominal wall. Eliciting board-like rigidity and percussion tenderness without causing unnecessary agony distinguishes generalized peritonitis from benign colic.

steps.text: Observe the patient posture: patients with generalized peritonitis lie motionless with knees drawn up, avoiding any cough, speech, or body movement.
Inspect the abdominal wall under tangential lighting, checking for complete absence of respiratory excursions of the anterior abdominal wall.
Ask the patient to cough gently before touching the abdomen, noting whether coughing provokes sharp localized or generalized abdominal pain.
Perform light percussion across all four quadrants, which elicits peritoneal tenderness with far less patient discomfort than abrupt manual rebound testing.
Palpate with warm flat hands starting gently in the least painful quadrant, assessing for true involuntary muscular rigidity that remains unyielding throughout respiration.
Elicit gentle release tenderness (Blumberg sign) by pressing slowly and deeply over the tender area and releasing hand pressure smoothly and swiftly.
Auscultate the abdomen continuously for at least two full minutes to confirm complete silence of paralytic ileus.

skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.normal: Abdominal wall moves smoothly with quiet respiration, soft non-tender abdomen without guarding or rigidity, painless light percussion, and active bowel sounds every five to ten seconds.
skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.abnormal: Still posture, completely absent abdominal respiratory excursion, board-like involuntary rigidity, percussion tenderness, positive release tenderness, and an entirely silent abdomen on prolonged auscultation.
skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.significance: Board-like rigidity and percussion tenderness establish generalized peritonitis from hollow viscus perforation or severe intra-abdominal sepsis, mandating urgent intravenous resuscitation and emergency laparotomy.
skill.exam.surg.peritonitis_signs.practice: Perform gentle examination for peritoneal signs on a simulated surgical patient, using light percussion tenderness and gentle cough provocation instead of aggressive manual rebound.
pitfalls: Performing violent manual rebound release, inflicting severe pain when gentle light percussion provides equal or superior clinical sensitivity.
Mistaking voluntary muscular guarding in an anxious, cold, or shivering patient for true involuntary peritoneal rigidity.
Failing to listen to the abdomen for a full two minutes before declaring bowel sounds completely absent.
Overlooking peritonitis in elderly or immunosuppressed patients who often present with minimal rigidity despite perforated viscera.

probes.q: Why is light percussion considered superior to traditional manual rebound release testing for peritonitis?
probes.a: Light percussion produces gentle vibrations of the parietal peritoneum that reliably elicit peritoneal irritation without inflicting the severe distress of abrupt manual release.

probes.q: How do you reliably differentiate voluntary muscular guarding from involuntary muscular rigidity?
probes.a: Voluntary guarding diminishes during expiration when the patient is reassured, flexes the hips, and breathes through the mouth; true involuntary rigidity is an unyielding reflex spasm that persists during expiration.

probes.q: What is the pathophysiological mechanism behind the silent abdomen in generalized peritonitis?
probes.a: Intense peritoneal inflammation and sympathetic overactivity inhibit the intrinsic enteric myenteric plexus and intestinal smooth muscle, producing paralytic ileus with cessation of peristalsis.

rubric.text: Observes patient posture and respiratory excursion before touching abdomen
Uses light percussion to screen for peritoneal irritation
Differentiates true involuntary rigidity from voluntary muscular guarding
Auscultates for at least two full minutes to verify silent paralytic ileus

teach.heading: The neurogenic reflex of muscular rigidity
teach.body:
When inflammatory exudate contacts the parietal peritoneum, somatic afferents transmit impulses to the spinal cord. This triggers an involuntary reflex arc through anterior horn motor neurons supplying the overlying muscles of the abdominal wall.

The resulting continuous tetanic contraction of the rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis, and obliques creates an unyielding board-like barrier that cannot be relaxed by conscious patient effort.

teach.heading: Humane elicitation of peritoneal signs
teach.body:
Classic textbook rebound tenderness (Blumberg sign) is elicited by pressing deeply and suddenly withdrawing the hand. While diagnostic, abrupt withdrawal causes intense pain and destroys patient rapport.

A far gentler and equally accurate approach is light percussion or asking the patient to cough. If light percussion over a quadrant provokes localized wincing, peritoneal irritation is confirmed without traumatising the patient.

teach.heading: Paralytic ileus and auscultation
teach.body:
Normal bowel sounds occur as gurgles every five to ten seconds due to coordinated peristaltic contractions advancing intraluminal gas and fluid. Generalized peritonitis activates visceral sympathetic reflexes that paralyse bowel peristalsis.

Auscultation in generalized peritonitis reveals a completely silent abdomen. Auscultation must be maintained continuously for at least two minutes in one quadrant before concluding that peristalsis is truly absent.

skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.title: Clinical signs of acute appendicitis
skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.oneLine: McBurney point, Rovsing sign, psoas and obturator tests, and Sherren triangle
skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.why: Acute appendicitis is the most frequent surgical emergency of the abdomen. Anatomical variation in appendix position (retrocaecal, pelvic, subcaecal) alters physical signs, making systematic provocative tests essential to secure an early diagnosis before perforation occurs.

steps.text: Identify McBurney point: located precisely at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the line joining the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine.
Palpate gently over McBurney point with the tip of one finger, confirming localized tenderness and release tenderness.
Elicit Rovsing sign: press deeply and steadily into the left iliac fossa; a positive test elicits referred pain in the right iliac fossa.
Perform the Cope psoas test: place the patient on the left lateral decubitus position and passively hyperextend the right hip joint, stretching the iliopsoas.
Perform the Cope obturator test: flex the patients right hip and knee to ninety degrees and passively rotate the hip internally, stretching the obturator internus.
Elicit Baldwin sign: with patient supine, lift the right lower limb with knee extended against resistance while palpating the right flank.
Test for cutaneous hyperaesthesia in Sherrens triangle (bounded by umbilicus, right anterior superior iliac spine, and pubic symphysis) using a pin or cotton swab.

skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.normal: No localized tenderness or guarding at McBurney point, negative Rovsing, psoas, and obturator tests, and symmetrical normal cutaneous sensation across Sherren triangle.
skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.abnormal: Exquisite point tenderness at McBurney point, pain referred to right iliac fossa on left iliac fossa pressure (Rovsing), pain on right hip hyperextension (psoas) or internal rotation (obturator), and cutaneous hyperaesthesia in Sherren triangle.
skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.significance: Localizes acute appendicular inflammation and establishes its specific anatomical position: a positive psoas sign confirms retrocaecal appendicitis, while a positive obturator sign indicates pelvic appendicitis.
skill.exam.surg.appendicitis_signs.practice: Demonstrate the exact anatomical location of McBurney point and perform the psoas, obturator, and Rovsing manoeuvres on a clinical skills simulator.
pitfalls: Assuming a negative McBurney point tenderness rules out appendicitis, missing a retrocaecal appendix shielded by the caecum or a deep pelvic appendix.
Failing to perform a digital rectal examination in suspected appendicitis with minimal abdominal signs, which detects pelvic appendicitis.
Confusing Rovsing sign with simply pressing across the transverse colon, failing to understand pressure transmission across the colonic gas column.
Overlooking acute appendicitis in pregnancy where the enlarging gravid uterus displaces the appendix upwards and laterally toward the right hypochondrium.

probes.q: State the exact surface anatomical landmarks used to locate McBurney point.
probes.a: The junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.

probes.q: How does the anatomical position of a retrocaecal appendix modify the clinical signs of acute appendicitis?
probes.a: Anterior abdominal wall tenderness and muscular rigidity are minimal or absent because the inflamed appendix is shielded by the gas-filled caecum; maximal tenderness is elicited in the right flank, and the psoas sign is positive.

probes.q: What is Sherren triangle, how is it tested, and what is its clinical significance?
probes.a: An area of cutaneous hyperaesthesia bounded by lines connecting the umbilicus, right anterior superior iliac spine, and pubic symphysis; testing with gentle pinprick detects sensory hyperaesthesia from T11-L1 spinal segments before perforation.

rubric.text: Accurately marks and palpates McBurney point
Demonstrates Rovsing sign correctly by pressing in left iliac fossa
Performs Cope psoas stretch test for retrocaecal appendicitis
Performs Cope obturator internal rotation test for pelvic appendicitis

teach.heading: Surface marking and the McBurney point
teach.body:
Charles McBurney described the point of maximum tenderness in acute appendicitis as lying exactly between one and a half and two inches from the right anterior superior iliac spine on a direct line to the umbilicus.

This landmark represents the anatomical base of the vermiform appendix where it arises from the posteromedial wall of the caecum, approximately two centimetres below the ileocaecal valve.

teach.heading: Provocative signs based on appendicular position
teach.body:
While the base of the appendix remains constant, its tip may lie in retrocaecal (sixty-five percent), pelvic (thirty percent), subcaecal, or pre-ileal positions.

A retrocaecal appendix lies upon the psoas major muscle; hyperextension of the right hip stretches the muscle and provokes pain (psoas sign). A pelvic appendix lies close to the obturator internus; internal rotation of the flexed hip stretches the fascia and causes pain (obturator sign).

teach.heading: Rovsing sign and Sherren triangle
teach.body:
Rovsing sign is elicited by applying deep pressure in the left iliac fossa. This displaces colonic gas retrogradely through the descending, transverse, and ascending colon into the caecum, distending the inflamed caecal pole and provoking sharp pain in the right iliac fossa.

Sherren triangle is a zone of cutaneous hyperaesthesia in the right lower abdomen reflecting spinal cord visceral sensory convergence at T11 and T12.

skill.exam.surg.cholecystitis_signs.title: Clinical examination for acute cholecystitis
skill.exam.surg.cholecystitis_signs.oneLine: Murphy sign, Murphy triad, Boas sign, and palpable inflammatory phlegmon
skill.exam.surg.cholecystitis_signs.why: Acute cholecystitis results from cystic duct obstruction by gallstones, triggering acute mucosal inflammation that extends to the peritoneal surface. Accurately eliciting Murphy sign and detecting Boas hyperaesthesia differentiates gallbladder inflammation from perforated ulcer, acute hepatitis, and pleurisy.

steps.text: Position the patient supine with the head slightly raised and knees gently flexed to relax the rectus abdominis muscle.
Inspect the right hypochondrium for localized fullness, lack of respiratory movement, and scleral icterus.
Place the fingers of the right hand gently beneath the right costal margin at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle (tip of the ninth costal cartilage).
Ask the patient to take a slow, deep breath in while maintaining steady upward palpating pressure.
Observe for Murphy sign: a sudden arrest of inspiration accompanied by a sharp wince of pain as the descending inflamed gallbladder touches the examining fingers.
Perform the identical manoeuvre under the left costal margin as a control; absence of inspiratory arrest on the left confirms a positive Murphy sign.
Examine the posterior right chest wall between the ninth and eleventh ribs for cutaneous hyperaesthesia (Boas sign).

skill.exam.surg.cholecystitis_signs.normal: Smooth, painless deep inspiration during palpation beneath both right and left costal margins, soft non-tender right hypochondrium without masses, and no posterior cutaneous hyperaesthesia.
skill.exam.surg.cholecystitis_signs.abnormal: Sharp arrest of inspiration during deep palpation beneath the right costal margin (positive Murphy sign), tender inflammatory phlegmon or mass in right hypochondrium, and posterior right hyperaesthesia (Boas sign).
skill.exam.surg.cholecystitis_signs.significance: A positive Murphy sign indicates acute cholecystitis with localized visceral and parietal peritoneal inflammation, while a palpable tender mass indicates inflammatory omental adhesions or mucocele of the gallbladder.
skill.exam.surg.cholecystitis_signs.practice: Perform Murphy test on a partner or simulator, demonstrating correct placement of fingers at the ninth costal cartilage and verifying with the contralateral control manoeuvre.
pitfalls: Pressing too hard or too quickly beneath the ribs, causing immediate voluntary guarding that prevents the patient from taking a deep breath.
Failing to perform the contralateral control palpation in the left hypochondrium to exclude generalized abdominal hypersensitivity.
Confusing Murphy sign with tenderness from acute hepatitis, right lower lobe pneumonia, or a high retrocaecal appendicitis.
Missing a palpable gallbladder mass because palpation is begun too close to the costal margin rather than starting low in the right iliac fossa.

probes.q: Describe how Murphy sign is elicited during physical examination of the abdomen.
probes.a: The examiner places fingers beneath the right costal margin at the lateral border of the rectus muscle and asks the patient to take a deep breath; inspiration arrests sharply due to pain as the inflamed gallbladder contacts the fingers.

probes.q: What anatomical landmark marks the fundus of the gallbladder on the anterior abdominal wall?
probes.a: The intersection of the lateral border of the right rectus abdominis muscle (linea semilunaris) with the right ninth costal cartilage.

probes.q: What is Boas sign and what is its neuroanatomical explanation in gallbladder disease?
probes.a: An area of cutaneous hyperaesthesia posteriorly between the ninth and eleventh ribs on the right, caused by visceral sensory impulses travelling from the gallbladder via the greater splanchnic nerves to spinal cord segments T7 to T9.

rubric.text: Positions patient comfortably with knees flexed to relax abdominal wall
Demonstrates Murphy sign correctly with fingers at right ninth costal cartilage
Performs contralateral control test under left costal margin
Checks for posterior cutaneous hyperaesthesia between right ninth and eleventh ribs

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of the Murphy sign
teach.body:
When a gallstone impacts in the cystic duct, stagnant bile provokes chemical mucosal injury, bacterial proliferation, and transmural inflammation that reaches the serosa of the gallbladder fundus.

During deep inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and descends, displacing the liver and gallbladder downwards by two to three centimetres. As the inflamed serosa impacts the examiners fingertips, acute peritoneal irritation causes reflex reflex cessation of diaphragmatic excursion.

teach.heading: Contralateral control and sonographic Murphy sign
teach.body:
A true Murphy sign requires that deep inspiration with palpation under the left costal margin causes no discomfort. This control step excludes anxiety, pleurisy, or generalized peritonitis.

In modern clinical practice, sonographic Murphy sign (maximal focal tenderness directly over the gallbladder during real-time compression with the ultrasound probe) carries a sensitivity of over eighty-five percent for acute calculous cholecystitis.

teach.heading: Boas sign and visceral referred hyperaesthesia
teach.body:
Visceral afferent fibres from the gallbladder and biliary tree accompany sympathetic nerves through the coeliac plexus to enter the dorsal horn of spinal cord segments T7, T8, and T9.

Sensory convergence in the dorsal horn with somatic afferents from the posterior primary rami produces cutaneous hyperaesthesia between the ninth and eleventh ribs posteriorly, one handbreadth to the right of the spine (Boas sign).

skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.title: Physical examination of acute intestinal obstruction
skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.oneLine: Ladder pattern visible peristalsis, mandatory hernial orifice check, and borborygmi
skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.why: Mechanical intestinal obstruction is an acute surgical condition where diagnostic delay risks strangulation, gangrene, and septic shock. Examining every hernial orifice is the single most critical physical manoeuvre, as an overlooked strangulated femoral hernia is frequently fatal.

steps.text: Inspect the abdominal contours for distension, noting whether swelling is central (small bowel) or predominantly in the flanks (large bowel obstruction).
Observe the abdomen under tangential lighting for visible peristalsis, looking for step-ladder waves across the central abdomen.
Systematically inspect and palpate all hernial orifices in both groins (inguinal and femoral canals), umbilicus, and surgical scars for tender, irreducible, non-expansile swellings.
Palpate the abdomen gently for localized tenderness, muscular guarding, or an underlying mass such as an intussusception, sigmoid volvulus, or neoplastic stricture.
Percuss the abdomen across all quadrants, noting high-pitched tympanitic hyper-resonance over gas-filled distended loops.
Auscultate for at least two full minutes to detect loud, high-pitched borborygmi with metallic tinkles and rushes coinciding with spasms of colicky pain.
Perform a digital rectal examination to determine rectal emptiness, exclude low rectal tumours and faecal impaction, and check for blood or mucus on the glove.

skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.normal: Symmetrical flat abdomen, no visible peristalsis, all hernial orifices clear with normal cough impulse, soft and non-tender, normal percussion, and quiet bowel sounds every five to ten seconds.
skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.abnormal: Marked distension, step-ladder visible peristalsis, a tense tender irreducible swelling at a hernial site, tympanitic hyper-resonance, loud high-pitched metallic borborygmi, or empty ballooned rectum.
skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.significance: Distension with visible peristalsis and loud metallic borborygmi confirms mechanical obstruction; localized tenderness with tachycardia and fever indicates impending or established bowel strangulation.
skill.exam.surg.bowel_obstruction.practice: Perform a systematic abdominal obstruction examination, demonstrating step-by-step palpation of inguinal and femoral canals, umbilicus, and previous surgical scars.
pitfalls: Failing to expose and palpate the groin, overlooking a small strangulated femoral hernia in an elderly or obese patient.
Confusing the hyperactive tinkling sounds of mechanical obstruction with the silent abdomen of paralytic ileus.
Assuming absence of distension rules out obstruction in high proximal jejunal obstruction, where vomiting decompresses the stomach early.
Missing bowel strangulation because colicky pain has given way to continuous severe pain with localized tenderness.

probes.q: Why is systematic examination of all hernial orifices mandatory in every patient with suspected bowel obstruction?
probes.a: Obstructed or strangulated external hernias (especially femoral and inguinal) are common causes of mechanical obstruction, and failure to detect an irreducible hernia leads to bowel gangrene.

probes.q: Describe the characteristic auscultatory finding in mechanical intestinal obstruction and its mechanism.
probes.a: Loud, high-pitched, metallic tinkling borborygmi occurring in rushes, caused by violent peristaltic contractions forcing fluid and gas through a narrowed, obstructed lumen under tension.

probes.q: What clinical signs indicate that simple mechanical bowel obstruction has progressed to strangulation?
probes.a: Constant severe pain replacing intermittent colic, localized abdominal tenderness with guarding, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and loss of hyperactive bowel sounds.

rubric.text: Distinguishes small bowel central distension from large bowel peripheral distension
Systematically examines inguinal, femoral, umbilical, and incisional orifices
Auscultates for high-pitched metallic borborygmi and tinkles
Identifies clinical signs distinguishing strangulation from simple obstruction
Performs digital rectal examination to assess rectal emptiness and impaction

teach.heading: The four cardinal symptoms of mechanical obstruction
teach.body:
Mechanical intestinal obstruction presents with four cardinal features: abdominal colic, vomiting, absolute constipation (neither faeces nor flatus), and abdominal distension.

In high small bowel obstruction, vomiting is early and profuse while distension is minimal. In low colonic obstruction, distension is immense while vomiting is delayed or absent until late in the disease.

teach.heading: Step-ladder peristalsis and distension anatomy
teach.body:
When obstruction is in the small bowel, peristaltic contractions of hypertrophied loops become visible through a thin abdominal wall as transverse bands stacked vertically like the rungs of a ladder.

Percussion yields a drum-like tympanitic note. In contrast, colonic obstruction creates prominent bulging in both flanks and across the upper abdomen, mapping the course of the colon.

teach.heading: The hernial orifices: a life-saving checklist

rows: Below and lateral to pubic tubercle
Overlooked as lymph node in obese women
Above and medial to pubic tubercle
