skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.title: Clinical examination of gastrointestinal perforation
skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.oneLine: Board-like rigidity, loss of liver dullness, motionless posture, and pelvic peritonitis
skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.why: Free perforation of a hollow viscus spills caustic gastroduodenal secretions or bacterial faecal fluid into the peritoneal cavity, precipitating immediate chemical peritonitis followed by septic shock. Recognizing board-like rigidity and loss of liver dullness dictates immediate resuscitation and surgery.

steps.text: Observe the patient general attitude: the patient lies rigidly supine with hips flexed, avoiding any cough, speech, or body movement.
Inspect the abdominal wall: respiration is entirely thoracic, and the abdominal wall appears retracted or flat (scaphoid) with zero respiratory excursion.
Palpate with extreme gentleness starting in a non-tender area: feel for unyielding, board-like involuntary muscular rigidity across all four quadrants.
Percuss the right mid-axillary line from the fourth intercostal space downwards over the liver, checking for obliteration of hepatic dullness (pneumoperitoneum).
Percuss gently across the rest of the abdomen to elicit exquisite percussion tenderness without causing unnecessary trauma.
Auscultate all four quadrants for at least two full minutes to confirm complete silence of paralytic ileus.
Perform a gentle digital rectal examination to detect exquisite tenderness of the pelvic peritoneum in the rectovesical or rectouterine pouch.

skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.normal: Soft, relaxed abdominal wall moving freely with quiet respiration, normal hepatic dullness extending from the fifth right intercostal space to the costal margin, and active bowel sounds.
skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.abnormal: Motionless supine posture, flat rigid abdomen without respiratory excursion, board-like muscular rigidity, obliteration of liver dullness replaced by tympany, and an entirely silent abdomen.
skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.significance: Board-like rigidity combined with loss of liver dullness provides definitive physical proof of hollow viscus perforation with free intraperitoneal gas, mandating immediate emergency laparotomy.
skill.exam.surg.perforation_peritonitis.practice: Perform liver percussion in the mid-axillary line on a healthy subject, then demonstrate how free gas obliterates hepatic dullness in a clinical simulation scenario.
pitfalls: Missing obliteration of liver dullness because percussion is performed in the mid-clavicular line rather than the mid-axillary line.
Assuming a soft abdomen excludes perforation in an elderly or debilitated patient with weak, atrophic abdominal wall musculature.
Mistaking the temporary symptomatic improvement of the second stage of perforation (illusion of recovery) for true clinical resolution.
Forgetting that colonic interposition between liver and diaphragm (Chilaiditi sign) can mimic loss of liver dullness in rare cases.

probes.q: What does obliteration of liver dullness to percussion in the mid-axillary line signify in a patient with acute abdominal pain?
probes.a: Free gas in the peritoneal cavity (pneumoperitoneum) resulting from perforation of a hollow muscular viscus, such as a peptic ulcer.

probes.q: Why is the anterior abdominal wall described as board-like in acute gastroduodenal perforation?
probes.a: Spillage of highly acidic gastric juice into the peritoneal cavity causes intense chemical irritation of the somatic parietal peritoneum, triggering a violent, continuous reflex spasm of the entire abdominal musculature.

probes.q: What is the three-stage clinical progression of perforated peptic ulcer described by classic surgical teaching?
probes.a: Stage 1: immediate prostration and agonizing pain (chemical peritonitis); Stage 2: illusion of recovery with diminished pain as peritoneal exudate dilutes the acid; Stage 3: diffuse bacterial peritonitis with septic shock and distension.

rubric.text: Identifies classic motionless supine posture with thoracic respiration
Demonstrates gentle palpation confirming board-like muscular rigidity
Percusses right mid-axillary line to detect obliteration of liver dullness
Performs digital rectal examination for pelvic peritoneal irritation

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of chemical versus bacterial peritonitis
teach.body:
When a duodenal or gastric ulcer perforates, hydrochloric acid, pepsin, and bile flood the peritoneal space. This generates an acute chemical burn of the parietal peritoneum, producing excruciating agonizing pain and instant board-like rigidity.

Within six to twelve hours, copious inflammatory peritoneal exudate dilutes the acidic fluid. The pain temporarily eases (the dangerous stage of delusion), before virulent bacterial peritonitis supervenes.

teach.heading: Percussion of the liver and pneumoperitoneum
teach.body:
Normal liver dullness is elicited by percussing downwards in the right mid-axillary line, where hepatic tissue lies directly adjacent to the thoracic wall between the sixth and tenth ribs.

When a hollow organ perforates, free gas rises to the highest anatomical point in the supine abdomen. Gas collects between the anterior liver surface and lateral abdominal wall, replacing dullness with a resonant tympanitic note.

teach.heading: The three clinical stages of perforation

rows: Sudden agonizing pain, cold clammy skin, subnormal temperature
Pain eases, pulse strengthens, but board-like rigidity and loss of liver dullness persist
Toxaemia, septic shock, abdominal distension, hypovolaemia, sunken facies

skill.annex.surg.alvarado_score.title: Alvarado score for acute appendicitis
skill.annex.surg.alvarado_score.oneLine: The 10-point MANTRELS clinical prediction rule for stratifying acute appendicitis
skill.annex.surg.alvarado_score.why: The Alvarado score is an internationally validated clinical decision rule that quantifies the probability of acute appendicitis. Standardising signs, symptoms, and laboratory markers reduces negative appendectomy rates and avoids unnecessary radiation from emergency CT scans.
skill.annex.surg.alvarado_score.practice: Calculate the Alvarado score for three clinical case vignettes, categorising each patient into discharge, observation, or immediate surgery groups.
pitfalls: Awarding two points instead of one point for symptoms like anorexia or nausea; only tenderness and leukocytosis receive two points.
Relying entirely on Alvarado score in reproductive-age females without performing pelvic ultrasound to exclude gynaecological pathologies.
Discharging a patient with an equivocal Alvarado score of 5 or 6 without mandatory observation and planned re-evaluation in four to six hours.
Overlooking acute appendicitis in children and elderly patients who may not mount marked leukocytosis or high fever.

probes.q: Which two components of the 10-point Alvarado score receive two points each?
probes.a: Localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leukocytosis (white blood cell count greater than 10,000 per microlitre).

probes.q: What clinical recommendation corresponds to an Alvarado score of 7 or 8?
probes.a: Acute appendicitis is probable; urgent surgical consultation is indicated, with preparation for appendectomy or targeted diagnostic imaging.

probes.q: List the eight components comprising the MANTRELS mnemonic in the Alvarado score.
probes.a: Migration of pain, Anorexia, Nausea/vomiting, Tenderness in right iliac fossa, Rebound tenderness, Elevated temperature, Leukocytosis, and Shift of neutrophils to the left.

rubric.text: Recalls the MANTRELS mnemonic and respective score weightings
Correctly assigns two points to tenderness in RIF and leukocytosis
Accurately categorises scores into discharge, observe, and surgical intervention groups
Applies diagnostic imaging caveats in reproductive-age women

teach.heading: The MANTRELS mnemonic and point allocation
Clinical risk stratification and management actions

rows: Admit for serial clinical observation or USG
Urgent surgical review; prepare for operation

teach.heading: Clinical utility and demographic limitations
teach.body:
The Alvarado score demonstrates high diagnostic sensitivity (over ninety percent) for ruling out appendicitis in scores below 5. It performs exceptionally well in adult males.

In women of reproductive age, gynaecological conditions (pelvic inflammatory disease, ruptured ovarian cyst, ectopic gestation) cause false positives; ultrasonography or laparoscopy is essential before committing to surgery.

skill.hx.surg.chronic_dyspepsia_ulcer.title: History in chronic peptic ulcer and dyspepsia
skill.hx.surg.chronic_dyspepsia_ulcer.oneLine: Periodicity, hunger pain, food relief vs sitophobia, and nocturnal waking
skill.hx.surg.chronic_dyspepsia_ulcer.why: The clinical history in chronic dyspepsia accurately differentiates duodenal ulcer from gastric ulcer and flags early malignant transformation. Recognising the food-pain relationship, seasonal periodicity, and alarm symptoms directs timely endoscopy before perforation or bleeding develops.

asks.text: How many months or years have you suffered from this indigestion or upper abdominal pain?
Does the pain come in distinct bouts lasting several weeks followed by symptom-free intervals of months (periodicity)?
What is the relationship between your pain and meals: does eating food relieve the pain or does food bring on or worsen the pain?
Does the pain wake you from sleep during the early morning hours, around two or three in the morning?
Do you have a good appetite, or do you avoid eating because you fear it will bring on the pain (sitophobia)?
Have you vomited large volumes of undigested, foul-smelling food eaten the previous day, or noticed unintended weight loss?

skill.hx.surg.chronic_dyspepsia_ulcer.practice: Take a structured dyspepsia history from a simulated patient, contrasting hunger pain of duodenal ulcer with food-provoked pain and sitophobia of gastric ulcer.
pitfalls: Failing to enquire about nocturnal pain, which is highly specific for duodenal ulceration and rarely seen in functional dyspepsia.
Overlooking the loss of periodicity in a long-standing ulcer, which signals penetration into the pancreas or malignant change.
Treating dyspepsia with long-term empirical antacids in a patient over forty-five without performing upper endoscopy to exclude gastric carcinoma.
Confusing sitophobia (fear of eating due to pain) with true anorexia (loss of desire to eat).

probes.q: How does the relationship of pain to food intake distinguish duodenal ulcer from gastric ulcer?
probes.a: In duodenal ulcer, pain occurs when the stomach is empty (hunger pain, two to three hours after meals) and is relieved by food or milk; in gastric ulcer, pain is aggravated within thirty to sixty minutes of eating.

probes.q: What is meant by periodicity in peptic ulcer disease and what does its loss signify?
probes.a: Periodicity refers to episodes of ulcer pain lasting several weeks alternating with symptom-free remissions of months; loss of periodicity indicates ulcer penetration into adjacent structures or malignant transformation.

probes.q: Why do patients with gastric ulcer frequently lose weight whereas patients with duodenal ulcer maintain or gain weight?
probes.a: Gastric ulcer patients experience pain shortly after eating and develop sitophobia (fear of food), avoiding meals; duodenal ulcer patients eat frequent snacks and drink milk to relieve hunger pain.

rubric.text: Documents chronicity and seasonal periodicity of dyspeptic episodes
Explores food-pain relationship (hunger pain vs postprandial exacerbation)
Asks specifically about nocturnal pain waking the patient at 2 to 3 AM
Screens for alarm features including vomiting, dysphagia, and weight loss

teach.heading: Periodicity: the rhythmic signature of peptic ulcer
teach.body:
A hallmark of uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease is periodicity. The patient describes distinct bouts of burning epigastric pain lasting two to six weeks, classically occurring during autumn and winter or periods of mental stress.

These exacerbations are followed by complete remissions lasting months where the patient feels entirely well. If pain becomes continuous without remission, deep penetration into the pancreas or retroperitoneal tissues has occurred.

teach.heading: The food-pain cycle: duodenal versus gastric ulcer
Alarm symptoms and malignant transformation
teach.body:
Gastric ulcers carry a definite risk of harboring or developing adenocarcinoma, whereas duodenal ulcers are almost invariably benign. Any change in chronic dyspeptic symptoms demands immediate upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.

Alarm features include persistent unremitting pain, true anorexia, early satiety, progressive dysphagia, vomiting of foul retained food, and unexplained iron deficiency anaemia or weight loss.

skill.exam.surg.gastric_outlet_obstructi.title: Clinical examination for gastric outlet obstruction
skill.exam.surg.gastric_outlet_obstructi.oneLine: Visible gastric peristalsis, succussion splash, and dehydration assessment
skill.exam.surg.gastric_outlet_obstructi.why: Chronic peptic ulcer scarring or antral malignancy narrows the pyloric canal, creating massive gastric dilatation with fluid and food retention. Identifying visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis and eliciting a succussion splash confirms gastric decompensation, alerting the clinician to life-threatening electrolyte derangements.

steps.text: Expose the abdomen and inspect the epigastrium under tangential lighting: observe for prominent fullness in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium.

Watch the upper abdomen patiently for visible gastric peristalsis: slow, deliberate peristaltic waves sweeping from beneath the left costal margin downwards and to the right toward the right hypochondrium.
Perform the flicking test: if visible peristalsis is faint, gently flick or tap the epigastric wall with fingertips to stimulate an active peristaltic wave.
Palpate the epigastrium and right upper quadrant for a hard, irregular, fixed mass indicating antral or pyloric adenocarcinoma.
Elicit a succussion splash: place the diaphragm of the stethoscope over the epigastrium, grasp both iliac crests or thighs, and shake the patient torso briskly from side to side.
Listen for a loud splashing sound (gargling/sloshing) produced by air and retained gastric fluid mixing in the dilated stomach.
Verify timing: confirm that the succussion splash is elicited at least four hours after the patient last ingested food or drink.
Examine for physical signs of severe dehydration and metabolic alkalosis: sunken eyes, dry tongue, reduced skin turgor, and shallow respiration.

skill.exam.surg.gastric_outlet_obstructi.normal: Flat epigastrium, no visible peristalsis, soft non-tender upper abdomen without palpable masses, negative succussion splash four hours after eating, and normal skin turgor.
skill.exam.surg.gastric_outlet_obstructi.abnormal: Fullness in epigastrium, visible gastric peristalsis traveling left to right, a palpable pyloric mass, positive succussion splash four or more hours postprandial, dry mucous membranes, and signs of tetany.
skill.exam.surg.gastric_outlet_obstructi.significance: Visible gastric peristalsis and a positive succussion splash establish gastric outlet obstruction; an associated palpable epigastric mass strongly favors antral gastric carcinoma over benign peptic cicatrization.
skill.exam.surg.gastric_outlet_obstructi.practice: Demonstrate the correct technique for eliciting a succussion splash with stethoscope auscultation, and describe the direction and features of visible gastric peristalsis.
pitfalls: Eliciting a succussion splash within one to two hours of a meal or large drink, which is a normal physiological finding.
Confusing the left-to-right wave of gastric peristalsis with the transverse step-ladder peristalsis of small bowel obstruction.
Overlooking hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria, which requires vigorous saline resuscitation before surgery.
Attempting forceful succussion without placing the stethoscope over the epigastrium, missing faint splashing sounds.

probes.q: Describe the direction of visible gastric peristalsis in gastric outlet obstruction.
probes.a: Peristaltic waves originate under the left costal margin, pass downwards across the epigastrium, and travel to the right toward the pylorus in the right hypochondrium.

probes.q: What is the diagnostic significance of a succussion splash elicited five hours after ingestion of food or water?
probes.a: A succussion splash present four or more hours after the last meal establishes delayed gastric emptying and gastric outlet obstruction.

probes.q: What metabolic and electrolyte abnormality characterises chronic vomiting in pyloric stenosis, and why does paradoxical aciduria occur?
probes.a: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; paradoxical aciduria occurs because aldosterone conserves sodium at the distal renal tubule by excreting hydrogen ions when severe potassium depletion is present.

rubric.text: Inspects epigastrium under tangential lighting for fullness and visible peristalsis
Correctly identifies direction of gastric peristalsis from left to right
Demonstrates correct succussion splash technique and confirms time criteria
Palpates for an epigastric or antral mass to differentiate benign from malignant causes
Assesses physical markers of dehydration and metabolic disturbance

teach.heading: Visible gastric peristalsis
teach.body:
When the pyloric canal is progressively narrowed by chronic peptic ulcer scarring or antral neoplasm, the gastric muscularis undergoes marked compensatory hypertrophy.

Powerful peristaltic waves travel across the dilated stomach. Seen through a thin abdominal wall under tangential illumination, these waves sweep characteristically from the left hypochondrium downwards and across to the right, resembling a golf ball rolling under the skin.

teach.heading: Technique and timing of the succussion splash
teach.body:
A normal stomach empties liquids within two hours and solids within three to four hours. In gastric outlet obstruction, several litres of food residues, saliva, and gastric secretions accumulate.

Placing a stethoscope over the epigastrium and rocking the patient from side to side produces a loud splashing sound. Finding a splash more than four hours after any oral intake is conclusive bedside evidence of delayed gastric emptying.

teach.heading: Metabolic derangements and paradoxical aciduria
teach.body:
Persistent vomiting of acidic gastric juice loses large amounts of hydrogen, chloride, water, and potassium. This produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

As hypovolaemia worsens, the kidney attempts to conserve sodium under aldosterone influence. In the presence of severe potassium depletion, the distal renal tubules excrete hydrogen ions instead of potassium, producing acidic urine despite systemic alkalosis.

skill.exam.surg.courvoisier_sign.title: Courvoisier law in obstructive jaundice
skill.exam.surg.courvoisier_sign.oneLine: Palpable gallbladder in painless progressive jaundice indicates malignant obstruction
skill.exam.surg.courvoisier_sign.why: Courvoisier law is a cornerstone of surgical differential diagnosis in obstructive jaundice. Recognizing that a palpable, distended, non-tender gallbladder in the presence of jaundice signals periampullary or pancreatic malignancy rather than gallstones guides urgent oncological staging and avoids inappropriate interventions.

steps.text: Expose the abdomen completely and inspect the sclera, skin, and mucosal surfaces under bright natural daylight for deep greenish-yellow jaundice and scratch marks.
Inspect the right hypochondrium for a visible smooth globular swelling that descends with quiet inspiration.
Begin palpation low in the right iliac fossa with a flat, relaxed hand, gradually working upwards toward the right costal margin with each expiration.
Identify the fundus of the gallbladder: a smooth, rounded, pear-shaped, cystic swelling projecting beneath the inferior liver margin at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage.
Confirm that the swelling is non-tender and moves smoothly downwards and upwards with respiration.
Assess for intrinsic lateral mobility: a distended gallbladder can be moved from side to side around its neck, but cannot be displaced downwards.
Percuss over the swelling: note uniform dullness that is continuous with hepatic dullness without any intervening zone of colonic resonance.

skill.exam.surg.courvoisier_sign.normal: Non-jaundiced sclera, no palpable fullness or mass beneath the right costal margin, non-palpable gallbladder, and normal liver span on percussion.
skill.exam.surg.courvoisier_sign.abnormal: Deep cutaneous and scleral icterus, excoriations from pruritus, and a palpable, smooth, rounded, non-tender cystic swelling in the right hypochondrium that moves with respiration.
skill.exam.surg.courvoisier_sign.significance: A palpable, enlarged gallbladder in a patient with progressive jaundice strongly indicates malignant obstruction of the common bile duct (such as carcinoma of the head of the pancreas or periampullary carcinoma) rather than a gallstone.
skill.exam.surg.courvoisier_sign.practice: Perform abdominal palpation on a jaundiced patient or mannequin, mapping the course of the gallbladder fundus at the lateral rectus border and stating the pathological basis of Courvoisier law.
pitfalls: Assuming a palpable gallbladder is always malignant, forgetting rare exceptions like double impaction of gallstones or mucocele with cholangitis.
Starting palpation directly beneath the costal margin, overriding a massively enlarged gallbladder that extends down into the right iliac fossa.
Confusing an enlarged gallbladder with a Riedel lobe of the liver or a hydronephrotic right kidney.
Failing to inspect the skin for excoriations (pruritus scratches), which are classic markers of obstructive cholestatic jaundice.

probes.q: State Courvoisier law precisely as formulated in surgical practice.
probes.a: In a patient with jaundice, if the gallbladder is palpably enlarged, the obstruction is unlikely to be due to a gallstone; it is usually due to a malignant neoplasm such as carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.

probes.q: Why does a gallstone obstructing the common bile duct rarely result in a palpably enlarged gallbladder?
probes.a: Cholelithiasis causes recurrent chronic inflammation and fibrous scarring of the gallbladder wall over years, rendering the gallbladder shrunken, fibrotic, and incapable of dilating when distal obstruction occurs.

probes.q: Name three recognized clinical exceptions where Courvoisier law does not hold true.
probes.a: Double impaction of calculi (one stone in cystic duct creating mucocele and another in common bile duct causing jaundice), Oriental cholangiohepatitis with soft pigment stones, and benign stricture of the distal common bile duct.

rubric.text: Inspects for jaundice, scratch marks, and right hypochondrial fullness in daylight
Starts palpation in right iliac fossa and ascends toward ninth costal cartilage
Identifies smooth, cystic, pear-shaped swelling moving with respiration
Explains pathological basis of Courvoisier law and names clinical exceptions

teach.heading: Ludwig Courvoisier original observation
teach.body:
In 1890, Ludwig Courvoisier analysed large autopsy and surgical series of biliary obstruction. He noted that when the common bile duct was occluded by a stone, dilatation of the gallbladder was rare.

Conversely, when obstruction was caused by other factors, especially malignant compression from carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, periampullary carcinoma, or cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder dilatation was almost universal.

teach.heading: The pathological basis of fibrotic non-distension
teach.body:
Gallstones do not form instantaneously; they arise over many years amidst chronic, low-grade cholecystitis. The muscular wall of the gallbladder undergoes recurrent bouts of inflammation, mural thickening, and fibrous replacement.

When a migratory calculus subsequently lodges in the common bile duct, the rigid, contracted, fibrotic gallbladder wall cannot yield or expand under elevated back-pressure.

Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis with pigment stones
Triad of mass, jaundice, and pain in child

skill.exam.surg.malignancy_stigmata.title: Physical examination for abdominal malignancy stigmata
skill.exam.surg.malignancy_stigmata.oneLine: Virchow node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Blumer shelf, and Krukenberg tumours
skill.exam.surg.malignancy_stigmata.why: Advanced intra-abdominal adenocarcinoma frequently disseminates to distant lymph nodes, peritoneal surfaces, and pelvic recesses before symptoms become prominent. Systematically seeking metastatic stigmata establishes inoperability and guides palliative planning, avoiding unnecessary non-curative exploratory laparotomies.

steps.text: Examine the left supraclavicular fossa: stand behind the seated patient, palpate deeply behind the clavicular head of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle to detect a hard, fixed, non-tender lymph node (Troisier sign / Virchow node).
Inspect and palpate the umbilicus thoroughly: feel for a firm, hard, irregular, fixed nodule within the umbilical ring (Sister Mary Joseph nodule).
Examine both axillae, particularly the left anterior axillary fold, for enlarged firm metastatic nodes (Irish node).
Inspect and palpate the abdomen for a hard, bosselated, irregular liver edge with central umbilication, and evaluate for shifting dullness of malignant ascites.

Perform a digital rectal examination with the patient in the left lateral position: sweep the examining finger across the anterior rectal wall above the prostate or cervix to palpate a shelf-like, rigid, nodular peritoneal deposit (Blumer shelf).
Perform a bimanual pelvic examination in female patients to detect firm, bilateral, mobile or fixed adnexal masses representing metastatic ovarian deposits (Krukenberg tumours).

skill.exam.surg.malignancy_stigmata.normal: Empty supraclavicular fossae without palpable lymphadenopathy, normal soft umbilicus without induration, sharp smooth liver edge, absence of ascites, and smooth anterior rectal wall.
skill.exam.surg.malignancy_stigmata.abnormal: Enlarged hard left supraclavicular node (Troisier sign), hard fixed umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule), hard nodular hepatomegaly, malignant ascites, anterior rectal shelf deposit (Blumer shelf), or bilateral adnexal masses (Krukenberg tumours).
skill.exam.surg.malignancy_stigmata.significance: Detection of any of these classical eponymous physical signs confirms distant transcoelomic, lymphatic, or haematogenous metastatic dissemination (Stage IV disease), proving systemic spread.
skill.exam.surg.malignancy_stigmata.practice: Perform a structured bedside examination for secondary malignant deposits on a surgical teaching patient, demonstrating palpation of Troisier node and examination of the umbilical ring.
pitfalls: Palpating the supraclavicular fossa from in front rather than standing behind the patient, missing small nodes deep behind the clavicle.
Dismissing a firm umbilical nodule as a small umbilical hernia or granuloma without verifying induration and fixation.
Omitting digital rectal examination in gastric cancer workup, missing pelvic peritoneal deposits on the Blumer shelf.
Confusing normal faecal masses or a retroverted uterus with a true Blumer shelf deposit on rectal examination.

probes.q: What anatomical structure carries metastatic cells from abdominal viscera to the left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow node)?
probes.a: The thoracic duct, which drains abdominal and lower body lymph into the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.

probes.q: Describe the anatomical route of tumour spread resulting in a Sister Mary Joseph nodule at the umbilicus.
probes.a: Direct contiguous spread along peritoneal surfaces, or retrograde lymphatic and venous permeation along the falciform ligament via remnants of the obliterated umbilical vein.

probes.q: What is a Blumer shelf, how is it palpated, and what primary malignancy is classically associated with it?
probes.a: A rigid, shelf-like peritoneal deposit palpable on the anterior rectal wall above the prostate or cervix, caused by transcoelomic seeding of cancer cells into the rectovesical or rectouterine pouch; classically seen in gastric adenocarcinoma.

rubric.text: Palpates left supraclavicular fossa correctly from behind the seated patient
Examines umbilical ring for induration and Sister Mary Joseph nodule
Demonstrates digital rectal examination seeking anterior peritoneal Blumer shelf
Palpates liver for bosselated irregular edge and umbilication

teach.heading: Virchow node and the Troisier sign
teach.body:
Rudolf Virchow observed that malignancies of the stomach, pancreas, and abdominal viscera frequently metastasise to a lymph node nestled behind the left clavicle. Charles-Emile Troisier demonstrated its universal clinical significance.

Tumour emboli ascend the thoracic duct to its terminal termination at the left jugulovenous confluence, back-flowing into the left supraclavicular sentinels (Troisier sign).

teach.heading: Sister Mary Joseph nodule at the umbilicus
teach.body:
Sister Mary Joseph Dempsey, surgical assistant to William Mayo, noted that patients with advanced intra-abdominal cancer often had a firm pebble-like nodule in the umbilical ring.

Tumour reaches the umbilicus via transcoelomic shedding, through subperitoneal lymphatics along the falciform ligament, or via persistent venous connections along the obliterated umbilical vein (ligamentum teres).

skill.exam.surg.abdominal_tuberculosis.title: Clinical examination for abdominal tuberculosis
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_tuberculosis.oneLine: Doughy abdomen, contracted omental cake, matted nodes, and ileocaecal mass
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_tuberculosis.why: Abdominal tuberculosis remains widespread in endemic regions and mimics Crohn disease, intestinal lymphoma, and peritoneal carcinomatosis. Recognizing physical signs such as a doughy abdomen, contracted transverse omental mass, and firm ileocaecal swelling prevents misdiagnosis and directs appropriate anti-tubercular chemotherapy.

steps.text: Inspect the abdomen for asymmetrical distension, sunken flanks, prominent superficial veins, and a retracted transverse fullness across the upper abdomen.
Palpate gently across all quadrants to elicit the characteristic doughy resistance of plastic peritoneal tuberculosis, where the abdominal wall feels thickened and spongy.
Palpate the epigastric and umbilical regions for a transverse, rolled, contracted, firm mass representing the rolled-up omental cake (omental mass of tuberculosis).
Palpate the right iliac fossa for a firm, nodular, slightly tender, restricted mass representing hyperplastic ileocaecal tuberculosis.
Palpate deeply around the root of the mesentery along an oblique line from the left of L2 to the right iliac fossa for matted, lobulated, firm lymphadenopathy (tabes mesenterica).
Percuss for loculated or free fluid: note shifting dullness or irregular areas of dullness interspersed with resonant bowel loops (checkerboard percussion note).
Auscultate for borborygmi over subacute partial mechanical strictures, and perform digital rectal examination for peritoneal nodularity.

skill.exam.surg.abdominal_tuberculosis.normal: Soft, supple abdominal wall without resistance, absence of palpable abdominal masses, normal percussion with central resonance, and quiet normal bowel sounds.
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_tuberculosis.abnormal: Doughy resistance on palpation, transverse contracted omental cake, firm nodular ileocaecal mass, matted mesenteric lymph nodes, and checkerboard percussion dullness with ascites.
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_tuberculosis.significance: The constellation of doughy abdomen, contracted omental mass, and ileocaecal swelling in a young patient in an endemic zone strongly points to abdominal tuberculosis, requiring tissue or molecular confirmation before considering surgical resection.
skill.exam.surg.abdominal_tuberculosis.practice: Perform abdominal palpation demonstrating the differentiation of an omental cake from an enlarged transverse colon or gastric neoplasm on a clinical case simulator.
pitfalls: Mistaking a hyperplastic ileocaecal tuberculous mass for appendicular mass or carcinoma of the caecum without taking a detailed constitutional history.
Performing emergency resection of an ileocaecal tuberculous mass instead of conservative anti-tubercular therapy, which resolves the majority of inflammatory masses.
Failing to recognise that a doughy abdomen reflects chronic adhesive plastic peritonitis with thickened omentum and fibrinous exudate.
Missing subacute intestinal obstruction from multiple circular tuberculous strictures of the small bowel.

probes.q: What does the term doughy abdomen describe during physical examination in surgery?
probes.a: A characteristic soft, spongy, inelastic resistance felt on abdominal palpation, caused by chronic plastic tuberculous peritonitis with thickened subperitoneal tissue and fibrinous adhesions.

probes.q: Describe the physical characteristics of an omental mass in abdominal tuberculosis.
probes.a: A firm, transverse, sausage-shaped, rolled-up mass lying across the epigastrium or above the umbilicus, with limited vertical mobility but slight lateral mobility.

probes.q: How do you distinguish hyperplastic ileocaecal tuberculosis from carcinoma of the caecum at the bedside in an Indian setting?
probes.a: Tuberculosis typically affects younger patients (second to fourth decade) with low-grade fever, night sweats, and a smooth or lobulated slightly tender mass; carcinoma affects older patients with severe anaemia, weight loss, and a hard, nodular, non-tender craggy mass.

rubric.text: Demonstrates gentle palpation to identify doughy peritoneal resistance
Palpates for transverse contracted omental cake across the upper abdomen
Identifies firm, restricted mass in right iliac fossa (ileocaecal TB)
Demonstrates checkerboard percussion note reflecting loculated fluid and gas

teach.heading: Clinical forms of abdominal tuberculosis
teach.body:
Abdominal tuberculosis presents in three primary pathological forms: ulcerative, hyperplastic, and peritoneal. The ulcerative form produces multiple transverse tuberculous ulcers in the ileum, healing with circular strictures and subacute intestinal obstruction.

The hyperplastic form produces a florid inflammatory granulomatous mass in the ileocaecal region, heavily loaded with lymphoid tissue in Peyer patches.

teach.heading: The doughy abdomen and omental contracture
teach.body:
In peritoneal tuberculosis, the parietal and visceral peritoneum are studded with thousands of greyish-white tubercles. Copious fibrinous exudate glues bowel loops together, creating a spongy resistance termed the doughy abdomen.

The greater omentum undergoes dense granulomatous infiltration and contracts, rolling up into a transverse, sausage-like cake across the epigastrium that is easily mistaken for a transverse colon tumour.

teach.heading: Tabes mesenterica and checkerboard percussion
teach.body:
Tabes mesenterica describes massive caseous enlargement of mesenteric lymph nodes along the attachment of the mesentery. Palpation reveals a lobulated, non-tender, fixed or semi-mobile chain extending obliquely from left upper quadrant to right iliac fossa.

In the encysted ascitic form, fluid is trapped in pockets between adherent coils, creating alternating zones of resonance and dullness called checkerboard percussion.

skill.exam.surg.carnett_test.title: Carnett test for abdominal wall masses
skill.exam.surg.carnett_test.oneLine: Head-raising and leg-raising manoeuvres to separate parietal from visceral masses
skill.exam.surg.carnett_test.why: Abdominal swellings may arise within the abdominal wall (parietal) or deep within the peritoneal cavity (intra-abdominal). Carnett test uses voluntary rectus abdominis muscle contraction to differentiate between the two, preventing unnecessary laparotomy for parietal conditions like rectus sheath haematoma or desmoid tumours.

steps.text: Position the patient comfortably supine with the abdominal wall fully relaxed and palpate the lump to determine its baseline size, edge, and tenderness.
Instruct the patient to cross their arms over the chest and actively raise their head and shoulders off the couch, contracting the rectus abdominis muscles.
Alternatively, ask the patient to keep both knees straight and raise both extended legs a few inches off the bed (straight-leg raising test).
Palpate the lump carefully while the abdominal wall muscles remain firmly contracted.
Note whether the swelling becomes more prominent, fixed, and easily palpable (parietal mass) or disappears, becomes indistinct, and is shielded by the tensed muscles (intra-abdominal mass).

Evaluate tenderness during the test (Carnett sign): if focal tenderness increases or remains unchanged during contraction, the pain originates within the abdominal wall; if tenderness decreases, the source is visceral.

If parietal, test mobility in the relaxed state: attempt to move the lump while the wall is relaxed, then re-test while contracted to identify whether it is subcutaneous, intramuscular, or preperitoneal.

skill.exam.surg.carnett_test.normal: Soft abdominal wall with no palpable mass or focal tenderness either when relaxed or during active head-raising or leg-raising.
skill.exam.surg.carnett_test.abnormal: A mass that remains palpable or becomes more prominent and tender during rectus muscle contraction (parietal swelling), or a mass that disappears or softens completely during contraction (intra-abdominal swelling).
skill.exam.surg.carnett_test.significance: Distinguishes abdominal wall pathologies (rectus sheath haematoma, desmoid tumour, lipoma, incisional hernia) from intra-abdominal visceral swellings, guiding surgical planning and preventing inappropriate abdominal exploration.
skill.exam.surg.carnett_test.practice: Perform Carnett head-raising and leg-raising tests on a simulated patient, explaining the anatomical physics of the tensed rectus sheath in shielding intra-abdominal viscera.
pitfalls: Allowing the patient to arch their back or flex their knees during head-raising, which fails to generate adequate tension in the rectus abdominis muscles.
Confusing an incisional or ventral hernia with a parietal tumour; an incisional hernia becomes prominent on head-raising but exhibits an expansile cough impulse and reducible contents.
Assuming a swelling that becomes less palpable during contraction is always intra-abdominal, overlooking deep preperitoneal lipomas.
Pressing with excessive force during muscle contraction, causing diffuse muscular pain that masks localized tenderness.

probes.q: How do you perform Carnett test at the bedside to distinguish an abdominal wall lump from an intra-abdominal lump?
probes.a: The patient is asked to contract the rectus abdominis muscles by raising the head and shoulders or raising extended legs off the couch; a parietal lump remains palpable or prominent, while an intra-abdominal lump disappears or becomes indistinct.

probes.q: Explain why an intra-abdominal lump becomes impalpable when the anterior abdominal wall muscles contract.
probes.a: Contraction of the rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis, and internal obliques tenses the anterior aponeurosis and rectus sheath into a rigid muscular shield that pushes the mass backwards into the peritoneal cavity.

probes.q: How do you determine whether a parietal abdominal wall swelling is subcutaneous, intramuscular, or preperitoneal?
probes.a: A subcutaneous swelling is mobile over relaxed muscle and remains freely mobile over contracted muscle; an intramuscular swelling is mobile when relaxed but becomes completely fixed when muscle contracts; a preperitoneal swelling becomes less distinct during contraction.

rubric.text: Palpates the lump carefully in the fully relaxed supine position
Instructs patient to raise head and shoulders to tense rectus muscles
Re-palpates during contraction to assess prominence and tenderness
Correctly categorises mass as parietal, intra-abdominal, or hernial

teach.heading: Anatomical basis of Carnett test
teach.body:
John Carnett in 1926 described how voluntary contraction of the abdominal wall musculature differentiates parietal abdominal wall pain and masses from deeper intra-abdominal visceral conditions.

The rectus abdominis muscles, enclosed within the anterior and posterior rectus sheaths, form an unyielding muscular barrier when actively contracted by head-raising or leg-raising.

teach.heading: Interpretation: parietal versus visceral mass
teach.body:
If a lump arises within the abdominal wall (such as a rectus sheath haematoma, desmoid tumour of the musculoaponeurotic layer, or subcutaneous lipoma), rectus contraction fixes and thrusts the mass forward, making it more easily palpable.

Conversely, if the lump is intra-abdominal (such as an enlarged liver, spleen, kidney, mesenteric cyst, or gastric neoplasm), the contracted rectus muscle covers and shields the mass, rendering it non-palpable or markedly indistinct.

skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.title: Systematic examination of an abdominal lump
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.oneLine: Region mapping, respiratory excursion, getting above the mass, and intrinsic mobility
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.why: A standardized physical examination localises an abdominal lump to its organ of origin before radiological imaging. Determining respiratory excursion, whether the examiner can get above the mass, intrinsic planes of mobility, and surface consistency narrows the differential diagnosis to one or two anatomical possibilities.

steps.text: Map the exact anatomical location of the swelling across the nine standard abdominal regions (epigastric, hypochondrial, lumbar, umbilical, iliac, and hypogastric).
Inspect the contour, skin changes, visible peristalsis, and cough impulse over the lump while the patient breathes quietly.
Observe the lump during deep inspiration: note whether it descends with the diaphragm (liver, gallbladder, spleen) or remains static (pancreas, retroperitoneum, pelvis).

Test whether you can get above the swelling: place the palpating fingers between the upper margin of the lump and the costal margin; if fingers cannot be inserted, the mass originates from an upper abdominal organ.
Palpate the margins (sharp, rounded, ill-defined), surface (smooth, bosselated, nodular), and consistency (soft, cystic, firm, hard, stony).
Assess intrinsic mobility: gently attempt to move the lump vertically and horizontally to determine fixation to deeper structures or mesentery.
Percuss over the swelling to distinguish uniform dullness (solid organ or fluid cyst) from overlying resonance (retroperitoneal or mesenteric mass covered by bowel loops).

skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.normal: Smooth, symmetrical abdomen with no visible or palpable mass across any of the nine regions, normal respiratory movement, and normal percussion resonance.
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.abnormal: A localized swelling in one or more abdominal regions, descending with respiration, inability to get above the upper border, firm nodular surface, or abnormal percussion dullness.
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.significance: Determining the anatomical region, respiratory mobility, ability to get above the swelling, and percussion note establishes the organ of origin (e.g. liver, spleen, kidney, gallbladder, mesentery, or pelvic organ).
skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.practice: Demonstrate the nine-region systematic examination of an abdominal mass on a clinical simulator, explaining the clinical significance of getting above the swelling.
pitfalls: Starting palpation directly over the mass rather than beginning in the opposite, non-tender quadrant, inducing voluntary guarding.
Failing to test whether one can get above the swelling, confusing an enlarged spleen or liver with a retroperitoneal or renal mass.
Overlooking movement on deep respiration, misclassifying a mobile gallbladder or hepatic tumour as a fixed retroperitoneal mass.
Palpating with the fingertips poked vertically into the abdomen rather than laying the warm palmar surfaces of the fingers flat.

probes.q: Name the nine anatomical regions of the abdomen used to describe the location of an abdominal lump.
probes.a: Right hypochondrium, epigastrium, left hypochondrium, right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar, right iliac fossa, hypogastrium (suprapubic), and left iliac fossa.

probes.q: What anatomical rule governs whether an abdominal lump moves downwards during inspiration?
probes.a: Swellings arising from organs intimately connected to the diaphragm (liver, gallbladder, spleen, and to a lesser degree stomach and kidneys) move downwards on inspiration; retroperitoneal, mesenteric, and pelvic swellings do not.

probes.q: What is the diagnostic significance of being unable to get above an abdominal swelling?
probes.a: Inability to insert the fingers between the upper border of the mass and the costal margin indicates that the swelling originates from a subdiaphragmatic organ, namely the liver or the spleen.

rubric.text: Accurately maps the lump to its anatomical region among the nine zones
Evaluates mobility of the swelling during quiet and deep inspiration
Tests whether the examiner can get above the upper border of the mass
Percusses over the swelling to identify overlying colonic resonance or dullness

teach.heading: The nine anatomical regions and visceral mapping
teach.body:
Topographical mapping divides the abdomen using two vertical mid-clavicular lines and two horizontal planes (subcostal plane passing through the lowest point of the tenth costal cartilages, and transtubercular plane through the iliac tubercles).

This creates nine regions. Correctly naming the primary region localises the underlying viscera: right hypochondrium (liver, gallbladder), left hypochondrium (spleen, stomach fundus), umbilical (small bowel, aorta).

teach.heading: Respiratory mobility and the diaphragm
teach.body:
During inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction displaces subdiaphragmatic structures downwards. The liver, gallbladder, and spleen descend prominently by two to four centimetres with each deep breath.

The kidneys move slightly (one to two centimetres). Conversely, retroperitoneal tumours, pancreatic pseudocysts, aortic aneurysms, and swellings arising from the pelvis (distended bladder, fibroid) remain immobile during respiration.

teach.heading: Can you get above it?
teach.body:
This classic physical sign provides instant anatomical discrimination. In an enlarged spleen or liver, the upper margin arises beneath the costal margin, making it impossible to insert fingers between the mass and the ribs.

In a renal, adrenal, pancreatic, or retroperitoneal mass, the examiner can usually press the fingers into the loin or beneath the ribs above the upper pole of the swelling.

skill.exam.surg.pulsatile_mass.title: Clinical examination of a pulsatile abdominal mass
skill.exam.surg.pulsatile_mass.oneLine: Distinguishing true expansile pulsation from transmitted aortic pulsation
skill.exam.surg.pulsatile_mass.why: A pulsatile abdominal mass may represent an abdominal aortic aneurysm (a life-threatening surgical disease) or a solid tumour or pancreatic pseudocyst overlying a normal aorta. Distinguishing expansile pulsation from transmitted pulsation prevents catastrophic biopsy or misdiagnosis.

steps.text: Inspect the epigastrium and umbilical region from the side under tangential lighting to detect visible rhythmic vascular pulsations.
Place the index fingers or palms of both hands gently on the lateral borders of the mass, with fingers separated and resting flat on either side.
Feel the nature of the pulsation: in true expansile pulsation, the examining fingers are actively pushed apart laterally in all directions with each systolic heartbeat.
In transmitted pulsation, the fingers are merely lifted straight anteriorly (anteroposterior thrust) without any lateral separation.
Perform the knee-elbow position test: place the patient in the knee-elbow position with torso supported, allowing the abdominal viscera to fall forward away from the spine.
Palpate the mass in the knee-elbow position: if pulsation disappears, the mass is anterior to the aorta and the pulsation was transmitted; if expansile pulsation persists, the mass is an aneurysm.
Auscultate over the mass with the bell of the stethoscope to detect a systolic murmur or vascular bruit.

skill.exam.surg.pulsatile_mass.normal: Normal aortic pulsation felt as a gentle vertical thrust in thin individuals without lateral expansion, no palpable abdominal mass, and absence of vascular bruits.
skill.exam.surg.pulsatile_mass.abnormal: A prominent epigastric or periumbilical mass exhibiting true expansile pulsation with lateral separation of examining hands, persistent pulsation in knee-elbow position, or an overlying systolic bruit.
skill.exam.surg.pulsatile_mass.significance: Expansile pulsation confirms an aneurysm of the abdominal aorta or major visceral branch, requiring urgent vascular ultrasound or CT angiography; transmitted pulsation indicates a pre-aortic mass such as a pancreatic cyst or retroperitoneal tumour.
skill.exam.surg.pulsatile_mass.practice: Perform the two-handed lateral palpation technique on a vascular model, contrasting lateral expansile separation with vertical transmitted displacement.
pitfalls: Attempting needle aspiration or percutaneous core biopsy of a pulsatile mass without first confirming vascular anatomy with colour Doppler ultrasound.
Mistaking the vigorous normal aortic pulsation of a thin, anxious young person or lordotic spine for an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Failing to perform the knee-elbow position test when the clinical distinction between transmitted and expansile pulsation remains equivocal.
Pressing with excessive force directly over a large, tender abdominal aortic aneurysm, risking rupture.

probes.q: How do you clinically distinguish an expansile pulsation from a transmitted pulsation in an abdominal mass?
probes.a: Placing hands on either side of the mass: in expansile pulsation, the hands are pushed laterally apart in all directions with systole; in transmitted pulsation, the mass is simply lifted forward without lateral separation.

probes.q: What happens to a transmitted pulsation when the patient is placed in the knee-elbow position, and why?
probes.a: The pulsation disappears or diminishes markedly, because gravity causes the mobile pre-aortic mass or tumour to fall anteriorly away from the retroperitoneal aorta.

probes.q: Name three pathological conditions that produce a transmitted pulsation across the abdominal aorta.
probes.a: Pancreatic pseudocyst, carcinoma of the body of the pancreas, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and stomach or transverse colon tumours overlying the aorta.

rubric.text: Inspects for rhythmic epigastric pulsation under tangential illumination
Places hands on lateral borders of mass to evaluate lateral separation
Demonstrates knee-elbow manoeuvre to separate mass from the aorta
Auscultates over the swelling for systolic bruits

teach.heading: The physics of expansile versus transmitted pulsation
teach.body:
An aneurysm is a pathological dilatation of an artery involving all three mural layers. Because blood enters the aneurysmal sac under systolic pressure, Pascal law dictates that pressure is exerted equally in all directions.

Placing the fingers on the lateral borders demonstrates that the fingers are pushed apart laterally as well as lifted forwards. A solid tumour overlying the aorta merely transmits the shock wave upwards without lateral expansion.

teach.heading: The knee-elbow test of Osler
teach.body:
When an anterior abdominal mass (such as a pancreatic pseudocyst, gastric carcinoma, or matted mesenteric lymph nodes) rests upon the abdominal aorta, it transmits aortic pulsation directly to the palpating hand.

Placing the patient in the knee-elbow position causes mobile peritoneal viscera to fall anteriorly under gravity away from the fixed retroperitoneal aorta. If the pulsation disappears, transmitted pulsation is confirmed.

rows: Lifted forward in vertical plane only

skill.exam.surg.mesenteric_omental_cyst.title: Clinical examination of mesenteric and omental cysts
skill.exam.surg.mesenteric_omental_cyst.oneLine: Tillaux sign, perpendicular mobility, and surrounding colonic resonance
skill.exam.surg.mesenteric_omental_cyst.why: Mesenteric and omental cysts are rare benign intra-abdominal cystic swellings that mimic ovarian cysts, hydronephrosis, and pancreatic pseudocysts. Eliciting Tillaux sign and demonstrating mobility at right angles to the line of mesenteric attachment confirms the mesenteric origin.

steps.text: Inspect the abdomen for a visible, painless, smooth, central abdominal swelling located around the umbilicus, with minimal movement on respiration.
Palpate the swelling gently, identifying a smooth, painless, well-defined, rounded or oval cystic mass with a distinct fluid thrill or fluctuance.
Test mobility along the line of mesenteric attachment: attempt to move the mass along the oblique axis from the left of the second lumbar vertebra down to the right sacroiliac joint.
Test mobility at right angles to the line of mesenteric attachment (Tillaux sign): gently push the mass transversely across the abdomen from right to left and left to right.
Confirm Tillaux sign: demonstrate that the mass is freely mobile in a direction perpendicular to the mesenteric attachment line, but relatively fixed along its longitudinal axis.
Percuss over and around the mass: note a central band of dullness surrounded by a resonant zone of gas-filled bowel, with a resonant band often traversing the cyst anteriorly.
Contrast with an omental cyst, which is located more superficially and is freely mobile in all directions without restriction.

skill.exam.surg.mesenteric_omental_cyst.normal: Soft, flat central abdomen with no palpable cystic masses, normal percussion resonance throughout, and normal active bowel sounds.
skill.exam.surg.mesenteric_omental_cyst.abnormal: A smooth, cystic, fluctuant swelling in the umbilical region that is freely mobile at right angles to the root of the mesentery but fixed along its axis (positive Tillaux sign), with surrounding resonant bowel loops.
skill.exam.surg.mesenteric_omental_cyst.significance: A positive Tillaux sign is pathognomonic of a mesenteric cyst, distinguishing it from ovarian cysts (which arise from the pelvis) and hydronephrosis (which is fixed in the loin).
skill.exam.surg.mesenteric_omental_cyst.practice: Demonstrate the elicitation of Tillaux sign on an abdominal model, moving the mass perpendicular to the anatomical line connecting L2 to the right sacroiliac joint.
pitfalls: Confusing a mesenteric cyst with a large ovarian cyst; an ovarian cyst arises from the pelvis, so the examiner cannot get below it, and dullness is central without a traversing resonant band.
Mistaking free ascites for a large mesenteric cyst, failing to recognize that mesenteric cysts do not cause shifting dullness in the flanks.
Attempting forceful compression of a suspected mesenteric cyst, which can rupture thin lymphatic or chylolymphatic cyst walls.
Failing to percuss for the band of resonance that characteristically traverses the anterior surface of a mesenteric cyst.

probes.q: What is Tillaux sign and what condition does it identify?
probes.a: An intra-abdominal cystic mass that is freely mobile in a direction at right angles to the root of the mesentery, but has very restricted mobility along the line of mesenteric attachment; it is characteristic of a mesenteric cyst.

probes.q: State the anatomical surface marking of the root of the mesentery across the posterior abdominal wall.
probes.a: An oblique line approximately fifteen centimetres long, extending from the duodenojejunal flexure (left side of the second lumbar vertebra) downwards to the ileocaecal junction (upper border of the right sacroiliac joint).

probes.q: How does percussion differentiate a large mesenteric cyst from an ovarian cyst at the bedside?
probes.a: A mesenteric cyst is surrounded by resonant gas-filled bowel with a band of resonance running across it; an ovarian cyst arises from the pelvis with central dullness and gas pushed laterally to the flanks.

rubric.text: Palpates smooth, well-defined mass and detects cystic fluctuance
Demonstrates Tillaux sign with mobility perpendicular to mesenteric root
Percusses surrounding resonance and identifies traversing resonant bowel band
Differentiates from pelvic ovarian cyst by getting below the lower border

teach.heading: Anatomy of the root of the mesentery
teach.body:
The root of the small bowel mesentery is approximately fifteen centimetres long and attaches the jejunum and ileum to the posterior abdominal wall.

It extends obliquely downwards from the duodenojejunal flexure at the left side of the second lumbar vertebra, crossing the third part of the duodenum, aorta, IVC, and right psoas to end at the upper border of the right sacroiliac joint.

teach.heading: Tillaux sign of perpendicular mobility
teach.body:
Paul Tillaux described the classic physical sign of mesenteric cysts. Because the cyst develops between the two peritoneal leaves of the mesentery, its attachment restricts movement along the mesenteric axis.

However, the mesentery has ample laxity in the transverse plane, allowing the cyst to be moved freely from side to side at right angles to the root of the mesentery.

skill.exam.surg.kidney_vs_spleen.title: Differentiating renal mass from splenomegaly
skill.exam.surg.kidney_vs_spleen.oneLine: Bimanual ballotability, the splenic notch, getting above the mass, and colonic resonance
skill.exam.surg.kidney_vs_spleen.why: A mass in the left hypochondrium is one of the classic examination dilemmas in surgery and medicine. Systematically testing for bimanual ballotability, an anterior notch, the ability to get above the swelling, and overlying colonic resonance reliably differentiates renal enlargement from splenomegaly.

steps.text: Inspect the left hypochondrium and lumbar region: note whether fullness fills the loin posteriorly (kidney) or projects downwards and medially toward the umbilicus (spleen).
Observe respiratory excursion: an enlarged spleen moves downwards and medially toward the right iliac fossa; an enlarged kidney moves downwards almost vertically and less extensively.

Attempt to get above the swelling: place the medial border of the hand between the top of the mass and the left costal margin; with splenomegaly it is impossible to get above it, whereas with a renal mass you can often insert fingers above the upper pole.

Palpate the anterior border: search for a sharp anterior margin with one or more distinct notches (splenic notch), contrasted with the smooth, rounded, cylindrical anterior surface of an enlarged kidney.
Perform bimanual palpation: place the left hand posteriorly in the left renal angle between the twelfth rib and iliac crest, and the right hand flat on the anterior abdominal wall.

Test for ballotability: gently push the posterior hand forward in quick, rhythmic taps; an enlarged kidney bounces anteriorly against the waiting right hand (ballotable), while an enlarged spleen is not ballotable.

Percuss over the swelling: an enlarged spleen is uniformly dull to percussion without intervening gas; an enlarged kidney has a band of colonic resonance (descending colon) running vertically over its anterior surface.

skill.exam.surg.kidney_vs_spleen.normal: Non-palpable spleen, left kidney not bimanually palpable or ballotable in healthy adults, and normal resonance across left lumbar and flank regions.
skill.exam.surg.kidney_vs_spleen.abnormal: A left hypochondrial mass: either a firm mass with a sharp notched anterior border moving towards the right iliac fossa that cannot be got above (spleen), or a smooth rounded bimanually ballotable mass with overlying colonic resonance (kidney).
skill.exam.surg.kidney_vs_spleen.significance: Accurately distinguishes splenomegaly (portal hypertension, haematological malignancy, visceral leishmaniasis) from left renal enlargement (renal cell carcinoma, hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney disease), preventing inappropriate interventions.
skill.exam.surg.kidney_vs_spleen.practice: Perform bimanual examination and ballotability on a renal teaching phantom, contrasting findings with splenic palpation and mapping colonic resonance.
pitfalls: Attempting to elicit ballotability with stiff, forceful movements rather than gentle, rhythmic posterior flicking with the resting anterior hand relaxed.
Assuming a massive spleen is a renal tumour because it fills the left flank, failing to trace the sharp anterior border and splenic notch.
Missing colonic resonance over a kidney mass because percussion is performed too lightly or without mapping the course of the descending colon.
Confusing the irregular bosselated surface of polycystic kidney disease with a neoplastic splenic mass.

probes.q: How do you test for bimanual ballotability of an enlarged kidney at the bedside?
probes.a: The examiner places one hand behind the loin in the renal angle and the other hand flat on the anterior abdominal wall; pressing forwards with the posterior hand bounces the kidney against the anterior hand.

probes.q: Why is an enlarged kidney typically resonant to percussion while an enlarged spleen is uniformly dull?
probes.a: The kidney is retroperitoneal and is covered anteriorly by the descending colon containing gas; the spleen is an intraperitoneal organ that displaces the splenic flexure downwards and medially, lying directly under the anterior wall.

probes.q: In which anatomical direction does an enlarged spleen expand, and why?
probes.a: An enlarged spleen expands downwards and medially toward the right iliac fossa, guided along the axis of the splenic vessels and restrained from expanding backwards or laterally by the phrenicocolic ligament.

rubric.text: Notes direction of movement with respiration (medial vs vertical)
Searches specifically for a sharp anterior border and splenic notch
Tests whether fingers can be inserted above the upper pole of the swelling
Demonstrates correct bimanual technique and assesses ballotability
Percusses for overlying band of colonic resonance over the kidney mass

teach.heading: Axis of enlargement and respiratory excursion
teach.body:
The spleen enlarges along its anatomical long axis. Supported laterally and inferiorly by the phrenicocolic ligament (sustentaculum lienis), it is directed downwards and medially across the abdomen toward the right iliac fossa.

The kidney enlarges downwards into the lumbar region and forwards into the hypochondrium, moving almost vertically during respiration and filling the posterior loin hollow.

teach.heading: Bimanual palpation and ballotability
teach.body:
A renal mass is retroperitoneal and occupies the posterior paravertebral gutter. Placing one hand posteriorly in the renal angle and one hand anteriorly permits bimanual capture.

Quick upward thrusts with the posterior hand toss the mobile kidney forward to impact the anterior examining hand (ballotability). A spleen is intraperitoneal, lies anteriorly, and cannot be ballotted from behind.

skill.hx.surg.rectal_bleeding_pain.title: Rectal pain and bleeding history
skill.hx.surg.rectal_bleeding_pain.oneLine: Characterise the pain, the timing of bleeding, and the change in bowel habit
skill.hx.surg.rectal_bleeding_pain.why: Anal symptoms are frequently trivialised as simple piles by patients, delaying the diagnosis of colorectal cancer or complicated anorectal sepsis. Differentiating the bright red splash of internal haemorrhoids from the painful tearing bleeding of a fissure or the dark blood mixed with mucus of malignancy changes the diagnostic pathway immediately.

asks.text: Where is the pain, what does it feel like, and how is it related to defecation? Severe sharp cutting pain during and after defecation indicates anal fissure; persistent throbbing pain indicates a perianal or ischiorectal abscess.
Describe the bleeding: is it bright red, dark red, or altered? Does it splash into the toilet pan, streak the surface of hard stool, or is it intimately mixed with faeces and mucus?
Does any lump protrude from the anus during defecation? Does it slip back spontaneously, require manual digital reduction, or remain permanently prolapsed outside?
Is there any perianal discharge of pus or mucus that soils the undergarments, or persistent itching (pruritus ani)?
Has there been any recent change in your bowel habit towards persistent constipation, morning diarrhoea, or spurious diarrhoea with a feeling of incomplete rectal evacuation (tenesmus)?
Have you experienced unintended weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue, or a family history of bowel cancer or polyps?

skill.hx.surg.rectal_bleeding_pain.practice: Take a history from a simulated patient presenting with rectal bleeding. Differentiate fissure, haemorrhoids, and rectal neoplasm in under four minutes.
pitfalls: Assuming painless bright rectal bleeding is benign haemorrhoids in a patient over forty without inquiring about altered bowel habit and weight loss.
Failing to ask whether blood is mixed with stool or coats the outside, which distinguishes colonic bleeding from anal verge pathology.
Not asking whether a prolapsed anal mass reduces on its own or requires manual replacement.

probes.q: What does bright red blood splashing into the pan after passing stool typically indicate?
probes.a: Internal haemorrhoids.

probes.q: How does the pain of an anal fissure differ from that of a perianal abscess?
probes.a: Fissure causes sharp cutting pain during defecation lasting for hours after, whereas perianal abscess causes persistent, progressive, throbbing pain independent of defecation.

probes.q: What is spurious diarrhoea or tenesmus in a patient with carcinoma of the rectum?
probes.a: A low rectal growth creates a false sensation of rectal fullness, provoking frequent straining to pass small amounts of mucus and blood without true faecal matter.

rubric.text: Characterises the nature, timing, and severity of anal pain
Differentiates blood coating stool, splashing in pan, or mixed with mucus
Inquires about prolapse of masses and reducibility
Screens for change in bowel habit, tenesmus, and weight loss

teach.heading: The three cardinal presentations of anorectal pathology
teach.body:
Patients presenting with anorectal disorders usually report pain, bleeding, or a protruding lump. Anal fissure produces exquisite burning or tearing pain during and after stool, often accompanied by a small streak of bright red blood on the toilet paper.

In contrast, uncomplicated internal haemorrhoids bleed painlessly with bright red blood splashing into the toilet pan. Persistent throbbing pain indicates an acute abscess or thrombosis.

rows: Fresh bright red, separate from stool
Bright red streak, severe tearing pain
Dark red or altered, accompanied by mucus
Blood mixed with pus, perianal discharge

skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.title: Inspection of the perianal region
skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.oneLine: Expose adequately in the left lateral position and separate buttocks gently
skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.why: More than half of all anal conditions are visible on simple inspection before a gloved finger ever touches the patient. Inserting a finger into a fissure without looking causes agonising pain and destroys patient trust, while a sentinel tag, external opening of a fistula, or thrombosed pile can be diagnosed on sight.

steps.text: Place the patient in Sims left lateral position with buttocks overhanging the edge of the couch and knees drawn up to the chest.
Ensure adequate lighting and explain each step calmly before touching.
Gently separate the buttocks with both hands using gloved fingers.
Inspect perianal skin for erythema, excoriation, maceration, or fungal dermatitis.
Look for external swellings: skin tags, sentinel pile at the midline, perianal haematoma (thrombosed external pile), or condylomata.
Look for openings: external fistula opening, noting whether it discharges pus or serous fluid.
Gently part the anal verge to inspect the anal canal lining for an anal fissure, usually at 6 o'clock (posterior midline) or 12 o'clock.
Ask the patient to bear down gently and observe for prolapse of internal haemorrhoids or rectal mucosal prolapse.

skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.normal: Perianal skin is intact, pigmented, and corrugated with normal anal reflex; anal verge is closed; no fissures, tags, sinuses, or masses visible on resting or bearing down.
skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.abnormal: Sentinel skin tag with visible posterior midline fissure; bluish tense perianal haematoma; external fistulous opening discharging pus; prolapsing haemorrhoids or concentric rings of rectal prolapse.
skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.significance: Identifying a fissure spares the patient a painful digital examination. A sentinel pile indicates a chronic fissure; radial mucosal folds indicate haemorrhoids whereas concentric mucosal rings indicate full-thickness rectal prolapse.
skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.practice: Inspect the perianal region in a surgical model, systematically identifying the twelve, three, six, and nine o'clock landmarks in the left lateral position.
pitfalls: Attempting digital examination before inspecting the perianal skin and anal verge.
Failing to ask the patient to strain or bear down, missing reducible internal haemorrhoids or mucosal prolapse.
Not noting the clock position of an external fistula opening or fissure relative to the anal verge.

probes.q: At which anatomical clock position is an anal fissure most frequently found?
probes.a: At 6 o'clock in the posterior midline.

probes.q: How do you distinguish mucosal rectal prolapse from full-thickness rectal procidentia on inspection?
probes.a: Mucosal prolapse shows radial mucosal folds and rarely exceeds three to four centimetres, whereas full-thickness rectal prolapse shows concentric circular folds and involves all rectal wall layers.

probes.q: What is a sentinel skin tag and what is its clinical significance?
probes.a: A sentinel tag is a tag of oedematous skin at the lower end of a chronic anal fissure caused by lymphatic oedema and chronic inflammation, signifying chronicity.

rubric.text: Positions patient correctly in Sims left lateral position with buttocks at bed edge
Inspects perianal skin, margin, and clock positions systematically
Identifies fissure and sentinel tag before attempting palpation
Asks patient to bear down to reveal prolapsing haemorrhoids or rectal procidentia

teach.heading: The clock face of the anal verge in left lateral position
teach.body:
By convention, anorectal descriptions reference a clock face: 12 o'clock is anterior toward the perineum and scrotum or vulva, 6 o'clock is posterior toward the coccyx, 9 o'clock is to the patient's right, and 3 o'clock is to the patient's left.

Acute fissures are located at 6 o'clock in over ninety percent of men and eighty-five percent of women. An off-midline fissure suggests atypical causes such as Crohn disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy.

teach.heading: Radial versus concentric folds in prolapsing tissue
teach.body:
When a mass protrudes on straining, look at the mucosal grooves. Internal haemorrhoids prolapse as separate lobes with radial furrows between them.

Full-thickness rectal prolapse descends as a cylindrical mass with circular, concentric mucosal folds that completely encircle the anal circumference. It can be grasped between thumb and finger, revealing a double thickness of rectal wall.

skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.title: Surgical digital rectal examination
skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.oneLine: Palpate anal sphincter, assess four rectal quadrants, and examine the gloved finger
skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.why: A surgical digital rectal examination is a tactile exploration of the distal eight centimetres of the alimentary tract and adjacent pelvic structures. Omission of DRE is a classic cause of late diagnosis of rectal cancer, prostatic tumours, and pelvic abscesses.

steps.text: Re-confirm consent and ensure a chaperone is present.
Generously lubricate a gloved right index finger with water-soluble jelly.
Rest the pulp of the index finger flat against the anal verge and apply gentle steady pressure until the sphincter relaxes, then slowly rotate and advance into the anal canal.
Assess resting tone of the anal sphincter, then ask the patient to squeeze to assess voluntary external sphincter contraction.
Palpate the anal canal walls circumferentially for induration, tenderness, or the internal opening of a fistula (a small depression or nodule).
Advance the finger fully into the rectal ampulla.
Palpate anteriorly: in men, evaluate the lateral lobes and median sulcus of the prostate and seminal vesicles; in women, palpate the cervix and pouch of Douglas.
Sweep the finger along both lateral walls (pelvic sidewalls and ischiorectal spaces) and posterior wall (sacrum, coccyx, presacral nodes).
Palpate for rectal tumours: note lower edge, ulceration, everted edges, induration, and mobility on muscularis.
Withdraw the finger gently and immediately inspect the glove for faecal colour, mucus, fresh blood, or melaena.

skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.normal: Smooth pliable mucosa, normal sphincter tone, no induration or mass felt; non-tender; in males, smooth, rubbery, symmetrical prostate with palpable median sulcus; glove stained with normal brown stool, no blood or pus.
skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.abnormal: Sphincter spasm or flaccidity; palpable indurated ulcer or cauliflower mass with indurated base; stony hard nodular prostate; tenderness in pouch of Douglas; fresh blood, dark blood, or mucus on glove.
skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.significance: Low rectal tumours (within 7 to 8 cm of anal verge) are easily palpated; consistency and fixation decide resectability. Tender fullness in pouch of Douglas suggests pelvic abscess or Blumer shelf (metastatic deposit).
skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.practice: Perform systematic quadrant palpation on an anorectal simulator, recording findings for anterior, right lateral, left lateral, and posterior walls.
pitfalls: Using the tip of the finger directly like a drill rather than placing the pulp flat to relax the sphincter.
Failing to advance the finger fully, missing tumours in the upper rectum (between 6 and 8 cm).
Forgetting to inspect the examining glove after withdrawal for blood, pus, or altered stool.
Palpating only the prostate and ignoring the posterior and lateral rectal walls.

probes.q: What must you inspect immediately upon withdrawing the finger after DRE?
probes.a: Inspect the glove for blood, mucus, pus, and the colour of the stool.

probes.q: What is Blumer shelf on digital rectal examination and what does it indicate?
probes.a: A palpable ridge or shelf-like mass in the rectovesical or rectouterine pouch anterior to the rectum, indicating transcoelomic peritoneal metastasis, classically from gastric adenocarcinoma.

probes.q: Why are uncomplicated internal haemorrhoids usually not palpable on digital rectal examination?
probes.a: Because internal haemorrhoids are soft vascular cushions that collapse under digital finger pressure, only becoming palpable when thrombosed, ulcerated, or chronically fibrosed.

rubric.text: Applies water-soluble lubricant and enters anal canal gently with pulp of finger
Assesses resting and voluntary sphincter squeeze
Systematically palpates anterior, lateral, and posterior rectal walls
Assesses prostate in males or pouch of Douglas for tenderness or shelf
Inspects glove on withdrawal for fresh blood, mucus, or melaena
