teach.heading: Quadrant sweep of the rectal ampulla
teach.body:
A complete digital examination covers all four quadrants of the rectal ampulla. Anteriorly lies the prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and rectovesical pouch in males, or the cervix, posterior vaginal fornix, and pouch of Douglas in females.

Posteriorly the finger follows the hollow of the sacrum and coccyx, detecting presacral tumours, chordomas, or enlarged retrorectal lymph nodes. The lateral walls abut the ischiorectal fossae and pelvic sidewalls.

teach.heading: Features of a palpable rectal carcinoma

points.d: Typically everted and raised, creating an ulcer with an indurated, crater-like base.
An annular growth encircles the lumen, creating a tight malignant stricture that may admit only the fingertip.
Assess whether the tumour moves freely on the muscularis, is tethered, or is fixed to the sacrum or pelvic sidewall.
Measure the distance from the anal verge to the lower edge of the tumour, which governs surgical choice (sphincter preservation vs abdominoperineal resection).

skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.title: Proctoscopic examination
skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.oneLine: Direct visualization of the anal canal and distal rectum using an illuminated proctoscope
skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.why: Digital examination cannot feel non-thrombosed internal haemorrhoids and cannot directly view mucosal colour, vascularity, or bleeding points. Proctoscopy allows direct inspection of the three primary haemorrhoidal positions and provides access for office treatments.

steps.text: Ensure the patient is in the left lateral position and that the DRE has already been completed to confirm the lumen is clear.
Inspect the proctoscope with its obturator fully locked in place; lubricate the instrument generously.
Warm the metal instrument or use a disposable plastic proctoscope to avoid sphincter spasm.
Direct the instrument toward the umbilicus initially, then alter direction posteriorly along the sacral curve as the sphincter gives way.
Advance the proctoscope fully, hold the flange firmly, and withdraw the obturator.
Inspect the rectal mucosa for colour, ulceration, granular proctitis, or tumours under direct light.
Slowly withdraw the proctoscope while asking the patient to strain gently.
Observe the mucosa collapsing into the open lumen of the scope at the anorectal ring to identify internal haemorrhoids bulging inward at 3, 7, and 11 o'clock.
Inspect the anal canal during final withdrawal for the internal opening of a fistula or an active fissure.

skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.normal: Smooth, pale pink rectal mucosa with visible branching submucosal vessels; no bulging vascular cushions or mucosal prolapse on withdrawal; no blood or purulent discharge.
skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.abnormal: Engorged, violaceous vascular cushions bulging into the proctoscope at 3, 7, or 11 o'clock; actively bleeding internal pile; red, granular, friable mucosa with contact bleeding in proctitis; ulcerating tumour.
skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.significance: Confirms the diagnosis and exact grade of internal haemorrhoids; localises primary sites for sclerotherapy or rubber band ligation; distinguishes haemorrhoids from proctitis or neoplasm.
skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.practice: Perform proctoscope insertion and withdrawal on a trainer, identifying simulated haemorrhoidal bulges at 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions.
pitfalls: Failing to perform DRE prior to proctoscopy, risking trauma from an unrecognised stricture or obstructing growth.
Withdrawing the proctoscope too quickly without asking the patient to strain, failing to see haemorrhoidal prolapse.
Inserting the proctoscope without locking the obturator in place, causing mucosal laceration.

probes.q: What are the three classical anatomical clock positions of primary internal haemorrhoids?
probes.a: 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions.

probes.q: Why do internal haemorrhoids occur precisely at 3, 7, and 11 o'clock?
probes.a: Because they correspond to the terminal branches of the superior rectal artery: the right branch divides into anterior (11 o'clock) and posterior (7 o'clock) branches, while the left branch continues as a single main trunk (3 o'clock).

probes.q: What mucosal appearance on proctoscopy distinguishes ulcerative proctitis from uncomplicated internal haemorrhoids?
probes.a: Ulcerative proctitis shows diffuse erythema, loss of the normal submucosal vascular pattern, granularity, and friability with contact bleeding, whereas haemorrhoids show localized bulging cushions surrounded by normal mucosa.

rubric.text: Checks proctoscope, ensures obturator locked, and lubricates instrument
Introduces toward umbilicus then angles posteriorly into rectal ampulla
Removes obturator and inspects rectal mucosa under direct illumination
Withdraws slowly, assessing haemorrhoidal cushions at 3, 7, and 11 o'clock on straining

teach.heading: Technique of proctoscopy and haemorrhoid detection
teach.body:
Proctoscopy is performed after digital examination has confirmed a patent lumen. The lubricated instrument with obturator engaged is inserted toward the umbilicus until the sphincter relaxes, then tilted backward into the sacral curve.

Once advanced to its hilt, the obturator is removed. As the barrel is slowly withdrawn, the mucosa falls into the lumen. Internal haemorrhoids bulge forward into the lumen as distinct pink or purplish mounds.

teach.heading: Vascular anatomy of internal haemorrhoids
teach.body:
Internal haemorrhoids are not mere varicosities; they are specialised vascular cushions composed of submucosal arteriovenous plexuses and smooth muscle fibers (Treitz muscle).

The superior rectal artery divides into a right and left branch. The right branch divides into anterior (11 o'clock) and posterior (7 o'clock) branches, while the left branch continues undivided (3 o'clock), dictating the three classical sites.

skill.annex.surg.haemorrhoid_grading.title: Classification of haemorrhoids and rectal prolapse
skill.annex.surg.haemorrhoid_grading.oneLine: Banov grading of internal haemorrhoids and distinction from full-thickness rectal prolapse
skill.annex.surg.haemorrhoid_grading.why: Treatment of haemorrhoids is determined entirely by clinical grade, from dietary fiber and banding for early grades to surgical excision for advanced prolapse. Misclassifying grade three or four haemorrhoids as grade one results in ineffective medical management.
skill.annex.surg.haemorrhoid_grading.practice: Review clinical photographs of internal haemorrhoids and assign the correct grade (1 to 4) according to degree of prolapse and reducibility.
pitfalls: Grading haemorrhoids based on bleeding severity rather than degree of anatomical prolapse.
Confusing third-degree haemorrhoids with fourth-degree haemorrhoids by not attempting manual digital reduction.
Misidentifying full-thickness rectal prolapse with circular folds as circumferential fourth-degree haemorrhoids.

probes.q: What defines a second-degree internal haemorrhoid?
probes.a: It prolapses through the anal canal during defecation but reduces spontaneously.

probes.q: What is the key difference between third-degree and fourth-degree internal haemorrhoids?
probes.a: Third-degree haemorrhoids prolapse and require manual digital reduction, whereas fourth-degree haemorrhoids are permanently prolapsed and cannot be reduced.

probes.q: What are the components of an external haemorrhoid versus an internal haemorrhoid?
probes.a: Internal haemorrhoids arise above the dentate line, covered by insensitive columnar epithelium and draining to the portal system; external haemorrhoids arise below the dentate line, covered by sensitive squamous anoderm and draining to the systemic system.

rubric.text: Defines first-degree internal haemorrhoids (bleed, no prolapse)
Distinguishes second-degree (spontaneous reduction) from third-degree (manual reduction)
Defines fourth-degree internal haemorrhoids (permanently prolapsed, irreducible)
Differentiates mucosal prolapse from full-thickness rectal procidentia

teach.heading: The four degrees of internal haemorrhoids (Banov classification)

rows: Bleed without prolapse outside the anal canal
Prolapse on straining, require manual reduction
All layers of the rectal wall
Sulcus felt between anal verge and mass
No sulcus if everted, or deep peritoneal pouch

skill.hx.surg.urinary_symptoms.title: Surgical urinary history
skill.hx.surg.urinary_symptoms.oneLine: Differentiate storage from voiding symptoms, renal colic from bladder pain, and timing of haematuria
skill.hx.surg.urinary_symptoms.why: Lower urinary tract symptoms and haematuria are cardinal presentations of benign prostatic hyperplasia, stricture, calculi, and urothelial malignancy. Dissecting obstructive (voiding) from irritative (storage) symptoms localises pathology, while macroscopic painless haematuria is urinary malignancy until proven otherwise.

asks.text: Do you have trouble starting urination (hesitancy), or do you need to strain? Is your stream weak, thinned, or interrupted (intermittency), and do you dribble at the end?
How often do you pass urine during the day, and how many times do you wake up at night to void (nocturia)? Do you experience sudden compelling urges to void that are difficult to defer (urgency)?
Do you leak urine: on coughing or laughing (stress incontinence), when rushing to the toilet (urge incontinence), or continuously without awareness (true or overflow incontinence)?
Have you noticed blood in the urine (haematuria)? Does it appear at the start of urination, at the very end, or is the entire stream uniformly coloured? Have you passed blood clots?
Where is the pain located: a dull persistent ache in the loin, severe spasmodic colic shooting from loin to groin or testis, or suprapubic strangury?
Have you experienced fever with rigors, previous urinary tract infections, stone passage, or previous urethral catheterisation or instrumentation?

skill.hx.surg.urinary_symptoms.practice: Take a structured urinary history from a simulated elderly male patient and calculate his preliminary IPSS score while screening for red-flag malignancy features.
pitfalls: Dismissing painless visible haematuria as a urinary tract infection without pursuing urgent urological investigation.
Confusing overflow incontinence with simple urge incontinence in a patient with a silent, chronic distended bladder.
Failing to ask about nocturnal frequency and daytime frequency as separate distinct quantities.

probes.q: What does painless visible haematuria throughout micturition (total haematuria) suggest in an older adult?
probes.a: Urothelial malignancy of the urinary bladder or upper tract until proven otherwise.

probes.q: Where does ureteric colic characteristically radiate?
probes.a: From the loin or flank down to the groin, scrotum, testis, or labium majus along the distribution of the genitofemoral and ilioinguinal nerves (T11 to L1).

probes.q: What is paradoxical or overflow incontinence and why is it dangerous?
probes.a: Involuntary dribbling of urine from an over-distended, chronically decompensated bladder; it is dangerous because back-pressure leads to silent bilateral hydronephrosis and progressive renal failure.

rubric.text: Separates voiding symptoms (hesitancy, stream, dribbling) from storage symptoms (frequency, nocturia, urgency)
Characterises haematuria: initial, terminal, or total, painless or painful, with clots
Clarifies loin-to-groin colic vs dull renal ache vs suprapubic strangury
Distinguishes stress, urge, and overflow incontinence

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Voiding versus storage lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
teach.body:
Lower urinary tract symptoms divide into voiding and storage categories. Voiding symptoms reflect mechanical or functional outlet obstruction, most commonly benign prostatic hyperplasia or urethral stricture.

Storage symptoms reflect bladder instability, irritation, or reduced functional capacity due to cystitis, stones, carcinoma, or secondary detrusor hypertrophy from long-standing bladder outlet obstruction.

rows: Beginning of stream only, clears midstream
End of micturition, often with straining

skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.title: Bimanual palpation and ballottement of the kidney
skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.oneLine: Palpate bimanually in the loin and ballot between anterior and posterior hands
skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.why: The kidney is a retroperitoneal organ that cannot be reliably felt with one hand alone. Bimanual palpation and ballottement distinguish a renal mass from an enlarged spleen, gallbladder, or liver, establishing its retroperitoneal attachment.

steps.text: Position the patient supine with knees semi-flexed and abdomen relaxed.
Stand on the patient's right side; expose the abdomen from xiphisternum to groins.
To examine the right kidney: place your left hand posteriorly in the right loin below the 12th rib, lateral to the sacrospinalis muscle.
Place your right hand anteriorly flat on the right lumbar region, lateral to the rectus abdominis.
Ask the patient to take a slow, deep breath in through the mouth.
As the patient inspires, lift gently with your posterior hand and press firmly inward and upward with your anterior hand to capture the descending kidney pole between your hands.
Assess size, surface, contour, consistency, and tenderness of the captured mass.
Test ballottement: with the anterior hand resting lightly, flex the fingers of your posterior hand briskly to bounce the kidney forward against the anterior examining hand.
Repeat for the left kidney: reach your left hand across the patient to support the left loin, or move to the left side.
Percuss anteriorly over the mass to demonstrate the overlying band of colonic resonance.

skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.normal: Normal kidneys are usually not palpable in muscular adults, though the lower pole of the right kidney may be palpable in thin individuals during deep inspiration; ballottement negative; no tenderness.
skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.abnormal: Enlarged bimanually palpable mass that moves downward on inspiration and is ballottable between anterior and posterior hands; band of colonic resonance on percussion.
skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.significance: Ballottement confirms a retroperitoneal organ. Resonance over the mass differentiates an enlarged kidney from an enlarged spleen or liver, which are dull to percussion and displace bowel away from the anterior surface.
skill.exam.surg.kidney_palpation.practice: Perform bimanual palpation and ballottement on a clinical partner or abdominal simulator, practicing coordinating posterior lifting with deep inspiration.
pitfalls: Attempting to palpate the kidney using only an anterior hand without supporting and lifting the loin posteriorly.
Confusing an enlarged left kidney with an enlarged spleen; failing to percuss for the band of colonic resonance.
Jabbing with fingertips rather than pressing with the flat pulp of the fingers, causing abdominal wall guarding.

probes.q: What physical sign distinguishes an enlarged left kidney from an enlarged spleen on percussion?
probes.a: An enlarged kidney has a band of colonic resonance across its anterior surface, whereas an enlarged spleen is uniformly dull to percussion.

probes.q: What is the physical mechanism of renal ballottement?
probes.a: A mass in the retroperitoneal loin can be bounced between the anterior and posterior examining hands because it is situated in a fluid-cushioned retroperitoneal space with anteroposterior mobility.

probes.q: Name three physical examination differences between an enlarged kidney and an enlarged spleen.
probes.a: The kidney is ballottable, has no notch, has colonic resonance in front, does not cross the midline, and you can get above its upper pole; the spleen is not ballottable, has a palpable notch on its anterior border, is dull to percussion, moves toward the right iliac fossa, and you cannot get above it.

rubric.text: Places posterior hand in renal angle and anterior hand flat on lumbar region
Coordinates palpation with patient taking slow deep inspiration
Demonstrates brisk posterior hand flick to ballot kidney forward
Percusses across anterior surface to confirm colonic resonance

teach.heading: Bimanual technique and ballottement mechanics
teach.body:
Because the kidney lies deep in the retroperitoneum against the quadratus lumborum, palpation requires two hands working in tandem. The posterior hand lifts the renal angle forward while the anterior hand depresses the abdominal wall below the costal margin.

On deep inspiration, the diaphragm pushes the kidney down by up to 3 to 5 centimetres, allowing its lower pole to be captured between the examining hands.

rows: Ballottable between loin and anterior hand
Sharp with a characteristic splenic notch
Can usually get fingers between rib margin and mass

skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.title: Examination of the distended urinary bladder
skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.oneLine: Palpate a cystic midline dome rising from the pelvis and confirm dullness to percussion
skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.why: A full urinary bladder is the commonest lower abdominal mass in clinical surgery. Failing to recognise urinary retention before abdominal paracentesis or misdiagnosing it as an ovarian cyst leads to catastrophic accidental trocar puncture of the bladder.

steps.text: Expose the abdomen from the xiphisternum down to the symphysis pubis.
Inspect the hypogastric region from the side and foot of the bed for a visible rounded dome rising above the pubic symphysis.
Warm hands and palpate gently from the epigastrium downward toward the pelvis with fingers flat.
Feel for the upper border of a smooth, tense, ovoid or globular midline swelling.
Confirm that you cannot get below the lower border of the mass because it emerges from behind the pubic symphysis.
Test for tenderness: marked tenderness is present in acute retention, whereas the mass is non-tender in chronic painless retention.
Percuss downward from the resonant umbilical area toward the pelvis: note the transition from tympanitic bowel resonance to sharp dullness at the bladder dome.
Map the lateral and superior margins of percussion dullness (convex upward).
In acute retention or chronic retention, catheterise or verify post-void disappearance of the mass.

skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.normal: Empty bladder is an entirely pelvic organ, neither visible, palpable, nor dull to percussion above the pubic symphysis.
skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.abnormal: Smooth, symmetrical, cystic, rounded midline hypogastric mass arising out of the pelvis; cannot get below it; dull to percussion; exquisitely tender in acute retention, painless in chronic retention.
skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.significance: Acute retention requires urgent catheter decompression. Chronic high-pressure retention carries a high risk of obstructive uropathy, hydronephrosis, and post-obstructive diuresis following decompression.
skill.exam.surg.distended_bladder.practice: Map out bladder margins on a distended bladder trainer, verifying that percussion dullness matches the upper rounded contour of the bladder.
pitfalls: Palpating upward from the pubis rather than downward from the resonant abdomen, missing a large bladder reaching the umbilicus.
Performing an abdominal tap or needle aspiration for suspected ascites without first emptying the bladder.
Mistaking chronic painless retention with overflow incontinence for simple urge incontinence.

probes.q: Why can you not get below the lower border of a distended bladder during palpation?
probes.a: Because the bladder emerges directly from behind the pubic symphysis within the pelvis.

probes.q: How does the clinical presentation of acute urinary retention differ from chronic urinary retention?
probes.a: Acute retention presents with agonizing suprapubic pain, extreme urge to void, and an exquisitely tender bladder containing 500 to 800 mL; chronic retention presents with a painless, massively distended bladder (often 1000 to 2000 mL) with overflow incontinence and renal impairment.

probes.q: What complication must you monitor for after relieving long-standing chronic urinary retention by catheterisation?
probes.a: Post-obstructive diuresis, where severe polyuria leads to dehydration, profound electrolyte wasting (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia), and cardiovascular collapse.

rubric.text: Inspects hypogastrium for smooth visible dome arising above symphysis
Palpates from resonant upper abdomen downward toward the pubis
Notes that the examining hand cannot get below the lower border
Demonstrates percussion dullness with an upward convex border

teach.heading: Physical signs of bladder distension
teach.body:
When the bladder contains more than 300 to 400 mL of urine, it rises out of the true pelvis into the hypogastrium. A visible and palpable dome can reach the umbilicus when distended with a litre or more.

Palpation must start high in the epigastrium, walking fingers down until the firm, smooth dome is encountered. The mass is non-mobile and anchored into the pelvis.

rows: Very large (1-2 L), soft or firm, non-tender
None; complete inability to pass urine

skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.title: Examination of the prostate per rectum
skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.oneLine: Assess prostatic size, consistency, symmetry, the median sulcus, and mobility of rectal mucosa
skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.why: Digital rectal examination is the primary clinical modality for detecting prostatic pathology. Distinguishing the smooth, elastic, symmetrical enlargement of BPH from the craggy, stony-hard induration with loss of the median sulcus in adenocarcinoma determines whether a biopsy is needed.

steps.text: Ensure patient understands the procedure, has an empty bladder if possible, and is positioned in the left lateral Sims position.
Lubricate the gloved index finger generously and enter the anal canal gently as the sphincter relaxes.
Advance the finger along the anterior rectal wall to locate the prostate gland.
Sweep the finger across the posterior surface: palpate the right and left lateral lobes.
Assess size: normal prostate is roughly the size of a chestnut (about 20 g); note if enlargement is mild, moderate, or massive.
Assess consistency: normal prostate is firm and rubbery (like the thenar eminence); note if it is soft, boggy, elastic, or stony hard (like the knuckles).
Feel for the median sulcus (vertical groove between the lateral lobes) to see if it is preserved, deepened, or completely obliterated.
Assess surface texture: note whether it is smooth, uniformly enlarged, or nodular.
Assess mobility of the overlying rectal mucosa: gently move the rectal mucosa over the gland; tethering suggests extracapsular malignant invasion.
Sweep above the upper border if reachable, feeling for indurated seminal vesicles or a pelvic shelf.

skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.normal: Prostate is heart-shaped, smooth, firm and rubbery in consistency, symmetrical, with a clearly palpable median vertical sulcus; non-tender; rectal mucosa moves freely over it; upper border reachable.
skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.abnormal: Symmetrically enlarged, smooth, elastic prostate with preserved median sulcus (BPH); or stony-hard, asymmetrical, nodular prostate with obliterated median sulcus and fixed rectal mucosa (carcinoma); or exquisitely tender, hot, boggy prostate (acute prostatitis).
skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.significance: Differentiates benign prostatic hyperplasia from carcinoma of the prostate and acute prostatitis. In acute prostatitis, vigorous prostatic massage is contraindicated because it can precipitate septicaemia.
skill.exam.surg.prostate_dre.practice: Palpate graded prostate models in a simulator, distinguishing normal, benign enlargement, and solitary or craggy malignant nodules.
pitfalls: Performing vigorous palpation or massage in a patient with suspected acute prostatitis, which can induce gram-negative bacteraemia.
Assuming a normal DRE excludes prostate cancer; anterior and central tumours cannot be felt by the rectal finger.
Mistaking prostatic calcification or phleboliths for malignancy without checking PSA and imaging.

probes.q: What does the normal prostate gland feel like on digital rectal examination?
probes.a: Firm and rubbery with a smooth surface, two symmetrical lateral lobes, and a distinct median vertical sulcus.

probes.q: What three features on digital rectal examination strongly suggest carcinoma of the prostate?
probes.a: Stony-hard consistency, irregular or nodular surface, and obliteration of the median sulcus with loss of mucosal mobility.

probes.q: Why is vigorous digital palpation strictly contraindicated if acute prostatitis is suspected?
probes.a: Because pressure on an acutely inflamed, infected prostate causes extreme pain and can force bacteria into the bloodstream, triggering severe urosepsis and bacteraemia.

rubric.text: Palpates both lateral lobes along the anterior rectal wall
Evaluates preservation or obliteration of the median sulcus
Assesses consistency (rubbery vs stony hard) and surface (smooth vs nodular)
Tests mobility of the overlying anterior rectal mucosa

teach.heading: Palpatory anatomy of the prostate gland
teach.body:
On DRE, only the posterior and posterolateral aspects of the lateral lobes are accessible. The anterior fibromuscular stroma and transition zone are positioned away from the examining finger.

Because benign hyperplasia originates primarily in the transition zone, extensive enlargement can occur with relatively modest rectal protrusion. Prostatic adenocarcinoma arises mainly in the peripheral zone (70%), directly under the examining finger.

teach.heading: Benign versus malignant prostate on palpation

rows: Fixed or puckered if locally advanced

skill.ix.surg.three_glass_test.title: Three-glass urine test
skill.ix.surg.three_glass_test.oneLine: Fractionate voided urine into three glasses to localise urethral, bladder, and prostatic hematuria or pyuria
skill.ix.surg.three_glass_test.why: The three-glass test is a classic bedside physical investigation that localises the anatomical origin of blood or pus in the lower urinary tract without invasive instrumentation.
skill.ix.surg.three_glass_test.practice: Perform fractional collection on a patient with visible urinary discharge or haematuria, recording turbidity and sediment across the three specimen containers.
pitfalls: Failing to instruct the patient to retain a full bladder before starting the test.
Allowing the patient to stop voiding between glasses rather than collecting continuously in fractionated aliquots.
Mistaking food dyes (beetroot) or drugs (rifampicin) for true macroscopic haematuria.

probes.q: In the three-glass test, what does blood in the first glass only indicate?
probes.a: A lesion in the anterior urethra, such as urethritis, trauma, or a urethral polyp.

probes.q: What does clear urine in glass 1 and 2, but blood and debris in glass 3 indicate?
probes.a: A lesion in the bladder neck, trigone, or prostate, expressed as the bladder contracts at the end of micturition.

probes.q: If all three glasses contain uniformly blood-stained urine, where is the source of bleeding?
probes.a: The upper urinary tract (kidneys or ureters) or the bladder cavity itself, where blood has thoroughly mixed with stored urine.

rubric.text: Instructs patient to collect urine continuously into three sequential vessels
Interprets first glass (initial 10-15 mL) representing urethral wash-out
Interprets third glass (terminal urine) representing prostatic and trigonal expression
Correlates visual turbidity with sediment microscopy for erythrocytes and pus cells

teach.heading: Principles of the three-glass test
teach.body:
The test fractionates a single continuous act of micturition into three clean glass containers. Glass 1 collects the initial 10 to 15 mL, washing out urethral exudate and blood.

Glass 2 collects the midstream sample (30 to 50 mL), reflecting the contents of the bladder. Glass 3 collects the final 10 mL passed with straining, which expresses secretions from the prostate and bladder neck.

rows: Upper urinary tract (kidneys, ureters) or bladder

skill.annex.surg.ipss_prostate.title: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)
skill.annex.surg.ipss_prostate.oneLine: Standardised scoring of seven urinary symptoms plus quality-of-life assessment
skill.annex.surg.ipss_prostate.why: The IPSS objectifies subjective urinary complaints, stratifying lower urinary tract obstruction into mild, moderate, and severe categories to direct medical versus surgical intervention.
skill.annex.surg.ipss_prostate.practice: Administer the IPSS questionnaire to an elderly male patient, calculate the total score out of 35, and assign the severity category.
pitfalls: Calculating IPSS while the patient has an active urinary tract infection or indwelling catheter.
Omitting the eighth Quality of Life question, which gauges subjective bother.
Using the score as a diagnostic test for prostate cancer; IPSS grades symptoms, not malignancy.

probes.q: What are the score ranges for mild, moderate, and severe lower urinary tract symptoms on the IPSS scale?
probes.a: Mild: 0 to 7; Moderate: 8 to 19; Severe: 20 to 35.

probes.q: Name four of the seven symptom questions evaluated in the IPSS questionnaire.
probes.a: Incomplete emptying, frequency, intermittency, urgency, weak stream, straining, and nocturia.

probes.q: What is the role of the eighth question (Quality of Life question) in the IPSS?
probes.a: It assesses the bother score ('If you were to spend the rest of your life with your urinary condition just the way it is now, how would you feel?'), scored 0 (delighted) to 6 (terrible), which often drives the decision to operate.

rubric.text: Lists the seven IPSS symptom questions scored 0 to 5
Correctly classifies total score: mild (0-7), moderate (8-19), severe (20-35)
Includes the separate 0-6 Quality of Life bother score

teach.heading: The seven components of the IPSS
teach.body:
Each question asks how often a symptom occurred over the past month, scored 0 (not at all), 1 (less than 1 in 5 times), 2 (less than half the time), 3 (about half the time), 4 (more than half the time), to 5 (almost always).

The seven items comprise four voiding symptoms (incomplete emptying, intermittency, weak stream, straining) and three storage symptoms (frequency, urgency, nocturia).

rows: Watchful waiting, lifestyle modification, fluid management
Ranges from delighted (0), pleased, mostly satisfied, mixed, mostly dissatisfied, unhappy, to terrible (6)

skill.hx.surg.groin_hernia.title: Groin hernia history
skill.hx.surg.groin_hernia.oneLine: Duration, reducible bulge, dragging discomfort, and precipitating causes of raised intra-abdominal pressure
skill.hx.surg.groin_hernia.why: A groin hernia history establishes whether the hernia is reducible or complicated, and identifies underlying chronic cough, bladder outlet obstruction, or constipation that must be treated before surgical repair to prevent recurrence.

asks.text: When did you first notice the swelling in the groin, and does it enlarge when you stand, walk, lift heavy weights, or cough?
Does the swelling disappear spontaneously when you lie flat, or do you have to push it back yourself (reducibility)?
Do you feel an aching or dragging sensation in the groin, or has there been sudden, severe agonizing pain in the swelling?
Have you ever experienced sudden irreducibility accompanied by nausea, colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, or failure to pass flatus or stool (obstipation)?
Do you suffer from a chronic cough, difficulty or straining during urination, chronic constipation, or heavy occupational manual lifting?
Have you had prior hernia repairs (recurrent hernia) or abdominal operations such as appendicectomy in the right iliac fossa?

skill.hx.surg.groin_hernia.practice: Take a focused groin hernia history, systematically checking for all five major causes of chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure.
pitfalls: Operating on a hernia without identifying and treating severe benign prostatic obstruction or chronic bronchitis, guaranteeing early recurrence.
Failing to ask about sudden irreducibility and vomiting, missing an acutely incarcerated or strangulated hernia.
Assuming a painless groin swelling cannot be a hernia.

probes.q: Why must you ask a patient with a hernia about urinary straining and chronic cough?
probes.a: Because chronic straining from BPH or chronic cough raises intra-abdominal pressure, causing the hernia and causing high recurrence rates if not addressed.

probes.q: What symptom triad indicates that a hernia has become obstructed or strangulated?
probes.a: Sudden severe pain in the swelling, irreducibility, and features of bowel obstruction (vomiting, abdominal distension, absolute constipation).

probes.q: Why does an appendicectomy scar in the right iliac fossa predispose to a right-sided direct inguinal hernia?
probes.a: A low appendicectomy incision can injure the iliohypogastric nerve, paralyzing the conjoint tendon and weakening the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

rubric.text: Asks about onset, posture-related appearance, and reducibility
Screens for red flags: severe pain, irreducibility, vomiting, obstipation
Systematically checks cough, urinary straining, constipation, and occupational lifting
Inquires about previous hernia repairs and abdominal incisions

teach.heading: The clinical presentation of an uncomplicated groin hernia
teach.body:
Most patients present with a groin swelling that appears when standing, walking, or straining and vanishes when lying supine. The patient often describes an aching or dragging sensation that worsens toward the end of the day.

Sharp, severe pain is not a feature of an uncomplicated hernia; severe pain implies acute distension, incarceration, or vascular compromise of strangulation.

teach.heading: Precipitating factors for raised intra-abdominal pressure

rows: Repeated sudden spikes in intra-abdominal pressure
Straining to empty bladder against outlet resistance
Chronic muscular straining and fascial stretching

skill.exam.surg.hernia_inspection.title: Inspection of a groin hernia
skill.exam.surg.hernia_inspection.oneLine: Inspect standing and supine for site, pyriform versus globular shape, and visible cough impulse
skill.exam.surg.hernia_inspection.why: A small hernia that is completely invisible when the patient is lying supine becomes immediately prominent on standing. Inspection establishes the precise anatomical location and differentiates an indirect bubonocele from a direct bulge.

steps.text: Expose the patient from the lower abdomen to mid-thighs with the patient in the STANDING position.
Stand or sit in front of the patient with eyes at the level of the patient's groin.
Inspect both groins simultaneously to detect asymmetry.
Identify the site: determine whether the swelling is centered above and medial to the pubic tubercle (inguinal) or below and lateral (femoral).
Note the shape: an indirect hernia is typically pyriform (pear-shaped) or oblong along the inguinal canal, whereas a direct hernia is typically hemispherical or globular.
Observe the extent: note if the swelling remains in the groin (bubonocele), extends to the external ring (funicular), or descends into the scrotum (complete scrotal hernia).
Ask the patient to turn their head away and cough firmly: observe for a visible expansile impulse over the swelling.
Ask the patient to lie flat on the examination couch and observe whether the swelling disappears spontaneously.
Inspect the contralateral groin and note any divarication of recti (Malgaigne bulgings).

skill.exam.surg.hernia_inspection.normal: Groins are symmetrical without visible bulges standing or on coughing; external rings not prominent; scrotum normal.
skill.exam.surg.hernia_inspection.abnormal: Visible pyriform swelling emerging through the inguinal canal and descending toward the scrotum, or hemispherical bulge in Hesselbach triangle; expansile impulse on coughing; disappears or reduces supine.
skill.exam.surg.hernia_inspection.significance: A pyriform swelling descending into the scrotum is almost always an indirect inguinal hernia. A globular bulge that does not enter the scrotum and appears directly forward is usually direct.
skill.exam.surg.hernia_inspection.practice: Inspect simulated groin swellings in standing and supine positions, correctly documenting site, shape, extent, and visible cough impulse.
pitfalls: Examining the patient only in the supine position, which causes a reducible hernia to vanish completely.
Failing to ask the patient to turn their head when coughing, risking droplet contamination.
Overlooking the contralateral groin, missing a bilateral hernia in up to twenty percent of patients.

probes.q: Why must a groin hernia always be inspected with the patient standing?
probes.a: Because gravity and intra-abdominal pressure cause a reducible hernia to emerge, whereas it often reduces and disappears when lying flat.

probes.q: What does an expansile impulse on coughing mean on inspection?
probes.a: It means that on coughing, the swelling visibly expands in all dimensions (expansile), not merely being pushed forward by abdominal wall muscles.

probes.q: What morphological shape suggests an indirect versus a direct inguinal hernia on inspection?
probes.a: An indirect hernia is pyriform (pear-shaped) or elliptical along the direction of the canal; a direct hernia is hemispherical or globular, protruding directly forward.

rubric.text: Examines patient in the standing position before lying down
Compares both groins simultaneously for asymmetry
Notes shape (pyriform vs globular) and extent (groin vs scrotum)
Asks patient to turn head and cough to look for visible expansile impulse

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Hernias, umbilicus and abdominal wall: clinical examination

teach.heading: Standing inspection and the cough impulse
teach.body:
Examination of a hernia begins with the patient standing upright. Gravity and the upright posture encourage peritoneal contents to descend through the fascial defect.

When the patient coughs, increased intra-abdominal pressure forces additional viscus into the sac. The resulting expansion is expansile, blowing up like a balloon rather than simply being displaced forward.

teach.heading: Morphological stages of indirect inguinal hernia

rows: Small bulge visible only on coughing above inguinal ligament
Extends through superficial ring to scrotal neck
Oblong swelling reaching upper border of testis
Descends fully into the fundus of the scrotum
Large pyriform swelling surrounding or obscuring the testis

skill.exam.surg.hernia_palpation.title: Palpation of a hernia and test of reducibility
skill.exam.surg.hernia_palpation.oneLine: Confirm you cannot get above the swelling, feel for an expansile cough impulse, and perform gentle taxis
skill.exam.surg.hernia_palpation.why: Palpation confirms whether a swelling arises from the abdomen (cannot get above it) or is confined to the scrotum (can get above it), and determines whether its contents are bowel (enterocele) or omentum (omentocele).

steps.text: Ensure the patient is comfortable; warm hands.
Test whether you can get above the swelling: place thumb and index finger at the root of the scrotum above the mass; if fingers cannot pinch the cord above the swelling, it emerges from the abdomen.
Assess consistency: smooth, elastic, and soft in an enterocele; granular, firm, and doughy in an omentocele.
Test for palpable expansile cough impulse: place the flat of the fingers over the swelling, have the patient turn their head and cough, and feel for expansion under your fingers.
Test reducibility (taxis): ask the patient if they can reduce the lump themselves, or have them lie supine.
If manual reduction is needed: support the fundus with one hand while the other hand guides the neck at the superficial ring; apply gentle, sustained pressure along the line of the canal.

Observe the mode of reduction: an enterocele reduces with difficulty initially, then slips back suddenly with a gurgle; an omentocele reduces easily at first, with the last portion doughy and difficult.
Percuss the swelling: tympanitic note confirms gas-filled bowel; dull note indicates omentum or fluid.
Auscultate over the swelling for bowel sounds (borborygmi).
Palpate the testis after reduction to confirm its presence, size, and normal position.

skill.exam.surg.hernia_palpation.normal: No mass in groin or scrotum; spermatic cord can be pinched clearly above the testis without thickening.
skill.exam.surg.hernia_palpation.abnormal: Cannot get above the mass; palpable expansile cough impulse; reducible with an audible or palpable gurgle (enterocele); or doughy reduction without gurgle (omentocele); tender and tense if strangulated.
skill.exam.surg.hernia_palpation.significance: Inability to get above the swelling definitively confirms an inguinoscrotal mass emerges from the abdomen. The gurgle on reduction confirms intestinal contents.
skill.exam.surg.hernia_palpation.practice: Demonstrate gentle reduction (taxis) on a hernia model, articulating the difference in feel between an enterocele and an omentocele.
pitfalls: Attempting forceful taxis on an exquisitely tender, irreducible, red swelling, risking rupture of gangrenous bowel into the peritoneal cavity.
Failing to check if you can get above the swelling, confusing a large hydrocele with a scrotal hernia.
Forgetting to palpate the testis once the hernia is reduced.

probes.q: What does the sign 'cannot get above the swelling' mean in a groin mass?
probes.a: It means the fingers cannot meet above the mass at the scrotal neck, proving the swelling arises from or extends into the abdominal cavity.

probes.q: How does the reduction of an enterocele differ from that of an omentocele?
probes.a: An enterocele is difficult to reduce at first and then slips back suddenly with an audible gurgle, whereas an omentocele reduces easily at first and its final part is doughy and difficult.

probes.q: Why is forceful reduction (taxis) strictly contraindicated in a strangulated hernia?
probes.a: Because forcing strangulated, ischaemic bowel back can rupture the necrotic wall, cause reduction en masse, or introduce infected gangrenous bowel into the peritoneal cavity causing fatal peritonitis.

rubric.text: Attempts to get above the swelling at the root of the scrotum
Palpates for an expansile cough impulse with flat hand
Tests reducibility gently along the direction of the canal
Distinguishes enterocele (gurgle, elastic) from omentocele (doughy, dull)

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Hernias, umbilicus and abdominal wall: clinical signs

teach.heading: Getting above the swelling: the cornerstone sign
teach.body:
To test if you can get above the swelling, grasp the neck of the scrotum between your thumb in front and index finger behind, above the upper limit of the mass.

In a pure scrotal swelling (such as a vaginal hydrocele), your fingers meet clearly across the normal spermatic cord above the mass. In a hernia or infantile hydrocele, the mass extends upward through the external ring, and you cannot get above it.

rows: Difficult at first, slips back with a gurgle
Easy at first, last part doughy and difficult

skill.exam.surg.deep_ring_occlusion.title: Deep ring occlusion test
skill.exam.surg.deep_ring_occlusion.oneLine: Occlude the internal inguinal ring to distinguish indirect from direct inguinal hernia
skill.exam.surg.deep_ring_occlusion.why: Surface marking and occluding the deep inguinal ring is the definitive clinical manoeuvre separating an indirect inguinal hernia from a direct inguinal hernia and a femoral hernia.

steps.text: With the patient lying supine, reduce the hernia completely.
Identify the surface landmarks: Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS) and Pubic Symphysis.
Determine the midinguinal point: midway between the ASIS and pubic symphysis (not the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, which is midway between ASIS and pubic tubercle).
Locate the deep inguinal ring: approximately 1.25 cm (half an inch) above the midinguinal point.
Firmly occlude the deep ring with the thumb of your hand (right thumb for right groin, left thumb for left groin).
Ask the patient to stand up, or have the patient turn their head and cough vigorously while you maintain firm thumb pressure over the deep ring.
Observe the groin: if the hernia is CONTROLLED and does NOT appear, it is an INDIRECT inguinal hernia.
If the hernia ESCAPES and bulges forward medial to your occluding thumb (through Hesselbach triangle), it is a DIRECT inguinal hernia.
Release your thumb: in an indirect hernia, the mass will suddenly emerge and shoot down along the canal into the scrotum.
Confirm relation to pubic tubercle: inguinal hernia neck is above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernia is below and lateral.

skill.exam.surg.deep_ring_occlusion.normal: Deep ring easily covered; no bulge appears with or without occlusion on coughing.
skill.exam.surg.deep_ring_occlusion.abnormal: Indirect hernia: controlled completely by deep ring occlusion. Direct hernia: bulges forward medial to the occluding thumb despite deep ring occlusion.
skill.exam.surg.deep_ring_occlusion.significance: Indirect hernia passes through the deep ring down the canal; direct hernia bulges through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. An indirect hernia has a higher risk of strangulation.
skill.exam.surg.deep_ring_occlusion.practice: Mark the deep ring on a colleague or anatomical model (1.25 cm above the midinguinal point) and perform the occlusion test.
pitfalls: Confusing the midinguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis) with the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (midway between ASIS and pubic tubercle).
Failing to reduce the hernia completely before applying thumb occlusion.
Applying too little pressure, allowing an indirect hernia to slip under the thumb and falsely diagnosing a direct hernia.

probes.q: Where is the deep inguinal ring located anatomically on the abdominal wall surface?
probes.a: 1.25 cm (half an inch) above the midinguinal point (the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis).

probes.q: What is the clinical finding in the deep ring occlusion test for a direct inguinal hernia?
probes.a: The hernia is not controlled by occlusion of the deep ring; it bulges forward medial to the occluding thumb through Hesselbach's triangle.

probes.q: How does the anatomical relationship to the pubic tubercle distinguish an inguinal hernia from a femoral hernia?
probes.a: The neck of an inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle, whereas the neck of a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

rubric.text: Accurately locates deep ring 1.25 cm above the midinguinal point
Ensures complete reduction of hernia before applying occlusion
Maintains firm thumb pressure while patient coughs or stands
Correctly identifies controlled = indirect, medial escape = direct
Checks relation to pubic tubercle (above/medial vs below/lateral)

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Hernias, umbilicus and abdominal wall: internal ring test

teach.heading: Surface anatomy of the deep inguinal ring
teach.body:
Accurate landmark identification is vital. Locate the Anterior Superior Iliac Spine and the Pubic Symphysis. The point midway between them is the midinguinal point, under which lies the external iliac / femoral artery.

The deep ring is a U-shaped condensation in the transversalis fascia located 1.25 cm above this point. Occluding this site closes the internal entrance to the inguinal canal.

rows: Sac originates lateral to inferior epigastric vessels through deep ring
Sac pushes directly through Hesselbach triangle medial to epigastric vessels
Sac emerges through the femoral canal below and lateral to pubic tubercle

skill.exam.surg.invagination_three_finge.title: Finger invagination test and Zieman three-finger test
skill.exam.surg.invagination_three_finge.oneLine: Invaginate the scrotum to feel the external ring and perform Zieman three-finger assessment
skill.exam.surg.invagination_three_finge.why: Finger invagination allows assessment of the superficial inguinal ring, its size, and the direction of impulse. The Zieman three-finger test tests all three groin hernia orifices simultaneously.

steps.text: With the patient standing, stand or sit on the side being examined.
Place the right little finger (or index finger in an adult with a lax ring) against the lower scrotum on the affected side.
Invaginate the scrotal skin upward along the spermatic cord toward the pubic tubercle to locate the superficial inguinal ring.
Rotate the examining finger so the pulp faces posteriorly toward the posterior wall of the canal and the fingertip points toward the deep ring.
Ask the patient to turn their head and cough firmly.

Assess the impulse: an impulse felt on the TIP of the finger coming down the canal indicates an INDIRECT hernia; an impulse pushing against the PULP of the finger from behind indicates a DIRECT hernia.
To perform the Zieman three-finger test: reduce the hernia and stand on the patient's right side.
Place the INDEX finger of your right hand over the deep ring (1.25 cm above midinguinal point).
Place the MIDDLE finger over the superficial ring (above and medial to pubic tubercle).
Place the RING finger over the saphenous opening / femoral canal (below and lateral to pubic tubercle).
Ask the patient to cough: impulse on index finger = indirect hernia; middle finger = direct hernia; ring finger = femoral hernia.

skill.exam.surg.invagination_three_finge.normal: Superficial ring admits only the tip of the little finger; no impulse on coughing; posterior wall feels firm and resistant.
skill.exam.surg.invagination_three_finge.abnormal: Dilated superficial ring; impulse felt on fingertip (indirect) or on pulp (direct); or impulse under ring finger (femoral).
skill.exam.surg.invagination_three_finge.significance: Distinguishes indirect from direct and femoral hernias; assesses weakness of the posterior wall (conjoint tendon).
skill.exam.surg.invagination_three_finge.practice: Perform the Zieman three-finger placement, identifying the exact anatomical structure under index, middle, and ring fingers.
pitfalls: Pushing the finger into the external ring aggressively, causing acute pain from cord compression.
Invaginating the skin from too high up on the scrotum, running out of mobile skin before reaching the ring.
Performing finger invagination in children or female patients, where it is inappropriate and painful.

probes.q: In the finger invagination test, how do you distinguish an indirect from a direct hernia by the feel of the impulse?
probes.a: An indirect hernia hits the tip of the examining finger; a direct hernia pushes against the pulp of the finger from the posterior wall.

probes.q: Which three anatomical structures are covered by the three fingers in the Zieman test?
probes.a: Index finger covers the deep inguinal ring; middle finger covers the superficial inguinal ring; ring finger covers the saphenous opening or femoral ring.

probes.q: Why is the finger invagination test strictly avoided in children and females?
probes.a: In children, the canal is very short, the ring is tiny, and invagination causes severe pain and trauma; in females, the lack of mobile scrotal skin and presence of the round ligament make it technically impossible and painful.

rubric.text: Invaginates mobile lower scrotal skin along the cord toward the external ring
Rotates finger so pulp faces posteriorly against the posterior wall
Correctly identifies fingertip impulse = indirect, finger pulp impulse = direct
Correctly places three fingers over deep ring, superficial ring, and femoral canal

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Hernias, umbilicus and abdominal wall: physical examination

teach.heading: The finger invagination technique
teach.body:
Finger invagination uses the loose, mobile skin of the lower scrotum. The little finger is placed at the bottom of the scrotum and pushes skin ahead of it along the spermatic cord.

The finger enters the triangular superficial ring just above and lateral to the pubic crest. When the patient coughs, an indirect hernia descending the canal strikes the fingertip, whereas a direct hernia pushes forward against the pulp.

rows: 1.25 cm above midinguinal point (Deep inguinal ring)
Above and medial to pubic tubercle (Superficial ring)
Below and lateral to pubic tubercle (Fossa ovalis / Femoral canal)

skill.annex.surg.nyhus_hernia.title: Nyhus classification of groin hernias
skill.annex.surg.nyhus_hernia.oneLine: Anatomical classification based on internal ring size, posterior wall integrity, and recurrence
skill.annex.surg.nyhus_hernia.why: The Nyhus classification standardises groin hernia defects to guide surgical repair selection, from simple ring narrowing in infants to posterior wall reconstruction or mesh placement in adults.
skill.annex.surg.nyhus_hernia.practice: Review operative scenarios of groin hernias and classify each into Nyhus Type I, II, III (A, B, C), or IV.
pitfalls: Classifying a femoral hernia as an inguinal hernia subtype rather than Nyhus Type IIIC.
Failing to categorize all recurrent groin hernias as Type IV regardless of previous repair type.
Confusing Type IIIA (direct) with Type IIIB (large indirect with posterior wall defect).

probes.q: What is a Nyhus Type I hernia?
probes.a: An indirect inguinal hernia with a normal internal ring and an intact posterior wall, typically seen in infants and children.

probes.q: How does Nyhus Type IIIA differ from Type IIIB and Type IIIC?
probes.a: Type IIIA is a direct inguinal hernia; Type IIIB is an indirect hernia with a dilated ring and defective posterior wall (or pantaloon hernia); Type IIIC is a femoral hernia.

probes.q: What defines Nyhus Type IV hernias?
probes.a: All recurrent hernias (A: direct recurrent, B: indirect recurrent, C: femoral recurrent, D: combined recurrent).

rubric.text: Defines Type I (normal ring) and Type II (dilated ring, intact wall)
Differentiates Type IIIA (direct), IIIB (indirect with defective wall), and IIIC (femoral)
Classifies Type IV as recurrent hernias

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Hernias, umbilicus and abdominal wall: classification

rows: Normal-sized deep ring, intact posterior wall
Dilated deep ring, intact posterior wall
Dilated deep ring with defective posterior wall
Large scrotal, sliding, or pantaloon hernias
Recurrent direct (A), indirect (B), femoral (C), or mixed (D)

points.d: Requires only high ligation and excision of the sac (herniotomy); the canal wall needs no reinforcement.
Requires herniotomy plus narrowing of the internal ring (Marcy repair) or posterior wall reinforcement.
Require tension-free prosthetic mesh reinforcement (Lichtenstein or laparoscopic TEP/TAPP) because the posterior wall fascia is fundamentally deficient.

skill.exam.surg.varicocele.title: Examination of varicocele
skill.exam.surg.varicocele.oneLine: Palpate the 'bag of worms' standing, note disappearance supine, and perform the refill test
skill.exam.surg.varicocele.why: Varicocele is the commonest treatable cause of male subfertility. Differentiating a primary idiopathic left-sided varicocele from a secondary varicocele caused by a left renal tumor compressing the renal vein is a vital diagnostic skill.

steps.text: Examine the patient in the STANDING position in a warm room to relax dartos muscle.
Inspect the scrotum: observe tortuous, dilated pampiniform venous plexus, typically on the left side; note any scrotal elongation or bluish hue.
Palpate the spermatic cord above the testis between thumb and fingers: feel for the classic sensation of a 'bag of worms' or compressible cords.
Have the patient cough or perform a Valsalva manoeuvre: feel for a thrill or expansile venous impulse (cough impulse in veins).
Ask the patient to lie flat on the examination couch: observe whether the dilated veins collapse and disappear completely (primary varicocele).

Perform the refill test: while supine, gently compress and empty the plexus; occlude the superficial ring with your thumb; ask patient to stand: if veins refill rapidly from above despite occlusion, the valves are incompetent.
Palpate both testes carefully to measure testicular volume (orchidometer) and detect left testicular atrophy.
Always palpate the left loin for a renal mass, especially in a man over forty with a newly diagnosed or non-emptying left varicocele.

skill.exam.surg.varicocele.normal: Pampiniform plexus is soft and barely distinguishable within the normal spermatic cord; no visible or palpable venous distension standing or coughing.
skill.exam.surg.varicocele.abnormal: Dilated, tortuous veins in the left scrotum feeling like a bag of worms; empties supine; thrill on coughing; left testicular softening or atrophy.
skill.exam.surg.varicocele.significance: Primary varicocele is left-sided (90%) and collapses supine. A right-sided varicocele or a left varicocele that fails to collapse when lying flat suggests retroperitoneal venous obstruction (renal cell carcinoma with renal vein thrombosis).
skill.exam.surg.varicocele.practice: Perform the standing versus supine varicocele examination on a model, grading severity from 1 to 3.
pitfalls: Examining only in the supine position, where a moderate varicocele collapses completely and is missed.
Failing to examine the left kidney when a varicocele is found in an older man or when it does not collapse supine.
Overlooking testicular atrophy, which is the primary indication for surgical or radiological varicocelectomy.

probes.q: Why does varicocele occur predominantly on the left side?
probes.a: Because the left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle (90 degrees) with higher pressure and often lacks effective valves, and may be compressed by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon).

probes.q: What does a left-sided varicocele that does NOT collapse when the patient lies supine indicate?
probes.a: Secondary varicocele caused by retroperitoneal venous obstruction, most commonly renal cell carcinoma invading the left renal vein.

probes.q: What are the three clinical grades of varicocele (Dubin-Amelar classification)?
probes.a: Grade 1: palpable only during Valsalva manoeuvre; Grade 2: palpable at rest while standing without Valsalva; Grade 3: visible through the scrotal skin at rest and easily palpable.

rubric.text: Examines patient standing in warm room, inspecting for visible tortuous veins
Palpates spermatic cord for compressible 'bag of worms' sensation
Observes disappearance of varicocele in supine position
Assesses testicular size for atrophy and palpates left loin for renal mass

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: The venous anatomy and clinical presentation of varicocele
teach.body:
Varicocele represents abnormal dilatation, elongation, and tortuosity of the pampiniform venous plexus. Over ninety percent occur on the left side due to anatomical disadvantages: the left vein is longer, joins the renal vein at 90 degrees, and lacks ostial valves.

Patients report a dragging dull ache in the scrotum after prolonged standing or present during evaluation for subfertility.

teach.heading: Dubin and Amelar clinical grading of varicocele

rows: Not felt clinically; detected on Doppler US
Palpable at rest standing without Valsalva
Visible through scrotal skin at rest
Gross tortuous plexus visible and palpable

skill.exam.surg.cord_swelling_traction.title: Examination of spermatic cord swellings and the traction test
skill.exam.surg.cord_swelling_traction.oneLine: Palpate swelling along the spermatic cord and demonstrate movement on downward testicular traction
skill.exam.surg.cord_swelling_traction.why: Encysted hydrocele of the cord and cord lipomas lie in the inguinal canal or upper scrotum and mimic an irreducible hernia. The traction test definitively proves attachment to the spermatic cord and differentiates it from a hernia.

steps.text: Expose the groin and scrotum with the patient standing and supine.
Confirm that you can get above the swelling: pinch the root of the scrotum between your thumb and index finger; in a cord swelling, the fingers can meet above the mass.
Palpate the swelling: note smooth, oval, cystic, non-tender character along the line of the spermatic cord.
Perform the traction test: grasp the body of the testis gently between the fingers of your left hand and pull it downwards toward the floor.
Observe the swelling: downward traction on the testis causes the encysted hydrocele to move downwards and become fixed in position.
Release traction: the cyst moves back up toward the external ring.
Test mobility: move the swelling gently from side to side across the line of the cord (mobile), but note it cannot be moved independently along the longitudinal axis of the cord.
Test transillumination: an encysted hydrocele of the cord transilluminates clearly because it contains clear serous fluid.
Test cough impulse: no true expansile cough impulse (may have an apparent impulse if pushed down by abdominal wall).

skill.exam.surg.cord_swelling_traction.normal: Spermatic cord is uniform, smooth, and slender without localized cystic or solid masses.
skill.exam.surg.cord_swelling_traction.abnormal: Smooth, tense, cystic oval swelling along the cord that moves down and becomes fixed when the testis is pulled downward; transilluminates brilliantly.
skill.exam.surg.cord_swelling_traction.significance: The positive traction test proves the cyst is an encysted hydrocele of the cord (persistent patent funicular process with fluid accumulation), distinguishing it from an irreducible bubonocele or inguinal node.
skill.exam.surg.cord_swelling_traction.practice: Demonstrate the downward testicular traction test on a groin/scrotal simulator, noting fixation of the cord mass.
pitfalls: Mistaking an encysted hydrocele of the cord for an irreducible inguinal hernia and attempting forceful taxis.
Pulling too vigorously on the testis, causing severe visceral pain from testicular traction.
Failing to transilluminate the swelling in a darkened room.

probes.q: What happens to an encysted hydrocele of the cord during the testicular traction test?
probes.a: When the testis is pulled gently downward, the cyst moves downwards and becomes fixed and restricted in mobility.

probes.q: What is the embryological basis of an encysted hydrocele of the cord?
probes.a: Failure of complete obliteration of the funicular process of the tunica vaginalis, leaving an isolated patent segment that fills with peritoneal fluid.

probes.q: How do you distinguish an encysted hydrocele of the cord from a lipoma of the cord?
probes.a: An encysted hydrocele is smooth, cystic, fluctuant, and transilluminates brilliantly, whereas a cord lipoma is soft, lobulated, doughy, and does not transilluminate.

rubric.text: Confirms that examining fingers can get above the swelling in the cord
Pulls testis gently downward to demonstrate downward movement and fixation
Tests side-to-side mobility and transillumination in darkened room

sources.locator: hydrocele: encysted hydrocele of the cord

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: The testes and scrotum: hydrocele of the cord

teach.heading: Embryology and anatomy of cord swellings
teach.body:
During testicular descent, the processus vaginalis obliterates from the deep ring to the upper pole of the testis. If the middle portion remains patent while both ends close, secreted fluid accumulates, forming an encysted hydrocele of the cord.

Because the cyst is enveloped within the layers of the spermatic cord (internal spermatic fascia), it is intimately bound to the vas deferens and testicular vessels.

teach.heading: Differential diagnosis of groin and cord swellings

skill.exam.surg.undescended_testis.title: Examination for undescended and ectopic testis
skill.exam.surg.undescended_testis.oneLine: Palpate the empty hemiscrotum, sweep along the inguinal canal, and elicit testicular sensation
skill.exam.surg.undescended_testis.why: An empty scrotum requires systematic search to distinguish a retractile testis from an undescended (cryptorchid) testis or ectopic testis. Uncorrected cryptorchidism leads to infertility and carries a thirty-fold increased risk of testicular malignancy.

steps.text: Ensure the examination room is warm and the examiner's hands are warm to avoid triggering the cremasteric reflex.
Place the child or patient supine with legs abducted in a frog-leg position.
Inspect the scrotum: note whether the hemiscrotum is hypoplastic, flat, or underdeveloped.
Palpate the scrotum between thumb and index finger to confirm the absence of the testis in the normal scrotal sac.
Place your non-dominant hand flat across the internal inguinal ring (anterior superior iliac spine toward the pubis) to prevent the testis from slipping back into the abdomen.
Gently sweep your right hand along the line of the inguinal canal from the deep ring toward the superficial ring.
Feel for a small, smooth, mobile, ovoid mass popping under your fingers; gentle pressure elicits a characteristic sickening dull testicular sensation.
If a testis is palpated in the canal, gently milk it down toward the scrotum: a retractile testis can be drawn fully to the bottom of the scrotum and stays there until the cremaster is stimulated.
An undescended testis cannot be brought into the scrotum, or snaps back immediately upon release (true cryptorchidism).
If not in the canal, inspect ectopic sites: Denis Browne superficial inguinal pouch, perineum, femoral triangle, and opposite scrotum.

skill.exam.surg.undescended_testis.normal: Both testes present in the dependent scrotum, symmetrical, smooth, firm, with normal testicular sensation.
skill.exam.surg.undescended_testis.abnormal: Empty, hypoplastic hemiscrotum; small ovoid swelling palpated in inguinal canal; cannot be brought to bottom of scrotum (undescended); or located in perineum/thigh (ectopic).
skill.exam.surg.undescended_testis.significance: Distinguishes physiological retractile testis (requires no surgery) from true undescended testis (requires orchidopexy before 12 to 18 months of age to preserve spermatogenesis).
skill.exam.surg.undescended_testis.practice: Demonstrate the two-handed sweeping technique along the inguinal canal on a paediatric pelvic manikin, milking the testis toward the scrotum.
pitfalls: Examining with cold hands or in a cold room, precipitating an exaggerated cremasteric reflex that mimics cryptorchidism.
Failing to check the ectopic sites (Denis Browne superficial pouch, perineum, femoral canal) when the testis is not felt in the canal.
Mistaking an enlarged inguinal lymph node for an undescended testis; failing to elicit the characteristic testicular sensation.

probes.q: What is the key clinical difference between a retractile testis and a true undescended testis?
probes.a: A retractile testis can be brought down fully into the bottom of the scrotum and remains there until the cremasteric reflex is triggered, whereas a true undescended testis cannot be brought into the scrotum or snaps back immediately upon release.

probes.q: What is the most common ectopic site for a testis?
probes.a: Denis Browne superficial inguinal pouch (subcutaneous tissue in front of the external oblique aponeurosis).

probes.q: Why must an undescended testis be surgically brought down into the scrotum (orchidopexy) by 12 to 18 months of age?
probes.a: To prevent progressive irreversible degeneration of spermatogonia (infertility) and to allow clinical surveillance for malignant transformation (seminoma/non-seminoma).

rubric.text: Ensures warm room, warm hands, and relaxed supine frog-leg positioning
Palpates hemiscrotum to confirm absence of testis and notes hypoplasia
Sweeps hand from deep ring to superficial ring along canal to locate testis
Milks testis into scrotum to differentiate retractile from true cryptorchidism
Checks Denis Browne pouch, perineum, and femoral triangle if not in canal

teach.heading: Clinical examination: sweeping the inguinal canal
teach.body:
Because the cremasteric reflex is active in boys, a cold hand or sudden touch triggers reflex contraction, drawing a normal testis into the groin.

Block the deep ring with one hand at the anterior superior spine, preventing retrograde retreat. The other hand sweeps along the canal from lateral to medial, catching the testis against the pubis.

rows: Halted along the normal path of descent
Deviated outside the normal descent path
Superficial inguinal pouch of Denis Browne
Perineum, femoral canal, pubic, opposite scrotum
Usually adequate length once ectopic attachments divided

skill.hx.surg.scrotal_swelling_pain.title: Scrotal swelling and testicular pain history
skill.hx.surg.scrotal_swelling_pain.oneLine: Tempo of onset, traumatic triggers, urinary symptoms, and rapid screening for torsion red flags
skill.hx.surg.scrotal_swelling_pain.why: Acute scrotal pain is a time-critical surgical emergency where testicular torsion must be differentiated from acute epididymo-orchitis within a 6-hour window to avoid ischaemic testicular loss. Insidious painless scrotal swelling demands differentiation of hydrocele from testicular tumour.

asks.text: When exactly did the pain or swelling start, and how many hours have elapsed? Sudden agonizing pain waking the patient from sleep suggests testicular torsion; gradual pain over days suggests epididymo-orchitis.
Does the pain radiate to the lower abdomen or groin, and is it accompanied by nausea or vomiting?
Has the swelling grown slowly over months or years (hydrocele, spermatocele), or has it enlarged rapidly over weeks (testicular tumour)?
Was there any recent scrotal trauma, sexual activity, urethral discharge, burning urination (dysuria), or recent instrumentation?
Have you had fever with chills, or a recent viral illness such as mumps with swelling of the face or parotid glands?
Have you noticed any unintended weight loss, chronic cough, backache, or a prior history of undescended testis?

skill.hx.surg.scrotal_swelling_pain.practice: Take an acute scrotal pain history from a simulated adolescent patient, establishing the exact duration from symptom onset to calculate the ischaemic window.
pitfalls: Assuming acute scrotal pain in an adolescent is epididymo-orchitis without excluding torsion, leading to an infarcted orchiectomy.
Dismissing a history of minor scrotal trauma as the sole cause of swelling, missing an underlying testicular malignancy.
Failing to ask about mumps or urethral discharge in a patient with suspected epididymo-orchitis.

probes.q: What is the critical golden time window within which testicular torsion must be surgically detorted to achieve testicular salvage?
probes.a: Within 6 hours of the onset of pain (salvage rate over 90 percent, dropping to under 20 percent after 12 to 24 hours).

probes.q: A 22-year-old man presents with a painless, rapidly growing firm swelling in the right testis. What diagnosis must be assumed until proven otherwise?
probes.a: Testicular cancer (germ cell tumour: seminoma or non-seminomatous germ cell tumour).

probes.q: What systemic and sexual history questions must you ask in a 25-year-old man presenting with acute epididymo-orchitis?
probes.a: Ask about sexual history, new partners, urethral discharge or dysuria (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae), and recent parotid swelling or fever (mumps orchitis).

rubric.text: Establishes exact onset and hours elapsed to assess ischaemic window
Asks about radiation to groin/iliac fossa and accompanying nausea or vomiting
Inquires about dysuria, urethral discharge, and sexual contacts
Screens for mumps, fever, weight loss, back pain, or haemoptysis

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: The acute scrotum: a surgical race against the clock
teach.body:
Testicular torsion is a true surgical emergency. Twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off venous outflow first, causing immediate engorgement, followed rapidly by arterial occlusion and ischaemia.

Irreversible germ cell death occurs within six hours of complete ischaemia. Immediate exploration is mandated if torsion cannot be definitively excluded.

rows: Months to years, heavy dragging sensation

skill.exam.surg.scrotal_palpation.title: Palpation of scrotal contents
skill.exam.surg.scrotal_palpation.oneLine: Get above the swelling, distinguish testis from epididymis, and test testicular sensation
skill.exam.surg.scrotal_palpation.why: Palpating the scrotum requires meticulous anatomical separation of the testis, epididymis, and spermatic cord. Determining whether a mass is testicular (often malignant) or epididymal (usually benign) dictates whether inguinal exploration or conservative treatment is warranted.

steps.text: Ensure the patient is in the standing position, then confirm findings supine.
Get above the swelling: grasp the spermatic cord at the neck of the scrotum between your thumb and index finger; feeling a normal slender cord proves the mass is confined to the scrotum.
Examine the normal side first to establish a baseline for size, consistency, and tenderness.
On the affected side, gently support the swelling with the flat fingers of your left hand.
Identify the body of the testis: palpate its anterior and lateral surfaces between your thumb and index finger; assess whether it is smooth, firm, soft, or hard.
Identify the epididymis: palpate posterolaterally to delineate the caput (head at upper pole), corpus (body), and cauda (tail at lower pole).
Determine whether the mass is in the testis itself or separate from it in the epididymis.
Palpate the vas deferens along the posterior aspect of the spermatic cord: roll it between your fingers to feel its characteristic smooth, firm, whipcord consistency.
Test testicular sensation: apply very gentle bilateral compression to the body of each testis; note the presence or absence of the normal sickening dull ache.
Test for fluctuation: place index fingers at right angles to test for fluid thrill or fluctuation in two planes.

skill.exam.surg.scrotal_palpation.normal: Both testes smooth, firm, ovoid, equal in size; normal testicular sensation present; epididymis distinct posterolaterally; vas deferens smooth and whipcord-like; no mass or fluid.
skill.exam.surg.scrotal_palpation.abnormal: Cannot feel testis separately (large hydrocele or haematocele); hard painless testicular lump with loss of testicular sensation (testicular tumour); craggy nodular epididymis with beaded vas (tuberculous epididymitis); acutely tender swollen epididymis (epididymo-orchitis).
skill.exam.surg.scrotal_palpation.significance: Any solid mass within the body of the testis is malignant until proven otherwise. Loss of testicular sensation is a classical feature of testicular tumours and syphilitic gumma. Beading of the vas deferens points to tuberculosis.
skill.exam.surg.scrotal_palpation.practice: Palpate scrotal manikins with simulated hydrocele, epididymal cyst, and testicular tumour, correctly documenting the anatomical relationship of each mass to the testis.
pitfalls: Pressing forcefully on the testis when testing sensation, causing severe agonizing pain.
Failing to separate the epididymis from the body of the testis, misdiagnosing an epididymal cyst as a testicular tumour.
Forgetting to palpate the vas deferens for thickening or beading.

probes.q: What does the normal vas deferens feel like on palpation of the spermatic cord?
probes.a: A firm, smooth, cord-like structure with the consistency of whipcord, easily rolled between thumb and fingers.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of a craggy, nodular epididymis associated with a 'beaded' vas deferens?
probes.a: It is the classical physical sign of tuberculous epididymo-orchitis.

probes.q: Why is testicular sensation lost in a testicular tumour?
probes.a: Because malignant infiltration destroys the testicular sensory nerve endings within the tunica albuginea, replacing normal sensitive parenchyma with insensitive tumour tissue.

rubric.text: Pinches cord at root of scrotum to confirm fingers can get above the mass
Distinguishes the body of the testis from the epididymis and cord
Rolls the vas deferens to confirm smooth whipcord feel and checks for beading
Gently tests testicular sensation (presence or loss of dull ache)
Assesses fluctuation in two orthogonal planes

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
