teach.heading: Anatomical localisation of scrotal swellings
teach.body:
The most important decision on scrotal palpation is whether the swelling is within the body of the testis or separate from it. If the testis can be felt distinct from the mass, the lesion is extra-testicular (epididymal cyst, spermatocele, or cord lipoma).

If the swelling replaces or arises from the testicular parenchyma itself, it is intra-testicular and must be treated as a malignancy until proven otherwise.

teach.heading: Characteristics of intra-testicular versus extra-testicular swellings

rows: No, mass is in the testis itself
Yes, testis felt distinct from the mass
Posterior, superior, or along the cord
Normal and preserved on the testis

skill.exam.surg.transillumination_scrotu.title: Transillumination test for scrotal swellings
skill.exam.surg.transillumination_scrotu.oneLine: Shine a focused light source from behind the swelling in a dark room and observe transmission of light
skill.exam.surg.transillumination_scrotu.why: Transillumination is the definitive clinical test that distinguishes clear fluid-filled scrotal swellings from solid testicular tumours and thick-walled sacs. Failure to perform it correctly leads to unnecessary biopsy or misdiagnosis of a haematocele.

steps.text: Darken the examination room as completely as possible (switch off overhead lights, close curtains or blinds).
Explain the procedure to the patient and have them lie supine.
Roll a sheet of paper or use a cardboard cylinder (such as a stethoscope tube or purpose-made hollow cylinder) to exclude ambient light.
Place the cylinder firmly against the anterior surface of the scrotal swelling.
Place a bright focused penlight torch directly against the posterior or posterolateral aspect of the scrotum, shining the beam directly toward the cylinder.
Look through the open end of the cylinder: look for red or amber light glowing brightly through the swelling.
Test in multiple directions and angles to ensure uniform light transmission throughout the mass.
Look specifically for the opaque shadow of the testis: in a hydrocele, the testis casts a dark, non-transilluminant silhouette usually at the posterior or lower aspect of the illuminated fluid.
Note whether the fluid transilluminates brilliantly (hydrocele, spermatocele) or is opaque (haematocele, pyocele, tumour, hernia).

skill.exam.surg.transillumination_scrotu.normal: Normal scrotum and testes do not transilluminate brilliantly; a faint reddish border may be seen through skin only.
skill.exam.surg.transillumination_scrotu.abnormal: Brilliant, diffuse red or amber illumination throughout the swelling (vaginal hydrocele, encysted hydrocele of cord, spermatocele); or completely opaque / dark mass (haematocele, gumma, tumour, hernia).
skill.exam.surg.transillumination_scrotu.significance: Brilliant transillumination confirms clear, serous fluid. An opaque swelling that does not transmit light indicates blood, pus, solid tumour, or thickened tunica.
skill.exam.surg.transillumination_scrotu.practice: Perform the transillumination test using a torch and paper cylinder on dark fluid models in a darkened room, identifying the silhouette of the testis.
pitfalls: Attempting transillumination in a brightly lit room without using a light-excluding cylinder.
Shining the light from the front rather than behind the swelling.
Assuming a completely opaque mass is an uncomplicated hydrocele, missing a testicular tumour or chronic thick-walled haematocele.

probes.q: What causes brilliant transillumination in a scrotal swelling?
probes.a: Clear, serous fluid enclosed by a thin wall, allowing light to pass freely through the mass (vaginal hydrocele, spermatocele).

probes.q: Name three scrotal swellings that do NOT transilluminate.
probes.a: Testicular tumour, haematocele, pyocele, chylocele, and an inguinal hernia containing bowel or omentum.

probes.q: Why does a congenital hydrocele transilluminate whereas an infantile inguinal hernia may not, even though both contain fluid?
probes.a: A hydrocele contains only clear peritoneal fluid, whereas a hernia contains bowel walls with mucosal layers and intraluminal gas or faeces, or thick vascular omentum that absorbs and blocks light.

rubric.text: Darkens room and uses paper cylinder to eliminate stray ambient light
Places torch firmly behind the mass, directing beam into the cylinder
Identifies the dark opaque silhouette of the testis within the fluid
Correctly identifies transilluminant = clear fluid, opaque = solid/blood/bowel

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
sources.locator: hydrocele: transillumination test and differential diagnosis

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Optics and mechanics of transillumination
teach.body:
Transillumination depends on the transmission of light through clear fluid. Clear serous fluid in a vaginal hydrocele or spermatocele scatters light without absorbing it, causing the entire mass to glow with a luminous red radiance.

Turbid fluid (pus in a pyocele), cellular fluid (blood in a haematocele), fat (chylocele), or solid tumour tissue absorbs and blocks the light beam completely.

rows: Vaginal hydrocele, encysted hydrocele of cord
Blood clots, pus, or bowel wall with omentum

skill.exam.surg.acute_scrotum_torsion.title: Clinical evaluation of the acute scrotum
skill.exam.surg.acute_scrotum_torsion.oneLine: Differentiate testicular torsion from epididymo-orchitis using Prehn sign, cremasteric reflex, and testicular lie
skill.exam.surg.acute_scrotum_torsion.why: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency with a narrow 6-hour salvage window. Misdiagnosing torsion as epididymitis and prescribing antibiotics without emergency exploration leads to testicular necrosis and loss of future fertility.

steps.text: Examine the patient immediately without delay; obtain a focused history while inspecting.
Inspect the scrotum: note whether the affected testis is retracted high in the scrotum (high-riding testis due to cord twisting) and lying horizontally (bell-clapper deformity).
Note scrotal skin changes: early torsion shows normal skin; late torsion or epididymitis shows erythema and oedema.
Test the cremasteric reflex: stroke the inner aspect of the upper thigh with a blunt object or fingertip; observe whether the ipsilateral testis elevates promptly.
Note reflex status: the cremasteric reflex is characteristically ABSENT in testicular torsion; it is typically PRESERVED in epididymo-orchitis and torsion of the testicular appendage.
Palpate gently: in early torsion, the twisted cord may be felt as a thickened, tender knot above the testis, with the epididymis located anteriorly or transversely rather than posteriorly.
Test Prehn sign: gently elevate the affected hemiscrotum toward the symphysis pubis.
Note response: in epididymo-orchitis, scrotal elevation relieves pain (positive Prehn sign); in testicular torsion, elevation typically does not relieve pain or worsens it (negative Prehn sign).
Inspect for the 'blue dot' sign at the upper testicular pole, which indicates torsion of the appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni).
If testicular torsion cannot be definitively excluded, immediately arrange emergency surgical exploration.

skill.exam.surg.acute_scrotum_torsion.normal: Testes hang symmetrically with vertical axis; prompt cremasteric reflex on inner thigh stroking; non-tender; no erythema.
skill.exam.surg.acute_scrotum_torsion.abnormal: High-riding testis with horizontal lie, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn sign, and extreme tenderness (torsion); or swollen, tender epididymis with preserved cremasteric reflex and positive Prehn sign (epididymo-orchitis).
skill.exam.surg.acute_scrotum_torsion.significance: Absent cremasteric reflex with high horizontal lie is the single most sensitive clinical sign of testicular torsion. When in doubt, exploration is mandatory; a normal ultrasound never overrides clinical suspicion.
skill.exam.surg.acute_scrotum_torsion.practice: Perform the acute scrotum examination on a simulator, practicing the cremasteric reflex, Prehn sign, and identifying horizontal testicular lie.
pitfalls: Relying on a negative urine dipstick or ultrasound scan to exclude torsion, delaying surgical exploration past the 6-hour golden window.
Assuming a teenager with severe lower abdominal pain has acute appendicitis without examining the scrotum for high-riding torsion.
Delaying immediate surgical consult while awaiting an ultrasound Doppler study.

probes.q: What is Prehn's sign and how does it help differentiate torsion from epididymo-orchitis?
probes.a: Elevation of the scrotum relieves pain in acute epididymo-orchitis (positive Prehn sign), whereas it does not relieve pain or worsens it in testicular torsion (negative Prehn sign).

probes.q: What is the status of the cremasteric reflex in testicular torsion versus epididymo-orchitis?
probes.a: The cremasteric reflex is absent in testicular torsion, whereas it is usually preserved in acute epididymo-orchitis.

probes.q: What anatomical abnormality predisposes to testicular torsion?
probes.a: Bell-clapper deformity (high insertion of the tunica vaginalis enclosing the testis, epididymis, and lower cord completely), allowing the testis to rotate freely within the tunica like a clapper in a bell.

rubric.text: Inspects for high-riding testis and abnormal horizontal lie
Strokes inner thigh to assess presence or absence of cremasteric reflex
Performs Prehn sign by gently elevating the hemiscrotum
Recognises threshold for immediate emergency surgical exploration

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: The testes and scrotum: torsion of the testis

teach.heading: The clinical triad of testicular torsion
teach.body:
Testicular torsion presents with three key physical findings: a high-riding testis pulled upward by cord shortening, a horizontal axis (bell-clapper lie), and an absent cremasteric reflex.

Pain often radiates to the ipsilateral iliac fossa, leading unwary clinicians to suspect appendicitis or ureteric colic. Never diagnose appendicitis in a boy without first examining both testes.

rows: Common in sexually active or older men
Sudden, acute, often waking from sleep
Normal vertical lie, swollen dependent testis
Absent in over 95 percent of cases

skill.exam.surg.penis_inspection.title: Examination of the prepuce, glans, meatus and penile shaft
skill.exam.surg.penis_inspection.oneLine: Inspect prepuce retractability, external urethral meatus, penile ulcers, and palpate corpora for induration
skill.exam.surg.penis_inspection.why: Penile examination identifies phimosis and paraphimosis, differentiates sexually acquired ulcers from invasive squamous carcinoma, and detects urethral meatal stenosis. Penile carcinoma is notoriously delayed by elderly patients who conceal malignant ulcers behind an unretracted prepuce.

steps.text: Ensure privacy and chaperone; examine in good light with gloved hands.
Inspect the prepuce (foreskin): note if circumcised or uncircumcised; look for inflammation (posthitis), scarring, or fissures.
Test prepuce retractability: gently retract the foreskin over the glans penis; in true phimosis, the foreskin cannot be retracted behind the corona.
If paraphimosis is present: note the retracted foreskin forming an oedematous constricting ring behind the coronal sulcus with a swollen glans; never leave the foreskin retracted.
Inspect the glans penis and coronal sulcus: look for balanitis, leukoplakia, condylomata, or an ulcerative/fungating mass.
Inspect the external urethral meatus: note position (normal terminal slit vs hypospadias on ventral surface or epispadias on dorsal surface) and caliber (meatal stenosis, pinhole meatus).
Gently compress the glans anteroposteriorly to open the meatus and inspect for urethral discharge, mucosal erythema, or papilloma.

Palpate any penile ulcer or growth: assess induration of the base, edge characteristics, and tenderness (hard painless ulcer with rolled edges in carcinoma; hard painless chancre with clean base in primary syphilis; painful ragged soft chancroid).
Palpate the shaft of the penis: compress the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum between thumb and index finger along their length; feel for dense fibrous plaques (Peyronie disease).
Always palpate both groins for enlarged superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
Reduce the foreskin completely back over the glans to prevent iatrogenic paraphimosis.

skill.exam.surg.penis_inspection.normal: Prepuce easily retractable over glans; glans smooth, pink; external urethral meatus a terminal vertical slit without discharge; penile corpora soft and elastic without plaques; inguinal nodes non-enlarged.
skill.exam.surg.penis_inspection.abnormal: Inability to retract foreskin (phimosis); tight constricting ring behind corona with glans oedema (paraphimosis); indurated ulcer or fungating cauliflower growth on glans/prepuce (carcinoma); fibrous plaques in corpora cavernosa (Peyronie disease); purulent urethral discharge.
skill.exam.surg.penis_inspection.significance: Distinguishes physiological phimosis from balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO/lichen sclerosus). Identifies penile carcinoma early. Reducing the foreskin prevents painful iatrogenic paraphimosis.
skill.exam.surg.penis_inspection.practice: Perform foreskin retraction, meatal inspection, corpus palpation, and foreskin reduction on a penile model, verbalizing the prevention of paraphimosis.
pitfalls: Leaving the foreskin retracted after examining or catheterising a patient, causing acute iatrogenic paraphimosis.
Forcing foreskin retraction in a young child with physiological adhesions, causing painful tearing, bleeding, and secondary cicatricial phimosis.
Failing to retract the prepuce in an elderly man with foul-smelling serosanguinous discharge, missing an advanced carcinoma of the glans.

probes.q: What is paraphimosis and why is it a surgical emergency?
probes.a: A condition where a tight, retracted prepuce cannot be pulled forward over the glans, forming a constricting ring behind the corona that impairs venous and lymphatic return, leading to massive glans oedema and arterial gangrene if unrelieved.

probes.q: What is the critical rule regarding the foreskin after performing a penile examination or catheterisation?
probes.a: Always reduce the foreskin back over the glans into its normal anatomical position to prevent iatrogenic paraphimosis.

probes.q: How does the primary chancre of syphilis differ from an ulcerating carcinoma of the penis on palpation?
probes.a: A syphilitic chancre is a painless, circumscribed indurated ulcer with a clean base and rubbery shotty non-tender lymph nodes, whereas penile carcinoma is an indurated, friable, irregular ulcer or cauliflower mass with everted edges and foul discharge, often fixed to underlying erectile tissue.

rubric.text: Assesses prepuce retractability gently without forceful tearing
Inspects glans, coronal sulcus, and opens meatus for discharge and stenosis
Palpates penile shaft along corpora cavernosa for Peyronie plaques
Reduces foreskin back over the glans immediately after examination
Palpates both inguinal regions for lymphadenopathy

teach.heading: Phimosis versus paraphimosis
teach.body:
Phimosis is the inability to retract the prepuce over the glans penis. In children up to three years, physiological adhesions are normal and require no intervention. Pathological phimosis in adults results from recurrent balanoposthitis or lichen sclerosus.

Paraphimosis occurs when a tight prepuce is left retracted behind the corona. The tight ring impedes venous return, engorging the glans and creating a vicious cycle of swelling.

rows: Fungating cauliflower mass or crater-like ulcer
Hard indurated base, everted rolled edges, foul discharge
Hard, enlarged, often fixed or ulcerated (metastatic)
Clean indurated base, clear exudate without pus
Ragged undermined edges, purulent sloughing base
Painful inflammatory bubo that may suppurate

skill.annex.surg.scrotal_swelling_matrix.title: Diagnostic matrix for scrotal swellings
skill.annex.surg.scrotal_swelling_matrix.oneLine: Systematic bedside algorithmic table for categorising scrotal masses by physical signs
skill.annex.surg.scrotal_swelling_matrix.why: Scrotal swellings represent a spectrum from harmless cysts to life-threatening malignancies and emergencies. A structured multi-axial physical sign matrix allows instant bedside differentiation based on getting above the mass, transillumination, testicular sensation, and testicular independence.
skill.annex.surg.scrotal_swelling_matrix.practice: Use the physical sign matrix to classify ten unknown clinical case presentations of scrotal swellings.
pitfalls: Assuming all transilluminant scrotal masses are simple hydroceles, missing a spermatocele or communicating hydrocele.
Diagnosing a scrotal hernia as a hydrocele because of fluid within the hernia sac.
Attempting percutaneous needle aspiration of an undiagnosed solid scrotal mass, breaching oncological tissue planes.

probes.q: Which physical sign distinguishes a vaginal hydrocele from an inguinal hernia that descends into the scrotum?
probes.a: In a vaginal hydrocele, you can get above the swelling at the scrotal neck and it transilluminates brilliantly; in a hernia, you cannot get above the swelling and it does not transilluminate.

probes.q: How does a spermatocele differ from a vaginal hydrocele on physical examination?
probes.a: A spermatocele lies distinctly above and behind the testis (which can be felt separately), often multiloculated with a 'snowstorm' translucency, whereas a vaginal hydrocele surrounds the front and sides of the testis, obscuring it completely.

probes.q: What physical signs define a chronic haematocele and why can it mimic a testicular tumour?
probes.a: A chronic haematocele is a firm, heavy, non-tender, non-transilluminant scrotal swelling that obscures the testis and may contain calcification in its wall, mimicking the size, weight, and opacity of a testicular tumour.

rubric.text: Uses 'getting above swelling' to separate inguinoscrotal from purely scrotal masses
Determines whether testis can be palpated separately from the mass
Applies transillumination to distinguish fluid from solid/cellular masses
Evaluates testicular sensation for loss in malignancy

teach.heading: The four-question algorithm for scrotal swellings
teach.body:
Any scrotal mass can be diagnosed at the bedside by systematically answering four physical examination questions:

1. Can you get above the swelling? (No = hernia or infantile hydrocele; Yes = purely scrotal).
2. Is the swelling cystic or solid? (Fluctuation and transillumination).
3. Can the testis be felt separately from the swelling? (Yes = epididymal or cord; No = testicular or tunica vaginalis).
4. Is testicular sensation present or absent? (Lost = tumour or gumma).

rows: Can get above it at scrotal neck
Moves down with traction on testis

asks.text: How old are you, and did this swelling first appear near puberty, a pregnancy, or the menopause?
Where have you lived all your life, and is your home district known for neck swellings in the community?
Has anyone in your family had a swelling in the neck, a thyroid operation, or thyroid medicines?

skill.history.thyroid.particulars.oneLine: Age, sex and home district set the prior probability of each thyroid disease

probes.a: Girls approaching puberty in iodine-poor districts present with diffuse simple goitre; nodular goitres present in women in their twenties and thirties; papillary carcinoma affects the young, follicular carcinoma mid life, and anaplastic carcinoma the elderly.
probes.q: How does the expected thyroid diagnosis shift with the age of the patient?

teach.heading: Age and sex set the prior probability
teach.body:
Most thyroid disorders favour women. Simple goitres of adolescence appear in girls near puberty, especially where iodine is scarce or need rises. Nodular and colloid goitres present in women in their twenties and thirties.

Cancer respects age bands rather than old age alone. Papillary carcinoma appears in young girls, follicular carcinoma in middle-aged women, and anaplastic carcinoma in the elderly. Primary toxicity affects the young, while Hashimoto disease affects middle-aged women.

teach.heading: Place matters: the goitre belts
teach.body:
Apart from endemic iodine-deficiency goitre, thyroid disease has little geography. But districts with iodine-poor soil and water, near rocky ranges such as the Himalayas, the Vindhyas and the Satpudas, carry whole communities with simple goitre.

Ask where the patient was born and brought up, not just where she lives now. In an endemic belt, several members of one family are often affected, and that clustering points toward iodine lack or an inherited enzyme defect rather than a solitary tumour.

skill.history.thyroid.particulars.title: Particulars in a thyroid swelling
skill.history.thyroid.particulars.why: A thyroid swelling is one of the few surgical lumps where age, sex and home district narrow the diagnosis before the lump is touched. Puberty plus a goitre belt means something quite different from rapid growth in an elderly man.

asks.text: Did you receive radiation treatment to the neck or head as a child?
Has anyone in your family had thyroid cancer, or tumours of other glands?
What treatment have you taken for this swelling so far, and did it shrink, stay the same, or keep growing?
Do you regularly eat cabbage, kale, turnip or soy, and is your household salt iodised?

skill.history.thyroid.risk.oneLine: Iodine, goitrogens, drugs, radiation and family history behind the swelling

probes.a: Childhood neck irradiation and a family history of thyroid cancer raise the suspicion of malignancy and lower the threshold for sampling the nodule.
probes.q: Which two background facts raise the suspicion of cancer in a thyroid nodule?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The thyroid gland: aetiology of simple goitre
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Four background questions that change the workup
points: Neck irradiation in childhood and a family history of thyroid cancer raise the suspicion of malignancy in any nodule.
Long residence in an iodine-poor district, or a diet heavy in brassica vegetables such as cabbage and kale, explains a diffuse simple goitre.
Goitrogenic medicines, including antithyroid drugs and iodine-containing preparations, can enlarge the gland and must be asked about by name.
A previous bursting or incised infected cyst in the midline of the neck points to a thyroglossal fistula rather than a thyroid nodule at all.

teach.heading: What past treatment tells you
teach.body:
Ask what treatment the swelling has already had and what followed. A diffuse adolescent goitre that shrank with iodine supports simple hyperplasia. A nodule that kept growing despite treatment, or one that was sampled before, needs its old reports traced, not repeated blindly.

Also ask about change in voice, breathing or swallowing since any previous neck procedure, since these mark nerve or airway injury that the next plan must respect.

skill.history.thyroid.risk.title: Past, personal, drug and family history in thyroid disease
skill.history.thyroid.risk.why: The background separates an endemic nutritional goitre from a sporadic tumour, and a previously treated gland from a fresh one. Radiation, family history and goitrogen exposure each push the same lump down a different path.

asks.text: Have you lost weight although your appetite is good, and do you feel too hot when others feel comfortable?
Do your hands shake when you hold a cup, and do you feel your heart racing or missing beats?
Do you have difficulty breathing when you lie flat, trouble swallowing solid food, or a change in your voice?
Have your eyes become staring or protruding, with difficulty closing the lids or double vision?

skill.history.thyroid.toxic.oneLine: Functional symptoms and pressure effects that grade the swelling

probes.a: Primary toxicity brings nervous symptoms such as tremor, excitability, insomnia and heat intolerance with eye signs, while secondary toxicity on a nodular gland brings cardiac symptoms such as palpitation, irregular pulse and breathlessness.
probes.q: Contrast the symptoms of primary and secondary thyrotoxicosis.

probes.a: Stridor or dyspnoea from tracheal compression, dysphagia from oesophageal pressure, and hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, which strongly suggests carcinoma.
probes.q: Name the three pressure effects of a thyroid swelling and state what hoarseness implies.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The thyroid gland: symptoms of thyrotoxicosis
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.heading: Primary toxicity is a nervous illness, secondary a cardiac one

rows: Palpitation, irregular pulse, breathlessness, ankle swelling
Staring, protrusion, lid lag often present

teach.heading: Hypothyroid symptoms point the other way
teach.body:
A few questions exclude the opposite state. Gain in weight despite poor appetite, intolerance of cold, dry skin, loss of hair including the outer eyebrows, puffiness of the face, constipation and dullness with failing memory all belong to hypothyroidism.

Mild hoarseness from oedema of the vocal cords and lethargy with muscle fatigue complete the picture. These symptoms associate with Hashimoto disease rather than with toxicity.

teach.heading: Three pressure symptoms localise the swelling
teach.body:
An enlarging gland can press on the trachea to cause dyspnoea and a whistling stridor, worse when the neck bends forward. It can press on the oesophagus, though true dysphagia is uncommon since the muscular tube is easily pushed aside.

Hoarseness means the recurrent laryngeal nerve is involved, and an infiltrating carcinoma is the usual cause. Sudden painful enlargement of a long-quiet swelling means bleeding into a nodule, which can threaten the airway.

skill.history.thyroid.toxic.title: Functional and pressure symptoms of thyroid disease
skill.history.thyroid.toxic.why: Function decides urgency as much as the lump does. A toxic heart can fail while the swelling looks modest, and hoarseness can be the first sign of an invasive cancer in a gland that still feels small.

skill.presentation.thyroid.summary.oneLine: Tempo, function, local findings and risk in three sentences

probes.a: The patient with relevant risks, the tempo in years, the syndrome in abstract terms with function and local findings, and the provisional diagnosis with any severity or red flags.
probes.q: What elements belong in a thyroid case summary?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: Examination of the thyroid gland: case summary
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.heading: Three sentences that contain the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with the risks that matter: age, sex, endemic district, radiation or family history. Then state the tempo: years of painless growth separates benign goitre from weeks of rapid change.

Then state the syndrome in abstract terms with function and local findings: a euthyroid multinodular swelling moving on swallowing with no nodes and no pressure effects. End with the provisional diagnosis and what is still missing, such as cytology.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 44 year old homemaker from a sub Himalayan district presents with six years of slowly enlarging painless anterior neck swelling. Examination shows an asymmetrical bosselated gland moving freely on swallowing, lower poles palpable, trachea central, no nodes, no bruit, clinically euthyroid.

This is a non-toxic multinodular goitre pending thyroid function, ultrasound mapping and needle sampling of the dominant nodule. No red flags are present, so surveillance with defined referral thresholds is the working plan.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: The tempo in years, since it is the single most discriminating detail.
The functional state: toxic, euthyroid or hypothyroid, with the evidence.
Pressure effects and nodes, stated as present or explicitly absent.
What would change the plan: cytology result, toxicity, or a new red flag.

skill.presentation.thyroid.summary.title: Summarising the thyroid case
skill.presentation.thyroid.summary.why: A thyroid summary must carry tempo, function and local staging together, because the plan follows from all three at once. Omitting any one of them leaves the listener unable to judge whether this patient needs reassurance, sampling or referral.

skill.hx.acute.appendicitis_risk.title: Background risks and previous episodes in suspected appendicitis
skill.hx.acute.appendicitis_risk.oneLine: Previous attacks, purgatives, diet, periods, past surgery and drugs that mask the signs
skill.hx.acute.appendicitis_risk.why: Appendicitis is a recurrent risk, not a first-ever event in every patient: previous similar attacks, purgative use and a missed period each redirect the whole workup. A gynaecological history omitted here is how an ectopic gestation or a twisted cyst gets opened as an appendix.

asks.text: Have you ever had a similar pain in the right lower abdomen before, even briefly, and what was it called at the time?
Did you take any purgative, laxative or home enema for constipation just before this pain began?
What do you eat on most days: meat at every meal with few vegetables, or a mixed diet with fruit and fibre?
For a female patient: when was your last menstrual period, is it ever late, and could you be pregnant?
Have you had any previous abdominal operation, tuberculosis, or worms passed in the stool, and what treatment did you take?
Are you taking steroids, immunosuppressants or regular painkillers that could blunt fever, tenderness or guarding?

teach.heading: Previous attacks and purgatives change the meaning of this one
teach.body:
Ask about earlier attacks of right lower abdominal pain by name, since recurrent brief episodes precede many acute presentations and point to a grumbling appendix rather than a first event.

Ask specifically about purgatives or a home enema taken for constipation just before the pain, because stimulating a loaded obstructed appendix can precipitate the acute attack.

teach.heading: The menstrual history is never skipped in an acute abdomen
teach.body:
In every female patient of reproductive age, record the last menstrual period, cycle regularity and any chance of pregnancy before anything else is decided.

A missed period with lower abdominal pain and faintness is a ruptured ectopic gestation until proved otherwise, and mid cycle pain with similar features can be a ruptured follicular cyst.

teach.heading: Past surgery, tuberculosis, worms and masking drugs
points: Previous abdominal operations raise adhesions and obstruction in the differential, while treated or untreated tuberculosis keeps ileocaecal tuberculosis on the list where it is prevalent.
In children, ask about worms passed in the stool, since roundworms can obstruct the appendicular lumen and precipitate appendicitis.
Steroids, immunosuppressants and habitual analgesics blunt fever, tenderness and guarding, so a soft examination in a patient on these drugs never excludes appendicitis.
Smoking and alcohol habits are recorded as for any surgical case, since they affect healing and anaesthetic risk rather than the diagnosis itself.

probes.q: Name two background questions that redirect the workup in suspected appendicitis.
probes.a: Ask about previous similar attacks of right lower abdominal pain and about purgative use just before this pain, and in a female patient always record the last menstrual period and any chance of pregnancy.

probes.q: Why can a soft abdominal examination be falsely reassuring in some patients?
probes.a: Steroids, immunosuppressants and regular analgesics blunt fever, tenderness and guarding, so the examination underestimates the inflammation in a patient taking these drugs.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.acute.appendicitis.title: Presenting the acute appendicitis case
skill.present.acute.appendicitis.oneLine: Tempo in hours, migration, localised peritonism, Alvarado band and what is still missing
skill.present.acute.appendicitis.why: An acute abdomen presentation fails when it reads like an elective history: the examiner needs the tempo in hours, the migration path, the exact peritoneal signs and the risk band, in that order, before the diagnosis is named.

teach.heading: Four sentences that contain the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with the risks that matter: age, sex and any previous similar attack. Then state the tempo in hours: pain first around the navel, then shifting to the right iliac fossa, followed by vomiting and then fever.

Then state the local findings in one breath: tenderness at the McBurney point with guarding and release tenderness, Rovsing sign, and the state of bowel sounds. End with the working diagnosis, the Alvarado band and what would change it.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 22 year old man presents with 18 hours of abdominal pain that began diffusely around the navel and shifted to the right iliac fossa six hours later, with anorexia, one episode of vomiting after the pain began, and fever since this morning.

Examination shows localised tenderness at the McBurney point with guarding and release tenderness, a positive Rovsing sign and sluggish bowel sounds. This is acute appendicitis of high clinical probability pending a leucocyte count and graded compression ultrasound.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: The pain vomiting fever sequence in order, since pain after vomiting points away from a surgical cause.
The migration path stated explicitly, since it is the single most discriminating detail in the history.
Relevant negatives: no missed period where relevant, no dysuria with loin pain, no previous similar attack, no purgative use.
The Alvarado band and what is still missing: blood counts, ultrasound findings, and the consent and fitness for theatre.

probes.q: What elements belong in an acute appendicitis case summary?
probes.a: The patient with relevant risks, the tempo in hours with the migration path, the localised peritoneal findings, the working diagnosis with its Alvarado band, and what investigation or review is still missing.

probes.q: Why does the order of pain and vomiting belong in the first minute of the presentation?
probes.a: Pain before vomiting fits a surgical cause such as appendicitis, while vomiting first fits gastroenteritis, so the sequence stated early lets the listener judge the whole case before the diagnosis is named.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.cholelithias.risk.title: Background risks behind gallstones
skill.hx.cholelithias.risk.oneLine: Age, parity, weight, family, blood and bowel history that raise the prior probability of stones
skill.hx.cholelithias.risk.why: Gallstones gather in particular people, so the background history sets the prior probability before the pain is even described. A multiparous woman above forty with an affected sister starts as stones until proven otherwise, while the same pain in a young man needs far more convincing.

asks.text: How old are you, and how many pregnancies and deliveries have you had?
Has your weight changed much in the last year, through dieting, illness or surgery, and what do you weigh now for your height?
Has anyone in your family had gallstones or surgery to remove the gallbladder?
Have you ever been told you have anaemia that runs in the family, yellow eyes since childhood, or needed repeated blood transfusions?
Have you had any operation on the intestine, long standing bowel disease, or prolonged fasting or rapid weight loss programmes?
Which regular medicines and hormones do you take, including contraceptive pills, hormone treatment, and any recent course of ceftriaxone?
Do you have diabetes, and what is your usual diet: fried food, long gaps between meals, or missed breakfasts?

teach.heading: Who carries stones
teach.body:
Stones favour women above forty, multiparity, obesity, and a family history of stones, the bedside five Fs that examiners still expect. Rapid weight loss, prolonged fasting, oestrogen and contraceptive pills, and diabetes each add further risk through bile that is supersaturated or a gallbladder that empties poorly.

Ask the bowel and blood history that juniors forget. Ileal disease or resection disturbs bile salt handling, and chronic haemolysis loads the bile with pigment, so both point toward pigment stones rather than cholesterol ones.

teach.heading: Why the background changes the question
teach.body:
Risk factors never diagnose on their own, but they decide how hard each later finding must work. In a high risk patient a typical fatty food attack with radiation to the scapula is nearly enough, while in a low risk patient the same story must be checked against ulcer, pancreas and heart before it is believed.

Record risks as facts with numbers where you have them: parity, weight change in kilograms, the drug with its duration. Vague phrases like high risk or obese help nobody at the bedside or in the viva.

probes.q: Name four background risk factors for gallstones you would ask about in every suspected case.
probes.a: Female sex above forty, multiparity, obesity, family history of stones, rapid weight loss, oestrogen or contraceptive pills, haemolytic anaemia, and ileal disease or resection.

probes.q: Why do chronic haemolysis and ileal resection point toward pigment rather than cholesterol stones?
probes.a: Haemolysis loads bile with unconjugated pigment that precipitates as calcium bilirubinate, while ileal disease disturbs bile salt handling; both favour black pigment stones over cholesterol ones.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.cholelithias.summary.title: Summarising the biliary case
skill.present.cholelithias.summary.oneLine: Patient, tempo, biliary syndrome, severity and the next step in four sentences
skill.present.cholelithias.summary.why: A biliary presentation must separate three stories that share one organ: passing colic, an inflamed gallbladder, and a blocked duct. The summary forces that separation in the open, with the tempo and the severity doing the work, so the consultant hears the plan inside the summary.

teach.heading: Four sentences that contain the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with the risks that matter: age, sex, parity, weight and family history of stones. Then state the tempo: a single evening attack that settled points to colic, while days of unrelenting pain with fever points to cholecystitis.

Then state the syndrome in abstract terms with the key positives and negatives: right hypochondrial pain with radiation to the scapula, a positive Murphy sign, fever, and no jaundice. End with the provisional diagnosis, the severity grade, and the next step, such as ultrasound or surgical referral.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 45 year old multiparous homemaker with recurrent fatty food related right upper abdominal pain over two years presents with two days of unrelenting right hypochondrial pain, fever and vomiting. Examination shows a positive Murphy sign with guarding and no jaundice.

This is acute calculous cholecystitis on background cholelithiasis, mild grade, and the next steps are an abdominal ultrasound with blood counts and liver tests, followed by early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

probes.q: What elements belong in a biliary case summary?
probes.a: The patient with relevant risks, the tempo of attacks, the syndrome in abstract terms with key positives and negatives, and the provisional diagnosis with severity and the next step.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: The acute abdomen: presenting the case

skill.hx.colorectal.risk.title: Risk, past, personal, drug and family history in colorectal cancer
skill.hx.colorectal.risk.oneLine: Age, polyps, bowel inflammation and family syndromes that raise the prior
skill.hx.colorectal.risk.why: Colorectal cancer is common after middle age, yet most patients who bleed per rectum do not have cancer. Knowing who carries higher risk before the examination lets you weight the same finding correctly: rectal bleeding with a first degree relative with bowel cancer, or with longstanding colitis, is a different case from identical bleeding with no risk at all.

asks.text: How old are you, and has there been unexplained tiredness, weight loss or iron deficiency anaemia? Risk rises with age, and a right sided growth can present with anaemia alone before bowel symptoms appear.

Have you ever had bowel polyps removed, a previous bowel cancer, or longstanding ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease of the large bowel? Adenomatous polyps are the precursor lesion, and chronic extensive colitis raises risk with duration.

Has anyone in your family had bowel cancer or many polyps, and at what age? Ask specifically about familial polyposis and Lynch type patterns: several affected relatives, or cancer under fifty, points toward a hereditary syndrome needing referral and family screening.

What regular medicines do you take, especially blood thinners, antiplatelet drugs, iron tablets or painkillers? Thinners make bleeding heavier without causing the growth, and iron may already have been started for anaemia.

Do you have diabetes, hypertension, heart or kidney disease, and what is your appetite, diet and weight trend? Comorbidity decides fitness for anaesthesia, bowel preparation and major resection, not the diagnosis.

Have you had any bowel test before: stool occult blood, sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy or barium enema, and what did each show? A recent normal full colonoscopy lowers the prior; a never examined patient with red flags needs complete colonic evaluation.

skill.hx.colorectal.risk.practice: Take past, personal, drug and family history from a simulated patient with rectal bleeding. Name the risk tier and what you would screen in the family, in under three minutes.
pitfalls: Accepting piles as the explanation in a patient over forty without asking about polyps, colitis and family history.
Forgetting that familial polyposis is hereditary, so never asking about relatives or screening the family.
Recording blood thinners as the cause of bleeding and stopping there, instead of asking what lesion is bleeding.
Not asking about a previous colonoscopy, so a metachronous second growth is never looked for.

probes.q: Name four risk factors for colorectal cancer you must ask about.
probes.a: Increasing age, adenomatous polyps or previous colorectal cancer, longstanding extensive inflammatory bowel disease, and a family history or hereditary syndrome such as familial polyposis or Lynch syndrome.

probes.q: Why does a history of villous adenoma matter more than a history of hyperplastic polyps?
probes.a: Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomatous polyps, and villous adenomas turn malignant about three times as often as tubular adenomas, while hyperplastic polyps are not the precursor.

probes.q: A 42 year old with rectal bleeding has two first degree relatives with bowel cancer under fifty. What does the family history change?
probes.a: It raises suspicion of a hereditary syndrome such as Lynch syndrome, which needs genetic counselling, tumour mismatch repair testing, and screening of the whole family, not just treatment of this patient.

rubric.text: Establishes age and anaemia as the background risk
Asks about prior polyps, cancer and inflammatory bowel disease
Takes a three generation style family history for polyposis and Lynch patterns
Records thinners, comorbidity and prior bowel tests for fitness and planning

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
sources.locator: colorectal_cancer: risk factors and hereditary syndromes

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum: aetiology and risk factors

teach.heading: Who carries higher risk
teach.body:
Risk rises with age, and most cancers develop from adenomatous polyps through an adenoma to carcinoma sequence. Only a minority of adenomas progress, with risk tied to size and histology: villous adenomas turn malignant about three times as often as tubular ones.

Longstanding extensive ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease of the large bowel adds risk with duration, as does a previous colorectal cancer or adenoma. These patients need surveillance of the whole colon, not reassurance from one normal test.

teach.heading: Hereditary syndromes to ask about
points: Familial polyposis coli is hereditary: multiple adenomas from youth, near certain progression without treatment, so ask about relatives and polyps directly.
Lynch syndrome may show few or no polyps and is easily missed; several relatives with bowel or related cancers, or cancer under fifty, is the clue.
A strong family history changes management toward genetic counselling, tumour mismatch repair testing and screening of relatives.
Record ages and relationships, not just yes or no: the pattern across generations is what names the syndrome.

teach.heading: What changes the plan
teach.body:
Risk history sets three things: how urgently the whole colon must be examined, whether the family needs screening, and whether the patient is fit for the workup and operation. Blood thinners explain heavier bleeding but never explain the lesion.

A never examined patient with red flag bleeding needs complete colonic evaluation whatever the risk tier, since synchronous polyps and cancers are common enough to look for every time.

skill.present.colorectal.case.title: Presenting the colorectal cancer case
skill.present.colorectal.case.oneLine: Tempo, site, rectal findings and stage in two minutes
skill.present.colorectal.case.why: A colorectal case fails when the site is vague, because right sided, left sided and rectal disease present, spread and operate differently. A presentation that names the site, the rectal findings in finger breadths, and the stage forces every later decision into the open.

probes.q: In what order should a colorectal case be presented?
probes.a: Problem representation with tempo and site, relevant bowel and systemic history with discriminating negatives, abdominal and rectal findings including nodes, diagnosis with stage and fitness, brief differential, then plan.

probes.q: Why must the rectal findings include distance, circumference and fixity?
probes.a: Distance from the anal verge decides whether the sphincter can be saved, circumference and fixity decide resectability, and all three are needed to stage and to plan the operation.

rubric.text: Opens with tempo in months and the site of disease
Gives distance, extent, edge character and fixity of any rectal growth
Includes discriminating negatives: obstruction, nodes, liver, fitness
States the stage with what is still missing, then the plan
Keeps a focused case to about two minutes

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
sources.locator: colorectal_cancer: clinical presentation by tumour site

sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Carcinoma of the rectum: clinical assessment and staging

teach.heading: The fixed order
teach.body:
Open with the problem representation: age, tempo in months, and site. Then the relevant bowel history with bleeding character and habit change, then systemic features and risk. Then abdominal findings, rectal findings, and nodes, positives before discriminating negatives.

Close with the diagnosis and stage, fitness for operation, a one line differential with what argues against each, and the next three steps: biopsy, staging scans, and referral to the colorectal unit.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 58 year old farmer presents with five months of bleeding per rectum with mucus, narrowing of stool and a feeling of incomplete emptying, with 6 kg weight loss and tiredness. Examination shows pallor, a soft abdomen with a loaded descending colon, and an ulcerated anterior rectal growth 4 cm from the verge involving half the circumference, mobile on the muscle, bleeding on touch, with no inguinal nodes.

This is carcinoma of the lower rectum, provisionally mobile and resectable, with iron deficiency anaemia, pending biopsy, pelvic MRI and contrast staging scans for nodes and distant spread.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: The tempo in months, since weeks of bleeding and months of habit change point differently.
Bleeding character and its relation to stool: mixed with stool, coating it, or separate with mucus.
Rectal specifics: distance from the verge, clock position, circumference involved, edge and fixity, and what the glove showed.
Nodes, liver, obstruction and fitness, stated as present or explicitly absent, since each changes stage or operability.

skill.hx.intestinal.risk.title: Past, personal, drug and family history in intestinal obstruction
skill.hx.intestinal.risk.oneLine: The cause is usually in the past: operations, hernias, TB, tumours and slowing drugs
skill.hx.intestinal.risk.why: The presenting symptoms say where the block is, but the past history says why it happened. Previous abdominal surgery points to adhesions, a known groin swelling points to hernia, and weight loss with altered bowel habit points to malignancy. Missing this history means missing a cause that needs its own operation.

asks.text: Have you ever had an operation on the abdomen or pelvis, including appendix, uterus, caesarean section or any emergency surgery, and when was it?
Do you have a swelling in the groin or scrotum, or have you ever been told you have a hernia, and has it recently become painful or irreducible?
Have you ever been treated for abdominal tuberculosis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis or diverticular disease, or had prolonged pain with diarrhoea?
Have you lost weight recently, noticed blood or mucus in the stool, or had a recent change in bowel habit towards constipation?
Have you had similar attacks of pain with distension before that settled on their own, as in recurrent volvulus or a passing gallstone?
Which medicines do you take regularly, especially opioid painkillers, anticholinergic drugs, iron tablets or verapamil that slow the bowel?
What is your usual diet and fluid intake, and do you depend on laxatives or enemas for constipation?
Is there cancer of the bowel in the family, and what are your smoking, alcohol and occupation details?

teach.heading: Previous surgery is the commonest clue
teach.body:
Postoperative adhesions cause about three quarters of small bowel obstructions, so any previous laparotomy, pelvic surgery or caesarean section is the single most important historical fact. Ask what operation it was and when it was done.

A known hernia is the second curable cause. Ask whether a groin or umbilical swelling exists, whether it reduces on lying down, and whether it has recently become painful, tense or irreducible, which suggests strangulation rather than simple obstruction.

teach.heading: TB, inflammation and tumour leave a trail
teach.body:
In India always ask about treated or partly treated abdominal tuberculosis, since strictures are a common benign cause of subacute obstruction. Inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis and previous pelvic radiotherapy point the same way.

For large bowel obstruction in an older patient, ask about weight loss, rectal bleeding, mucus, tenesmus and a recent change towards constipation. These favour an obstructing colorectal growth over volvulus, and they change the operation from decompression to resection.

teach.heading: Drugs, diet and recurrent attacks
points: Opioids, anticholinergics, tricyclics, iron and verapamil slow transit and precipitate obstruction, especially in the elderly and constipated.
Chronic constipation with laxative dependence and a redundant sigmoid sets up sigmoid volvulus. Recurrent self-limiting attacks of distension suggest it.
Intermittent colicky pain that settles and returns can mark a gallstone tumbling down the ileum before final impaction, typically in an older woman with gallstone history.
Family history of bowel cancer and personal history of polyps raise the probability of a malignant stricture.

probes.q: Name two past-history facts that each point to a specific cause of intestinal obstruction.
probes.a: Previous abdominal or pelvic surgery points to adhesive obstruction, and a known groin hernia points to a strangulated hernia.

probes.q: An elderly man has large bowel obstruction. Which historical points favour carcinoma over sigmoid volvulus?
probes.a: Weight loss, rectal bleeding or mucus, tenesmus and a recent change in bowel habit favour an obstructing growth, while chronic constipation with previous self-limiting attacks of distension favours volvulus.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.intestinal.summary.title: Presenting the intestinal obstruction case
skill.present.intestinal.summary.oneLine: Tempo, the four cardinal symptoms, the likely level and cause, and strangulation yes or no
skill.present.intestinal.summary.why: An obstruction presentation must answer four questions in order: is it obstruction, small or large bowel, what is the likely cause, and is the bowel strangulated. A presentation that lists symptoms without committing to these four leaves the consultant unable to decide between continued conservative care and theatre.

teach.heading: The four-sentence structure
teach.body:
Start with the patient and the tempo: age, sex, and hours or days of colicky pain with vomiting, distension and absolute constipation. State which of the four cardinal symptoms dominate, because vomiting dominates high small bowel obstruction while distension dominates large bowel obstruction.

Then give the risk context in one line: previous surgery, hernia, TB treatment, weight loss or constipating drugs. Follow with the examination in the same order: dehydration and vitals, distension pattern and visible peristalsis, tenderness or rigidity, hernial orifices and rectal findings.

teach.heading: Commit to level, cause and strangulation
points: State the level: small bowel if central distension with early profuse vomiting, large bowel if peripheral distension with late vomiting and marked constipation.
State the likely cause with its evidence: adhesions after previous laparotomy, strangulated groin hernia, sigmoid volvulus in an elderly constipated patient, or growth with weight loss and bleeding.
State strangulation explicitly, present or absent, with the evidence: constant pain, tenderness with guarding, fever, tachycardia, leucocytosis or raised lactate favour it.
Close with the plan in one line: resuscitate and decompress with serial review, or resuscitate and operate, and say which.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 58 year old man with an open appendicectomy twelve years ago presents with two days of central colicky pain, repeated bilious vomiting, progressive central distension and absolute constipation for one day. He is dehydrated with tachycardia but no fever. The abdomen is centrally distended with visible peristalsis and increased bowel sounds, there is no tenderness or rigidity, hernial orifices are clear and the rectum is empty.

This is a small bowel obstruction, most likely adhesive, with no strangulation at present. The plan is nasogastric decompression with fluid and electrolyte correction under surgical review, proceeding to operation if strangulation appears or the obstruction fails to resolve.

probes.q: Which four questions must an intestinal obstruction presentation answer?
probes.a: Is it obstruction, is it small or large bowel, what is the likely cause, and is there strangulation.

probes.q: Why must the presentation state strangulation explicitly even when it is absent?
probes.a: Because strangulation is the decision point between continued conservative care and urgent operation, so the team needs to know it was looked for and what the evidence showed.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.varicose.riskfactors.title: Risk, past and family history in varicose veins
skill.hx.varicose.riskfactors.oneLine: Occupation, family, pregnancies, hormones, bowel habit, past thrombosis and prior treatment
skill.hx.varicose.riskfactors.why: Two patients can show identical varicosities yet need opposite operations: one has simple primary valve failure and the other has a blocked deep system or a pelvic tumour doing the obstructing. The risk and past history is what separates them, and missing it turns a routine ablation into a congested, ulcerated leg.

teach.heading: Risk factors decide the operation, not the diagnosis
teach.body:
The visible veins only say that surface pressure is high. Whether that pressure comes from weak walls and leaky surface valves, from deep valves wrecked by an old thrombosis, or from a blocked outflow higher up is decided almost entirely by the story: the job, the family, the pregnancies, the bowels and any past swollen leg.

Ask every one of these even when the leg looks straightforward. A patient who stands all day, whose mother and sisters have the same veins, and whose veins worsened in each pregnancy is telling you primary disease with a real chance of recurrence, and that changes consent.

teach.heading: Questions you must never skip
points: Occupation and hours on the feet: conductors, police, traffic staff, nurses, hawkers and farm workers who stand all day.
Family history in the mother and sisters, which points to inherited wall or valve weakness.
Obstetric history: veins appearing or worsening in pregnancy, and any white swollen leg after delivery.
Hormonal pills taken for many months, which raise the chance of deep venous thrombosis.
Constipation, straining, chronic cough and any abdominal or pelvic lump, which raise outflow pressure.
Any past painful swelling of the whole leg, long immobility, major surgery or prolonged travel.
Prior injection treatment or vein surgery, and what happened afterwards.

teach.heading: Secondary causes hide in the abdomen and the pelvis
teach.body:
A pelvic fibroid, an ovarian cyst, a growth of the cervix or rectum, swollen abdominal nodes, or a uterus heavy with pregnancy can all press on the iliac veins and produce secondary varicosities. Constipation with a loaded colon does the same on a smaller scale.

So a new varicosity in an older patient, a varicosity only on one side with swelling of the whole limb, or veins that appeared suddenly all demand an abdominal and pelvic history and examination, not just a look at the leg.

asks.text: What work do you do, and how many hours a day do you spend standing or walking without sitting?
Do your parents, brothers or sisters have similar prominent leg veins or leg ulcers?
For women: in which pregnancy did the veins first appear or worsen, and did a leg ever swell up white and painful after a delivery?
Have you taken hormonal contraceptive pills, and for how long?
Do you suffer from constipation, and do you strain for long at stool?
Have you noticed any swelling in the abdomen, and have you lost weight or appetite recently?
Have you ever had a whole leg swell painfully, after surgery, childbirth, injury or a long journey?
Have you had any injection treatment or operation for these veins before, and did the veins return?

pitfalls: Recording the veins while never asking about a past deep vein thrombosis, which is the one fact that can forbid surface surgery.
Forgetting the obstetric and pill history in a young woman, and so missing a preventable thrombotic cause.
Dismissing constipation or an abdominal lump as unrelated to the leg, when either can be the whole cause.

probes.q: A bus conductor stands all day and reports heaviness that is worst in the evening and gone by morning. What two facts point to venous rather than arterial pain?
probes.a: Evening worsening after dependent standing and overnight relief on lying down both point to venous hypertension, while arterial claudication comes on with walking and eases with rest.

probes.q: Why must you ask about a past painfully swollen leg before planning varicose vein surgery?
probes.a: A past deep vein thrombosis can leave deep veins blocked or their valves destroyed, so the surface varicosities are carrying essential return flow and removing them risks severe congestion.

probes.q: A woman says her varicosities appeared in pregnancy and her mother has them too. What do these two facts tell you?
probes.a: Pregnancy raises venous pressure through the weight of the uterus and hormonal relaxation of vein walls, and a first-degree family history points to inherited valve or wall weakness, and both raise the chance of recurrence after treatment.

rubric.text: Establishes hours of standing and straining in the daily work
Records family history and the full obstetric and hormonal story
Screens for outflow obstruction and past deep vein thrombosis

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.varicose.summary.title: Presenting the varicose vein case
skill.present.varicose.summary.oneLine: Tempo, system, tests and CEAP grade in under two minutes, ending with fitness for intervention
skill.present.varicose.summary.why: A varicose vein presentation fails in two predictable ways: the student recites every test without saying which system is diseased, or describes the veins without ever stating whether the deep veins are open. The consultant needs the system, the junction, the perforators, the deep patency and the grade, in that order.

teach.heading: Five lines that contain the case
teach.body:
Open with the patient and the tempo: age, sex, standing occupation, and years of evening heaviness and swelling. Then name the system: long or short saphenous trunk, the junction, and any perforator level.

Then give the two test results that matter: Trendelenburg for the junction and perforators, and Perthes for deep patency. Then the skin grade and any ulcer, past or present. Close with your diagnosis, the CEAP class, and whether the leg is fit for ablation or surgery.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 44 year old woman constable on traffic duty presents with six years of left leg heaviness and evening ankle swelling. There are tortuous long saphenous varicosities with a saphena varix showing an expansile cough impulse, a palpable medial calf perforator defect, and pigmentation with eczema above the medial malleolus.

Trendelenburg shows saphenofemoral and perforator incompetence, and Perthes shows patent deep veins. This is primary varicose veins of the left great saphenous system, CEAP C4a, fit for duplex mapping and ablation.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: The deep history: past swollen leg, pregnancies, pills, constipation and abdominal symptoms.
The negatives that protect the plan: no bursting pain on walking, no whole-limb swelling, pulses present.
The arterial check: pulses and the ankle-brachial index before any compression is advised.
The secondary screen: abdomen examined, no pelvic lump, so primary disease can be stated.
The plan: duplex mapping first, then ablation or surgery, with compression and surveillance after.

pitfalls: Listing Trendelenburg and Perthes steps without stating what each proved in this patient.
Presenting the veins while omitting the deep venous history, so the plan hangs on an unchecked assumption.
Ending on the diagnosis with no statement of fitness for intervention and no next test.

probes.q: In what order should a focused varicose vein case be presented?
probes.a: Patient with tempo, the diseased system with junction and perforators, the Trendelenburg and Perthes results, the skin grade, then the diagnosis with CEAP class and fitness for intervention.

probes.q: Your presentation omits the deep veins entirely. Why does the consultant stop you?
probes.a: Without deep patency from the history and Perthes, and without duplex confirmation, no surface vein can be safely removed, since blocked deep veins make the varicosities essential collaterals.

rubric.text: Names the trunk, junction and perforator level
States what Trendelenburg and Perthes each proved
Gives the CEAP grade and fitness for intervention
