skill.hx.acute.pancreatitis_risk.title: Risk factors for acute pancreatitis
skill.hx.acute.pancreatitis_risk.oneLine: Gallstones, alcohol and triglycerides first, then drugs, trauma and recent procedures
skill.hx.acute.pancreatitis_risk.why: The cause decides the cure: stones need a cholecystectomy, alcohol needs abstinence counselling, and high triglycerides need lipid treatment. A pancreatitis history that never asks the cause questions leaves the recurrence unprevented.

teach.heading: Gallstones and alcohol explain most cases
teach.body:
Gallstones cause roughly 40 to 70 percent of attacks and alcohol roughly 25 to 35 percent, so these two questions come first. Ask about prior biliary colic, fatty food intolerance and known gallstones, then about the quantity, frequency and type of alcohol, including country liquor, in a non-judgemental way.

Where neither is present, ask about diabetes, obesity and a high fat diet, and send a fasting lipid profile: triglycerides above 1000 mg per dL point to hypertriglyceridaemia as the likely cause.

teach.heading: Drugs, trauma, procedures and the Indian context
teach.body:
Ask about recent drug starts, particularly azathioprine, thiazides, sodium valproate and oestrogens, and about recent ERCP, abdominal trauma and scorpion sting, which is a recognised precipitant in parts of India.

Past attacks matter: recurrent unexplained episodes raise the possibility of small stones, sludge or an anomaly. Above the age of 40 with no clear cause, keep a pancreatic tumour in mind and ask about weight loss.

asks: Have you had this kind of pain before, or pain after fatty food suggestive of biliary colic?
Do you drink alcohol? How much, how often, and for how many years?
Are you diabetic, or have you been told your cholesterol or triglycerides are high?
What regular tablets do you take, and has any new drug been started recently?
Have you had any injury to the abdomen, a recent ERCP, or a scorpion sting?
Is there anyone in the family with gallstones or pancreatic disease?

probes.q: Name the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis.
probes.a: Gallstones and alcohol.

probes.q: No gallstones and no alcohol. What single blood test points to the next most likely cause?
probes.a: Fasting triglycerides. A level above 1000 mg per dL makes hypertriglyceridaemia the likely cause.

probes.q: Why does the cause change the operation you plan before discharge?
probes.a: Mild gallstone pancreatitis needs cholecystectomy on the same admission to prevent recurrence, while alcohol related disease needs abstinence counselling and hypertriglyceridaemia needs lipid treatment instead.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.acute.pancreatitis.title: Presenting the acute pancreatitis case
skill.present.acute.pancreatitis.oneLine: Tempo, pain, cause clues, severity and plan in under two minutes
skill.present.acute.pancreatitis.why: The consultant needs the tempo, the cause and the severity grade in the first minute, because those three decide fluids, feeding and whether the gallbladder comes out on this admission. A presentation that buries them under examination detail wastes the decision window.

teach.heading: The one minute scheme
teach.body:
Open with age, sex and tempo: an acute severe epigastric pain of stated hours or days, radiating to the back, with vomiting. Follow with the cause clues: prior biliary colic or known stones, alcohol use, triglycerides, drugs and trauma.

Then give the severity: pulse, pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen need, urine output and creatinine, and the revised Atlanta class. Close with lipase, ultrasound and CT findings, and the plan: fluids, feeding, antibiotics only if infected, and gallbladder surgery where indicated.

teach.heading: Say the negatives that exclude the mimics
teach.body:
State what is absent and why it matters: no board-like rigidity or free gas against perforation, no Murphy sign or thick walled gallbladder against cholecystitis, no colicky pattern with distension against obstruction.

End with a crisp diagnostic line, for example: acute gallstone pancreatitis, moderately severe by the revised Atlanta classification, with a plan for fluids, early feeding and same admission cholecystectomy.

probes.q: What three facts open an acute pancreatitis presentation?
probes.a: The tempo, the pain with its radiation, and the cause clues.

probes.q: Which severity facts must appear before the plan?
probes.a: Pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen need, urine output, creatinine and the revised Atlanta class.

probes.q: Why name the absent findings in the presentation?
probes.a: Because named negatives exclude the close mimics, perforation, cholecystitis and obstruction, without further tests.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

asks.text: What is your daily diet and water intake like? A diet poor in fibre and fluids with hard stools and prolonged straining underlies most piles and fissures.
Do you pass stool daily without straining, or do you sit a long time and strain hard? Ask about ignoring the urge, prolonged sitting on the pan, and chronic constipation.
What work do you do? Prolonged sitting or standing, heavy lifting, and long hours without moving raise venous pressure in the anal cushions.
Have you ever had a painful swelling beside the anus that burst on its own or needed a cut to drain pus? A previous anorectal abscess is the usual origin of a fistula-in-ano.
Have you had tuberculosis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, or repeated bouts of dysentery or severe diarrhoea? These explain recurrent or multiple fistulae and rectal prolapse.
For women: how many pregnancies and deliveries, and was labour prolonged? Pressure on the rectal veins in pregnancy and pelvic floor weakness afterwards predispose to piles and prolapse.
Do you pass urine with difficulty, a thin stream, or dribbling? Urethral stricture or an enlarged prostate with chronic straining raises pressure on the superior rectal veins.
Do you use purgatives or enemas regularly to open your bowels? Increasing purgative requirement with alternating diarrhoea can mark an annular growth higher up.

Has anyone in your family had piles, fissure, rectal prolapse, bowel cancer, or multiple bowel polyps? Polyposis is hereditary, and patients often volunteer a family history of piles or rectal cancer.

probes.a: Chronic constipation with hard stools and prolonged straining is the commonest background, with low fibre diet, ignoring the urge, pregnancy, and any cause of raised intra-abdominal pressure such as a pelvic tumour, urethral stricture or enlarged prostate.
probes.q: Name three background factors you must ask about in every patient with piles or fissure.

probes.a: A previous anorectal abscess that burst spontaneously or was incised and drained, because most fistulae-in-ano begin as a cryptoglandular abscess that fails to heal completely.
probes.q: What single past event explains most new fistulae-in-ano?

probes.a: Tuberculosis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, lymphogranuloma inguinale and colloid carcinoma of the rectum, so recurrent or multiple tracks should trigger questions about chronic cough, weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, genital sores and bowel symptoms.
probes.q: A patient has recurrent multiple fistulae. Which systemic diseases must your past history exclude?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: Examination of a rectal case: past and family history
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body: Most anorectal disease is a habit disease before it is a surgical disease. Chronic constipation, hard stools, prolonged sitting on the pan and repeated straining congest the anal cushions and tear the anal lining. A low fibre diet with poor water intake, regularly ignoring the urge to defecate, and occupations that keep a person sitting or standing for hours all belong in the history, because correcting them is part of the treatment.
teach.heading: Bowel habit comes first

teach.body: Pressure above the anus matters as much as habit at the anus. Pregnancy presses on the superior rectal veins while progesterone relaxes vein walls. Urethral stricture, an enlarged prostate, a large pelvic tumour, and chronic cough all raise intra-abdominal pressure and congest the same veins. In a woman, ask about pregnancies and prolonged labour; in a man with piles, ask about urinary stream and straining to pass urine.
teach.heading: Causes of raised pressure

teach.body: A fistula is an abscess that never finished healing. Ask every discharging patient about a past painful perianal swelling that burst on its own or was cut open to let pus out. Where fistulae are multiple or keep recurring, widen the net: tuberculosis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis and colloid carcinoma of the rectum all produce tracks that refuse to heal, so ask about chronic cough, weight loss, prolonged diarrhoea and genital sores.
teach.heading: Past sepsis explains the track

teach.body: Prolapse has its own past. Repeated dysentery or severe diarrhoea with tenesmus, wasting that weakens rectal support, and chronic straining in childhood or old age all precede it. Family history is volunteered more often here than elsewhere: patients mention piles, fissure or rectal cancer in relatives, and multiple bowel polyps in the family point to hereditary polyposis.
teach.heading: Prolapse and family history

skill.hx.anorectal.riskfactors.title: Risk factors and background in anorectal disease
skill.hx.anorectal.riskfactors.why: Piles, fissure and fistula recur when the ground that grew them is left untouched. Constipation, straining, pregnancy, raised abdominal pressure and a past abscess are the ground, and tuberculosis or inflammatory bowel disease is the mimicker that punishes a surgeon who never asked.

probes.a: Age, sex, occupation and bowel habit, the complaints in chronological order with bleeding pattern, pain and its relation to defecation, prolapse and its reducibility, and discharge, followed by inspection findings, digital findings, proctoscopy, and a statement naming the condition with its grade or type.
probes.q: What must a rectal case presentation contain, in order?

probes.a: Radial folds of mucosa over separate cushions mean prolapsed piles, while concentric rings of full thickness wall mean complete rectal prolapse, and stating which one you saw decides between banding or excision and prolapse surgery.
probes.q: Why must the presentation state whether prolapsing tissue showed radial or concentric folds?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The anus and anal canal: clinical examination
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.body: Open with age, sex, occupation and bowel habit, then the complaints in the order they appeared. Describe bleeding by colour, amount and relation to stool: splash in the pan, streak on the surface, or mixed with mucus. Describe pain by character and timing against defecation: cutting pain during and after stool for fissure, throbbing continuous pain for abscess, intermittent pain relieved by discharge for fistula, and no pain at all for uncomplicated piles.
teach.heading: Present the story in order

teach.body:
Report examination in the order it was done: inspection first, palpation second, digital examination last. Give position and clock-face sites of piles, the midline site of a fissure with its sentinel tag, and the position of a fistula opening against the transverse anal line with its discharge.

Record whether prolapsing tissue reduced on its own, needed a finger, or stayed out. Close with the diagnostic statement: the condition, its degree or type, and the key negatives that exclude cancer and inflammatory bowel disease.
teach.heading: Report inspection before the finger

skill.present.anorectal.summary.title: Presenting the anorectal case
skill.present.anorectal.summary.why: A rectal presentation fails when bleeding is reported without its pattern or a prolapse without its reducibility, because grade and type are the whole treatment decision. Inspection findings lead, the finger follows, and the closing line names the condition with its degree.

skill.hx.bph.riskfactors.title: Background history in prostatic disease: past, drugs, family and habits
skill.hx.bph.riskfactors.oneLine: Why it blocked now, what treatment is safe, and what the family story warns of
skill.hx.bph.riskfactors.why: The urinary story describes the obstruction, but the background history explains why it blocked this week and what treatment is safe. A retention that followed a cold remedy needs different counselling from one built on repeated infections, and a family history of prostate cancer changes how every future test is read.

asks.text: Have you had similar difficulty before, attacks of being unable to pass urine, or repeated burning or fever with urination?
Have you had any discharge from the urinary passage, injury to the passage, or any tube, camera test or operation through the passage?

Which tablets do you take regularly, including cold and cough remedies, allergy tablets, sleeping tablets, nerve or mood tablets, strong painkillers and water tablets? When did each start compared with the urinary trouble?
Do you have sugar disease, fits, Parkinson disease, a stroke with weakness, piles with straining, or chronic constipation?
How much water, tea and coffee do you take, especially in the evening and at night? How many times do you wake to pass urine?
Have you noticed changes in erection or in discharge at climax, and has any prostate medicine changed this?
Did your father or any brother have prostate trouble, a prostate operation, or prostate cancer, and at what age did it start?

skill.hx.bph.riskfactors.practice: Take the background history from a simulated elderly man with retention, listing every medicine by purpose and by timing against the first urinary symptom.
pitfalls: Accepting retention as pure prostatic enlargement without asking about the cold remedy started last week.
Forgetting that a bladder relaxant for urgency can worsen emptying when the residual urine is already large.
Recording prostate trouble in the family without asking whether it was cancer and at what age.

teach.heading: Drugs that precipitate retention
teach.body:
Some commonly used medicines tighten the bladder outlet or weaken the bladder squeeze. Cold and cough remedies with decongestants, allergy tablets, bladder relaxants, gut spasm tablets, some nerve and mood tablets, and strong painkillers can all turn a narrow passage into a complete blockage. Ask for each medicine by its purpose, not by its chemical name, since patients rarely know the names.

Water tablets taken in the evening fill the bladder overnight and unmask a weak stream as night-time frequency. Note the timing of every diuretic, and ask about recent anaesthesia, operations with a catheter, loaded bowel, and alcohol excess, all of which can trigger the first episode of retention.

teach.heading: Past events that change the plan

rows: Earlier attacks of being unable to pass urine
An outlet that has blocked before and will block again
Plan follow-up and definitive treatment, not just relief
Repeated burning or fever with urination
Infection behind residual urine, or stone forming in stagnant urine
Send urine for test and culture before antibiotics
Discharge, injury or instruments through the passage
A scarred stricture rather than a large prostate
Examine the whole urethra and arrange a flow study
Blood in the urine, even once
A bladder growth or bleeding vessels on the prostate surface
Never accept infection as the whole answer; refer onward

teach.heading: Family, fluids and bowel habit
teach.body:
A father or brother with prostate cancer, especially at a young age, raises the stakes of every raised marker and every firm or nodular gland. Evening tea, coffee and alcohol increase night-time urine, and chronic constipation with straining shares the same pelvic floor effort as voiding.

Sort these contributors before blaming the prostate alone. Record erectile and ejaculatory function before treatment starts, since both the disease and its medicines affect them, and a baseline lets later changes be recognised as drug effects.

probes.q: Name two groups of medicines that can precipitate urinary retention in a man with prostatic enlargement.
probes.a: Decongestant cold remedies and anticholinergic medicines such as allergy tablets, bladder relaxants and gut spasm tablets tighten the outlet or weaken bladder contraction; opioid painkillers and evening diuretics can also precipitate retention.

probes.q: A man taking a bladder relaxant for urgency is found to have a large residual volume. What is the risk of continuing it?
probes.a: The relaxant weakens bladder contraction and can convert incomplete emptying into complete retention. It should be stopped or changed and the residual rechecked, with referral if emptying does not recover.

probes.q: Why record erectile and ejaculatory function before starting treatment for prostatic enlargement?
probes.a: Both the disease and its medicines affect sexual function: some prostate medicines reduce libido and erection or abolish ejaculation, so a baseline lets later changes be recognised as drug effects rather than new disease.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: History and examination of the urinary tract

skill.present.bph.summary.title: Summarising the urinary retention case
skill.present.bph.summary.oneLine: Tempo, retention type, the trio of dome, kidneys and prostate, and what is still missing
skill.present.bph.summary.why: A retention case is judged on structure as much as content: the listener must hear within a minute whether this is a painful acute blockage, a silent chronic build-up, or an overflow the patient never noticed, and what the kidneys have already paid. Presenting in the order collected buries exactly that.

teach.heading: Three sentences that contain the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with the risks that matter: age over 50, years of slow stream symptoms, sugar disease or nerve disease, and the drugs that precipitate retention. Then state the tempo: years of progressive voiding difficulty ending in hours of painful inability, which is acute on chronic retention, or painless dribbling with a silent dome, which is chronic retention.

Then state the syndrome in abstract terms with the bedside evidence: an obstructed bladder with a palpable suprapubic dome and a smooth enlarged prostate, with the kidney numbers and the urine test. End with the provisional diagnosis and what is still missing, such as the counselled marker result, the residual volume, and the upper tract scan.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 68 year old retired teacher presents with three years of weak stream and night-time frequency, now unable to pass urine for ten hours with lower abdominal pain. Examination shows a tense tender suprapubic dome dull to percussion and a symmetrically enlarged smooth firm prostate with a preserved central groove.

This is acute on chronic retention from benign prostatic enlargement, pending urine testing, kidney function, a counselled prostate marker, and an ultrasound of the prostate, residual urine and upper tracts. Immediate relief by catheter with a planned trial without catheter is the working plan.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: The tempo in years for the symptoms and in hours for the retention, since it names the type.
The retention type: painful acute, painless chronic, or overflow leakage the patient mistook for age.
The prostate feel: smooth or nodular, groove present or lost, lining free or tethered.
Kidney function and upper tracts, stated as checked or as still awaited, never skipped.
What would change the plan: a raised marker, a nodular gland, infection, or stones.

probes.q: What elements belong in a urinary retention case summary?
probes.a: The patient with relevant risks, the tempo in years and hours, the retention type, the dome and prostate findings with kidney numbers, and the provisional diagnosis with what is still awaited.

probes.q: Why does the tempo need two time scales in a retention summary?
probes.a: Years of progressive symptoms establish the chronic obstruction while hours of inability establish the acute event; together they name acute on chronic retention and justify both immediate relief and definitive follow-up.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: History and examination of the urinary tract: case summary

skill.hx.breast.risk.oneLine: Reproductive history, family clustering, hormones and radiation sort background risk before the lump is judged
asks: Ask age at first childbirth, number of children, and total months of breastfeeding, since nulliparity and absent lactation raise background risk.
Ask whether mother, sisters or daughters had breast or ovarian disease and at what age, since clustering in the family changes surveillance.
Ask about hormonal pills, postmenopausal hormones, chest wall irradiation, smoking, alcohol and chest trauma, each in plain dated language.
Ask menstrual pattern and menopausal age, and whether any lump or pain fluctuates with the monthly cycle.

probes.a: Nulliparity, late first childbirth, absent breastfeeding, early menarche, late menopause, a first degree relative with breast cancer, chest irradiation and prolonged combined hormone exposure all raise background risk.
probes.q: Which reproductive and family facts raise the background risk of breast carcinoma?

probes.a: Cyclical pain and fluctuation with menstruation favour benign hormonal change and argue against carcinoma, though they never excuse skipping examination and triple assessment of a discrete lump.
probes.q: What does a clear menstrual rhythm in the symptoms tell you, and what does it not excuse?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The breast: aetiology and risk factors of breast carcinoma
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Breast cancer feeds on lifetime hormone exposure, so the reproductive story is risk arithmetic. Early first period, late menopause, no children, a late first child, and little or no breastfeeding each add risk, while early childbearing and prolonged nursing subtract it. Take each as a dated fact, not a judgement.

Family clustering matters independently. A mother or sister with breast or ovarian disease, especially when young or bilateral, should prompt questions about the wider family and about surveillance for the patient herself.
teach.heading: Hormone years and family clustering

teach.body:
Ask drugs by name and year: contraceptive pills, postmenopausal hormones, and any tablets that swell male breasts such as certain heart, ulcer and tuberculosis drugs all belong in the record. Add chest irradiation in youth, smoking, regular alcohol, and any remembered blow to the breast.

Close with the cycle. Pain and swelling that rise before menstruation and melt after it mark benign hormonal change, while steady painless growth without rhythm warns of tumour. The rhythm guides suspicion but never replaces examination.
teach.heading: Drugs, irradiation, habits and the monthly rhythm

skill.hx.breast.risk.title: Risk factors in breast disease
skill.hx.breast.risk.why: The lump is the presenting fact but the background risk decides how hard to chase it. A painless lump in a nulliparous woman with an affected sister is a different proposition from the same lump in a nursing teenager, and only the risk history tells them apart.

skill.present.breast.summary.oneLine: Patient, tempo, lump in five features, skin nipple nodes, and a staged impression with the next test

probes.a: Age and risk context, tempo in weeks or months, the lump in site, size, consistency, margin and fixity, skin and nipple findings, nodal status, and a staged impression with the next investigation.
probes.q: What are the elements of a complete breast case summary?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The breast: clinical method and case summary
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.body:
Open with the woman and her risk context in one line: age, parity and lactation, and any family clustering. Follow with tempo, because weeks of steady growth and years of quiet swelling tell opposite stories.

Then describe the lump in fixed order: quadrant and size, consistency and surface, margin, mobility within the breast, and fixity to skin, muscle and chest wall. Add skin, nipple and discharge, then the axilla and supraclavicular fossae on both sides.
teach.heading: Patient, tempo, lump, nodes

teach.body:
Close with an impression that stages, not merely names: which side and quadrant, benign or malignant character, nodal status, and the clinical stage it implies. Name the triple assessment arm that comes next and what each possible result would change.

A worked close reads: this is a right sided upper outer carcinoma with mobile axillary disease, operable clinical stage IIB (T2N1M0), for core biopsy with receptor testing and risk adapted staging before any surgical plan. Say what is still unknown, and offer the relevant negatives that exclude the mimics.
teach.heading: Stage it, state the next test, admit the gaps

skill.present.breast.summary.title: Summarising the breast case
skill.present.breast.summary.why: A breast presentation fails when it lists findings without forcing them into a staged impression. The fixed order of patient, tempo, lump, nodes and next test guarantees the consultant hears the diagnosis, its evidence and its plan in under a minute.

skill.hx.head.riskfactors.title: Risk factors and background in head injury
skill.hx.head.riskfactors.oneLine: Blood thinners, alcohol, age, comorbidity and past fits that turn a blow into a bleed
skill.hx.head.riskfactors.why: Two identical blows behave differently in different patients. Anticoagulation turns a minor knock into an expanding haematoma, alcohol hides the examination, and age with comorbidity decides which lesion to expect. Missing this background means misreading both the severity and the scan.

asks.text: Do you take any blood thinning tablets such as warfarin, acitrom, aspirin or clopidogrel, and when was the last dose taken?
Do you consume alcohol regularly, and had you consumed alcohol or any sedative tablet in the hours before the injury?
How old is the patient, and is there an unsteady walk, poor eyesight, or repeated falls at home?
Do you suffer from high blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease or fits, and which tablets do you take daily for these?
Have you ever had a head injury, a fit, or a stroke like weakness before this accident?
What is your occupation, and were you wearing a helmet or a seatbelt at the time of the accident?
Is there fits, diabetes or high blood pressure running in the family?

teach.heading: Blood thinners turn a minor blow into a bleed
teach.body:
A patient on warfarin or an antiplatelet tablet can grow a large intracranial haematoma from a blow that would barely bruise anyone else. Ask the exact tablet name and the timing of the last dose in every head injury, because reversal of anticoagulation and correction of clotting start from that answer.

An elderly patient who fell at home while on a blood thinner deserves a scan even when fully alert and talking. Never let a normal examination overrule the drug history in such a patient.

teach.heading: Alcohol hides the examination
teach.body:
Alcohol both causes the injury and confuses its assessment. A drunk patient may look drowsy from drink rather than from brain compression, and a head injury may be missed behind the smell of alcohol. Ask the quantity and timing honestly, and repeat the examination as the alcohol wears off.

Chronic heavy drinking also raises the risk of falls, assaults and road accidents, and of bleeding from minor trauma. Record it as a risk factor, not as a moral judgement.

teach.heading: Age, comorbidity and past fits set the lesion
teach.body:
A blow to the front or back of the head in an old man with signs of compression should raise suspicion of a subdural haematoma at once. Children recover faster but deteriorate faster too, and a fit after injury may localise the site of cortical irritation.

High blood pressure, diabetes and kidney disease affect fitness for surgery and for contrast imaging, while past fits, past head injury and current tablets decide whether a fit today is new disease or old disease showing itself again.

probes.q: Which two drug groups must you ask about in every head injury, and why?
probes.a: Anticoagulant and antiplatelet tablets such as warfarin, acitrom, aspirin and clopidogrel, because they convert minor trauma into an expanding intracranial haematoma, plus alcohol and sedatives because they confound the level of consciousness.

probes.q: An alert elderly man on warfarin fell from bed and has only a scalp bruise. Scan or observe?
probes.a: Scan. Anticoagulation plus age makes even trivial trauma capable of producing an intracranial haematoma, and a normal examination does not overrule that combination.

probes.q: Why does a fit after head injury matter beyond the fit itself?
probes.a: A fit may localise the site of cortical irritation, as in Jacksonian fits from middle meningeal bleeding, and a first fit can be the earliest sign that something more serious than simple concussion is present.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.head.injury_summary.title: Presenting a head injury case
skill.present.head.injury_summary.oneLine: Mechanism, timeline, GCS trend, localising signs and plan in two minutes
skill.present.head.injury_summary.why: A head injury presentation fails when it reads as a list of injuries rather than a story with a direction. The listener needs the mechanism, the exact timeline of consciousness, the trend of the coma score, and the one lesion that explains the signs, in that order, before any plan can be judged.

teach.heading: Open with mechanism and timeline, not with the scan
teach.body:
State the age, the exact mechanism, and the time since injury first. Then give the consciousness timeline in one breath: conscious or not at the scene, any lucid interval, and the direction of change since arrival. This single timeline carries more weight than any other sentence in the presentation.

Name the helmet, seatbelt, alcohol and anticoagulant status early, because each changes what the scan is allowed to mean. A scan read without the timeline is only a picture.

teach.heading: Make the GCS trend the spine of the examination
teach.body:
Present the coma score as a trend with its components, not as one number: what it was on arrival, what it is now, and which component moved. A fall of two or more points is deterioration until proved otherwise and must be said out loud.

Follow with the pupils, the scalp and base of skull signs, and the focal deficit in that order. End the examination with the spine and the rest of the body, to show that associated injuries were actively sought.

teach.heading: Commit to a lesion, a severity and a next step
teach.body:
Close with one diagnosis that names the mechanism, the lesion and the severity, for example a moderate head injury with a right extradural haematoma under observation. Then state the two findings that support it and the one finding that would change it.

Finish with the plan in order: airway and spinal protection, the scan that is due or done, the neurosurgical referral, and what would force an operation. Never end on the diagnosis without a plan.

probes.q: What three things must open every head injury presentation?
probes.a: The exact mechanism of injury, the time since injury, and the full timeline of consciousness including any lucid interval and the direction of change.

probes.q: Why present the coma score as a trend with components rather than one number?
probes.a: Because a fall of two or more points signals deterioration and expanding compression, and the components show which function is failing while the total alone hides it.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.inguinal.risk.title: Past, personal, drug and family history in inguinal hernia
skill.hx.inguinal.risk.oneLine: The pressure factors and past repairs that decide whether a hernia recurs after surgery
skill.hx.inguinal.risk.why: A hernia is the meeting of a weak wall and raised pressure. Repair closes the defect but does nothing about a chronic cough, constipation or bladder outlet obstruction, so a patient sent to theatre without these asked after returns with a recurrence that was preventable.
asks: Do you have a long-standing cough, and what brings up sputum day to day?
Do you strain to pass stools, and how often do your bowels move?
Do you pass urine frequently at night, wait for the stream to start, or feel the bladder never empties?
What work do you do each day, and does it involve lifting heavy weights?
Have you ever had a hernia repair before, on this side or the other side?
Have you had any earlier operation on the abdomen, including appendicectomy?
Do you smoke beedis or cigarettes, and for how many years?
Has anyone in your family had a hernia or a groin operation?
Which medicines do you take every day, including blood thinners and steroids?

teach.heading: Ask after pressure before promising a repair
teach.body:
Four chronic strains raise pressure inside the abdomen and push bowel through a weak groin: a persistent cough, habitual constipation, bladder outlet obstruction from an enlarged prostate or a urethral stricture, and repeated heavy lifting. Patients rarely volunteer them, because they seem unrelated to a groin lump, so each needs a direct question.

Treating the cause is part of treating the hernia. A cough worked up before surgery, constipation eased with diet and fluids, and prostatic symptoms examined per rectum all lower the chance that the repair fails in the first year.

teach.heading: Past operations change the plan
teach.body:
Ask about every earlier abdominal operation. Division of nerves during appendicectomy can weaken the groin wall and precede a direct hernia, and any previous hernia repair on the same side means this swelling may be a recurrence, which needs a different operative approach from a first hernia.

Record daily drugs with bleeding in mind. Blood thinners and antiplatelet tablets matter for the timing of elective surgery, and long steroid use weakens tissues and wounds. Diabetes, hypertension and heart or lung disease decide fitness for anaesthesia rather than the hernia itself.

teach.heading: Risk factors and what each one changes

rows: Repeated pressure spikes that formed the hernia and threaten the repair
Examine the chest and treat the cause before elective surgery
Daily pressure loading on the groin wall
Fibre, fluids and habit before and after the operation
Possible outlet obstruction straining the wall with every void
Rectal examination of the prostate and urology review
Occupational strain that continues after discharge
Counsel on load and leave after repair
Refer to a surgeon experienced in redo groin surgery
Connective tissue weakness shared in the family
Examine the other groin; counsel, do not alarm

probes.q: Name three chronic strains you must ask after in every hernia history.
probes.a: A persistent cough, habitual constipation with straining, and bladder outlet obstruction such as prostatic enlargement, plus repeated heavy lifting.

probes.q: Why does a previous appendicectomy matter in a patient with a new groin swelling?
probes.a: Division of nerves during appendicectomy can weaken the muscles of the groin region and precede a direct inguinal hernia on that side.

probes.q: A patient with a reducible hernia also reports nocturia, hesitancy and a poor stream. What do you do before booking elective repair?
probes.a: Examine the prostate per rectum and arrange urology review for outlet obstruction, because unrelieved straining threatens the repair, and treat constipation and cough in the same sitting.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.inguinal.summary.title: Summarising the inguinal hernia case
skill.present.inguinal.summary.oneLine: Side, extent, contents and complications in three sentences
skill.present.inguinal.summary.why: A hernia summary fails when it names the lump but not its behaviour. The consultant needs side, extent, reducibility, contents and complications in one breath, because each word changes the urgency from routine list to tonight.

teach.heading: The shape of the summary
teach.body:
State the patient with age and work, the tempo of the swelling, then the syndrome in abstract terms: a right inguinoscrotal swelling with an expansile cough impulse, reducible with a gurgle, consistent with an indirect inguinal hernia containing bowel.

Close with complications and fitness: no tenderness, no obstruction, no strangulation, and the pressure factors and comorbidity that decide fitness for elective mesh repair.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 48 year old farm labourer presents with a two year history of a right groin swelling that descends into the scrotum on standing and coughing and disappears on lying down, with a dragging ache late in the day.

Examination shows a pyriform right inguinoscrotal swelling with an expansile cough impulse, from which one cannot get above, reducible with a gurgle and resonant to percussion. This is an uncomplicated right indirect inguinal hernia, an enterocele, with chronic constipation as a contributing strain and no features of obstruction or strangulation.

teach.heading: What never to omit
points: Side, extent and shape: groin only or down to the scrotum, pyriform or spherical.
The two classical signs: expansile impulse on coughing and reducibility.
Contents in one word where known: enterocele or omentocele, with the evidence.
The ring tests and what they showed: deep ring occlusion and the invagination finding.
Complications stated as negatives: no tenderness, no tension, no obstruction, impulse present.
Fitness and causes: comorbidity, drugs that bleed, and the cough, bowel and bladder history.

probes.q: What six facts must every hernia summary contain?
probes.a: Side, extent, cough impulse, reducibility, contents, and complications with fitness for surgery.

probes.q: Why must complications be stated even when they are absent?
probes.a: Because a reducible hernia and a strangulated one differ only in tension, tenderness, impulse and bowel function, and the listener cannot grade urgency without hearing those negatives.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
