asks.text: Ask about diabetes: known sugar illness, tablets or insulin, recent sugar readings, and whether wounds elsewhere have healed slowly.
Ask about hypertension and heart disease: known high pressure, chest pain on effort, and swelling of both feet by evening.
Ask about tobacco in every form: bidis, cigarettes, chewing tobacco, and years of use, plus alcohol and usual diet.
Ask about vein history: visible varicose veins, a past clot with prolonged leg swelling, calf swelling in pregnancy, and any prior vein operation or injection treatment.
Ask about past ulcers: an earlier sore on either leg, how long it took to heal, and what dressing or bandage was used.
Ask about medicines and local applications: steroids, water tablets, blood thinners, and every powder, oil, ointment or home remedy applied to the wound.
Ask about family and work: varicose veins or non healing sores in parents or siblings, hours spent standing, walking barefoot, and the footwear used daily.

skill.hx.leg.risk.oneLine: Sugar, pressure, tobacco, clot and vein history, drugs, family, standing work and footwear
pitfalls: Recording the ulcer in detail while never asking about diabetes, so a neuropathic or infective component is missed.
Forgetting tobacco in chewed form, which many patients do not volunteer when asked only about smoking.
Missing a past deep vein thrombosis, which explains a venous ulcer in a leg with no visible varicosities.

probes.a: Diabetes with poor sugar control, which impairs healing and invites infection, and a past deep vein thrombosis, which damages valves and produces lasting venous hypertension.
probes.q: Name two background conditions that decide whether a leg ulcer will heal.

probes.a: Steroids and immunosuppressants delay healing, water tablets alter swelling, blood thinners affect bleeding, and caustic powders and oils applied to the wound can cause contact allergy and chemical injury.
probes.q: Why do you ask about medicines and about powders or oils applied to the wound?

probes.a: Long hours standing still, walking barefoot on rough ground, and open or ill fitting footwear that causes repeated minor trauma, all of which turn a fragile gaiter skin into a chronic ulcer.
probes.q: What work and footwear details matter in a venous or neuropathic ulcer?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
A leg ulcer is the visible end of a background process, so the history must name that process. Diabetes slows healing and invites infection, hypertension underlies the small vessel disease of a Martorell ulcer, and tobacco damages both arteries and skin healing.

Ask each of these directly. Patients rarely volunteer chewed tobacco, old water tablets, or a swollen leg years ago unless each is asked by name.
teach.heading: The background decides the healing

teach.body:
A past deep vein thrombosis destroys deep valves and leaves lasting venous hypertension, so a venous ulcer can arise in a leg with no visible varicose veins at all. Ask about a leg that once swelled painfully for weeks, a long hospital stay, or swelling first noticed in pregnancy.

Ask the same way about past sores on either leg, vein operations, and injection treatment, since a recurrent ulcer at the same site changes both the diagnosis and the plan.
teach.heading: An old clot explains a new ulcer

teach.body:
Record every medicine and every local application. Steroids and immunosuppressants delay healing, blood thinners change bleeding, and powders, oils and strong ointments can cause contact allergy that mimics a spreading ulcer.

Close with family, standing work, barefoot walking and footwear. Long hours standing still raise venous pressure, barefoot trauma seeds tropical and neuropathic ulcers, and tight or open footwear concentrates pressure on the same spot.
teach.heading: Drugs, dressings, family and feet

skill.hx.leg.risk.title: Risk factors in leg ulcer: veins, arteries, nerves and skin
skill.hx.leg.risk.why: The ulcer you see is the result of a background process you cannot see, and that process decides whether the wound will heal. Diabetes, an old deep vein thrombosis, tobacco in every form, and the drugs and dressings already tried each change the diagnosis or the plan, and none of them is visible on the leg.

skill.present.leg.ulcercase.oneLine: Patient, tempo, ulcer description, circulation and nerve status, diagnosis and plan

probes.a: The patient with venous risk factors, the tempo in months, the ulcer in abstract terms with site and edge, the arterial and nerve status, and the provisional diagnosis with red flags and the plan.
probes.q: What elements belong in a leg ulcer case summary?

probes.a: Whether arterial disease has been excluded by pulse examination and the ankle brachial index, because compression bandaging is unsafe until that question is answered.
probes.q: What is the one safety statement a leg ulcer presentation must never omit?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: Examination of an ulcer: case summary
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.body:
Open with the patient and the risks that matter: age, sex, standing work, varicose veins, an old clot, diabetes, tobacco. Then state the tempo: months of a non healing sore separates a venous ulcer from days of spreading infection.

Then describe the ulcer in abstract terms with site, size, edge, floor and surrounding skin, followed by the circulation and nerve status: pulses, colour and warmth, and sensation. End with the provisional diagnosis, red flags, and what is still missing.
teach.heading: Four sentences that contain the ulcer case

teach.body:
A 54 year old woman who stands all day selling vegetables presents with eight months of a painless oozing sore above the inner ankle. Examination shows a shallow ulcer with a sloping edge and pale granulation tissue, pigmented eczematous surrounding skin, palpable foot pulses, and normal sensation.

This is a venous leg ulcer pending duplex mapping and the ankle brachial index. No rolled edges, severe pain, or spreading redness are present, and compression awaits arterial exclusion.
teach.heading: A worked example

skill.present.leg.ulcercase.title: Presenting the leg ulcer case
skill.present.leg.ulcercase.why: A leg ulcer presentation fails when it describes the wound at length but never states whether the leg can safely be compressed. The listener needs the circulation and nerve status in the same breath as the ulcer description, because that combination is what makes the diagnosis and the next step obvious.

skill.hx.lymphadenopa.node_story.title: History of an enlarged lymph node
skill.hx.lymphadenopa.node_story.oneLine: Age, duration, pain, fever pattern, the primary focus and pressure effects
skill.hx.lymphadenopa.node_story.why: Most node diagnoses are already half made before touching the neck. A short painful history with a visible septic focus points one way, while months of painless growth with evening fever and weight loss points quite another, and the group first affected often names the cause.

asks.text: How old are you, and how long has this swelling been present: days, weeks or months?
Is the swelling painful or painless, and has the pain changed as the swelling grew?
Have you had fever with it: evening rise, periodic attacks, or prolonged bouts that come and go?
Is there any sore throat, tooth pain, scalp sore, skin cut, ulcer or discharge in the area that drains into these nodes?
Have you lost weight or appetite, had drenching sweats at night, or felt unusually tired for weeks?
Is there any pressure symptom: noisy or difficult breathing, trouble swallowing, change in voice, or swelling of the face?
Which group did you notice first, and have other groups in the neck, armpit or groin enlarged since?
Have you had tuberculosis, syphilis, filarial attacks or a similar swelling before, and is there tuberculosis at home?

teach.heading: Age and duration set the field
teach.body:
Tuberculous nodes and syphilis belong to the young, acute lymphadenitis can strike at any age, primary malignant lymphomas gather in the young adult, and secondary deposits favour the old. A history counted in days suggests acute infection, while one counted in months suggests tuberculosis or malignancy.

Ask which group enlarged first. Cervical nodes lead in Hodgkin disease and tuberculosis, while the groin leads in filariasis and venereal bubo, though this clue guides rather than decides.

teach.heading: Pain, fever and the primary focus
teach.body:
Painful nodes mean inflammation, whether acute or chronic. Painless nodes mean syphilis, primary lymphoma or secondary carcinoma until shown otherwise. Evening rise favours tuberculosis, periodic fever with pain favours filariasis, and intermittent prolonged bouts favour Hodgkin disease.

Always hunt the primary focus in the drainage territory: a septic throat, bad teeth, a scalp sore or a small cut can explain the whole illness, and finding it confirms acute or chronic septic adenitis.

teach.heading: Weight, sweats and pressure effects
points: Ask about weight loss, night sweats and persistent tiredness in every case: they mark tuberculosis, lymphoma and disseminated disease.
Ask about pressure effects of deep nodes: facial puffiness, breathlessness, dysphagia, voice change and limb swelling.
Ask past history of tuberculosis, syphilis and filariasis, and family history of tuberculosis running in the household.

probes.q: A neck swelling of three days is hot, red and exquisitely tender. What does the tempo and pain tell you?
probes.a: An acute inflammatory process, most likely acute lymphadenitis from a septic focus in the drainage area.

probes.q: Which fever patterns point towards tuberculosis, filariasis and Hodgkin disease?
probes.a: Evening rise in tuberculosis, periodic fever with pain in filariasis, and intermittent prolonged bouts of remittent fever in Hodgkin disease.

probes.q: Why must you ask which node group enlarged first?
probes.a: Because the first group hints at the cause: cervical first favours tuberculosis or Hodgkin disease, while inguinal first favours filariasis or venereal disease.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: The lymph nodes: history in lymphadenopathy

skill.hx.lymphadenopa.risk_factors.title: Past, personal, drug and family history in node enlargement
skill.hx.lymphadenopa.risk_factors.oneLine: Contacts, exposures, habits and drugs that change what a node means
skill.hx.lymphadenopa.risk_factors.why: Two identical necks mean different things in a student with a consumptive roommate and in a lifelong tobacco chewer. Contacts, occupation, exposures and a few drugs decide which cause climbs to the top of the list.

asks.text: Has anyone at home, in the hostel or at work had tuberculosis or a chronic cough, and have you been treated for tuberculosis before?
What work do you do: barefoot labour, farming, fishing, butchery or health work with exposure to cuts, cattle, fish or patients?
Do you smoke, chew tobacco, drink alcohol regularly, and have you had more than one sexual partner recently?
Have you lived in or visited a filarial belt, kept cats, suffered scratches or thorn pricks, or drunk unboiled milk?
Do you take regular medicines, especially drugs for fits, and have you had fever with rash or gum swelling since starting them?
Is there tuberculosis, lymphoma or cancer in the family, and which childhood immunisations did you receive?

teach.heading: Contacts and household
teach.body:
Ask every patient about tuberculosis contact at home, in the hostel or at work, and about their own past tuberculosis and its treatment. Tuberculosis runs in households, and a past episode makes relapse or nodal reactivation far more likely.

Ask about family tumours and lymphomas. A household with several consumptives, or a family with lymphoid tumours, changes the pre-test odds before a single test is ordered.

teach.heading: Work, habits and exposures
teach.body:
Barefoot walking on cracked earth seeds groin nodes in labourers, oral sepsis and scalp lesions seed cervical nodes, and fishing or butchery injuries seed regional nodes. Tobacco and alcohol raise the odds that a hard neck node in an older adult is metastatic.

Ask about filarial residence, cat scratches and thorn pricks, and recent sexual exposures, since bubo, cat scratch disease and secondary syphilis each need their own question to surface.

teach.heading: Drugs that enlarge nodes
points: Ask about regular medicines, particularly drugs taken for fits, which are a classic cause of generalised nodal enlargement.
Ask about recent vaccination, serum or new drugs where nodes followed within weeks.
Record BCG and childhood immunisation where tuberculosis is in the differential, without over reading the scar.

probes.q: Name three exposures you must ask about in every enlarged node.
probes.a: Tuberculosis contact, occupation and barefoot exposure, and tobacco, alcohol or sexual exposures.

probes.q: Why do you ask a young man with groin nodes about his feet and his sexual history?
probes.a: Because infected cracks from barefoot walking cause chronic septic adenitis, while venereal bubo and primary syphilis present in the groin.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: The lymph nodes: past and personal history

skill.present.lymphadenopa.summary.title: Presenting the lymphadenopathy case
skill.present.lymphadenopa.summary.oneLine: Patient, tempo, node description, spread and provisional diagnosis
skill.present.lymphadenopa.summary.why: A node case is presented as a story of spread: who the patient is, how long the nodes have grown, exactly what the fingers found, how far the disease has travelled, and what it most likely is. Without that order the listener cannot judge urgency or the next step.

teach.heading: Four sentences that contain the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with the risks that matter: age, occupation, tuberculosis contact and habits. Then state the tempo: days of painful swelling versus months of painless growth.

Then describe the nodes in abstract terms: site and group, size, number, consistency, matting, fixity, skin and sinus. End with spread: other groups, liver, spleen and pressure effects, and the provisional diagnosis with what would confirm it.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 19 year old male student, with a consumptive roommate, presents with two months of painless right neck swelling with evening fever and weight loss. Examination shows multiple matted firm right deep cervical nodes with a fluctuant area and a healing sinus, with no other groups and no liver or spleen enlargement.

This is tuberculous lymphadenitis with cold abscess formation, awaiting needle sampling and molecular confirmation, for antitubercular treatment under the national programme.

probes.q: What elements belong in a lymphadenopathy summary?
probes.a: The patient with relevant risks, the tempo, the node description with consistency and fixity, the spread to other groups and organs, and the provisional diagnosis.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.obstructive.jaundice.title: History of jaundice in a surgical patient
skill.hx.obstructive.jaundice.oneLine: Painful and intermittent points to stone, painless and progressive to growth
skill.hx.obstructive.jaundice.why: In a jaundiced surgical patient three answers carry the whole differential: whether the yellow colour deepens steadily or comes and goes, whether pain travels with it, and whether fever with shivering joins the attacks. Those three answers separate a stone that shifts in the duct from a growth that tightens around it, before a hand is laid on the abdomen.

asks.text: When did you first notice the yellow colour in the eyes or urine, and has it deepened steadily week by week or faded and returned?
Is the jaundice painful or painless? Does pain come in attacks in the right upper abdomen, going through to the back or the right shoulder?
Do you itch, especially on the palms and soles or at night, and have you scratched until the skin broke?
Has your urine turned dark like strong tea while the stool turned pale like clay, and have the motions become bulky, pale and foul smelling?
Have you had fever with shivering or shaking chills alongside the yellow colour, and has any attack needed hospital admission?

teach.heading: Painless and progressive points to growth, painful and intermittent to stone
teach.body:
Ask first about pain and course together, since the pair is more telling than either alone. Painful jaundice that follows attacks of upper abdominal colic and then fades belongs to a stone in the common bile duct, while painless jaundice that deepens week by week without relief belongs to a growth at the head of the pancreas, the ampulla or the bile duct itself.

Fever with rigors riding on top of pain and jaundice means infection behind the block and changes the urgency entirely. That trio should be named the moment it appears, because it calls for admission and drainage rather than routine work-up.

teach.heading: Stone jaundice and growth jaundice side by side

rows: Colicky attacks before and with the jaundice
Painless, or a dull constant ache late

teach.heading: Urine, stool and itch place the block below the liver
teach.body:
Dark urine with pale stools means conjugated bilirubin is reaching blood but not gut, which is the signature of obstruction rather than liver cell failure. Ask about the stool in plain words, since few patients volunteer that the motion has turned white unless asked directly.

Itching comes from bile salts held back in the blood and can precede any visible yellow by days. Scratch marks on the chest, back and limbs may then be the first sign on examination, so the history of itch should always be followed by a deliberate look at the skin in daylight.

probes.q: What three features in the history of jaundice separate a stone from a growth?
probes.a: Whether pain travels with the jaundice, whether the course is intermittent or steadily progressive, and whether the gallbladder is palpable later on examination. Painful intermittent jaundice favours a stone, painless progressive jaundice favours a growth.

probes.q: A patient reports jaundice that faded for two weeks and then returned. Does that exclude a growth?
probes.a: No. Jaundice from a growth at the ampulla can ease briefly when part of the tumour sloughs and the passage opens, then deepen again. Intermittent jaundice favours a stone but never proves one, and the rest of the picture still decides.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.obstructive.risk.title: Risk factors and background in biliary obstruction
skill.hx.obstructive.risk.oneLine: Stones have company, growths have warnings, and the past rewrites both
skill.hx.obstructive.risk.why: The same yellow patient means something different with a decade of gallstone attacks behind them, a cholecystectomy scar on the abdomen, or a family where gallstones struck young. Risk factors set the pre-test probability before the examination begins, and past operations and drugs decide which investigations are safe to order next.

asks.text: Have you had attacks of upper abdominal pain after fatty food before, or has anyone told you that you carry gallstones?
Have you had fever with shivering alongside the yellow colour before, or any operation on the gallbladder or bile duct, including keyhole surgery or endoscopy?
What medicines do you take every day, including pills for tuberculosis, fits, hormones or herbal preparations, and how much alcohol do you drink in a week?
Has anyone in your family needed gallstone surgery young, had jaundice in pregnancy, or liver disease that ran in the family?

teach.heading: Stones have company: who gets calculous jaundice
teach.body:
Middle-aged women, obesity, rapid weight loss and repeated pregnancies all raise the chance that a blocked duct is blocked by a stone, as does a long story of flatulent dyspepsia with pain after fatty food. Chronic haemolysis, biliary infection and parasites produce pigment stones by a different route and matter in patients from endemic belts.

A previous attack of acute cholecystitis leaves a scarred, fibrotic gallbladder that cannot distend, which is exactly why the gallbladder stays impalpable when a stone later blocks the duct. Ask for that past attack in every patient, since it explains the examination before it happens.

teach.heading: Age, weight loss and anorexia warn of a growth
teach.body:
A new, painless, deepening jaundice in an older patient with steady weight loss and loss of appetite should be treated as malignant until proved otherwise. New back pain passing through from the upper abdomen, new diabetes or an attack that looks like pancreatitis in an older patient all raise the same warning.

Inflammatory bowel disease points toward sclerosing cholangitis rather than a stone, and an old cholecystectomy with a clip or stricture history points toward a benign postoperative narrowing. Both change the choice of the next investigation.

teach.heading: Past, drug and family history that changes the plan
points: Earlier endoscopy with a cut at the papilla or a stent in the duct, and any earlier cholecystectomy, since retained or reformed stones and strictures follow procedures.
Drugs that injure bile flow, so list every regular tablet rather than accepting that the patient takes nothing.
Alcohol in honest weekly amounts, smoking, and diabetes, which colour both fitness for surgery and the risk of pancreatic disease.

Family gallstones at a young age, jaundice in pregnancy, or inherited bile disorders, which should raise the thought of an ABCB4-related low-phospholipid stone syndrome and referral for family testing.

probes.q: Why do you ask about a past attack of cholecystitis in a patient with a suspected duct stone?
probes.a: A past attack leaves a scarred fibrotic gallbladder that cannot distend, which explains why the gallbladder stays impalpable when a stone blocks the duct, and it confirms the stone-forming background.

probes.q: A young adult has repeated gallstones and a sister who had jaundice in pregnancy. What inherited thread do you consider?
probes.a: An ABCB4-related bile disorder of the low-phospholipid stone spectrum, which runs in families, produces cholesterol stones and intrahepatic lithiasis, and needs genetic counselling and family testing rather than surgery alone.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.obstructive.summary.title: Presenting the surgical jaundice case
skill.present.obstructive.summary.oneLine: Tempo, discriminators, Courvoisier status, level, cause and plan in six sentences
skill.present.obstructive.summary.why: A jaundice presentation fails when it lists findings without committing: the consultant needs the tempo, the two or three discriminators that split stone from growth, the state of the gallbladder, and a named level and likely cause with the next investigation. Six sentences in that order carry the whole case and invite exactly one question, which test of the diagnosis comes first.

teach.heading: Six sentences carry the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with age and background, then state the tempo in one clause: painless and progressive over weeks, or painful and intermittent over months. Name the syndrome next in abstract terms, an extrahepatic biliary obstruction with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, rather than reciting every symptom.

Then give the discriminators that split the causes: state of the gallbladder, fever pattern, weight and appetite, and the urine and stool change. Close with the provisional level and cause, the fitness for procedure, and the single next step, usually an ultrasound already done and the scan that must follow.

teach.heading: A worked presentation
teach.body:
A 58 year old farmer presents with six weeks of painless, steadily deepening jaundice with itching, pale stools and dark urine, with anorexia and steady weight loss. Examination shows deep icterus with scratch marks and a smooth, non-tender, palpable gallbladder moving with respiration, with no fever at any stage.

This is an extrahepatic biliary obstruction, clinically malignant with a positive Courvoisier sign, most likely a periampullary growth. He is fit with normal cardiorespiratory reserve, and the next step is contrast imaging with MRCP to define the level and stage before hepatobiliary referral.

probes.q: What must a surgical jaundice summary contain that a medical jaundice summary may omit?
probes.a: The tempo as painful intermittent or painless progressive, the state of the gallbladder with the Courvoisier reading, a named level and likely cause, and the fitness and next procedural step, since the endpoint is an intervention rather than a prescription.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.peripheral.risk.abnormal: Heavy beedi use, long-standing poorly controlled diabetes, hypertension, past heart attack or stroke, and a family history of early vascular disease all raise the prior probability of arterial disease and of a poor outcome.

asks.text: How many beedis or cigarettes do you smoke each day, and since what age?
Do you have diabetes? Since when, what treatment do you take, and was your last sugar controlled?
Do you have high blood pressure, and do you take its tablets regularly?
Have you ever had a heart attack, angina, a stroke, or a clot in the leg or lung?
Has anyone in your family lost a toe, foot or leg to poor blood supply or diabetes?
Do you walk barefoot, and how do you cut your toenails?

skill.hx.peripheral.risk.normal: No tobacco use, no diabetes, blood pressure normal on treatment, no past heart attack or stroke, and no family history of early vascular disease or amputation.
skill.hx.peripheral.risk.oneLine: The risk factors that decide how likely arterial disease is before the leg is examined

probes.a: Beedi or cigarette smoking, diabetes, hypertension, past heart attack or stroke, and a family history of early vascular disease or amputation.
probes.q: Name four risk factors you must ask about in every suspected ischaemic limb.

probes.a: Because beedis deliver the same arterial injury as cigarettes, dose and duration set the risk, and quitting is the single most effective treatment for claudication distance and graft survival.
probes.q: Why do you count beedis separately instead of writing smoking as yes or no?

probes.a: Ask when the diabetes was found, what drugs or insulin are taken and whether doses are missed, and what the last fasting sugar or HbA1c showed, since uncontrolled sugar drives both atherosclerosis and poor healing of any foot wound.
probes.q: What exactly do you ask a diabetic patient beyond do you have sugar?

skill.hx.peripheral.risk.significance: Risk factors do two jobs at once: they raise the probability that leg pain is arterial, and they decide the treatment, since revascularisation fails early in a patient who keeps smoking with uncontrolled sugar.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: Arterial disease: risk factors and prevention
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Four exposures cause most peripheral arterial disease in Indian practice: tobacco (beedis included), diabetes, hypertension, and disturbed lipids. Each multiplies the others, so a diabetic beedi smoker with hypertension carries many times the risk of a patient with one factor alone.

Ask every factor in every case, even when the leg already looks gangrenous. The risk history decides the diagnosis in an atypical limb and decides the treatment in every limb, because bypass grafts and angioplasties block early in patients who keep smoking.
teach.heading: Four exposures cause most disease

teach.body:
Count tobacco as dose times duration: how many beedis or cigarettes a day, since what age, and whether the patient still smokes. A bundle-a-day habit since youth is the commonest history behind Buerger disease in young men, and continued smoking is the commonest reason a claudicant deteriorates.

Record diabetes the same way: age at detection, tablets or insulin with missed doses admitted honestly, and the last fasting sugar. Barefoot walking and careless nail paring then complete the diabetic foot story, since trivial trauma starts the ulcer that ischaemia prevents from healing.
teach.heading: Dose and duration, not yes or no

teach.body:
Ask about the heart, brain and the other leg in the same breath: angina or heart attack, stroke or transient weakness, and claudication or coldness in the opposite limb. Atherosclerosis is a generalised disease, and the patient who presents with a toe may die of the coronary artery.

Finish with family: early heart attacks, strokes, or amputations in parents and siblings. Familial predisposition is reported in Buerger disease, and a young non-smoker with claudication needs a different differential from a sixty-year-old diabetic smoker.
teach.heading: Heart, brain, other leg, family

skill.hx.peripheral.risk.title: Risk-factor history in the ischaemic limb
skill.hx.peripheral.risk.why: The risk history sets the prior probability of arterial disease before the leg is touched, and it decides the treatment afterwards, since no revascularisation survives continued smoking with uncontrolled diabetes.

skill.present.peripheral.padcase.oneLine: Present the ischaemic limb: tempo, level, stage and plan in under three minutes

probes.a: Age and risk factors, tempo from claudication to rest pain to tissue loss, level of pulses and key bedside findings, ABPI and imaging, Fontaine or Rutherford stage, and the plan including revascularisation and foot care.
probes.q: What six elements must every ischaemic limb presentation contain?

probes.a: Because the stage decides the treatment: claudication is exercised and risk-managed, rest pain and tissue loss need urgent revascularisation, and a threatened limb cannot wait for the next routine list.
probes.q: Why do you state the Fontaine or Rutherford stage out loud in the summary?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: History and examination of arterial disease
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.body:
Open with the patient and the risks in one sentence: a 62 year old diabetic beedi smoker with two years of calf pain on walking. That single line tells the consultant the tempo and the cause before any finding is mentioned.

Then walk the story forward in time: claudication distance shrinking month by month, night pain relieved by hanging the foot down, then blackening of the toe. Tempo is the diagnosis in arterial disease: gradual means atherosclerosis, sudden means embolus.
teach.heading: One line for the patient, then the tempo

teach.body:
Give the level before the lesion: femoral present, popliteal weak, tibial and dorsalis pedis absent, with a vascular angle under 30 degrees and an ABPI under 0.5. Findings read proximal to distal, pulses before skin changes, measurements before adjectives.

Close with stage and plan: Fontaine stage IV chronic limb threatening ischaemia with dry gangrene of the great toe, for urgent vascular referral, risk factor control, and foot care with a guarded prognosis for the toe already lost.
teach.heading: Level, measurements, stage, plan

skill.present.peripheral.padcase.title: Presenting the ischaemic limb case
skill.present.peripheral.padcase.why: A consultant judges an ischaemic limb presentation by whether the tempo, the level of disease, the stage and the urgency all appear in order, since each decides a different part of the plan.

skill.hx.peritonitis.risk.title: Ulcer past and perforation risk in the acute abdomen
skill.hx.peritonitis.risk.oneLine: Hunger pains, painkillers and old bleeding that explain why this ulcer gave way
skill.hx.peritonitis.risk.why: Most perforated ulcers do not arrive without warning. A past of rhythmic hunger pains, painkiller use or an old bleed turns a sudden catastrophe into the expected end of a known disease, and each of these facts changes what you do after the operation.

asks.text: Ask about rhythmic upper abdominal pain in the past months or years, and what relieved it.
Ask about regular painkiller tablets, especially for joint or back pain, taken without stomach protection.
Ask about smoking bidis or cigarettes, alcohol use, and irregular or missed meals.
Ask about any previous vomiting of blood or black stools, and any past treatment for ulcer.
Ask about known diabetes, steroid tablets, and any previous abdominal operation.

teach.heading: The past that predicts the perforation
teach.body:
Ask every acute abdomen with upper abdominal pain about earlier ulcer type pain. Hunger pains that woke the patient at night, burning pain eased by food or antacids, and pain returning in episodes over months are the classic past of a chronic duodenal ulcer.

Many patients ignored these episodes or treated them with tablets from a chemist. That neglected past is exactly why the perforation happened, and it also tells you the ulcer is chronic, which matters for the definitive plan later.

teach.heading: Painkillers, smoke and drink
teach.body:
Ask directly about painkiller tablets taken regularly for joint pain, backache or headache. Self taken anti inflammatory drugs without food or stomach protection are among the commonest precipitants of perforation in Indian practice.

Ask about bidi or cigarette smoking and regular alcohol in the same breath. Both delay ulcer healing and both raise the chance that an ulcer bleeds or perforates rather than healing quietly.

teach.heading: Old bleeding and old treatment
points: Vomiting of blood or black tarry stools in the past means the same ulcer has already bled once, and the disease is proven chronic.
Ask whether the patient ever took a course of tablets for ulcer or for H pylori, and whether it was completed.
Ask about diabetes and steroid tablets, since both impair healing and worsen infection.
Ask about any previous abdominal operation, since old scars change both the examination and the operative plan.

probes.q: What past pain history points to a chronic duodenal ulcer behind a perforation?
probes.a: Rhythmic hunger pains over months, waking at night, eased by food or antacids, returning in episodes.

probes.q: Which two habits or drugs most raise the risk that an ulcer perforates?
probes.a: Regular painkiller tablets taken without protection, and smoking with regular alcohol use.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.present.peritonitis.summary.title: Summarising the perforation case
skill.present.peritonitis.summary.oneLine: Tempo, peritoneal signs, gas under the diaphragm, and the clock that is running
skill.present.peritonitis.summary.why: A perforation summary is judged on whether the listener feels the urgency. Tempo first, then the two bedside proofs of perforation, then the film, then the plan, all inside a minute, because this is a disease measured in hours.

teach.heading: The order that carries urgency
teach.body:
Open with the patient and the tempo in one sentence: a middle aged man with sudden severe upper abdominal pain of a few hours. Then name the syndrome in abstract terms: an acute abdomen with generalised peritonitis.

Follow with the examination proofs: board like rigidity, absent bowel sounds, and loss of liver dullness. Then the investigation that confirms: gas under the diaphragm on erect film. Close with the diagnosis and the immediate plan.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 48 year old mason presents with sudden stabbing upper abdominal pain of six hours, now spread all over the abdomen, with one episode of vomiting and no flatus since. He gives a past of hunger pains relieved by food and daily painkiller tablets.

On examination he lies still, the abdomen is rigid like a board with rebound tenderness, bowel sounds are absent, and liver dullness is obliterated. Erect chest film shows free gas under the right diaphragm. This is generalised peritonitis due to perforated peptic ulcer, for urgent resuscitation and laparotomy.

teach.heading: What never to leave out
points: The tempo in hours, since it separates perforation from slower surgical illness.
The ulcer past and the painkiller history, since they explain the cause.
Relevant negatives: no distension early, no previous similar catastrophe, no chest findings that suggest a thoracic mimic.
The resuscitation state: pulse, pressure, urine output, and what fluids and antibiotics have started.

probes.q: What four elements must a perforation summary contain in order?
probes.a: Tempo in hours, the peritoneal examination proofs, the confirmatory film finding, and the immediate resuscitation and operative plan.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.renal.risk.title: Stone risk: past, personal, drug and family history
skill.hx.renal.risk.oneLine: The background that makes a stone likely, and the causes worth treating
skill.hx.renal.risk.why: A first stone is often treated as bad luck, but recurrence is the rule when the background is ignored. Low fluid intake, gout and the metabolic syndrome, a high purine diet, chronic bowel fluid loss, and some drugs each point to a cause that can be treated, so this history decides the prevention plan as much as the scans do.

asks.text: Have you ever passed a stone before, or seen blood or grit in the urine? Was a stone ever analysed, and what treatment followed?
Do your joints ever swell painfully, especially the big toe? Have you been told you have gout, diabetes, or high uric acid?
How much water do you drink in a day, and what colour is your urine by evening? Do you work long hours in heat without drinking?
What do you eat most days: how often meat, offal, or beer, and how much salt? Have you lost or gained weight recently?
Do you have chronic loose motions or bowel disease, and have you had bowel surgery? Do you take water tablets, excess vitamin C, calcium or antacid tablets, or treatment for gout?
Has anyone in your family had kidney stones, gout, or kidney failure? At what age did their trouble start?

teach.heading: A past stone is the strongest predictor
teach.body:
Ask every patient with loin pain about earlier colic, passage of grit or a stone, and any prior analysis or procedure. A stone that was never analysed is unfinished business: composition decides whether dissolution, diet change, or a drug has a role.

Recurrence clusters in families and in hot climates where fluid intake lags behind sweat loss. A young patient with repeated stones needs a metabolic workup, not reassurance.

teach.heading: The metabolic cluster behind uric acid stones
teach.body:
Gout, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and the metabolic syndrome travel with persistently acidic urine, and acidic urine is what lets uric acid crystallise. Ask about joint attacks, thirst and weight, and check for diabetes where the story suggests it.

High purine intake from meat and rapid cell turnover add urate load. Chronic diarrhoea depletes volume and alkali together, which concentrates the urine and keeps it acidic.

teach.heading: Drugs, bowel loss, and family
teach.body:
Some drugs raise stone risk: thiazide-like water tablets alter calcium handling, excess vitamin C can convert to oxalate, and calcium-based antacids add load. Starting allopurinol during an acute gout attack without cover can worsen the joint, a separate trap worth knowing.

Ask about bowel disease and resection, which waste fluid and alkali. A family history of stones, gout, or early kidney failure marks a patient for full metabolic study rather than a single episode of care.

probes.q: Name three background factors that raise the risk of a uric acid stone.
probes.a: Persistently acidic urine, low fluid intake with concentrated urine, and gout or the metabolic syndrome with diabetes and obesity.

probes.q: Why does chronic diarrhoea predispose to uric acid stones?
probes.a: It causes volume depletion with alkali loss, leaving a scanty, concentrated, persistently acidic urine, which favours uric acid crystallisation.

probes.q: A 30-year-old has passed three stones in two years. What does the history need to establish?
probes.a: Stone composition from analysis, fluid intake and heat exposure, purine diet, gout and diabetes, bowel disease, relevant drugs, and a family history of stones or kidney failure, leading to a full metabolic evaluation.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
sources.locator: Urinary stone disease: risk factors and prevention

skill.present.renal.summary.title: Presenting the renal colic case
skill.present.renal.summary.oneLine: Three sentences that carry the patient, the syndrome, and the plan
skill.present.renal.summary.why: A colic presentation fails when it becomes a list of pain adjectives with no syndrome, no severity, and no plan. The consultant needs the tempo, the radiation path, the stone evidence, and whether infection or obstruction makes this an emergency, in under a minute.

teach.heading: The shape of the summary
teach.body:
Name the patient with the risk background, state the tempo as sudden colicky episodes with pain-free gaps, describe the syndrome in abstract terms with its radiation path, and close with severity and plan.

A worked example: a 38-year-old truck driver with low daily fluid intake presents with sudden severe left loin pain radiating to the groin in waves, with vomiting and blood in the urine. Examination shows a restless patient with left renal angle tenderness and no guarding or fever. This is a left ureteric stone with mild hydronephrosis on imaging, uncomplicated, for analgesia, fluids, medical expulsive therapy, and planned review for passage.

teach.heading: What must never be missing
points: Tempo and behaviour: sudden, colicky, restless between waves, pain-free intervals.
Radiation path stated plainly: loin to groin, and what the level of the stone suggests.
Relevant positives and negatives: haematuria and strangury present; fever, rigors, guarding, and anuria absent.
Stone evidence: imaging finding with size and site, urine pH, and whether infection markers are present.
Plan in one line: analgesia, fluids, expulsive therapy or intervention, and how passage will be confirmed.

probes.q: What five elements belong in a renal colic case summary?
probes.a: The patient with risk background, the sudden colicky tempo, the syndrome with its radiation path, the stone evidence from imaging, and the severity with the plan.

probes.q: Why do the negatives matter as much as the positives in this summary?
probes.a: Absence of fever, guarding, and anuria is what keeps the case uncomplicated and suitable for conservative care; their presence would convert it into an emergency needing drainage.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.sinus.riskfactors.title: Past, personal, drug and family history in sinus and fistula disease
skill.hx.sinus.riskfactors.oneLine: The background illnesses and drugs that keep a track open
skill.hx.sinus.riskfactors.why: A sinus or fistula persists because something keeps it open, and that something is usually in the past history rather than at the opening itself: tuberculosis, diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, a retained suture or mesh, or a drug that slows healing. Missing this history means treating the track while the cause continues.

asks.text: Ask about past or household tuberculosis: prolonged cough, evening fever, night sweats, weight loss, lymph node swellings, bone or joint tuberculosis, and antitubercular treatment taken, including whether the full course was completed.
Ask about diabetes and recurrent skin sepsis: known diabetes, excessive thirst and urination, recurrent boils, carbuncles or perianal abscesses, and the most recent blood sugar value if tested.
Ask about bowel symptoms that point to Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis: chronic diarrhoea, blood or mucus in the stool, mouth ulcers, weight loss, and any previous colonoscopy or bowel surgery.
Ask about every previous operation, drainage procedure, implant, mesh repair, suture material left in the wound, fracture fixation device, and any bone chips or discharge of bony particles since.
Take a full drug history: steroids, immunosuppressants, anticancer drugs, recent prolonged antibiotics, and native or over the counter medicines applied to the wound.

Ask about personal habits and nutrition: smoking, chewing tobacco, alcohol use, occupation with exposure to dust or minor trauma, footwear and foot care where the leg is involved, and recent weight change.
Ask the family history: tuberculosis, inflammatory bowel disease, or fistula in ano in close relatives, and living conditions that favour spread of tuberculosis.

teach.heading: Why the past history decides the fate of the track
teach.body:
A fresh sinus from a drained pyogenic abscess usually closes once the cavity collapses and the cause is gone. A sinus that has discharged for months has a keeper, and the keeper is named in the past history far more often than at the bedside.

Tuberculosis, retained dead bone or suture material, Crohn disease, actinomycosis, diabetes with poor control, and continued pressure or movement at the site are the usual keepers. Each one changes the plan completely, from sequestrectomy to antitubercular therapy to bowel workup.

teach.heading: Drugs and habits that hold healing back
teach.body:
Steroids and immunosuppressants blunt the inflammatory response that walls off infection, so abscesses in these patients spread quietly and sinuses close slowly. Prolonged unguided antibiotics select resistant organisms while the deep nidus survives untouched.

Smoking impairs small vessel flow to healing tissue, and protein energy undernutrition does the same from the inside. Both are correctable, and both should be recorded and addressed rather than merely noted.

teach.heading: Family history is an exposure history here
points: Tuberculosis in a household contact raises the prior probability that a chronic cold sinus is tuberculous, and should trigger a contact and BCG history in children.
Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis cluster in families, so bowel symptoms in a relative strengthen the case for colonoscopy in complex perianal fistulae.
Fistula in ano itself is seen in more than one member of a family often enough that the question is worth asking directly.
Record who gave the history and how reliable it is, since operative details from years ago are often approximate.

probes.q: Name four background conditions you must ask about in every chronic discharging sinus.
probes.a: Tuberculosis, diabetes mellitus, inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn disease, and actinomycosis, plus any previous operation with retained material.

probes.q: Why do you ask about steroids and immunosuppressants in a patient with a persistent sinus?
probes.a: Because they blunt the inflammatory response that walls off infection, so abscesses spread quietly and sinuses close slowly while the drug continues.

probes.q: A young man has complex multiple perianal fistulae. His brother has chronic diarrhoea with blood. What does the family history change?
probes.a: It raises Crohn disease as the shared cause, so the patient needs bowel assessment with colonoscopy and the fistulae should not be laid open as if they were simple cryptoglandular ones.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.sinus.summary.title: Summarising the sinus or fistula case
skill.present.sinus.summary.oneLine: Site, track, keeper and state, in one breath
skill.present.sinus.summary.why: A sinus case summary fails when it lists the discharge but never names the keeper of the track. The listener needs the anatomy of the lesion, the cause that keeps it open, and the current state of activity, because each one points to a different operation or drug.

teach.heading: A fixed order for every sinus summary
points: Open with the patient and the tempo: age, occupation, and how many weeks or months the discharge has lasted.
State the anatomy: single or multiple openings, exact site, and whether it is a blind sinus or a communicating fistula with what leaks through it.
Name the keeper: sequestrum, retained suture or mesh, tuberculosis, Crohn disease, pilonidal disease, or none found yet.

Close with the state of activity and the plan: active inflammation with fever and cellulitis, or quiet chronic discharge, then the investigation that proves the keeper and the operation or drug that removes it.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 34 year old sugarcane cutter presents with a single discharging sinus over the middle third of the left shin for eighteen months, following an open fracture fixed with a rod. The discharge is purulent with occasional bony particles, the track is fixed to irregular thickened tibia, and a probe strikes bare gritty bone.

This is a chronic osteomyelitic sinus kept open by dead bone, currently in an active flare with fever and surrounding cellulitis. The plan is a radiograph for sequestrum, pus culture, sugar testing, then sequestrectomy with saucerisation once the flare settles.

teach.heading: What to leave out
teach.body:
Leave out the full dressing chronology, every normal systemic finding, and the entire drug list. Keep one line for relevant negatives: no bowel symptoms, no diabetic history, no household tuberculosis contact.

End with the question the summary answers: what keeps this track open, and what will close it. If the summary cannot answer that, the workup is not finished.

probes.q: What four elements must a sinus case summary contain, in order?
probes.a: The patient with tempo, the anatomy of the track, the keeper that holds it open, and the current state of activity with the plan.

probes.q: Why does the summary name the keeper rather than just describing the discharge?
probes.a: Because the discharge looks similar whatever the cause, while the keeper decides the treatment: dead bone needs removal, tuberculosis needs drugs, and a fistula needs its abnormal passage made patent or repaired.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease
sources.locator: Examination of a sinus or fistula

skill.hx.oesophagus.risk.title: Risk factors and background history in carcinoma oesophagus
skill.hx.oesophagus.risk.oneLine: Tobacco, alcohol and diet exposures, predisposing oesophageal disease, and family history
skill.hx.oesophagus.risk.why: Carcinoma of the oesophagus is strongly linked to exposures the patient can report and to long standing oesophageal disease already in the notes. Asking about them takes two minutes, separates a high risk from a low risk story, and tells you which relatives need counselling about the same habits.

asks.text: Do you smoke bidis or cigarettes, chew tobacco, gutka or betel nut, and for how many years? How much alcohol do you drink each week?
Do you drink very hot tea or food, and what does your daily diet look like, especially fresh fruit and vegetables?
Have you had heartburn or acid coming up for many years, difficulty swallowing in the past, or treatment for achalasia or a long standing narrowing of the food pipe?
Have you ever swallowed a corrosive such as acid or alkali, received radiation to the chest or neck, or had repeated instrumentation of the gullet?
Have you been told you are anaemic or low in iron, with a sore tongue or brittle nails, and is there any cancer of the food pipe or stomach in the family?
What medicines do you take regularly for acidity or pain, and have you lost weight or changed what you eat because of swallowing trouble?

teach.heading: Why exposure history matters here
teach.body: Most squamous cancers of the gullet follow years of injury to its lining. Tobacco and alcohol act together, so the combined habit carries far more weight than either alone. Chewed tobacco with areca nut, frequent very hot drinks, and old corrosive burns each add their own risk, and all of them are common in Indian practice.

teach.heading: Ask about tobacco, alcohol and heat in every case
points: Smoke: bidis as well as cigarettes, number per day and years of use; chewing: tobacco, gutka, betel nut with areca.
Alcohol: type, amount and years; ask about both together, since the two potentiate each other.
Heat: habitually drinking tea or food scalding hot, a repeated thermal injury to the lining.
Diet: low intake of fresh fruit and vegetables goes with higher risk; record what the patient actually eats.

teach.heading: Diseases that predispose to cancer
points: Long standing achalasia: stagnant food and chronic irritation over many years.
Plummer-Vinson pattern: iron deficiency with webs in the upper gullet, a recognised precancerous setting.
Old corrosive stricture and prior chest radiation: both leave scarred lining that can turn malignant decades later.
Chronic reflux with Barrett change: the main background for adenocarcinoma near the junction with the stomach.

teach.heading: Drugs, weight and family
teach.body: Record regular antacids and acid suppressing medicines, since they may have masked years of reflux. Ask about painkillers that injure the lining. Document weight loss with dates, any change in diet texture to cope, and cancers of the gullet or stomach in close relatives.

pitfalls: Asking only about cigarettes and missing bidi smoking, tobacco chewing and areca nut, which dominate the exposure in many Indian patients.
Forgetting to ask about scalding hot tea, an exposure the patient will not volunteer unless asked directly.
Skipping the corrosive and radiation history because it was decades ago, when that long interval is exactly the pattern.

probes.q: Name four exposures or background conditions that raise the risk of squamous carcinoma of the oesophagus.
probes.a: Tobacco smoking or chewing, alcohol use, very hot beverages, areca nut chewing, long standing achalasia, Plummer-Vinson syndrome with iron deficiency, old corrosive stricture, and prior radiation.

probes.q: A 62 year old man chews tobacco and drinks alcohol daily. Why does the combination matter more than either habit alone?
probes.a: Alcohol and tobacco act synergistically on the oesophageal lining, so the combined habit multiplies the risk of squamous carcinoma rather than simply adding to it.

probes.q: Which reflux related change in the lower gullet predisposes to adenocarcinoma, and what history points to it?
probes.a: Barrett metaplasia from years of gastro-oesophageal reflux: long standing heartburn and regurgitation, often masked by regular antacid or acid suppressing treatment.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.approach.surg.intimate_chaperone.title: Intimate surgical examination: chaperone, informed consent and respectful exposure
skill.approach.surg.intimate_chaperone.oneLine: Explain the examination, secure verbal consent, arrange an independent chaperone, and maintain privacy
skill.approach.surg.intimate_chaperone.why: Intimate surgical examination of the breast, groin, genitalia, or anorectum without an independent chaperone and informed consent breaches professional standards, increases patient anxiety, and leaves both clinician and patient unprotected.

steps.text: Introduce yourself clearly, confirm patient identity, and explain the precise clinical indication for the intimate examination.
Explain exactly what the examination involves, including the anatomical structures to be inspected and palpated, and the expected duration.
Obtain explicit voluntary verbal consent, confirming that the patient understands they may ask questions or pause the examination at any stage.
Offer and summon an independent healthcare chaperone (nurse or female attendant), recording the chaperone name and professional role.
Ensure complete privacy by drawing curtains, closing examination room doors, and providing a clean sheet or gown.
Expose only the specific anatomical area under direct examination, keeping all other areas draped until examination begins and promptly covering when finished.

skill.approach.surg.intimate_chaperone.practice: Rehearse requesting a chaperone and explaining an intimate groin or rectal examination with a colleague in 45 seconds without using technical medical jargon.
pitfalls: Proceeding with an intimate examination without offering or documenting an independent healthcare chaperone.
Allowing an accompanied family member to act as the official chaperone instead of a neutral healthcare worker.
Uncovering the patient completely rather than exposing only the region being actively examined.
Failing to explain what you are about to do before touching sensitive anatomical areas.

probes.q: Why is an independent healthcare chaperone required during an intimate surgical examination?
probes.a: A chaperone provides emotional support to the patient, safeguards patient dignity, and protects the clinician against misunderstanding or false allegations.

probes.q: Can a family member or friend of the patient serve as the formal chaperone?
probes.a: No, a formal chaperone should be a qualified healthcare professional who understands the clinical examination and can witness that it was conducted appropriately.

probes.q: What should the clinician do if a patient declines an intimate examination when a chaperone is present?
probes.a: Respect the patient refusal, explore their concerns, explain the clinical consequences of not examining, document the refusal, and offer alternative options.

probes.q: What specific documentation is required in the surgical record after an intimate examination?
probes.a: Document that consent was obtained, the identity and designation of the chaperone, the presence of the chaperone throughout, and key physical findings.

rubric.text: Explains the clinical necessity and nature of the intimate examination clearly
Obtains explicit voluntary verbal consent before touching the patient
Offers and arranges an independent healthcare chaperone and documents their presence
Ensures physical visual privacy with screens, curtains, and closed doors
Drapes the patient with a clean sheet, exposing only the region under active evaluation
Maintains continuous professional communication, warning before touching and allowing questions

teach.heading: Principles of chaperone and intimate surgical examination
teach.body:
An intimate examination includes physical evaluation of the breasts, genitalia, groin, and perineum or anorectum. These examinations can evoke significant emotional vulnerability, anxiety, or embarrassment.

A qualified chaperone is a healthcare worker such as a staff nurse or resident doctor who understands the professional boundaries of physical examination.

skill.approach.surg.consent_operation.title: Informed consent for an emergency or elective surgical operation
skill.approach.surg.consent_operation.oneLine: Assess capacity, explain diagnosis and surgical procedure, disclose material risks, and document voluntary consent
skill.approach.surg.consent_operation.why: Informed consent is a legal and ethical prerequisite for surgical intervention. Operating without valid consent constitutes battery except in life-threatening emergencies where the patient lacks decision-making capacity and no surrogate is available.

steps.text: Conduct the discussion in a quiet, private setting at an appropriate time before sedation or theatre transfer.
Assess decision-making capacity: confirm the patient can understand, retain, weigh the information, and communicate a choice.
Explain the diagnosis, the proposed operation, the primary objective, and what will happen during surgery in accessible language.
Disclose common complications and rare but severe material risks, including bleeding, infection, visceral injury, and anaesthetic hazards.
Discuss reasonable alternative management strategies, including conservative or non-operative care and the consequences of declining surgery.
Invite questions, confirm understanding using teach-back, and verify that consent is given voluntarily before obtaining signatures.

skill.approach.surg.consent_operation.practice: Deliver a simulated consent conversation for an emergency appendicectomy or laparotomy to a peer within six minutes, addressing a major surgical risk.
pitfalls: Obtaining consent from a premedicated, heavily sedated, or drowsy patient.
Listing surgical risks rapidly without checking whether the patient understood the explanation.
Delegating complex surgical consent to an intern who cannot describe the operative procedure or potential complications.
Failing to explain the realistic alternative of conservative management and the risks of refusing treatment.

probes.q: What are the four components of assessing mental capacity to give surgical consent?
probes.a: The patient must be able to understand the relevant information, retain it long enough, weigh it to reach a decision, and communicate their decision.

probes.q: What constitutes a material risk that must be disclosed during surgical consent?
probes.a: A risk is material if a reasonable person in that patient position would attach significance to it, or if the doctor knows this particular patient would attach significance to it.

probes.q: Under what circumstances may a surgeon operate on an adult without explicit consent?
probes.a: Only in an emergency to save life or prevent severe harm when the patient lacks capacity and no legal surrogate or advance directive exists.

probes.q: Can a surgeon perform an incidental procedure during surgery if the consent form only named the primary procedure?
probes.a: No, incidental procedures without prior consent are unlawful unless immediately necessary to save the patient life or avoid severe detriment to health.

rubric.text: Ensures private setting and conducts discussion before sedation or premedication
Assesses and confirms patient decision-making capacity
Explains diagnosis, proposed operative procedure, and surgical objectives in plain words
Discloses common side effects and rare but serious material risks
Discusses non-operative alternatives and the implications of refusing treatment
Confirms voluntary consent without coercion and signs consent documentation

teach.heading: The modern legal standard of informed consent
teach.body:
Informed consent requires a collaborative dialogue between clinician and patient. The clinician shares medical knowledge while the patient contributes their values, anxieties, and priorities.

Consent is not a signature on a paper form but an ongoing clinical process that respects patient autonomy and personal bodily integrity.

skill.tx.surg.atls_primary_survey.title: Trauma primary survey: ATLS ABCDE approach
skill.tx.surg.atls_primary_survey.oneLine: Systematic identification and immediate life-saving treatment of lethal injuries in order of physiological priority
skill.tx.surg.atls_primary_survey.why: Trauma patients die from preventable physiological failure within the golden hour. The ABCDE algorithm prioritises airway compromise, tension pneumothorax, massive haemorrhage, and intracranial herniation before secondary diagnostic workup.
skill.tx.surg.atls_primary_survey.dosingNote: CliniX is a teaching aid and does not prescribe or administer medication. Trauma resuscitation protocols follow ATLS 10th Edition guidelines.

steps.text: Ensure scene safety, wear universal personal protective equipment, and approach patient while maintaining in-line cervical spine stabilisation.
Assess Airway: evaluate patency, suction blood or vomitus, insert simple airway adjunct if obtunded, and protect cervical spine with a rigid collar and blocks.
Assess Breathing: inspect chest wall excursion, auscultate bilaterally, administer high-flow oxygen, and decompress tension pneumothorax immediately if present.
Assess Circulation: apply direct pressure to external haemorrhage, palpate central pulses, assess capillary refill, and establish two large-bore 16G IV lines.
Assess Disability: determine Glasgow Coma Scale score, assess pupillary size and reactivity to light, and check capillary blood glucose.
Expose fully to inspect for occult wounds while preventing hypothermia with warmed blankets and warmed intravenous isotonic fluids.

skill.tx.surg.atls_primary_survey.practice: Simulate leading a trauma primary survey on a mannequin, verbalising ABCDE assessments and immediate interventions within 180 seconds.
pitfalls: Tilting or hyperextending the neck to open the airway in a blunt polytrauma victim.
Delaying needle or finger thoracostomy in a tension pneumothorax while waiting for a chest radiograph.
Failing to expose the back by gentle log-roll, missing posterior penetrating lacerations.
Allowing the patient to become hypothermic during exposure, triggering trauma-induced coagulopathy.

probes.q: What is the very first action when managing the airway in blunt polytrauma?
probes.a: Maintain manual in-line cervical spine stabilization to prevent spinal cord injury during airway maneuvers.

probes.q: What physical signs indicate immediate needle decompression for suspected tension pneumothorax?
probes.a: Respiratory distress, absent unilateral breath sounds, hypotension, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation to the opposite side.

probes.q: What are the components of the trauma lethal triad, and how is each prevented during primary survey?
probes.a: Hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy; prevented by rapid hemorrhage control, warm environment, warm IV fluids, and balanced blood transfusion.

probes.q: Where are the primary anatomical compartments of occult blood loss in hypotensive blunt polytrauma?
probes.a: The five compartments are the chest, abdomen, retroperitoneum with pelvis, long bone fractures, and external blood loss on the scene.

rubric.text: Assesses airway patency while maintaining manual in-line cervical spine stabilisation
Assesses breathing, delivers high-flow oxygen, and identifies life-threatening chest pathology
Performs immediate decompression without delay if tension pneumothorax is identified
Controls external haemorrhage with direct pressure and assesses pulses, perfusion, and blood pressure
Places two wide-bore 16G intravenous cannulae and initiates warmed balanced crystalloid or blood
Evaluates GCS and pupils, then exposes the patient completely while preventing hypothermia

teach.heading: The chronological imperative of the primary survey
teach.body:
The primary survey follows an uncompromising hierarchy. The physiological insult that kills the patient fastest is treated first: airway loss before tension pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax before exsanguination.

If the patient deteriorates at any point, stop and re-evaluate the sequence beginning from Airway.

teach.heading: Immediate life threats and their interventions

skill.tx.surg.catheterisation.title: Urinary bladder catheterisation: aseptic technique and balloon inflation
skill.tx.surg.catheterisation.oneLine: Aseptic urethral catheterisation with confirmation of urinary drainage before Foley balloon inflation
skill.tx.surg.catheterisation.why: Urethral catheterisation relieves acute urinary retention and monitors hourly urine output in shock and surgery. Inflating the retaining balloon within the urethra causes severe urethral rupture, haemorrhage, and permanent stricture.
skill.tx.surg.catheterisation.dosingNote: CliniX is a teaching aid and does not prescribe or administer medication. Catheter sizes and balloon volumes are standard surgical practice.

steps.text: Verify indication, explain procedure to patient, ensure privacy, and position patient supine with thighs abducted.
Inspect the external urethral meatus: confirm absence of meatal blood, stricture, or active purulence before proceeding.
Perform surgical hand scrub, don sterile gloves, and arrange sterile drape around the genitalia.
Cleanse the glans and meatus with aqueous chlorhexidine; instill 10 mL of 2% sterile lignocaine gel and wait 3 to 5 minutes.
Hold penis vertically on stretch, introduce Foley catheter gently without force, and advance fully to the side-arm junction.
Confirm free urine flow into the drainage tube before slowly inflating the balloon with 10 mL of sterile water, then gently withdraw to seat at bladder neck.

skill.tx.surg.catheterisation.practice: Demonstrate sterile Foley catheterisation on a male catheterisation trainer, highlighting the tactile stop and urine flashback.
pitfalls: Attempting urethral catheterisation when blood is visible at the external meatus after pelvic trauma.
Inflating the balloon before urine is seen draining freely from the catheter lumen.
Inflating the balloon with normal saline instead of sterile water, risking valve crystallisation and balloon non-deflation.
Forcing the catheter past an obstruction when resistance is encountered at the prostate or sphincter.

probes.q: What is the crucial confirmation required before inflating a Foley catheter balloon?
probes.a: Urine must be seen flowing freely from the catheter lumen, confirming that the catheter tip is inside the urinary bladder.

probes.q: Why must sterile water rather than normal saline be used to inflate the retention balloon?
probes.a: Normal saline can crystallize within the narrow inflation channel and valve mechanism, preventing balloon deflation during removal.

probes.q: What are the clinical signs of urethral injury in pelvic trauma that contraindicate blind urethral catheterisation?
probes.a: Blood at the external urethral meatus, perineal or scrotal haematoma, and a high-riding prostate on digital rectal examination.

probes.q: What is the immediate management if catheterisation encounters impassable resistance at the prostatic urethra in acute retention?
probes.a: Stop immediately without forcing, seek urological assistance, consider a coude tip catheter, or perform an ultrasound-guided suprapubic cystostomy.

rubric.text: Prepares sterile field, performs hand hygiene, and dons sterile gloves
Inspects external urethral meatus for blood, discharge, or stricture
Instils 10 mL of 2% sterile lignocaine gel into urethra and allows adequate dwell time
Advances catheter gently along the anatomical curve of urethra without applying force
Verifies free urine drainage before attempting any balloon inflation
Inflates balloon with 10 mL of sterile water only and connects closed drainage system

teach.heading: Anatomical safety principles in urethral catheterisation
teach.body:
The male urethra is approximately 20 cm long and has two natural curvatures. Traction on the penis perpendicular to the abdominal wall straightens the anterior urethra, facilitating smooth passage.

Resistance at the membranous urethra is usually due to voluntary sphincter spasm. Reassuring the patient and asking them to breathe deeply relaxes the pelvic floor.

skill.tx.surg.nasogastric_tube.title: Nasogastric tube insertion and position verification
skill.tx.surg.nasogastric_tube.oneLine: Aseptic insertion of a wide-bore nasogastric tube with NEX measurement and pH verification of gastric placement
skill.tx.surg.nasogastric_tube.why: Nasogastric tube decompression empties the stomach in intestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, and acute peritonitis, preventing pulmonary aspiration of enteric contents. Blind tracheal placement risks pneumothorax, aspiration pneumonia, and fatal enteral infusion.
skill.tx.surg.nasogastric_tube.dosingNote: CliniX is a teaching aid and does not prescribe or administer medication.

steps.text: Explain the procedure, agree on a stop signal with the patient, and position patient sitting upright with head in neutral position.
Measure insertion length using the NEX method: Nose tip to Earlobe to Xiphisternum, noting the marked centimeter graduation.
Inspect nostrils for patency, select the clearer nostril, and lubricate the distal 10 cm of the tube with water-soluble gel.
Insert tube horizontally along the floor of the nasal cavity towards the occiput until the posterior pharyngeal wall is reached.
Ask the patient to flex the neck forward and take small sips of water through a straw, advancing the tube synchronously with each swallow.
Advance to the predetermined NEX mark, aspirate gastric fluid with a 50 mL syringe, and confirm pH <= 5.5 using CE-marked pH indicator paper.

skill.tx.surg.nasogastric_tube.practice: Measure NEX distance on a partner and demonstrate horizontal insertion vector along the nasal floor on a mannequin.
pitfalls: Directing the tube upwards towards the cribriform plate instead of horizontally along the nasal floor.
Using the 'whoosh test' (air insufflation with epigastric auscultation) to confirm gastric placement; this is unreliable and unsafe.
Advancing the tube against persistent coughing, respiratory distress, or cyanosis indicating tracheal intubation.
Administering feed or medication before objective verification of gastric placement with pH paper or radiograph.

probes.q: How is the insertion length of a nasogastric tube accurately determined?
probes.a: Measure the distance from the tip of the nose to the earlobe, and then down to the xiphisternum (the NEX measurement).

probes.q: Why is the air insufflation 'whoosh test' no longer recommended to confirm nasogastric tube position?
probes.a: Auscultating air over the epigastrium cannot reliably distinguish between tube placement in the stomach, oesophagus, or respiratory tract.

probes.q: What is the threshold gastric aspirate pH confirming that a nasogastric tube is in the stomach?
probes.a: A pH of 5.5 or lower on CE-marked indicator paper confirms gastric acid secretion and correct gastric placement.

probes.q: What is the primary contraindication to nasogastric tube insertion via the nasal route?
probes.a: Suspected basilar skull fracture with CSF rhinorrhoea or midface trauma, where cribriform plate disruption risks intracranial tube entry.

rubric.text: Positions patient sitting upright with head neutral and agrees on a stop signal
Measures NEX distance (nose to earlobe to xiphisternum) and notes mark on tube
Lubricates tip and passes horizontally along nasal floor, avoiding upward trajectory
Advances tube synchronously with patient swallowing sips of water with neck flexed
Withdraws tube immediately if patient coughs persistently, stridors, or desaturates
Aspirates gastric fluid and confirms pH 5.5 or less on pH indicator paper

teach.heading: Safe passage and verification of nasogastric decompression
teach.body:
The nasogastric tube must travel parallel to the hard palate along the floor of the inferior meatus. Aiming upwards impacts the middle turbinate, causing severe epistaxis.

Neck flexion closes the laryngeal inlet and steers the tube into the retrocricoid pharynx and upper oesophagus during swallowing.

rows: Required if pH > 5.5 or no aspirate
Do not use; must use narrow-range pH
