skill.tx.surg.suture_wound.title: Wound debridement, infiltration anaesthesia and simple interrupted suturing
skill.tx.surg.suture_wound.oneLine: Aseptic wound preparation, local anaesthetic infiltration, non-viable tissue excision, and perpendicular interrupted skin closure
skill.tx.surg.suture_wound.why: Proper surgical wound closure restores the anatomical barrier, minimizes scar hypertrophy, and prevents wound infection. Inverting wound edges or tying sutures under strangulating tension produces ischaemic necrosis and dehiscence.
skill.tx.surg.suture_wound.dosingNote: CliniX is a teaching aid and does not prescribe or administer medication. Local anaesthetic doses and suture techniques are standard surgical practice.

steps.text: Assess wound location, check distal neurovascular and tendon function before local anaesthetic infiltration, and ensure tetanus prophylaxis status.
Irrigate wound copiously with sterile 0.9% saline under gentle pressure to remove particulate contamination.
Infiltrate 1% plain lignocaine (maximum 3 mg/kg) intradermally and subcutaneously through clean wound margins, aspirating first.
Perform surgical debridement: excise non-viable ragged edges and foreign material using scalpel or tissue scissors.
Mount curved reverse-cutting needle at junction of middle and posterior third with needle holder, and enter skin at 90 degrees 4-5 mm from margin.
Pass needle across wound bed at equal depth, exit perpendicularly 4-5 mm from opposite edge, and tie square knot with instrument tie without excessive tension.

skill.tx.surg.suture_wound.practice: Place five simple interrupted sutures on a silicone practice pad, ensuring equal bite depth and wound edge eversion with square instrument ties.
pitfalls: Failing to document distal sensation and motor function before infiltrating local anaesthesia.
Using lignocaine with adrenaline on fingers, toes, penis, or ears, causing end-artery vasospasm and gangrene.
Tying knots so tightly that the skin blenches, causing dermal ischemia and transverse suture railroad tracks.
Permitting wound edges to roll inward (invert) rather than everting the skin margins.

probes.q: Why must the suture needle enter and exit the skin at a 90-degree angle to the surface?
probes.a: A perpendicular entry takes a wider bite in the deeper dermis than at the surface, ensuring that wound edges evert when the knot is tied.

probes.q: What is the maximum safe dose of plain lignocaine (without adrenaline) in an adult for local infiltration?
probes.a: The maximum safe dose of plain lignocaine is 3 mg per kg of body weight (or approximately 200 mg in an average 70 kg adult).

probes.q: Why must adrenaline never be used in local anaesthetic for lacerations on the digits or earlobe?
probes.a: Adrenaline produces intense vasoconstriction in end-arteries without collateral supply, causing irreversible tissue ischemia and gangrene.

probes.q: What is the recommended timing for skin suture removal across different anatomical regions?
probes.a: Face sutures are removed at 3 to 5 days, scalp at 7 days, trunk and upper extremities at 7 to 10 days, and lower extremities or over joints at 10 to 14 days.

rubric.text: Examines and documents distal neurovascular integrity before infiltrating local anaesthetic
Irrigates wound copiously with sterile normal saline to remove particulate contaminants
Aspirates before infiltrating local anaesthetic, staying within safe weight-based dose limits
Excises devitalised tissue and foreign debris while preserving viable anatomy
Enters and exits skin at 90 degrees taking equal bites of skin and subcutaneous tissue
Ties square knot off the incision line, achieving wound edge eversion without strangulation

teach.heading: Principles of atraumatic wound closure
teach.body:
The goal of wound suturing is precise anatomical approximation with gentle eversion of skin edges. Everted edges heal flat, whereas inverted edges produce a depressed, disfiguring scar.

Sutures should approximate, never strangulate. Tissue oedema invariably occurs during the first 48 hours; tying knots too tightly leads to dermal necrosis and cross-hatching marks.

asks.text: Have you had repeated painful swellings of the same gland before, and did they settle on their own or need treatment?
How much water do you drink in a day, and do you work long hours in heat without drinking?
Do you chew tobacco, betel quid or areca nut, or smoke beedis or cigarettes, and for how many years?
Which daily medicines do you take, especially any that dry the mouth such as allergy tablets, water tablets or tricyclic medicines?
Have you had neck radiation, mumps with face swelling in childhood, or diabetes and kidney stones?
Has anyone in your family had a neck lump removed, thyroid disease, or dry eyes with joint pains?

skill.hx.salivary.risk.oneLine: Dehydration, oral sepsis, tobacco, dry-mouth drugs, radiation and family tumours behind the swelling

probes.a: Poor fluid intake with heat labour, poor oral hygiene with dental sepsis, tobacco and betel habit, and daily medicines that dry the mouth all favour duct blockage with mineral deposit and ascending gland infection.
probes.q: Which four background habits favour a blocked salivary duct with infection?

probes.a: Childhood neck irradiation and a family history of salivary or thyroid tumours raise the suspicion of cancer in a lump and lower the threshold for needle sampling.
probes.q: Which two background facts raise the suspicion of cancer in a salivary lump?

teach.heading: Ask about water, mouth, drugs and habits first
points: Daily fluid intake and hours of heat labour without drinking, since stagnant saliva precipitates mineral deposit.
Oral hygiene, dental caries and gum sepsis, since ascending mouth bacteria infect a slow gland.
Tobacco, betel quid and smoking history, since smoking clusters with Warthin tumour and betel with oral disease that mimics gland swelling.
Every daily medicine by name for dry-mouth effects, plus diabetes and debility that slow salivary flow.

teach.heading: Past episodes and family set the threshold
teach.body:
Ask about earlier swellings of the same gland and what settled them: mealtime swellings that pass suggest a duct deposit, while childhood face swelling with fever points to mumps and protects against mislabelling a new lump.

Ask about neck irradiation in childhood and about salivary or thyroid lumps in the family. Either answer raises the suspicion of cancer in the current lump and lowers the threshold for needle sampling rather than watching.

skill.hx.salivary.risk.title: Risk, past, personal, drug and family history in salivary swelling
skill.hx.salivary.risk.why: The background separates a preventable duct blockage from a tumour that needs sampling. Dehydration, oral sepsis, tobacco and dry-mouth drugs each push the same swelling down a different path, while radiation and family history set the threshold for cancer.

skill.present.salivary.summary.oneLine: Gland, tempo, mealtime behaviour and red flags in three sentences

probes.a: The patient with relevant exposures, the gland and the tempo, the mealtime behaviour with local findings, and the provisional diagnosis with red flags stated as present or absent.
probes.q: What elements belong in a salivary case summary?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: Salivary glands: examination and case summary
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.heading: Three sentences that contain the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with the exposures that matter: age, sex, field labour with low fluid intake, tobacco or betel habit. Then name the gland and state the tempo: months of mealtime swelling separates duct blockage from years of painless growth.

Then state the local findings in abstract terms: a tense tender submandibular swelling at meals with bimanual palpability and a dry duct orifice, or a firm lobulated painless parotid lump lifting the ear lobule with an intact facial nerve. End with the provisional diagnosis and what is still missing, such as ultrasound or needle sampling.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 38 year old male field worker presents with eight months of recurrent right submandibular swelling that tenses painfully during meals and eases between them. Bimanual examination finds a firm tender gland caught between the fingers above and below the mylohyoid, with a dry ipsilateral duct orifice on lemon stimulation.

This is an obstructive submandibular swelling favouring a duct calculus, pending occlusal radiograph and ultrasound. No facial weakness, skin fixity or hard nodes are present, so the working plan is conservative with defined thresholds for stone retrieval or gland surgery.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: Which gland is swollen, and whether the swelling is single or bilateral.
The mealtime behaviour: swelling that tenses with food versus a lump that ignores meals.
Facial nerve status in every parotid lump, stated as intact or palsied.
Nodes, skin fixity and duct discharge, stated as present or explicitly absent.

skill.present.salivary.summary.title: Summarising the salivary case
skill.present.salivary.summary.why: A salivary summary must carry the gland, the tempo and the mealtime behaviour together, because the plan follows from all three at once. Omitting the nerve status in a parotid lump or the duct findings in a submandibular swelling leaves the listener unable to judge urgency.

skill.hx.scrotal.risk_factors.title: Background history in scrotal swelling: past, personal, drug and family
skill.hx.scrotal.risk_factors.why: A scrotal swelling is rarely only what it looks like today. The age at onset, a forgotten fever with a swollen cord, an old urethral discharge, or treatment for tuberculosis each reframes the same lump, and none of them is visible on examination.
asks: At what age did the swelling first appear, and was it present in infancy or early childhood with any change on crying or straining?
What work do you do each day, and do you stand for most of the day without sitting?
Have you had repeated attacks of fever with pain and swelling of the cord or scrotum, and where have you lived for most of your life?
Have you ever been treated for tuberculosis, or lived with anyone who coughed for months and took prolonged treatment?
Did you have mumps with a painful swollen testis in childhood or adolescence?
Have you had burning on passing urine, a urethral discharge, or treatment for a sexually transmitted infection?
Have you ever injured the scrotum, had a swelling tapped or drained, or been operated on for hernia or hydrocele?
Do you have children, and has fathering a child ever been difficult?
Which medicines do you take every day, including blood thinners, and have you taken steroids for weeks at a time?
Has anyone in your family had a similar scrotal swelling, an undescended testis, or a testicular tumour at a young age?

teach.body:
A painless swelling that has grown slowly for months in a man past forty usually proves to be a primary vaginal hydrocele. A swelling in a man between twenty and forty more often proves secondary, following infection, trauma or torsion. A testicular tumour is a disease of the young, and torsion strikes boys and teenagers, so the age alone already narrows the list before the examination begins.

In infants a communicating hydrocele comes and goes and usually settles within the first year or two of life. Operating before that window closes treats many children who would have recovered on their own.
teach.heading: Age points at the diagnosis before you touch the patient

teach.body:
Ask directly about periodic fever with a painful swollen cord, because filarial funiculitis leaves exactly this story and is common in coastal and eastern districts. Ask about tuberculosis treatment and household contact, since tuberculous disease reaches the epididymis through the urinary tract and also scars the seminal vesicles.

Ask about mumps orchitis, urethral discharge and urethritis, because each seeds the epididymis by a different route and changes which investigations you order. A trivial knock that the patient blames for the swelling deserves attention too, but remember that trauma more often draws notice to a lump than causes it.
teach.heading: Ask after filariasis, tuberculosis, mumps and urethritis
Background factors and what each one changes

rows: Infantile communicating, primary past forty, secondary at twenty to forty
Decide whether to watch, scan or refer urgently
A varicocele that appears on standing and vanishes lying down
Examine standing then supine; look for a renal cause if sudden
Filarial infection of the cord and lymphatics
Night blood smear, urine check, antifilarial course by guideline
Epididymal disease with beaded vas and cold abscess
Urine tests, chest film, full antitubercular course if proved
Urine culture, treat the urinary infection alongside
Recurrence, a plugged sac, or a missed secondary cause
Scan before promising a simple operation
Bleeding and poor healing at elective surgery
Plan stopping and cover with the anaesthetist
Shared infection exposure or undescended testis
Examine brothers, screen the household where relevant

probes.a: The age at onset and tempo, standing work, periodic filarial fever, tuberculosis past and contact, mumps and urethritis, trauma and earlier tapping or repair, fertility, daily drugs, and a family history of similar swelling.
probes.q: Name five background facts you must ask after in every scrotal swelling history.

probes.a: Because filarial fever with cord swelling, tuberculosis of the urinary tract, mumps orchitis and urethritis each seed the epididymis or cord, and each needs a different investigation and a different definitive treatment.
probes.q: Why do you ask about periodic fever, tuberculosis, mumps and urethral discharge in a man with a chronic scrotal swelling?

probes.a: A varicocele that fills on standing in a young man is usually idiopathic, but a varicocele of sudden onset in a middle aged man can follow a renal tumour obstructing the testicular vein, so examine the kidney and arrange an ultrasound rather than reassuring him.
probes.q: A middle aged man reports a varicocele that appeared within weeks. What must you exclude, and how?

skill.present.scrotal.summary.title: Summarising the scrotal swelling case
skill.present.scrotal.summary.why: The consultant decides the plan from your summary, not from your examination. Side, duration, pain, whether you can get above the swelling, translucency, the state of the testis and cord, and the one urgency flag must all land in under a minute.

teach.body:
State the patient with age and work, the duration and tempo of the swelling, then the syndrome in abstract terms: a painless right scrotal swelling of eight months with a brilliantly translucent cystic feel, from which one can get above, the testis impalpable within it.

Close with the discriminators and fitness: no cough impulse, cord felt separately above, no nodes, no fever or urinary symptoms, and the comorbidity and drugs that decide fitness for elective repair.
teach.heading: The shape of the summary

teach.body:
A forty six year old bus conductor presents with a painless swelling of the right scrotum that has grown slowly over eight months, heavy by evening but never painful, with no fever, urinary burning or discharge.

Examination shows a pyriform right scrotal swelling that is cystic, fluctuant and brilliantly translucent, from which one can get above, with no cough impulse. The testis cannot be felt apart from the swelling, the cord is normal above it, and there is no lymphadenopathy. This is an uncomplicated primary vaginal hydrocele, with prolonged standing as the occupational background and no feature of hernia, tumour or acute torsion.
teach.heading: A worked example
What never to omit
points: Side, duration and tempo: months of painless growth versus hours of acute pain.
Pain characterised exactly, since a painless swelling and an agonising one take different roads.
Whether you can get above the swelling, and whether it has a cough impulse.
Transillumination and fluctuation, stated as positive or negative with the method.
The testis, epididymis and cord: felt separately, impalpable, thickened, beaded or nodular.
Nodes, fever and urinary symptoms as stated negatives where they exclude infection or spread.
Fitness and causes: comorbidity, bleeding drugs, and the TB, filarial and urethritis background.

probes.a: Side, duration and tempo, pain, whether one can get above the swelling, cough impulse, translucency and fluctuation, the state of testis, epididymis and cord, nodes, and fitness with the infective background.
probes.q: What must a scrotal swelling summary always contain?

probes.a: No. An impalpable testis inside a hydrocele can hide a tumour, so the summary must flag the uncertainty, state that ultrasound assessment of the testis is still awaited, and give the referral threshold rather than closing the case.
probes.q: The testis cannot be felt within the swelling. Can you still close the summary as a simple hydrocele?

rubric.text: States side, duration, tempo and pain
States get-above, impulse, translucency and the state of testis and cord
Closes with a diagnosis, negatives, fitness and follow up

skill.hx.gi.risk.title: Background risks behind gastrointestinal bleeding
skill.hx.gi.risk.oneLine: Drugs, drink, liver disease and past ulcer or bleed behind the current bleed
skill.hx.gi.risk.why: Most gastrointestinal bleeds are not bad luck. A daily painkiller, regular alcohol with liver disease, a blood thinner, or a past ulcer that was never tested for cure each changes the likely source and the urgency, and none of them is volunteered unless asked directly.

asks.text: Which painkillers do you take, including aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac or any tablet for joint pain, and for how many weeks or months?
Do you take any blood thinner such as aspirin, clopidogrel or warfarin, and who prescribed it and for what heart or vessel problem?
How much alcohol do you drink in a week, for how many years, and have you ever been told you have liver damage, jaundice or swollen veins in the food pipe?
Have you vomited blood or passed black stools before, were you told you have an ulcer, and were you tested for the stomach germ after treatment?
Do you smoke beedis or cigarettes or chew tobacco, and do you eat irregularly with long gaps or frequent spicy outside food?
Do you have heart failure, kidney disease or chronic lung disease, and which daily medicines do you take for them?

teach.heading: Ask about painkillers by name, not as drugs
points: Name aspirin, ibuprofen and diclofenac one by one, since many patients do not count a painkiller bought without prescription as a medicine.
Ask the dose, the number of weeks or months, and whether it is taken on an empty stomach, because risk rises with duration rather than with any single tablet.
Ask about low dose aspirin for the heart separately, since even a small daily dose can injure the stomach lining.
Record self medication from chemists and herbal powders too, since undisclosed powders often contain hidden painkillers.

teach.heading: Map drink to liver before asking about varices
teach.body:
Ask quantity in local measures, frequency and years of drinking, then ask directly about jaundice, swelling of the feet or abdomen, and vomiting of blood in the past. A patient with years of heavy drinking and fluid in the abdomen bleeds from a different source than a painkiller user, and the resuscitation plan differs.

Ask about blood transfusions, jaundice after injections, and needle sharing as well, since chronic viral liver disease is another route to the same portal pressure.

teach.heading: Past ulcer, past bleed and the stomach germ
teach.body:
Ask whether an ulcer was ever diagnosed, whether black stools or vomiting of blood happened before, and what treatment was given. Then ask whether a breath, stool or biopsy test confirmed the stomach germ was cured, because an ulcer that was never tested stays a likely source.

A bleed without warning is common, so the absence of past dyspepsia never excludes an ulcer as the source.

teach.heading: Comorbidity changes the transfusion threshold
points: Heart failure and ischaemic heart disease, since anaemia is tolerated poorly and the transfusion threshold is set higher.
Chronic kidney disease and chronic lung disease, since both worsen the tolerance of sudden blood loss.
Diabetes and steroid use, since both slow ulcer healing and raise infection risk after admission.
Allergy to penicillin or aspirin, recorded before any eradication or antiplatelet plan is written.

probes.q: Name four background facts you must ask in every gastrointestinal bleed.
probes.a: Painkiller and aspirin use, alcohol with liver disease, blood thinners, and a past ulcer or bleed with whether the stomach germ was cured.

probes.q: Why do you ask about heart failure and kidney disease in a bleeding patient?
probes.a: Because comorbidity changes how much blood loss the patient tolerates and where the transfusion threshold is set, and it changes drug choices during resuscitation.

skill.present.gi.summary.title: Presenting the gastrointestinal bleed case
skill.present.gi.summary.oneLine: Patient, bleed pattern, volume clues and scores in three sentences
skill.present.gi.summary.why: A bleeding case summary must carry the bleed pattern, the evidence of volume loss and the risk score together, because the plan follows from all three at once. Omitting the score or the evidence of shock leaves the listener unable to judge whether this patient can wait for a morning list.

teach.heading: Three sentences that contain the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with the risks that matter: age, painkiller or alcohol use, liver disease, blood thinners. Then state the bleed in pattern terms: vomiting of bright red blood or coffee ground material, black tarry stools or fresh blood per rectum, with the number of episodes and the time course.

Then state the evidence of volume loss and the scores: pulse and blood pressure with any postural fall, haemoglobin and urea, the pre endoscopy risk score and the post endoscopy score where available. End with the working source and what is still missing, such as urgent endoscopy or colonoscopy.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 54 year old male farm worker and regular painkiller user presents with two episodes of vomiting of dark blood and one black tarry stool over twelve hours. He is pale and restless with a pulse of 112, a systolic pressure of 98 lying flat, and a haemoglobin of 8.1 g per dL with a raised urea.

This is an upper gastrointestinal bleed with haemodynamic instability and a high pre endoscopy risk score, for resuscitation and urgent inpatient endoscopy within 24 hours. No chest pain, breathlessness or calf swelling is present, and the rectal examination confirms melaena without a local anal source.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: Upper or lower pattern stated from the history, not left for the listener to infer.
Volume evidence: pulse, blood pressure, postural change, haemoglobin and urea.
Risk scores with the band they place the patient in, and what that band changes.
Resuscitation status: access, fluids, transfusion given or threshold set.
Relevant negatives: no chest pain, no breathlessness, no calf swelling, no local anal source where claimed.

probes.q: What elements belong in a gastrointestinal bleed summary?
probes.a: The patient with relevant risks, the bleed pattern with tempo, the volume evidence with scores, and the working source with what is still missing.

rubric.text: States the bleed as upper or lower with the evidence
States volume evidence and risk scores
Links the summary to resuscitation and endoscopy timing

skill.hx.deep.leg_swelling.title: History of a painful swollen leg
skill.hx.deep.leg_swelling.oneLine: One leg, days old, calf pain with swelling, and the chest symptoms that warn of embolism
skill.hx.deep.leg_swelling.why: Deep vein thrombosis is mostly silent, so the history has to do the work the examination cannot: a sudden painful swelling of one leg within days, made worse by standing and walking, is the story that earns a scan, while new breathlessness or pleuritic pain in the same patient warns that part of the clot has already travelled to the lungs.

teach.heading: Tempo and side carry the diagnosis
teach.body:
Ask which leg, and how many days. Thrombosis typically declares itself over hours to a few days with pain and swelling of one leg, often starting in the calf. A swelling that has built over months or years, or that affects both legs equally, points instead toward chronic venous disease, lymphoedema, or a systemic cause of oedema.

Remember that most thrombosis never announces itself at all, so the absence of a dramatic story does not exclude it. In a patient with a recent operation, delivery, long journey or period of bed rest, even a modest new calf ache with mild swelling deserves the same questions as a grossly swollen leg.

teach.heading: What to ask about the leg
points: Which leg is swollen, and is the swelling around the ankle and calf or the whole limb from thigh down.
When it started and whether the onset was sudden, and whether pain or swelling came first.
The character of the pain: a cramp-like calf ache that worsens on standing and walking and eases with elevation.
Whether the leg feels warm or looks red compared with the other side, and whether the surface veins look more prominent.
Whether walking has become difficult, and whether the calf is tender to touch or to gentle squeezing.
Any fever, and any recent knock, strain or long walk that could explain a muscle injury instead.

teach.heading: Always ask the chest questions
teach.body:
Every patient with a suspected leg thrombosis must be asked about breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, cough and coughing of blood. The clot can embolise silently, and breathlessness may be the first symptom the patient volunteers once asked.

Also ask whether anyone has noticed the patient breathing fast, and whether there has been faintness or collapse. A yes to any of these moves the case from a leg problem to a possible emergency, and the examination and investigations must then cover the chest as well as the leg.

asks.text: Which leg is swollen, and did the pain or the swelling come first?
How many days ago did this start, and did it come on suddenly?
Does the calf ache worsen when you stand or walk, and does raising the leg ease it?
Is the swollen leg warmer or redder than the other one, and are the surface veins more visible?
Have you had any breathlessness, chest pain on breathing in, cough, or blood in the sputum since the leg swelled?
Have you had any fever, recent injury to the leg, or an unusually long walk or strain before this started?

pitfalls: Accepting bilateral ankle swelling as thrombosis without asking why only one deep system would block.
Forgetting the chest questions, so an embolism that has already happened goes unasked about.
Dismissing a mild calf ache in a postoperative or postpartum patient because the leg is not dramatically swollen.

probes.q: A patient reports a left calf ache with ankle swelling that began two days ago after a long bus journey. Why does this story raise suspected thrombosis?
probes.a: A sudden unilateral calf pain with swelling within days, following prolonged immobility, is the classic tempo and setting of deep vein thrombosis.

probes.q: Why must you ask about breathlessness and pleuritic pain in every patient with a suspected leg thrombosis?
probes.a: Because part of the clot may already have embolised to the lungs, and breathlessness or pleuritic pain with haemoptysis would reveal a pulmonary embolism needing urgent assessment.

rubric.text: Establishes side, suddenness and days since onset
Records pain character, swelling extent, warmth, redness and walking effect
Screens for breathlessness, pleuritic pain, cough and haemoptysis

skill.hx.deep.risk.title: Risk, past, drug and family history in suspected thrombosis
skill.hx.deep.risk.oneLine: Stasis, injury and clotting tendency: surgery, stillness, cancer, hormones, past clots and family
skill.hx.deep.risk.why: Whether a swollen leg is thrombosis, and whether it will happen again, is decided by the risk story: a recent operation or delivery, days of stillness, an active cancer, hormonal pills, or a past clot each raise the likelihood before a hand touches the leg, and each changes how long treatment must continue.

teach.heading: Stillness after surgery or delivery is the commonest setting
teach.body:
Ask about any operation under general anaesthesia, any delivery or miscarriage, any fracture or plaster, and any long period in bed with a debilitating illness. Calf muscles idle during anaesthesia or bed rest fail to pump blood through the deep veins, and thrombosis follows stasis.

Ask the same about travel: a long bus or train journey sitting still for many hours is a standard history in Indian practice. Record the date of the operation or journey and count the days to the swelling, because thrombosis typically declares itself within days to a couple of weeks.

teach.heading: Conditions and drugs that thicken the tendency to clot
points: Any active cancer or its treatment, and any recent unexplained loss of weight or appetite that could hide one.
Pregnancy and the weeks after delivery, when clotting tendency is physiologically raised.
Hormonal contraceptive pills taken for many months, which raise the chance of venous thrombosis.
Known diabetes, obesity, smoking, and dehydration during illness or travel, which add to the risk.
Long-term medicines: steroids, diuretics, and any anticoagulant already being taken, with doses missed.
Past history of a painful swollen leg, pulmonary embolism, miscarriages, or known protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency.

teach.heading: Family history and the inherited tendency
teach.body:
Ask whether parents or siblings have had leg clots, pulmonary embolism, repeated miscarriages, or lifelong anticoagulant treatment. Inherited states such as factor V Leiden, the prothrombin gene change, and deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C or protein S run in families.

A young patient with an unprovoked clot, a clot in both legs, or relatives with the same story needs referral for thrombophilia assessment after the acute treatment. Record the pedigree briefly rather than writing family history positive without detail.

asks.text: Have you had any operation, delivery, fracture, plaster, or long stay in bed in the last few weeks, and on which date?
Have you undertaken any long bus, train or air journey sitting still for many hours before this started?
Do you have any cancer or its treatment, or recent loss of weight or appetite?
For women: are you pregnant or delivered in the last few weeks, and have you taken hormonal contraceptive pills, and for how long?
Have you ever had a painful swollen leg or a lung clot before, and are you taking any blood-thinning medicine?
Has anyone in your family had leg clots, a lung clot, repeated miscarriages, or lifelong blood-thinner treatment?

pitfalls: Recording a postoperative swollen leg without asking the date of surgery, so the link to stasis is never made.
Forgetting the pill and pregnancy history in a young woman with an otherwise unexplained clot.
Writing family history positive without names, ages and events, which cannot guide thrombophilia referral.

probes.q: Name three risk settings you must ask about in every suspected deep vein thrombosis.
probes.a: Recent surgery or anaesthesia, prolonged immobility or travel, and a prothrombotic state such as cancer, pregnancy, hormonal pills or a past clot.

probes.q: A 24 year old woman has an unprovoked calf thrombosis and her mother had a lung clot at 30. What does the family story add?
probes.a: It raises an inherited thrombophilia such as factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene change or protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency, needing referral for assessment after acute treatment.

rubric.text: Records operation, delivery, bed rest and travel with dates
Screens for cancer, hormones, pregnancy, past clots and current anticoagulants
Records family clots and miscarriages with enough detail for referral

skill.present.deep.summary.title: Presenting the deep vein thrombosis case
skill.present.deep.summary.oneLine: Tempo, Wells likelihood, duplex result and provoked or not, ending with duration and follow up
skill.present.deep.summary.why: A thrombosis presentation fails when the student lists the swelling without ever stating the clinical likelihood, the scan result, or whether the clot was provoked: those three facts decide treatment and its duration, so the consultant needs them in the first minute, not buried at the end.

teach.heading: Five lines that contain the case
teach.body:
Open with the patient and the setting: age, sex, and the provoking event with its date, such as a hysterectomy ten days ago. Then give the tempo: sudden calf pain with swelling over days, and whether the chest questions were positive or negative.

Then state the clinical likelihood by the Wells assessment and the scan result: a non-compressible segment on duplex confirms thrombosis, while a negative d-dimer in a low-likelihood patient excludes it. Close with provoked or unprovoked, the chosen anticoagulant class, planned duration, and advice on mobilisation, compression, bleeding watch and follow up.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A 52 year old homemaker presents ten days after abdominal hysterectomy with a three-day painful swelling of the left leg from calf to ankle, without breathlessness or chest pain. The calf is tender and warmer than the right, with pitting oedema to the mid shin.

The Wells assessment gives high clinical likelihood, and duplex shows a non-compressible left popliteal segment with absent flow. This is an acute provoked proximal deep vein thrombosis, started on therapeutic anticoagulation with a planned three-month course, graduated compression, early mobilisation, and review for bleeding and post-thrombotic symptoms.

teach.heading: Never omit these
points: The provoking event with its date, because provoked or unprovoked decides duration.
The chest screen result, because a missed embolism is the dangerous error.
The Wells likelihood and exactly which test confirmed or excluded the clot.
The negatives that protect the plan: pulses present, no whole-limb blue congestion, no bleeding risk stated.
Duration, compression, mobilisation, bleeding advice, and when the patient must return.

pitfalls: Describing the swelling in detail while never stating the Wells likelihood or the duplex result.
Omitting the provoking event, leaving the listener unable to judge whether three months or longer treatment is planned.
Closing without bleeding advice and follow up, as if starting anticoagulation ends the case.

probes.q: What three facts must the first minute of a thrombosis presentation contain?
probes.a: The provoking setting with its date, the Wells clinical likelihood, and the confirmatory test result, because together they decide treatment and duration.

rubric.text: States the provoking event with its date and the tempo
States Wells likelihood and the duplex or d-dimer result
States provoked or not, duration, compression, mobilisation and bleeding advice

skill.hx.abdominal.trauma_risks.title: Background risks in abdominal trauma
skill.hx.abdominal.trauma_risks.oneLine: Mechanism, bleeding risk, bladder clues, tetanus cover and comorbidity before the belly is touched
skill.hx.abdominal.trauma_risks.why: In a penetrating wound the history decides how fast the patient must reach theatre, and a missed detail such as blood thinners, an unprotected wound or a full bladder changes the risk of bleeding, infection and a missed bladder injury. Asking it in one pass keeps the primary survey moving.
skill.hx.abdominal.trauma_risks.body: Take the mechanism, the bleeding and contamination risks, and the bladder and tetanus history together, since each one changes urgency, wound care or the operation planned.

asks.text: Mechanism and weapon: What exactly caused the wound, a knife, a sharp object, a bullet or a fall onto something sharp? How long was the blade, how hard was the thrust, and was it one wound or several? A long blade or a high velocity missile damages widely beyond the visible track.

Time and place of injury: When did it happen, and how long did it take to reach care? Ask what was done to the wound meanwhile, since delay favours infection and a longer prehospital time means more blood already lost.

Blood loss and faintness: How much blood was seen at the scene, did the patient faint, feel giddy on standing, or become less responsive? Restlessness and air hunger after injury point to continuing internal bleeding rather than pain alone.

Vomiting and its content: Did the patient vomit after the injury, and did the vomit contain blood? Blood in vomit suggests upper gut involvement, while repeated vomiting with a tense abdomen follows developing peritonitis.

Urine passage since injury: Has the patient passed urine, and was there blood in it? Ask also about an intense desire to pass water with only a few drops of blood coming out, which suggests bladder or urethral injury, and about no desire at all, which fits an intraperitoneal bladder rupture.

Drugs that bleed and drugs that mask: Is the patient on blood thinners, aspirin, painkillers or steroids, and when was the last dose taken? Painkillers and steroids blunt the guarding you rely on, while thinners turn a contained haematoma into free bleeding.

Past operations, hernia and pregnancy: Any previous abdominal operation, hernia repair, or current pregnancy? Old scars tether bowel to the wall so a wound over a scar injures gut more easily, and pregnancy displaces organs and changes resuscitation priorities.

Tetanus cover and comorbidity: When was the last tetanus injection, and does the patient have diabetes, hypertension, heart disease or alcohol dependence? A dirty penetrating wound in an unimmunised diabetic patient needs both prophylaxis and tighter wound watch.

keyPoints: Record mechanism, weapon length, force and number of wounds first, since a gunshot or a long blade means wide hidden damage even when the entry wound looks small.
Ask urine passage and blood in urine in every case, plus the desire to pass water with only drops of blood, which separates urethral and bladder patterns.
Confirm blood thinners, painkillers and steroids with the last dose, because they change bleeding risk and hide peritoneal signs.
Check tetanus immunisation and diabetes together in a contaminated wound, since both decide prophylaxis and follow up.
A previous scar over the wound line and a current pregnancy both change what lies under the blade and must be stated, not assumed.

teach.heading: Mechanism tells you the hidden track
teach.body:
Ask what caused the wound, how long the weapon was, how hard the thrust was, and how many wounds there are. A stab wound injures along a fairly predictable track, while a bullet transfers energy widely and injures beyond the visible path.

Note the time since injury and what was done at the scene. Penetrating wounds expose the peritoneal cavity to the outside, so infection risk grows with every hour of delay.

teach.heading: Urine and tetanus are never skipped
teach.body:
Ask whether urine has been passed and whether it contained blood, and distinguish the patient who strains to pass a few drops of blood from the one with no desire to pass water at all. The first pattern fits the lower urinary passage, the second an intraperitoneal bladder leak.

Ask the date of the last tetanus injection in the same breath. A contaminated wound in an unprotected patient needs prophylaxis urgently, and diabetes makes infection more likely.

teach.heading: Drugs and scars that change the picture
teach.body:
Ask about blood thinners, painkillers and steroids with the last dose taken. Thinners convert a contained bleed into a free one, and painkillers with steroids blunt the very guarding and rebound you will rely on.

Ask about previous abdominal operations, since adhesions fix bowel under the scar and make gut injury more likely beneath a wound that crosses it.

probes.q: In a stab wound to the abdomen, what three history points besides the wound itself must you always record?
probes.a: The mechanism and time since injury, whether urine has been passed and if it contained blood, and the date of the last tetanus injection.

probes.q: Why do you ask about painkillers and steroids in abdominal trauma?
probes.a: Because painkillers and steroids blunt guarding and rebound tenderness, so they can hide the peritoneal signs you rely on to decide for operation.

skill.present.abdominal.case_summary.title: Presenting the abdominal trauma case
skill.present.abdominal.case_summary.oneLine: Sixty-second bedside summary from wound and vitals to the theatre decision
skill.present.abdominal.case_summary.why: In trauma the senior clinician needs stability, wounds, belly findings and the plan in the first minute, because the decision to operate cannot wait for a long story. A crisp order, stability first and mechanism woven in, is what makes the presentation safe to act on.

teach.heading: The sixty-second trauma presentation
teach.body:
Open with age, sex, mechanism and time since injury, then state stability in one line with pulse, pressure and urine passage. Name each wound by site, size and what is visible at its mouth, then give the belly findings of guarding, rebound, distension and bowel sounds.

Close with the FAST result, the erect film, blood grouping status and your plan: immediate operation, wound exploration under cover, or serial examination with clear review timing.

teach.heading: What the senior listens for
teach.body:
Four decision points must be audible: first, stable or not, with the numbers that prove it; second, peritonitis present or absent, with the signs found; third, the urinary and chest screen, urine blood, chest findings and back inspection; fourth, tetanus cover, antibiotics started, blood arranged and consent for operation.

State what you have excluded as well as what you found, since a negative rectal examination, a clear chest and an intact back are part of the safety net.

skill.present.abdominal.case_summary.practice: Rehearse presenting a stable stab wound case in sixty seconds: mechanism, vitals, wound description, belly and chest findings, FAST and film results, and whether the patient needs theatre now or serial review.
pitfalls: Opening with past history and comorbidity before stating stability, mechanism and wounds.
Describing the belly without saying whether peritonitis is present or absent as a clear verdict.
Omitting the back and flank inspection, the urine finding and the tetanus status from the plan.

probes.q: What is the first line of a trauma case presentation?
probes.a: Age, mechanism and time since injury, followed at once by stability with pulse, pressure and urine passage.

probes.q: Which negatives must a complete abdominal trauma presentation include?
probes.a: No peritonitis or a clear verdict on it, a clear chest, an intact back and flanks, blood in urine excluded, and tetanus cover confirmed.

rubric.text: States mechanism, time since injury and stability with vitals in the first lines.
Gives wound description, belly verdict on peritonitis, chest and back screen, and urine finding.
Closes with FAST and film, blood and consent status, and a clear theatre or review decision.

skill.hx.burns.story.title: History of the burn: what burned, how, and what happened first
skill.hx.burns.story.why: Two burns of the same size behave differently when one is a brief scald and the other is a flame burn in smoky clothing. The agent, the setting, the time since injury and what was done first decide the depth, the airway risk and the fluid plan, and none of it can be recovered from looking at the wound.
asks: What exactly caused the burn: an open flame, hot liquid or steam, contact with a hot object, a chemical, or an electric current?
Did clothing or hair catch fire, and was the patient in an enclosed or smoky room, kitchen or vehicle?
When exactly did the burn happen, and how much time has passed since then?
What was done immediately: was the area cooled with clean running water, for how long, and was anything applied to the wound?
Where is the pain worst now, and has the pain grown, eased or changed character since the injury?
Have blisters appeared or burst, and has the red area spread since the first hour?
Is there any difficulty in breathing, change in the voice, cough with black sputum, or burning inside the nose or mouth?
Has urine been passed since the burn, and how does its amount and colour compare with usual?

teach.heading: Mechanism before measurement
teach.body:
Ask the agent first, then the setting, then the clock. An open flame with ignited clothing burns deeper and longer than a splash that runs off, and a burn inside a closed room adds smoke and heat injury of the airway to the skin loss.

Fix the time of injury early in the interview. Resuscitation formulae run from the moment of the burn, not from arrival, and a patient who arrives six hours late is already behind on fluids.

teach.heading: The first aid that counts
points: Cooling with clean running water in the first minutes limits the depth; ask whether it happened and for how long.
Ask what was put on the wound after cooling: toothpaste, oil, ice and raw food worsen contamination and cooling injury.
Clothing, jewellery, belts and watches near the burn act as heat reservoirs and tourniquets, so ask if they were removed.
Tetanus protection, pain relief and keeping the patient covered and warm matter from the first contact, not later.

probes.q: Name the four facts about the burn mechanism you must fix before estimating anything.
probes.a: The causative agent, whether clothing ignited, whether the setting was enclosed or smoky, and the exact time since the burn.

probes.q: Why does cooling in the first minutes change the depth of the wound?
probes.a: Because heat continues to injure tissue after contact ends, and prompt cooling with running water halts that progression.

probes.q: A burn happened six hours ago and no fluid has been given. Why does the delay itself change your plan?
probes.a: Because resuscitation is timed from the moment of the burn, so a late arrival is already behind and needs catch-up assessment rather than a routine start.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.hx.burns.risk.title: Background risks in a burn: past, personal, drug and family history
skill.hx.burns.risk.why: A burn lands on a whole patient. Diabetes slows healing, a seizure disorder explains an unsupervised kitchen fire, smoking and alcohol raise inhalation and infection risk, and tetanus protection decides one injection today. The background also decides who will change dressings at home.
asks: How old is the patient, and what work is done each day: cooking over an open flame, a kerosene stove, or factory work with heat or chemicals?
Is there diabetes, and is the sugar controlled with tablets or insulin?
Has there ever been a fit, faint or fall near fire or hot water?
Is there smoking, chewing tobacco, or regular alcohol use?
What regular medicines are taken, including tablets for sugar, pressure, fits, blood thinners or steroids?
When was the last tetanus injection, and was any booster given in the last ten years?
Has there been a burn before, or any scar, contracture or skin graft from an old injury?
Who lives at home and can help with dressings, feeding and follow-up visits?

teach.heading: Why the background changes the burn
teach.body:
Age sits at both ends of risk: small children reach for hot vessels and cannot escape, while the elderly have thin skin, slow healing and blunted warning signs. Occupation and cooking method explain most Indian burns, from the kerosene stove and the open chulha to factory chemicals and live wires.

Comorbidity rewrites healing and danger. Diabetes invites infection and slow closure, epilepsy explains repeated unsupervised contact with flame, and smoking and alcohol raise the odds of airway injury and chest infection after any smoke exposure.

teach.heading: Drugs, protection and home
points: Blood thinners and steroids change bleeding and healing, so list every regular tablet by name.
Tetanus protection must be verified, never assumed: an unknown history means protection is due.
An old burn scar or contracture marks skin that heals badly and joints that stiffen fast.
A crowded home with one carer and a distant hospital argues for admission where a supported home manages dressings.

probes.q: Which three background facts change burn healing and infection risk most?
probes.a: Diabetes and its control, smoking and alcohol use, and regular drugs such as steroids or blood thinners.

probes.q: Why does a seizure history matter specifically in a kitchen burn?
probes.a: Because a fit near an open flame explains unsupervised contact with fire and warns that the same setting may burn the patient again.

probes.q: Tetanus history is unknown in an adult burn patient. What follows?
probes.a: Protection is treated as absent and tetanus prophylaxis is given rather than assumed from childhood.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

skill.exam.burns.wound.title: Examination of the burn wound: depth, extent and circulation
skill.exam.burns.wound.why: Depth decides grafting, extent decides fluids, and a circumferential deep burn decides escharotomy. All three are read from the wound itself in minutes, and a wrong extent entered on the chart mistreats the patient for the next two days.
steps: Ensure analgesia, consent and privacy first, then uncover one region at a time so the patient never lies fully exposed and shivering.
Note the site and pattern: splash marks on the front of the body, glove or stocking contact marks, ignited clothing zones, and any sparing of flexures.
Estimate the extent with the palm of the patient as about one percent, and confirm against the rule of nines chart later.
Record blanching: press the reddened skin and watch the colour return, area by area.
Test sensibility to light touch over the burn and compare with unburned skin nearby.
Feel the wound edge and base for leathery firmness, thrombosed vessels and dry inelastic eschar.
Where the burn rings a limb, finger or the chest, feel distal pulses, check capillary refill, and watch chest movement with breathing.
Glance at the face, nostrils, mouth and voice for soot, singed hair, black sputum and hoarseness before finishing.
skill.exam.burns.wound.normal: Unburned skin nearby blanches briskly on pressure, feels light touch sharply, and shows no blister, pallor or leathery change.
skill.exam.burns.wound.abnormal: A superficial burn is red, blistered and exquisitely painful with brisk blanching. A deep partial burn is blotchy red and white, blanches sluggishly and feels touch dully. A full thickness burn is white, charred or leathery, does not blanch, and is insensate to light touch.
skill.exam.burns.wound.significance: Depth read this way decides whether the wound can heal alone or needs excision and grafting. Extent read with the palm decides the resuscitation volume. A tight circumferential burn with failing pulses or chest movement demands escharotomy, and any airway sign demands escalation before the swelling closes the airway.
pitfalls: Counting painful red erythema as burn area for fluids, which over-resuscitates and swells the patient.
Palpating and testing sensibility without analgesia, so guarding hides the true findings.
Missing a circumferential band: pulses checked early can fade within the hour.

rows: Red, painful, brisk blanching, no blister loss
Heals within days from surviving epithelium, no grafting
Heals in about two weeks with dressings if kept clean
Blotchy red and white, dull feeling, sluggish blanch
Slow healing with scar; often needs excision and grafting
White, brown or charred, leathery, insensate, no blanch
Cannot re-epithelialise; needs excision and grafting

teach.heading: Extent and circulation in the same pass
teach.body:
Confirm the palm estimate on a Lund-Browder chart, counting only partial and full thickness areas, since the erythema around a burn needs no fluid and heals on its own.

Then test what the burn may be strangling. A deep ring around an arm, leg or finger weakens pulses and refill, and a ring around the chest stiffens breathing; both are released by escharotomy, not by more fluid.

probes.q: How do you separate a superficial partial burn from a full thickness burn at the bedside?
probes.a: By blanching and sensibility: the partial burn blanches and is painful to touch, while the full thickness burn does not blanch and is insensate.

probes.q: Why is erythema left out of the resuscitation area?
probes.a: Because erythema is superficial vasodilatation that heals on its own, and counting it overestimates the burn and over-resuscitates the patient.

probes.q: A circumferential forearm burn shows weakening pulses an hour after injury. What does it need?
probes.a: Escharotomy through the inelastic eschar to restore perfusion, since no amount of fluid opens a tourniquet of dead skin.

Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.present.burns.summary.title: Summarising the burns case
skill.present.burns.summary.why: The receiving unit decides fluids, referral and theatre from your summary, not from your chart. Agent, time since burn, depth, extent, airway signs, circulation, urine and tetanus status must all land in under a minute, with the resuscitation already running.

teach.heading: The shape of the summary
teach.body:
State the patient with age and setting, the agent and time since burn, then the wound in abstract terms: depth in plain words, extent as a percent with the method, and whether the burn rings any limb or the chest.

Close with the living patient: airway signs present or absent, pulses and perfusion, urine output, pain control, tetanus protection, and whether referral criteria are met and the centre has been called.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A twenty eight year old homemaker sustained a flame burn from a kerosene stove three hours ago when her saree caught fire in an open courtyard. There is no enclosed smoke exposure and no soot, singed hair or voice change.

Examination shows mixed superficial and deep partial thickness burns of the right arm and anterior trunk, about eighteen percent by chart, with brisk pain and blanching over most areas. Pulses are full, urine has been passed once since injury, tetanus protection is unknown, and she meets referral criteria for a burns centre.

teach.heading: What never to omit
points: Agent and exact hours since burn, since fluids are timed from injury, not arrival.
Depth in words and extent as a percent with the chart named.
Airway signs stated as present or absent, never skipped.
Perfusion beyond any circumferential burn and urine output so far.
Tetanus status, analgesia given, cooling done, and referral decision with reason.

probes.q: What seven facts must every burns handover contain?
probes.a: Agent and time since burn, depth, extent with method, airway signs, perfusion and urine output, and tetanus and referral status.

probes.q: Why is time since burn stated before anything about fluids?
probes.a: Because resuscitation is timed from the moment of injury, so the hours already passed decide catch-up rather than a routine start.

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB
Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

skill.hx.carcinoma.stomach_risk.title: Risk factors and background history in carcinoma stomach
skill.hx.carcinoma.stomach_risk.oneLine: Tobacco and diet exposures, Helicobacter and ulcer background, and family and prior stomach history
skill.hx.carcinoma.stomach_risk.why: Carcinoma of the stomach clusters where chronic irritation of the lining meets advancing age: tobacco in smoked and chewed forms, long standing Helicobacter infection, an old ulcer story that has changed its tune, and close relatives with stomach or bowel cancer. Two minutes on these exposures separates a high risk dyspepsia from a low risk one and decides who needs an early scope.

asks.text: Do you smoke bidis or cigarettes, or chew tobacco, gutka or betel nut, and for how many years? How much alcohol do you drink each week?
What does your daily diet look like: heavily salted, smoked or pickled foods, and how much fresh fruit and vegetables?
Have you had ulcer type pain in the past with pain free intervals, and has that pattern changed recently into a constant ache with loss of appetite?
Have you been told you carry Helicobacter pylori, or taken treatment to clear a stomach infection, and do you use painkillers such as aspirin regularly?
Have you had anaemia with a sore tongue, or surgery on the stomach long ago, and is there cancer of the stomach, bowel or breast in close relatives?
What medicines do you take for acidity, and have you lost weight or changed to softer foods because eating has become difficult?

teach.heading: Why exposure history matters here
teach.body: Most cancers of the stomach follow years of injury to its lining. Tobacco in smoked and chewed forms adds risk, and heavy alcohol use travels with the same habit. Long standing Helicobacter infection drives the slow sequence from chronic gastritis through atrophy and intestinal metaplasia toward cancer of the intestinal type, so the infection history is as important as the smoking one.

teach.heading: Ask about tobacco, alcohol and diet in every case
points: Smoke: bidis as well as cigarettes, number per day and years of use; chewing: tobacco, gutka and betel nut with areca.
Alcohol: type, amount and years; ask about both habits together, since they cluster in the same patients.
Diet: frequent heavily salted, smoked or pickled food, and low intake of fresh fruit and vegetables; record what the patient actually eats.
Occupation and home: dusty field work matters less here than the kitchen and the tobacco pouch, so ask where meals and chewing happen.

teach.heading: The stomach background that predisposes to cancer
points: Chronic atrophic gastritis and pernicious anaemia: a thinned, intestinalised lining is the recognised precancerous field.
Old gastric ulcer with recent change: loss of periodicity, a constant dull ache, and new loss of appetite point toward malignant change.
Previous partial gastrectomy many years ago and adenomatous polyps of the stomach: both carry a small but real later risk.
Family history: close relatives with stomach, bowel or breast cancer, and the rare diffuse familial pattern presenting young, change the threshold for scoping the family.

teach.heading: Drugs, weight and family
teach.body: Record regular antacids and acid suppressing medicines, since they may have masked years of ulcer type pain. Ask about aspirin and other painkillers that injure the lining. Document weight loss with dates, any shift to soft or liquid foods to cope, and cancers of the stomach or bowel in close relatives.

pitfalls: Asking only about cigarettes and missing bidi smoking and tobacco chewing, which dominate the exposure in many Indian patients.
Accepting a reassuring old ulcer story without asking whether its periodicity and appetite have changed, which is exactly how malignant change presents.
Never asking about Helicobacter testing or treatment, so a curable driver of the whole sequence stays unknown.

probes.q: Name four exposures or background conditions that raise the risk of carcinoma of the stomach.
probes.a: Tobacco smoking or chewing, heavy alcohol use with tobacco, a diet high in salted, smoked or pickled food and low in fresh fruit, long standing Helicobacter pylori infection, chronic atrophic gastritis, an old gastric ulcer that has changed character, and stomach cancer in close relatives.

probes.q: A 60 year old man reports twenty years of ulcer type pain with pain free intervals, but for three months the pain has become constant with loss of appetite. Why does the history worry you?
probes.a: The loss of periodicity with a constant dull ache replacing the rhythmic ulcer pain, plus new anorexia, is the classic story of malignant change supervening on a chronic gastric ulcer.

probes.q: Which step in the intestinal type sequence does Helicobacter treatment aim to interrupt, and why does that matter for counselling?
probes.a: It aims to clear the chronic gastritis that starts the Correa sequence of atrophy, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia, so treating proven infection and scoping the atrophic stomach turns a vague risk into a managed one.

rubric.text: Covers tobacco, alcohol and diet in locally relevant forms
Asks about ulcer history, Helicobacter, anaemia and prior stomach surgery
Establishes whether an old rhythmic pain has changed character
Records stomach and bowel cancer in close relatives

skill.present.carcinoma.stomach.title: Presenting the carcinoma stomach case
skill.present.carcinoma.stomach.oneLine: Tempo, discriminators, lump and spread, fitness and next step in six sentences
skill.present.carcinoma.stomach.why: A stomach cancer presentation fails when it lists symptoms without committing: the consultant needs the tempo in months, the two or three discriminators that split ulcer from cancer, the state of the epigastric lump and liver, the metastatic stigmata checked and the fitness for staging and surgery. Six sentences in that order carry the whole case and invite exactly one question, what the scope and scan showed.

teach.heading: Six sentences carry the case
teach.body:
Name the patient with age and background, then state the tempo in one clause: months of anorexia and weight loss with a recent change. Name the syndrome next in abstract terms, a suspected malignant gastric process with or without outlet features, rather than reciting every symptom.

Then give the discriminators that split ulcer from cancer: loss of periodicity, pain no longer relieved by food or vomiting, new anorexia, and coffee ground vomit or melaena.

State the lump and the spread check: epigastric mass with its mobility and movement with respiration, liver for hard nodules, ascites, the left supraclavicular fossa, the umbilicus and the rectal shelf. Close with fitness and the single next step, usually the staging scan after an already done endoscopy with biopsy, and the referral route.

teach.heading: A worked presentation
teach.body:
A 58 year old farmer presents with four months of anorexia, early satiety and steady weight loss, with a constant epigastric ache for six weeks that food no longer relieves. Examination shows a wasted man with pallor, a firm irregular mildly tender epigastric mass moving slightly with respiration, a nodular liver edge, and a hard left supraclavicular node, with shifting dullness present.

This is a suspected carcinoma of the antrum with clinical spread to liver, peritoneum and distant nodes, in a patient still ambulant with acceptable cardiorespiratory reserve, and the next step is contrast staging imaging with a surgical oncology referral after the biopsy result.

probes.q: What must a carcinoma stomach summary contain that a benign ulcer summary may omit?
probes.a: The tempo in months with the point of change, the loss of periodicity and appetite, the state of the epigastric lump and liver, the metastatic stigmata checked including Virchow node, umbilicus and rectal shelf, and the fitness with the staging and referral plan, since the endpoint is a cancer operation or palliation rather than acid suppression.

skill.hx.neck.risk_factors.title: Background history in neck swellings: past, personal, drug and family
skill.hx.neck.risk_factors.oneLine: Tuberculosis exposure, tobacco and alcohol, voice change and the draining area past
skill.hx.neck.risk_factors.why: A neck lump is rarely only what it looks like today. A treated tuberculosis course, a household cough, beedi smoking with regular drink, or an old head and neck operation each reframes the same swelling before a finger touches it.
asks: At what age did the swelling first appear, and was it present in infancy or early childhood with any change on crying or straining?
What work do you do each day, and do you smoke beedis or cigarettes or chew tobacco, and drink alcohol regularly?
Have you ever been treated for tuberculosis, or lived with anyone who coughed for months and took prolonged treatment?
Have you had a recent sore throat, toothache, mouth ulcer, ear discharge or scalp boil on the same side?
Has your voice changed, or have you noticed noisy breathing or difficulty in swallowing solids?
Have you lost weight or appetite, or noticed fever rising in the evening with night sweats?
Have you ever had an operation, radiation or a needle test on the neck, mouth or throat?
Do you have diabetes, HIV infection, or take steroids or other drugs that lower immunity?
Which medicines do you take every day, including thyroid tablets, blood thinners and painkillers?
Has anyone in your family had a similar neck swelling, tuberculosis, or a cancer of the mouth or throat?

teach.heading: Age and tempo already narrow the list
teach.body:
A swelling since infancy that swells on crying is congenital, whether hygroma, branchial remnant or thyroglossal. A painless lump growing over months in a young adult in India is tuberculous until the aspirate says otherwise.

A hard lump growing over weeks in a tobacco chewer past forty is secondary carcinoma until the primary is found. Sudden pain with fever is acute infection, and sudden painless growth in an old cyst is bleeding inside it.

teach.heading: Ask after tuberculosis, tobacco and the voice
teach.body:
Ask about treated tuberculosis and household cough directly, since scrofula follows the lungs and the kitchen table more often than the textbook admits. Ask about beedis, chewing tobacco and regular drink in the same breath, since these three seed the cancers that shed to the jugular chain.

Ask about voice change, noisy breathing and dysphagia even when the patient came only for the lump. The larynx shares the drainage, and a hoarse voice moves a routine node into the immediate band.

teach.heading: Background factors and what each one changes

rows: Congenital in infants, TB in young, cancer past forty
Decide whether to watch, aspirate or refer urgently
Scrofula with matted nodes and cold abscess
Aspirate with CBNAAT, chest film, TB unit referral
Primary in mouth, throat or larynx
Full oral and ENT exam with every hard node
Laryngeal spread or pressure on the airway
Urgent head neck review, airway first
Reactive nodes that settle with the source
Treat the source, watch the node six weeks
Recurrence, second primary, or chylous fistula risk
Old records and scar exam before any cut
Screen immunity, plan cover with the physician
Shared TB exposure or familial cancer

probes.q: Name five background facts you must ask after in every neck swelling history.
probes.a: Age at onset and tempo, tuberculosis past and household contact, tobacco beedi and alcohol use, voice breathing and swallowing change, throat teeth and scalp sepsis, earlier neck treatment, immunity drugs, and a family history of similar swelling.

probes.q: Why do you ask about beedis, chewing tobacco and drink in a man with a hard neck node?
probes.a: Because cancers of the mouth, throat and larynx follow tobacco and alcohol, and the node is only the metastasis: finding the primary decides the operation.

probes.q: A young woman has matted nodes and her husband took tuberculosis treatment last year. What changes?
probes.a: The contact makes scrofula the working diagnosis: aspirate with CBNAAT, chest film and HIV screen, household screening, and referral to the tuberculosis unit rather than excision.

StewardMD Clinical KB

skill.present.neck.summary.title: Summarising the neck swelling case
skill.present.neck.summary.oneLine: Side, level, movement, character and urgency in under a minute
skill.present.neck.summary.why: The consultant decides the plan from your summary, not from your examination. Side, duration, nodal level, movement with swallowing and tongue, consistency and fixity, and the urgency band must all land in under a minute.

teach.heading: The shape of the summary
teach.body:
State the patient with age and work, the duration and tempo of the swelling, then the syndrome in abstract terms: a painless right upper lateral neck swelling of four months, matted and firm, fixed to deep structures, with evening fever.

Close with the discriminators and fitness: movement tests, skin and sinus, nodes elsewhere, drainage area findings, and the comorbidity and drugs that decide fitness for biopsy or surgery.

teach.heading: A worked example
teach.body:
A twenty four year old tailor presents with a painless swelling on the right side of the neck that has grown slowly over four months, with evening fever and loss of appetite.

Examination shows matted firm nodes of levels two and three, fixed to deep structures with intact skin and no sinus, not moving on swallowing or tongue protrusion, with no nodes elsewhere and a normal mouth and throat. This is right sided tuberculous lymphadenitis of the jugular chain in the early band, with household tuberculosis contact.

teach.heading: What never to omit
points: Side, duration and tempo: months of quiet growth versus weeks of hard growth versus hours of pain.
Level or triangle stated exactly, since the referral and the incision both follow it.
Movement with swallowing and with tongue protrusion, stated as positive or negative with the method.
Consistency and fixity: cystic, matted, rubbery or stony hard, and fixed to skin or deep structures.
Skin, sinus, pulsation and bruit as stated negatives where they exclude mimics.
Nodes elsewhere, drainage area and chest findings, with fitness, drugs and TB background to close.

probes.q: What must a neck swelling summary always contain?
probes.a: Side, duration and tempo, nodal level, movement with swallowing and tongue, consistency and fixity, skin and nodes elsewhere, and fitness with the tuberculosis and tobacco background.

probes.q: The node is stony hard and fixed but the mouth looks normal. How do you close the summary?
probes.a: As secondary carcinoma with unknown primary under evaluation, stating the level, the negative mouth exam, the planned contrast scan with ENT review, and the immediate band, without promising a simple excision.

rubric.text: States side, duration, tempo and exact level
States movement tests, consistency, fixity and skin
Closes with a diagnosis, band, negatives and the next move
