asks.text: Do you chew tobacco, khaini, gutka, pan masala, betel quid with areca nut, or mishri, and where do you keep the quid in the mouth? Ask how many times a day, for how many years, and whether it stays tucked in the cheek overnight.

Do you smoke bidis, cigarettes, chillum or hookah, or drink country liquor, beer or spirits? Work out the daily amount and the years of use, since tobacco and alcohol raise risk together more than either alone.

What do you eat most days, and is there a sharp tooth, loose tooth, broken denture edge or chronic cheek bite that keeps hurting the same spot? A sore that never heals because something keeps injuring it needs the cause named.

Was there a white patch, red patch, burning on spicy food, tightness on opening the mouth, or an earlier sore at this same site? Ask about any past biopsy, cautery, or white patch that was told to be watched.

Do you have diabetes, anaemia, tuberculosis, syphilis, HIV, or any long illness, and what tablets, capsules or injections do you take regularly? Steroids, immune suppressing drugs and long antibiotic courses change what a mouth ulcer can mean.

Has anyone in the family had cancer of the mouth, throat or food pipe, and what work do you do? Outdoor sun exposure matters for lip sores, and dust, smoke or chemical fumes at work matter for chronic irritation.

skill.hx.oral.risk.oneLine: Quid, smoke, drink, sharp teeth and past patches that set the prior for a mouth ulcer
pitfalls: Asking about smoking and stopping there, while the quid sitting in the cheek pouch goes unrecorded.
Forgetting to ask where the quid is kept, so the link between the habit site and the ulcer site is missed.
Never asking about an earlier white or red patch at the same spot, so a known premalignant lesion is treated as a new problem.
Recording diabetes or steroids without linking them to poor healing and to fungal overgrowth that can coat the ulcer.
skill.hx.oral.risk.practice: Take risk, past, personal, drug and family history from a simulated patient with a two month mouth ulcer. Name the risk tier and the single habit change you would counsel first, in under three minutes.

probes.a: Smokeless tobacco or areca nut quid kept in the cheek, smoking, heavy alcohol use, a white or red patch, oral submucous fibrosis, a sharp tooth or denture edge, poor oral hygiene, older age and male sex.
probes.q: Name five risk factors for cancer of the mouth you must ask about.

probes.a: Because the ulcer usually sits exactly where the quid rests, in the gingivobuccal sulcus or against the cheek, so matching the site to the habit separates a habit driven cancer from a chance sore elsewhere.
probes.q: Why must you ask exactly where the patient keeps the quid?

probes.a: A white patch needs whole mouth palpation for induration and a low threshold for biopsy, a sharp tooth needs smoothing or extraction and the ulcer reassessed, and neither is managed by repeated courses of vitamins or mouth paint alone.
probes.q: A patient has a white patch and a sharp molar edge beside a small ulcer. What does each finding change?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The mouth and tongue: premalignant lesions and risk factors
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Most cancers of the mouth in India are squamous cancers driven by chewable tobacco and areca nut, with smoking and alcohol adding to the risk. The quid is usually tucked into the cheek pouch, and the cancer follows the habit: the gingivobuccal sulcus and the cheek are the commonest sites. Ask the habit, the site of keeping, the daily count and the years, in that order.

A student who records smoking alone has taken half the history. Smokeless forms dominate this disease, and alcohol multiplies the effect of tobacco rather than adding a little extra.
teach.heading: The habit comes first

teach.body:
Premalignant change often precedes the ulcer by months or years. A white patch that cannot be wiped off, a velvety red patch, burning on spicy food, or progressive tightness on opening the mouth are all warnings that the mucosa was already diseased before the sore appeared.

Ask about each of these directly, and about any earlier biopsy or advice to watch a patch. Patients rarely volunteer a painless patch, and a sore that arose inside a longstanding patch is a different case from a sore on previously normal mucosa.
teach.heading: What came before the sore

points: Past sores at the same site and what was done: extraction, biopsy, cautery, or repeated vitamin courses without examination.
Sharp teeth, dentures, cheek biting and oral hygiene, since chronic trauma keeps a benign ulcer open and confuses the picture.
Diabetes, anaemia, immune suppression, tuberculosis and regular drugs, which decide healing, fitness for operation, and whether a coated ulcer is fungal.
Family cancers of the mouth and throat, occupation, sun exposure for lip lesions, and diet, stated briefly since they rarely decide the plan alone.
teach.heading: Past, personal, drug and family

skill.hx.oral.risk.title: Risk, past, personal, drug and family history in oral cancer
skill.hx.oral.risk.why: A mouth ulcer in a young non user that heals in ten days and the same sized ulcer in a sixty year old quid chewer with a white patch are two different diseases until proven otherwise. The risk history sets the prior before the mouth is even opened, and it is the only part of the case that can still change the outcome by changing the habit.

skill.present.oral.case.oneLine: Tempo, ulcer detail, nodes and stage in two minutes

probes.a: Problem representation with tempo in weeks or months and risk, ulcer detail with site size edge base fixity and function, nodes by group size consistency fixity, diagnosis with stage, brief differential with what argues against each, then plan.
probes.q: In what order should an oral cancer case be presented?

probes.a: Because a mobile ulcer on the cheek without nodes and a fixed ulcer with hard submandibular nodes and trismus differ in stage, in the extent of resection, and in whether the neck needs dissection, so the plan cannot be stated without them.
probes.q: Why must fixity, nodes and mouth opening appear before the plan?

rubric.text: Opens with tempo in weeks or months and the tobacco or quid habit
Gives site, size, edge, base induration, fixity, bleeding and functional loss
Gives nodal groups with size and fixity plus measured mouth opening
Includes discriminating negatives: opposite side, distant spread, fitness
States the clinical stage with what is still missing, then the plan

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The mouth: case presentation and staging
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Open with the problem representation: age, sex, tempo in weeks or months, site of the sore, and the habit with its site of keeping. Then the ulcer story with pain, bleeding, growth and functional loss, then risk and background with discriminating negatives.

Then the findings in the order you examined: mouth opening, the ulcer with edge base and fixity, the neck by group, and the general survey. Close with the diagnosis and clinical stage, a one line differential, fitness for operation, and the next three steps: edge biopsy, contrast staging scans, and referral to the head and neck unit.
teach.heading: The fixed order

teach.body:
A 58 year old sugarcane cutter who keeps khaini in the right cheek pouch presents with a two month painless ulcer at the same site, now painful with spicy food, foul smell and reduced opening. Examination shows a 3 cm ulcer of the right lower gingivobuccal sulcus with a raised everted edge, stony induration, fixation to the cheek, two finger mouth opening, and a 2 cm firm submandibular node.

This is squamous cancer of the right buccal mucosa with nodal disease, pending edge biopsy and contrast scans of the face, neck and chest for stage, fitness and the plan for wide resection with neck dissection.
teach.heading: A worked example

points: The tempo in weeks, since days point to aphthous or dental ulcers and months point to cancer.
Ulcer specifics: site against the habit site, size in centimetres, edge, base induration, fixity, bleeding on touch, and what the glove showed.
Nodes by group with size, number, consistency and fixity on both sides, since bilateral examination is mandatory even for a one sided sore.
Mouth opening, tongue movement, loose teeth, ear pain and weight loss, stated as present or explicitly absent, since each changes stage or the operation.
teach.heading: Never omit these

skill.present.oral.case.title: Presenting the oral cancer case
skill.present.oral.case.why: An oral cancer case fails when the ulcer is described without its edge and base, because the edge and base are the diagnosis at the bedside. A presentation that names induration, fixity, nodes and opening forces the stage into the open before any scan is ordered.

asks.text: How old is the mother, how many pregnancies has she had, and are the parents related by blood? Record parity, maternal age and consanguinity, since both frame the background risk for congenital anomalies.
Did the mother attend antenatal checkups, and did she take folic acid and iron tablets in early pregnancy? Ask when she started them and whether she took them regularly.
Did the mother smoke or chew tobacco, drink alcohol, or breathe heavy smoke at home or at work during this pregnancy? Ask about bidis, cigarettes, khaini, gutka and country liquor by name.

What tablets or injections did the mother take in the first three months of pregnancy, and was she ill with fever, diabetes, fits or any long illness? Record any regular medicine for fits, sugar, blood pressure or thyroid.

Has anyone in the family had a cleft of the lip or palate, pits of the lower lip, or another birth defect? Ask about previous children with a cleft, and about relatives with hearing loss, heart defects or learning difficulty that could hint at a syndrome.
Where was the baby delivered, what is the baby fed on, and has any doctor already seen the cleft? Note the place of delivery, the feeding method, weight gain so far, and any referral already given.

skill.hx.cleft.risk.oneLine: Pregnancy, habits, medicines and family pattern behind an orofacial cleft
pitfalls: Asking only about the current feed and never about the pregnancy, so folate, tobacco and medicines in early pregnancy go unrecorded.
Recording smoking alone while the mother chewed tobacco or drank country liquor through pregnancy, which matters as much here.
Never asking about lip pits or affected relatives, so a familial pattern that changes counselling is missed.
Forgetting previous children with a cleft or another defect, which is the single most practical recurrence question the parents will ask.
skill.hx.cleft.risk.practice: Take pregnancy, drug and family history from the mother of an infant with a cleft. Name the risk factors found and the one counselling line about recurrence you would give, in under three minutes.

probes.a: Young or late maternal age is background only, but consanguinity, absent folate, tobacco or alcohol exposure in early pregnancy, maternal diabetes or fits medicines, and a family history of clefts or lip pits all raise the prior and change counselling.
probes.q: Name five background factors you must ask about when a baby is born with a cleft.

probes.a: Because lip pits mark Van der Woude syndrome, the commonest syndromic form, and a positive family history turns an isolated anomaly into a familial one with a different recurrence pattern for the next pregnancy.
probes.q: Why must you look at the lower lip of the parents and ask about affected relatives?

probes.a: Folate started before conception protects best and starting late in pregnancy cannot redo the weeks when the face fused, while stopping tobacco and alcohol still helps growth and healing, so record the timing honestly and counsel for the next pregnancy rather than promising repair of this one.
probes.q: A mother started folic acid in the seventh month. What do you tell her it can and cannot do?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: Cleft lip and palate: aetiology and risk factors
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
An orofacial cleft is made in the first weeks of pregnancy, long before the mother feels movements, so the risk history is a pregnancy history. Take it in a fixed order: mother and parity, consanguinity, antenatal care with folate and iron, tobacco and alcohol by name, medicines and illness in the first three months, then family pattern and previous affected children.

Ask each habit by its local name. Bidis, khaini, gutka and country liquor are all used in pregnancy in India and none is volunteered unless named. A student who asks only about cigarettes has taken half the history.
teach.heading: The cleft was made in early pregnancy, so start there

teach.body:
Two answers change everything downstream. Consanguinity raises the background for recessive syndromes, and lower lip pits in the baby or either parent point to Van der Woude syndrome, the commonest familial form. Both must be looked for, not just asked about, because parents rarely volunteer pits.

Close with place of delivery, feeding method and weight gain. These decide whether this baby needs urgent feeding support today or can wait for the routine cleft clinic, which is the most immediate use of the whole history.
teach.heading: Pits, relatives and the feeding position today

skill.hx.cleft.risk.why: The face fuses in early pregnancy under the joint influence of genes and exposures, so a cleft history that skips the pregnancy misses the cause, the recurrence counsel and the feeding urgency all at once. This skill fixes the order so nothing is skipped.
skill.hx.cleft.risk.title: Pregnancy, drug and family history behind a cleft

asks.text: When was the gap first noticed, and exactly what does it involve: the lip alone, the palate alone, or both, on one side or both sides? Ask whether it was seen at birth or picked up later, and whether milk or sound escapes through it.

How does the baby feed, and how long does one feed take? Ask about breast versus cup and spoon versus special bottle, milk coming out of the nose, coughing or choking during feeds, and the number of feeds in a day.
Is the baby gaining weight, and what does the growth card show? Ask the birth weight, the current weight, and whether feeds have become slower or more tiring over recent weeks.

Is breathing noisy, is there difficulty in breathing, and does the baby sleep better in any particular position? Ask about snoring sounds, pauses in breathing, blue spells, and recession of the chest, which matter most where the jaw looks small.
Is there discharge from the ears, and does the baby turn to sounds and to the mother's voice? Ask about repeated ear discharge, poor response when called, and startling to loud claps.
What sounds does the baby make, and for an older child, is speech nasal or hard to understand? Ask about cooing and babbling by age, and about escape of air or fluids through the nose while speaking.

Was anything else unusual noticed: the heart, the limbs, the eyes or the growth? Ask about sweating or breathlessness during feeds, murmurs already mentioned, extra digits, and whether any doctor has suggested a syndrome.

skill.hx.cleft.story.oneLine: Defect detail, feeding, breathing, hearing and growth in the cleft history
pitfalls: Recording the lip gap and stopping there, while the palate, which decides feeding and speech, is never asked about.
Calling poor weight gain a separate feeding problem instead of the expected result of a palatal cleft that prevents suction.
Missing noisy breathing and apnoeic pauses in a baby with a small jaw, where the airway rather than the cleft is the urgent problem.
Never asking about ear discharge and response to sound, so the hearing loss that will later cost the child speech goes unrecorded.
skill.hx.cleft.story.practice: Take the presenting history from the mother of a four month old with a unilateral cleft lip and palate. Cover defect, feeding, breathing, hearing and growth, then state the single most urgent issue, in under four minutes.

probes.a: Whether lip alone, palate alone or both are involved, one side or both, complete or incomplete, feeding time with nasal leak and choking, weight gain, noisy breathing or apnoea, ear discharge with response to sound, and sounds or speech by age.
probes.q: What must the presenting history of a cleft always cover beyond the visible gap?

probes.a: Because a palatal cleft breaks the seal the baby needs for suction, so feeds run long, milk escapes through the nose, the baby tires, and weight gain falters, which is why feeding time and the growth card belong in the presenting complaint itself.
probes.q: Why do feeding time and weight gain belong in the presenting history, not the personal history?

probes.a: Noisy breathing with recession, apnoeic pauses or blue spells, especially with a small receding jaw, which points to Pierre Robin sequence where airway positioning and urgent referral outrank every other cleft question.
probes.q: Which answers in this history would make you stop and manage the airway first?

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: The head and face: history of a congenital defect
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.body:
Start with the defect in the mother's own words, then pin it down: lip alone, palate alone or both, one side or both, noticed at birth or later. A lip gap is obvious at birth, but a palate gap hides inside the mouth and may present only as feeding trouble, so ask about the palate even when the complaint is only the lip.

Then move to function in a fixed order: feeding, breathing, hearing, sounds and growth. Each maps to one complication of the cleft, so the order doubles as a checklist that stops the common error of admiring the lip while the palate starves the baby.
teach.heading: Defect first, then function in a fixed order

teach.body:
Feeding is the urgent function. A baby with a palatal cleft cannot seal the mouth to suck, so ask how long one feed takes, whether milk escapes through the nose, and whether the baby coughs or tires. Then check the growth card, because faltering weight is the objective proof that feeding support cannot wait.

Breathing is the dangerous function. Where the jaw is small and the tongue falls back, ask about snoring sounds, pauses and blue spells, and which sleeping position helps. Those answers point to Pierre Robin sequence, where the airway comes before everything else.
teach.heading: Feeding is urgent, breathing is dangerous

skill.hx.cleft.story.why: Parents present the visible lip, but the hidden palate decides feeding, hearing and speech, and a small jaw can threaten the airway. A fixed order of defect then function keeps the student from treating the photograph while missing the patient.
skill.hx.cleft.story.title: History of the cleft: defect, feeding, breathing and growth

skill.present.cleft.case.oneLine: Defect, function, examination and team plan in two minutes

probes.a: Problem representation with age and defect since birth, feeding breathing hearing and growth, examination of lip alveolus and palate with extent and septum, nodes and general survey, diagnosis with completeness and laterality, brief differential, then feeding support and referral to the cleft team.
probes.q: In what order should a cleft lip and palate case be presented?

probes.a: Because the plan differs completely: an isolated lip needs lip repair and feeding reassurance, while a palatal cleft needs urgent feeding support, hearing surveillance and palate closure timed for speech, so the palate answer must come before any plan is stated.
probes.q: Why must lip versus palate involvement be stated before the plan?

rubric.text: Opens with defect since birth with laterality and completeness, then feeding, breathing, hearing and growth
Gives lip, alveolus and palate findings with extent, septum attachment and nodes
Includes discriminating negatives: airway, syndrome features, weight trend
States the full diagnosis with classification, a one line differential, and feeding plus team referral

sources.source: StewardMD Clinical KB

sources.locator: Cleft lip and palate: principles of management
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Open with the problem representation: age and sex, defect noticed since birth, lip versus palate with side and completeness, then function in one breath, feeding with nasal leak and time per feed, breathing, hearing response, and weight trend. Then risk in one line: pregnancy exposures, consanguinity and family pattern.

Then the findings in the order examined: general survey with growth and any dysmorphism, the lip gap with nasal deformity, the alveolus and premaxilla, the palate with extent and whether the septum hangs free or is attached, and the neck nodes. Close with the diagnosis, a one line differential, and the plan.
teach.heading: The fixed order

teach.body:
A four month old girl presents with a complete gap of the left lip and palate noticed since birth. She takes forty five minutes per feed with milk escaping through the nose and her weight has faltered. Examination shows a complete left cleft lip with flattened nostril, notched alveolus, cleft of soft and hard palate with the septum attached to the right, and no nodes.

This is a complete unilateral left cleft lip and palate, and she needs feeding support today and referral to the cleft team.

State what is still missing: hearing assessment, cardiac check for a syndrome, and growth review. A presentation that ends without the next three steps is unfinished.
teach.heading: A worked example

skill.present.cleft.case.why: A cleft case fails when the lip is described beautifully while the palate, the hearing and the plan are left out. A fixed order forces defect, function, full findings and team referral into every presentation.
skill.present.cleft.case.title: Presenting the cleft lip and palate case
